[He says] regarding the two fire-sticks that are not taken up: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as lord of the house."
When his entire lifespan has been exhausted and he has been led away from here, he utters the name of his son; thus he has extended his progeny.
Indeed, he returns only to the human realm, for he utters the name of a human. When he says, "The divine thread is severed;
let not the human one be severed," he has thus extended both the divine and the human; may I not be cut off from the divine abode.
"May we not [fall] from man"—by saying this, both conquer this world together and come to exist in the heavenly world.
It became: "bhūd" (from *abhūt*).
Having crossed over those gods who were destroyers of the sacrifice and plunderers of the sacrifice on earth, he ascended to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*);
having crossed over those gods who were destroyers of the sacrifice and plunderers of the sacrifice in the intermediate space, he went to heaven—those very gods...
Having crossed over those destroyers of sacrifice and stealers of sacrifice in heaven, he has established him in the preeminence among his kinsmen.

The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *vedī* grass-bundle is its hair. When he wipes the sacrificial cake with the *vedī*, it is for the completeness of the sacrifice and for its purity. Sacrifice indeed went away from the gods; the gods found it by means of the *vedī*.

That is the "Veda-ness" of the Veda that it rests upon what is to be known by the Veda; he thereby finds the sacrifice for himself. He hands the Veda to his wife; for the sacrifice is difficult to find in the world beyond, and thus he finds the sacrifice for her. He hands it over three times, for the gods are threefold in truth. She sits down on her lap; she becomes one who desires a male child. The Veda is indeed cattle, for it is the plants, and it is this [sacrifice].
Verily, that which is between the two fires is the world of cattle; thus, in his own world, the sacrificer appropriates the cattle of his rival.

The sacrifice is indeed interrupted every half-month; he goes from the Āhavanīya fire, scattering [grass] continuously, for the continuity of the sacrifice. He performs the sacrifice continuously in the subsequent half-month with the words: "O Agni, may this sacrifice be rich in cattle, rich in sheep, and rich in horses."

"He has made the sacrifice possessed of cattle, possessed of sheep, and possessed of horses; it is rich in food, O Asura, and full of offspring; it is long-lasting wealth, broad-based, and fit for the assembly"—with these words he invokes a blessing. "May the wife go with her husband to the world of the well-performed"—this indeed is the wife’s participation in the sacrifice;
they both come to share in the heavenly world. Whosoever is his wife, she stands right behind him.

If he were to sit down behind her at this very moment, he would consume her offspring. When he says, "O wife, wife, this is your place," he has made a place for her; her offspring will not be consumed. With the words, "She who is Sarasvatī, the bringer of settlement," he provides him with a settlement by means of that; and his kinsmen wait upon him with life, [saying] "Truly, [it is] speech!"

"We shall serve this Brāhmaṇa or Rājanya," [they say]; however, they should not cook meat on that fire, for if they were to cook meat on it, they would make it a flesh-eater; indeed, they do not cook meat on that fire upon which they offer oblations.

With the words, "O Agni, thou art the swift one (ayās) and the blameless one," [he offers]; for "the swift one" is indeed the name of this dear body of Agni, [and he says] "O swift ones, with your swift course."
Indeed, they say: whatever is done here at this sacrifice and whatever is not done, whatever expiation for the sacrifice we know and whatever we do not know—for both of these, this is the expiation.

One should consecrate what has been spilled with the mantra: "O gods, [I have] entered the assembly of this one who possesses speech; the sacrifice has gone to the assembly. For it is indeed to the assembly of the sacrifice that this goes.

Whatever a person spills, that is lost to us; however, by saying, "I take thee for the support of the five winds," he secures the blessing of the sacrifice that has gone to the people. The sacrifice is fivefold; having grasped the entire extent of the sacrifice, he takes it. This wind that blows is indeed the sacrifice; he has thus taken that very sacrifice. By saying, "I take thee for the support of the five quarters," [he takes] these...

Thus he took hold of the five directions with the formula, "I take thee for the support of the five waters. The waters are indeed cattle; verily, he took hold of cattle. With the formula, "I take thee for the support of the five backs," he took hold of the *pṛṣṭha* chants. Therefore, his *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices possess the *pṛṣṭha* chants; they become continuous and uninterrupted. [With the formula,] "I take thee for the five *pañcajana*s..."
"I take you for the support," he says; the five *chandases* are indeed the five peoples, and thus he took hold of the *chandases*.
"I take you for the support of the five-holed cauldron (*caru*)," he says; these worlds are indeed the five-holed cauldron, and thus he took hold of these very worlds.
Thou art the beloved abode of the gods, the inviolable place of sacrifice for the gods;
I take thee for the enjoyment of the gods.
Thus, having taken the clarified butter with the formula, he says: "By the path it has come; may there be prosperity for us, oblation for the gods, and blessings for the sacrificer.
He thus invokes prosperity for himself; the oblation for the gods and blessings for the sacrificer. With the words, "For the deities thee!
By the deities I take thee," he has indeed taken it for the deities by means of the deities.
The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the abode of the gods; that which is between the two fires belongs to the cattle; the Gārhapatya fire is for humans;
and the Odanapacana fire is for the ancestors. Truly, all the deities come to the sacrifice of one who is about to sacrifice and who knows thus.

Having strewn the grass around both the eastern and the western fires, he says: "Human habitation is indeed dear; [I have made] this a new habitation for the sake of its purity. With the words, "Thou art the tongue of Agni, the release of speech," he pours out the grains for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
This is indeed the seizing of the deities; the deities have seized this. Regarding this, Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say when the oblations had not yet been offered:

"Or rather, may I cause the deities to go to the oblation in the offerings; through the completed sacrifice, may I reach completion"—he who knows thus, for him the deities go to the oblation in his very offerings, and he reaches completion through the completed sacrifice. [With the words:
"From the two mortars, from the two millstones, O preparer of the oblation, come!"...
Thus the gods drove away the Rākṣasas from the sacrifice when they cause the mortars to resound and strike the two millstones together.
O preparer of the oblation, come!
Thus he says. Having poured forth the waters for the warding off of the *rakṣases*, he restrains his speech. Prajāpati indeed extended the sacrifice with his mind.

When the mortar and pestle have been lifted up, both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer should restrain their speech; having become Prajāpati himself, they extend the sacrifice with their minds. Not all the sacrificial implements are to be thrown into the fire together, lest it be human.

That [offering] is not performed as a single unit; rather, it is dedicated to the ancestors and the gods in two parts, for two by two are offered together. This is the form of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. He fasts; thereby he wins both kinds of cattle, those of the village and those of the forest.

In that he does not eat of what belongs to the village, he wins the village cattle; and in that he eats of what belongs to the forest, he wins the forest cattle. Moreover, the forest [food] is indeed power (*indriya*).

One should maintain the sense-faculties within oneself; one should not eat beans, for beans are unfit for sacrifice. One should not eat in the evening that for which he intends to sacrifice in the morning. By means of an offering that has not been consumed [by others], the gods attained greater prosperity, while by means of a consumed offering, the Asuras met with defeat. Thus, by means of an offering that has not been consumed, the sacrificer attains greater prosperity.
His rival perishes; he who performs sacrifice without having grasped faith (*śraddhā*) becomes more wicked.

Water is indeed faith; they are not grasped by speech nor by the *yajus* formula. Indeed, these [waters] overflow beyond speech, but they do not overflow beyond the mind. When one should take up the waters, then one should meditate upon this [earth] with the mind; for this [earth] is the vessel of them.
By this very [verse] he has seized them; having offered faith, he sacrifices and does not become worse off.

The exponents of Brahman say: "They sprinkle the fuel first; the fuel is the first of the oblations. Why is it that for other oblations there are both the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, but for the fuel there are none?"
Recite the invitatory verse for Agni as he is being kindled.

Thus [are] the *puronuvākyā*, the *sāmidhenī*s, the *yājyā*, the *upavāka*, and the *vaṣaṭkāra*. Whatever redundant element is performed in the sacrifice, that becomes redundant in the person of the sacrificer; if the sacrifice is interrupted because it was not fully attained, the sacrificer becomes hungry.
By means of the *paridhānīyā* of the *sāmidhenī*s, he completes the final part of the fuel-bundle (*idhma*); thus the sacrificer does not become hungry.

Nothing extra arises for him from himself; he who knows Prajāpati as the seventeenfold one inherent in the sacrifice—his sacrifice does not falter, and he is firmly established in Prajāpati through the sacrifice.
"O, cause to hear!"—thus consists of four syllables.
So be it; let there be hearing.
Thus is the four-syllable [mantra].
We sacrifice to those [gods].

Thus, there is the five-syllable [formula] and the two-syllable *vaṣaṭ*-call; this indeed is Prajāpati, the seventeenfold, who is dependent upon the sacrifice. Whether it goes from the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) or from the offering verse (*yājyā*), if it does not go away from that very place, his sacrifice does not falter; he becomes firmly established in Prajāpati through the sacrifice. Truly, we do not know whether we are Brahmins or non-Brahmins, if it belongs to him.

"Whether we belong to a seer or to another, for whomsoever we declare [our lineage], that very one whom he, while declaring it, worships—his sacrifice reaches him; it does not go to another. This is what one should say when the *pravara* (the invocation of ancestral lineages) is being recited.
The gods are the fathers, the fathers are the gods; being who I am, I sacrifice; being who I am, I act. May my sacrifice be auspicious, may my peace be auspicious, may my deed be auspicious.
Thus, whosoever performs that sacrifice while being truly existent, to him alone does that sacrifice go; it does not approach anyone else.
I encompass you with the forward-measure, the toward-measure, the around-measure, and the upward-measure of the sacrifice.

Thus, the Gāyatrī is indeed the measure of the sacrifice, the Triṣṭubh its height, the Jagatī its circumference, and the Anuṣṭubh its expansion; these meters carry the sacrifice, and with them he encompasses it.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases asked Keśin Dārbhya, "How is it that the sacrificer is equal to his rival sacrificer? He replied, "I know. They said, "Come now, explain the sacrifice to us.
He explained the sacrifice to them. They said, "Would the sacrificer not thereby become worse off than his rival sacrificer?"
Thus they said to him: "We shall indeed arrange the sacrifice for you in such a way that you, as a sacrificer, will overcome your rival sacrificer.
For him, they arranged the oblations within the sacrifice. Thereupon Keśin overcame Śaṇḍika Audbhāri;
he overcomes his rival through the sacrifice who knows thus. The *āghāra* libation is indeed the vital breath; it should be offered in the eastern part, from the front.

Thus he bestows breath upon him; for the *āghāra* libation is indeed breath, and it should be offered in the middle; verily, he bestows breath in the middle of him. He should offer the *āghāra* more abundantly than the other oblations (*āhutis*); for the *āghāra* is breath, and thus he makes his breath most abundant. He should offer the *āghāra* continuously; for the *āghāra* is breath, and this is for the continuity of breath. He should offer the *āghāra* upwards.

The *āghāra* libation belongs either to the sacrificer who desires heaven or to the sacrificer himself; it causes the sacrificer to go to the heavenly world. If he should hate someone, he should pour the *āghāra* for that person downwards; that person becomes worse off. One libation goes forward, one goes backward, and one is established.
That which he offers while stepping forward is the one that goes forward; that which he offers while stepping backward is the one that goes backward.

That which one offers while standing still is established. If one should desire of someone, "May he become more prosperous and better," one should offer for him while stepping forward; by that, he becomes more prosperous and better. Then, if one should desire of someone, "May he become less prosperous and worse," one should offer for him while stepping backward; by that, he becomes less prosperous and worse.

Now, if he should desire of someone, "May he become neither better nor worse," he should offer for him while standing in the same place; by that, he becomes neither better nor worse. The *prayāja* offerings are indeed the seasons; they should be offered in the same place for the stability of the seasons. That which belongs to Agni’s butter-portion (*ājyabhāga*) should be offered on the northern half; that which is further north has the Rakṣases as its deity.

That [oblation] which belongs to Soma and the *ājyabhāga* should be offered in the southern half; from that, it becomes one whose deity is the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*). This indeed is the intermediate space between the offerings; thus his offerings are properly arranged and are offered in their proper sequence for him who knows this. If he offers in the smoke, he offers it in darkness; consequently, the sacrificer becomes lusterless. That which he offers on the embers is the *andhāhuti* (the blind offering); from that...

The sacrificer’s sight becomes liable to perish; both [oblations] should be offered with light, for the sacrificer becomes radiant and his sight does not perish. Whatever a non-Brahmin eats [of the offering] is a spilt oblation; regarding this, Vasiṣṭha alone knew the expiation.
O Bradhna, protect us!

Thus he should touch the sacrificial cake: "May I, who am entitled to a share, receive my portion; may I not be without a share. This oblation belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, to those worthy of Soma, to the drinkers of Soma. Here there is no place for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. May it not fail me as I perform this rite; may it not diminish for me as I give."

Thus he establishes the sacrifice among those worthy of offerings so that it is not spilled and remains undisturbed; furthermore, whatever an un-Brahmin eats of it becomes for him as if already offered.

If one's unstrained ghee spills, that is indeed the oblation called *citrā*; consequently, the sacrificer’s fortune becomes liable to perish. A *citrā* (variegated) gift should be given; that is the expiation for it. Now, if one's strained ghee spills, that is indeed the oblation called *skannā*;
consequently, the sacrificer becomes liable to perish. A *vara* (boon) should be given; that is the expiation for it. Now...

If one's two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are badly baked, that oblation belongs to Yama; when that oblation has been completed, one should then cook a mess of rice in four bowls and offer it to the Brahmins like rice with its husks intact—this indeed is the expiation for that.
Now, if one's two sacrificial cakes burn, Varuṇa seizes that sacrifice; when that oblation has been completed, then...

One should offer that very same oblation, for sacrifice is indeed the atonement for sacrifice. Now, one should know that he who sacrifices with a sacrifice lacking a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is sacrificing with a sacrifice lacking a dakṣiṇā, and yet he does not become better off;
therefore, a fertile field should be given as a gift—this is his atonement. Now, if his potsherd should break...
One should join it with the verse: "With the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables, I join you."

Thus, the Gāyatrī is indeed speech, consisting of a hundred syllables; by means of speech he thus joins it together. Now, for him whose potsherd is lost, this earth indeed separates him from the heavenly world. When that oblation has been completed, he should then offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. This Agni is indeed Vaiśvānara; he thus approaches this very earth with its own share, [and so gains] the heavenly world.
For the sake of the world's non-disappearance, if now an oblation spills outside the enclosing sticks, that is indeed a living oblation; he should say to the Āgnīdhra: "This is a living oblation."
Having drawn this [sacrificial ladle] together with the sacrifice,
offer it!

Thus, Agni is indeed all the deities; by means of all those deities, his offering becomes truly offered. A full vessel should be given to the *agnīdh*; that itself is its expiation. The sacrificer is the *juhū* ladle, and the rival is the *upabhṛt* ladle. One should not offer as if emptying [the ladle]; for if one were to empty it, one would empty the sacrificer. One should offer as if scattering [the oblation], for these are indeed the arrows of the gods.

When there are oblations, he should then meditate in his mind upon whomsoever he hates; verily, with the arrows of the gods, he pierces him and lays him low. The oblations are indeed cattle, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is Rudra; they should not be offered together. For if he were to offer them together, he would deliver over his cattle to Rudra. They should be offered in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire], so that there may be no confusion of the oblations; and thus it is for him.
Rudra becomes one who does not feel animosity toward his cattle.

One who is about to undertake the New and Full Moon sacrifices should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu. Agni is indeed all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; having thus grasped both the deities and the sacrifice, he undertakes the New and Full Moon sacrifices. They also offer the Jaya oblations.
Indeed, the gods and the Asuras were in conflict; Prajāpati saw these Jaya oblations and [performed] them.
He offered them to Indra; with them, he conquered the Asuras step by step, pillar by pillar.
He for whom these are offered conquers his rival step by step, pillar by pillar.
Intention and purpose.
Thus, the sacrifice is indeed intention (ākūta), and the sacrificial gift is purpose (dakṣiṇākūti).
And mind, and mentation.
Thus, the mind is indeed thought, and speech is the act of thinking.
That which has been studied and the act of studying.
Thus, offspring are the thing meditated upon, and cattle are the meditation.
That which has been cognized and the act of cognition.
Thus, the Ṛgveda is indeed what is known, and the Sāmaveda is the act of knowing.
And Bhaga and Kratu.
Thus, Prajāpati is indeed Bhaga, the sacrifice, and the ritual.
The New Moon sacrifice and the Full Moon sacrifice.

Thus, the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves are those [twelve]; twelve months make a year; having attained the year, he secures it for himself. Prajāpati bestowed the Jaya offerings upon Indra, the bull, the fierce one, the conqueror in battles.
With these twelve, may we, seeking booty, win the prize; with them, may we overcome all hostile armies.
Thus he should offer the thirteenth oblation; there is a thirteenth month, and having obtained it by means of this [oblation], he secures it for himself.
O Agni, giver of strength, grant power and vigor to me as I stride forth, so that I may be one who cannot be censured by those who would otherwise seek to censure me.
For the preeminence of this people, svāhā!
Thus one should offer [the oblation] wherever one might desire, "May I be conspicuous in this assembly. Indeed, he becomes conspicuous in that assembly, but a speckled mark arises upon his own body.

He who desires, "May I be fortunate and an eater of food," should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni Bhagin. Bhaga is indeed Prajāpati; he is the sacrifice, the ritual. Therefore, everyone thinks, "Bhaga will come to me," and "Bhaga will come to me. In that he offers to Agni Bhagin, he directly attains and secures Bhaga himself; he becomes fortunate and an eater of food, both together.
If one undertakes the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he is released from his fetters like an ox tied by its horns. Of these two, the New Moon is the first and the Full Moon is the latter;

yet they perform the Full Moon sacrifice first. That is done out of order. Therefore, when performing the Full Moon sacrifice, he should offer a pap to Sarasvatī and a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvant. For the New Moon is indeed Sarasvatī, and the Full Moon is Sarasvant.
Sarasvant, having restored both of them as they were before, sacrificed them; he prospers through prosperity, and it is also for the sake of pairing.
Approaching the sacrifice, let us address a hymn to Agni,
who hears us even from afar.
Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord of this earth.
He quickens the seeds of the waters.
O Indra and Agni, I invoke you both; may you both together rejoice in the gift of wealth.
Both of you are givers of food and riches; I invoke you both for the winning of strength.
This [Agni], the most excellent invoker, worthy of praise at the sacrifices, was established here by the creators as the first;
he whom Apnavāna and the Bhṛgus caused to shine forth, the wonderful and pervasive one, for every tribe within the woods.
Following his ancient splendor, the bold ones have milked the bright milk from the seer who wins a thousandfold.
This is your seasonal womb, from which once born you shone forth;
knowing it, O Agni, ascend it, and from there increase our wealth.
I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited steed;
may he make our mouths fragrant and may he prolong our lives.
O Agni, purify our lifespans; pour forth upon us strength and nourishment; drive misfortune far away.
Agni is the seer, the purifying one, the domestic priest of the five peoples;
we implore him for great wealth.
O Agni, purify yourself, you who are skillful of hand; bestow upon us splendor and heroic strength, granting me nourishment and wealth.
O Agni, purifier, with your radiant glow and your pleasant tongue, O god,
bring the gods here and worship them.
O purifying, radiant Agni, O god, bring the gods here to us,
to this sacrifice and to our oblation.
Agni, whose vows are most pure, is pure as a sage, pure as a seer;
being offered oblations, he shines forth with purity.
O Agni, your pure, bright, and radiant flames rise upward;
your lights are your rays of fire.
O Agni and Soma, you two bulls, hear this my invocation well; graciously accept these hymns and be a source of joy to the donor.
May Agni, sharp and of sharp splendor, burn against the Rakṣas;
may he overcome the enemy and drive away the one who speaks evil.
O Agni, subduer of rivals, overcome my rivals; let him who seeks to cross over me not cross over.
O Agni, you possess the splendor of the sun; endow me with long life and luster. O Agni, you have united yourself with the light of the sun.
May I be united with the praise of the seers, with the beloved abode, with long life, with luster, with progeny, and with the increase of wealth.

Kindling thee for a hundred winters, may we kindle thee with splendor— being full of vigor, O maker of vigor; being powerful, O maker of power, O Agni, the subduer of rivals, possessed of noble heroes, and invincible.

Thou art the fuel of Agni; protect me from imprecation. Thou art the fuel of Soma; be thou my protector against enemies. Thou art the fuel of Yama; protect me from death. O Agni, thou art the bestower of life; bestow life upon me. O Agni, thou art the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me. O Agni, thou art the guardian of sight; guard my sight. O Agni, thou art the guardian of hearing; guard my hearing. O Agni, thou art the guardian of the body.

Protect my body; O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that up for me. O Agni, with that heat which is yours, burn him who hates us and whom we hate. O Agni, with that flame which is yours, scorch him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Agni, with that radiance which is yours, blaze against him who hates us and whom we hate.
And we hate him, O Agni; with that heat of yours, strike back at him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Agni, with that brilliance of yours, burn him up who hates us and whom we hate.
O Lord of lights, homage to your light; bestow light upon me, O Citrāvasu! May I reach your far shore in safety, O Arvāgvasu!

May it be well with you; may I reach the further shore of the waters; may I partake of you, O waters. You are greatness; may I partake of you, O greatness. You are vigor; may I partake of you, O vigor.
You are the increase of wealth; may I partake of you, O increase of wealth.
O Revatīs, rejoice in this womb, in this stall; this is your kinship; do not depart from here, become many, and do not abandon me.
You are the collection, possessing all forms; unite me with vigor, with the people, with cattle, with offspring, and with the increase of wealth.
May riches rest upon you; may I attain for you nourishment that increases a thousandfold.
O Agni, illuminator of the darkness, we approach you day by day with our prayer,
bringing homage.
Shining over the sacrifices, the radiant guardian of the cosmic order,
increasing in his own abode.
O Agni, be easy of access to us like a father to his son;
attend to us for our own well-being.
O Agni, be our closest kinsman, our protector, and our gracious guardian.
To you, O most radiant and shining one, we now pray for the welfare of our friends.
Agni is the Vasu, of excellent fame; come hither and grant us most resplendent wealth. Be mindful of us, hear our call, and protect us from every one who intends us evil.
"I have overcome all hostile armies; this Agni has declared, and Soma has declared this.
Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, Indra, and Pūṣan have established me in the world of the righteous."
With vigor I look upon you; with vigor look upon me. With wealth I look upon you; with wealth look upon me.
I behold the offspring, the human progeny of Iḍā;
may they all be in our home.
You are Ida-s, honey-makers; enter me, you who bring delight and exhilaration.
May I enjoy your thousandfold nourishment.

Thou art the world, nourishing a thousandfold prosperity; grant us of that, and may we be partakers of thee. Thou art the *iḍā*, the upholder of vows; in thee is the vow; thou art the upholder of vows.
May the great, celestial protection of the three—of Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa—be ours; it is invincible and unassailable.
For there is no enemy, nor any speaker of evil, who has power over those virtuous ones, whether they are at home or on their journeys through the forests.
For those sons of Aditi bestow eternal protection and grant desirable boons to the donor.
O Brahmaṇaspati, make Kakṣīvat— the son of Uśij— our praiser and our singer.
May he who is wealthy, the dispeller of disease, the finder of treasure, and the increaser of prosperity—
may he who is auspicious be gracious unto us.
The glory of the divine Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is winning;
his splendor possesses most wonderful renown.
Never are you barren; never do you fail.
May your unassailable chariot reach us from every side— the chariot with which you protect those who offer oblations.
You are the crusher; may I crush him who hates us and whom we hate. You are the overcomer;
may I overcome him who hates us and whom we hate. You are the surpasser; may I surpass him who hates us and whom we hate.
May Pūṣan, the protector of paths, protect me; may Pūṣan, the protector of cattle, protect me; may Pūṣan, the sovereign protector, protect me. The eastern direction has Agni as its deity:

whoever would attack me from this direction, may he encounter Agni. The southern direction has Indra as its deity: whoever would attack me from this direction, may he encounter Indra. The western direction has the Maruts as its deity: whoever would attack me from this direction, may he encounter the Maruts.

May she strike down the northern direction; Mitra and Varuṇa are its deity. Whoever would attack me from this direction, may Mitra and Varuṇa strike him down. May she strike down the upward direction; Soma is its deity. Whoever would attack me from this direction, may he strike down Soma. May Dharma protect me from Dharma; may Vidharma protect me from Vidharma. And may Āyus and Prāyus, Cakṣas and Vicakṣas [protect me].
And from the east and from the west, O broad one, may we come together with you, the broad one, through speech and through shared food, O Agni, Lord of the House.
Or, for whomsoever the *stoma* is joined to the *agnihotra*, heaven becomes his; for that at which the *stoma* is not joined is indeed no sacrifice.

With the verse, "Approaching the sacrifice,"—for this [earth] is indeed the *upoti*—he joins the *soma* from this very place, and thus he joins this very earth as the *stoma*. Moreover, those creatures that have come into being and possess names, them he joins as the *stoma*.
With the verse, "Following its ancient splendor," he yokes the *stoma* from that world above, for "the ancient" refers to yonder world.
Moreover, the gods are indeed the ancient; he thus yokes the *stoma* unto them. He yokes the *stoma* from both sides, from here and from there.
Having set the gods in motion, he goes to the heavenly world when he says: "O Maghavan, may we now indeed increase, may those [powers] now indeed increase."
Thus this is the *upoti*; he finds firm support in this very [earth]. Now, when he utters the word "upa-vat," he yokes those very subjects who are destined to come into being to the *stoma*.

With the verse, "Thy hard-to-overcome chariot," he encloses the yoked *stoma* on both sides, from here and from yonder. By the words "Agni is the head," he [attains] heaven; by the words "The summit of heaven," he [attains] heaven; by the words "The lord," he [attains] heaven.
"This [is] of the earth"—thus he approaches with a pair; "thereby do thou quicken the seeds of the waters"—thus she is possessed of seed, fit for cattle, and complete in every respect.
He has approached with a *gāyatrī* verse, for Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature and has the *gāyatrī* as his metre; thus he has approached him with his own metre.
"Both you, O Indra and Agni, I call upon"—for these two indeed go together; for this [Agni] enters yonder [sun] when it has become day; therefore...

"That one shines by day, this one by night; therefore, this [fire] shines by night. When he says, "Both of you," he approaches both of them so that his effort is not in vain; they shine in both worlds, in this one and in yonder one. He has approached with a *triṣṭubh* verse:
"This one was first established here by the establishers. For Agni was indeed first established upon this earth as the most excellent invoker at the sacrifices.

"Worthy of praise"—for he is indeed the Hotṛ, the most skilled in sacrifice, worthy of praise at the rituals; "whom Apnavāna and the Bhṛgus caused to shine"—for the Bhṛgus did indeed cause him to shine; "wondrous and pervasive among the woods, for every clan"—for he is indeed all-pervasive here, having approached with the world of living beings; "according to his ancient splendor"—the ancient [splendor] is indeed the heavenly world, and thus [he approaches] in the heavenly world itself.
"He stands firm with the words, 'This is your seasonal womb. For this is indeed his seasonal womb; Agni has taken his stand after the sun and the anuṣṭubh."

With the verse, "Approaching the sacrifice," he causes [the seed] to be sown; with the verse, "O Aṅgiras, the head," he places the seed once it has been sown. With the verse, "Both you, O Indra and Agni, I invoke," [he does so]; for Indra and Agni are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing, and it is out-breathing and in-breathing that are placed at the beginning of the sacrifice.
With the words, "This [Agni] was established here by the establishers as the first," he has indeed deposited his embryo; with "according to his ancient splendor," he has made manifest his udder;
with "this is your seasonal womb," he has both generated and nourished him. He worships with six verses;
for there are six *pṛṣṭha* chants, and thus he has fashioned the *pṛṣṭhas*. With the verse addressed to Dadhikrāvan, "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan," he worships.
This, indeed, is Agni’s dear body, the Dadhikrāvatī, which is beneficial for cattle and complete in all respects. By means of this [verse], he approaches the dear abode of Agni;

moreover, he becomes possessed of cattle; and moreover, by means of this, the sacrificer purifies himself. He worships with seven [verses]; the Śakvarī meter has seven feet, and cattle are connected with the Śakvarī; thus he wins cattle. This animal, once established, indeed grows old.

Indeed, Agni is that; therefore, one should offer these very oblations of the *agnyādheya* every year. By this, he does not age, and by this, he makes him new again. One need not concern oneself with that; rather, one should worship with these very *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Agni and Pāvamāna for the *agnyādheya*. By this, he does not age, and by this, he makes him new again.
He performs with twelve [verses]; he worships for twelve months; the year consists of twelve months; having obtained the year, he secures it.
With the thirteenth [verse] dedicated to Agni and Soma, he should worship; there is a thirteenth month; having obtained that very month by means of this [verse], he secures it.

The exponents of Brahman say: "Why do they worship Agni in the evening, but not in the morning? It is because yonder sun impels [the world] in the evening; therefore they worship him in the evening. He impels [the world] in the morning; therefore they do not worship him in the morning.
Therefore, the performer of the Agnihotra should not eat until the evening Agnihotra has been offered; likewise, he should not eat until the morning [Agnihotra] has been offered.

Therefore, they give to the guest in the evening because he is blameless and meritorious, but they give in the morning [only] after [the guest] has performed the *prātar-avanega* (morning washing). One should approach [the fire] in the morning.
While the oblation is being placed on the fire or while it is being ladled out, one should wash one's hands. Therein, there are four verses of the *vihavya*.
He should recite [the Prātaravanega hymns] at dawn; by means of the Prātaravanega, he obtains what has not been obtained and secures what has not been secured.

Thus, by this very act, he obtains that which was unobtained and secures that which was unsecured. Indeed, when it is drawn out, it fears; the gods strewed around it with the meters (*chandas*). In that he stands in attendance, he strews around it with the meters; both [worlds] are for him.

One should worship with an offering to Agni and Soma during the first half of the month; for the first half of the month belongs to Agni and Soma, and thus he entrusts him to the second half of the month.

One should worship with an offering to Indra and Agni during the second half of the month; for the second half of the month belongs to Indra and Agni, and thus he entrusts him to the first half of the month.
Indeed, all the deities protect him who knows this, handing him over to one another and never neglecting him.
He pays homage to Agni.

"O Agni, you are of solar luster"—with these words he prays for a blessing for one who is more prosperous or better; "unite me with life and luster"—with this he prays for himself. "You, O Agni, have united with the light of the sun"—for at that time those two lights indeed become united. "With the praise of the seers"—the praise of the seers is the meters; verily, by means of the meters he brings him into harmony. "Unite..."
With the words, "By his dear abode,"—the oblations are indeed Agni's dear abode; verily, by means of the oblations, he causes him to prosper.

"May I be united with life, united with luster, united with offspring, united with the increase of wealth"—thus he invokes a blessing. "Kindling thee for a hundred winters"—this is the invocation of the *pṛtanājit* (victor of armies); with it a *rājanya* should perform the worship, for when a *rājanya* conquers an army, he becomes [a victor]. Or rather, everyone should perform the worship, for everyone desires to conquer an army. Everyone...

Manu desired to have offspring. Manu had ten wives: one who had ten sons, one who had nine sons, one who had eight sons, one who had seven sons, one who had six sons, one who had five sons, one who had four sons, one who had three sons, one who had two sons, and one who had one son. Of those who had nine sons, one approached them;
of those who had eight, two approached them; of those who had seven, three approached them; of those who had six, four approached them; and indeed, of those who had five, five approached them.
These five groups of ten divided these five [fires]. Whatever belonged to Manu, they seized it all;
therefore, they indeed fled to Manu for refuge and cried out to him for protection. He gave them these kindling-sticks (*samidh*).
With them, they indeed burnt those [enemies] away; with them, they brought about their defeat. He who knows thus brings about the defeat of his evil rival.

The learned man places these kindling-sticks upon the fire with the formulas: "Thou art the kindling-stick of Agni; protect me from imprecation"—thus he protects him from imprecation. "Thou art the kindling-stick of Soma; be a protector for me from afar"—thus he becomes a protector for him from afar. "Thou art the kindling-stick of Yama; protect me from death"—thus he protects him from death. Indeed, Nārada used to say this: "This, truly, is the ritual attendance upon Agni."
He protects him from false accusation; he becomes his protector against others; he protects him from death.

"O Agni, you are the bestower of life; grant me life"—thus he bestows life upon him. "O Agni, you are the bestower of luster; grant me luster"—thus he bestows luster upon him. "O Agni, you are the protector of sight; protect my sight"—thus he protects his sight.
"O Agni, you are the protector of the ear; protect my hearing"—thus he protects his hearing. "O Agni, you are the protector of the body;

protect my body"—thus he protects his body. "O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that for me"—whatever is deficient in his own self, in his offspring, or in his cattle, that he fills with this [mantra] and causes it to swell. "O Agni, that heat which is yours..."

"These indeed are the luminous bodies of Agni. For Āruṇa Aupaveśi used to say: "When I perceive rivals who are more prosperous or better than myself, may I overcome them with these luminous bodies of Agni. He who, knowing this, worships Agni with the words, "O Agni, Lord of Splendors," overcomes his evil rival.

"Homage to thee, O Radiance; bestow radiance upon me"—with these words, he places radiance, which is indeed peace, within himself; he becomes resplendent and endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*).
"O Citrāvasu, may I reach thy further shore in safety!"—Citrāvasu is indeed the night, and Arvāgvasu is the day;
the night is Agni and the day is yonder Āditya. These two are the breakers; he invokes them three times, for the gods are threefold in truth; thus it shines.
Truly, for one who knows thus, his sacrifice or his sacred formulation (brahman) is preserved. "You are waters; may I partake of you"—for these indeed are waters.
"You are greatness; may I partake of you"—for these indeed are greatness. "You are strength; may I partake of you"—for these indeed are strength.
"You are the increase of wealth; may I partake of you"—for these indeed are the increase of wealth. "O wealthy ones, rejoice in this!"

"In this womb, in this stall"—thus he causes them to settle in their own womb, in their own stall. "This is your kinship; do not depart from here; become many; do not abandon me"—with these words he invokes a blessing. He seizes a calf, for cattle are fond of their calves. He indeed rules over a thousandfold prosperity; he prospers with a thousand and does not fall short of a thousand who acts thus.
"You are the Vedic collection, you who possess all forms"—for she is indeed collected form by form; thus he causes her to prosper through her very forms.
"He has grasped their names; with them he has made a friend"—for when he utters the name of Mitra, he thereby makes him a friend.

Seven indeed are the *bandhumatī* bricks that are placed upon the piled fire-altar; they are those seven domestic bricks for that world above. They are to be placed here: the cow, the horse, the mule, the donkey, the goat, the sheep, and the man. When he immolates the cow, they become piled with the cow; moreover, having been immolated, they are placed [as bricks]. Turning away...

Verily, he goes to the heavenly world by means of the meters, ascending one meter after another with the verse, "O Agni, day by day we approach thee. When he worships with this three-verse hymn in the Gāyatrī meter, the Gāyatrī is indeed this earth; thus he finds firm support on this very earth.
With the verse, "O Agni, thou art our nearest [friend]," he approaches that body of Agni which is invulnerable, dear, and protective; verily, he attains that very form.

"No one shall harm him; he overcomes [the enemy]. With four two-footed verses he worships. Cattle are four-footed, the sacrificer is two-footed, and the Gārhapatya fire is the house. Thus he finds firm support both in his houses and in his cattle. "With vigor I look upon you;
with vigor may they look upon me"—thus he looks upon them with vigor, and they look upon him with vigor. "With wealth I look upon you; with wealth may they look upon me."
Through wealth he sees them; through wealth they see him.
I behold the offspring, the human progeny of Iḍā;
may they all be in our home.
Thus these creatures are both of Iḍā and of Manu; he has indeed won them. "You are the iḍās that have not been eaten, the honey-makers," for these are indeed the iḍās, the honey-makers.

"Enter me, O pleasant ones, bestowing delight," for these are indeed the bestowers of delight. "You are the world, nourishing with thousandfold prosperity," for this is indeed the world, nourishing with thousandfold prosperity. "Grant us of that; may we be partakers of you"—this is the blessing.
Thus he prays: "Thou art Iḍā, the bearer of vows," for she is indeed Iḍā, the bearer of vows; "In thee is the vow, O bearer of vows," for she is indeed the bearer of vows.
"May there be great protection for us three"— with this triplet addressed to Prajāpati, he worships, for these creatures indeed belong to Prajāpati.
Having thus secured those very [powers] and made them his own, he then approaches Prajāpati; indeed, he finds firm support in the deities through Prajāpati.

With the verse addressed to Bṛhaspati, "The Soma-presser, the one who makes sound," he worships; he finds firm support in the *brahman*, and furthermore, he secures spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Whoever competes with one who is firmly established in the *brahman* falls before him first. Both kinds...

The deities expect [offerings] from the Agnihotra-sacrificer—both those for whom he offers and those for whom he does not. With the verse, "Of Mitra, the supporter of men," he worships with a verse addressed to Mitra; by this, he establishes Mitra on both sides, both here and yonder.
With two *bṛhatī* verses addressed to Indra, beginning with "Never art thou barren," he worships; for cattle belong to Indra, and thus he wins them and secures them.
"May thy steeds, difficult to overcome, carry thee"—for that sun is indeed a chariot difficult to overcome;
he indeed traverses both these worlds. With this [verse], he encompasses everything. "Thou art a crusher;
may I crush him who hates us and whom we hate"—with this, if he should compete with one who is more wicked, he should press down with his heel. "Thou art the overcomer."

"May I surpass him who hates us and whom we hate," with these words he should press down on the footprint from the south, if he should compete with one of equal status. "You are powerful; may I surpass him who hates us and whom we hate," with these words he should press down with his forefoot, if he should compete with one of superior status. In this way, he overcomes all of them.

"He surpasses all, he transcends all; may Pūṣan, the guardian of paths, protect me"—thus [he says], for this earth indeed is Pūṣan. "May Pūṣan, the guardian of cattle, protect me"—thus [he says], for the intermediate space indeed is Pūṣan. "May Pūṣan, the guardian of lords, protect me"—thus [he says], for yonder sky indeed is Pūṣan. Having thus approached these very worlds, he encloses himself within these worlds for the sake of non-injury. "The eastern direction, Agni as its deity"—thus [he says] regarding the directions that protect the body.

Then, he who competes with him or whom he seeks to overcome, having encountered these very deities, perishes first. There are indeed seven greatnesses in man; they are to be praised by means of this [sacrifice], and they are those very Seven Seers. The Seven Seers are the vital breaths; it is the vital breaths that he thus praises. He praises his own vital breaths and appropriates the vital breaths of his rival; those who seek to harm him do not succeed.
He who knows thus spreads [the sacrifice]. May Dharma protect me from non-dharma; may Non-dharma protect me from dharma.
Life and further life, sight and wide-sight, the forward breath and the backward breath—the "wide one" (uruka) is indeed this [fire], for he distributes;
and what he distributes, that he bestows back again upon him. "O Agni, lord of the house, I kindle thee. He kindles the fire.

The sacrificer: "This indeed is the sacrificer’s own, namely Agni; this is Agni’s, namely the sacrificer. Thus it is as if a dwelling-place is being created. Saying, "For light, for the thread," he should speak while sitting between the two fires; whatever blessing he previously desired and whatever he [desires] afterwards, that he places within himself.
Thus he has obtained [it].

"One gives while saying 'mā' (me/not)," for he who offers the *agnihotra* indeed gives perpetually. Whatever he may desire, that the *agnihotrī* should ask of Agni; verily, it bows down to him. Regarding this they say: "He indeed incurs the wrath of the gods who asks them perpetually. Therefore, at that time, he should not approach [the fire] for sexual intercourse. Yama, indeed, died; those gods [prepared] Yami for Yama.

When they asked her, she replied, "Today I have died. They said, "Indeed, she does not tolerate this [state] of his. "Let us create night," they said. At that time there was only day, not night; those gods created night.
Then there became a tomorrow, and then she tolerated him. Therefore they say, "Day and night indeed tolerate suffering."
When that night was created, it closed in upon the cattle. The gods beheld the cattle by means of the metres alone;

by means of the metres they called them back again. In that he performs the *upatiṣṭhana* (reverential standing), he thereby beholds the cattle by means of the metres and calls them back again by means of the metres. Moreover, they say: "Varuṇa indeed, having become that night, [seized] the cattle."
"Let them devour!"—with these words, those gods released the cattle from Varuṇa by means of the meters; with the meters they called them back again.

When he stands in attendance, he thereby releases the cattle from Varuṇa by means of the meters and calls them back again by means of the meters. Sacrifice after sacrifice indeed comes into conflict; therefore, some think that Soma alone is what comes into conflict.
Before the *agnīṣomīya* offering, he should recite four verses of the *vihavya*; for the cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni, he should provide two *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.
With this alone, he should touch the oblations when they have been placed on the altar. He appropriates the sacrifice of another, and another does not appropriate his sacrifice;
he becomes one who possesses a sacrifice, while the other remains without a sacrifice.
Let us create;
[he] closed his eyes completely.
They released [the fires]:
those who have established the sacred fires and perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed piling up the fire-altar; for them, the days and nights themselves are the bricks.

Where the five nights are laid down, there one should offer [the oblation] after staying for the *saṃhitā* period; [thus] there would be five nights and five days, which would amount to ten. But it should not be done in that way. It should be offered at the very end during those same ten nights; in that way it is done in an orderly manner (*yata*). It should not be offered when all [the fires] have been joined (*yukta*); nor should it be offered on the site (*vāstu*) when they are unjoined (*ayukta*), for in that case it is done in a disorderly manner (*ayata*).
All other [oxen] should be yoked; the one standing by the fire should be yoked first, and the thong of the left-hand one should be fastened.
Then he should offer the oblation. He does not offer it on the site itself. Whichever [ox] is released first, that should not be noticed.
The offering should be made only when all have been yoked, for this is an offering to Vāstoṣpati. One must not bring back what has been left behind, for that which is left behind is offered to Rudra.

They would have brought Rudra upon themselves; they would have brought the manifested being upon themselves. If there were a carrying forward [of the oblation], they should first carry it forward or remove it; for if it were to be set down, it would indeed be lost; therefore, one should offer it.
May he indeed depart:
O Vāstoṣpati, driving away disease, entering all forms,
be a most gracious friend to us.
O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us; be a gracious refuge for us and free from disease.
Whatever we implore of you, grant that to us; be a blessing to our bipeds and a blessing to our quadrupeds.
O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle; guard them for me until my return.
O Agni, thousand-eyed, hundred-headed, a hundred are your out-breaths and a thousand your in-breaths; you are the lord of thousandfold wealth; to you, for that strength, we pay homage.
O manly one, protect my offspring; guard it for me until my return. O Agni, Lord of the House, may I be a good lord of the house through you as lord of the house;
may you be a good lord of the house through me as lord of the house. Be mindful of my food; protect it for me until my return.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect these houses of mine;
O Pūṣan, guard them unharmed and undisturbed until our return.
"O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle; guard them for me until my return," with these words he worships the Āhavanīya fire.
Having entrusted the cattle to the Āhavanīya, he departs, saying: "O Agni, thousand-eyed, hundred-headed! For he is indeed thousand-eyed and hundred-headed.
"A hundred are your out-breaths, a thousand your in-breaths! For his out-breaths are indeed a hundred and his in-breaths a thousand.
"You, O Apāna, are the lord of a thousandfold wealth; to you, for that strength, we pay homage"—with these words he invokes a blessing.
"O manly one, protect my offspring; guard them for me until my return," with these words he worships the *gārhapatya* fire.
Having entrusted his offspring to the *gārhapatya*, he departs, saying: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good master of the house through you as my master of the house;
may you be a good master of the house through me as your master of the house. Thus they both grow old together, possessing everything.
"Life has not brought me here to suffering; O Food, protect me, be mindful of me, and guard me until my return," with these words he worships the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire);
having entrusted his food to the *dakṣiṇāgni*, he departs.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two protect these houses of mine;
let Pūṣan guard them unharmed and undisturbed until our return.
Thus, having entrusted the cattle to Day and Night, to Mitra and Varuṇa, and to Pūṣan, he returns from Day and Night and from Mitra and Varuṇa.
Kindle the fire.
Thus he spoke; [the teacher] then stands worshipping the ashes.
The reciters have protected my cattle for me; give them back to me.
Having thus returned to the Āhavanīya fire, he worships it; by means of the Āhavanīya itself, he places the protected cattle within himself.
O Agni, thousand-eyed, hundred-headed, a hundred are your out-breaths and a thousand your in-breaths; you are the lord of thousandfold wealth; as such, we pay homage to you for the sake of strength.
O hero, you have protected my offspring; give it back to me.
Having thus returned to the Gārhapatya fire, he worships it; by means of the Gārhapatya itself, he places protected offspring within himself.

O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as lord of the house. Food has protected me with my intellect; give that back to me.
Having thus returned to the Dakṣiṇāgni, he worships it; by means of the Dakṣiṇāgni itself, he places protected food within himself.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, may you two protect these houses of mine—unimpaired and unharmed; may Pūṣan guard them until our return.
Thus, Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night, and Pūṣan is the cattle; by means of day and night and by means of Mitra and Varuṇa, he places his house protected within himself.
Forward for you go the strengths, seeking the heavens, accompanied by oblations and the ladle dripping with ghee;
it approaches the gods, desiring their favor.
O beloved Agni, let my ladles, dripping with ghee, approach you; graciously accept our oblations.
O Agni, let that flame of yours shine forth from the ghee when it is offered, kissing the sacrificial ladles in your mouth.
O Agni, cause the subjects and the quarters to dwell together here along with the cattle;
bestow upon this man those kingdoms which existed at the impulse of Savitṛ.
This is your seasonal womb, from which once born you shone forth;
knowing it, O Agni, ascend it, and from there increase our wealth.
This spotted cow has come; she has settled before her mother, and as she moves toward heaven, she approaches her father.
The thirtyfold abode shines forth; speech is offered to the winged one;
the buffalo has ascended to heaven.
He moves within the ocean, from his out-breath and in-breath;
the sun faces you both through the days.
From this, his own womb, Jātavedas was first born;
may he, knowing all, carry the oblations to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Anuṣṭubh meters.
O fathers, that immortal Agni who has entered into us mortals within our hearts—
him we embrace here within ourselves, so that he may not depart from us, leaving us behind.
The two milch-cows are for you, filled with milk; these two earths are yours. I bestow upon you your allotted portion; with them I establish you. The Gharma is your head;
may this Agni be dear to you through the cattle. You are the soil-covering (purīṣa); O bright one, with that which is your bright light, may you attain luster through that luster.
In me I first take up the fire, together with progeny, splendor, and wealth;
in me I place sovereign power, in me riches; may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons.

"Bhūr bhuvaḥ! With the vow of the Aṅgirases, the gods, I place you; with the vow of the god Agni, I place you; with the vow of Indra accompanied by the Maruts, I place you; with the vow of Manu the leader of the host, I place you. I place you as the Āchadi meter. You are the sky in greatness, the earth in abundance.
In your lap, O goddess Aditi, I place the eater of food, Agni, for the sake of obtaining food."
O Agni, you purify lives; Agni is the seer; O Agni, purify yourself.
O Vājin, bring hither that dear body of Agni which is Pavamāna; O Vājin, bring hither that dear body of Agni which is Pāvaka; O Vājin, bring hither that dear body of Agni which is Śuci.

When you first neighed at birth, rising from the ocean or from the primordial waters, your wings were like those of a falcon and your forelegs like those of a deer; that birth of yours, O steed, is worthy of praise.
I lift you up for vigor, for strength, for manly power; you are the subduer of rivals, the slayer of Vṛtra.

Go forth toward the eastern quarter, O Agni, as the knowing one; be here as the fire that precedes the fire. Shining brightly, illumine all the directions; bestow strength upon our bipeds and our quadrupeds.
"I have overcome all hostile armies and enemies"—this Agni has declared, and this Soma has declared;
Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, Indra, and Pūṣan have declared it for me: "He has established me in the world of the well-performed deed."

By the vow of Bhuvas, Svar, and the Aṅgirases, the gods, I set thee down; by the vow of the god Agni, I set thee down; by the vow of Indra accompanied by the Maruts, I set thee down; by the vow of Manu the leader of the host, I set thee down. I have laid upon thee the Āchadi metre; thou art the sky in greatness, the earth in abundance.
In the lap of thee, O goddess Aditi, I set down Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of obtaining food.
O pure one, with that which is your pure light, your pure, eternal abode—with that I establish you.
O Jātavedas Agni, we place you upon the navel of the earth, in the station of Iḍā, so that you may carry our oblation.

O Agni, you who have the two bodies known as Samrāj and Svarāj—grant me vigor through them. O Agni, you who have the two bodies known as Virāj and Prabhū—grant me vigor through them. O Agni, you who have the two bodies known as Vibhū and Paribhū—grant me vigor through them.

From the ocean a honeyed wave has arisen; through the *upāṃśu* cup it has attained immortality. That which is the secret name of clarified butter is the tongue of the gods and the navel of immortality.
Let us proclaim the name of the clarified butter; let us uphold it with reverences at this sacrifice.
May the Brahman hear the hymn being recited; the four-horned bull has bellowed this.
He has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands;
bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly. The great god has extended himself across the mortal world.
Those fires which, with one mind, have entered into the plants and the trees—
let them all come together toward Virāj; bestow strength upon us, for our bipeds and our quadrupeds.
Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven the ṛṣis, and seven your beloved abodes.
Seven officiating priests worship you in seven ways; as one who knows the seasons, fulfill the seven sacrificial roles. Fill the seven wombs with clarified butter—svāhā!
Those fires which are from heaven and those which are from earth, coming together and clothing themselves in nourishment and vigor—
having given wealth to this Agni for us, being sacrificed to, gratified, and having become partakers of the oblations, go back again to your respective worlds, svāhā!
Varuṇa, firm in his vows and wise in action, sat down within the dwellings for the sake of universal sovereignty.
And may Ahi Budhnya hear us, and Aja Ekapād, Earth, and Ocean;
may the hymns praised by seers protect us; O King, rejoice in this oblation.
Now indeed Brahmanaspati utters the hymn worthy of praise,
in which Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and the gods have made their dwellings.
Heat is the head; may this Agni be dear to the cattle. You are the soil; grant well-being and security to our children and descendants.
The hymn is the light; may this Agni be dear to the cattle. You are the soil; grant well-being and security to our children and descendants.
Wind is the breath; may this Agni be dear to the cattle. You are the soil.
And grant welfare and peace to our children and descendants.
Cook for us food that is free from poison.
May Heaven and Earth be in harmony; may the waters and the plants be in harmony;
may the fires, being of one accord, be in harmony individually for my preeminence.
Those fires which, being of one mind, have entered into the plants and the trees—let them all come together toward Virāj; bestow strength upon us, for our bipeds and our quadrupeds.

In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. Creepers climbed over him; for these plants are indeed of the nature of the Asuras. Desiring to overcome them, he was unable to overcome them. He grieved and performed austerity; from that, Agni was created.
When Agni was created, the vital energy of the creepers went into him; they withered away, for they had never withered before that time. That Prajāpati—

"He establishes the fire with the words, 'May these [worlds] overcome! He indeed overcame them; therefore, this fire is established for the sake of overcoming. Just as Agni overcomes the plants during the spring and winter, even so he who, knowing this, establishes the fire, overcomes his rival, his enemy, and misfortune.
Indeed, that much of this earth remains unconsecrated as far as the altar is enclosed; having dug it up and poured water upon it, [he establishes] the fire."
He establishes it; having made it fit for sacrifice and pure, he establishes it. Indeed, when Agni was created, this earth was afraid, thinking, "He will burn me excessively.

In that one pours water and then establishes the fire, it is to prevent her from being burnt excessively. Water is indeed that all-encompassing body of Prajāpati; thus offspring and cattle surround him on every side with merit, for him who acts in this way.

The wise man, having poured out water, establishes the fire. As large as the snout of a boar was at first, so large was this earth; when he establishes the fire after placing down what has been dug up by a boar, he does not miss this very earth, but establishes it upon its own measure.
Therefore, this earth growls at the boar, for it bears its measure. The Asuras were indeed called "God-hand" (devapāṇayaḥ).
The divine cows were away; he followed after them and drove them back. Their milk was lost. They said, "That which was their best has been lost. Becoming a boar, he went from the Asuras to the gods.
Therefore, cows run after a boar, knowing it as their own milk. Thus, one obtains for oneself as much of the cattle and bipeds as is dear.

He who, knowing this, establishes his fire on ground trampled by a boar, becomes as dear to four-footed animals as the milk is to them; he becomes dear to both two-footed and four-footed creatures. Now, that which is an anthill is the part of this earth that has not been touched [by man]. When he scatters the mound of an anthill and establishes his fire upon it, he establishes it upon that very part of her which has not been touched. Indeed, the anthill is the essence of this earth that has risen up.

In that he establishes the fire after scattering the mound of an anthill, he establishes it upon the very sap of this earth; for the anthill is indeed the vigor (*ūrj*) that has risen from her. In that he establishes the fire after scattering the mound of an anthill, he establishes it upon the very vigor of this earth.
The anthill is indeed the breast of Prajāpati; in that he establishes the fire after scattering the mound of an anthill, [he establishes it] as Prajāpati.

Thus he closes the breast for him; he wins food for himself; he becomes the leader of his kinsmen, free from hunger, for one who knows thus. Indeed, the saline soil (ūṣas) here is the sacrificial portion of that [earth] over there. When he scatters saline soil and establishes the fire, he establishes it upon the sacrificial portion of that very earth.
Cattle do not deposit seed here unless there is saline soil. Therefore, [he scatters] the saline soil.
He scatters [sand] and establishes the fire; verily, he thus bestows seed for the nourishment and procreation of cattle.

This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed that sun yonder; what was its ash when it was here on earth is these sands. In that he scatters sands and establishes the fire, he establishes it in its own womb, in its own ash. In the beginning, this earth was loose; Prajāpati [stabilized] it.
He made it firm with pebbles; when one scatters pebbles and establishes the fire, one thereby makes this very earth firm for the sake of stability.

Just as Prajāpati made this earth firm with pebbles, so do cattle become firm upon him who, knowing thus, scatters pebbles and establishes the fire. Indra, indeed, hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra; those which were its scattered drops—

They became gravel. When one scatters gravel and establishes the fire, he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival and adversary. At that moment, he should meditate in his mind upon whomsoever he hates; verily, he hurls the thunderbolt at him and lays him low. "He is a householder," they say, "who has a store of grain. Now, the mole-hill is indeed the form of that grain-store. When...
Having scattered mouse-droppings, he establishes the fire; he becomes a householder who possesses dung.

He establishes [the fire]. The gods were unable to divide the fire. When they carried it eastward, it was entirely in front; when they carried it westward, it was entirely behind. They carried it forward with a horse yoked as the lead animal; that is why the horse yoked as the lead animal is called *pūrvavāh*.

The horse is indeed given at the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) by way of distribution for Agni; for the fire of him who does not give a horse at the *agnyādheya* remains undistributed and unestablished. Now, he who gives a horse at the *agnyādheya* establishes it after having distributed it, for the sake of distribution.
The gods, preceded by the *stoma*, conquered the Asuras; this horse is indeed the *stoma*. Therefore, when one places the horse in front—

They lead [the horse] while overcoming it; verily, having overcome it, he establishes it. Prajāpati’s eye swelled; that which was its swelling became the horse. In that they lead the horse in front, he bestows sight upon the sacrificer.

It must not be let loose to go away; for if he were to let it loose to go away, he would deprive the sacrificer of his sight and he would become blind. It should be established after being drawn back toward him.
He took back the eye for the sacrificer alone; it should not be placed on the footprint, for he would make it a dwelling-place, and Rudra would become intent on harming his cattle.
It should be placed from the side, either from this side or that; thus he does not make it a dwelling-place, and Paśupati does not become a slayer of his cattle.
The gods sent the Gāyatrī toward the sacrifice; she returned empty, and Agni [took] her [portion].
He bestowed radiance upon him; he became a goat. In that one gives a goat at the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), one secures radiance for oneself.

It should be given to the Agnīdh; for the Agnīdh is the mouth of the sacrifice, and thus by means of the mouth of the sacrifice, he brings the mouth of the sacrifice to fulfillment. He gives a cow and a bull;
thereby he secures all vital power, for the cow and the bull are indeed all vital power. These two are it.

The cow and the ox are indeed the mother and father of the sacrifice; the clarified butter and the milk belong to the cow, while the sacrificial cake and the boiled rice belong to the ox. Regarding this, they say: "He who gives a cow and an ox at the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) secures for himself a wish-fulfilling cow. Therefore, he who desires the greatest prosperity for his livestock should give a two-year-old cow that has had one calf.
A two-year-old bull with testicles—this is a pair for the nourishment and procreation of cattle. Speech, indeed, is the Soma-purchasing cow;
a two-year-old cow is the Soma-purchasing cow of life. In that he gives a two-year-old cow of life, he wins speech itself;
he who knows thus speaks beautifully. A pillow with all its threads intact should be given; for this pillow is the very form of the meters.

He gives a pillow made of all kinds of thread; verily he wins the meters. The meters are cattle; verily he wins cattle. One who is unfit for sacrifice, impure, and born of violence suckles human milk;
he gives gold, and thereby he purifies himself. It is a hundred mānas in weight; man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundredfold strength.
Verily, one obtains life and vigor through the two former oblations; thirty measures are to be given for each of those two, while forty measures are to be given for the latter.

By that, he has lifted him up; therefore, he becomes more prosperous and better in the future. Indeed, a man is not truly born so long as he does not establish the sacred fire; he is born at the very moment he establishes the fire. Wearing linen garments, [they establish] the fire.
The two [garments] to be given to the *adhvaryu* priest are the very form of the womb; verily, they strip away the womb itself. One should place the gold upon it before the fire is established;

for gold is the brilliance of Agni—verily, he establishes him with his own brilliance. That gold must not be cast away; if one were to cast it away as if it had been left behind, that would be so. If he were to cast it away, he would become brooding and hungry.
If he does not reflect upon that which has been refuted, he becomes contentious.
He performs [it].
He who is this human fire—by worshipping him one eats food; by worshipping him one finds offspring;
by worshipping him cattle attend upon him. If one were to remove him without a share, he would cut him off from his thoughts.

He would be hungry. Therefore, of those forest trees that grow in the wild and bear the most abundant edible fruit, one should take two leaves from such a tree, gather upon them a cake of barley and a cake of rice, and set them down as an offering.
By this, he has presented him with a twofold portion, both domestic and wild; therefore, it does not fail him. Barley is not to be thought of [with longing], for it makes one free from hunger.

Indeed, at the beginning of the season, [the sacrificial cake] is cooked from here; they indeed draw this one out facing eastward. Therefore, the sacrificial cake for the animal on the west side is made of barley, while that in front is made of rice. Thus, for whomsoever he should desire [this], he should offer a cake of barley on the west side and one of rice in front.
These two are indeed the breasts of Prajāpati; by means of them, the gods subsist upon his sacrifice, humans upon the rain, and [other beings] upon food.
He wins for himself the food of his kinsmen who do not starve; he becomes the leader of those who call him their own—he who knows thus.

Indeed, Keśin Sātyakāmi used to say this regarding Keśin Dārbhya: "We have won food for him from the people at this establishment of the sacred fires, so that he eats food. Regarding this, they say: "Everything here is indeed the food of this sacrificer."
He indeed places this [lid] over it; thus one should know it, but one should not act upon it in that way—for three times Prajāpati uttered this truth.
A human being: [emended from *manuṣo*]. He should worship; he rises up. M2:
[emended from *atti*]. M2: [emended from *upāsītonnamati*].
Sitting nearby, [he said]: "upāsīnonna-" (M1);
"upāsīnonna-" (Bb); "upāsītonna-" (Amano, p. 223, n. 477).
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.
Thus, this indeed is *bhūḥ*, this is *bhuvaḥ*, and that is *svaḥ*. One should place [the fire] for a Brāhmaṇa who is an Āṅgirasa with the formula:
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ! By the vow of the divine Āṅgirasas, I place thee. [He places it] twice behind with "bhuvaḥ," twice in front with "svaḥ," twice behind, and twice in front.
Thus the sacrifice is established twofold upon truth, and the lord of the sacrifice is established twofold; now, as for the Brāhmaṇa...
Vaiśvānara would be [the deity] for that [offering]; he should place it with: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ! By the vow of the god Agni, I place thee.

Behind [with] "bhuvaḥ," and in front [with] "svaḥ"—twice behind, twice in front; thus the sacrifice is established twofold in truth, and the lord of the sacrifice is established twofold. Then he should place it for a Rājanya with: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ! By the vow of Indra accompanied by the Maruts, I place thee."

Thus [he places the fire] behind with "Bhūḥ" and in front with "Svaḥ"; twice behind and twice in front—that sacrifice is thus established twofold upon the Truth, and the lord of the sacrifice is established twofold. For the Rājanya has Indra as his deity, while the Viś has the Maruts; indeed, a Rājanya becomes prosperous through the Viś, and he wins the Viś for himself. Now, for a Vaiśya, he should establish [the fire] with: "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ! O Manuṣ, you, the village-leader..."

With "By the vow he bestows" [he places] behind; with "Bhūḥ! Svaḥ! [he places] in front—twice behind, twice in front. Thus the sacrifice is established twofold upon truth, and the lord of the sacrifice is established twofold. Indeed, through the leadership of a village (grāmaṇīthya), a Vaiśya becomes prosperous;
he secures for himself the leadership of a village. When Agni was created, he was unable to cast off his caul (ulba); Prajāpati [acted for him].

With the *āgneyapāvamānī* verses he tore away the caul; in that he places fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood with the *āgneyapāvamānī* verses, he indeed tears away its caul and purifies it. Just as a mother licks her young or a cow her calf, so does he lick him.
When Agni was created, his brilliance blazed up and entered the *aśvattha* tree; therefore, [he uses] fuel-sticks of *aśvattha*.
He places [the fuel sticks]; verily he wins splendor. Agni, when created, was flickering and stood still without being kindled.
Prajāpati was afraid, thinking, "He will surely harm me. He kindled him with a *śamī* branch; he pacified him.
That is why the *śamī* is called *śamī*. In that he places fuel sticks made of *śamī*, he kindles him and indeed pacifies him.
He brings well-being to the sacrificer and well-being to the cattle. When the gods distributed strength (*ūrj*), from that the Udumbara tree arose;
in that he places a fuel-stick of Udumbara wood, he secures strength for himself.
This one is indeed placed apart from cattle; for this Agni is Rudra. He should cause [the sacrificer] to recite: "The Gharma is the head;

therefore, become this Agni, dear to cattle; you are the soil. Thus he makes him dear to cattle and possessed of soil. With the words, "O bright one, with your bright light, may you attain luster through that luster," he indeed bestows luster upon him.
This Agni Vaiśvānara has indeed come from there—namely, that sun. If he were to carry [the fire] from the north, it would be as if this [sun] were here and this [Agni] were there;

he would surely burn him alive. Therefore, it should be carried from the south alone. When they have reached the midpoint of the way, the sacrificer should give a boon. Thus, he has established the Virāj in the middle; verily, the Virāj bestows the fires upon him.
The Virāj is indeed cattle; it was from the midst of cattle that he emitted this [fire]. Now, Agni had been created, and then Prajāpati created offspring;
they perished into this blind darkness of these worlds. He grieved; he performed austerity; from that, Agni was created.
Having created that Agni, he placed him below. Those [beings] who were in this world returned to him.
He lifted it up until it reached his ankles; those who were in the world above gathered around it.
He lifted it up until it reached his knees, then until it reached his navel, then until it reached his shoulders, and finally until it reached his ears;
those who were in the world above gathered around it. One should not lift it higher than the level of the ears; for if one were to lift it higher than the level of the ears—

The sacrificer is the highest of animals; if Agni were to burn the sacrificer from above, they say: "How could they now cause this one, established by the *brahman*, to fall? They have indeed made him loose; they are casting him away. Therefore, without setting him down, he should lift him up knee-high, then navel-high, and then shoulder-high. Just as it was...

Just as creatures turned back toward Prajāpati from these worlds, even so do cattle turn back toward the sacrificer from these worlds who, knowing this, establishes the sacred fire. By means of Agni as the deity and Viṣṇu as the sacrifice, the gods, having overwhelmed the Asuras, struck them down with the thunderbolt; this applies to one who has rivals or enemies.

They should turn the chariot wheel three times around; just as the gods, having crushed the Asuras with Agni as the deity, with Viṣṇu, and with the sacrifice, then released them upon with the thunderbolt, even so the sacrificer who, knowing this, establishes the fire, crushes his rival and adversary with Agni as the deity, with Viṣṇu, and with the sacrifice, and then releases him upon with the thunderbolt.
This full ladle is indeed Prajāpati in form; when he offers the full ladle, he attains Prajāpati himself.
"Seven, O Agni, are your fuel-sticks, seven your tongues"—for these are the bodies of Agni, sixfold and seven by seven.
Whoever, when establishing this fire, causes these [bodies] of his to thirst, he himself becomes thirsty; [the verse] "of wood from the *śamī* tree" satisfies them for him.
He places three fuel-sticks on the fire, anointed with ghee and accompanied by verses containing the word "ghee. He kindles him completely and thus pacifies him;

he becomes auspicious for the sacrificer and for his cattle. Those fires which exist in these three worlds come together and think, "We shall take away his wealth. [The sacrificer should think,] "He has stepped over us; let him be the bearer of our oblations," and then he should offer the oblation.
We take [it] up:
those fires which are from heaven and those which are from earth, coming together, clothed in food and strength—
having given wealth to this Agni, being sacrificed to, pleased, and having become partakers of the oblation, go back again to your respective worlds.

With "Svāhā!"—having thus made this very [sacrifice] possessed of wealth, the deities, being gratified and having become partakers of the oblations, return again to their respective worlds.
