He should cause [the sacrificer] to recite: "The Gharma is the head; may this Agni become dear to the cattle; thou art the soil.
By this he makes him dear to the cattle and rich in soil. "That which is thy bright, bright light..."
"Thou art the bright, eternal abode; with that, I establish thee"—thus he establishes it endowed with splendor.
O Jātavedas Agni, we place you upon the navel of the earth, in the station of Iḍā, so that you may carry the oblation.
Thus he made him the carrier of oblations. When Agni was created, the cattle fell away from his eyes;
Prajāpati then created the Vāravantīya [sāman] and held them back. Indeed, he is now being created at the very moment he is established.
Just as the cattle fell away from him when he was created, so do the cattle fall away from him when he is established. This is that [Agni].
For Rudra is that which is Agni; therefore, he who, knowing this, sings the Vāravantīya, truly wards off cattle [from harm].

Prajāpati, having created the Vāravantīya, attained whatever desire he desired; even so does the sacrificer attain whatever desire he desires when, knowing this, he establishes the fire while singing the Vāravantīya. Agni, indeed, is the consumer of raw flesh (kravyād).
Viśvadāvya burnt these worlds; Prajāpati, singing the Vāravantīya and carrying the Varaṇa tree, went toward him and pacified him.

Whatever of his was flesh-eating and whatever was Viśvadāvya, that he pacifies who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya. Therefore, a Varaṇa tree should be used as a sacrificial implement, but one should not offer an oblation with it. For this [which is here]...
That which has been, that which is becoming, and that which will be—whatever exists between heaven and earth—that is the Vāmadevya;
he who, knowing this, sings the Vāmadevya, secures that very thing. The Yajñāyajñiya is indeed the essence of the Brahman;
when he sings the Yajñāyajñiya, he places the essence in the Brahman.
When Agni was created, Prajāpati fanned him from the front with the Pavamāna; when he offers to the Pavamāna, he thus fans him.
When [he offers] to the Pāvaka, he purifies him; when [he offers] to the Śuci, whatever in him is unpurified, that he purifies by this.
When he offers to the Pavamāna—since the Pavamāna is cattle—he wins cattle. When [he offers] to the Pāvaka, [it is] food.

Verily, he who offers to Pāvaka wins food; he who offers to Śuci places luster in him as one who is purified. If he should desire of someone, "May he become more wretched and more evil," he should offer the oblations to him one by one; thus he has seized him away, and thereby that person becomes more wretched and more evil. But if he should desire of someone, "May he be neither better nor worse," he should offer all [the oblations] to him simultaneously.

He should offer the oblations; that indeed restrains him, and by that he becomes neither better nor worse. Now, if he should desire of someone, "May he become better and more prosperous in the future," for him he should first offer to Agni Pavamāna, and then the two subsequent oblations to Agni Pāvaka and Agni Śuci on the same sacrificial grass-bundle. That indeed elevates him, and by that he becomes better in the future.

He becomes more powerful and better; however, if one were to have two *triṣṭubh*s, two *anuṣṭubh*s, or a *jagatī* as the *saṃyājyā* verses, he would overstep the *gāyatrī*, and he would fall away from the meters. Therefore, for one who desires this, he should use two *gāyatrī*s as the *saṃyājyā* verses; for Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature and has the *gāyatrī* as his meter. Thus, he establishes him in his own womb, in his own meter.

One should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; for Agni is all the deities and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice—thus he seizes both the deities and the sacrifice. He should offer a pap in clarified butter at the three-night rite to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. In that it is offered to Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he seizes the sacrifice itself. In that it is offered to Śipiviṣṭa—Śipiviṣṭa being cattle—he secures cattle for himself.

In that it is threefold, and there are these three worlds, he thereby obtains these very worlds. In that it is in ghee—ghee being indeed brilliance—he wins brilliance. He who desires cattle should offer a caru-oblation of rice in ghee to Āditya; for ghee is the milk of the cow and the rice-grains are the milk of the ox;
that is a productive pair for the nourishment and procreation of cattle. He should subsequently offer a second cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Agni and Soma.

Therefore, let this oblation come back to us; no one else has power over it. When the Brahmins offered it in former times, then none of them had power over it, for they do not offer it now; thus, everyone has power over it. As for that which belongs to Agni:

Agni is brilliance, so he wins brilliance. As for that which belongs to Soma: Soma is indeed the bright one, the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); [thus] he wins the luster of sacred knowledge.

Thus he secures it. Now, that *caru* of ghee which is for Āditya, they should carry it around to the Brahman; four should consume it, and an equal boon should be given to them. For in the beginning, this pair was produced fourfold: one and one, two and two, three and three, and four and four; such is the pairing of cattle.
For nourishment and for procreation.

One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to receive the consecration on the full moon of Phalgunī; for the full moon of Phalgunī is the beginning of the seasons, Agni is the foremost of the gods, and the Brāhmaṇa is the foremost of men. One should cause a Rājanya to receive it in summer; for in summer Indra slew Vṛtra, and indeed, a Rājanya who desires preeminence seeks to slay his enemies. One should cause a Vaiśya to receive it in autumn; for autumn is food, and by means of food the Vaiśya prospers.

He becomes prosperous; he wins food for himself. If he were to establish [the fire] in another season, then that one season alone would be auspicious for him, while the others would be inauspicious and difficult for him to dwell in. Therefore, if he should desire this, he should establish it on the full moon of Phālguna. Then all the seasons become auspicious for him, and all the seasons quicken him throughout the year.

This day of the Phalgunī full moon is indeed the mouth of the year; if one were to install [the fire] on the day of the Phalgunī full moon, he would place it within the mouth of the year and thereby close it off.

It should rather be installed two days or even one day before that; thus he takes hold of the second season and does not close off the year at its mouth. This is why he takes hold of the second season.
Verily, he goes forth seizing the power, cattle, and field of his rival and adversary. He should establish the fires under the Kṛttikās for a Brāhmaṇa;

the Kṛttikās belong to Agni, and the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni; thus he establishes them on their own birthplace, on their own day. The Kṛttikās are indeed the head of Prajāpati; Agni is the mouth, and food is eaten by means of the head. He secures for himself the eating of food. There are seven [Kṛttikās].

There are seven *kṛttikās* in the head; [the breaths] are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); he thus places the vital breaths in him. For one desiring cattle, he should install [the fire] under Rohiṇī. Rohiṇī is indeed the lunar mansion of Soma; Soma is the placer of seed; he thus places seed in him. In the beginning, this earth was rough; upon it, the gods caused plants to grow during Rohiṇī. Just as these plants have grown upon her, so does [he cause them to grow] in him.

Cattle thrive for one who, knowing this, establishes the sacred fire under Rohiṇī; one desiring heaven should establish it under Rohiṇī, for under Rohiṇī the gods went to heaven—he indeed goes to heaven. The Kālakāñjas, the Asuras, were building bricks with the thought, "We shall ascend to heaven. Indra, calling himself a Brāhmaṇa, approached them; he laid down that first brick.
As if ascending to heaven, he then pulled that [brick] out; those Asuras, becoming worse off, fell away.

Those two which were the highest became the two Yama-horses; those which were lower became the woolly ones (*ūrṇāvatī*). That brick which he pulled out became Citrā. He who has rivals or enemies should establish his fire on the Citrā day; this is its significance.

Just as when this [lunar mansion] has been entered, the Asuras, becoming more wretched, were utterly cast down, even so his rival, the enemy, becoming more wretched, is utterly cast down by him who, knowing thus, establishes the sacred fires under Citrā; and he who desires,
"May I be fortunate and an eater of food," should establish the fires under the earlier Phalgunīs, for that day belongs to Bhaga.

If one establishes the sacred fires under the *pūrvā-phalgunī* constellations, he becomes fortunate and an eater of food. Now, if one should desire, "May my offspring be desirous of giving," he should establish the fires under the *uttarā-phalgunī* constellations. The *uttarā-phalgunī*s are indeed the day of Aryaman;
Aryaman is the giver, and thus his offspring become desirous of giving to him. Under those [constellations], he should establish them for a *rājanya*, for he is the giver of offspring.
The Noble One lives by means of giving; his subjects become desirous of giving. These two, the full moon and the new moon, are indeed the two breasts of Prajāpati.

When one establishes the sacred fires on either the full moon or the new moon day, one milks Prajāpati himself when he is offered. These two, the full moon and the new moon, are the Sadas and Havirdhāna sheds of the gods. When [one performs] on the full moon...
Or one may establish the sacred fires on the new moon day, or on two auspicious days, or on two sacrificial days.
Before the rising of the sun, the fire was churned by the Asuras, who were godless; it was established when the rays had risen.

Being churned, it is established as possessing the gods, together with Indra, in the form of both days. It should be established at twenty-four steps, for the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables.

The Gāyatrī is indeed the Gāyatra metre of Agni; he thus places him in his own womb, in his own metre. Therefore, for one whom he desires [to prosper], he should place him in an unlimited [metre]; for that which is limited is liable to perish, and he secures for him an unlimited life-span.
When Agni was created, he stepped forth from Prajāpati; Prajāpati was afraid, thinking, "He has become something here."

Saying "This am I," he follows it out and offers it; for indeed, at the very moment it is established, this [Agni] is being created. Regarding this, they say: "One should run after [the fire] from the *amhas* and then offer the *agnihotra*. One should not do it thus; that would be a violation of the sequence.
That which is done beyond the womb [of the fire-pan] is a defect of the sacrifice; if one were to place what is posterior before what is prior, one would be unable to procreate.
Having offered the first oblations, he should then perform the evening *agnihotra* sacrifice.
Agni is light, light is Agni; svāhā!
Thus, by means of that evening light, he places the seed within the middle.
The sun is the light, the light is the sun; svāhā! Thus at dawn.
That seed, placed in the midst by means of the evening light.

In the morning he brought forth offspring. Now, the gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict; then Indra established the sacred fire. Those gods were afraid, thinking: "There he will remain, guarding this very Agni and guarding the *agnihotra*; he will not come to us, and they will defeat us. They said: "Whatever you do, whether it be wealth or sacrifice..."
"Whatever you win, that we shall perform as your *agnihotra*; now, come! He indeed went there. Therefore, the *agnihotra* of a *rājanya* should not be offered.

For whatever he does, whatever he kills, whatever he conquers, whatever he wins, and whatever the subjects wait upon him—that is the *agnihotra* of the *rājanya*. Should the *agnihotra* of a *rājanya* be offered, or should it not be offered? It should not be offered.

Thus they deliberate: if one were to offer after having already offered, he would either cut asunder the sacrifice, or he would be defeated, or he would perish. Therefore, one should offer on the full moon day or the new moon day; moreover, one should perform the attendance upon the fires or pile them up again. By this means, his New and Full Moon sacrifices remain continuous and uninterrupted.

If one should desire, "May he be rich in cattle," they should fetch the fire from the house of one who has many well-nourished animals; for just as animals were created following him when he was being created, so do animals follow him when he is being fetched, since Agni is indeed Rudra. And if one should desire, "May he be an eater of food," they should fetch the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni) from his frying pan.

This [fire] among the fires is indeed the eater of food and the maker of food; he secures for himself the consumption of food through the hearth. Regarding this they say: "As a low-born man, a domestic servant, might practice medicine, so does he [who establishes the fire in such a manner]. He should rather be produced by friction; that is auspicious for the sacrificer and auspicious for his cattle. He who, not intending to sacrifice with Soma, establishes the sacred fires, should not offer oblations before a year has passed.

Rudra might become intent on seizing his cattle; for rice and barley are indeed cattle. Having cooked four-śarāva-measures of their boiled rice so that the grains remain whole, he should offer it to the Brahmins. If he were not to sacrifice to those deities for whom he established the fire, he would cut them off from him; they would be anxious and hungry for him. Therefore, an oblation of clarified butter should be offered to them.
Therefore, he does not shrink from them; being free from anxious thought, he becomes free from hunger. At the end of a year he offers the oblations;

thus Rudra, being kept at a distance for a year, does not harm his cattle. He offered the Agnihotra for a year; he found that heat and ascended to the heavenly world together with everything. For three times indeed did the Virāj stride this [universe].
The Gārhapatya, the Āhavanīya, and the Sabhya—these he obtains as the Virāj; the Virāj is indeed food, and thus he obtains food.
He should offer on the middle of the gaming board for a Rājanya with a verse addressed to Varuṇa; Varuṇa is the king of the gods, and thus he secures royal power for him.
Having placed gold down, he offers; he offers upon that which possesses fire and possesses a foundation. If he does not do so, the Adhvaryu becomes blind.
It may be that he should sacrifice in a non-abode; he should give him a hundred dice and have him sort them.

Man indeed has a life-span of a hundred years and a strength of a hundred; thus he obtains life and strength. On that day, they should gamble with his cow in the assembly hall, and they should not harm its joints. He should present it to the members of the assembly; whatever he wins with it should be given to the Brahmins.
Thus he obtains suitable food.

On the morning of whichever night he is about to establish the sacred fires, on that night he should cook four śarāva-measures of rice and offer it to the Brahmins like rice with its grains still intact. Aditi, indeed, desiring offspring, cooked rice; she ate the remains, and from her Dhātṛ and Aryaman were born. She cooked again; she ate the remains, and from her Mitra and [Varuṇa] were born.

Varuṇa and Ajāyata were born; she cooked again, and he ate the remnant. Aṃśa and Bhaga were born to her; she cooked again, and he thought: "Two by two are being born to me while I am eating the remnant. Surely it would be better for me if I were to eat first.
Having eaten first, she offered [the remainder]. While they were still within the womb, they spoke.
"We two shall become this, namely the Ādityas," they said. The Ādityas sought one to strike them down; Aṃśa and Bhaga struck them down.
Therefore, people perform sacrifice for these two; they are sharers of the portion, for Aṃśa received his share of the sacrifice, while Bhaga went to the people.
Therefore, they say, "One should go where the people are, there one meets with Bhaga. He, indeed, was Indra.

He indeed sent forth the breath upward; the other egg fell down dead. He is truly Mārtāṇḍa, from whom these human beings are descended. She, Aditi, went to the Ādityas for help, saying, "Let this [egg] be mine; let it not fall away from me in vain. They said, "Then let him speak for us alone; let him not disregard us. He is truly Vivasvat.
Āditya, Manu Vaivasvata, and Yama—Manu indeed is in this world and Yama in that world;

these Ādityas guard the paths of the gods. They repel the one who desires to sacrifice without having informed them, and they repel from the heavenly world the one who establishes the sacred fire without having announced it to them. The Ādityas have the remnants as their portion; therefore, having turned [the fire] toward the remnants...
He places the fuel-sticks; thus he declares the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) to the Ādityas, and they do not repel him from the heavenly world.

One who is about to establish the fires should let [the fire] go out for a year. They should not carry his fire away from the house, nor should they bring it from elsewhere. In a year, embryos are born fully developed; he establishes the fire for him when it is born and fully developed. He should let it go out for twelve nights; twelve [months make up a year].

The nights are indeed the counterpart of the year; embryos grow in the year and are born when they have grown. He establishes this [fire] when it has grown and been born. He should omit three [nights]; for these worlds are three; he thus attains these very worlds. He should omit one [night]; Prajāpati is indeed one; he thus attains Prajāpati. Purūravas, the son of Iḍā, found Urvaśī.

From her was born Āyu. He rose up toward the heavenly world along with the gods; they said, "We gods are going there; where will this man go? He replied, "There are many of my equals who will say of me, 'What has this son of a goddess done for his mother's brothers among the gods? Let there be something for me indeed. Therefore...

Agni gave up his sacrificial body; placing it in his lap, he carried it away and deposited it in a fire-pan. That became the *aśvattha* tree which grows upon it, while the pan itself became the *śamī*. Therefore, these two are used in the sacrifice, for they are of auspicious birth. Indeed, Agni went to Varuṇa to practice studentship (*brahmacarya*). While Varuṇa was away on a journey, Agni had intercourse with his wife. [Varuṇa found him] from the front...
Seeing him approaching, he ran back toward him. He realized, "He is carrying away all my vital power, manly strength, and seed, having torn it out.
So, pursuing him, he tore it out. That which was the seed became the *aśvattha* tree;
that which was the womb became the *śamī* tree. Therefore, these two are used in the sacrifice, for they have a holy origin. Indeed, Prajāpati, having created the creatures, was emptied.

He thought, "Having become a horse, let me lie down on the earth for a year with my head turned downward. As he stood there, a *aśvattha* tree sprouted from his head; that is the reason for the *aśvattha*'s name as *aśvattha*. Therefore, this [wood] is used in the sacrifice, for it belongs to Prajāpati.
prāṇamān;
māturbhrātrebhyāḥ.

Manu, desiring offspring, was about to establish the sacred fires; he offered oblations to each deity one by one. Then, from the oblation to Mitra and Varuṇa, a female phantom (prapharvi) arose. Ghee flowed from her feet. She went to Mitra and Varuṇa, and they said to her:
"By our oblation indeed you were born; you belong to Manu; go to him. She went to Manu, and he...

He said, "These Asuras, thinking themselves meritorious, are establishing the sacred fires; go to them! She went to them. They established that fire first, then this one, then this one. She returned and asked him, "What did they obtain?
He replied, "They established that one first, then this one, then this one. He said, "The Asuras have indeed once reached the end of prosperity; but they shall perish."

He said, "These gods, who consider themselves meritorious, are establishing the sacred fire; go to them. She went to them; they established this [fire] first, then that one, and then this one. She returned and asked him, "What did you find? He said, "They established this very one first, then that one, and then this one. He said, "The gods have indeed once for all [attained] the heavenly world together with everything."

Thinking, "From this gift they shall ascend and subsist upon the sacrifice," he who is to give away all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*) should place this [fire] first, then that one, and then this one. Just as the gods ascended to the heavenly world together with everything,
even so the sacrificer, knowing thus, ascends to the heavenly world together with everything.

He established the sacred fire. He said, "These seers, who consider themselves meritorious, are establishing the fire; go after them! She went after them. They established this [fire] first, then this one, then that one. She returned and asked him, "What have they attained? He said, "They have established this one first, then this one, then that one. He said, "I alone have discovered the true nature of the establishment of the fire."

"Indeed, the seers established themselves in all these worlds. He who, knowing this, establishes the fire, establishes himself with offspring and cattle. If one were to establish this [terrestrial] fire after having established that [celestial] one, he would establish it wrongly; or if, having established this one, he were to establish that one, he would establish it wrongly. Therefore, having first established this one, then this one, and then that one—it is thus successful.
It is established on ground sloping toward the east; thus it is established in a prosperous manner. It is established from the middle beam toward the east;
thus it is established in a prosperous manner. That which was indeed the *prapharvi* became a cow;
she is *iḍā*, she is of Manu, she is *ghṛtapadī*, and she belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa.
He rose up:
from this offering.
FN: Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.
But that which you, most gracious one, cast away in anger when provoked—O Agni, that act of yours is well-ordered; we kindle you anew.
That which you, when struck down by wrath, have scattered across the earth—
that the Ādityas, all the gods, and the Vasus have brought back again.
That which you, being powerless, have scattered from your heart through your fury.
Then Indra, Agni, and the Vasus fashioned it together once again.
May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmins, O Agni, who possess the wealth of the earth, kindle you again.
May you cause your body to grow with clarified butter; may the abundance of wealth attend the sacrificer.
The thirty-three threads that extend this [sacrifice] and bestow it with ambrosia—with those we plug the hole here. Svāhā! May the sacrifice go unto the gods.
May the mind, the light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice.
May the gods come with benevolent minds to this sacrifice of seven threads that has been stretched out for us.
May Bṛhaspati restore this interrupted sacrifice for us with our oblation of clarified butter;
those dawns that have been sacrificed and those offerings that are to be made, these I join together with my mind and with clarified butter.
O Agni, you who turn toward us, turn toward me with life-span, with splendor, with offspring, with wealth, with gain, with wisdom, with riches, and with nourishment.
O Agni Aṅgiras, may there be a hundred turnings for you, and a thousand approaches for you. Then, by the increase of prosperity, restore to us what we have lost; restore wealth to us once again.
Return again with vigor, O Agni, return with food and long life;
protect us again from distress.
Return with wealth, O Agni; overflow with a stream that nourishes all, from every side.

Salila, Saliga, Sagara—may those Ādityas, enjoying our oblation, partake of it; Svāhā! Keta, Suketa, Saketa—may those Ādityas, enjoying our oblation, partake of it; Svāhā! O Vivasvat, impelled by the gods, O Āditya, may you gods speed our true invocation of the gods among the gods; Svāhā to the Ādityas!

The re-establishment of the fire (*punarādheya*) is indeed the portion of Agni. By desiring to obtain this portion, one actually diminishes it. If, while about to establish the fires, he should think, "May it prosper for me," he should remove them and establish them again. Thus, having obtained that very portion which he previously diminished, he makes it prosper. Everything is made to belong to Agni; whatever there is, by giving all of it as a portion to Agni, he prospers.

"He attains all prosperity; there are no materials to be collected, nor is there a sacrificial formula (*yajus*) to be performed," so they say, for he has already collected the materials and his sacrifice is already performed.

However, others say that the materials must indeed be collected and the sacrificial formula must be performed. A garment that has been mended, a chariot that has been renewed, and an ox that has been let out again—these, indeed, are the forms of the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*).

Having reached the forms themselves, he wins them. When Agni perishes, he perishes along with the waters and the plants; for Darbha grasses are indeed waters and plants. In that there are Darbha upolapa grasses, he wins and secures him from the waters and the plants.
When the gods were about to depart for victory over the Asuras, they deposited their beloved bodies in Agni, [thinking]: "If they should conquer us, these [bodies]..."

"Let us run toward them if we should conquer; let us turn back toward them," they said. Having conquered, those gods sought [the cattle], thinking, "May they be ours in common. Agni said, "Only he who shall establish me as his deity with my own portion shall become one with these bodies.
The gods established him; he became one with these bodies. Cattle, indeed, are the dear bodies of the gods.

They became one with cattle; therefore, he who, knowing this, performs the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), becomes one with these very bodies of Agni. Cattle are indeed the dear bodies of the gods; he becomes one with cattle. Manu, desiring prosperity, established the fires; he prospered in these nourishments, and by that he attained success. Tvaṣṭṛ, desiring cattle, established the fires; these [cattle] are his.

The animals of Tvaṣṭṛ were born; by that, Prajāpati, desiring offspring, prospered. These creatures, belonging to Prajāpati, were born; by that he prospered. Verily, he who first established [the fire] became endowed with that wealth; that is the reason for the name Punarvasu. Therefore, it should be established under Punarvasu, for he indeed became endowed again with that wealth.
He who established that [fire] indeed prospered; therefore, it should be established under the Anurādhās, for the sake of prosperity—he surely prospers—and also for the sake of pairing.
If the fire goes out, it goes out after [the lapse of] a year. Seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses should be recited:
five seasons and twelve months—this is the year. Having reached him from the very year, he wins him. Regarding this they say:
"Fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses should be recited, not seventeen; for this [fifteenfold set] is the most effective means of transition within the year, by which [the year] is best attained."

Fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses are obtained; there are fifteen nights in a half-month, and by means of those very [verses], they are obtained. As many as are the syllables of the *sāmidhenīs*, so many are the days of the year; by means of those very [syllables], those [days] are obtained. Agni, indeed, when he goes out, goes out after the year; for the year consists of six seasons, therefore there are six case-endings (*vibhakti*).
Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; in that there are six case-forms (*vibhakti*), he wins him by obtaining him from the year itself.

Now, because Agni is distributed in many ways, he has nourished these prosperities; therefore, Agni has attained as many case-forms as no other deity. Furthermore, although they consist of two syllables, they are made to have four syllables, for cattle are fourfold.

The *prayāja* offerings are the seasons, and the seasons are indeed pairs or couples. If he were to omit the *prayājas*, he would omit the seasons; and if he were to omit the seasons, he would omit food. The *prayājas* are the mouth of the sacrifice; if he were to omit the *prayājas*, he would omit the mouth of the sacrifice.

Therefore, for one who desires [to attain something], he should employ the case-endings (*vibhakti*) after the *prayājas*. The *prayājas* are indeed vigor, and the case-endings are vigor; [he thus secures it] from vigor.

Thus he utters the *vaṣaṭ* over it; he attains immediate prosperity. Why is the offering to Agni not performed separately? And why are the *vibhakti*-formulas recited together with the *prayāja* offerings?
The *prayāja* offerings are indeed sacrificed throughout the year. Why, then, is the offering to Agni performed [separately]? Therefore, the offering to Agni is not performed separately.
Return again with vigor, O Agni, return with food and long life;
protect us again from distress.
Thus he should offer [the oblations] before the fore-sacrifices (prayāja).
Return with wealth, O Agni; swell with a stream that is worthy of universal praise, from every side.
Thus he should offer after the subsequent offerings (anuyāja). For he who prospers through strength and cattle perishes along with them;
[with the words] "Return again with strength," he thereby secures for himself strength and cattle once more. Moreover, he makes those very deities sharers [in the sacrifice].
Furthermore, he thus fulfills the blessings of the sacrifice on both sides. Why is no offering made to Agni, yet the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) are nevertheless sacrificed?

Thus, these two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice; if one were to omit the butter-portions, he would omit the eyes of the sacrifice. He should perform [the verse] "O Agni, purify the lives" in the place of Soma; since it belongs to Agni, it is addressed to Agni, and since it is a Pavamāna verse, it is addressed to Soma.
Thus, the rite is not deprived of Agni, nor do they exclude Soma. [He should recite] "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit" for one desiring offspring.

Or, one who desires cattle should perform [this] in the world of Soma; for in that it is paired, it is productive of offspring, and in that it contains seed, it belongs to Soma. He who sets aside the sacred fires is deprived of the sacrifice; since the sacrifice is fivefold, and this [offering] is on five potsherds, he thus recovers the sacrifice itself. It should be made on eight potsherds, for Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature, his metre is the Gāyatrī, and this [offering] indeed belongs to Agni.

As for the fact that the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is performed with an offering on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*), that should not be heeded; it should rather be performed on five potsherds (*pañcakapāla*).
For from the fifth season the sixth season arose; thus, the fifth and the sixth seasons are the same.
By means of the five-potsherd cake, having obtained him from the very year, he secures him. The seasons are indeed procreation, and Agni is procreation.
In that it consists of five potsherds, the progenitor indeed procreates him from the very act of procreation.
Or rather:

"He who neglects the *agni* is a slayer of the hero among the gods. A hero is one who bestows a hundredfold. Since these *paṅkti* verses consist of a hundred syllables, he thereby recovers for the gods their hero. Indeed, the *ādheya* (initial establishment) is for one purpose, while the *punarādheya* (re-establishment) is for another."
Verily, one does not thereby rescue [the fire] by means of what is to be placed upon it; rather, for whomever there is a re-establishment, he rescues it by means of that very re-establishment.

Old age, indeed, is the lifespan ordained by the gods; for so many years does one go. In that these are *pañkti* verses of a hundred syllables, he attains and rescues as much life and vigor as there is; he secures it. Yet, he is deprived of life and vigor.

He who extinguishes the fire loses his life-span and vigor; in that he gives gold, he endows him with life-span and vigor. It is a hundred mānas in weight; for man has a life-span of a hundred years and a vigor of a hundredfold; thus he attains both life-span and vigor.
The Ādityas, indeed, were the last to go from here to the heavenly world; they became thirsty, for the gods [derive their power] from the sacrificial gift given from here.
They indeed live off this [fire] when they set it up again; they prospered. The Ādityas prospered in this world, and the Ādityas in yonder world;

the cattle in this world, and the seasons in yonder world. Therefore, he who, knowing thus, sets up the fire by re-installation (punarādheya), prospers in both worlds—both in this one and in yonder one. Salila, Saliga, Sagara—those Ādityas [are the guardians] of our oblation.
"May they partake with favor, Svāhā! May their intention, their good intention, and their shared intention—O Ādityas, may they partake with favor of our oblation, Svāhā!

O Vivasvat, impelled by the gods, O Āditya, may you gods speed our true invocation of the gods among the gods; Svāhā to the Ādityas! With these [formulas], they indeed re-established that fire and prospered. Therefore, when one re-establishes it with these [formulas], he prospers.
Then he prospers, for the re-establishment of the sacred fires belongs to the Ādityas.

Prajāpati created living beings; he first created Agni from his head. When he created Agni, he wiped [his hand] around it; from that, redness flowed away, and he wiped it down. From that, the Udumbara tree arose.
Therefore, the Udumbara belongs to Prajāpati; therefore, its fruit ripens red. Once created, it went away from him toward its own portion.
Desiring that very thing, Prajāpati did not find what he was to offer; taking his own eye, he offered it as an oblation.
Agni is light, light is Agni; Svāhā!
Thus, they consider that eye to be yonder sun; for they consider that they are offering this [oblation] to yonder [sun] while offering it into this [fire].

The eye is indeed truth; with truth one offers the Agnihotra when he who knows thus offers it. He becomes prosperous and becomes truth, he who knows thus. "To whom and for what purpose is the Agnihotra offered? the exponents of the Veda ask; [the answer is: "To Agni."

That which one offers in the evening is offered for support and protection; by it one sustains the night. That which one offers in the morning is for the day; by it one sustains the day. They conclude all sacrifices in the fire. Now, the exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ) ask: "Why is this alone called the Agnihotra? [They reply: "The Hotṛ-offerings indeed departed from the gods, seeking their share in the Agnihotra."
The Agnihotra sacrifice.

Thus he said; by that [formula] he causes the Hotṛs to partake, and by that he makes them sharers. This, indeed, was the first oblation offered into Agni; that is the reason for the Agnihotra’s name as "Agnihotra. Once created, it went away from him, seeking its own portion. It did not find anything there that Prajāpati might have offered. His own Speech spoke to him, saying, "Offer! He wiped it out from this very place and offered.
Svāhā!
Thus his own speech indeed addressed him; that is the origin of the *svāhā*-utterance. Therefore, in the *agnihotra* there is the *svāhā*-utterance.

For this reason, there is no hair on the forehead or on the hand, because he took it from those places and offered it. Therefore, they say of one whose hair has been shaved on the right side that he possesses "the mark of the eldest," for Prajāpati, being the eldest, shaved himself with this first.
The *sruk* ladle should be made according to this measure. In the beginning, an oblation was offered into the fire; from that oblation, man was created.

He offered a second oblation; from that, the horse was created. Therefore, the horse eats both kinds of food, for it was created not separated from man. Therefore, they consider the horse standing facing them, thinking, "Is this a horse or a man? He offered a third oblation.

From that, the cow was created; he offered the fourth oblation, and from that the sheep was created. He offered the fifth oblation, and from that the goat was created. He offered the sixth oblation, and from that barley was created. He offered the seventh oblation, and from that rice was created. These seven domestic animals were thus created; he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, secures them for himself.

He offered the eighth oblation; from that, spring was created. He offered the ninth; from that, summer was created. He offered the tenth; from that, the rainy season was created. He offered the eleventh; from that, autumn was created. He offered the twelfth; from that, winter was created.
The thirteenth oblation remained unoffered, and then the cool season was created. Therefore, this [unoffered state] belongs to the seasons.

From the unoffered oblation, indeed, the unappeased and cruel arose; from the unoffered oblation it was created. Regarding this, the exponents of sacred knowledge say: "Were the seasons created first, or the cattle? One should reply: "Both the seasons and the cattle," for both of these were created together.
Verily, he (Agni) entered him again from this very place. That which is the hand is indeed the fire-receptacle of the hand; therefore, one should offer from here.
Fire burns the hand most severely when, being scorched, one stretches out both hands toward it; for one thus seeks a refuge in the fire.

Indeed, animals enter into fire, and fire enters into animals; verily, animals enter into him who knows this, and he enters into animals. Regarding this, Nārada used to say: "When one perceives a cow lying down as dead..."

"Let one who does not know this think thus," for these [beings] enter into Agni, and Agni [enters] them; therefore, during all the seasons, animals crawl toward Agni, for they do not exist without Agni. Because he found the cattle when born, that is the "Jātavedas-ness" of Jātavedas.
He poured her into the waters; she burned the waters; they became thunderbolts for Agni; therefore, the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*).

Fire should not be sprinkled over; if one were to sprinkle over it, he would sacrifice with a ruined sacrifice. Prajāpati sought her; he found her in the waters. He rubbed her into the plants; therefore, the plants, though unsmeared, hum.
From the plants come cattle, from cattle men. He who knows this hums, though unsmeared. That [which occurs] in spring and winter...
That armpit is what is to be conditioned; this indeed is Agni’s beloved abode, and this truly is that oblation which comes forth.

By means of it, he approaches Agni’s beloved abode; moreover, he becomes possessed of cattle, and furthermore, by means of it, the sacrificer purifies himself. These two, Agni and Sūrya, were together in a common womb—the red iron—and then that Āditya rushed upward.

His semen fell away; Agni received it with his womb (the fire-pan). It burned him up; therefore iron burns lead, tin, fresh milk, and curdled milk. Therefore they offer this [oblation]. This is indeed the milk of cattle, namely rice and barley;
therefore they offer this. It must not be over-boiled, lest it dry up the semen; if it should overflow, there will be madness among his offspring.
This seed of that very Āditya is offered; it is impure, uncooked, and incomplete.
It must be offered when it is cooked, for then it is pure, fit for procreation, and productive as a pair.
Thus: [the text] has been emended; the edition reads *manyate*.
On this page (I,118):
"They milk with this vessel, or rather they sit down near it; for it does not spill from here or there, because it is fashioned by the Āryas, so that nothing may be spilled."
It has its rim turned upward for the sake of being with the gods; for this vessel, when made by a potter and shaped like a wheel, belongs to both the gods and the Asuras.
Wherever it might spill, one should pour water there; for water is peace, water is restoration, and water is medicine.
Indeed, wherever these waters reach her (the earth), there more excellent and more abundant plants are born. If she should break while being milked...

Having washed [the vessel] with another pot, [another cow] should be milked, for sacrifice is indeed the atonement for sacrifice. If [the milk] should spill while being placed on the fire, or while being taken down, or once taken down, or while being ladled out, or once ladled out, or if it has been carried forward before the offering—having poured it back again and having milked another [cow], [one should offer it], for sacrifice is indeed the atonement for sacrifice; having recited a verse addressed to Varuṇa...
One should offer with a verse addressed to Varuṇa; for Varuṇa seizes that part of the sacrifice which falters, and this is the atonement and the remedy.

It should not be sprinkled with water by one who desires splendor, by one who desires sacred luster (*brahmavarcasa*), or by one who is striving for success; likewise, by one who desires, "May a heroic son be born to me. For the *gharma* when unsprinkled is indeed splendor and sacred luster; [the sacrificer thus becomes] possessed of splendor and possessed of sacred luster.

He prospers and overcomes him who desires to overcome; a hero is born to him. One should offer with clarified butter for one whose [sacrificial substance] is not to be poured out, for this indeed is unpoured-out;

yet there is no expiation for what has been spilled, and moreover, he does not become possessed of cattle. This is the milk of cattle that is being offered; it places sorrow among the cattle, and its unappeased brilliance consumes the cattle.

Therefore, it should indeed be sprinkled with water; for that which one would sprinkle with water, Dhara would lead away by means of the milk-vessel's rinsing-water. That [which is thus prepared] is indeed neither water nor milk. Regarding this they say: "This spills when it is being carried away from the milking place; at that moment it has spilled, for its trees have vanished. Therefore, it should be sprinkled with water alone.
With a single small portion, Hara does not take away one's sorrow; cattle pacify it, for cattle are indeed *tejas* and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Water and milk are a pair; from a pair, indeed, offspring and cattle are produced. That is a pair;
therefore, from that very pair, the sacrificer is propagated with offspring and cattle. One whose [offering] it is should offer with boiled rice (*odana*).
He is fit for consecration, for he has been sprinkled, is tranquil, pure, united with a wife, and ready to procreate.
Prajāpati created offspring; he indeed created them through *tapas* alone. He, for his part, restrained speech; [for] *tapas* is indeed speech.

He who restrains his speech approaches this very creation of offspring; for the Agnihotra creates offspring from both sides, both from here and from there. Speech should be restrained when the sun has set, and also while the milk is being milked, and also when it is placed on the fire and while it is being ladled out—this is most appropriate.
You two are the source of arising.
Thus one should observe.
May I indeed increase through offspring and cattle.

Thus, for the sake of the creation of offspring and cattle, he thereby indeed causes it to flow for the sake of its purity. Regarding the Agnihotra, the husband and wife may fall into discord; the world of the sacrificer is the eastern one, and that of the wife is the western one.
If he were to remove the fire to the east, the sacrificer would die; if to the west, the wife [would die]. "Whom has he caused to heat the Gharma? so say the exponents of sacred knowledge.

They say that one should remove [the fire] only toward the north; [then] the two who do not take [the portions] consume [the fire], and he does not lead it to distress from this world before reaching a full lifespan.

He draws [the butter] four times; by that, he wins four-footed cattle. He offers twice; by that, he wins two-footed humans. If he should desire of someone, "May he prosper among his offspring according to seniority," he should draw the first portion full for him, then less, then less still; thus he prospers according to seniority.

"He prospers through offspring. Regarding this they say: "He indeed enters a lesser sacrificial rite; he has fewer offspring, fewer cattle, and less food to eat; he becomes worse off. One should fill the ladles to the brim at first, then more, then more, and the last one full, for the sake of surpassing the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "He indeed enters a greater sacrificial rite; he has more..."
He becomes more prosperous with offspring, more prosperous with cattle, and more prosperous with food; his son becomes the youngest.
However, if he should desire, "May they all be equal," he should pour out all [the portions] equally; then indeed they all become equal.
He should not set them down behind, for that is a departure from the sacrifice; wherever he pours them out, there he should set them down, and even further forward.

Or rather, this is a further transgression against the sacrifice for one who meditates upon it: that they heat [the coals] on the western fire while offering on the eastern one, and carry them across to the middle of the fire.

By that very act he gratifies him; moreover, this is the purifier of the Agnihotra, and he has indeed wiped it away from the western fire. From the western fire the eastern was created; they made him rest at this point, and therefore—
Having run forward, he offers the oblation.
He becomes possessed of offspring; *ardhukaḥ*. (Notes: *prajāṃ* is a correction and conjecture for the entire work;
*bhavati* is likely *bhavatīti*;
*ardhukaḥ* is a correction and conjecture for the entire work.)
Bestow life upon me.
Thus he sets it down; verily, he bestows life upon him.
Bestow radiance upon me.

Thus he deposits [the fuel-stick]; verily, he bestows splendor upon him. These plants, indeed, the Rudras anointed with poison; the cattle did not eat them. Those gods ran to Prajāpati for help. Prajāpati said, "Let me choose a boon; let there be a share for me. They said, "Choose it.
He said, "Let the fuel-stick (samidh) have me as its deity. Therefore, the fuel-stick belongs to Prajāpati.

For among the gods, this [earth] was chosen by her for the sake of desirable things; two kindling-sticks are to be made, for there are two oblations. Only one is to be made, for Prajāpati is indeed one.

When he is kindled in a single way, many oblations are indeed offered; he swept them away with fire, he made them palatable, and they were born again renewed. Now, indeed, all plants belong to the Agnihotra-performer who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
In that he places the kindling wood, he has made all plants into a self-offering for him.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.
Thus one should say before the Hotṛ: "This indeed is Brahman, this is Truth, this is Right; for there is no sacrifice without this; therefore it must be spoken thus."
Agni is light, light is Agni; svāhā!

Thus, by means of speech containing a fetus, he bestows a fetus; by means of paired speech, he causes a pair to be born. In that he offers both with speech and with a *yajus* formula, that is a pairing; in that he offers both silently and mentally, that is a pairing. The first oblation is indeed a fixed stump; the second oblation must be offered after passing over the first, for the second oblation serves to avoid making the fixed stump a failure.
They should be offered again for the advancement of the sacrifice; by the first oblation he wins cattle, and by the second, spiritual luster. The evening oblation belongs to Agni;

with it he pours forth seed, and that poured seed he places as an embryo within the night. By means of the morning [oblation] belonging to Sūrya, he causes it to be born. This [earth] is to be offered to, then the other [heaven], and again from below in the morning, for from below indeed is the birthplace of creatures.

For procreation is indeed generation; that belongs to Sūrya, so it must not be overlooked. It should be offered only toward the east and the west for the advancement of the sacrifice; he points it out toward the north.
O Jyotis, be gracious to the one who does not shine; O Dhūrta, homage be to you; O Rudra, be gracious.

"These indeed are the cruel bodies of Rudra, these are his names; by means of these he subjects cattle to himself. He pacifies them with their own share. In the evening he wipes downward; therefore, in the evening, one urinates downward.
He wipes upward toward the sky; therefore, one urinates upward toward the sky. The Agnihotra is, as it were, turned away from oneself, since it is performed in front."
He recites the Yajus formula for stability so that there shall be no neglect. He who knows the Vaiśvadeva portion of the Agnihotra, Paśupati does not harm him;

Paśupati does not harm his cattle. Sitting facing the east, he offers the oblation; thereby he gratifies the gods. Having offered, he leaves a remnant; he leaves a remnant for the sake of the sacrificer’s cattle. He directs it toward the north; thereby he propitiates Rudra.
He wipes [the vessel] toward the south; thereby he gratifies the plants and the ancestors. He eats [the remnants]; thereby he gratifies human beings.
He eats with his finger for the sake of giving it away [to the ancestors]; he should not let it pass between his teeth. If he were to let it pass between his teeth, serpents would seek to kill him;
thus he pacifies the serpents themselves for the sake of non-violence.
For the sake of the true being (saddharmatva).
*Corrections and conjectures for the entire work. Ed:*
Having given this, he should recite the Yajus formula: "Thou art Pūṣan. Pūṣan is indeed cattle; verily, he secures cattle for himself. This [fire] is indeed unappeased and unsatisfied;
it awaits the Puruṣamedha sacrifice. When he heats the Agnihotra-ladle, he makes the sacrificer himself the oblation.
It is not calmed; therefore, having heated the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the hand should be placed upon it, or the hand should be heated and placed upon the *agnihotra-havaṇī*.

By that very act he calms it, by that he gratifies it; being calmed and gratified, it does not harm him. He turns [the ladle] in this manner, for in this manner the sacrifice turns; moreover, he turns following the revolution of yonder sun. It must be offered.
"Should one not offer in the Gārhapatya fire? they deliberate; "For this [fire] is contemplative and parched; one must indeed offer in it."
O Agni, lord of the house, seated in the assembly, accept [this offering]; Svāhā!
Thus he should sacrifice; by that very act he pacifies him, by that he gratifies him, and furthermore, by that he makes him free from malice and not harsh.

Now, when, having offered the first oblation, he waits while about to offer the subsequent one, by that very act he pacifies him, by that he gratifies him, and furthermore, by that he makes him free from malice and not harsh. Now, as for the first oblation...

Having offered the northern oblation, when he is about to offer the next, he gazes back at it; by that very act he pacifies it and by that he gratifies it. Moreover, by that very act he makes it free from resentment and unrough. Furthermore, whatever is brought to his house, and whatever those sitting around this fire ask for, by that very act he pacifies it and by that he gratifies it; moreover, by that very act he makes it free from resentment and unrough.
He performs [it].
They milk two for the Agnihotra; for greater than the world of one who has milked only one is the world of an Agnihotra-performer when they milk two.

Thus the sacrificer conquers a greater world. Manu and Manāvī brought forth this [world] through union; when they milk with both the vessel and the milking-pail, it is from that very union that offspring is produced.
This:
*sajūr* Jātavedas, together with heaven and earth, enjoying this oblation, accept it; *svāhā*.
Thus he should offer; for this is his Jātavedas-form, and by its cruelty he harms cattle; he pacifies that very form of his with its own share, should it harm them excessively.
O Agni of well-formed body, accept this; Svāhā!
Thus he should offer; for this is his listening body, and by its cruelty he harms the cattle; he pacifies that very body of his with its own share, even if it should harm them excessively.

For twelve nights he should offer oblations every evening. Twelve nights indeed are the image of the year; Agni Vaiśvānara is the year. Those who have established the sacred fires kindle him with the New and Full Moon sacrifices. For them, the seasons are the logs; the largest embers are the months; the smallest embers are the half-months; the sparks are the days and nights; and that which is smoky is...
That light which is reddish belongs to the Viśvedevas; that which is dark-red belongs to Varuṇa; that which is golden belongs to Bṛhaspati;

that which is neither reddish nor golden belongs to Mitra; and that which, when the embers have subsided, flickers as if shining intensely—that is the mouth of the gods. Furthermore, they consider this to be the splendor of both yonder sun and of Agni; therefore, at that time—
One must offer the oblation; for when one places it down after it has been set out, he thereby strengthens it. This offering is indeed called "manifest" (āvis);

it goes to a state of manifestation among gods and men for him who knows thus. One should not offer over a kindling-stick (*samidh*), for that offering is unestablished, as if it were to fall away or slip off. It should be offered in such a way that it passes across the fire; for that [offering] is steady.

Therefore, the fuel for the *agnihotra* should be large. Indeed, he who has given much and sacrificed much, if he lets the fire go out, that [fuel] of his is imperishable. Those who have sacrificed well reach that world;
these, indeed, are the stars. When they say, "A light has fallen," or "A star has fallen," these very things fall down after having reached [the earth].

While they remain there, they enjoy these things according to their merit; but when they fall away from that world, then for him who has given much, who has sacrificed much, who offers the *agnihotra*, who performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, who performs the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, and who undertakes many sacrificial sessions (*satra*), this [merit] becomes inexhaustible and immeasurable. Indeed, the sacrifice surpasses the one who merely sacrifices by means of these two.

"He should be burned by both fires; for he ascends after his own sacrifice. "He should be burned by the western fire," "or by the eastern one"—thus they deliberate. Having brought both together, he should be burned between them; that is most appropriate.
One should take hold [of him] at night, for the night belongs to the Asuras; with light indeed he overcomes the darkness. By day, indeed, he becomes established in this world.
That world shines forth for him who knows thus.
vīva: FN Corrections and Conjectures to the Entire Work. FN Corrections and Conjectures to the Entire Work. Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ.
Thus he should speak before the oblation: "It is for these worlds that he places these bricks; for the attainment of the heavenly world.
When he offers in the evening, by that he wins a thousand wish-fulfilling cows; when he offers in the morning, by that [he wins] another thousand;
and when his fire is established, by that [he wins] another thousand. By means of the Agniṣṭoma, he conquers the kingdom of Yama, and the kingdom of Soma.

Through the Ukthya one attains the sovereignty of Sūrya; through the Ṣoḍaśin, self-rule (svārājya); and through the Atirātra, these [other] realms. Indeed, by means of all these, Indra became everything;

he who sacrifices with them becomes all this. He who knows thus becomes all this. One is a sacrificer of oblations (haviṣmant), another a sacrificer to the gods (devayājī), and another a sacrificer of a thousand (sahasrayājī). He who performs the Agnihotra is the sacrificer of oblations; he who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices...
He who sacrifices is a sacrificer to the gods; he who sacrifices with the Cāturmāsya offerings is a thousand-sacrificer. Indeed, all sacrificial rites are contained within the Agnihotra.
He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, secures for himself all sacrificial rites.

[Page I,125] All the Prayamedhas, together with Brahmā, knew [the truth]; they perfected themselves through the Agnihotra. Among them, one offered oblations three times, another twice, and another once. They asked him who offered three times: "For whom did you offer?"

Thus he spoke: "This [sacrifice] is indeed threefold—for Agni, for Prajāpati, and for Sūrya. Then they asked him who had sacrificed twice, "For whom did you sacrifice? He replied, "This is indeed twofold—for Agni and Prajāpati in the evening, and for Sūrya and Prajāpati in the morning. Then they asked him who had sacrificed once, "For whom [did you sacrifice]?"
"Have you offered? he asked. He replied, "In one way indeed, this was for Prajāpati alone.
Among them, he who offered twice prospered, while the others attained kinship with him. He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, prospers;
his kinsmen attain kinship with him. The Agnihotra should be offered at the onset of night and in the morning after dawn, [for the sake of] the mature embryos.
He procreates; regarding this they say, "The Agnihotra of one who does not offer it at nightfall indeed falls away. If he should think, "I have passed over the season," [he should perform the rite].
Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ.
Thus one should speak before the Hotṛ; by that alone he does not omit anything in between.
To the faults of the bladder, homage, svāhā!

Thus he should offer; for one does not indeed overstep the season. "Should it be offered or should it not be offered?"—thus they deliberate. If the sun should rise upon one whose *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, it must certainly be offered to Agni for support and protection; however, [if unoffered], it frustrates procreation.
If he should think, "I have overstepped the season," [he should offer].
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.
Thus one should speak before the offering; by that alone, one does not miss anything in between.
Bhūr!
At the break of dawn, homage, Svāhā!
Thus he should offer; verily he does not overstep the season. As they offer for one who hates craftsmen, so is his offering made.

If the sun should set upon one whose fire has not been lifted up, a learned Brāhmaṇa should lift it up; with the entire Veda he thus lifts him up. He should run toward the Agnihotra; with its own portion he leads it forth, and indeed with its own portion he leads it forth.

The *vara* (choice) fulfills; the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial gift) causes him to move away from all directions by means of that *vara*. For one whose two fires both go out at sunset, or for one whose two go out at sunrise, the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is indeed the expiation. Just as there are two tracks on a road, so are the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); just as there is the space between them, so is the Fire-oblation (*agnihotra*). Thus it is for the one who maintains the Fire-oblation and the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

"The heavenly world shines forth; they consume the other oblations and dwell [therein]. But why do they not fast for the *agnihotra*? so ask the exponents of the Veda. "For he eats meat continuously, in unlimited measure, without restraint, and approaches his wife. Therefore they do not fast. One should observe the vow of the sacrificial animal (*paśu-vrata*); for animals exist in silence. Thus they say.

When he approaches his wife silently, he becomes even more pure; he should approach her after uttering the *hiṃ* sound, for it is in this manner that cattle approach for the sake of purity. They deliberate: "Should the Agnihotra be concluded, or should it not be concluded?
If he were to conclude it, he should offer a blade of grass after anointing it; for that is the conclusion of the Agnihotra. Regarding this, they say: when...
"When one is defeated, when one dies, or when one meets with misfortune, then the Agnihotra should be concluded"—this [view] is not to be followed;

for Prajāpati encompassed this [earth] with his mind. This earth is indeed the altar of the Agnihotra; this [earth] is the *upayāma*; the plants are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); the dewdrops are the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*); the quarters are the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); whatever is added [to the fire] is the fuel-wood (*idhma*); and the sacrificer is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
While being led forward, one should stand thus, for the sacrificial post is like this for prosperity. Indeed, this Agnihotra is extended from the middle of the sacrifice;

therefore, the performer of the Agnihotra who is also performing the New and Full Moon sacrifices gives everything belonging to the sacrificial grass (barhis). For that which is to be offered in the Agnihotra is given from the very center of the sacrifice.
Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should the Agnihotra be offered by a Rājanya, or should it not be offered?"
This kṣatriya is, as it were, raw; he indeed practices much that is unfit for sacrifice and impure, and he overcomes the Brāhmaṇa with food that is not to be eaten.
Therefore, the Agnihotra of a kṣatriya should not be offered. The Agnihotra is indeed the *ṛta* and the truth, and the Brāhmaṇa is the *ṛta* and the truth;
therefore, it should be offered by the Brāhmaṇa alone. Moreover, they should bring it to his house first for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa.

Thus his Agnihotra becomes indeed an ascetic practice (dhuta); moreover, for one who would act as if it were the cosmic order (ṛta) and as if it were truth (satya), the offering should be made for the sake of continuity.
The New and Full Moon sacrifices.
(FN emended. Ed: darśaparṇamāsau.)
The *pruṣvās* (drops);

the *prokṣaṇīs* (sprinkling waters). If a cow set loose for the *agnihotra* should sit down, one should give her to that person whose food one would not eat; for she brings misfortune to the sacrificer through lack of endurance.

He sits down together with her; thus he makes amends for her. But thereafter, no one in his house should eat; if he were to eat, he would meet with misfortune. If, while the Agnihotra has not yet been offered, the former fire should go out, he should carry it forth along with the fire and the Agnihotra;
verily, he leads it forth by means of its own portion, and moreover, he prospers it by means of its own portion. Then he should address it with a mantra.
From this very place, Agni Jātavedas was first born from these wombs;
may he, knowing all things, carry the oblations to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Anuṣṭubh meters.
These indeed are its wombs; he thus causes it to be born from its own wombs.
Rejoice for the sake of food, wealth, power, splendor, vigor, and progeny.
Thus he wins these very things; moreover, he truly causes him to delight.
You are the sovereign; you are the self-sovereign; sit upon the good seat.
Thus, he settles it in a comfortable seat.
But may the two springs of Sarasvatī flow forth for us.

Thus, the *ṛc* and *sāman* are indeed the two springs of Sarasvatī; by means of them he protects him and by means of them he brings him to fulfillment. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat and a pap of barley to Varuṇa for one whose first fire goes out before his *agnihotra* has been offered. Verily, darkness seizes the sacrifice of him whose first fire goes out before his *agnihotra* has been offered.
In that [he offers] to Agni Jyotiṣmat, he prospers his sacrifice by means of light itself. Night belongs to Varuṇa;

in that [he offers] to Varuṇa, he rescues his sacrifice from Varuṇa himself. If another fire should go out after the Agnihotra has been offered, one should take it out from that very place toward the east, settle it, and offer the Agnihotra; then one should address it with a mantra.
"May you two be of one mind, of one dwelling, of one thought, and stainless"—with this he makes them of one mind for the non-injury of the sacrificer.

Regarding these two, those who discourse on sacred knowledge say: "No single crooked thing can encompass two tigers. He whose fire is carried out from another fire should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnimat; for such a person creates strife among the deities.
For him whose fire they lift up from the fire, he produces for himself more numerous deities through that which is for Agni Agnimat; he becomes more prosperous.
Agni has followed the vanguard of the dawns; Jātavedas, the first, has followed the days.
He has followed the rays of the sun in many places, and he has stretched himself across heaven and earth.
Thus he should consecrate [the fire] for one whose *agnihotra* has not been offered when the sun rises; by thus consecrating it, he recovers it again.

Regarding this they say: "He causes that world to rise up together with the sacrificer's offspring and cattle; therefore, even one who has maintained the sacred fires for a long time becomes destitute of cattle. Therefore, he should worship [the fire].
Be secure right here; do not abandon me, [the son] of such-and-such a lineage.
Thus, in this very world, he supports him; the sacrificer prospers along with his offspring and cattle.
He should offer a *caru* oblation to Mitra and a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya for one whose *agnihotra* has not yet been offered when the sun rises.
Mitra indeed seizes the sacrifice of him whose *agnihotra* has not been offered when the sun rises, for the day is Mitra.

Through Mitra himself, Maitra protects his sacrifice from above; and because it belongs to Sūrya, he thereby causes the sacrifice to prosper from the front by means of that very Āditya. If the sun should rise while the Agnihotra has not yet been offered, the husband and wife, having kindled the fire and restrained their speech, should remain waiting for the entire day; they should offer the evening Agnihotra with two cows, [offering] both [the milk of the evening and the morning].

Thus he bestows upon him his share, both that of the evening and that of the morning. For when a man is ill, people say of him, "Does he eat, or does he not eat? If they say, "He does not eat," then indeed he has partaken of the immortal.
When he neither eats nor speaks, they have partaken of the immortal along with him; through austerity, they recover him again for Agni Vratapati.

"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds; Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods. He [Agni] approaches him with his own portion; he causes him to undertake the vow. For one whose fire should go out, having rekindled it at the very place where it went out and having settled it, he should perform the *agnihotra* offering.
Indeed, when the fire goes out, Agni departs; from the very place where he goes out, he brings him back again."

One whose fire goes out should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the maker of the path). He whose fire goes out indeed goes astray from the path; Agni is the maker of the path among the gods. He approaches him with his own portion, and he leads him back onto the path. An ox is the sacrificial fee, for it carries one along the path. [He should also offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Śuci (the Pure).

One should offer [an oblation] for him whose fire becomes mixed with that used for cooking; for that which is used for cooking is indeed very impure. By offering to Agni Śuci (the Pure), he makes that [fire] pure and fit for sacrifice. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat (the Earth-possessing) for one who, having established the sacred fires, has his house burnt by fire; for Agni, as the earth-possessing, overflows his house and thus burns it further.
With the offering for Agni Kṣāmavat, he pacifies by means of his portion that very body of his which is the beloved *kṣāmā*;
thus Agni does not burn his house in the future. If one's fire should go out, it should be churned from those very embers;
thus he produces it from its own womb. If such embers are not available, [it should be churned] from the ashes with the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*).

Having touched it, it should be churned; thus he produces him from his own womb. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat, for one whose fire goes out. Indeed, no covering is placed over this [fire], yet it goes out.
The plants are indeed purifying (pāvaka); verily, he provides the purifying plants as its portion for the sake of procreation.
The thirty-three threads which extend this [sacrifice] and bestow this sacrifice with ambrosia—with those we close whatever gap there may be here. Svāhā! May the sacrifice go to the gods.

Thus he should offer if either a cart or a chariot should pass between [the fires]. For these are indeed the threads of the sacrifice; these are the deities. He has severed them, and now he joins them together. Regarding this, the Dākṣāyaṇas used to say: "He has severed the threads; let him drive a cow back. For the cow is sacrificial and fit for the altar. [He recites: "Viṣṇu strode across this [world]," [and offers] upon the footprint.
He makes it swell; indeed, he performs the stride of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice. He sprinkles along the waters for the sake of pacification.
The milk in the cow is for Rudra; when released [into the vessel] it is for Vāyu; while being milked it is for the Aśvins; once milked it is for Soma; when placed on the fire it is for Varuṇa;
when taken up into the ladle it is for Mitra; when forming drops it is for the Maruts; when rising up it is for Pūṣan; when trickling out it is for Sarasvatī;

when being carried back it is for Viṣṇu; when removed from the fire it is for Heaven; when being lifted up it is for Tvaṣṭṛ; when lifted up it is for Dhātṛ; and when being poured out it is for Viśvakarman.

The Sāvitra [offering] when raised; the Dyāvāpṛthivīya while being carried forward; the Aindrāgna when thrown into the fire; the Prājāpatya when it has been placed near; the Vaiśvadeva when the fuel-stick has been added; and the [oblation] to the All-gods when it has been offered.

Intelligence is the sacrificial ladle, thought is the clarified butter, speech is the altar, reflection is the sacred grass, insight is the fire, understanding is the *agnīdh* priest, the lord of speech is the *hotṛ* priest, mind is the *upavaktṛ* priest, breath is the oblation, the *sāman* chant is the *adhvaryu* priest; go to Indra, *svāhā*! Earth is the *hotṛ* priest, heaven...

Tvaṣṭṛ is the Adhvaryu, Agni is the Hotṛ, Mitra is the Upavaktṛ. O Lord of Speech, with the most powerful vigor of speech you sacrifice for the sake of the lord of the sacrifice; bestow what is desirable upon him. The Lord of Speech has drunk the Soma; he has generated Indra for power.
Let the bright Soma drink of the Soma; let the bright one drink of the bright. These Soma-draughts of yours, O Indra—blazing, full of milk, and hearing the call—are [for] Agni.

The Hotṛ is the Aśvins, the Adhvaryus; Rudra is the Agnīdh; Bṛhaspati is the Upavaktṛ. O Vācaspati, you who provide the two-fold name, we worship your name; do you provide us with our name. Vācaspati has drunk the Soma; may he bestow manly vigor upon us. Let Soma drink of Soma;
let the bright one drink of the bright. These Somas of yours, O Indra—well-cooked, mixed with milk, and heard at the invocation—are for the great oblation.
The Hotṛ is the one with true oblation; the Adhvaryu is he of inconceivable luster; the Agnīdh is he of inconceivable mind; the Upavaktṛ is the unassailable and the unassailable invoker;
the Udgātṛ is Ayāsya. O Vidha, whose name is Vidha, we pay homage to your name; you, Vidha, [pay homage] to our name.
May the thread of the gods not be severed, nor that of men. Homage to Mother Earth!

Agni [is honored] with *yajus* formulas; Savitṛ with *stomas*; Indra with *uktha* and *madas*; Bṛhaspati with the meters (*chandāṃsi*); Aditi and the Waters with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); the Ādityas with the clarified butter (*ājya*); the Maruts with the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds; Viṣṇu with consecration (*dīkṣā*) and austerity (*tapas*); and Mitra and Varuṇa [with the *prauga*].

The Aśvins [are associated] with the *dhiṣṇya* hearths; Tvaṣṭṛ with the *āśira* mixture; Pūṣan with the fuel-stick (*samidh*); Vāc, the wife of Vāyu, with the *svāhā*-utterances; Pathyā, the wife of Pūṣan, with the earth; Agni’s [is] the army; Indra’s [is] the lowing cow (*dhenā*); Bṛhaspati’s [is] the *gāyatrī*; that of the Vasus [is] the *triṣṭubh*; that of the Rudras [is] the *jagatī*; that of the Ādityas [is] the *anuṣṭubh*; Mitra’s [is] the *virāj*; Varuṇa’s [is] the *paṅkti*; and Viṣṇu’s [is] the consecration (*dīkṣā*), while Soma’s [is] the [consecration].

Prajāpati alone was here. He desired, "May I, having become the sacrifice, create offspring. He fashioned himself as the sacrifice consisting of the Daśahotṛ. He made thought his offering-spoon, intention his clarified butter, speech his altar, and the sacred study his sacrificial grass.
Having divided himself tenfold and formed a pair, he sought a dwelling place. That dwelling place, indeed, was the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) consisting of the threefold set.
He gazed with them and created offspring; he drew up the first fortnight consisting of fifteen [days], and by it he created the gods.

Those gods swelled upwards; he who knows thus swells upwards. He drew down the latter fortnight consisting of fifteen [days], and by it he created the Asuras. Those Asuras collapsed headlong; his rival collapses, he who knows thus.

By day he created the gods, and by night the Asuras. Those gods became fair, while the Asuras became dark. By means of truth he created the gods, and by means of untruth the Asuras. Those gods became truth, while the Asuras became untruth. With his right hand he created the gods, and with his left the Asuras. Those gods became vigorous, while the Asuras were weak. Thereupon the gods prevailed.

His enemies were defeated; he who knows thus becomes [victorious] in himself, and his rival is defeated. He thought, "Where shall I offer? Prajāpati did not find that place where he might have offered, for there was nothing else for him to offer than his own vital breath (*prāṇa*).
He perceived Indra alone as the abode within himself. He said, "Go to Indra, svāhā! and he exhaled his vigor. Indeed, it is vigor.
Breath is vigor; Indra is vigor; he offered vigor itself as the oblation of vigor.
It occurs thus:

"Those very Caturhotṛs sat down with Soma as their householder, thinking, 'We shall procreate Indra. Pṛthivī was the Hotṛ, Dyau was the Adhvaryu, Tvaṣṭṛ was the Agnīdh, and Mitra was the Upavaktṛ. They indeed drew these two cups [of Soma] with the words, 'O Lord of Speech, of speech...'"
"With the most fully gathered vigor, you shall win what is desirable for the lord of the sacrifice; bring it to yourself! Thus they chose the twenty-first as their abode;

by means of that, they generated Indra. Having generated Indra, they said, "Let us go to heaven. Then the five Hotṛ-priests sat down with Varuṇa as their Gṛhapati: Agni was the Hotṛ, the Aśvins were the Adhvaryus, Rudra was the Agnīdh, and Bṛhaspati was the Upavaktṛ.

With the words, "O Aśvins," they took up the Pañcahotṛ cup. These two indeed drew these cups: "O Lord of Speech, you who have many forms, we worship your name; may you worship our name. They perceived the Triṇava as their abode; having made it a bridge, they ascended to heaven.
With it, they released the cattle and led them to the deities. They led a horse to Yama; half of its vital power departed.
He saw this means of acceptance.

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. For Yama I receive you; Varuṇa gives you to me. May I attain immortality. May there be joy for the giver;
may there be joy for me, the receiver.
Thus he deposited half of his sensory power; he who, knowing this, accepts a horse, deposits half of his sensory power.
But for him who accepts it without knowing this, half of his sensory power departs. They led a cow to Rudra;
a third of his sensory power departed from him. He saw this means of acceptance.
Varuṇa gives you to me, to Rudra; may I attain immortality. May there be joy for the giver, and joy for me, the receiver.
Thus he deposited a third part of his vital power; indeed, he who, knowing this, accepts a cow, deposits a third part of his vital power.

But he who accepts it without knowing this—of him a third part of his vital power departs. When they presented gold to Agni, a fourth part of his vital power departed from him; he then beheld this means of acceptance.
The sense-organ departed:
"Varuṇa gives thee to me for Agni; may I attain immortality. May there be joy for the giver, and joy for me, the receiver."
Thus he bestowed the fourth [part] of his power upon the gold; he who, knowing this, accepts gold, bestows the fourth part of his power upon it.
But he who accepts it without knowing this, the fourth part of his power departs from him. They brought a garment for Bṛhaspati;
the fifth part of his power departed from him. He saw this means of acceptance.

"The skillful ones cut out the limbs; they stretched out the prayers; they wove them for Bṛhaspati. Varuṇa gives thee to me; may I attain immortality through him. May there be joy for the giver, and joy for me, the receiver. Thus he deposited the fifth part of the sense-power. He who, knowing this, accepts a garment, deposits the fifth part of the sense-power;
but from him who accepts it without knowing this, the fifth part of his sense-power departs. [He said: "To Uttāna Āṅgirasa, thou didst breathe forth."
Through this, the sixth sense-organ departed from him; he saw this means of reception.
Varuṇa gives you to me, the son of Aṅgiras, Utāna; may I attain immortality. May there be joy for the giver, and joy for me, the receiver.

Thus he bestowed the sixth sense; he who, knowing this, accepts [a gift] while not breathing, bestows the sixth sense. But for him who accepts without knowledge, the sixth sense departs from him. "Who gave this to whom? Desire gave it to desire. Desire is the giver, desire is the receiver. For desire I accept you; O Desire, this is yours. [Page I, 135]
