Thus, the ocean is indeed desire, and the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) is desire; by means of desire itself, one accepts the sacrificial gift. Verily, he who knows that deity who first brought the sacrificial gift becomes worthy of the sacrificial gift; he brings the sacrificial gift.
As they were departing for heaven, they said, "Give us a sacrificial post from here; by what means shall you recognize us right here?

They, the seven *hotṛ*s, sat down with Aryaman as their householder: Mahāhavis was the *hotṛ*, Satyahavis the *adhvaryu*, Acittapājas the *agnīdh*, Acittamanas the *upavaktṛ*, and Anādhṛṣya and Apratidhṛṣya were the two *abhigara*s.
Ayāsya was the Udgātṛ. They indeed took this cup for him, saying: "O Vidhi, we worship your name; you are Vidhi, our name.

They found the thirty-threefold abode; by means of that they brought this [universe] into harmony. By the Saptahotṛ and the thirty-threefold [stoma], this world is continuous—this which gods and men hand over to one another, namely, the vital breath.

The *daśahotṛ* is indeed sight; the *caturhotṛ* is hearing; the *pañcahotṛ* is speech; and the *saptahotṛ* is the self. The *agnihotra* is the *daśahotṛ*; the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are the *caturhotṛ*; the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*) are the *pañcahotṛ*; and the Soma sacrifice is the *saptahotṛ*. The *agnihotra* is offered for the sake of life; he who knows this attains a full lifespan. The new- and full-moon sacrifices are performed for the sake of sight.
For one who knows thus, there is no harm to the eye; the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are performed for the sake of the ear—for one who knows thus, there is no harm to the ear;
the Soma sacrifice is performed for the sake of speech and for the self—for one who knows thus, there is no harm to speech nor to the self.
Prajāpati, indeed, though being only one, is the greatest sharer of the *vyāhṛtis* as the ten-fold Hotṛ; being only one, he is the greatest.
He who knows thus becomes radiant. For the sake of splendor, the Full Moon sacrifice is performed. The Brāhmaṇa has Soma as his deity and the Gāyatrī as his metre;

Agni is of the Gāyatrī metre. Thus, he places these two deities together for him; no one else has power over his acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*). For the sake of long life, the New Moon sacrifice is performed. Indeed, he is drawn near to death [at that time], yet he attains a full lifespan if he knows thus, for the sake of the heavenly world.
"To whom does the gentle sacrifice go when it is offered? To the heavenly world, for he who knows thus. One should touch the Agnihotra when it has been ladled out with the *daśahotr* formula;

for by means of the *daśahotr*, the gods created the Agnihotra, and having been created, they seized it once it was produced. One should touch the New and Full Moon sacrifices with the *caturhotr* formula; for by means of the *caturhotr*, the gods created the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and having been created, they seized them.

Having been created, he should touch the Cāturmāsya sacrifices with the Pañcahotṛ formula; for the gods created the Cāturmāsya sacrifices by means of the Pañcahotṛ, and having been created, they were touched once they had been produced. Having been created, he should touch the Soma sacrifice with the Saptahotṛ formula; for the gods created the Soma sacrifice by means of the Saptahotṛ, and having been created, it was touched once it had been produced. He should recite the Daśahotṛ formula.

Before the *sāmidhenī* verses, Prajāpati is indeed the *daśahotṛ*; the *sāmidhenīs* are the mouth of the sacrifice; verily, he thus places this couple at the mouth of his sacrifice. He should recite the *caturhotṛ* formula before the *prayāja* offerings; for by means of the *caturhotṛ*, the gods generated Indra; verily, he thus generates Indra in this sacrifice, and he sacrifices with a sacrifice accompanied by Indra. [He should recite] the *pañcahotṛ*.

One should recite the Pañcahotṛ formula before the oblations; by means of the Pañcahotṛ, the gods created cattle and deprived the Asuras of them. He creates cattle for himself and deprives his rival of them. One should recite the Saptahotṛ formula before the after-offerings (anuyājas); by means of the Saptahotṛ, the gods went to heaven; he goes to heaven himself. One should recite the Daśahotṛ formula before the Bahiṣpavamāna chant; Prajāpati...

The *daśahotṛ* is indeed the beginning of the sacrifice, the *bahiṣpavamāna*; he thus places this couple at the very beginning of the sacrifice. He should recite the *caturhotṛ* before the *ājya* chants; he should recite the *pañcahotṛ* before the midday *pavamāna*; he should recite the *saptahotṛ* before the *ārbhava-pavamāna*.
By means of the *saptahotṛ*, the gods went to heaven; verily, he goes to heaven himself.

He who knows the Caturhotṛs who are to be gratified at each pressing (anusavana) prospers with offspring and cattle. These indeed are the Caturhotṛs to be gratified at each pressing: they are the learned Brāhmaṇas. He gratifies them alone;
they, being gratified, gratify him in turn with offspring and cattle.
*acittapājā*: [Note:
emended; edition reads *acittapājā*. Cf. 1.9.1:131.11.]
In the house: FN emended. Ed: gṛhe. The seven-hotṛ sacrifice: FN emended. Ed: saptahotāraṃ.
The Saptahotṛ [rite].

He who is not propagated with offspring or cattle should, for twelve days, put on a coarse garment, drink hot water, and sleep on the ground. By performing austerity, Prajāpati indeed fashioned himself, created a pair, and [was] propagated with offspring and cattle.

And he does not procreate, for this [fire] is indeed unordained and without a mate; therefore it does not procreate. Having performed austerity and having fashioned himself, having made a mate, he procreates through offspring and cattle. Prajāpati is indeed the Daśahotṛ; Prajāpati is greater than the oblation (homa), therefore they do not offer that. Having breathed out, one breathes in; thus one offers the out-breath (apāna) into the in-breath (prāṇa). [This applies to] one who is engaged in battle.

One should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Caturhotṛ formula. Having prepared the clarified butter taken in four ladlings, one should recite the Caturhotṛ formula; one should offer one half with the first part of the formula and the other half with the latter part. By means of the Caturhotṛ, the gods generated Indra. In whichever battle Indra is present, he indeed conquers. Verily, by this [rite], one has generated Indra for oneself in battle; thus one conquers the battle. [This is for one] desiring offspring.

One should cause him to sacrifice with the Caturhotṛ formula. Having prepared the clarified butter taken in four ladlings, he should recite the Caturhotṛ; he should offer one half with the first portion and the other half with the latter. By means of the Caturhotṛ, the gods indeed generated Indra; it generates offspring for this man. Yet another is not born after him; however, he becomes full of splendor, for he generates him with his entire vital power. [This applies] for one who desires cattle.

One should cause him for whom one performs the sacrifice with the Pañcahotṛ to offer; having prepared the clarified butter taken in four ladlings, he should recite the Pañcahotṛ formula. He should sacrifice half with the first portion and half with the latter. By means of the Pañcahotṛ, the gods indeed created cattle; thus he creates cattle for himself. One who has rivals should cause him to sacrifice with the Pañcahotṛ; having prepared the clarified butter taken in four ladlings, he should recite the Pañcahotṛ formula, sacrificing half with the first portion...
One should offer the first half with the *pañcahotṛ* formula; for by means of the *pañcahotṛ*, the gods overcame the Asuras. He thus causes his evil rival to be overcome.
For one who desires heaven, he should perform the sacrifice with the *pañcahotṛ*. Having prepared the clarified butter in four ladlings, he should recite the *pañcahotṛ* formula.
He should offer one half with the first part of the formula and the other half with the latter part. By means of the *pañcahotṛ*, the gods went to heaven; verily, he goes to heaven himself.
If one should consider himself worse off after the completion of a sacrifice, one should have him perform the Saptahotra sacrifice. By means of the Saptahotra, the gods indeed accomplished this;
they attained it completely, and quickly he becomes just as he was before when he performed the sacrifice.

The exponents of Brahman say: "Since there is one sacrifice consisting of the *caturhotṛ* formulas, why then are all [of them] called *caturhotṛ*s? Indeed, these are four sacrifices; they have four *hotṛ* priests, and that is the reason for the *caturhotṛ* nature of the *caturhotṛ* formulas.
One of the four should not eat for a year; that is the vow. The *caturhotṛ* formulas are indeed food; he who knows thus becomes possessed of food.
Now, if one who has studied the Vedas should find that [the knowledge] does not come to him, he should go to the forest, make a Brāhmaṇa his witness, and recite the Caturhotṛ formulas.

This is indeed the extraction (*udaraṇa*) of the Brahman, namely the Caturhotṛ formulas; the Brāhmaṇa is the witness. At the end, through the witness, the Brahman becomes manifest (*āviḥ*). He causes him to reach that which has become manifest and known. Now, if two should dispute, saying "I..."
"I know more, I know more!"—he indeed knows more who knows the *caturhotṛ* formulas.
For the *caturhotṛ*s are the womb of the sacrifice; the sacrifice was fashioned from the *caturhotṛ*s, and it does not harm him when it is defective.
One desiring food should recite the *caturhotṛ*s on the tenth day; for the *caturhotṛ*s are food, and the tenth day is the end. Having reached the very end, he attains the eating of food.
He wins this; for at this time, that [part] of his remains unapplied and unobtained, and he now applies it and obtains it.

This earth is indeed the Queen of Serpents (Sarparājñī), and the Caturhotṛ formulas are her hymn (uktha). When the Hotṛ recites them, he recites in accordance with what has been chanted (stuta); for there is no chanting that is not followed by recitation.

The gods and the Asuras were in conflict; they proceeded performing the sacrifice in exactly the same manner. Whatever the gods did, the Asuras did that too, and thus they did not attain distinction. Those gods said, "Come, let us extend this sacrifice over the heads of the Asuras. Taking it up with these [verses], they stepped forward: Agni with the *yajus* formulas.
With the *stomas* Savitṛ, with the *ukthas* and *madas* Indra, and with the *chandases* Bṛhaspati—they wove that [sacrifice] across and above the Asuras.

The Asuras could not follow that sacrifice of theirs; by it they drove them away. Thereupon the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows thus weaves his sacrifice across and above his rival; he prevails in himself and his rival is defeated.

He becomes an enemy; he should offer with these very [verses] at a sacrifice performed for a rival. At each of the four [sessions], he should offer after the *anvākhyāna*—in the morning before the *prātaranuvāka*. For the sacrifice is as great as this; he appropriates the entire sacrifice, and thus he becomes one who possesses the sacrifice, while the others become those without a sacrifice.
He should offer with these very [verses] before the initiation (*dīkṣā*); for this is the initiation in its direct form; having seized that very [initiation] by means of these, he offers.
One should offer thus before the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). This [fire] is indeed the manifest twelve-day sacrifice;

having seized it, one should touch the guest-offering (*ātithya*) with these [verses]. Thus, by means of the sacrifice itself, one has seized the sacrifice. To the south, the Asuras conquered the sacrifice from the gods;
they fled northward together with the wives and entered the *agnīdhra* shed. Having driven them out along with the wives, [the gods] were ashamed of them.

The Asuras turned back; rising up from that very place, they conquered them. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows this prospers in himself, while his rival is defeated. His rival does not ascend to his houses or his cattle;
rather, he who knows this ascends to the houses and cattle of his rival. These [same verses] belong to the Āgnīdhra.

One should recite [the invitatory verse]; the Āgnīdh indeed sacrifices for the Pātnīvata offering. Satisfied, the wife (patnī) conceives seed; he is procreated with offspring and cattle. One should offer with these very [verses] between Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives (patnīs). He who desires offspring [should do so] for a year; for Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives are indeed a couple. Verily, he has impelled Tvaṣṭṛ toward this couple for the sake of procreation.

Therefore, from that very pair, the sacrificer is procreated with offspring and cattle; he finds offspring, and a hero is born to him. Even if, while offering for a year, he does not find [offspring], it is not to be disregarded.
For one who is ashamed [of his conduct]: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan,
a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, clotted curds (āmikṣā) for the Viśve Devās, a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth, and the whey-offering (vājina) for the Vājins.
An offering on eight potsherds for Agni; a pap for Soma; an offering on eight potsherds for Savitṛ; a pap for Sarasvatī; a pap for Pūṣan;
an offering on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni; curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Maruts; curdled milk for Varuṇa; a single-potsherd offering for Ka; and the whey of the Vājins.
In the morning, an offering on eight potsherds for Agni Anīkavant; at midday, a pap for the Sāṃtapana Maruts; [and] for the Maruts...

For the householders, [there is] boiled rice cooked in the milk of all [the cows] in the evening; [there is] the scrapings of Indra's [oblation]; for the sporting Maruts, [an offering] together with the rays on seven potsherds; [there is] an offering on eight potsherds for Agni; a pap for Soma; an offering on eight potsherds for Savitṛ;
a pap for Sarasvatī; a pap for Pūṣan; an offering on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni; a pap for Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; and one for Viśvakarman.

A cake on one potsherd for Agni; a cake on eight potsherds for Soma; a pap for Savitṛ; a pap for Sarasvatī; a pap for Pūṣan; a barley-gruel for Vāyu; or curdled milk for Indra Śunāsīra; a cake on twelve potsherds; a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya; a cake on six potsherds; parched grains; a stirred drink; cakes for each person; and additionally, a pap for Aditi.

O Agni, accept the office of the Hotṛ; accept the office of the messenger. The sacrifice has stood upright. May Heaven and Earth favor us. Be the maker of good offerings for Indra and for the gods. Accepting this oblation of clarified butter, enjoy it—*svāhā*!
We invoke the Praghāsya Maruts, the bearers of the sacrifice, who are in harmony with the *karambha* offering.

O Indra, O God, be with us here in the battles; for you, O Mighty One, are our protection. Even the great song of the worshipper, rich in oblations, praises the Maruts, the bounteous ones who move in youthful vigor.

Whatever sin we have committed in the village, whatever in the forest, whatever in the assembly, or whatever in the senses; whatever offense we have committed, or whatever we have done in secret— that [sin] rests upon the mind of one person alone, and upon the dharma of one person alone.
You are the expiation for all that evil.
Performers of ritual action, having performed the work with a voice full of bliss for the sake of the gods, go to your home, O bounteous givers.
O ladle, fly away full; fly back again well-filled.
Like two merchants bargaining for goods, O Śatakratu, let us exchange food and strength.
Give to me; I give to you. Take from me; I have taken from you.
Gather it back like a loan; who indeed would take back what has been given?
O ancestors, rejoice here!
O Vasu, O Maghavan, may we gladden you who are so beautiful to behold.
Now indeed, with your chariot-seat full, being praised, you go according to your will; O Indra, yoke now your two bay steeds.
Whatever harm we have done to the mid-air, to the earth, or to the sky, or to our mother or our father—
may Agni Gārhapatya, Jātavedas, deliver us from that sin and from our evil deed.
The fathers have rejoiced; homage to you, O fathers, for food; homage to you, O fathers, for strength; homage to you, O fathers, for vigor; homage to you, O fathers, for sap;
homage to you, O fathers, for that which is life; homage to you, O fathers, for that which is terrible; *svadhā* to you, O fathers, homage, homage to you, O fathers.
This is your father; these are our living ones; may we, being alive, exist here among you who are alive.
Depart, O Soma-loving Fathers, by the deep and ancient paths;
bestow upon us wealth that is auspicious, and grant us riches consisting of all heroic sons.
By this manifestation, generating mighty deeds— for he is indeed the glowing one, the wide path for the seeker—
he has come forward as the supporter of the first of the honeyed draught, when he extended his own body within his body.
Turning toward us, they have eaten and rejoiced; the dear ones have shaken themselves free.
The self-luminous sages have offered praise with their newest hymn: "Now, O Indra, yoke your two bay steeds!"
We invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa hymn and with the prayers of the fathers.
May our mind return to us again for the sake of will, for skill, and for life, so that we may long behold the sun.
May our fathers and the divine folk grant us back our mind;
may we be united with the company of the living.
O Agni, may we today accomplish that [work] for you with our hymns— as one would a horse— with auspicious resolve that touches the heart,
through these offerings.
O Rudra, I make the mouse your sacrificial animal; this, O Rudra, is your portion; accept it together with your sister Ambikā, Svāhā!
O Mother, we have appeased Rudra; we have appeased the divine Tryambaka,
so that he may make us more prosperous, so that he may make us better, so that he may make us more numerous, so that he may prolong our lives, and so that he may inspire us with resolve.
Medicine for the cow, medicine for the horse, medicine for man;
and also for us, may there be excellent medicine, so that there may be a good path for the ram and the ewe.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May I be liberated from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not be separated from immortality.
O Rudra, this is your portion; with that favor, pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains.
Pināka in hand, clad in a skin, with his bow unstrung.
The gods and the asuras were both in this world. Prajāpati desired, "May I drive away the asuras; may I create offspring.
He saw the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; indeed, by means of the Cāturmāsyas he drove away the asuras, and by means of the Cāturmāsyas [he created offspring].

He created offspring. Therefore, he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Cāturmāsyas, drives away his rival and is propagated with offspring and cattle. Having fashioned the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice from the Agniṣṭoma, Prajāpati created offspring;
having fashioned the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice from the Ukthya, he caused these offspring to be seized by Varuṇa; [he did so] from the Atirātra.
Having fashioned the Sākamedha sacrificial rite, Indra slew Vṛtra. Some creatures were already created, while others were yet uncreated;
then Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring. The sacrifice is indeed the year, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice.
He placed these two pairs of milk within himself—the *udhanya* and the *vahya*—and then [offered] these [oblations] to those deities.

He offered the oblations as their respective portions and thereby created offspring; from the seasons indeed those offspring were born, for these five oblations are the seasons, since there are five seasons; from them one is born. Agni alone caused [the seed] to be sown; Soma indeed deposited the seed. Agni and Soma are a pair; Savitṛ impelled it for procreation, and the year [is the result].

Verily, Savitṛ is the twelve months of the year; therefore, the cake is offered on twelve potsherds. Moreover, it is offered on twelve potsherds for the sake of its being dedicated to the All-gods (vaiśvadeva). He offers it in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), for the year is undefined. Sarasvatī indeed bestowed speech upon the creatures when they were created;
they were emitted toward Pūṣan as their support. Sarasvatī is speech, and Pūṣan is cattle; thus, speech and cattle constitute a productive pair.

And from the middle they were created by Prajāpati; from that pair at the end, offspring were born spreading in all directions. Thus, in this way, they are now created by Prajāpati from the middle, and then, from that pair at the end, offspring are born spreading in all directions. These oblations are indeed slayers of Vṛtra; for with Agni as his vanguard, Indra slew Vṛtra, impelled by Savitṛ and accompanied by Sarasvatī, with Soma as his king.
Then Pūṣan supported him with his own vigor. These oblations are indeed the victory. Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra;
he was scattered in all directions by his vigor, and he entered into this entire world—the waters, the plants, and the trees. Because of that, the gods grew weary;
they gathered it together, and that is why the *sānnāyya* (the milk-offering) is called *sānnāyya*. Therefore, one who knows this [should offer] with the *sānnāyya*.
He who sacrifices prospers.
Curds and boiled milk indeed form a pair; now, that which is mixed together appears like an egg or like curdled whey, and it is truly an embryo.
From fervor (tapas), indeed, creatures were born. He who attains the state of being boiled (śṛtatva) attains the state of fervor;
from that he is born. Now, this is the Vaiśvadeva Āmikṣā. Prajāpati created offspring; he created them by means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice itself.
Therefore, these offspring belong to the Viśvedevas; he sacrifices to the Viśvedevas, for the drops are indeed the Viśvedevas, and it is them he thus worships.
Moreover, from that which is bestowed from above, human beings subsist upon the sacrifice. This [offering] is the womb of offspring;

the Maruts desired it, and from that they were released when seized by distress. When [he offers] to those who possess their own property (*svatavadbhyas*), it is for the sake of their own property and for atonement.
This cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts is indeed the procreator of cattle, for there are seven Maruts; moreover, it is for the sake of expiation, and by this he secures domestic food.
Created by the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, they indeed dispersed in all directions; Prajāpati enclosed them with the offering to Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivīya).

In that there is an offering to Heaven and Earth, it is for the sake of enclosing the creatures once they have been created. In that there is a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla), it belongs to Prajāpati;
thus the sacrificer finds firm support among the deities in Prajāpati himself. The cake on one potsherd is the sacrificer, and the Āhavanīya fire is the heavenly world.

In that he offers it as a complete oblation, he causes the sacrificer—who has become an offering—to go to the heavenly world. When the sacrificer falters, the offspring falter after him; when the sacrificer is firmly established, the offspring are established after him. It should be offered straight for the sake of stability. He offers it as a complete oblation for the sake of stability. The one-potsherd cake is indeed the sacrificer; the clarified butter is the cattle.
It should be filled; thus he prospers him with cattle.
If he were to fill it, he would place him below his cattle, and the cattle would attend upon him without feeding him. It should be made with the back exposed;
thus he places him above his cattle, and the cattle attend upon him while feeding him. One should not heed that; it must indeed be filled, for cattle do not [attend] otherwise.
If [the offering] should fall while facing east, the sacrificer would die; if facing south, it would burn up his offspring;
if facing west, the wife would die; if facing north, it would burn up his cattle; if it should fall face upwards, Parjanya would fail to rain.
Having picked it up again and sprinkled it with ghee, it should be offered for the firm establishment of the sacrificer; a boon is the sacrificial fee.
By means of the choice itself he wins the choice, for the self is indeed the choice. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is tied in three bundles;
the fuel-stick (*idhma*) is tied in three bundles; the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices are arranged in three parts. The *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices are indeed the year;
by means of the year they churn the fire. Offspring are born after the fire; this fire is churned as a procreator, and moreover, as a bull.
They produce this for the sacrificer: one should sacrifice in spring for the sake of procreation; one should sacrifice on sloping ground for the sake of procreation.
They do not throw up a high altar for the sake of procreation. There are curdled milk-mixtures (prasva); [the thought is], "May he procreate me.

The speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) is indeed cattle, and cattle are of various forms; therefore it is of various forms: the ghee belongs to Agni, the curds belong to Indra, and the speckled butter belongs to Indra and Agni.

The speckled butter belongs to the deity; Indra and Agni are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing. Mithuna (the couple) is out-breathing and in-breathing, and offspring have their origin in the couple.

From a couple, indeed, offspring and cattle are produced. It is from that very couple that the sacrificer is propagated with offspring and cattle. If he should sacrifice in the spring, he should spread [the butter] twice and pour it over once.

Cattle are indeed plants; verily, he establishes cattle in plants. If he should sacrifice in the rainy season, he should spread [the ghee] once and pour [the butter] over it twice; verily, by means of rain itself, he sprinkles cattle.

From the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), indeed, those creatures were born; these nine oblations are the vital breaths, for there are nine vital breaths. The deity is the self (*ātman*); from that one is born. There are nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and nine after-offerings (*anuyāja*), two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), and eight oblations; he offers them together to Agni and sacrifices to the Vājins. That makes thirty; the *virāj* consists of thirty syllables; verily, he finds firm support in the *virāj*.
From the womb of Virāj, Prajāpati indeed created offspring; from this same womb of Virāj, the sacrificer is born.
There are thirty nights in a month; that which is a month is the year, and the year is Prajāpati.
Thus, from this union—the womb of Prajāpati and the womb of Virāj—the sacrificer is born. Indeed, with each single oblation...
For twelve nights each they separated; as many as there are nights in a year by calculation, for so many nights they separated.

Verily, they separate the year itself from the enemy. With the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice they separated four months; with the Varuṇapraghāsas, another four; with the Sākamedhas, another four. It is these very months that they separate from the enemy. One who performs the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyājī*) is indeed one thing.
He who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices by sacrificing with the thought, "Spring has been," "The rainy season has been," and "Autumn has been," he is a performer of the seasonal (ṛtu) sacrifices.
Now, he who completes a thirteenth month and sacrifices for that thirteenth month, he is a performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Having performed three straight [seasonal] sacrifices, he should omit the fourth; having performed two straight [seasonal] sacrifices, he should omit the third. Those which are the three...

Their years are thirty-six full months; of those two [additional] months, there are twenty-four. Those thirty-six that are in excess, he brings them together within these twenty-four. This indeed is that thirteenth month;
it is this very one that he thus brings about. He sacrifices toward it. One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva, but not with the Varuṇapraghāsas.
Not everyone is born with a thousandfold [wealth] through the Sākamedha offerings; rather, one attains it according to one's vital strength.

This Vaiśvadeva oblation is indeed procreation; when one sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva, one sacrifices for the sake of procreation, thinking, "May I attain my own measure. When he has acquired a thousand cattle, then he should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings.
Whatever thousandfold [offense] they have committed, he expiates that sin with this.
Virāj: [the reading] *virāḍ* has been emended to *virājaiva*;
[the reading] *yajeta* has been emended to *yajate*.
When he sacrifices with the *barhis* at the *prayāja*s, he sacrifices to the plants; when he sacrifices with the *barhis* at the *anuyāja*s, he sacrifices to the fruit;
when he sacrifices with the *barhis* of the *vāritī* grasses, he sacrifices to that which is produced from this fruit. When he sacrifices to the two doors, he sacrifices to the lap;

when he sacrifices to Dawn and Night, he sacrifices to both the dawning and the setting; when he sacrifices to the two *joṣṭrī* goddesses, he sacrifices to that which has been born and that which is yet to be born.

And as for the *ūrjāhuti* (the offering of vigor): it is that which he eats and drinks; and as for the two divine *hotṛ*s: they are these very [two], for the three goddesses are indeed speech—the three goddesses being speech—and it is speech that he thus sacrifices to. Moreover, the meters are indeed speech, and it is the meters that he thus sacrifices to.
The sacrifice is indeed *tanūnapāt* (the body-protector) when unextended, and *narāśaṃsa* (praised by men) when extended; therefore, he sacrifices to *tanūnapāt* in the *prayāja* offerings.
For at that time the sacrifice is not yet extended; therefore, he offers to Narāśaṃsa in the after-offerings, for at that time the sacrifice is indeed extended.
He offers to Vanaspati; Vanaspati is Soma, and these creatures belong to Soma; verily, he bestows sap upon the creatures.
He offers to Tvaṣṭṛ, for Tvaṣṭṛ fashions forms. He offers to the Vājins; the Vājins are cattle; verily, he [bestows] them.
He sacrifices this; moreover, the *vājins* are indeed the meters, so it is the meters that he sacrifices here. The *vājins* are cattle;

therefore, one must not conclude [the sacrifice]. If he were to conclude it, he would be concluding those very cattle, for these are never concluded, as they are born perpetually. Indeed, this is not like a well-performed sacrifice, for he offers when the enclosing-sticks have been cast away and there is no separation [between the fire and the altar].

He sacrifices; by that, the sacrifice is performed. He performs the secondary sacrifice for the sake of firm establishment through the *samiṣṭayajus*. Sprinkling the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he draws [the butter]; thus he places seed in the bulls. Sitting with his knees raised, he sacrifices, for cattle have their knees raised; thus they place seed in the cattle. Moreover, Prajāpati, having his knees raised, created offspring. He offers to the quarters; these...

Thus he moistens the quarters with the essence; he offers the eastern one last. They turn back toward the eastern quarter and call out together, for this is like a draught of Soma; the officiating priests consume it.
May the vigorous ones carry my sacrifice.
Thus they consume it in equal portions; indeed, they distribute the strength (*vāja*) in equal portions, while he eats it himself, thereby placing the strength within himself.
Created by means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, they were seized by Varuṇa in their youth. Regarding this, they say: "Those creatures indeed transgressed against Prajāpati;

while they were transgressing, Varuṇa caused them to be seized. Therefore, a father should not be transgressed against. By means of the Vaiśvadeva, Prajāpati created offspring; the Maruts scattered his oblation, and consequently, those seized by misfortune (aṃhas) were born.

He sought a remedy for them; he sought it within himself. He fashioned this milk from out of himself and with it he sacrificed away their distress. Therefore, these Varuṇapraghāsa offerings are indeed an averting of distress (*aṃhas*).

When one sacrifices with the Varuṇapraghāsas, it is for the averting of all distress. Varuṇa seized those creatures because they had eaten [forbidden food]; therefore, they are called Varuṇapraghāsas.
As much sin as there was in the unborn embryo, so much sin falls upon him who performs the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.
There is a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ; for Savitṛ among the gods is connected with the Gāyatrī. There is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni by way of deity.
When those seized by Varuṇa were as if trembling, then Indra and Agni bestowed strength upon them, for they were indeed feeble.
Varuṇa seized the creatures; Indra and Agni bestowed strength upon them. Indeed, Indra and Agni are vigor and virility;
this vigor and virility are placed in the midst of the creatures. They did not breathe; Varuṇa seized those who were breathless.
Indra and Agni are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing; this out-breathing and in-breathing are placed at the beginning of the creatures. Now, these are five.
The offering to the Maruts is for continuity; the offering to Varuṇa is for release from Varuṇa; the offering to Ka is for pleasure.
For when that [suffering] became pleasure for those seized by Varuṇa, therefore it is the offering to Ka. Ka is Prajāpati; Prajāpati indeed made those creatures subject to Varuṇa.
By means of the offering to Ka, he releases them from Varuṇa for his own sake.
He sacrifices.

*Ṛta* is truth, the sacrifice; falsehood is woman. She who, having been purchased by her husband, acts otherwise, commits falsehood. Having thus removed that very falsehood, she attains *ṛta* and truth. If she were to answer falsely with her most beloved [husband], [she would incur sin].

He should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice; furthermore, in that he causes [him] to recite, he makes her pure for the sacrifice. They are ground raw for the removal of every evil. If they were roasted, the evil would not be removed. Varuṇa seized those creatures by means of the vessels;
in that there are vessels, he releases them from Varuṇa by means of the vessels themselves. There is one for each person; thus he removes the evil for each person individually.
One [ladle] is for the embryos; with it he makes atonement. Varuṇa seized those offspring because of food;

they carry food with a winnowing-basket, therefore they offer with a winnowing-basket. A man and a woman offer; verily as a pair they release the offspring from Varuṇa. Standing in front, facing west, they offer; thus they drive away misfortune from the front.
In that he offers the *prātrāṇi*, he thereby removes the distress from before those bipeds, the animals that are in pairs;
and in that [he offers] the ram and the ewe, he thereby removes the distress from behind those quadrupeds, the animals that are in pairs.
Thus, he removes the distress from both sides—from before and from behind.
When Varuna seizes offspring, he does not seize even the *śamyā* and the barley; for winter is Varuna.
By means of those two which are not seized by Varuna, he frees them from Varuna. Barley indeed belongs to Varuna and has Varuna as its deity;
thus, by its own portion, he frees them from Varuna. For Varuna seized those offspring on account of untruth (*anṛta*). When...
These are animals of falsehood; verily by means of falsehood he releases them from Varuṇa. They become a pair, for it is as a pair that offspring are released from Varuṇa.

They have wool, for the sake of purity; for those animals which have taken up hair attain the sacrificial essence (*medha*). There are leaves of the *śamī* tree, for the sake of peace. This tree is indeed named *bhūrja*; its ladles should be made, for Prajāpati is indeed the food-eater.

He was not able to encompass it; he encompassed it with a hundred pieces of firewood for the sake of encompassing food. Indeed, a thousand pieces of firewood suffice to contain the expiation for sin; more than a thousand should be used for the expiation of every sin. When they offer the vessels, then he cleanses the fire-altar; in that very place where they have cast away their sin, the deities abide once it has been purified.

"Yaja!"—Indra indeed gave the *yatīs* over to the hyenas; their heads are these date-palms (*kharjūra*). This is his drinking of Soma which has risen up here, namely the *karīra* fruits. The *karīra* fruits are indeed related to Soma; for the oblation related to Soma causes rain to fall from yonder sky. That there are *karīra* fruits is for the attainment of food through rain.
Thus from distress:
indeed, this is the eldest offspring of Prajāpati; those mountains were once winged, and they flew away.

Wherever they desired [to settle], this earth was then unstable for them. Indra cut off their wings; with those he made firm this earth. Those which were the wings became clouds; therefore, these [clouds] constantly rush against the mountain, for this is their place of origin. Then, that first essence which flowed forth became the *karīra* fruits; that is this very thing.

In the rainy season, the clouds float; they sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, and there are *karīra* fruits. By means of these, he extends the rain. Therefore, it rains most abundantly at that time, for he extends the rain. Indeed, they do not throw up an *uttaravedi* (high-altar) at the Vaiśvadeva; they throw it up here [at this sacrifice], thinking, "May he sustain the offspring already born. This which is the northern altar—whatever...

The Atris are offspring; this [altar] is their womb, and they are born after it. This southern altar is the womb of those who are the first-born offspring, and they are born after it. Thus he procreates both kinds of offspring: the Atris and the first-born.
Indeed, this [hand] was the hand, but that [other hand] was not so; this southern altar was that [hand], and by means of it they found him. Therefore, this [altar] belongs to him.

The younger indeed serves as the attendant; therefore, the younger serves the elder. They are both turned toward the east, for these two hands are likewise directed forward. They remain unjoined, for the purpose of warding off all evil. If they were to join them, the evil would not be warded off. He joins them behind one [of the two spoons] for the sake of continuity, and he scatters this [grain] upon it so that he may not step over it.

Indra is the kṣatra and the Maruts are the viś; they sacrifice separately for the sake of distinction between the worse and the better. Whatever the adhvaryu does, that the pratiprasthātṛ does; therefore, what the king (rājā) does, that the people (viś) do. Indeed, there are not thirty oblations in the Vaiśvadeva nor in the Sākamedhas; it is only in the Varuṇapraghāsas that there are thirty oblations, which belong to the Vairāja metre.

Verily, man consists of ten fingers, ten toes, and ten vital breaths. When they descend into the *avabhṛtha* bath, it is for the sake of the sacrificer’s freedom from Varuṇa. Whatever part of the sacrifice does not reach the state of being properly consecrated (*svagākṛti*), that Varuṇa seizes.
When they descend into the *avabhṛtha* with the residue of the offering, this is the removal of whatever has been attached to Varuṇa therein.

They come without looking back so as not to follow after Varuṇa; they cleanse themselves outside the cow-pen; thus they appease Varuṇa outside the cow-pen. "Thou art fuel; may we thrive," they say; having thus become free from Varuṇa, they approach for the purpose of thriving.
"Thou art kindling-wood; may we prosper," they say; it is for the sake of kindling itself.
They might split [it];
for the purpose of ascending after [the others].
FN emended. Ed: anvabhyārohayat. KS.36.7: 74.19:
for the sake of non-ascension.

Having created offspring and driven away his distress, he desired, "May I slay Vṛtra. He, having become united with these deities—the Maruts as the people, Agni as the vanguard—rushed forward. Having approached Vṛtra, upon seeing Vṛtra, he stood there unable to attack him, held back by the pillar of his thighs. The Maruts reflected upon him; they sought to overcome him, and when they reached his vital parts...

Then he exerted himself; they indeed heated him thoroughly, therefore they are called the Sāṃtapana (the Heaters). Or rather, Indra slew Vṛtra with Agni as his vanguard; that is for the sake of having a vanguard. Moreover, Agni is indeed the commander-in-chief of the gods; thus this [offering] is for the raising of the army.
Indra, indeed, was unable to lift the thunderbolt against Vṛtra; he offered up this portion to the Maruts, and that—

They heated him with fervor by means of that vigor; indeed, they heated him thoroughly by that. Therefore, the Sāṃtapana [offering] is to be prepared as a pap at midday, for at that time he heats both ends. There should be a pap, for it heats him from all sides.
The gods, indeed, could not find the vital spot of Vṛtra; the Maruts pierced him with a razor-edged thunderbolt. Indeed, they heated him thoroughly by that.
Therefore, they are called Sāṃtapana.
To be expelled from the community:
FN emended. Ed: senotthāpanīyam.
On the following day, as they were about to slay Vṛtra, they sat down together and said, "To whom will this belong tomorrow?
Whose meat shall we cook? They cooked this rice-porridge and sought to discern the cattle by means of it. They knew:
"Whichever ones these [cattle] will return to, those will be ours. With this [porridge] they set out toward them, and with this they captured them.
This [offering] indeed belongs to the cattle; they were about to conquer on the morrow, and they said, "To whom will this belong on the morrow?
For whom shall we cook it? They cooked this rice-porridge and said, "Let us not eat it without having offered it.
They offered it to the Maruts Gṛhamedhas; for the Maruts Gṛhamedhas are indeed cattle, and it was for the sake of cattle that they [cooked it].
They were indeed engaged in conflict. Those Asuras sent hunger against the gods; the gods, having perceived it, cooked this rice-porridge.
It, not finding a place among the gods, entered back into the Asuras. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
Therefore, he who, knowing thus, cooks this rice-porridge, prospers in himself and his rival is defeated—even so.

If he were to cook for a neighbor, he would indeed send hunger to his rival. That which belongs to the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed the Pākayajña; among these, the Gṛhamedha is most conducive to cattle. He does not offer the Prayājas, nor the Anuyājas, nor does he recite the Sāmidhenī verses; he offers the two Ājyabhāgas for the sake of the sacrifice. He makes an oblation to Agni Samavat; for Agni is the completion (sam-iṣṭi), Agni is the foundation; [it is] by means of the completion.
Having thus established [the sacrifice], they invoke the *iḍā*. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *gṛhamedha* is related to cattle; therefore they invoke the *iḍā*.
He sets aside the scrapings for the sake of continuity.
They,
having failed to obtain [it]— for Indra had deserted both of them— the gods set aside this portion for Indra, [thinking], "To us tomorrow..."
"Having set aside a portion, he chooses," they say; thus they call upon this bull, Indra. The bellowing is the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Moreover, they call out to this bull of the Asuras, saying, "May he procreate for us. The cows stay with their calves for the sake of the *Sākamedha* sacrifice.
A woman eats for the sake of the *Sākamedha* sacrifice; if a woman were not to eat, they would be without the *Sākamedha*. Now...

Whatever a woman eats is for the sake of the Sākamedha sacrifice; indeed, Nirṛti seizes that part of the sacrifice which a woman eats, for a woman is Nirṛti. The wooden ladle (darvī) is possessed by Nirṛti, for it moves about while heated; and this ladle is truly the hand of a woman. When he offers with the ladle, he expiates Nirṛti by means of her very own possession by Nirṛti. This, indeed, occurs on the following day.

He went forth to slay Vṛtra; the Maruts were playing around him. They reached him and diverted his attention; they overpowered him. Therefore they are called *krīḍayaḥ*. Now, when they were engaged in battle, those gods could not see the furthest limit of the Asuras. But they saw the Maruts playing, and [thought], "These are surely those with conquered minds. To them...

They offered this portion; from that they conquered. Having conquered that, this very one—Indra, who is yonder sun—[consists of] the *krīḍayas*, the rays; he moves together with the rays for the sake of victory. The gods, indeed, did not recognize Vṛtra when he was slain;
the Maruts played upon him, therefore they are called *krīḍayas*. Now, these five oblations are for the sake of continuity; and this [is as follows].

The offering to Indra and Agni: Indra and Agni indeed bore the thunderbolt for him; Indra and Agni brought the thunderbolt down upon him. Now, this [offering] belongs to Indra; for having slain Vṛtra, Indra extracted this as his share. That is his very portion, his extraction; therefore, when a king has won a battle, he carries away the booty. Now, this [offering] belongs to Viśvakarman; all...
Thinking, "My deeds have been performed," he indeed became Viśvakarman; then, after slaying Vṛtra, this was the Āghāra libation for the continuity and the completion of the thirty offerings.
Having created offspring while playing, and having warded off evil by slaying Vṛtra, those gods desired immortality alone. The heavenly world is indeed immortality;
the year is the heavenly world. In that there are twelve oblations, he thereby wins immortality.

This indeed is a calamity; he has either fallen short of or exceeded the year by offering twelve oblations. He turns back toward the year itself. This indeed is a calamity; he has either failed to reach or has overreached the year in that he brings them together six by six. There are six seasons; it is these he thus brings together, he causes them to attain their full measure, he establishes them.
He followed after those who were following; for this year is indeed calamity, and the seasons are the fathers.

He thus procreates them, and he is procreated after them as they are being procreated; from that he is procreated. This year has indeed become sacrificed for him, and the seasons have become sacrificed; but his fathers have not yet been sacrificed for him—therefore, by means of this Pitṛyajña, it is for them that he sacrifices.

The ancestors become beloved and pleased when the offering is set out on the south side, for the south belongs to the ancestors. Now, some say that the offering should be set out on both sides, because both [classes of deities] are worshipped there; however, that need not be heeded. It should be set out on the south side alone, for the south belongs to the ancestors. There is a cake on six potsherds; there are indeed six seasons, and thus these very seasons become beloved and pleased by this [offering].

The sacrifice is indeed not with the parched grains nor with the stirred drink; since this cake exists, by that it is a sacrifice. Now, these parched grains are the *svadhā* offering in yonder world. Moreover, the nights of the year are truly unlimited;

they are thus worshipped and gratified by him through these [grains]. The sacrifice to the ancestors is indeed not with the parched grains nor with the cake; since this stirred drink exists, by that it is a sacrifice to the ancestors.

It should be the milk of a cow that has been approached for milking, for that is the most proximate *dakṣiṇā* for the ancestors. He churns while sitting toward the south, for the south belongs to the ancestors. He churns with one [hand], for the ancestors have one [hand]. He churns with a stalk of sugarcane, for that belongs to the ancestors. He does not dig up the ground toward the east, for the sacrifice to the ancestors is not an eastern sacrifice. He digs up between both directions, for both [classes of ancestors] are honored.
He cuts the sacrificial grass (barhis) including its roots; with that which is rootless, it belongs to the ancestors, and with that which has roots, it belongs to the gods; for both are worshipped.

They enclose [the altar] on all sides, for the ancestors are indeed hidden from yonder sun, and the ancestors are hidden from both gods and men; therefore they enclose it. He strews the sacrificial grass all around, for these seasons are encompassed on every side.
"Furthermore, [he thinks], 'May the fathers not come together from all sides. For in that former [fire] the other deities are sacrificed to;
if he were to offer oblations there, he would mingle the offerings and cause a conflict. They prepare the cooked food on the Gārhapatya fire for the sake of the sacrifice;
they bring the fire from the rice-cooking hearth, and they do not bring it from anywhere else."
The ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*):
"Desiring you, we call upon you; desiring you, we kindle you."
Desiring them, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation.

Thus he recites the *anuṣṭubh*, for the fathers desire the end; the *anuṣṭubh* is indeed the end, and the fathers are the end. Therefore, he recites the *anuṣṭubh*. He recites one [verse], for the fathers are of one world. He recites three times, for the fathers are in the third world. In that he recites one, by that he honors the fathers; in that he recites three times, by that he honors the gods. Thus both are honored. He does not choose a *hotṛ* nor an *ārṣeya*, [for fear] of death.

Thus he releases them; he performs the fore-offerings (prayāja) excluding the one for the sacrificial grass (barhis). The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring; verily, he releases offspring from death.

When about to act for men, he wraps his garment around himself; he wraps it over the right shoulder for the gods. Now, here he must wear it over the left shoulder (prācīnāvīta) for the sake of distinction.
Having made the portioning on the south side, having stepped across toward the north, standing on the south side, he offers; [this is] toward the south.

For he first sacrifices Soma to the Fathers; Soma is indeed the deity of the Fathers, for Soma has the Fathers as his deities. When he sacrifices to Soma accompanied by the Fathers, he thereby sacrifices to those Fathers who drink Soma. When [he sacrifices] to those seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*), he sacrifices to the sacrificers; when to those consumed by the fire (*agniṣvātta*) who perform the domestic sacrifice (*gṛhamedhin*), he sacrifices to them.
When he sacrifices to Agni Kavyavāhana, there are two bodies of Agni: with his body that carries the oblation (*havyavāhanyā*), he carries the oblation to the gods.
With the *kavyavāhanī* verse he offers to the fathers for the sake of firm establishment through the *samiṣṭi*. Indeed, the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) of the gods are two;

with one he impels [the offering], and with the other he causes it to go. But here three should be performed, for the fathers are beyond the gods; thus, by this third [verse], he has indeed given [the offering] beyond them.
He cuts five times; the sacrifice is fivefold; having encompassed the sacrifice in its entirety, he seizes it.
With the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta).
Svadhā! Adoration!
Thus he utters *vaṣaṭ*; the *svadhā* call belongs to the ancestors, the *namas* call to the gods; for both are worshipped. He places [the portions] on the corners;

for humans follow after the gods and the ancestors. He has sacrificed to the gods and the ancestors. He places them three times, for there are these three men here: the father, the son, and the grandson; he mentions three subsequent ones for the sake of continuity.
He places [the offering] in all the corners, for the ancestors are in all directions; thus he causes him to go to all the directions. He does not place it in that [specific] direction;
for if he were to place it in that direction, he would encircle them with death. They follow after that very [direction], and when he wipes [the vessel] in that direction, he thereby gratifies her.

"O fathers, rejoice here! Having said this, they depart; they stand near the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse, "Thee, who art fair to behold," until they are exhausted. Having made the fire their witness, they reach the end of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having said, "The fathers have rejoiced," they enter; they lay down a tuft of wool or a fringe.
This is the expiation for whatever they step upon there. He says, "Go forth, O Soma-loving fathers," lest the fathers should become attached to them;
it is for the sake of separation. He goes around, sprinkling water all around; this is their purification. Not sprinkling [again], he returns.

Those who perform the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) go to that world beyond; however, Prajāpati alone is able to lead them back from there. In that he recites a verse addressed to Prajāpati, it is Prajāpati himself who leads them back. Furthermore, when they return by the same way they went without sprinkling water, they turn back again toward this world, or toward the ancestors.

The sacrifice has come to this; the sacrifice is fivefold, for they return with the *paṅkti* [verse]. They return together with the sacrifice; they return with verses containing the word "mind" (*manasvatī*);
they thus call the mind back again.
Verily, for him the year has been sacrificed to, and the seasons have been sacrificed to; but the Rudras were not yet sacrificed to for him.

Since these cakes are for Tryambaka, by that very means the Rudras become sacrificed to and gratified for him. They are prepared on one potsherd; for man is not composed of many potsherds, but he obtains him all at once. Moreover, this earth is indeed one, and upon her alone he finds firm support.
"Should it be sprinkled with clarified butter or not? they deliberate. "If one were to sprinkle it," they say, "he would deliver over his cattle to Rudra;
therefore, that should not be heeded. It must indeed be sprinkled, for there is no oblation that is not sprinkled. They carry a single firebrand, for a single firebrand belongs to the Rudras.
They carry it smoking, for what is smoking belongs to the Rudras. They carry it toward this direction, for this is the direction of the Rudras."
They carry it away facing away; they thus carry away Rudra facing away. "O Rudra, I make the mole your victim," he says, and he scatters one [grain] for the mole-trapper;
thereby he makes atonement for his cattle. Therefore, Paśupati is a slayer of them. One should cause him to sacrifice at a crossroads;
for the dwellings of the Rudras are indeed at the crossroads. Thus he makes atonement for Rudra in his very own dwelling. This is for you, O Rudra...
"Accept this portion together with your sister Ambikā, svāhā! Autumn is indeed the womb of Rudra, and Ambikā is his sister;
he follows after her, and therefore he kills most in autumn. By means of her, he propitiates him.
He offers with the middle leaf, for that is untouched by demons. He offers with a wild plant; thus he propitiates Rudra in the forest itself.

If one were to offer with a vessel, one would bring Rudra down upon the offspring; therefore, he offers with a forest-branch. With the words, "O Mother, we have appeased Rudra," they have indeed become free from debt. With the words, "A remedy for the cow, for the horse, a remedy for man," having indeed become free from debt, they have provided a remedy.
With the words, "We worship Tryambaka," they walk around; there also, a woman desiring a husband walks around as a means of winning a husband.
Having thrown those [beans] upwards for her, they obtain fortune; indeed, they obtain fortune itself. They pour them together for the sacrificer;
they pour fortune itself together for him. For a woman who desires a husband, they should pour them together for her;
they pour fortune itself together for her. Having placed them in a cloth, she hangs them on a tree.
Not killed by a non-protector.
(FN emended. Ed: arakṣohatam)
Thus they were:
"O Rudra, this is your portion; with that favor, go beyond the Mūjavat mountains, O you who hold the *pināka* bow in hand, who are clothed in a skin, and whose bow is unstrung."

Thus, the mountain is indeed the womb of Rudra; from there, he bestows peace upon creatures as they descend. By means of his own portion, he causes them to go to their own womb. They return without looking back, so that they may not be overtaken by Rudra. They cleanse themselves outside the cow-pen; thus they appease Rudra outside the cow-pen. A woman is indeed called *ambī* and *bhagā*; therefore, they are called *tryambakāḥ*.
He whose sacrificial offering is unstable is himself unstable; his Tryambaka offerings become unstable.
He should offer a pap of cooked rice in clarified butter to Āditya upon returning home. This earth is indeed Aditi; this earth is the foundation.
Since Āditya is this very earth, he finds firm support in her.
O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for his fortune.
May the celestial Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, purify our intention; may the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet today.
Now, at the impulse of strength, we celebrate with our speech the great Mother named Aditi;
for into her has entered every living being, and in her may the god Savitar impel the cosmic order.
Within the waters is immortality, within the waters is healing; and in the praises of the waters, O horses, become swift and vigorous.
Either Vāyu has yoked you, or Manu, or the twenty-seven Gandharvas;
they first harnessed the horse, and they placed speed in him.
O Son of the Waters, swift-moving one, with that wave of yours which is impetuous, lofty, and a winner of booty— with that, win us the prize!
In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, whose impulse is true, may I ascend to the highest firmament.
In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, whose libations are true, may we, as the vigorous ones of Bṛhaspati, conquerors of the prize, win the prize.
O prize-winners, win the prize; holding fast the paths, measure out the stages of the journey.
Go to the limit!
May the Vājins be auspicious to us in our invocations, they who are swift as measured paces, well-praised in the assembly of the gods;
crushing the serpent, the wolf, and the demons, may they drive away all diseases far from us.
O swift ones, protect us in every contest for booty; O wise, immortal, knowers of the Eternal Law, drink of this honeyed mead and rejoice! Satisfied, go by the paths traveled by the gods.

May all those coursers, who hear our invocation, hear our call— the swift ones of measured speed, winners of thousands, eager for gain at the winning of the prize, they who have gathered great riches in the battles.
This steed hastens toward the whip; bound by the neck, he reaches up to the shoulder-blades.
Following the intention of Dadhikrā, he springs along, leaping repeatedly over the curves of the paths.
And indeed, as he runs and hastens forward, eager for the prize, the wind blows after him like the wing of a bird;
it follows Dadhikrāvan as he speeds along his flank, crossing over with might and vigor.
May the impulse of strength come to me; may Heaven and Earth, the source of all prosperity, come to me; may you fathers of every form come to me; may Soma come to me with immortality.

Speak speech to Indra; speak speech together for Indra; make Indra win the prize. "O Indra, may I win the prize for you!"—that was the true speech which you uttered in concert with Indra. O trees, you have caused him to win;
release your voice for Indra! O two prize-winning steeds, winners of the prize, having won the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati, O prize-winners!

Winners of the prize, having won the prize, may you both wipe yourselves upon the portion of Bṛhaspati. Let us ascend to heaven; come, let us ascend to heaven; let us ascend to heaven. Through sacrifice, vital breath is perfected; through sacrifice, out-breath is perfected; through sacrifice, sight is perfected; through sacrifice, hearing is perfected;
through sacrifice, mind is perfected; through sacrifice, speech is perfected; through sacrifice, the Brahman is perfected; through sacrifice, the *pṛṣṭha* is perfected.

It prospers through the sacrifice; the sacrifice prospers through the sacrifice. Svāhā to strength! Svāhā to instigation! Svāhā to the after-born! Svāhā to the ritual will! Svāhā to the lord of days! Svāhā to the lord of speech! Svāhā to Vasu! Svar! The head is Vaiyaśana; Vyaśyan is Āntya; Āntya is Bhauvana. Svāhā to the lord of the world, the overlord! For food thee, for strength! Svāhā!
Thee for the winning of booty; thee for brilliance; thee for vigor; thee for wealth; thee for prosperity. To the light of heaven have the gods gone; we have become immortal;
we have become the offspring of Prajāpati.
O Agni, speak here to us; turn toward us with a gracious mind.
Bestow upon us, O Lord of the People; you are the giver of wealth to us.
May Aryaman grant us [blessings], may Bhaga, may Bṛhaspati, may the gods, and may Sūnṛtā grant them; may the goddess Vāc bestow them upon us.
Urge Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, and Indra to grant gifts;
urge Vāc, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and the vigorous Savitṛ.
We take hold of King Soma, Varuṇa, and Agni;
the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati the Brahman.
We invoke Indra and Vāyu here, who are beautiful to behold and easy to call upon,
so that all people may be well-disposed toward us at our gathering.
This impulse of strength first brought forth King Soma in the plants and in the waters;
may he, knowing all, encompass the Virāj, increasing progeny and prosperity for us.
The impulse of strength has taken its stand upon this heaven; may it anoint all plants with clarified butter.
May they be full of sweetness for us; may we remain watchful in the kingdom as our domestic priests. This impulse of strength has come forth toward all these worlds on every side.
May he, knowing all, cause him who is unwilling to give to bestow, and may he grant us wealth consisting of all heroic sons.

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the speech of Sarasvatī, and with the restraint of the restrainer, I consecrate Bṛhaspati for sovereignty; I consecrate Indra for sovereignty. You are taken with a support;
I take you, who sit upon the wood, who sit among men, who sit in life, as one pleasing to Indra. This is your womb; for Indra, you!
Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, who sittest upon the earth, who sittest in the atmosphere, who sittest in the firmament, as one pleasing to Indra.
This is thy womb; for Indra, thee! Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, who sittest in the waters, who sittest in the clarified butter, who sittest in all beings, as one pleasing to Indra.
This is thy womb; for Indra, thee! Thou art taken with a support; O cup, belonging to all people, O restrainer, we offer [thee] to the sage.
Of those three first-born divine vessels that have been sprinkled together, from them— when they are being separated— I have gathered nourishment and vigor.
I take you, acceptable to Indra; this is your resting place; for Indra you are taken with a support.
The essence of the waters, swelling with power, the bright [essence] gathered from the sun—
the highest essence of the essence of the waters, that I take for you.
I take you, acceptable to Indra; this is your resting place; for Indra, you!
Surely, just as those possessing barley reap the grain in due order, separating it out,
so bring here the food for those who have not come with the sacrificial grass and the utterance of homage.
You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. This is your womb; for Prajāpati, you!
With this placement, [I take] you for Prajāpati.

The gods indeed saw various sacrifices, but they all saw this one [the *agniṣṭoma*]. They strove for it; they ran a race for it. Bṛhaspati won it. Bṛhaspati is indeed the domestic priest (*purohita*) of the gods.

Whatever a Brāhmaṇa hears as a domestic priest, he reports that to the king. With that [knowledge], he caused Indra to sacrifice. He attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). This very [sacrifice] is self-sovereign.

The sacrifice goes to self-sovereignty for him who sacrifices with this; because Bṛhaspati won [victory] by means of it, therefore a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice. Because they caused Indra to sacrifice with it, therefore a Rājanya [should sacrifice]. Indeed, the gods brought various sacrifices, saying, "I shall bring this one, you shall bring that one"; then Prajāpati brought this one. They desired a share in it; for them, the meters [were assigned].
He bestowed the *ujjitī*s. Now, Prajāpati sacrificed with this [rite]; he attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). This sacrifice is the self-sovereign;

he who sacrifices with it attains self-sovereignty. Food indeed is *vāja*; therefore, he who, knowing thus, eats food, causes that food to be victorious (*vājayati*). Soma is indeed the *vājapeya*; therefore, he who, knowing thus, [drinks] Soma...

He drinks the *vāja* (strength/food) and indeed attains it; for as many gods as drank the *soma*, they all attained the *vāja*. Therefore, everyone desires to drink *soma* and indeed attains the *vāja*. For speech (*vāk*) is the source of *vāja*. That speech, once created, became fourfold:
three quarters are in these worlds, one quarter is in cattle. That which is on earth is in the fire, and that is in the *rathantara* [sāman].
That [speech] which was in the intermediate space, that went to the *vāta* [sāman] and to the *vāmadevya*; that which was in heaven, that went to the *bṛhat* and to the thunder.

Then, that speech which remained over, they deposited it in the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa speaks both kinds of speech: that which he knows and that which he does not know. That [speech] which was in the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, by that he approaches him from the sacrifice; that which was in the animals, by that [he approaches him] outside the sacrifice.
Therefore, he who knows thus—verily, [the gift] goes to him unrefused; for as much as there is speech, that he knows, since gifts are given by speech and bestowed by speech.
He who wins [a gift] with the *gāthā* and *nārāśaṃsī* verses—for him there is nothing to be refused. For he wins it through untruth;
nor is it [to be refused] from one who is intoxicated, for when his intoxication passes away, then it torments him.
These two sets of cups dedicated to Prajāpati are seventeen; man, dedicated to Prajāpati, consists of seventeen parts:
four limbs, the head, the neck, the trunk, speech as the seventh, and the ten vital breaths. Indeed, evil clings to every limb of man;
in that he draws the cups in an interlocking manner, he releases him from evil limb by limb. Soma is indeed prosperity, and evil is [the enemy].

When the time for the *suropayāma* offerings has arrived, they step forward with the *soma* cups and step backward with the *suropayāma* cups; they purify him from evil through these very [offerings]. Therefore, they say, "Only one who has sacrificed with the *Vājapeya* is truly purified," for it is indeed through these that they purify him from evil. He offers at every joint with the words, "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice, impel the lord of the sacrifice, bestow fortune! This sacrifice is indeed one that has fallen into ruin.

Who indeed knows what is done for this [chariot], whether it is for the sake of completeness or for impulsion? Now, at the impulsion of strength (*vāja*), he brings down the chariot with the words, "The great mother. For Aditi is this earth; by her, and impelled by Savitṛ, he brings it down.
For the winning of strength. With the words, "In the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing," they wash the horses; for horses are born from the waters.

They generate them from their own womb. With the words, "Either Vāyu shall yoke thee, or Manu shall yoke thee," he yokes them; for humans are not worthy to yoke these; verily, by means of the deities, he yokes them. With the words, "O Son of the Waters, swift-coursing," he wipes the forehead-straps;
he merely repeats the sacrificial formula that has already been uttered. They cause the drums to resound; for Speech entered the forest.
Verily, he elevates that very speech; moreover, whatever speech is in the trees, that he secures for himself. It consists of seventeen parts and is complete;

Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold, so he attains Prajāpati. This sacrifice is one that has fallen away; indeed, from the year this fallen-away sacrifice is recovered. Having attained it from the year itself, he secures it.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, whose impulse is true, may I ascend the highest firmament"—with this thought the Brahman priest creeps toward the chariot wheel; impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed creeps toward the thunderbolt for the winning of booty. Moreover, the Brahman is Prajāpati of the sacrifice; thus Prajāpati himself impels him from the thunderbolt for the winning of booty. The Sāman is sung as truth.

The *sāman* is indeed truth; by truth he conquers, for conquest is victory. *Vāja* is food; it is for the conquest of food. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, at the impulse of the true impeller Bṛhaspati, may we, as possessors of *vāja*, conquerors of *vāja*, win the *vāja*"—with these words he mounts the chariot;
thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he mounts the chariot for the conquest of *vāja*. He recites the verses of the *vājins*.

They run the race for the winning of strength; they run with chariots assigned as sacrificial gifts. By means of the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) alone, one goes to the heavenly world. In that they run with chariots assigned as sacrificial gifts, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world together with the sacrificial gift. Now this [offering] of seventeen jars of wild rice: when the plants had ripened, the gods ran a race for them.
Bṛhaspati won them; he chose these *nivāra* grains, and that is why they are called *nivāra*. Bṛhaspati indeed won them;
he makes him a sharer [in the sacrifice] for the sake of non-injury. They carry him down below the *catvāla* pit.
For here, indeed, was this sun; they took him from here to yonder world. Since they took him from here to yonder world, that which...

They place [the chariot] in the *cātvāla* pit; they thus lead the sacrificer himself to the heavenly world. With the formula, "May the impulse of strength come to me," he offers an oblation when the chariots have returned. Whatever strength they won in the contest, that he now places within himself.
With the formula, "The trees have sung; for Indra, release your speech," he offers the *rathavimocanīya* oblation; by means of the sacrificial formula (*yajus*), they are indeed unyoked.
"By means of the *yajus*, the two prize-winning steeds are unyoked; having won the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati!"—thus he makes them sharers.

"O prize-winning steeds, having won the prize, wipe yourselves on the portion of Bṛhaspati!"—thus he gratifies all of them. They carry away the half-ox and the vessels for the liquor for those who run the race.
The prize (*vāja*) which they have won, that he purchases; a honey-ladle for the Brahmin—for by that he purchases it from the Brahmin himself.
The prince eats the *kakubh* verses; the *kakubh* is indeed vigor; verily, he places vigor within himself.
He causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *ujjitī* verses:
"Svarga! Ascend! Svarga! Ascend! Svarga! Ascend! Indeed, being about to ascend to heaven (*svar*), he thus converses with his wife; furthermore—
This is indeed the taking hold of the sacrifice together with the wife; you two shall be in the heavenly world. "May life be perfected by the sacrifice;

may breath be perfected by the sacrifice"—for man is as much as this [formula]. As much as man is, so much he attains; having become whole, he goes to the heavenly world. The garment is made of darbha grass for the sake of purity; the top-ring is made of wheat, belonging to Prajāpati.
Wheat indeed constitutes half of these plants; together with the food he goes to yonder world. "To strength, svāhā! To impulsion, svāhā!"—these are thirteen oblations, for thirteen months are a year.
Verily, he thus places him in the year; in that very heavenly world he finds firm support. "For food thee! For strength thee!"

With the words, "For the winning of strength, thee! they fix [the horse] with bags of saline soil. Saline soil, indeed, belongs to Prajāpati; it becomes more abundant day by day. Verily, they fix him with food. He who goes to that world (the heavenly world) indeed departs from this world.
In that they fix him with bags of saline soil, he does not depart from this world; thereby he is supported in this world. He descends toward gold; gold is indeed splendor.
Gold, he establishes himself in splendor. He descends onto a goat-skin; the goat-skin is indeed cattle;
verily, he establishes himself in cattle. With each kind of food he offers oblations using the Vājaprasavīya formulas; "vāja" is indeed food, for the attainment of food.
He offers both that which is domestic and that which is wild, for the attainment of both kinds of food, with a ladle made of udumbara wood.
He offers; the udumbara is indeed strength, [offered] for the attainment of strength. He offers with seven [verses]; there are indeed seven meters;
verily by means of the meters he secures food for him. Moreover, the meters are speech; verily by means of speech he bestows food upon him.
Now, these *atigrāhya* cups are drawn for the sake of securing that supreme food which has not yet been secured;
furthermore, these animals are sacrificed for the sake of securing the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). Insofar as it belongs to Agni, one secures the *agniṣṭoma* by means of it.

By that which is the *ukthya* for Indra and Agni, [he obtains it]; by that which is the bull for Indra, [he obtains] the *ṣoḍaśin*; by that which is the ewe for Sarasvatī, he thereby obtains and secures that seventeen-fold chant (*stotra*) which was previously unattained and unsecured. Now, this is the barren cow (*vaśā*). The gods and the Asuras were in conflict; some were gods and some were Asuras. Those gods [sought] this barren cow.

Not seeing [the world], he enclosed a second world, the world of the Asuras. That for which he cuts off [the portion] is the world of the gods; that for which he does not cut off is the world of the Asuras.

By means of this [offering], the sacrificer likewise encloses a second world, namely the world of his rival. The Sarasvatī [offering] is the last of the others, and the Sarasvatī is the first of the others. Sarasvatī is indeed Speech; by Speech the sacrifice is performed.

By means of speech alone he continues the sacrifice. Whatever of the sacrifice a man who knows does not perform, and whatever an ignorant man omits, that becomes a flaw; that he rectifies by means of Sarasvatī, speech. The morning pressing is unexpressed; thereby he attains Prajāpati.
The Vājapeya belongs to Prajāpati, yet it is of a different womb; since it has a Sāman with expressed syllables while the morning pressing is unexpressed, [it is thus made consistent].
Therefore, the *rathantara* chant becomes its own source for the sake of obtaining blessings and for victory; moreover, the *rathantara* is indeed this [earth], and thus it is generated upon her.

At the midday *pavamāna*, there are verses containing the word *vāja*; *vāja* is food, [and they serve] for the attainment of food. At the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, there are verses containing the word *citra*; [they serve] for the complete attainment of the heavenly world. [They are recited] over verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*.

They chant praises; this indeed is Prajāpati’s body established in cattle, namely Śipiviṣṭa. Therefore, they chant praises in verses containing the word "Śipiviṣṭa. The eighteenth hymn becomes the last of the *ukthas*; thus he extends [the sacrifice] further toward the two higher chants.
Whatever is redundant in the sacrifice is redundant for that world (the heavenly world); yet the *Bṛhat* alone is capable of reaching that world and [attaining] sensory power.
Verily, this is great vigor; for when they praise with the Bṛhat, they do so in Indra’s power and vigor; from that, the sacrificer finds firm support in the sacrifice.
They praise:
Agni won the one-syllable [meter], the Aśvins the two-syllable, Viṣṇu the three-syllable, and Soma the four-syllable.

Savitṛ [created] the five-syllabled [meter], Pūṣan the six-syllabled, the Maruts the seven-syllabled, Bṛhaspati the eight-syllabled, Mitra the nine-syllabled, Varuṇa the ten-syllabled, Indra the eleven-syllabled, the Viśve Devās the twelve-syllabled,
the Vasus the thirteen-syllabled, the Rudras the fourteen-syllabled, the Ādityas the fifteen-syllabled, and Aditi the sixteen-syllabled.
Prajāpati, the seventeenfold [stoma], won speech with the one-syllable [meter]; the Aśvins won out-breathing and in-breathing with the two-syllable;
Viṣṇu won these three worlds with the three-syllable; Soma won four-footed cattle with the four-syllable;
Savitṛ won the five directions with the five-syllable; Pūṣan [won] the six seasons with the six-syllable.

The Maruts won by means of the seven-syllabled [meter], the *śakvarī* consisting of seven feet; Bṛhaspati won the eight quarters by means of the eight-syllabled [meter]; Mitra won the four quarters and the four intermediate directions by means of the nine-syllabled [meter]; Varuṇa won the nine vital breaths by means of the nine-syllabled [meter];
Indra won the *virāj* by means of the ten-syllabled [meter]; and the Viśvedevas won the *triṣṭubh* by means of the eleven-syllabled [meter].
The gods conquered the *jagatī* with twelve syllables; the Vasus conquered the thirteenth month with thirteen syllables;

the Rudras conquered the fourteenth month with fourteen syllables; the Ādityas conquered the fifteenth month with fifteen syllables; Aditi conquered the sixteenth month with sixteen syllables; and Prajāpati is the seventeenth.

Agni won this earth by means of the one-syllable [meter]; the Aśvins, the intermediate region by means of the two-syllable; Viṣṇu, the heavenly world by means of the three-syllable; Soma, the quarters by means of the four-syllable; Śrīvir, the stars by means of the five-syllable;
Savitṛ won the *akṣarapaṅkti* by means of the five-syllable [meter], for that which is the *akṣarapaṅkti* is indeed the *paṅkti*, since it consists of four sets of five syllables each—Pūṣan [won it].
