With the six-syllable [foot], Ṣaḍakṣara conquered the Gāyatrī; for it has four times six syllables. With the seven-syllable [foot], the Maruts conquered the Uṣṇih; for it has four times seven syllables. With the eight-syllable [foot], Bṛhaspati conquered the Anuṣṭubh;
for it has four times eight syllables. With the nine-syllable [foot], Mitra conquered the Bṛhatī; for it has... four times.
Varuṇa won the Virāj with its ten syllables by means of this [gāyatrī] which has nine new syllables, for there are four sets of ten syllables in it.
Indra won the Triṣṭubh with its eleven syllables by means of this [gāyatrī] which has eleven syllables, for there are four sets of eleven syllables in it.
The Viśve Devas won the Jagatī with its twelve syllables by means of this [gāyatrī] which has twelve syllables, for there are four sets of twelve syllables in it.

The Vasus won the thirteenth month with a verse of thirteen syllables; the Rudras won the fourteenth month with a verse of fourteen syllables; the Ādityas won the fifteenth month with a verse of fifteen syllables; Aditi won the sixteenth month with a verse of sixteen syllables; Prajāpati, the seventeenth, [won] with fire; [to] the one-syllabled metre, Svāhā! To the Aśvins!

Hail to the two-syllabled metre for Viṣṇu, svāhā! Hail to the three-syllabled metre for Soma, svāhā! Hail to the four-syllabled metre for Savitṛ, svāhā! Hail to the five-syllabled metre for Pūṣan, svāhā! Hail to the seven-syllabled metre for the Maruts, svāhā! Hail to the eight-syllabled metre for Bṛhaspati, svāhā! Hail to Mitra!
Svāhā to the nine-syllabled metre; svāhā to Varuṇa, the ten-syllabled metre; svāhā to Indra, the eleven-syllabled metre;
svāhā to the Viśvedevas, the twelve-syllabled metre; svāhā to the Vasus, the thirteen-syllabled metre;
svāhā to the Rudras, the fourteen-syllabled metre; [svāhā] to the Ādityas, the fifteen-syllabled metre.
Svāhā to the *chandas* [meter] for *Chandas*; svāhā to the *chandas* consisting of sixteen syllables for *Āditi*; Prajāpati is the seventeenth.

He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni for one whose kinsmen have departed; Indra and Agni are indeed vigor, strength, and virility; by means of vigor, he [thereby] overcomes them.

Furthermore, one should worship with vigor; he who has rivals should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and strength; by means of that very vigor and strength, he overcomes them. He who desires offspring, being capable of procreation yet not obtaining offspring, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. For Indra and Agni hid away the offspring of Prajāpati; those two...

He approached them with this portion; they gave offspring back to him. Indeed, Indra and Agni conceal the offspring of one who, though being capable of having offspring, does not obtain offspring. He approached those very deities with their portion;

they gave offspring back to him. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word "finding" (*vindat*). For the sake of finding [offspring], there is an offering to Indra and Agni on eleven potsherds.
One who is about to go forth to battle should offer [an oblation]; for Indra and Agni are indeed might and vigor; by means of that very might and vigor, he goes forth to battle.

One should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Indra and Agni when engaged in battle; for Indra and Agni are indeed might and vigor; by means of that very might and vigor, he conquers it. When he has won the battle, then he should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Indra and Agni with might.
Verily, he who wins a battle prospers through vigor; Indra and Agni are vigor and power. With vigor and power, they endow him.
He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni and a pap to Pūṣan when setting out toward a people.
Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and power; with vigor and power he sets out toward them. Pūṣan is the bestower of vigor. He...

He bestows vigor upon him. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni, a pap to Pūṣan, and a pap to the Lord of the Field when settling upon a field. Indra and Agni are indeed vigor and strength; by means of vigor and strength, they find a world for him.
Pūṣan is the bestower of vigor; he bestows vigor upon him. This earth is the mistress of the field.
He becomes firmly established in this very [state].

One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara for the sake of desire. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year, and the year is desire; he attains the year, and it fulfills his desire for whatever he may wish. One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara when about to enter upon a year-long term; Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year.

One is bound for a year; having reached the year itself, one commits an offense against Varuṇa’s desire. He should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara when seeking to win a prize. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; it is for the year that one receives [the prize]. Having reached the year itself, he wins the prize that was to be won. When he has won it, then [he should offer] to Agni Vaiśvānara.

One should offer an oblation on twelve potsherds. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; he employs the year, and the year wins this [sacrificer] for him. He makes that very one a sharer. Whomever he hates, for him he should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); by means of a noose, indeed, he moves about—he fastens that very [noose] upon him. A one-year-old bull is the sacrificial fee, for it is he.

One who desires to eat what is not food should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara, for Agni Vaiśvānara is the year; he thus places that [food] within the year itself. When he eats what is not food, he should then offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara; whatever unedible thing he has eaten, the year makes palatable for him, and it becomes well-digested.

He should give lead or black cloth as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Lead is indeed non-food; black is non-food. By means of non-food he strikes away non-food and bestows food-eating upon himself. He who is about to set out for battle should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara.
Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; by means of the year he sets out toward him. To Agni...

One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when about to engage in battle. Of two combatants, whichever has the more secure foundation (*āyatanavat*) is the victor. Indeed, Agni Vaiśvānara is this [earth]; he has made this very earth his foundation and exerts his prowess upon it; thus he conquers the battle. When he has won the battle, then he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara.
One should offer [an oblation]; Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; he thus employs the year, and the year wins for him.

He has made that [year] a sharer; he has released it. One who desires, "May I establish these kings with barley or rice," should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara; for Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year.
The year is the giver of food; he should approach it with its own portion. It bestows food upon him.

He should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara and a pap of barley to Varuṇa for one who is ill. For he who is ill is indeed seized by Varuṇa; by this [offering], he releases him from Varuṇa. That sun, indeed, is Agni.
Vaiśvānara [is the deity]; for Varuṇa seizes this man when he has been thus restrained by that [deity]. Having released him from that, he frees his entire self from Varuṇa.

He should offer a *caru* of barley to Varuṇa, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara for one who desires prosperity. One who desires prosperity is indeed seized by Varuṇa; [therefore, the priest] should release him from Varuṇa.

Therefore, there is a porridge offering for Iḍā; for the self is only as much as this [offering]. Having released him from Varuṇa, he causes him to take hold of that [sun], for Agni Vaiśvānara is yonder sun; he thus makes him reach the measure of yonder sun.

To Agni Jātavedas he should offer an oblation on eight potsherds; to Dadhikrāvan, one on eleven potsherds; and to Agni Vaiśvānara, one on twelve potsherds—this is for him who performs the first sacrifice after having given away all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*). Indeed, Agni knows that of this man where he has sacrificed. *Note:* *iyantam*: Corrections and conjectures to the entire work. (This appears to be a marginal note or a reference to a critical apparatus.)

In whatever place his good deed exists, Agni himself finds that for him; for he who gives everything is indeed impure. Dhīkkrāvā makes him pure again. Agni Vaiśvānara is the year; the year knows where his sacrifice was and where his good deed lies.
The year itself finds that for him. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat.

One should perform the *rathaprotīya* sacrifice for one who is being falsely accused. Now, they accused Dārbhya Rathaproti. The two Kaulakāvatis said to him, "We will perform the sacrifice for you in such a way that people will eat your food, yet you shall not hear the sound of domestic animals;
go to a place where you do not hear anything, and let whoever approaches you remain silent. And indeed, tigers used to approach him silently, sniffing him.

Thus they depart; indeed, on the following day, having followed after with the sacrificial implements and having churned the fire, the two of them offered an eight-potherd cake to Agni Surabhimat. Thereupon, they did not exclude him from the sacrifice. One whom they might suspect should be made to sacrifice with this [offering]. For they suspect him of being ill-smelling; the fragrant one is indeed the healing body of Agni, for fragrance is a medicine.

Thus he has made him fragrant for him; he indeed pacifies him. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna, a cake on eleven potsherds to Dadhikrāvan, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara, having returned home. Pavamāna purifies him, and Agni burns away [his impurity]. Indeed, he whom they accuse is unpurified; even Dadhikrāvan would not have been able to purify him.
Thus indeed they say: "The Dadhikrāvan [offering] purifies him; Agni Vaiśvānara is the year;

it is the year itself that makes him palatable. One who desires to win a battle, or wishes to overcome his enemy in combat, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma, and a cake on two potsherds to Heaven and Earth. The offering to Agni is for the sake of prosperity.

By means of the power of Agni and Soma, Indra indeed slew Vṛtra. He who conquers in battle or overcomes an enemy in human conflict, he truly slays Vṛtra; therefore, this [offering] is indeed "Vṛtra-slaying. Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra, but Heaven and Earth did not approve of it. They approved of it through this sacrificial portion, namely, the offering to Heaven and Earth.

"By the approval of Vajra, and by Vajra’s approval, [the enemy] shall become non-existent. When he wins a battle or conquers in a wager, he should then offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, one on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni, and one on two potsherds to Heaven and Earth. The offering to Agni is for prosperity; for it was through the power of Agni and Soma that Indra slew Vṛtra, and he was deprived of his vigor and strength.

He saw this [offering] to Indra and Agni; with it he placed vigor and strength within himself. Indeed, he who wins a battle or wins a prize among men is deprived of vigor and strength; Indra and Agni are vigor and strength, and by means of their vigor and strength they endow him with success.
Now, as for the offering to Heaven and Earth: those two who approved the thunderbolt for him, to them belongs this share.
It is performed.

A Brāhmaṇa desiring [a specific] object should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma. For the Brāhmaṇa has Agni-Soma as his deity; he thus approaches his own deity with a share for the sake of his desire. Those two fulfill that desire for him, whatever desire he may have. One desiring prosperity should cause a Brāhmaṇa to sacrifice with an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma. The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Agni, Soma, and Indra were sitting at Kurukṣetra. They said, "Whichever among us first attains glory, he shall be the strongest of us.

Of them, glory indeed attained Soma; they gathered around him. Therefore, they gather around Soma, for he is the most glorious. Soma desired that glory for himself; he went to the mountain, and Agni followed after him.
Through the word *gir*, Agni and Soma came into being; therefore, Agni always burns with *gir* (song), and Soma is in the *giri* (mountain).
Indra, however, felt as if he were weak. He went to Agni and Soma and said to them, "Sacrifice for me.
Agni and Soma sacrificed for him with this [rite]; Agni bestowed brilliance upon him, and Soma bestowed sensory power (*indriya*). Thereupon, he became Indra.
One who desires prosperity should cause him to sacrifice with this [offering]; Agni bestows splendor upon him, and Soma bestows sensory power.

One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake of *śyāmāka* grain on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma in the spring; for Agni and Soma are indeed the bestowers of spiritual luster. He approaches them with their own portion, and they grant him spiritual luster.
One should sacrifice in spring while bestowing [the gift]. Spring is indeed the season of the Brāhmaṇa; thus, he bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon him in his own season.

In that there is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), by that it belongs to Agni; in that there is śyāmāka grain, by that it belongs to Soma. He has thus bestowed the entire oblation upon Agni and Soma together; they bestow upon him the entirety of spiritual luster. The two *saṃyājyā* verses should belong to Soma and Agni.

Agni is indeed brilliance (*tejas*), and Soma is the sense-power (*indriya*); by means of both brilliance and sense-power, he thus encompasses spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) on both sides for him.
One desiring cattle should offer a pap (*caru*) to Soma and Pūṣan, half-ground; Soma is indeed the placer of seed, and Pūṣan is the progenitor of cattle;
Soma bestows seed upon him, and Pūṣan procreates cattle. [He should offer] a pap to Soma and Indra.

One who desires the office of domestic priest should offer [this sacrifice]. The Brāhmaṇa has Soma as his deity, and the Rājanya has Indra; indeed, Soma bestows non-falling-off. He approaches him with his own share, and he bestows upon him a kingdom from which there is no falling-off.

One who, having committed an offense against an equal, is afflicted by disease, or who commits falsehood—since he who offends an equal commits falsehood—should offer a *caru* oblation to Agni and Varuṇa.

This man who acts falsely offends the deity; Agni is indeed all the deities, and thus he releases him from whichever deity he has offended. Since it belongs to Varuṇa, he thereby releases him from Varuṇa.
This is indeed a swift rite: the *aveṣṭi* for everything, the atonement for everything.

One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a pap of white rice cooked in ghee to Soma and Rudra. Indeed, Svarbhānu the Asura pierced the sun with darkness; Soma and Rudra healed it, and by means of this very [offering], they removed its impurity (*śamala*) and placed vital energy (*tejas*) within it. One who desires spiritual luster should cause such a person to sacrifice with this [rite]; [it removes] his impurity.

Thus he strikes away its brilliance and places it within him. This oblation-pot (caru) consists of rice; for the self is only so great as this, and thus he places brilliance in him to the full extent of his self. The rice grains are white, and white cows are milked for the clarified butter (ājya); thus brilliance itself is gathered together.
Ghee is used for sprinkling, they purify themselves with ghee, and the offering is in ghee; in this way, he increases his brilliance even further.

He bestows splendor upon him who is about to sacrifice on the morning of that night; they should not throw water into his house during that night, for water is indeed peace—it would surely pacify [the heat]. They cause the sacrifice to be performed in an enclosed space for the sake of enclosing the splendor. They proceed with the ritual together with the rays [of the sun]; thus they drive away his impurity together with the rays. One should cause the sacrifice to be performed at the full moon of the Tiṣya constellation; Soma...

The moon is indeed Rudra Tiṣya; he approaches these [plants] at this very time. The plants belonging to Soma face eastward, while those belonging to Rudra face westward; for they do not wither facing eastward, but they wither facing westward. The verses belong to Manu; whatever Manu spoke was indeed medicine—he spoke it for the sake of being medicine. These [verses] are the Śakvarīs.

The *nārāśaṃsa* verses are used for power and for peace; indeed, his fear arises from being afflicted by consumption, for he strikes it away. One desiring cattle should offer a pap of rice to Soma and Pūṣan, half-ground. The Brāhmaṇa has Soma as his deity, and cattle belong to Pūṣan;
thus he causes his own deity to increase through cattle. He has indeed fashioned a skin.

*ati*: [FN emended]. Ed: One practicing sorcery should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra made of black rice. For plants belong to Soma; thus, having extorted him from them, he delivers his cattle over to Rudra. The rice is black; black is indeed darkness.

Death is darkness; by means of death itself he causes him to grasp it. The sacrificial grass is made of *śara* reeds, and the fuel is of *vaibhīdaka* wood; [the mantra says] "May he pierce," for the *śara* grass serves as sacrificial grass for piercing, and the *vaibhīdaka* fuel is for splitting. One who desires, "May I be born a second time in this world," should offer a pap of rice-grains that have not been winnowed to Soma and Rudra, with the formula "The one who goes upward. Or [it may be] those belonging to Soma.

These creatures produce for him a second [self] in this world; neither is this sacrificial grass made of *śara* nor is it made of non-*śara*, neither is the fuel-stick made of *vaibhīdaka* nor is it made of non-*vaibhīdaka*; thus he produces for him a second [self] in this world. He should offer a curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) to Soma and Rudra; he should cause one who is ill to sacrifice. For he who has died belongs to Agni, while he who lives belongs to Soma; from both sides, therefore, he [the sacrificer] [is protected].
Milk indeed is man; milk fails him when he is ill. By means of milk, one ransoms his milk.
The Hotṛ priest should have his eyes bound; having led him away into the forest, one should cause him to be proclaimed. One should give him an ox; one should kill it and eat of it.
If one were not to eat of it, he would die.

One who practices sorcery, or against whom sorcery is practiced, should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; he should also sacrifice to Sarasvatī with clarified butter. Agni is indeed all the deities; thus, by means of the deities, he counteracts his deities. Viṣṇu is the sacrifice;

thus, by means of the sacrifice, he counteracts the sacrifice. Sarasvatī is speech; thus, by means of speech, he counteracts speech. This is done for the purpose of counteracting the sorcery, and furthermore, for the purpose of counteracting it.

One who desires sight should offer a caru-oblation of rice cooked in ghee to Agni and Viṣṇu, as has been previously prescribed. Agni indeed is the bestower of sight upon men, and Viṣṇu is the bestower of sight upon the gods; these two are truly the bestowers of sight. He approaches them with their respective portions, and they grant him sight. Ghee is indeed the milk of the cow, and rice grains are the milk of the ox; that is a pair, for a pair is productive of offspring.
By means of a pair, they produce for him a pair, the eye; ghee is indeed milk, and the eye is milk; by means of milk, they produce for him milk, the eye;
ghee is indeed brilliance, and the eye is brilliance; by means of brilliance, they produce for him brilliance, the eye.
He gives gold; gold is indeed life, and the eye is life; by means of life, he bestows upon him life, the eye—a hundred-māna weight.

A man indeed lives for a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold vigor; he thus attains both life and vigor. One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu. Agni is indeed all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus, for the sake of overcoming both the deities and the sacrifice, he enters into their midst. In battle, one should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, and also to Sarasvatī.

One should sacrifice with clarified butter; for Agni is indeed all the deities. By means of the deities, he drives away his [rival's] deities. Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice, he [drives away] the sacrifice. Sarasvatī is speech; by means of speech, he [drives away] speech. If he should think, "She moves forward against me," he should make two invitatory verses (*puronuvākyā*) and one offering verse (*yājyā*). By means of the two, it is made equal; by means of the one, he overcomes. [He offers] to Agni and Viṣṇu.

In the morning, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati; at midday, a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati; in the afternoon, a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati—for one whose rival is sacrificing with Soma. Agni, indeed, is all.

By means of the deities themselves, he obtains the deities of this [sacrifice]: Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and by the sacrifice he obtains the sacrifice; Sarasvatī is speech, and by speech he obtains speech;
Bṛhaspati is the Brahman, and by the Brahman itself he obtains the Brahman of this [sacrifice]. By means of the potsherds he obtains the meters, and by the sacrificial cakes the pressings.
He should offer a cake on one potsherd to Mitra and Varuṇa, or a dish of curd (payasyā); by this he obtains the Anūbandhyā cow. This is the Adhvarakalpa-iṣṭi.
By this [verse], one attains the sacrifice itself.
One desiring rain should offer a *caru* oblation to Agni and the Maruts. They should prepare both the *caru* and the water-jar from the same clay.

In whichever fire they cook the *caru*, in that same fire they should fumigate the jar; for its smoke goes to yonder sky, but its flame does not. Therefore, they fumigate it but do not cook it. When they have set down the sacrificial offerings, then they place the jar on the southern buttock [of the altar].

If they should fill [the vessels] with water upon reaching them, he should say, "It will rain today before the sacrifice concludes. If [they do so] when the sacrifice has concluded, he should say, "It will rain tomorrow. If it should rain as if after a long time, he should say, "We do not know for certain. Indeed, Agni prays for rain from here, and the Maruts cause it to fall from there; these are the givers of rain, and he approaches them with their respective portions.
They bestow rain upon him. One who desires a village or desires cattle should offer a pap of millet cooked in milk to the Maruts;
it should be prepared in the milk of spotted cows, and its ghee should be from spotted cows. Therein, they should also drop some cow-urine.
For that which the spotted cow milked became millet; this spotted cow is indeed Speech, and this is her milk.

Because he approaches her with Priyaṅgu seeds as her own milk, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word "dear" (*priya*); thus he makes him dear among his kinsmen. There are both two-footed and four-footed [verses]; verily, he wins for himself both two-footed and four-footed cattle. Just as a calf goes toward the udder, or as a cow toward her calf, so do his kinsmen [approach him].
They approach one another. He should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to the Maruts for one whose twin sons or twin cattle are born.

For a man who has a twin [son] aspires to the state of being without virility; a cow that has a twin [calf] aspires to the state of being without offspring. In that there are thirteen potsherds—Prajāpati is indeed the thirteenth—he thereby attains Prajāpati himself. In that there are twelve, he attains him through the year. As for the fact that the invitatory verse is in the Gāyatrī metre...

Because the *jagatī* was used as the *yājyā* for the year, it was for the sake of cattle; because the *mārutī* sacrifice was performed, it was for the sake of cattle. He should offer a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts where the common people (*viṭ*) might seek to harm the king. The *sāmidhenīs*, as well as the *yājyās* and *anuvākyās*, should belong to Agastya. Indeed, Agastya consecrated bulls for the Maruts and offered them to Indra; they [the bulls] were [then] slaughtered.

Taking up the thunderbolt, he rushed at them; with this [offering] he pacified them, and with this he pacifies them now. It consists of seven potsherds, for there are seven Maruts; he pacifies them by means of their own share.
One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts; one should cause a Rājanya who desires prosperity to sacrifice.

For the Rājanya has Indra as his deity and the people (viś) have the Maruts as their deity; verily by means of his own power (*indriya*), he brings the people under his control for him, and makes the people obedient and free from dispute to him.
One who [desires this] should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
If he should desire, "May I create strife between the commoners and the nobility," he should recite the verse for Indra over the offering for Indra and sacrifice with the verse for the Maruts;

he should recite the verse for the Maruts over the offering for the Maruts and sacrifice with the verse for Indra. Thus, he creates strife among them regarding their own respective portions. If he should desire, "May there be mutual confusion," he should place one cow from another community in the eastern half [of the altar] and the other in the rear half.

If he should desire, "May they both come together and may there be no confusion," he should offer these two oblations and sacrifice according to their respective order; then it succeeds for him. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on seven potsherds to the Maruts when performing sorcery.
He should take the portion from the Indra-oblation above and from the Marut-oblation below; thus he sets them ablaze from both sides.
One should cause a Kṣatriya who desires a village to sacrifice with an offering to Indra on eleven potsherds and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Maruts.

Having placed the sacrificial cake in the middle of the curdled milk, he should take portions from both. Indra is indeed the nobility (kṣatra) and the Maruts are the common people (viś); thus he enters the midst of the common people. He takes the portions by surrounding them; verily, by means of the common people, he surrounds him.
One practicing sorcery should offer a cake on twenty-one potsherds to the Maruts. The Maruts are indeed the host of gods, and a host does not slay what has been surrendered.
Having thus extorted him from the very host of gods, he lays him low. Having placed it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), he should strike it through the middle with the wooden sword (sphya).
With this thunderbolt of Indra, I cut off the head of such-and-such a person, the son of such-and-such a person.
Thus, with the very thunderbolt of Indra he cuts off his head; and as for the wooden sword—the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt—he lays him low with the thunderbolt itself.
Embracing the tiger, they groom the lion for great wealth;
they groom our well-formed buffalo standing firm, and the leopard within the waters.
Thus, the waters are indeed the thunderbolt; in that this sacrificial formula contains the word "apsumat" (containing water), he strikes him down with the thunderbolt itself.

One whose well-known sacrifice should be delayed should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Way). He who has his well-known sacrifice delayed goes astray from the path. Agni is indeed the maker of the way for the gods; he approaches him with his own portion, and he leads him back onto the path. An ox is the sacrificial fee, for it carries one along the path. [He should offer] to Agni Vratapati (Lord of Vows)...

"One who, having established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), goes on a journey, should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*). For he who, having established the sacred fires, goes on a journey, greatly transgresses his vow; for on a day when the vow is in force, he approaches a woman or eats meat. Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods; he approaches him with his own share, and he causes him to adhere to his vow for Agni."

One who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and sheds tears should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati. He who has established the fires is indeed led toward the gods; therefore, he must not shed tears, for the gods do not shed tears. Agni is the guardian of vows (*vratabhṛt*) among the gods, and it was to Agni that his vow went; therefore, he offers this victim as a substitute for his vow. [He should also offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha.
One who is being practiced against with sorcery should offer oblations; by means of those very applications with which the other practices against him, Agni Yaviṣṭha drives them away from him.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vājasṛt in battle; for he who desires to win a battle desires to win booty (*vāja*). Agni is indeed among the gods the winner of booty; he [Agni] approaches him with his own share, and he [Agni] bestows it upon him.

One should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Anīkavant for one who runs after booty in battle. Whatever front of Agni goes astray, that cannot be withstood; Agni himself wins the fronts for him. He should also sacrifice to Viṣṇu with clarified butter;
for from there Viṣṇu won these worlds; following Viṣṇu’s victory, he wins these worlds and prevails over them.

He who desires, "May I shut away his cattle from Rudra," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rudravat; for Agni is indeed Rudra, and thus he shuts away his cattle from Rudra himself. If he should desire, "May he be appeased," he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat; for that which is fragrant is the healing body of Agni.
He has indeed made medicine for him; he has made him fragrant. He pacifies Agni, the possessor of food, the eater of food, and the lord of food.

He who desires, "May I be possessed of food, an eater of food, and a lord of food," should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. Agni, indeed, among the gods, is the possessor of food, the eater of food, and the lord of food. He approaches him with his own portion; he [Agni] makes him possessed of food, an eater of food, and a lord of food.
He performs [it].

One who fears demons should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the demon-slayer. Indeed, the demons attached themselves to Indra; he entered into Agni, and they seized him from all sides. He produced those drops which scatter when [the oblation] is being stirred. Those [demons] were indeed driven away by Agni himself. Agni is the slayer of demons among the gods; by him alone one drives away the demons.
One should perform the sacrifice at night; for the *rakṣas* set forth at night, and when they set forth, it is then that one strikes them down.

There should be fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses and *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses belonging to Vāmadeva. Vāmadeva and Kusitāyī once engaged in a race; then Kusitāyī cut off the pole of Vāmadeva’s chariot, and she plunged away into the water.
Thinking, "I will cut their yoke, or their pole," he looked at the fire in the pan (ukhya). He saw this mantra; its flame blazed up.

Being consumed by that flame, it entered a lake. That lake was indeed the Kausita; by means of it, he struck down the Rakṣases. Thus, by this very act, one strikes down the Rakṣases. One who [seeks to establish] himself in the kingdom should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni.

Whoever should desire, "May I be an eater of food," [should perform this]. Indeed, the gods and the Asuras were in rivalry. Gāyatrī, having encompassed all food, stood between them. They knew: "Whichever side she will join, theirs shall this world become. Both sides desired her; they sought to win her by means of their names.
"Dābhi!"—thus the Asuras called out.
O Viśvakarman!
Thus the gods [spoke]; she did not turn toward either side. The gods appropriated her by means of this sacrificial formula (yajus).

You are vigor, you are endurance, you are strength, you are splendor; you are the abode of the gods by name; you are the universe, you are the life of the universe; you are all, you are the life of all, the overcomer.

Thus, the Gāyatrī is indeed the year; the year stood firm there. They appropriated that food of theirs for a year. Therefore, by this means, the sacrificer appropriates the food of his rival for a year. This is the Gāyatrī sacrifice;
moreover, they say it is "the seizure of the kingdom."

One who is a ruler but does not attain preeminence should offer an oblation to Indra and Bṛhaspati. Aditi indeed cooked a mess of rice for her offspring; she ate the remains, and while Indra was still within the womb, she bound him with an iron fetter.
Bound thus, he was born. Bṛhaspati caused him to sacrifice with this very offering to Indra and Bṛhaspati.

That rope of his broke of its own accord; he then turned around these quarters with the thunderbolt. One who is a ruler of a kingdom but cannot prevail should sacrifice for him with this offering to Indra and Bṛhaspati. For he is indeed encompassed on all sides by evil and thus does not prevail. An oblation is offered to Bṛhaspati and prepared for Indra; it releases him from every side with the thunderbolt. These [quarters]...
It revolves around the quarters.
O Ādityas, I shall prepare a portion for you; cause such-and-such a person, the son of such-and-such, to understand this.

Thus he should say when about to pour out the oblation; he should offer this pap of ghee to Āditya. For these creatures belong to Āditya; he approaches them, and they lead him forward. Seven shoots of the *aśvattha* tree should lie within the altar; when the sacrifice is completed, he should fix them into the middle hole of the chariot-stand.
"Here I bind the Ādityas for the sake of the attainment of such-and-such."

Thus, he binds these [stems] to the Ādityas; they, being released, cause him to attain [his goal]. Vital energy departed from the people (viś); it entered the aśvattha tree; by that vital energy it became "bharbharā. By this [rite], he wins for himself the vital energy of the people.
If he does not attain [success] in seven [days], he should add those [stems] to the fuel-wood and offer this very oblation. For these [worlds] belong to the Ādityas.

He should approach those very *prajā* (progeny) [verses]; they cause him to attain [his goal]. If he should attain it in the seven [verses]—for thrice seven is indeed seven—he should approach those very Ādityas; they cause him to attain [his goal]. If he should attain it in the *ekatayīs* or the *dvayīs*, they would be likely to obstruct him;
but when he attains it in all [the verses], thus he attains it without being obstructed. When he should attain it...

Then he should offer a pap of cooked rice with ghee to the Ādityas who uphold [the world]. The Ādityas are indeed the repellers; the Ādityas are the ones who cause one to understand. They establish him firmly.
O Aditi, give your consent; may the blessing of truth be here in this mind.
Thus, when the king has been overthrown, whoever among those previously acting like commoners might seize his position, they should surround the windward side of his assembly hall and destroy it.
O self-strong Maruts, with these [songs], protect that king as the lord of the people.
Thus, they should bring rice from his house; he should divide it into three parts. Those that are black, having bound them upon a black antelope skin, he should set them aside.

Those that are white, he should offer as a pap of ghee to Āditya. For these creatures belong to Āditya; thus he approaches them, and they lead him to success. Then, those [grains] from which he has separated [the others], having gone northward and dug up an anthill, he should sacrifice them.
Whatever terrible seat of yours I offer today for the sake of releasing these bonds—
O you whom people joyfully hail as "the Earth," yet I know you from every side to be Nirṛti.

Thus, he who is obstructed is indeed seized by Nirṛti; by this [rite], he releases him from Nirṛti. When the people have gone away, his sovereignty has followed after them. Therefore, he should offer a *caru* of black rice cooked in ghee to Varuṇa.
Varuṇa is indeed the king of the gods; he is the one who causes sovereignty to be attained. He approaches that very deity with his own share, and he (Varuṇa) [releases] him.
This makes one understand sovereignty; for it belongs to various subjects. By means of this, one understands both types of subjects:
the divine and the human.

[Page II,16] One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of white rice to Sūrya in ghee. There should be a gold ornament weighing a hundred *mānas* beneath, and a silver ornament weighing a hundred *mānas* above; for indeed, this sun was here. It—

Having grasped them with these two, they placed them above these creatures; for yonder sun is above these creatures, lest he should sit upon them. The silver one is this [earth] and the golden one is yonder [sky]. Having grasped him with these two, he places him above these creatures, so that he sits above these creatures. He should also offer five *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces during the *prayāja* offerings.

By means of these, this Āditya follows these five seasons; he makes him radiant by means of these very five directions. One who desires long life should offer an oblation of ghee and a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces to Prajāpati. Having slain the Asuras, the gods were afraid of death; those gods then sought refuge with Prajāpati, and Prajāpati caused them to sacrifice with this [offering]. Thereupon...

The gods attained immortality; gold is indeed immortality, and life is immortality. Having obtained immortal life for them by means of immortality, he established it. One who desires long life should sacrifice with this [offering]. This indeed is the immortality of a human being: that he reaches his full span of life.
Gold is indeed immortality, and life is immortality. By means of immortality, he obtains immortal life for him and bestows it upon him.

By this, he reaches his full lifespan and does not die before his time; he becomes one possessing a hundred *kṛṣṇalas*, for man has a hundred-year life and a hundredfold vigor; verily, he attains both life and vigor. He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas* each for the sake of prosperity. He says, "All must be handed over to the Brahman"; thus he establishes the entire sacrifice in the Brahman, and the Brahman [establishes] everything in him.
He bestows vigor; moreover, the Brahman is indeed the Brahmā; by means of the Brahman, the Brahmā bestows the lifespan of the Brahman upon him.

One who desires the office of a domestic priest should offer a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati. For him, there should be two verses for the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, containing the word "light" (*jyotiṣmatī*), addressed to Bṛhaspati.

Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; the one addressed to Bṛhaspati is a Brāhmaṇa by deity. Thus, he approaches his own deity for the sake of the office of a domestic priest, and his own deity leads him to that office. That which flickers as it were and shines is light; therefore, [these verses should contain the word "light"].

If one who possesses the light (the Brahmin) should not go before [as a domestic priest], he should offer an oblation to Indra and Bṛhaspati; thus he has united both the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*), and they immediately place him at their head. He who desires a village or desires cattle should offer a pap (*caru*) to Bṛhaspati in milk; for that offering to Bṛhaspati, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses should contain the word "host" (*gaṇa*), if he is one who has many followers.

They should fetch milk from his house; it should be the milk of his own cows, and water—this very nourishment is thereby gathered. Bṛhaspati is indeed Brahman, and Bṛhaspati is the meters; through the meters Bṛhaspati is possessed of a host. Thus he endows his own deity with abundance and makes him possessed of a host through his kinsmen. One should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) dedicated to Brāhmaṇaspati.

In battle, for one seeking the favor of Brahmaṇaspati, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses should be those addressed to him, containing the words "heroic" (*vīravatī*) and "possessing strength" (*vayasvatī*). He should perform the *darśa* sacrifice with a roof-covering as the offering material;

the *barhis* grass should be the *prastara* bundle, and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be provided with arrows. When the birds enter the next village, he should know: "I shall be victorious. For Brahmaṇaspati is indeed the Brahman; he has resorted to the Brahman, [offering] that which belongs to Brahmaṇaspati.

One should offer a *caru* oblation wherever he should desire, "May there be the power of the *brahman*. For that [offering], the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākye*) should belong to Brahmaṇaspati and the Maruts. Brahmaṇaspati is indeed the *brahman*, and the Maruts are the people (*viś*). He thus establishes the people upon the *brahman* for the sake of firmness and to prevent looseness.

One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* oblation of *garmut* beans to Bṛhaspati. Prajāpati created cattle; once they were created, they went away from him. Bṛhaspati and [Prajāpati] pursued them, and where they halted, from that place the *śakna-garmut* was born. *Lelāyat*: Corrections and conjectures for the entire work. One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* oblation of *garmut* beans to Bṛhaspati. Prajāpati created cattle; once they were created, they went away from him. Bṛhaspati and [Prajāpati] pursued them, and where they halted, from that place the *śakna-garmut* was born.
He said to him, "Sacrifice for me with this. He sacrificed for him with it; cattle came to him.

For one who desires cattle, he should sacrifice with this; indeed, cattle come to him. When he sacrificed for him with this, then cattle came to him. One desiring cattle should offer a pap of *garmut* beans to Soma and Pūṣan. Prajāpati—

He created cattle; once they were created from him, they went away from him. He made Pūṣan their guardian. Wherever they settled, from that place the śakna-garmut was born. He took it, thinking, "By this may I have a firm foundation. Soma said, "Mine indeed is that which ripens without being ploughed. He offered it as a sacrifice to Soma and Pūṣan. The cattle returned to him; he who desires cattle [should perform this].

One should cause him who desires cattle to sacrifice with this [offering]; indeed, cattle turn toward him. For when Soma caused him to sacrifice with this, then cattle turned toward him. Soma is the bestower of seed; Pūṣan is the progenitor of cattle;
Soma bestows seed upon him, and Pūṣan procreates cattle. One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* oblation of *garmut* beans to Prajāpati, using spotted grains.

There should be the milk of spotted cows and the clarified butter of spotted cows; there too, they should add drops of cow’s urine. For that which she, the spotted one, milked became *garmut*. This earth is indeed the spotted one, or rather, speech is the spotted one; and this *garmut* is her head. Therefore, it is like an egg and like colostrum. One desiring cattle should offer this *caru* oblation to Prajāpati, for cattle belong to Prajāpati.

Paśus is Prajāpati, the progenitor of cattle; he approaches him with his own portion, and he (Prajāpati) procreates cattle for him. One should offer a *caru* of *vāstūmaya* grain to Rudra where Rudra might afflict the offspring. For *vāstūmaya* is born from the dwelling (*vāstu*), and *vāstūmaya* indeed belongs to Rudra; verily, he pacifies him with his own portion.
With that [sacrifice], one should cause the Niṣāda chief to sacrifice; for that is his iṣṭi; the sacrificial fee is either a piece of wood or a donkey with an ear cut off.
One who desires, "May I become a supreme lord," should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Parameṣṭhin.

For he who is a supreme lord among the gods is indeed Parameṣṭhin, and the kṣatriya who is a supreme lord among men is Parameṣṭhin. He approaches him with his own portion; he makes him a supreme lord. To him he should present a bow and three arrows.
May Agni bestow splendor upon you, Indra bestow sensory power, and the paternal kinship.

Thus Agni indeed bestows brilliance upon him, Indra bestows sensory power, and the ancestral kinship [bestows] the Vaiśvadeva offering on twelve potsherds. One who has rivals should offer this; having placed it upon the sacrificial grass, he should strike it through the middle with the wooden sword.
This I separate from both myself and that [other].

Thus, whatever he should hate—if that [clod] should sink down or if it should stick to the wooden sword (sphya)—he should offer it to Viṣṇu Urukrama; Viṣṇu himself strides between them. He should then gather it back together, saying:
"Here I gather myself and him."

Thus, whoever may be dear to him—for these creatures belong to the Viśvedevas—he separates the other [enemy] by means of them and unites himself with them. He should offer a *caru* oblation to Indrāṇī when the army is rising up; for Indrāṇī is the army. By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), he sharpens it from the front for the sake of victory. There should be *balbaja* grass in the fuel, or these [grass-blades] should be placed upon the fire-sticks; thus he brings her into subjection through the proper method.
Whatever one might obtain in that army, that is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). One who desires prosperity should offer a pap (caru) to Vācaspati.
He who is indeed the overseer of speech is Vācaspati; this is truly a means for achieving prosperity.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus, a *caru* of millet to Soma accompanied by the Rudras, a cake on eleven potsherds of *nīvāra* rice to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and a *caru* of barley to Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas. The gods, each striving for preeminence over the other, went forth in four divisions: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, and Indra with the Maruts.

Varuṇa, together with the Ādityas, had Bṛhaspati perform this very sacrifice for them, the Saṃjñānī; they then turned toward Indra and reached a common understanding regarding Indra. Therefore, those who perform this sacrifice turn toward him and reach a common understanding regarding him. Regarding this, they say:
"An offering on eleven potsherds should be made for Indra," for it was toward Indra that they turned and it was regarding Indra that they reached a common understanding.
May there be consciousness for our cattle by day, and consciousness for our horses by night.
Grant us recognition from our own kin, recognition from strangers; O Aśvins, bestow upon us here that recognition.
O Indra, may we grasp wealth, may we grasp nourishment, may we grasp spoils that are many-glittering and resplendent;
may we grasp divine providence, which is rich in heroic vigor, preeminent in cattle, and abundant in horses.
We invoke Indra and Vāyu, who are beautiful to behold and easy to call, here with this [offering] consisting of cows and excellent horses.
So that all people may be well-disposed toward us at our gathering.
Your minds have been brought together, your vows have been brought together, and your intentions have been made to accord. Those of you who are of contrary intent, we cause them to submit to you.
Alike indeed are your intentions, alike are your hearts; let your mind be one, so that you may act in perfect harmony.
The mantra is common, the assembly is common, the vow is common, and their thought is shared.
Address yourselves with a common purpose; I offer for you with a common oblation.
Come together, agree with one another; let your minds be in harmony, as the gods of old, being in agreement, attend to their portion.

One whose gold is lost, or who finds gold, should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, a *caru* to Savitṛ, barley-gruel or fresh milk-curd to Vāyu, and a cake on one potsherd to the Earth. For Agni first found the gold;
he addressed Savitṛ, [saying], "There is indeed nothing whatsoever that has not been reached by Vāyu. It was upon this earth that he [found it].

The cake for Agni is for the sake of finding through the act of finding; that for Savitṛ is for instigation; that for Vāyu is for leading forward. Now, as for the one for the Earth: he found it on this earth, for she indeed found it there. These are indeed the givers; he approaches them with their own share, and they bestow it upon him.
When he has found it, then he should offer these very cakes to those by whom he found it; thus he makes them sharers, so that there may be no injury.

Prajāpati gave his daughters, the constellations, to King Soma. He dwelt only with Rohiṇī and not with the others. The others, being neglected, went back to him. He seized him with *rājayakṣma* (kingly consumption), and he flowed away. Therefore, one seized by *rājayakṣma* flows away. He indeed fled to Prajāpati; Prajāpati said to him, "Speak the truth! He spoke the truth.
He said, "May I dwell equally in all [the nights]. Therefore, he dwells equally in all of them.
For him, Prajāpati sought an atonement; for him, he offered a *vaiśvadeva* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
By that, he found atonement for him. He swelled along with that which was swelling; he became more prosperous. Whoever...
He would be seized by consumption; therefore, on the new moon day, he should offer a *caru* oblation to the Viśvedevas. By this means, indeed, he found the atonement for him;
by that very means he finds atonement for him. Following that very [moon] as it waxes, he himself waxes; he becomes more prosperous.

Prajāpati indeed apportioned the sacrificial portions to the gods. Indra said, "Whatever remains over, that shall be mine. That which remained was indeed the *indriya* (vital power). It rose upward through these worlds; he could not reach it with one [verse], nor with two. Having reached it with the third, he secured it. As for there being three sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), it is for these [worlds].

Verily, having obtained and secured from these worlds power and vigor, each subsequent sacrificial cake becomes larger, for each subsequent world is larger. The first is for Indra the King, the middle one is for Indra the Self-Ruler, and the last is for Indra the Overlord;
for Indra indeed became all these—sovereignty, self-rule, and overlordship. He who [performs this] becomes all these.

He who knows thus sacrifices with these [verses] and becomes this whole world. Having recited the first [verse], he should sacrifice with the middle one; having recited the middle one, he should sacrifice with the last one; having recited the last one, he should sacrifice with the first one. In this way, all [the verses] become his invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) and all become the offering verses (*yājyā*). This is for the sake of the recognition of these worlds, and also for their continuity. [The verse is: "To Indra, accompanied by the Gharma and by Sūrya..."
One desiring splendor should offer a cake on eleven potsherds; for splendor is indeed the *gharma*, and splendor is the sun; verily, he secures splendor for himself.
One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, the possessor of power; for cattle are indeed power, and Indra is the giver of power.
He approaches him with his own portion; he bestows upon him power and cattle.
Regarding this:
one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*; he should perform this sacrifice for one who has been besieged.
For he who is besieged has reached the end; the *arka* is the end, and the *aśvamedha* is the end. By means of the end, he provides an end for him. A barren cow is the sacrificial fee.

Thinking, "Lest he bring me under his control," one who desires, "May I prosper among the people," should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*. For the people are the limit of prosperities; the *arka* is the limit, and the *aśvamedha* is the limit. By means of this limit, he establishes him within that limit. A cow is the sacrificial fee, thinking, "Lest he bring me under his control. [He should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*.

One whose prosperity has departed should offer [this sacrifice]; for when one reaches the end of prosperity, he becomes worse off. The *arka* is an end, and the *aśvamedha* is an end; having grasped the very end, he does not become worse off. He who desires, "May the great sacrifice come to me," should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*. These two indeed are Indra’s sacrificial bodies.

Arka and Aśvamedha—these two were indeed sacrificed; with them he performed the great sacrifice. One desiring prosperity should cause [a patron] to sacrifice: one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra possessed of heat (gharmavat) and possessed of the sun (sūryavat); [one should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra possessed of wrath (manyumat) and possessed of mind (manasvat); [one should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra possessed of power (indriyavat);
[one should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra possessed of Arka and possessed of Aśvamedha. This [is for one] desiring prosperity.
Or Indra’s heat and Sūrya; this is his wrath and this is his mind; this is his Indra and this is his power;
this is his Arka and this is his Aśvamedha. Indeed, Indra became all these;
he who sacrifices with these becomes all these; he who knows thus becomes all this.

One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc; he should cause one who is ill to sacrifice. This, indeed, is Indra’s healing body, namely Aṃhomuc. He approaches him with his own portion; he (Indra) releases him from distress.
One who fears loss through old age, death, or confinement should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Trātar. Indra is indeed the protector, Indra...

The one who has been seized by an enemy should approach that very [deity] with his own portion; he protects him. He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Anvṛjvan when there is a dispute among kinsmen. The kinsman who is the eldest is indeed power (*indriya*); verily, by means of power, he makes them submissive.
He should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Prababhru in battle. Indra, being tawny (*prababhru*), hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.
Prabhūvan indeed struck them; he strikes the thunderbolt at them. One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vaimṛdha in battle.

He who conquers in battle strikes down the adversaries (*mṛdhas*); having struck down the adversaries, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Abhimātighna in battle. He who conquers in battle slays the assailants (*abhimātīs*); [having slain] the assailants...
One who desires, "May I overcome [my enemies] and may there be safety for me," should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Hata-abhimātiṣāha (Indra, the slayer of those who attack).
Indeed, Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra; the Dānavas did not approve of it, but they approved of it through this sacrificial portion.
Thereupon he struck down his attackers; he struck down Vṛtra. Verily, he who conquers in battle strikes down Vṛtra.
That, indeed, is the slaying of Vṛtra.
[He offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Vaimṛdha.
(FN emended. Ed: vai mṛdhāyaikādaśakapālaṃ)

One who has been besieged should offer a cake on one potsherd to Indra; for him, the invitatory and offering verses should be "Come forward from the furthest distance" and [the other]. For he who is besieged has indeed gone to the furthest distance; having reached him from the furthest distance, it causes him to come back. One who has been besieged should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to Indra; for the thirteenth is redundant, and the besieged one is redundant.

Having obtained the redundant from that which is redundant, he causes it to reach him. One whose rival is performing a *soma* sacrifice should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Slayer of Vṛtra, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Overcomer of Vṛtra.
He who sacrifices with *soma* raises up a thunderbolt against his rival; in that [offering] to Indra the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, by means of the thunderbolt itself, he [strikes] him.

He strews the *vajra* for Vṛtrahan; Vṛtra is indeed the rival, and he thus slays him. For Vṛtratūr, [he strews it]; Vṛtra is indeed the rival, and he thus overcomes him. He who disputes over a field or cattle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Kṣetrajit. Indra is indeed the field-conqueror among the gods; he approaches him with his own portion, and he (Indra) [grants it] to him.
One who desires to win fields and cattle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Ādhirāja where kings are as if equal.
Indra is indeed the overlord (*adhirāja*) of the gods; he approaches him with his own share, and he causes him to attain overlordship.
One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Manyumat Manasvat in battle; for by fury (manyu) valor is performed and by power (indriya) one conquers.
Thus he bestows both valor and power upon them for the sake of victory. One should offer a pap (caru) to Manyu in battle;
for by fury valor is performed. Thus he bestows valor upon them for the sake of victory, [in the case] of one whom they should capture alive.

They would cut him down; indeed, he has truly performed this for Indra with his mind through wrath. He who desires, "May I be prosperous and unassailable," should offer a cake on eleven potsherds. Mind is indeed prosperity and splendor; verily, he bestows prosperity and splendor upon him.
For one year he must not mention [the name] before the mind; for by a year that which is unattained is attained, and by means of the year itself, he [attains it].
Having obtained glory, he bestows radiance.
If the moon should rise over one for whom the *sānnāyya* has been prepared, he should divide those rice-cakes (*puroḍāśa*) intended for the sacrifice into three parts.

Of these, he should offer the middle-sized ones as an eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Dātṛ; the largest ones as a pap (*caru*) of curds to Indra Pradātṛ; and the smallest ones as a pap of boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. For Agni is the giver of the middle-sized portion, and Indra is the giver of the large.

Now, that which is the smallest portion given to the eldest is Śipiviṣṭa; he obtains cattle thereby. Indeed, Soma overflows for him whose *sānnāyya* offering the moon rises upon; he who desires cattle truly overflows with cattle himself.
He who desires cattle should, after performing the sacrifice on the new-moon day, drive away the calves; those that are fit for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he should divide into three parts.

He should perform [the sacrifice]. Those [grains] which are the smallest, he should offer as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Samanamat; those which are of medium size, he should offer as a cooked mess (*caru*) in boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; those which are the largest, he should offer as a curd-mess (*dadhi-caru*) to Indra Pradātṛ. Agni indeed finds for him that which is here [on earth], Viṣṇu that which is in the intermediate space, and Indra that which is in heaven; thus the warriors seek cattle.

When these rice grains are being divided, these beings are indeed the seekers and the appropriators. One who has attained prosperity should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; a cow that has calved for the first time is the sacrificial fee for this. Having gone forward to the east, he should offer a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu;

a mare that has calved for the first time is the sacrificial fee for this. Having gone forward to the east and having reached a mountain, or else water, he should offer a pap cooked in ghee to Prajāpati.
A man’s cow is its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In that it belongs to Agni, he thereby steps upon this [earth]; in that it belongs to Viṣṇu, he thereby [steps upon] the intermediate space;

in that it belongs to Prajāpati, he thereby [steps upon] yonder world. In that he proceeds facing eastward, he has indeed stepped toward [the goal]; in that he goes to the mountain or to the waters, he has indeed arrived at the end. In that three cows are the sacrificial fees—and these worlds are three—he [bestows] these worlds upon him.

The cow made these worlds yield for him; indeed, these worlds yield what is given to him who knows thus. One should offer a sacrificial pap of *śyāmāka* grain to Soma-Indra for one who has vomited Soma. Indra, it is said, drank Tvaṣṭṛ’s Soma without being invited;
his Soma-draught fell upward and became these *śyāmāka* grains. This [sacrificer] is indeed possessed of the Soma-draught.

He who vomits Soma is deprived [of it]; when there is an offering to Soma, he thereby satisfies him with the very drinking of Soma. He who vomits Soma is deprived of sensory power and vigor; when there is an offering to Indra, he thereby satisfies him with sensory power and vigor. For his drinking of Soma has become as it were loose, and thus he vomits Soma; when he mixes it with the grains of *śyāmāka* millet, [he thereby strengthens it].
For the support of the drinking of Soma.

In this case: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a dish of curdled milk to Mitra and Varuṇa; one should cause one afflicted by disease to sacrifice for the sake of prosperity. Now, the offering to Agni is [for] prosperity;
furthermore, having made him possessed of bones, he establishes him. Indeed, the dish of curdled milk is liable to be unappeased without an animal victim."
Even a beast that has been wiped clean is to be sacrificed for the sake of peace and to prevent its being rubbed away. Indeed, rice and barley are these very beasts;
when there is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) made of rice, by that very means the beast is sacrificed for the sake of peace and to prevent its being rubbed away.

For a Brāhmaṇa, it should be dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa has Mitra and Varuṇa as his deity; for a Rājanya, it should be dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa, for the Rājanya has Indra and Varuṇa as his deity.

Indeed, the deity for the Rājanya should be Agni-Vāruṇa; for the Vaiśya, it should be Agni alone, since Agni is indeed all the deities. Here, one should cause even the Vaiśya who is afflicted by disease to sacrifice; he approaches his own deity as an expiation. For he who is diseased is seized by Varuṇa; by this [offering], he releases him from Varuṇa. Man is indeed milk; it is milk that afflicts him when he is diseased; thus, by means of milk, he heals him.
He redeems it with milk; for when he arranges [the oblations], they extract the barb from the middle after having cut it out, and so they extract this consumption (yakṣma) from his very center.

Then, when he has gathered them together again and makes the portions for Agni, it is just as when, having extracted a barb, they bind it with a turban—thus one should cause him who desires prosperity to sacrifice. He has approached his own deity for expiation, though seized by Varuṇa.

He who desires prosperity is indeed this [sacrifice]; by means of it, he releases him from Varuṇa. Man is indeed milk; he who desires prosperity desires milk. By means of milk, he secures milk for him. When he separates [the fires], it is for the protection of the sacrifice; then, when he brings them together again, he brings him together through prosperity. He should cause one who desires a village to sacrifice; by means of the expiation, he reaches his own deity.

He who desires a village is indeed seized by Varuṇa; verily, by this [offering], he releases him from Varuṇa. Man is indeed milk, and he who desires a village desires milk; verily, by means of milk, he secures milk for him. In that he separates [the fires], it is for the protection of the sacrifice;
and in that he brings them together again, he brings him together with the village. He offers oblations on single potsherds here and there.

These indeed are Varuṇa’s nooses; therefore, he releases him from them. If one were to offer the oblations separately, that would be a dragging away of the sacrifice. They should all be offered into the fire together for the sake of prosperity.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, with that body of yours which is powerful, we worship you; with that, release this man from distress.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, with that body of yours which is victorious, we worship you; with that, release this man from distress.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, with that body of yours which is to be invoked, we worship you; with that, release this man from distress. O Mitra and Varuṇa... [with that body of yours... we worship you; with that, release this man from distress.

With that body of yours which is demonic, with that we shall worship you; with that, release this one and that one from distress. O Mitra and Varuṇa, with that body of yours which is powerful, victorious, capable of attack, and demonic—with that we have worshipped you; with that, release this one and that one from distress. O King Varuṇa, that noose of yours which is among the gods, that I release for you by means of this [offering]; for that, Svāhā! O King Varuṇa, that [noose] of yours which is in food...

That noose of yours, O King Varuṇa, which is among bipeds and quadrupeds—by this [oblation] I appease it for you; to that of yours, svāhā! That noose of yours, O King Varuṇa, which is among plants, trees, waters, the earth, and the quarters—by this [oblation] I appease it for you; to that of yours, svāhā!
These indeed are the bonds of Varuṇa; therefore, he releases him from them.
One who has rivals should offer a *caru* oblation to the Viśve Devas. The gods and the Asuras were in conflict; those gods performed a sacrifice with a means of gathering (*saṃgrahaṇa*).

Whatever property of the Asuras there was, they gathered it together; indeed, they gathered their very minds. Being deprived of their minds, the Asuras were defeated. One who has rivals should sacrifice; for this is a seizing of the mind—it gathers the minds [of the enemies].

Verily, he thus seizes the minds of his rivals; they, being mindless, perish. One desiring a village should sacrifice; this is indeed a seizing of the mind. Verily, he thus seizes the minds of his kinsmen; they, their minds seized by him, do not depart from him. They should bring clarified butter from the houses of all his kinsmen—of as many as there are, however few. Of those from whose houses they bring the clarified butter, [their minds are likewise seized].
He wins over the minds of all; they, their minds won over by him, do not depart from him. He offers with *āmana*; he thus makes them well-disposed toward himself.

O God of Mindfulness, those who are my kinsmen, being of one mind, I desire them with my heart; may they desire me with their hearts; make them mindful of me, Svāhā! O God of Mindfulness, those who are my sons, being of one mind, I desire them with my heart; may they desire me with their hearts; make them mindful of me, Svāhā! O God of Mindfulness, those women who are of one mind...

I desire them with my heart; may they desire me with their hearts. Make them well-disposed toward me, Svāhā! O God, those animals that are well-disposed, I desire them with my heart; may they desire me with their hearts. Make them well-disposed toward me, Svāhā!

[Page II,29] These indeed are his own people—like kinsmen, like sons, like women, like cattle—with them he unites himself; through them he becomes [prosperous]. A spotted cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for she belongs to the Viśvedevas; and as for the fact that this is a sacrifice to the Viśvedevas...

These creatures indeed belong to the Viśvedevas; he has won them for himself and made them edible. The fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and after-sacrifices (*anuyāja*) are the outer self, while the deity is the inner self. If he were to offer either before or after the fore- and after-sacrifices, he would place his kinsmen outside of himself.
But since he offers in the middle, he places his kinsmen in the very center of his own self. If he should so desire, [they will be] swift.

If he should desire, "May they go quickly and depart," he should offer with a wooden [ladle], for trees are both moving and unmoving. But if he should desire, "May they be firm and depart only with difficulty," he should offer with one made of clay.

For this [earth] is firm; you are firm; may you be firm among the gods. May I be firm among my kinsmen, dear to my kinsmen, fierce, a perceiver, and a finder of wealth. May I be a conqueror among my kinsmen; may I be dear to my kinsmen—mighty, a guardian, and a finder of wealth.

You are the encompasser; be an encompasser among the gods. May I be an encompasser among my kinsmen; may I be dear to my kinsmen—mighty, a guardian, and a finder of wealth. You are a patron; be a patron among the gods. May I be a patron among my kinsmen; may I be dear [to them].
He is the fierce guardian of his kinsmen and the finder of wealth.
These indeed are the kinsmen; he places them in him and makes them not depart from him.
Now, this horse is accepted; once accepted, it indeed devours both his own power (*indriya*) and his cattle.

The horse belongs to Varuṇa and has Varuṇa as its deity; whoever accepts a horse, he falls into the power of Varuṇa. Therefore, one should sacrifice with an oblation of a horse to become free from Varuṇa’s grasp. There are four potsherds, for the horse is four-footed, [and it is freed] by means of the potsherds.

Thus he attains him; there are as many sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) as there are horses, for he thus releases him from all sides. One cake remains over; it is for that which he forgets. He who is about to receive [the horse] again should not sacrifice; for if he were to receive it again, he would fall back into Varuṇa’s power. Now, he who is about to receive it again...
Its border-stones should belong to Varuṇa; they should be border-stones belonging to both Sūrya and Varuṇa. In that they belong to Varuṇa, he thereby releases him from Varuṇa;

and in that they belong to Sūrya, he accepts his own deity for the sake of his own safety. There are twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses; this Āditya is the twenty-first, and Prajāpati is this Āditya; the horse belongs to Prajāpati—just as great as the horse is.
All other animals that have a womb and originate from the human womb attain it; the horse alone is without a womb, being born from the waters.
Since this oblation for Apām Napāt is a pap, he thereby makes him one who has a womb and establishes him in his own womb.

O King Varuṇa, that bond of yours which is in the Gāyatrī metre and established in the Brahmin, I release it from you with this; to it, Svāhā! O King Varuṇa, that bond of yours which is in the Triṣṭubh metre and established in the Kṣatriya, I release it from you with this;
to it, Svāhā! O King Varuṇa, that bond of yours which is in the Jagatī metre and established in the Vaiśya, I release it from you with this.
To that of yours, Svāhā! O King Varuṇa, that noṣṭubh-metered noose of yours which is established in the quarters—to that of yours I sacrifice with this; to that of yours, Svāhā!

The *chandāṃsi* are indeed Varuṇa’s nooses; with those by which he seizes him, he releases him. He offers two oblations with the verses addressed to Aponaptr; thus Varuṇa, who is of the waters, releases him from there.
You are the life-span of Agni; with that, grant life to this [person], to so-and-so. You are the breath of Indra;

grant breath to so-and-so, whose breath is yours—svāhā! You are the breath of the Fathers; grant breath to so-and-so, whose breath is yours—svāhā! You are the breath of the Viśve Devas; grant breath to so-and-so, whose breath is yours—svāhā! You are the breath of Bṛhaspati.
Give breath to this one, whose breath is yours; svāhā! You are the breath of Prajāpati; give breath to this one, whose breath is yours; svāhā!
That which was fresh became fresh butter (*navanīta*); that which flowed became clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*); that which was solidified became ghee (*ghṛta*).
The path of clarified butter, the navel of immortality, given by Indra and presented by the Maruts—
Vishnu beheld that, and Ida impelled it toward you with the products of the cow.

With the hymn of the purifying one, with the course of the Gāyatra, with the power of the Upāṃśu, I release you; with the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, with the course of the Triṣṭubh, with the power of the Śukra, I lift you up; with the measure of Agni, with the course of the Jagatī, may the god Savitṛ lead you up for the sake of living, for the sake of vitality.
This splendor has come, given by Agni; great is the gift, together with vigor and strength. For the sake of long life for a hundred autumns, I accept it for the sake of great sensory power.
O Agni, grant him long life and splendor; O King Varuṇa and Soma, bestow upon him sharp vigor.
Like a mother, O Aditi, extend protection to him, so that all the gods may grant him a full lifespan.
Agni is life; men are the makers of his life; through that life, be long-lived! Brahman is life; Brāhmaṇas are the makers of its life;

through that life, be long-lived! Sacrifice is life; sacrificial fees are the makers of its life; through that life, be long-lived! Immortality is life; the gods are the makers of its life; through that life, be long-lived! You are the breath of the Aśvins; may they both grant you breath!
By that live! You are the breath of Mitra and Varuṇa; may they both grant you breath. By that live! You are the breath of Bṛhaspati;
may he grant you breath. By that live! You are the breath of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin; may he grant you breath. By that live!

[Page II,32] One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati; one should cause him who is afflicted by illness to sacrifice on the previous day. For Agni is all the deities and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus, by means of the deities and by means of the sacrifice, he [is restored].
Speech bestows life; Sarasvatī is speech and Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation (*brahman*). Verily, by means of speech and by means of the sacred formulation, he bestows life upon him.

Moreover, the deities are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); having taken hold of the vital breaths on the previous day, he observes the fast. On the following day, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap in milk to Soma, a pap in clarified butter to Aditi, and a barley pap to Varuṇa.

One should cause him who is ill to sacrifice this twelve-potherd cake to Agni Vaiśvānara. For whoever dies, his body goes to Agni and his vital sap to Soma; by means of the offering to Agni, he ransoms his body, and by means of that to Soma, his vital sap. Having thus ransomed him in his entirety, [he thinks]: "Aditi is indeed this earth; upon her offspring are born. Upon her [he offers].

Thus he causes him to attain consciousness. There is a porridge (caru) of this size; for the self is indeed as large as this. Having released him from Varuṇa, he establishes him in the year, for Agni Vaiśvānara is the year; verily, he establishes him in the year and makes his life-span equal to the year.
[He says: "Thou art the life of Agni; by that, grant life to such-and-such a person. For Agni is the source of the life of men.

He is the giver; he bestows life upon him. He offers with five [verses]; man is fivefold: as great as man is, him he impels. Having impelled him as great as man is, this one who blows here is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

This [wind] blows from these quarters; for these quarters have those deities as their presiding powers; thus, according to the respective deities, he [the sacrificer] is established by means of these quarters.
Having drawn forth the vital breaths from all directions, he places them within this [person].
That which was newly brought forth became fresh butter; that which flowed became clarified butter; that which was solidified became ghee.

Thus he proclaims the greatness of the clarified butter; moreover, he indeed magnifies it. "With the praise of the Pavamāna, with the course of the Gāyatra, with the strength of the Upāṃśu, I release thee! Just as here one releases what is to be slain, lifting it up and drawing it out, so it is here.
Indeed, there is only this much: the Stomas, the Grahas, and the Metres; by whatever exists, he bestows life upon him.

He bestows life upon him by means of the sacrifice; all the officiating priests proclaim it around him. Indeed, all of them attend to him for this purpose, and thus all of them bestow life upon him. Having taken hold of the hand of the Brahman priest, they proclaim it around him. The Brahman priest is indeed the Veda (brahman); by means of the Veda itself, the Brahman priest bestows the Veda—life—upon him. From the gold they cause him to drink clarified butter; gold is indeed immortality, and clarified butter is life.
From immortality itself they cause him to drink out life; he drinks it out as it were, and thus he places life within himself.

He binds it to him, and thereby he prospers through life. He binds it with a verse addressed to Agni; for Agni is all the deities, and thus he bestows life upon him through all the deities. Agni is life, and humans are the makers of his life; by that life he becomes long-lived.

"Prosper!"—he who indeed knows the gods who are long-lived and life-givers reaches a full lifespan; he does not die before his time. These breaths are indeed the gods who are long-lived and life-givers; they bestow life upon him [with the words]: "Thou art the breath of the Aśvins; may they two grant thee breath; live by that! For these are indeed the breaths; he places them within him. Those...
He makes [the sacrificer] one who does not depart from this world; ten [cows] are to be given, for there are ten vital breaths in the self; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him.
