A horse is to be given, a garment is to be given, gold is to be given, a cow is to be given, a boon is to be given—much is to be given.
They bestow [the deities].
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on five potsherds to Indra; curd, honey, ghee, parched grains, and water.

That becomes commingled; there is a pap for Aryaman. It is for the sake of nourishment that it is for Agni. There is a cake on five potsherds for Indra; the sacrifice is fivefold, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are fivefold, cattle are fivefold, and man is fivefold. As great as man is, him he obtains; having become whole, he obtains cattle, for this commingled [offering] is like cattle. Moreover, as many as...
In this way he unites the cattle with him. Regarding this they say: "An eleven-potherd cake should be offered to Indra," for cattle belong to Indra;
then again they say, "It should be offered to Prajāpati," for cattle belong to Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the progenitor of cattle.
He approaches him with his own share, and he causes cattle to be born for him. Now, this [cake] is for Aryaman.

He who gives a *caru* offering is Aryaman; Aryaman is the gift, and his offspring become desirous of giving. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Radiant and a *caru* to Sūrya, and then a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Radiant for one who desires sight.
For by the eye of Agni, men see at night, and by the eye of Sūrya, they see by day; these two indeed are the bestowers of sight.

He approaches those very [deities] with their respective portions; they bestow sight upon him. Indeed, sight is common; when the same deity is on both sides of the *caru*, he restores the two eyes to him separately.
As much as one sees with one eye, so much would one see with both, were it not for the *caru* being between them. Now, as for the *caru*...
It exists in between; therefore this [mixture] is in between. For the sake of supporting the two eyes, there are white *vrīhi* grains;

they milk white cows for the clarified butter (*ājya*), for such indeed is that sun. It is for the sake of success that it is in milk; clarified butter is indeed milk, and the eye is milk; verily by means of milk he bestows milk and the eye upon him. He establishes [the fire] with verses addressed to Sūrya; he bestows the eye upon him.
The gods entered into the service of the Asuras, but Indra did not enter into their service; indeed, their powers and strengths departed from them:

the *Rathantara* of Agni, the *Bṛhat* of Indra, the *Vairūpa* of the Viśve Devas, the *Vairāja* of Savitṛ, the *Revatī* of Tvaṣṭṛ, and the *Śakvarī* of the Maruts. Indra followed after these; with them he equipped himself, and with them [he strengthened himself].
Whoever should desire prosperity, one should cause him to sacrifice with this [offering]. By means of these very senses and powers, he unites himself; through them, he becomes prosperous.

It is offered on twelve potsherds, for the sake of its being dedicated to the Viśvedevas. He places the potsherds face upwards; thereby he has made it a *caru* (porridge), so that there may be no burning. One should cause him who is being falsely accused to sacrifice; for when the gods eat the food of one, they truly eat it.
Human beings are his food; indeed, all these deities are his food, for he has caused all these deities to eat it;
thus human beings eat his food.
Recite for Indra associated with the Rathantara [Sāman].
Having recited a verse of the Rathantara, one should sacrifice with a verse of the Bṛhat.
Recite the verses in the Bṛhatī metre for Indra.
Having recited a verse of the Bṛhat-sāman in this manner, one should perform the offering with a verse of the Rathantara-sāman.
Recite for Indra Vairūpa.
Having recited a verse of the Vairūpa, one should sacrifice with a verse of the Vairāja.
Recite the invitatory verse for Indra Vairāja.
Having recited a verse of the Vairāja [Sāman], one should sacrifice with a verse of the Vairūpa [Sāman].
Recite for Indra Raivata.
Having recited the Revatī verses in this manner, one should sacrifice with the Śakvarī verse.
Recite the invitatory verse for Indra Śākvara.
Having recited the *śakvarī* verse, he should sacrifice with the *revatī* verse; by these very powers (*indriya*) and these deities, he interweaves him.
He cuts off the portions while surrounding them; by these very powers and these deities, he surrounds him.

The *bṛhatī* is indeed cattle, and Agni is Rudra; if he were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with the *bṛhatī*, he would deliver over his cattle to Rudra. Furthermore, [he should not do so] with the *bṛhatī*.
For from that which is not exhausted in its power, cattle are born after it. He omits four syllables from the *anuvākyā* and adds them to the *yājyā*;
he thus completes both the *anuṣṭubh* and the *paṅkti*. The *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and the *paṅkti* is Prajāpati;
verily, he has caused Prajāpati to enter into speech for the sake of procreation. That is a productive pair; from that very pair, the sacrificer [is blessed] with offspring.
And he is born with cattle.
I unite you— the sweet with the sweet, the sharp with the sharp, the bright with the bright,
the goddess with the god, the immortal with the immortal— with Soma.
Thou art Soma; be prepared for the Aśvins, be prepared for Sarasvatī, be prepared for Indra the Good Protector.
May the daughter of the Sun purify your flowing Soma with her eternal,
continuous fleece.
Purified by the filter from the wind, Soma has flowed back; he is the worthy companion and friend of Indra.
Just as those who possess barley reap the grain in due order, separating it out,
so bring here the food for those who have not come with the sacrificial grass (barhis) and the utterance of homage.

"You are taken with a support; I take you, the flawless one, with the flawless [vessel], as one pleasing to the Aśvins. This is your womb; for the Aśvins, you are taken with a support. You are taken with a support; I take you, the flawless one, with the flawless [vessel], as one pleasing to Sarasvatī.
This is your womb; for Sarasvatī, you are taken with a support. You are taken with a support; I take you, the flawless one, with the flawless [vessel], as one pleasing to Indra Sutraman."
This is your source; for Indra, the Good Protector, you are pressed.
Of this pressed juice of the Soma-possessor, that which remains here— of which Indra drank by his powers— I, with my mind and with clarified butter, partake here of that King Soma.
For indeed, separate seats have been prepared for you both by the gods; do not mingle in the highest heaven!
You are Surā, the spirited one, and this is Soma; do not harm me as you both enter your own respective wombs.
I have heard of two paths of the fathers, and of the gods as well as of mortals—
those two by which all this that moves comes together, that which lies between the father and the mother.
Those who, while consuming [the offerings], did not obtain riches, and for whom the hearth-fires (dhiṣṇyā agnayaḥ) felt remorse—
whatever ill-sacrificed portion belongs to them, may Viśvakarman make that into a well-sacrificed offering for us.

Thinking those unworthy of sacrifice to be worthy of sacrifice, though wise in the encounter like a skilled man, he has committed a great sin and is bound; O Viśvakarman, release him for his well-being!
The seers, feeling remorse, have declared the sacrificer to be guilty of sin because he abandoned his offspring;
may Madhavya and Stoka have granted them [atonement], and may Viśvakarman unite us with them again.

He mixes the cup for the Aśvins with flour of *kuvala* fruits; that for Indra with flour of *badara* fruits; and that for Sarasvatī with flour of *karkandhu* fruits. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; verily, by means of speech, he bestows sweetness upon him. Now, whatever harsh or improper speech addresses him, saying, "He has overstepped," or "He has perished," she makes it speak auspiciously to him again. The Adhvaryu meditates on lions, the two Vyāghras...

The Pratiprasthātṛ and the sacrificer are two wolves; this is the *surā* liquor. Whatever powers and vital strengths he has lost, they recover those for him and bestow them upon him. It is to be placed on the head of a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of purity.

Indeed, *surā* is food, and food is pure; thus it is made pure by means of that. There is one *puroruc*, one *yājyā*, and [one *anuvākyā*]; in this way, he bestows vigor upon him all at once, [making him] a Brāhmaṇa.
He should cause it to be drunk; by that, the oblation is prepared for himself, and he places vigor within himself. All [oblations] are to be offered into the fire for the sake of prosperity.

He who passes through the middle is seized by evil from the very center; thus, he releases him from evil from the very center. If he were to offer into the Āhavanīya fire, he would not be turned away from evil; a remedy would be applied, but then, if [he offers] into the Dakṣiṇa...

He offers; he turns away from evil; a remedy is prepared. Now, as for why he sprinkles it: for in this very way does it leak. It consists of a hundred syllables; man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor; verily, he attains life and vigor.
Whatever of his was torn asunder, whatever was wasted—that has gone to the fathers; when they consecrate it with verses addressed to the fathers, it goes to the fathers.
By this they impel him: because there are three [verses] for the third world, the ancestors are thereby impelled; and because there are four [verses], they impel him from the quarters.

Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was the nephew of the Asuras; he had three heads. With one head he drank Soma, with another he drank Surā, and with the other he consumed food. Indra thought, "He will surely become all this"; he struck him with that [thunderbolt]. With that...
He fell upon the carpenter at a distance of a yoke’s length; standing there, he said to him, "Run up and cut off his heads!
The carpenter leaped upon him and cut off his heads with an axe. Therefore, the head was held for the carpenter; therefore, food is his portion.
That which had been his Soma-drinking head became the *kapiñjala* partridge; that which had been his liquor-drinking head became the *kalaviṅka* sparrow.

That by which he caused the food to swell became the partridge (*tittiri*). When his son was slain, Tvaṣṭṛ indeed fetched Soma; he challenged Indra to a contest and pressed it in a vessel with a hundred holes—or, as some say, in one with a thousand holes. Indra desired an invitation to that [Soma], but Tvaṣṭṛ did not invite him. Seizing it by force, Indra drank it through a tube; he was deprived of the right to drink Soma thereafter. Therefore...

Soma is not to be drunk by one who has not been invited; indeed, such a person becomes deficient in his right to drink Soma. That which was released from here became lions; that which [was released] from there became tigers; that which [was released] from there became wolves. What he spat out first became the *kuvala* fruit; what he spat out second became the *badara* fruit; what he spat out third became the *karkandhu* fruit; and what was below became the *surā* liquor.

The Aśvins indeed caused him to sacrifice with this Sautrāmaṇī; whatever powers and strengths he had lost, they recovered and restored them to him. One should cause him who has over-poured Soma to sacrifice; for he who over-pours Soma is deprived of power and strength. By means of this, having recovered as much power and strength as there was, they place it within him. [One should also cause] one consecrated by the Rājasūya to sacrifice.
One should cause him to sacrifice with [this rite]. He who is consecrated by the Rājasūya falls away from his sensory power and vigor;

having obtained as much sensory power and vigor as there is, he bestows it upon him. One should cause him who desires prosperity to sacrifice. He who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, falls away from his sensory power and vigor; having obtained as much sensory power and vigor as there is, he bestows it upon him. [One should cause] one who has been long ill to sacrifice.

He for whom there is long-standing illness is deprived of his senses and his vigor; by means of this [sacrifice], one obtains and bestows upon him whatever sense-power and vigor he possesses. "One should not sacrifice when afflicted," they say, for this is indeed like a sacrifice performed by one who is ill.
To this they reply: "One must certainly sacrifice, for every man is afflicted, and everyone desires to thrive. Because it belongs to the Aśvins, for the Aśvins were the physicians.

That which is addressed to Sarasvatī: Sarasvatī is indeed speech; for with speech those two performed the healing. That which is addressed to Indra: for in Indra those two, having obtained those powers and heroic strengths, deposited them.
Regarding food:
lead is indeed untruth, for it is from a eunuch that the work is performed; the eunuch is untruth, and liquor is untruth; thus, by means of untruth he purchases untruth from untruth.
Regarding this they say: "A mare is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)," for she is indeed swift, and the swift mare belongs first to the Aśvins.

They immolate the victim for Sarasvatī, and then the one for Indra; in this very way he proceeds with the omenta, whereby Indra prevails over them. The offering for Indra becomes the first among those performed again, for they thus immolate the victim for Indra once more for the sake of possessing power.
The omentum of the offerings belongs to Indra as the last, while the cake for Indra is the first among the cakes; Indra is indeed vigor, and thus he places him in vigor itself.
The Sāvitra [offering] is for the sake of impelling procreation; the Vāruṇa is for the sake of release from Varuṇa’s noose, for he is seized by Varuṇa in the middle.
Since she was created from behind with her head turned backward, when the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is placed on top, it serves as a covering to prevent leakage.
The portions are gathered together, and they invoke the Iḍā together, for the sake of cohesion and so that there may be no omission regarding the Iḍā. Now, whatever...

That [Sautrāmaṇī] is unsuccessful; it is successful in this [Agniṣṭoma] in that there are sacrificial cakes for other deities and animals for other deities—thus, what was unsuccessful in that becomes successful here. Half of Prajāpati’s own self was firmness and half was softness;
he placed that which was firm in front and covered that which was soft behind.

That which is steadfastness is indeed Soma; from that he created the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, every Brāhmaṇa is by nature steadfast in the sacred word (*brahman*). That which is intoxication is indeed Surā; from that he created the Rājanya. Therefore, both the elder and the younger, the daughter-in-law and the father-in-law, sit and chatter after drinking Surā, for that intoxication is evil. Evil, indeed, is intoxication.

Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not drink *surā*, lest he unite himself with evil. This very point one should explain as a sacred instruction (*brāhmaṇa*) to a member of the royal class (*rāṣṭrīya*). If one who knows this drinks *surā*, it does not harm him; for this is indeed the powerful body of Prajāpati. Prajāpati is power; he bestows power upon him.
Then that Soma which remained over, he caused to flow into the fire:
"Svāhā! O enemy of Indra, grow strong!"
Thus, he did not wish to make this [Soma] Indra’s enemy; rather, he made Indra his enemy. Thereupon, Speech itself departed.
That Soma which he caused to flow forth, and that fire upon which he caused it to flow forth—those two deities, Agni and Soma, became the out-breath and the in-breath.
He stopped at such a distance as he could strike with his arms raised, whether on level ground or on a slope.
At first he was as large as a fire, or perhaps as much as that; indeed, he grew by the measure of an arrow’s length across in one day and by the measure of an arrow’s length along.
Now they say he grew by the measure of an arrow’s length across in a day and night, and by the measure of an arrow’s length along;
others say in half a month, or a month, or a year. He indeed lay encompassing all these rivers; therefore—

Indra was afraid of him, and Tvaṣṭṛ was afraid of him as well. Indra sought a match for him and gave it to him; Tvaṣṭṛ poured the *vajra* for him. That *vajra* was indeed heat (*tapas*). He was unable to lift it up. At that time, Viṣṇu was another deity present there; he said, "Viṣṇu, come! We two shall take up this [weapon] by means of which he [Tvaṣṭṛ] will be struck down. He...

He divided himself threefold; he was afraid because of being turned around. One third [of himself] he placed in this [earth], one third in the intermediate space, and one third in heaven. With that which was his third part in this [earth], he raised the thunderbolt, urged on by Viṣṇu. Seeing the raised thunderbolt, he was afraid. He said: "Indeed, there is this vigor within him; I shall give that to you."
"Do not kill me! he said; then he gave it to him, and he accepted it.
"Then to me..."—with these words, he offered it to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu accepted it.
May Indra bestow power upon us; may the generous lords of wealth attend to us;
may our prayers be fulfilled.
Thus he knew: "Truly, there is indeed heroic power within him. With that which was the third [part] in the intermediate space, he raised his thunderbolt, urged on by Viṣṇu.
Seeing the raised thunderbolt, he was afraid. He said: "Truly, there is this heroic power within him; I will give that to you; do not kill me! So he gave it to him, and he accepted it.
Twice, O Madhus!
Thus he offered it to Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu accepted it.
May Indra bestow power upon us; may the generous lords attend to us;
may our prayers be fulfilled.
Thus he knew: "Truly, there is indeed heroic power within him. That which was the third [part] in heaven, with that he raised his thunderbolt, impelled by Viṣṇu.
Seeing the raised thunderbolt, he was afraid; he said: "Truly, there is this heroic power within him; I shall give that to you; do not kill me!"
"Let us indeed form an alliance, so that I may enter into you," he said. He replied, "If you were to enter me, what would be mine from that?
He said, "I would kindle you; I would enter you for the sake of your enjoyment. He granted this to him, and he accepted it.
Three times he placed [the oblation] within me.

Thus, that indeed is the Traidhātavī; he has given him a thousand—that is, the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas. Whatever exists here, that is the Traidhātavī; he thereby obtains cattle alone.

Vṛtra is indeed the belly; evil is hunger, the enemy of man. When he undergoes ascetic heat (*tapas*), he strikes down this evil, his enemy, and hunger itself. It was these two that spoke against him;
then this speech of his rose upward from her.
Both of you have conquered; you are not defeated, nor has either of you been vanquished. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two strove together, you divided the thousandfold [booty] into three parts.

"He has spoken the truth," he said. "There are indeed two [shares] for the giver and one for the receiver. Those two remained right there. Therefore, the Traidhātavī offering is performed for the sake of attaining the three-night sacrifice (*trirātra*). Whatever one obtains through the three-night sacrifice, that much one secures through the Traidhātavī. Therefore they say, "It has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He recites the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses; it is the *gāyatrī*.

Or the *uṣṇih*—now, those four syllables which are upon the *ṛc*: these cattle are indeed four-footed; just as there is cake upon cake in this sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), even so are these syllables upon the *ṛc*. The *gāyatrī* is indeed breath;
by breath cattle are restrained. In that he recites the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*, it is for the restraining of cattle.
O Agni, three are your strengths, three your abodes, and three are your many tongues, O you born of Truth. Three are your bodies beloved by the gods; with these, protect our songs without failing.

Thus he concludes for the sake of heroism, and also for the sake of form. If he were to conclude with a Jagatī verse, he would reach the end; but since he concludes with a Triṣṭubh verse, he does not reach the end. The Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor and strength; thus he finds firm support in vigor and strength.

"The sacrifice is brought for all the deities," they say; for this entire sacrifice is indeed brought for all the deities. He recites all the meters, for all the meters are employed in the sacrifice. One practicing sorcery should bring [the offering]; for this entire sacrifice is [all-encompassing], and thus he practices sorcery against him with the whole sacrifice. However, it should be without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*).

One has indeed committed a sin; for one who gives no sacrificial fee is a sinner. Now, if someone who has said "I shall sacrifice" does not sacrifice, one should cause him to sacrifice with this [offering].

This sacrifice is indeed everything; by means of the whole sacrifice, he finds atonement for himself. Each subsequent cake becomes larger, for each successive world is larger. Just as this [earth] is, so is that [heaven]; and the intermediate space is likewise.
It has neither the form of this [earth] nor that of yonder [heaven]; therefore it is made of barley in the middle, for such indeed is the form of the intermediate space.

It consists of twelve potsherds; whatever is three-by-three is perfect for the Traidhātavī offering. He cuts off from all [the cakes] to avoid failure, for with as much as one would not reach, so much would constitute a failure. This, indeed, is that.
As for what they say, "The *chambaṇ* is the nose": the sacrifice is indeed woven like a garment; when they sew on the *tārpya* cloths, that is the form of the *yajus*.

When cows are given, that is the form of the *ukthāmadāni*. When gold is given, that is the form of the *sāman*, for they say of the *sāman*, "It is to be sung as something bright. By means of this [sacrifice], the Sṛñjayas performed a sacrifice; they reached the end of prosperity.
Therefore, one should not sacrifice too much, for the Lord turns his face away from overstepping. He who sacrifices with this [offering] cuts himself off;
a son should be made to sacrifice for the sake of continuity.
One desiring prosperity should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, and a pap to Bṛhaspati. (ṇāsā: FN emended. Ed: ṇāsā. cf. note 3)
Indra, indeed, felt as if he were weak. He said to Agni and Bṛhaspati, "Sacrifice for me.

Agni and Bṛhaspati sacrificed for him with this [offering]. Agni bestowed radiance upon him, Indra bestowed power, and Bṛhaspati bestowed sacred formulation (brahman). Thereupon Indra became [great]. One who desires prosperity should have him sacrifice with this; verily, radiance is placed within him.

Agni bestows sensory power (*indriya*), Indra [bestows] might, and Bṛhaspati becomes the sacred formulation (*brahman*). Because they placed three powers within him, it is therefore called *tridhātu*. They join the other [bricks] to the *aindra* brick for the sake of possessing sensory power.
[Page II,44] "O east wind, roar! Svāhā! O wind-borne rain, terrible roarer! Svāhā! O thundering rain, fierce roarer!
Svāhā! Having rained for an *atirātra* sacrifice, fulfilled roarer! Svāhā!"—"Indeed, he has rained much," so it was heard.

Roaring, the one who shines while raining, the Virāj—svāhā! Roaring, the one who flashes as lightning while raining, the radiant one—svāhā! Roaring, the one who strikes with thunderbolts while flashing and raining, the elemental being—svāhā!
Sparkling forth,
sparkling down— ye gentle, ruling, luminous, resounding ones; cleanse yourselves, ye level plains, moistening, well-foaming!
O you who support our friends, who support the ruling power, and who dwell in the beautiful land, protect us here!
You are the tethering-rope of the stallion; I bind you for the sake of rain.
O gods who possess wealth, O Agni, Soma, Sūrya, and Waters, give us [rain]! Break open the ocean.
From heaven, from Parjanya, from the intermediate space, and from the earth—from those places, favor us with rain.
O gods who grant protection—Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman—give us water; cleave open the ocean.
From heaven, from Parjanya, from the intermediate space, and from the earth, favor us with rain from there.

O gods who drink together, O Apāṃ Napāt, O Narāśaṃsa, O Waters, give us [the gift] and cleave the ocean! From heaven, from Parjanya, from the intermediate space, and from the earth—from those places, protect us with rain.
Even by day they create darkness when, with Parjanya, the water-bearer,
they drench the earth.
The bounteous heroes have come; they have shaken down the treasury of heaven for the donor.
Let Parjanya pour forth rain upon the two worlds, Rodasī; let the showers flow along the desert wastes.
When you, O Maruts, send forth rain from the ocean and from heaven, showering down the watery abundance,
your milch-cows, O wonder-workers, never fail; for the sake of glory, your chariots have rolled forward.

"Create rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters! O gods who have your portion in heaven, you who have your portion in the intermediate space, and you who have your portion on earth—enter this field, enter into this field! Indeed, food for the gods departed in the form of rain, and consequently all this world withered away. Those gods then sought refuge with Prajāpati; with this Kārīrī sacrifice, Prajāpati caused them to perform a rite, and he secured for them rain and food."

Where Parjanya does not rain, one should cause the eldest son or the domestic priest to perform this sacrifice; for where Parjanya does not rain, the food of these people departs from them. In that they cause the Kārīrī sacrifice to be performed, it is for the attainment of rain and food.

There are eight Vāta-offerings and [offerings] to the eight quarters; by means of these, they bring back the rain from the very quarters. [The verses are: "The gentle ones," "The submissive ones," and "The luminous ones."

"Amasvarī"—these indeed are the names of the waters. Just as one here calls out by name, saying "So-and-so, so-and-so," even so does he cause the waters to move by means of their names. With the words, "Thou art the fetter of the stallion," for the horse is a stallion and Parjanya is a stallion; this is for the sake of prosperity and rain. With the words, "I bind thee for rain," for he binds it for the sake of rain. O gods who possess wealth!
With the deities Agni, Soma, and Sūrya, he thus seeks rain day by day. If it should not rain, they should remain right there;

for by means of day and night they cause the rain to fall. There are *karīra* fruits, for the attainment of food through rain. They are honey-sweet, for this is indeed the essence of the waters and the plants; with the very essence of the waters and the plants, he thus seeks [rain].

With this [offering], he causes them to move. For one who desires rain, he should sacrifice for Agni Dhāmachad an eight-potherd cake, for the Maruts a seven-potherd cake, and for Sūrya a one-potherd cake. One should cause him to sacrifice; for Agni indeed prays for rain from here, the Maruts cause it to move from yonder, and Sūrya rains it down with his rays. These, indeed, are the bestowers of rain; it is to them that he has approached with their respective portions.
They bestow rain upon him [with the words]: "Release rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters. Thus he has caused these and those worlds to flow together; by means of these, he reaches those.

"O gods who have your portion in heaven, you who have your portion in the intermediate space, you who have your portion on earth—enter this field; enter this pasture! In this way, he touches these very worlds for the sake of rain.
He enclosed.
(FN emended. Ed:
avarunddhe. cf. 3.3.1:32.16)
"I gird you for prosperity.
(FN emended. Ed:
"I gird you for prosperity. Cf. 2.4.7:44.9.
One desiring cattle should offer a gentle, tawny, hairy, and reddish-brown animal to Soma. For plants belong to Soma, and cattle are plants;
thus he offers the animal directly to him. It is hairy, for this is the form of prosperity;
verily he wins prosperity. It is tawny and reddish-brown, the form of Soma, for the sake of success—for one who belongs to the Traita lineage.
The best [bull] should be born; one desiring cattle should sacrifice a victim to Soma and Pūṣan. Soma, indeed, is the placer of seed; Pūṣan is the progenitor of cattle.

Soma places the seed for him, and Pūṣan procreates the cattle. Two of these are born with the teat, while the third is vigor; cattle are indeed vigor. Having obtained vigor and cattle through vigor, he secures them for himself. Three times...
This [sacrificial post] indeed distinguishes itself from other animals of the year; this is the form of prosperity (*puṣṭi*); verily, he wins prosperity.
Some creatures have their share, while others have no share; in that the sacrificial post is made of *udumbara* wood, he makes both kinds of them partakers.
Indeed, month by month, it ripens within among other trees; this is the form of prosperity.
He obtains form and nourishment. One desiring cattle should sacrifice a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati;
for cattle belong to Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the progenitor of cattle. He approaches him with his own share, and he (Prajāpati) procreates cattle for him.
Prajāpati is indeed the womb; verily, from the womb he is born. Indeed, this (goat) possesses the forms of all cattle, as in the case of a human being.

Its beard is like that of a horse, its head like that of a donkey, its ears like those of a dog, its forefeet like those of a cow, and its hindfeet like those of a sheep; indeed, the goat attains and secures all the forms of animals, and all the forms of animals attend upon it. The *āghāra* oblation is accompanied by verses addressed to Hiraṇyagarbha, and those which are the *sāmidhenī* verses of Prajāpati are these.
The *sāmidhenī* verses which are the *āprī*s of Prajāpati—those are the *āprī*s [of this sacrifice]. Gold should be given for the sake of possessing brilliance;

a silk garment (*tārpya*) should be given for the sake of having a common origin; an upper garment (*adhīvāsa*) should be given. By means of it, having attained the forms of the sacrifice, he secures them.
By this very [offering], Upakeru prospered; he who sacrifices with this prospers. Indeed, he divided his property into twelve portions; therein were twelve each.

Because he granted twelve boons, this [rite] is his counterpart. One desiring prosperity should offer a white [animal] to Vāyu, or one should cause him to sacrifice. Vāyu is indeed the strongest and swiftest of the gods; he leads him toward prosperity. Regarding this, they say: "The deity is unsteady and fickle; he is liable to lead him to ruin. But he overcomes that [objection]; it is he himself who leads him toward prosperity.

One desiring a village should offer a white [animal] to Vāyu with his team (*niyut*). He should perform the sacrifice for one who desires a village; for Vāyu leads these creatures hither and thither like those bound by a nose-rope. In that he offers to Vāyu, Vāyu himself leads the people (*viś*) bound by the nose-rope toward him. There are two verses, the *yājyā* and the *anuvākyā*, containing the word "team" (*niyutvatī*); he secures the village for him. It is white, which is the form of Brahman, for the sake of prosperity. [He should offer] a white [animal] to Vāyu.

One should sacrifice an animal with the *niyut* (team) for one who is ill; one should perform the sacrifice for him. Vāyu is indeed breath (*prāṇa*), for it is his breath that has departed and thus he falls ill.
By [offering] to Vāyu, Vāyu pours breath back into him. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word *niyut*. He thereby establishes breath in him.
It is white, for white is the form of the Brahman; this is for the sake of prosperity. One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu with the *niyut*.

One desiring cattle should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice. Vāyu is indeed breath; cattle run toward breath when they smell the wind during the rains. When [the offering] is for Vāyu, Vāyu himself brings cattle to him. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word "niyut.
He has thus established cattle in him. The horse is white; this is the form of Brahman, for the sake of prosperity.
vai: FN emended.
Ed: khalu. B:
khalu vai. M3: khalu vā.

Svarbhānu the Asura pierced the sun with darkness. The gods struck away that darkness from him. That darkness which they first struck away became a black cow; that which they struck away second became a red one; that which they struck away third became a white-spotted one; and that which they cut away from the top became a brindled cow. They said, "Let us immolate this divine beast for our desire."

Or rather, at that time this earth was a boar, hairless. They said, "Let us immolate her for that desire so that plants and trees may be born upon her. For that desire they indeed immolated her, and from that plants and trees were born upon her. Whoever should desire offspring or desire cattle, he should [immolate] this ewe.

One should sacrifice a barren cow (*vaśā*); he is propagated with offspring and cattle. Now, they say: "The first [ray] that drove away the darkness—the ray of the sun—uncoiled itself upon the *caṣāla* of the sacrificial post; she became the manifest barren cow. Thus, by both means, the animal for the gods is sacrificed:
whether that birth of hers is this one or the other, the manifest barren cow is sacrificed for the sake of every desire. [The victim] for Agni is...
One who desires prosperity should sacrifice a barren ram to Varuṇa. One should cause such a person to be sacrificed for; for the bones of a man belong to Agni, while the flesh belongs to Varuṇa.

By means of the [offering] belonging to Agni, he ransoms what belongs to Agni from him, and by means of that belonging to Varuṇa, what belongs to Varuṇa. He should sacrifice a ewe to Sarasvatī for one who is seized by speech; Sarasvatī is indeed speech. Verily, by means of speech he heals his speech—[an ewe] whose teeth have not fallen out.
It becomes all-encompassing and unassailable for prosperity. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice a white, long-eared cow:
one dedicated to Agni, one to Bṛhaspati, and one to Sūrya. The one dedicated to Agni in spring, the one to Bṛhaspati in the rainy season, and the one to Sūrya in the cold season.

In that she is dedicated to Agni, he thereby gains brilliance; in that she is dedicated to Bṛhaspati, he thereby gains spiritual luster; in that she is dedicated to Sūrya, he thereby gains radiance. Truly, it becomes threefold for him.

This bestows abundant spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). They are sacrificed to over the course of a year; for by means of the year, that which is unattained is attained. Having attained it through the year, he bestows upon him splendor and spiritual luster. It is white, for that is the form of Brahman, for the sake of prosperity. One who is being accused should sacrifice a goat to Vāyu, a ewe to Sarasvatī, and a goat to Aditi.
One should cause him to sacrifice; for Vāyu indeed carries about among the people the foul odor of him whom they accuse, since Vāyu reaches all this.
When [one sacrifices] to Vāyu, Vāyu makes that odor fragrant for him;
thus that fragrant odor of his stands about among the people. For with speech they accuse him whom they accuse, and Sarasvatī is speech.
In that there is [an offering] to Sarasvatī, it is by means of speech itself that he pacifies their speech. He whom they accuse is indeed without a firm foundation;

this earth is Aditi, and this earth is the foundation. In that there is [an offering] to the Ādityas, he finds a firm foundation on this very earth. He whom they accuse is deprived of power and vigor; the fetus is power and vigor. In that the [cows] become pregnant, he [restores him] by means of power itself.
They bring [their goals] to fulfillment through vigor.
[He] breathed forth.
The gods and the Asuras were in conflict; they were indeed performing the sacrifice equally. Whatever the gods [performed],... [Page II,50] ...the gods.

The Asuras did that; they did not attain distinction. Those gods saw this dwarf animal; they sacrificed it to Viṣṇu. Thereupon Viṣṇu conquered these worlds. Thereupon the gods drove the Asuras away from these worlds.
Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who has rivals or has enemies, he should [perform] this.

One should sacrifice a dwarf (vāmana) dedicated to Viṣṇu; for through this, Viṣṇu indeed conquered these worlds. Following Viṣṇu’s conquest, he conquers these worlds; he repels his rival from these worlds. He should sacrifice one that is uneven, for the gods conquered these worlds as if they were uneven. Indra slew Vṛtra; he [Vṛtra] was facing eastward.
As she was falling, she seized Indra with seven coils; therefore, the animals dispersed in all directions.

The Vaideha women rose up from his head; therefore, their birth is in front and their dwelling is in front, while the Vaideha bull rose up behind them. He perceived him, thinking, "He alone can surely deliver me from this distress," and he [approached] that [bull] belonging to Indra.

One should sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni first; he, by means of Agni alone, having scorched the coils of Vṛtra, then took the sensory power and vigor into himself. He who feels seized by evil and darkness should sacrifice this bull dedicated to Indra, but [he should] sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni first;
by means of Agni alone, having scorched the coils of evil, he then takes the sensory power and vigor into himself by means of Indra.
Indra indeed held Vala; from that, a thousand emerged. From the front of that thousand, Kubhra emerged.
Therefore they say of him, "He is the thousandfold mark," both he who knows it and he who does not.
They say: "Verily, seeing this world, he rose up toward it; he strove, and he is this one who has striven, called 'Kubhra'. One should sacrifice this [animal] dedicated to Indra.

One who desires cattle should sacrifice to Indra; for cattle belong to Indra, and Indra is the progenitor of cattle. He approaches him with his own share, and he (Indra) procreates cattle for him. When he has acquired a thousand cattle, then he should immolate this dwarf (vāmana) dedicated to Viṣṇu.
For it was upon this (dwarf) that the thousand rested; he stretched out crosswise, therefore he is crosswise.

As it were, he was impelled by this; with this, indeed, he encompassed that thousand. This is for the sake of encompassing the thousand and for the sake of non-disturbance. Now, the gods and the ancestors were together in this world; whatever belonged to the gods, Yama seized that.
Those gods then ran to Prajāpati for help. Prajāpati [gave] these two animals as a pair.
He saw a bull and a cow; he sacrificed them. He first sacrificed the cow to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa.

Having caused him to be seized by Varuṇa himself, he drove him away by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice. Then he sacrificed a bull to Indra among the gods; through that, having obtained the powers and strengths within them, he bestowed them upon them. Whoever should have rivals or enemies, he should perform these two [sacrifices].
He should sacrifice a pair of animals, a bull and a cow; he should first sacrifice the cow dedicated to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa.
Having caused them to be seized by means of Varuṇa, he drives them away by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice; then, by means of the [oblation] to Indra, he places power and vigor within himself.

One who, having previously been virtuous, later falls into sin, should sacrifice a *punarutsṛṣṭa* (relinquished) animal dedicated to Savitṛ. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of prosperity; he approaches him with his own share, and thus Savitṛ impels him toward prosperity. He who, having previously been a bull, later becomes a steer, is like one who, having previously been virtuous, later attains prosperity through sin. Just as this [animal], so too is he.
He attains glory; in this very way, he causes him to attain glory. One desiring offspring should offer a barren cow to the plants.

This is indeed the favorite of the plants; they indeed obstruct her from giving birth. Truly, the plants hide away the offspring of that man who, though capable of having offspring, does not obtain offspring. He approaches them with their own portion; they [then] yield it to him.
The waters give back progeny; the plants are indeed the waters, for it is from the waters that they dig them up, and thus they dig up progeny for him.
One who desires food should offer two milch-cows, mother and daughter, to Heaven and Earth; for when it rains there above, it settles here below.
Heaven and Earth are the masters of food; he approaches them with their own portion, and they bestow upon him the enjoyment of food.

He should offer a calf to Vāyu; for Vāyu is the calf of these two [worlds]. Vāyu causes these two to bestow [wealth]; indeed, he who knows this milks these two when they have been bestowed. He should offer a barren cow that has recently calved to Indra; he should perform the sacrifice for a Kṣatriya desiring prosperity. From her, indeed, Indra was born; being born, he brought forth this womb, and she became a barren cow that had recently calved. Moreover, they say:

Having generated this very same sensory power (*indriya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and brilliance (*tejas*) once, the Sūta did not hope for another; thus she became subject to the Sūta. Therefore, he who, being capable of prosperity, does not become prosperous, is deprived of sensory power and vigor. It belongs to Indra; it bestows sensory power upon him. Now, if one should find that [bull] by whose birth the Sūta became subject to the Sūta, one should sacrifice it to Indra.

One who desires brilliance attains that very sense-power, vigor, and brilliance. He who should dispute over a field or cattle should sacrifice a barren cow sacred to Sarasvatī; for Sarasvatī is Speech—it is by means of Speech that he seizes their speech. This [cow], though being a milch-cow, does not yield milk; thus he renders their speech barren. One should sacrifice a cow that has miscarried, dedicated to Heaven and Earth.
If a kṣatriya who has been excluded from the people should wander about, he is indeed separated from both Heaven and Earth, and thus he wanders about excluded from the people;

Heaven and Earth alone establish him among the people. She becomes one who has gone around [in pregnancy], for this kingdom is as if gone around when a kṣatriya wanders about excluded from the people; having established him among the people, Heaven and Earth [protect him].
On the following day, he should offer a calf to Vāyu. Vāyu is indeed the calf of these two; Vāyu causes these two abodes and the people to yield their milk.
Verily, those two abodes and the people yield their milk for him who knows thus.

One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a goat to Agni and a tawny, reddish-brown bull to Soma. One should cause him to sacrifice for the sake of prosperity. The [goat] belongs to Agni; indeed, he who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, is deprived of power and vigor. As for the [bull] belonging to Soma:
having obtained power and vigor through his own deity, he secures them for himself and indeed prospers. It is tawny and reddish-brown.

One should sacrifice a Gomṛga for the sake of prosperity; one who is being falsely accused should perform this sacrifice. Indeed, he whom they accuse is impure. Vāyu is indeed the purifier of the gods; by means of Vāyu as his purifier, he purifies him. Indeed, he whom they accuse is neither in the village nor in the forest; and truly, he is neither a domestic animal nor a wild animal. Therefore...

This [offering] is successful for him in respect to the deities among cattle; he whose father and grandfather have not drunk Soma should offer an unconfined (anusṛṣṭa) victim to Indra and Agni. He whose father and grandfather have not drunk Soma is deprived of sensory power and vigor; in that it is dedicated to Indra, he endows him with sensory power and vigor. He is deprived of the deities who... [whose father... has not drunk Soma.

If his father and grandfather do not drink Soma, he is consecrated to Agni; for Agni is indeed all the deities—verily, he prospers through the deities themselves. He becomes "released," for the Soma-drinking of one whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma is, as it were, released. Therefore, this [offering] of his is successful among cattle by virtue of its deity. He should sacrifice a bull to Tvaṣṭṛ that is smeared with [the remains of the offering].

One who desires cattle [should sacrifice]; for cattle belong to Tvaṣṭṛ, and Tvaṣṭṛ is the progenitor of cattle. He approaches him with his own share, and he (Tvaṣṭṛ) procreates cattle for him. One should offer a hermaphrodite to Soma and Pūṣan; one should cause a eunuch to perform the sacrifice.
Wherever it should be born from the earth, there one should seek to understand it; for when this [hermaphrodite] was being born, its organ and vigor departed from it.
Having obtained that very power and vigor for him, he bestows it; for when he was being born, Soma and Pūṣan appropriated his power and vigor.

Pūṣan is indeed this earth, and Soma is the plants. Since the offering belongs to Soma and Pūṣan, he obtains and secures power and vigor for him through his own deity; thus he indeed comes into being. With those portions which are not to be cut off, they first proceed with the offerings to Nirṛti.

This woman who has the form of a man is seized by Nirṛti; this man who has the form of a woman is seized by Nirṛti. By that [rite], he releases him from Nirṛti. Indeed, an oblation to Nirṛti does not reach Agni; when one offers it upon the embers, does he offer it in Agni, or does he not? For when Indra was enamored of Vṛṣaṇaśva’s daughter, then Nirṛti, evil, seized him.

That evil which he struck away became a neuter. Whoever thinks himself seized by evil and by darkness should sacrifice this neuter animal dedicated to Indra. By that very means through which Indra struck away evil, he strikes away evil;
and by means of the offering to Indra, he places power and vigor within himself. Prajāpati created cattle; he indeed created this [animal] first.
He created the neuter; after it, the domestic animals were created. Now they say: "When he had first created this neuter, he offered it to Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives;
by means of that, he created offspring. Whoever should desire offspring or desire cattle, he should offer this neuter to Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives. Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the couple.
And he has created this pair—the wife and Tvaṣṭṛ—for procreation; from that very pair the sacrificer is propagated with offspring and cattle.
By means of the wind alone he [attains him].
(FN emended. Ed: vāyunavainaṃ.)

Prajāpati created offspring; once they were created, they despised him. Because they were showing such contempt, he caused them to be seized by Varuṇa. (Tvaṣṭṛ... [Note: *tvaṣṭāram* is the corrected form; the edition reads *tvaṣṭhāram*.]

Seized by Varuṇa, they were afflicted; a black ram leaped upon them, and following after him, he seized his foot. His hoof was torn off, and he became one with a single white foot. He perceived this: "This very one among these creatures is seized by Varuṇa; through him, I shall release these creatures from Varuṇa. He offered it as a victim to Varuṇa; then these creatures were released from Varuṇa.

This [sacrifice] is indeed for the release from Varuṇa; he who has been long ill, him one should cause to sacrifice with this. For he is seized by that evil which is Varuṇa, and thus he is long ill. Since it belongs to Varuṇa, he thereby releases him from Varuṇa.
It consists of a one-footed white-spotted [bull], for such was its form; [this is] for the sake of success. One should cause him to sacrifice on an island; these indeed...

Since the waters are visibly Varuṇa’s, he thus visibly expiates Varuṇa in his own womb. The waters flow around him on all sides so that the Rākṣasas may not follow after him. One practicing sorcery should offer a black dog as a victim to Varuṇa; by means of Varuṇa, he causes the enemy to be seized by Varuṇa himself and then lays him low. It is black, for the black is darkness and darkness is death.

Death itself causes him to be seized; for that which is black is the form of evil, since evil is, as it were, black. Verily, he presses him out by means of evil; one should yoke that [black horse] to the chariot.
I bind this animal for King Varuṇa; the bull is the exclusive portion for Indra.
May the gods enter into its limbs; may Yama seize it, and Nirṛti seize my rivals.
Having thus begged him from these very deities—Yama being indeed death—he causes him to be seized by death itself.

One who intends to commit an offense against a fellow-year-longer should sacrifice a black ram to Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; he is kindled for the sake of the year. Having reached the year, he commits an offense against his fellow-year-longer according to his will.

One who desires preeminence should sacrifice a black-spotted animal dedicated to the Aśvins; he should cause one who is of low birth to perform the sacrifice. The Aśvins are indeed the lowest-born among the gods, and the Aśvins are the deities of him who is of low birth. He approaches those very deities with their own portion; they lead him to the forefront.
It is black, for he thus drives away evil. It has a spot on its forehead; he thereby places splendor upon his face. [Dedicated to] the Aśvins.
One should sacrifice a black-spotted bull; one should cause a sick man to perform the sacrifice. The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; the Aśvins are the deities of him who is sick.
He approaches them with their own share, and they heal him. It is black; he thus drives away evil. It has a spot on its forehead; he thereby bestows brilliance upon him from the front.
The *chandasyas* indeed did not submit to the sacrifice. That *vaṣaṭ*-call, having approached, cut off the head of the *gāyatrī*.

From that severed head, the essence which flowed forth became those *vaśā*s; that is the reason for the name of the *vaśā*s. Furthermore, they say: "They flowed (*akṣaran*) according to their will (*vaśam*), therefore they became *vaśā*s; that is the reason for the name of the *vaśā*s. Moreover, they say: "That [essence] was indeed fat (*vasā*)."
"These indeed are the fat of yours. Then, the first essence that flowed forth, Bṛhaspati seized it;

she became the ruddy Rohiṇī, belonging to Bṛhaspati. Then, what flowed forth after that, Mitra and Varuṇa seized it; she became the two-colored Dvirūpā, belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa. Then, what flowed forth after that, the Viśve Devas seized it; she became the multiform Bahurūpā, belonging to the Viśve Devas. Then, what flowed forth after that, Agni [seized it].

She was Pṛśni, belonging to Agni and the Maruts; moreover, they say she was Kṛṣṇaśabalī. And those drops which were [left behind], these are other forms. Then the first drop that fell away, Bṛhaspati, having approached it, seized it;
it became a bull (ukṣan), and that is the bull-nature of the bull. Moreover, they say that because he sprinkled (vyaukṣata) according to the deities, it became a bull (ukṣā).

Regarding that [verse], "So [the bull] attained the state of a bull," one should sacrifice a bull dedicated to Bṛhaspati for a Brāhmaṇa who desires prosperity; he should cause such a Brāhmaṇa to sacrifice.

Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and the Brāhmaṇa has Bṛhaspati as his deity. By means of his own deity, he obtains and secures power and vigor; he surely prospers. One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice a red cow dedicated to Bṛhaspati.

Bṛhaspati is indeed Brahman; the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Bṛhaspati by deity. Having obtained [the sacrifice] through his own deity, he bestows brilliance and spiritual luster upon him. It is a Rohiṇī cow, for that is the form of Brahman; it serves for prosperity. One desiring cattle should offer a two-colored Maitrāvaruṇī cow. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night, and along with day and night, cattle are produced; it is these very ones [he obtains].
He approaches with his allotted portion; they bring forth cattle for him. This is indeed the essence of the meters;
by means of the essence of the meters, they bestow cattle upon him. It is two-colored for the sake of prosperity.

He should offer a multiform cow to the Viśvedevas for whatever desire he may wish; for all these deities are present here, and it is to all these deities that he approaches with his allotted portion for the sake of that desire.
They fulfill his desire, whatever desire he may have; for this is the essence of the meters, and they bestow upon him the essence of the meters itself.
It is multiform for the sake of prosperity. One who desires rain should sacrifice a speckled cow to Agni and the Maruts.
Agni indeed prays for rain from here, and the Maruts cause it to fall from there; these are indeed the givers of rain. To them—
Thus he approaches them with their own share; they bestow rain upon him. This [cow] is indeed the essence of the meters, and rain is the essence;
by means of the essence of the meters, they pour down the essence, rain, for him. It is a speckled cow, for the Maruts have speckled mothers.
One desiring food should offer a black-spotted cow born of the earth; this earth is indeed the giver of food; he thus approaches her with her own share.

She bestows food upon him; they should not even bring a hide, for a hide is indeed non-food, and black is non-food. By means of non-food he strikes away non-food and takes food unto himself. Indeed, when that brilliance, sensory power, and vigor fell away from the severed head, she became a tawny cow (vaśā). That cow is truly food, while the others are merely [ordinary] cows. One practicing exorcism should sacrifice this cow to Brāhmaṇaspati.

Brahman indeed is Brahmaṇaspati; the Brāhmaṇaspatya [victim] has the Brāhmaṇa as its deity. With the entirety of the Brahman, he thus practices sorcery against him; with splendor he cuts him down and lays him low. It is a tawny [animal], for that is the form of the Brahman, for the sake of success. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice a white [cow] dedicated to Sūrya; for yonder sun is indeed the source of spiritual luster.

The giver approaches him with his own portion; he bestows upon him spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). It is white for the sake of prosperity, for it is the form of Brahman. One desiring rain should sacrifice a cow to Mitra and Varuṇa that is black-eared; day and night indeed are Mitra and Varuṇa, and after day and night it rains. That which is white is the form of the day, and that which is black is the form of the night.
It is of two forms for the sake of prosperity.

One should offer a spotted beast to Indra the Wrathful, the Mindful, in battle. For by wrath indeed is heroism performed, and by power one conquers; thus he bestows both heroism and power upon them for the sake of victory. It is spotted; for this wrath is foremost, and so with the sacred word (*brahman*) he sharpens them from the front for the sake of victory. [He offers] to Indra the Slayer of Enemies.

One who has rivals should sacrifice a bull; for the rival is indeed the evil-minded adversary. By means of his own power (*indriya*), he strikes away the evil-minded adversary, the evil. He should sacrifice that [bull] to Indra, the subduer of Vṛtra; for the rival is indeed the evil-minded adversary.
Having struck away the evil-minded adversary, the evil, by means of his own power, he becomes a subduer of Vṛtra and attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).

"He goes forth, the subduer of Vṛtra"—so they say of him who attains self-sovereignty. One should cause a Kṣatriya who desires a village to sacrifice an Aindrāmāruta animal with speckled thighs. For the Kṣatriya has Indra as his deity, and the Maruts are the people (*viś*); verily, by means of power (*indriya*), he unites the people with him. It has speckled thighs; thus he places the people behind him, according to his desire.

He makes the uneven [territory] free from dispute. One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a bull to Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt; he should cause a Kṣatriya who desires prosperity to perform this sacrifice.
For when a Kṣatriya becomes a wielder of the thunderbolt, then he attains prosperity. In that he sacrifices to the wielder of the thunderbolt, he places the thunderbolt itself within him;

by means of it, he attains victory and prosperity. It kindles him for prosperity and excellence. Because it is "to the wielder of the thunderbolt," that part of it is intended for malevolent magic (*abhicaraṇīya*).

If he should hate someone, he should then meditate upon that person with his mind; he hurls a thunderbolt at him and surely strikes him down. One who is fit for kingship but does not obtain it should sacrifice a gentle, brown, tawny bull. Soma is indeed the king, and Soma is the deity of this [sacrificer]; for Soma is the king. He approaches his own deity for the sake of kingship, and by means of his own deity, [the deity] bestows kingship upon him.
The tawny one makes it go; he becomes reddish-brown for the prosperity of Soma’s form.

He who is born on the first *ekāṣṭakā*—he whom one intends to sacrifice—should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. For Agni is the womb of cattle; verily, he ransoms them from their own womb so that they may become fit for sacrifice. Month by month, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara. For Agni Vaiśvānara is the year.
He ransoms him after a year; when he reaches the state of being fit for sacrifice, then one should offer a victim to Indra Abhimātighna.

Evil is indeed the adversary and the rival; by means of his own power (*indriya*), he strikes away the adversary, evil, and the rival. A horse that has not been castrated is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
for this [horse] is turned away from evil, and thus he turns him away by means of evil itself. Now, as for [the offering] on the later *ekāṣṭakā*—
One should release that very [victim] in this manner and then offer it to Indra, the subduer of Vṛtra. Hostility, evil, and the rival are indeed the same;
having struck down hostility, evil, and the rival by means of his own power (*indriya*), he becomes a subduer of Vṛtra and attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
For they say of one who attains self-sovereignty, "He is a subduer of Vṛtra. A hundred cows that do not drop their loads are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
They are indeed turned away from evil; by means of evil itself, he turns him away. There are a hundred [of them]; man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor;

verily, he attains life-span and vigor. The gods and the Asuras were contending. They said, "Let us two contend for victory in this Brahman. Aruṇa Tūpara Caitreya was on the side of the gods, and Śyeta Ayaḥśṛṅga Śyaineya was [on the side] of the Asuras.

"The Asuras moved about among the gods, shouting in anger: 'Arāḍa belongs to us, but Tūpara belongs to them! They both sacrificed together. The gods made his head a razor-edged disk; having placed his head between his two horns, they split it apart in all directions.
The Asura-speech that spoke entered this [earth]; that which conquered entered the trees. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa [should not eat] from an earthen vessel."

One should not drink with ungodly speech, lest one defile oneself. Therefore, he who, knowing this, becomes a drinker from an earthen vessel, attains the very victory of speech. He who practices sorcery should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Brāhmaṇaspati;

for Brāhmaṇaspati is the Brahman, and the sacrificer is of the nature of Brāhmaṇaspati through his deity. By means of the entire Brahman, he thus practices sorcery against him, and by means of its splendor, he [overcomes] him.
He cuts [the grass] and indeed spreads it; it is a ruddy hornless goat (tūpara), for such was its form. This is for prosperity.

The gods, having slain the Asuras, drove them out from these worlds; they entered the night, and the two Aśvins followed after them and entered. Darkness enveloped them; they offered this Āśvina animal victim, and by means of it, they struck away the darkness. He [the sacrificer] strikes it away with this.

The Āditya came toward him from the east with his light; he drove away the darkness from these two. He who thinks himself seized by evil and by darkness should sacrifice this ointment for the Aśvins. By that very means with which the Aśvins struck away the darkness, he strikes away the evil.
That Āditya comes toward him from the east with his light, and he drives the darkness away from him.

Śyaineya says: "Yonder sun was deprived of its splendors; thereupon all this became darkness. Prajāpati saw these ten bulls—or, as they say, Indra saw them—and he offered them to Indra. By means of them, [he restored] it in him."
Having obtained the senses and the powers, he bestowed them; with those [bulls] that were marked with white spots on their foreheads, he bestowed brilliance upon him from the front;
with those that had white humps, he bestowed it from above; with those that were white and shining, he bestowed it from behind. Therefore, this sun became brilliant on all sides.
He who desires brilliance should sacrifice these bulls dedicated to Indra; for when those marked with white spots on their foreheads are sacrificed, [he bestows brilliance].
With those [bricks] he places brilliance in its mouth; with those that are white on the hump, he places it above; with those that are white-backed, he places it behind.

Thus he makes it brilliant on every side and causes it to attain the measure of yonder sun. He should offer the tenth animal dedicated to Prajāpati in the twelfth month; twelve months are a year; having thus attained the year, he secures it.
Nine are taken; there are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the vital breaths are truly the vigor in a person; he thus bestows vital breaths and vigor upon this [person].
Ten are taken; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is these very senses and vigors; having placed them within himself, he becomes this *virāj* and finds firm support in her.
Homage to the greatness, to the eye of the Maruts, O Father; that I praise for you.
Being offered, go by the paths traveled by the gods; take your stand among the plants with your bodily parts.
This was the grievance of the gods: "The Lord of Waters is the bull of the plants.
Pūṣan chose a drop of Soma; the great rock became that which had been there.
The drop has fallen upon the earth and upon heaven; it has followed this womb and that which was before.
I offer the drop as it moves along toward the common womb, following the seven priestly offices.

He is the father of the calves, the lord of the cows; and he is the father of the great jars. He is the calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, the first milk, the curd, the whey, and the clarified butter; his source is the womb.
The cattle chose you for kingship; the Maruts, who sing beautiful hymns, strengthen you. Resting upon the heights with the peaks of dominion, from there, O fierce one, distribute wealth to us.

One who desires prosperity should sacrifice a goat to Vāyu, a ram or a bull to Indra, or a castrated sheep to Varuṇa. Because it is for Vāyu, Vāyu leads him toward prosperity. He who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, is deprived of power and vigor; because the offering is to Indra, Indra endows him with power and vigor. [He is] seized by Varuṇa.

He who, though capable of prosperity, does not attain it, belongs to Varuṇa; by means of that [offering] which is dedicated to Varuṇa, he releases him from Varuṇa. One practicing sorcery should sacrifice these very [animals]. In that there is one for Vāyu, Vāyu hurls the thunderbolt for him; for the thunderbolt belongs to Indra, and the thunderbolt is indeed hurled with power (*indriya*). In that there is one for Indra, he hurls the thunderbolt at him; in that there is one for Varuṇa, he [delivers him] by means of Varuṇa himself.

Having caused [the victim] to be seized, he spreads [the grass]. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice a white-footed wild ram (*petva*). Yonder sun, indeed, is the bestower of spiritual luster; he approaches him with his own portion, and he bestows spiritual luster upon him.
In that it is white-footed, it is perfect; in that it is uncastrated, it is perfect; in that it is fat, it is perfect; thus it is threefold.

Verily, he bestows upon him this prosperous spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). One should sacrifice a multiformed *āditya* [animal] for one for whom the sun does not rise while the *āśvina* hymn is being recited. For those rays indeed dawn away from him for whom the sun does not rise while the *āśvina* hymn is being recited;
by means of the *āditya*, he raises up yonder sun for him. It is multiformed; for there are many forms of the rays of the sun.

Thus, having obtained these forms for him, he brings them forth. Agni, indeed, when created, did not shine. He offered a goat with a black neck to Agni Tejasvin; by that, he became radiant. He desired, "May I prevail everywhere.
He offered a goat with a black neck to Agni Vibhūtimat; by that, he prevailed everywhere. He desired...
Thinking, "May I have a share everywhere," he offered a black-necked goat to Agni Bhāgin; through that, he obtained a share everywhere.
He desired, "May my offspring be inclined to give"; he offered a black-necked goat to Agni Dātṛ;
through that, his offspring became inclined to give. Whoever should desire, "May I be radiant and may I possess power everywhere," [should offer this].
"May I have a share everywhere; may my offspring be desirous of giving. He should sacrifice these goats with black necks;
he becomes radiant, he prevails everywhere, he has a share everywhere, and his offspring become desirous of giving to him.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice a multi-colored animal dedicated to Prajāpati; for cattle belong to Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the lord of cattle.

The progenitor approached him with his own portion; he (the progenitor) procreates cattle for him. It is multiform; indeed, many are the forms of cattle. Having obtained the forms of cattle, he secures them for himself. He who desires, "May I prosper in the world of Yama," should offer a black-necked, parrot-colored, or white-eared animal; by this means, indeed, Yama prospered in that world.

Yama has attained sovereignty over that world; one should approach him with his own portion. He causes him to attain sovereignty over that world. Indeed, by means of this [sacrifice], one prospers in the world of Yama in a single way during the latter part of life; for he dies suddenly, or he becomes emaciated, or he becomes tawny like a parrot, for he is indeed perfected among cattle through his deity.
[Page II,64] They offer a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati for those who pass beyond the yoke-pin to the west; that [cake] for Nirṛti is on one potsherd.
They cook both together. They proceed first with the offering to Nirṛti. Having gone to the south, [they proceed] at a natural saline hollow.
Having placed a single firebrand, he makes an offering with two stalks of the *visraṃsikā* plant.
May Nirṛti, being pleased, accept this; svāhā!

A black garment with frayed edges is the sacrificial fee; having returned, they proceed with an offering to Anumati on eight potsherds, for which a cow is the sacrificial fee. Then, those who have moved beyond the yoke-pin toward the north, having gone further north and having dug up an anthill, they should offer an oblation.
This hereditary disease of such-and-such a person, born of the wife, do I expiate.
He then covers it again.
This seed of the field belonging to such-and-such a person of such-and-such a lineage, I shut away.

On the following day, there is a caru-oblation of ghee for the Ādityas accompanied by the word *bhuvat*; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a choice gift. On the following day, there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu; the sacrificial fee is a dwarf ox. On the following day, there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Soma; the sacrificial fee is gold.
On the following day, there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni; the sacrificial fee is a bull-ox. On the following day, there is [a cake] for Agni.
A cake on eight potsherds for Mahendra, curdled milk, and a linen garment as the sacrificial fee.

One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni, or one to Agni and Indra; a pap for the Viśve Devas, a pap of *śyāmāka* grain for Soma, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. The sacrificial fee is a first-born calf, or a plough with twelve yokes, or a draft-ox.
There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a porridge of barley for Varuṇa, a porridge of Gavidhuka seeds for Rudra, and curd for Indra; a milch-cow and an ox are the sacrificial fees.

From the place where the waters flow out, they bring Apāmārga plants; having made them into groats, they go toward the south, deposit a single firebrand in a natural depression, and offer with a ladle made of Parṇa wood.

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, and with the might of Indra—you are the slayer of Rākṣasas; Svāhā! The Rākṣasa is slain; we have struck down the Rākṣasa.
The bridegroom is the sacrificial fee.
Those gods who sit in the east, led by Agni, slayers of demons—may they protect us, may they guard us; to them, Svāhā!
Those gods who sit in the south, led by Yama, slayers of demons—may they protect us, may they guard us; to them, Svāhā!
Those gods who sit in the west, led by the Maruts, slayers of demons—may they protect us, may they guard us; to them, Svāhā! Those...
The gods who sit in the north, led by Mitra and Varuṇa, slayers of demons—may they aid us, may they protect us; to them, svāhā!

The gods who sit above, possessing wealth, led by Soma, slayers of demons—may they aid us, may they protect us; to them, svāhā! Here I drive away the demon; O Agni, burn up the demon! The demon is burnt up; to Agni, who sits in front, [svāhā]!

Svāhā to Yama, who dwells in the south; svāhā to the Maruts, who dwell in the west; svāhā to Mitra and Varuṇa, who dwell in the north; svāhā to Soma, who dwells above, who possesses the lower world, the slayer of Rākṣasas; svāhā! A chariot drawn by five horses is the sacrificial fee.

An oblation of cooked rice for Anumati, an oblation of cooked rice for Rākā, an oblation of cooked rice for Sinīvālī, an oblation of cooked rice for Kuhū; a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ, with a four-year-old cow as the sacrificial fee; a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, an oblation of cooked rice for Indra-Viṣṇu, and a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu, with a dwarf bull as the sacrificial fee;
a cake on eleven potsherds for Soma-Pūṣan, an oblation of cooked rice for Indra-Pūṣan, and an oblation of cooked rice for Pūṣan, with a dark-grey animal as the sacrificial fee.
To Dakṣiṇāgni Vaiśvānara, a cake on twelve potsherds; a porridge of barley for Varuṇa; and gold and a horse are the sacrificial fees.

A pap of *bārhaspatya* grain is for the house of the Brahman priest; a white-backed bull is the sacrificial fee. A cake on eleven potsherds for Indra is for the house of the King; a bull is the sacrificial fee. A pap for Aditi is for the house of the Queen; a milch-cow is the sacrificial fee. A pap for Nirṛti is for the house of the Parivṛktī (the discarded wife), who has plucked out her nails; a brindled cow that is crippled and maimed is the sacrificial fee. A cake on eight potsherds for Agni is for the house of the Commander of the Army; gold is the sacrificial fee.

A cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins is offered in the house of the charioteer; a pair of mares is the sacrificial fee. A cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ is offered in the house of the chamberlain; a white horse is the sacrificial fee. A barley cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa is offered in the house of the herald; a large, reddish-brown castrated bull is the sacrificial fee.
A cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts is offered in the house of the village headman of the Vaiśyas; a spotted four-year-old cow is the sacrificial fee. There is a pap for Pūṣan.

In the house of the *bhāgadugha*, a dark-colored animal is the sacrificial fee; [the offering] for Viṣṇu is a cake on three potsherds. In the house of the carpenter and the chariot-maker, all-iron objects are the sacrificial fee; [the offering] for Rudra is a pap of *gāvīdhuka* grain. In the house of the dice-player and the cow-slaughterer, a sword is the sacrificial fee, placed upon a braid of hair;
or else a brindled bull of three years, or a halter, or a tuft of hair.

One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman; a bull is the sacrificial fee. There is a vessel made from a branch of the *aśvattha* tree that has broken off by itself. Then they milk a white cow with a white calf;
that [milk] coagulates by itself, it is churned by itself, and the clarified butter becomes liquefied by itself. Then there is an offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati.
They offer the oblation; those rice grains which are the smallest, they cook them as a *caru* for Bṛhaspati.

Having covered that vessel there and poured clarified butter over it, they add the rice grains which are the largest. They cook both together. They proceed first with the offering to Mitra. A white horse is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the offering to Mitra; a white-backed one for the offering to Bṛhaspati; [and] for Agni...
Householders, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Āpatant; a *caru* of millet to Soma Vanaspati;

a cake on eight potsherds of *satīna* beans to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ; a *caru* of wild rice to Bṛhaspati Vācaspati; a cake on eleven potsherds of *hāyana* grains to Indra Jyeṣṭha; a *caru* of *nāmba* grains to Mitra Satyasya Pati; [and a *caru*] of *nāmba* grains to Varuṇa Dharma.
To Pātayitṛ, an oblation of barley; to Rudra Paśupati, an oblation of Gāvīdhuka grain.
May Savitṛ impel you among those who impel; Agni among those belonging to the household; Soma among the lords of the forest; Bṛhaspati among speeches;

Indra among those characterized by preeminence; Mitra among the truthful; Varuṇa among the laws; Rudra among cattle. O gods, impel this man so that he is without rivals—him, the descendant of such-and-such, the son of such-and-such, in such-and-such a clan—for great dominion, for great...
For the sovereignty of the people: Śukrajyotis, Citrajyotis, Satyajyotis, Jyotiṣmat, Satya, Ṛtapā, Atyaṃhas, Ṛtajit, Styajit, Senajit, Suṣeṇa, Antimitra, Dūremitra,
and the host [consisting of] Ṛta, Satya, Dhruva, Dharuṇa, Dhartṛ, Vidhartṛ, and Vidhārayas.
O divine waters, you are the offspring of the waters; you are givers of sovereignty. Grant us sovereignty, svāhā! O divine waters, you are the offspring of the waters;

you are givers of sovereignty. Grant sovereignty to so-and-so! You are the surging wave; you are the vigorous army; you are the lord of the waters; you are the unassailable ones; you are the flowing ones; you are the powerful ones; you are the gladdening ones; you are those who dwell in the enclosure; you are those whose splendor is like the sun; you are those whose skin is like the sun.
You are the vigor of the Maruts; you are the willing ones; you are the powerful ones; you are the sustainers of all; you are the sustainers of men. You are the essence of the waters and the plants;
you are the most excellent; you are the givers of kingship. Bestow the kingdom upon that man!
O divine Waters, full of sweetness, mingle together, winning great dominion for the Kṣatriya;
sit down unassailable and full of vigor, bestowing great splendor upon the Kṣatriya.
I have taken up the divine waters, honey-sweet, full of vigor, shining in the Rājasūya;
those with which they anointed Mitra and Varuṇa—with those they led Indra beyond his enemies.
You are unassailable, the kinsman of speech, born of heat, the gift of Soma.
I purify you, the bright ones, with the bright; I purify you, the radiant ones, with the radiant.
May the divine Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer,
with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya.
Svāhā! The Rājasūya sacrifices.
Rejoicing together with splendor and vigor, the unassailable ones, active and clothed in waters, have made their dwelling place within the houses;
Varuṇa, the infant of the waters, has taken his seat within those most motherly ones.

O Rudra, that name of yours which is beyond the mountains—in that you are offered as a libation; in Yama you are sacrificed; *svāhā*! May Soma, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni—those gods who uphold the cosmic order (*dharma*)—uphold the cosmic order.
You are the womb of the kṣatra; you are the caul of the kṣatra; you are the navel of the kṣatra. Agni, the lord of the house, has been won over;
Indra of far-reaching fame has been won over; Mitra and Varuṇa, whose vows are firm, have been won over; Heaven and Earth, who increase the cosmic order, have been won over;
Pūṣan, the all-knowing, has been won over; the goddess Aditi has been won over. This man here, the son of such-and-such a lineage and of such-and-such a mother, has been won over.

"In this clan, for great sovereignty, for great lordship over the people—this is your king, Soma; he is the king of us Brāhmaṇas. You are Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; with you may he slay Vṛtra. You are the repellers of enemies; protect him from the front, protect him from behind, protect him from the side, protect him from below, protect him from above, and protect him from all directions. You are Mitra; you are Varuṇa."
O Varuṇa and Mitra, at the dawning of the ruddy dawn and at the rising of the sun, you ascend the golden-colored, iron-pillared chariot-seat; from there, you ordain both non-bondage and bondage.

Mount the fuel-stick! May the *gāyatrī* among the meters protect you; the *trivṛt* hymn-form, the *rathantara* chant, and Agni as the deity—may these grant you the wealth of sacred knowledge (*brahman*). Mount the fierce [chariot]! May the *triṣṭubh* among the meters protect you; the *pañcadaśa* hymn-form, the *bṛhat* chant, and Indra as the deity—may these grant you the wealth of sovereign power (*kṣatra*). Mount the eastern direction! May the *jagatī* among the meters protect you; the *saptadaśa* hymn-form...

The Stoma is the Vairūpa, the Sāman; the Viśve Devas are the deity; the people are the wealth. Ascend toward the north; may the Anuṣṭubh among the meters protect you. The Stoma is the twenty-onefold, the Sāman is the Vairāja; Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities; prosperity is the wealth. Ascend upward; may the Paṅkti among the meters protect you. The Stomas are the twenty-sevenfold and the thirty-threefold; the Sāmans are the Śākvara and the Raivata; Bṛhaspati [is the deity].
