If he should desire, "May I endow the sacrifice with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the *ṛcs* the final [verses]; thus he endows the sacrifice with the glory of the sacrifice. If he should desire [the same] for the sacrificer...

Thinking, "May I endow him with the glory of the sacrifice," one should perform the final *yajus* formulas; for it is thus that he endows the sacrificer with the glory of the sacrifice. By the forward progression of the oblations, the sacrificer prospers. If he should desire of someone, "May he prosper," he should recite all the formulas for him once and offer them; he then prospers. But if he should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," he should offer for him separately.
"He becomes more wicked; 'Fulfill the hymn with the *ṛc*,' he says—for the sake of fulfillment. 'With the *gāyatra*, the *rathantara*:
the *gāyatrī* is indeed this [earth], and the *rathantara* is this [earth]; the *bṛhat* is yonder [sky]. This [rite] is performed at the end for the pervasion of these two worlds.
Indeed, there are eight of these sacrificial formulas (*yajus*); the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables. Thus, he gratifies the *gāyatrī* syllable by syllable. Now, as for that which..."

The ninth oblation is therefore [offered]; by this he goes from the threefold beginning of the sacrifice. Now, because he offers one oblation with eight sacrificial formulas (*yajus*), therefore many bring tribute to one man; many indeed become the ones who bring tribute for him.
The sacrificial formulas are the last; the sacrificial formula is indeed the Brahman; thus the sacrificer finally finds firm support in the Brahman at the end of the sacrifice.
He takes up the spade with verses addressed to Savitṛ for the sake of impulsion. He takes it up with four [verses]; the meters are indeed four;

verily, by means of the meters he takes it up. Moreover, the meters are the Brahman; verily, by means of the Brahman he takes it up. This earth is the Gāyatrī, the intermediate space is the Triṣṭubh, the sky is the Jagatī, and the quarters are the Anuṣṭubh. Impelled by Savitṛ, he thus [takes it] from these worlds, by means of the meters and the quarters.
And he gathers the fire. For when Agni fled in fear from the office of the Hotṛ, he dwelt among all beings;
where he dwelt among the trees, there he dwelt in the bamboo. Where he burned them down, those became the speckled spots;
that by which he moved about became the hollow; where he dwelt, that became the joint. Since the spade is made of bamboo, it is by its own [nature] that he [wins it].
He gathers it with the *yoni* (womb). Of trees, that which bears fruit most abundantly is the most powerful among them;

of trees, the bamboo (*veṇu*) bears fruit most abundantly, and it is the most powerful among them. Fruit is indeed food; food is the *arka*; the *arka* is Agni. With the *arka*, he thus gathers the food, the *arka*, namely Agni. It should be made a fathom in length; for this much indeed—

In a man, strength is exerted according to his vigor; moreover, such indeed is the greatness in a man, and it is for the attainment of that greatness [that the sacrificial post] should be made one cubit long, measured according to the man who is the sacrifice. It should be made one span long, measured by Viṣṇu the sacrifice. It should be sharpened on both ends for the attainment of both kinds of food. It should be sharpened on one end only, for the blade of a plowshare is sharpened on one side; it should be made of that same measure.

One makes it of *arka* wood; for *arka* is indeed food, [and it serves] for the attainment of food. It should be made of *udumbara* wood; for the *udumbara* is strength, [and it serves] for the attainment of strength. It should be made of unlimited size; for the attainment of the unlimited. Or it may be made of whatever tree bears fruit, for the attainment of food.

By means of the horse, indeed, the gods first won the victory; when they proceed with the horse, it is for the sake of victory. Wherever Agni went, Prajāpati beheld him; the horse is of Prajāpati’s nature; when they proceed with the horse, it is for the sake of following after Agni. Prajāpati, intending to collect the fire-altar, having fashioned the horse out of these worlds and having brought together the fire from the quarters, [performed this rite].

As it is said: "In heaven is your highest birth; in the intermediate space is your navel; upon the earth is your womb. Thus, having fashioned the horse from these worlds according to their respective deities, he gathers the fire from the quarters.

He says, "Yoke the donkey, you two," and thus he gathers [the fire] with the donkey for the sake of joining; for this [donkey] among animals is the least fit to be lived upon by others, and so is Agni.
When the seed of this [horse] was first created, it scorched its source; therefore, he deposits seed as much as other animals, yet he is the smallest.
They lead the horse first and the donkey afterwards, for the sake of distinguishing the inferiority of the latter.
Therefore, the more wretched follows behind the one who is superior as he goes before. If he should desire the distinction of inferiority...
They should lead the donkey first and the horse last; for by this means Vipūjana Saurāki brought about a state of greater wretchedness.

By this very rite, he brings about that same state of greater wretchedness. With the verse "More powerful in every undertaking," which contains both the word *ūti* (aid) and the word *vāja* (food), they proceed.
*Vāja* is indeed food, and *ūti* is a way; and Agni is piled for the sake of both food and a way. Because it contains the word *ūti*, [the verse is used].

They proceed with verses containing the word *vāja* for the attainment of food and cattle. He who piles the fire-altar indeed becomes everything; when one becomes everything, he becomes envious. The horse is indeed the thunderbolt belonging to Prajāpati. When he says, "Come forward, overcoming, treading upon the curses," he thus overcomes the curses and the one who acts with hostility by means of the thunderbolt. Cattle belong to Rudra, and the fires are [also] Rudra's.
If one were to pile the fire-altar without having asked Rudra for leave regarding the cattle, Rudra would be intent on seizing his cattle.
When he says, "O bringer of bliss, come from the attendants of Rudra," he piles the fire-altar after having asked Rudra for leave regarding the cattle;
thus Paśupati does not harm his cattle. He says, "Traverse the wide mid-air," for the separation of these worlds from the Rakṣases.

Verily, these two seek to destroy him who is about to collect the fire. When he says, "Creating security for the pastures and making [them] free from fear," he has indeed secured well-being for them both. Earth (purīṣa) is the abode of Agni; the Aṅgirases first collected this [fire].
When he says, "Bring Agni Purīṣya like the Aṅgirases," he collects him together with his own abode and the deities.

With which man he might associate, him he should consecrate with the mantra, "I have reached the fire of the soil, in the manner of Aṅgiras. By this means, he indeed appropriates the strength from that man.

They say that the fire should be piled after having announced it to Prajāpati. From where the sun rises, from there, while striking away the ant-hill, he should say, "I shall bear the fire of the soil in the manner of Aṅgiras. This earth, indeed...

Prajāpati is this ant-hill, which is its ear; it is for him alone that he piles the fire after announcing it. They indeed hear of him when he has piled the fire, saying, "That one has piled the fire. Therefore, the ear of an inferior person speaks to the ear of a superior; the ear speaks to the ear.
"O you who possess the prize," he says;
"Agni has followed at the head of the dawns," he says, for the sake of following after. Having arrived, the prize-winner shakes off all obstacles along the path.
Thus he separated the enemies; for Prajāpati found him with the first verse and sought him with the second; indeed, he found him with the first verse and found him with the second.
"The sky is your back, the earth your seat"—for the sky is indeed his back and the earth his seat. "The self is the atmosphere, the ocean the womb"—for the atmosphere is indeed his self.
"The ocean is your womb; having looked with your eye, trample upon him who attacks you. He indeed tramples upon the one who attacks him;
he should say this regarding whomever he hates.
Tread upon that one.
Thus he steps upon that very [spot] and says, "Step forth! It is for the sake of stepping forth; for wherever in the sacrifice something corresponding is performed, there the sacrificer prospers.
He says, "Step forth! He has stepped forth! This is indeed done as a corresponding act for the attainment of the sacrifice.
Having become black, Agni entered the horse; he reached that place where the hoof-mark of the deer is, which is in the footprint of the horse.
He offers into the fire that possesses [the word] *agni*, he offers into that which possesses a foundation; the Adhvaryu would become blind if he were to offer where there is no foundation.
This is indeed what they say regarding the "deer's hoofprint" and the "trackless chariot": he offers with two verses containing the word *manas*, for offerings are obtained through the mind.
He offers with two *triṣṭubh* verses for the attainment of power (*indriya*). He offers with two verses containing the word *anna* (food) for the attainment of food.

He traces around with a *gāyatrī* verse; by that he encloses it from this [earth]. With a *triṣṭubh* verse [he traces] from the intermediate space; by that [he encloses it]. He traces around with an *anuṣṭubh* verse;
for the *anuṣṭubh* indeed encompasses all the meters, therefore he traces around with an *anuṣṭubh*. He takes up the spade with verses addressed to Savitṛ for instigation.
He digs with two [verses]; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability. For here there is heat (*śuc*).
Where the fire is dug out or piled up, the progeny comes to harm; when he says, "Auspicious to the progeny, non-injurious," he makes it auspicious for the progeny.
"Thou art the back of the waters," he says; for this is indeed the back of the waters; by means of the back, he has made it the back, the womb of Agni.
Thus, this lotus leaf is indeed the womb of Agni, and the Vadhaka grass is the navel; so it is gathered with its own womb and its own navel.

With the words, "Spread yourself out with the measure and the width of heaven," he causes it to spread out with the very measure and width of these two [worlds]. With the words, "You two are a shelter and you two are a protection," he spreads the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf together; these two, heaven and earth, he thus provides for him.
He spreads [the two skins] with the words, "Widely extending, may you two dwell together. For humans are not able to lie upon these; he thus encloses him by means of them.
He gathers [the sacrificial materials] on a black antelope skin, for that is the one among animals least fit for subsistence;

thus he afflicts the wild animals with pain. He gathers them with the hair side up, for from that side the black antelope skin possesses its divine essence; it is indeed by means of the sacrifice itself.
He prepares the sacrifice with a lotus leaf; he prepares it with a lotus leaf because the lotus leaf is the womb of Agni;
verily, he prepares him with his own womb. He prepares it for a Brāhmaṇa with Gāyatrī verses, for the Brāhmaṇa is connected with the Gāyatrī;
for a Rājanya with Triṣṭubh verses, for the Rājanya is connected with the Triṣṭubh; for a Vaiśya with Jagatī verses, for the Vaiśya is connected with the Jagatī.

If he should desire of someone, "May he prosper," he should collect [the earth] for him with *gāyatrī* and *triṣṭubh* verses; thus he prospers. With the words, "Thou art the filler of the soil, the all-supporter; Atharvan was the first to churn thee forth from Agni"—for Atharvan is indeed Prajāpati;
he churned this [Agni] first and generated it. Thus, he churns him in his own [place] and generates him. He collects [the earth] with three verses.

There are indeed these three worlds; from these very worlds he gathers him. The *yajus* is the fourth; by it he gathers him from the quarters. The wind indeed establishes itself after the east wind, the rain after the rain, the plants after the rain, the cattle after the plants, and human beings after the cattle. These are the foundations; the sacrificer secures them for himself. The divine waters...

"Pour forth the honeyed ones," he says, for the firm establishment of the plants. "From their standing place, let the plants rise up with good fruit"—therefore, from their standing place, these plants rise up with good fruit. "May Vāyu Mātariśvan join together for you"—therefore, whatever of this [earth] is ploughed and whatever is dug, that is joined together by means of ghee.

He should offer [the oblation]; he thus drives away impurity. Now, as for the fact that he pours water upon it: he thereby pacifies it. With the words, "O God, you who move with the breath of the gods—to whom, O God, let there be *vaṣaṭ* unto thee," [he offers]. There are six seasons; verily, he establishes rain in the seasons. Therefore, all the seasons are possessed of rain. With the words, "Well-born, with light... he has made him worthy of heaven. "A garment of every form, O Agni... [he says].

"Clothe yourself with the flames," he says; for the meters are indeed the garment of Agni, and he (Agni) clothes himself in the meters. Verily, by means of the meters he entrusts him [Agni] to him [the sacrificer].

For one who knows thus, clothing becomes available to him in this world, and he remains unclothed in that world. This [Agni] is now the "Varuṇa-stake" (varuṇamenī). "Arise, O you of fair sacrifice!"—he thus makes the Varuṇa-stake stand upright.

He releases [the calf] with two verses; he releases with two, for the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability. "Once born, you are the embryo of the two worlds"—for this [Agni] is indeed the embryo of these two, and from these two he is born; verily, from these two he causes him to be born. "O Agni, lovely among the plants, distributed"—therefore Agni is in all plants. "Crying out from his mothers, he goes forth"—he goes forth from his mothers.

Thus, the plants are indeed his mothers; from them he causes him to move forward. Prajāpati either covered him with the first half-verse or stood over him with the second; in the same way, he either covers him with the first half-verse or stands over him with the second.

"Be firm, O you of strong limbs," with these words he places [the fire] on the donkey; he thereby bestows vigor upon it, and therefore the donkey is the most vigorous of all animals, for he has bestowed vigor upon it. Indeed, this [donkey], having become a dweller in the intermediate space, is liable to injure offspring; when he says, "Be auspicious to offspring," he makes it auspicious toward offspring, so that it may not strike them down.
"In the front of life"—verily, he bestows life upon him for the sake of attainment. "Bearing Agni, the bull, the bull," for he is indeed a bull;
"bearing the bull, the offspring of the waters, the oceanic," for he is indeed the offspring of the waters, the oceanic.
"Come to the fire for the feast," for by means of Agni as their mouth, the gods conquered these worlds; indeed, by means of this very mouth, [he conquers].
The sacrificer conquers these worlds: *ṛta*, truth, *ṛta*, truth; he becomes firmly established in both *ṛta* and truth.

This earth is indeed *ṛta* and yonder sky is truth; he becomes firmly established in these two. Day is indeed *ṛta* and night is truth; he becomes firmly established in day and night. "O plants, receive this Agni!"—verily, he makes him go straight into the plants.

With the words, "She bears flowers and possesses good fruit," he causes the plants themselves to take on fruit; therefore, the plants bear fruit upon their heads. This [victim] is now bound as the noose of Varuṇa; with the verse, "Shining forth with broad splendor," he releases the noose of Varuṇa by means of the *anurūpa* verse. He releases it with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.
With the verse, "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," he pours water; for water is the pacifier of that which is unpacified, therefore he pours water for the sake of pacification.
He pours with three verses, for Agni is threefold. At this stage, he is Varuṇa’s bolt, yet he is Mitra;
thus, by saying, "Mitra, having mixed with the earth," he mixes Varuṇa’s bolt with Mitra. By saying, "The Rudras, having mixed with the earth... [he continues].
Verily, these deities first created this [earth] for Prajāpati; with them he now unites it. He unites it with five; the sacrifice is fivefold; thus he seizes the sacrifice in its entirety.
"Truth. [The text] likely reads *satyam iti gṛhṇanti* (they take it as "truth"); the Corrigenda notes this, while the edition reads *gṛhṇāti*.
He says, "Thou art the head of Makha"; the sacrifice (*yajña*) is indeed Makha, and the fire-pan (*ukhā*) is its head; for it is from the mouth that this [is offered].

"Having seized the sacrifice, may the Vasus fashion you with the Gāyatrī metre"—for this [sacrificial vessel] is indeed fashioned by means of both the metres and the deities; thus he fashions it with both the metres and the deities. "Thou art firm, thou art the earth"—this is the benediction for the metres. "Thou art Aditi’s girdle; may Aditi grasp thy opening"—with a *yajus* he fashions it, for humans fashion things without a *yajus*.

They do this for the sake of turning away [the fire]. Aditi gave her to her sons, saying, "Cook her! For these humans are indeed the Ādityas; he has thus bestowed her upon them. It should be made with three elevations, for there are these three worlds;
this fire-pan (ukhā) is made as a counterpart of these worlds. It should be made with eight nipples, for that is the form of the Gāyatrī. Or it should be made with four nipples for the Ādityas.
It should have two udders for milking; the atmosphere is indeed the cart, and these two worlds are the two udders. Verily, he who knows this milks these two worlds when they are offered.
It should be made a fathom in length, for so much is the vigor in man; it is made commensurate with vigor. Moreover, such is the greatness in man;
it is made for the attainment of that greatness. It should be made a cubit in length, commensurate with the sacrificial person (yajñapuruṣa); [or] a span in length.

It should be made by Viṣṇu, commensurate with the sacrifice, and for the sake of not overstepping Prajāpati. He fumigates it with seven [verses]. For there are seven vital breaths in the head; this [altar] is the head of the sacrifice; he thus places the vital breaths in the head by means of the Yajus formula.
He fumigates it with seven [verses]; for there are seven meters; he fumigates it with the meters. Moreover, the meters are indeed the Brahman.

He fumigates it with *brahman*-wood; for this vessel belongs to Viṣṇu, and if he were to fumigate it with other deities, he would deprive it of its own deity. When he says, "May Viṣṇu fumigate thee, like Aṅgiras," he endows it with its own deity. He fumigates it with a horse that has not yet been castrated, for the horse is a bull and Agni is a bull; this is for the sake of prosperity, and also—
The horse belongs to Prajāpati, and Agni belongs to Prajāpati; therefore, he fumigates with horse-dung for the sake of common origin.

Prajāpati indeed thought: "Whoever digs into this [earth] first shall suffer injury. He saw this sacrificial formula (*yajus*): "May the goddess Aditi, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, dig the pit for you on the seat of the earth, like Aṅgiras.
Now, this earth is indeed the goddess Aditi, accompanied by the Viśvedevas; with her he thus dug into it for the sake of non-injury, for one does not injure oneself.

"He injures himself [if he does otherwise]. 'May the divine wives of the gods, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, place thee, O fire-pan, like Aṅgiras, in the seat of the earth'—the divine wives of the gods, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, are indeed the plants; verily, he establishes it upon the plants.
'May the divine Dhiṣaṇā, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, kindle thee like Aṅgiras in the seat of the earth.'"

"The cauldron"—Vāc indeed is the divine Dhiṣaṇā, possessed of all the gods; verily by means of Vāc he kindles it. "May the divine Gnas, possessed of all the gods, bake thee on the seat of the earth, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, O cauldron!"—the divine Gnas are indeed the meters, possessed of all the gods; verily by means of the meters he bakes it. "May the divine Varūtrī, possessed of all the gods..."
"In the dwelling-place of the earth, let the cauldron be cooked like Aṅgiras"—the two goddesses Varūtrī and Viśvadevyavatī are indeed day and night;

verily, by means of day and night he cooks it. "Let the goddesses, the women with unbroken wings, accompanied by all the gods, cook thee, the cauldron, in the dwelling-place of the earth, like Aṅgiras"—the women with unbroken wings, accompanied by all the gods, are indeed the stars.
Verily, he cooks it with the constellations; for these deities cooked it first for Prajāpati, therefore these sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) consist of five parts;
with them he cooks it. He cooks it with two [formulas]; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.
This [fire] is now the wrath of Varuṇa when kindled; [he says], "With Mitra, the supporter of the people," and thus by means of Mitra he [appeases] the wrath of Varuṇa.

"May the god Savitṛ approach thee; may he of the good hands and beautiful fingers dig thee up"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he digs her up for his own safety. "Arise, become great! he says, for the sake of stability so that she does not waver. "Fill the quarters and the intermediate directions," he says;
therefore Agni shines toward all the directions.
O Mitra, I entrust this fire-pan to you; may it not break, for it must not be shattered.
Thus he entrusts her to Mitra for the sake of non-fracture; for if she were not entrusted to Mitra, she would break, and she would have to be made again.
"May the Vasus anoint thee with the Gāyatrī metre," he says; for this [brick] is indeed fashioned by means of both the metres and the deities;
thus he anoints it with both the metres and the deities. He anoints it with goat’s milk, which is its own proper abode.

This goat’s milk is indeed related to Agni; this cauldron is related to Agni. Thus, with its own milk, he besprinkles its own vessel. This goat’s milk is indeed the highest kind of milk; this cauldron is the highest kind of vessel.
Thus, with the highest milk, he besprinkles the highest vessel.

He offers these six yajus-formulas that have been studied. There are indeed six seasons; it is by means of the seasons that he raises up the vigor of the earth. He offers them separately, for these vital breaths (prāṇas) possess separate vigor; it is for the sake of the separation of the vital breaths. If he should desire of someone, "May he become deaf," he should offer all [the formulas] for him at once after reciting them together; he confounds his vital breaths, and he becomes deaf. Therefore...

The deaf man speaks with his voice but does not hear it, for his organ of speech has failed; these other *chandas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech. In that he offers the seventh oblation with an *anuṣṭubh*, he thereby unites speech with the vital breaths. Therefore, this speech is the seventh among the vital breaths. With the words, "Do not be shattered! Do not be harmed! he digs out [the earth]; this is the magic power of the Asuras.

This [earth] was indeed hers; the gods took it away by means of this sacrificial formula: "Thou art the magic power of the Asuras, fashioned by the *svadhā*. By this very formula, the sacrificer likewise takes away the magic power of his rival. He draws the fire with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability.
One who desires prosperity should draw the fire; for we live upon what is yet to come, and he attains that which is yet to come; day by day he becomes better.

One who has lost his prosperity should place [the fire] on what is already born; for he who has lost his prosperity is indeed "one who is born. By means of that which is already born, he causes him to be born.

He should fetch it from a frying pan if he should desire of someone, "May he be an eater of food"; for this [fire] among the fires is the eater of food and the maker of food; he thus secures for him the eating of food.
He should fetch it from a place where it has been burning down if he should desire of someone, "May his kingdom be prone to birth through its army."

By means of *prasena*, his kingdom becomes productive; from wherever he may bring [the wood], he should place it on the fire if he should desire, "May a sinful rival, a second [to me], be born to him. This indeed is the station of the sacrificer;
verily, he thus produces a sinful rival, a second, in his own station for him. With the words, "Eating wood, anointed with ghee," he places a piece of *krumuka* wood that has been anointed with ghee.
He establishes this: the *krumuka* wood is indeed the dear body of Agni, and ghee is his brilliance; thus he endows him with his own dear body and with brilliance.
With the words, "From the highest gathering-place," he takes a branch of *udumbara* wood; when the gods divided their vigor (*ūrj*), from that the *udumbara* arose;
therefore, by taking the *audumbarī*, he secures vigor for himself. With the words, "From the furthest distance," he takes a branch of *vaikaṅkata* wood.
When Agni was created, his radiance departed; it entered the *vikaṅkata* tree. By [offering] a splinter of *vikaṅkata*, he secures that very radiance.

With the verse, "O Agni, whatever things... he offers a splinter of *śamī* wood for the sake of pacification. Indeed, nothing that had been cut with an axe was palatable to Agni; for him, Āsaṅga Prāyogin made everything palatable by means of this [verse], "O Agni, whatever things..."—that [was done] for Agni.

Verily, by this [verse], he makes everything palatable; everything becomes palatable for him. With the words, "Bringing [oblations] night after night without failing," he indeed invokes a blessing. With the words, "Kindling Agni at the navel of the earth," he has made him a conqueror of armies.
When Agni was created, the Rakṣases sought to destroy him; they indeed drove them away with these [verses], namely those which concern the attacking armies.

Thus, by means of these very [verses], he drives away the *rakṣases* from the fire. One should place these same kindling-sticks (*samidh*) where one fears the *rakṣases*, for they drive away the *rakṣases*. Furthermore, in such a year, thieves indeed become prone to seizing. One practicing sorcery (*abhicaran*) should place a stick from a *tailvaka* tree;
this is indeed the thunderbolt among trees. He against whom he has enmity perishes instantly if he then [addresses him] with his mind.

Whether it be the mind or the breath that meditates, or the blessing that is the offering of speech—he, having become such, consigns this very thing to Agni with the words, "He who acts with hostility toward us and whoever hates us, O people. Therefore, one who has piled the fire-altar must not utter anything unseemly, nor one who knows the fire.

[With the words] "Sharpened is my sacred power (*brahman*), sharpened is my vigor and strength," he thereby sharpens the ruling power (*kṣatra*) by means of the sacred power, and [the sacred power] by means of the ruling power.
"Brahmā, and indeed Brahma, and Kshatra—these he made into companions. This very [truth] has been declared in this verse.
The one who applies the effort [says]: "The *brahman* and the *kṣatra* do not waver when they are joined as companions. Thus, for the *kṣatriya*, the *brahman* invigorates the *kṣatra*;
for the *brāhmaṇa*, the *kṣatra* invigorates the *brahman*. When they perform heroic deeds together in harmony, [they are inseparable].

"To the fires"—thus they are seized for the sake of desire; whatever desire one has, that desire is fulfilled for him. They propitiate them; they make them worthy of sacrifice and fit for the altar. Having carried fire around them, they release them so that there may be no exhaustion of their vigor. They conclude with a single [verse] for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice. There are lotus[-shaped vessels] for the sake of possessing sensory power. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.

If the sense organs become obstructed, then there is this offering on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; Vaiśvānara is the dear body of Agni. Verily, he endows him with his own dear body, and also for the sake of freshness, for Vaiśvānara is indeed fresh. To Vāyu Niyutvat, [he offers] a white [animal].

One who desires brilliance should offer it; for Vāyu is the brilliance of Agni, therefore Agni follows after Vāyu. If [the offering] were made to Vāyu alone, it would be for the sake of Agni’s possession of brilliance; but if it were offered to Vāyu in a single portion, the sacrificer would become insane. Because it is offered to Niyutvat, it serves as a second [portion], and furthermore, for the sake of stability and to prevent insanity. Indeed, this [offering] corresponds to the forms of all animals; if it were offered to Vāyu in a single portion, the sacrificer would become insane.
The sacrificer should offer this cake on twelve potsherds for Prajāpati; this is for the sake of being second, as well as for support and to prevent madness.

Then there is this cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu; Agni is indeed all the deities and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus he has obtained both the deities and the sacrifice. Then there is this oblation of ghee for Aditi; the Ādityas, indeed, were the last to go from here to the heavenly world; for them—
Having spoken thus, they went to the heavenly world. Indeed, the Ādityas prospered in this world, and the Ādityas [prospered] in yonder world.

By means of the *puroḍāśa* the gods prospered in this world, and by means of the *caru* in yonder world. Verily, by means of the *puroḍāśa* he prospers in this world, and by means of the *caru* in yonder world. Now, this [offering] for Agni Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the abode of the gods.
Having established it in a temple of the gods, he maintains the fire; furthermore, Vaiśvānara is indeed desire, so whatever desire he may have, that desire inclines toward him.
Thus ends the first chapter of the upper section (uparikāṇḍa) concerning the juhū ladle.

"Visible like a gold ornament, shining far and wide"—with these words he fastens on the gold ornament. Gold is indeed immortality; Agni is the form of death, and the noose is death. Thus, by means of immortality, he places a barrier between himself and death. Now, regarding these *nirbādhas*: once the gods and the Asuras were contending. The gods saw these *nirbādhas* and, with them, [expelled] the Asuras from these worlds.

They pressed him out; that is the reason for the pressing-out of the *nirbādhas*. By means of these very *nirbādhas*, the sacrificer presses his rival out from these worlds. There are twenty-one *nirbādhas* for the sake of stability.
He holds a *nirbādha* above and places a *nirbādha* below for the expulsion of the rival. "Night and Dawn, of one mind, though diverse in form... [he says].

Thus, by means of day and night alone, he establishes the fire. With the verse, "The two united ones suckle the one infant," for these two indeed suckle that one infant. With the words, "The golden disk shines between heaven and earth," for this [sun] indeed shines as a golden disk between those two.
With the words, "The gods, bestowers of wealth, supported Agni,"—the gods who bestow wealth are indeed the vital breaths; thus, by means of the vital breaths, he raises up the fire.

"The sage assumes all forms"—for Agni has indeed brought forth all forms; "he has sent forth what is auspicious for the two-footed and the four-footed," he says, for the sake of procreation. "Savitṛ, the excellent one, has opened up the firmament"—impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed maintains the fire.
"She shines following the departure of the Dawn"—therefore, Agni is established following the dawning of the Dawn; he is the fair-winged bird.
"If Garuḍa is threefold, your head is the Trivṛt, your eye the Gāyatra"—this is indeed the gathering of Agni; he thus gathers Agni.

Therefore he gathers [the materials]; therefore an animal is born with all its limbs, for Agni is an animal. "Go to heaven, fly to the light," he says, for the attainment of the heavenly world. Now these are the strides. The gods and the Asuras...

The gods contended with them; they saw these strides and, by means of them, drove the Asuras away from these worlds and conquered them so as to be invincible. Therefore, by means of these very strides, the sacrificer drives his rival away from these worlds and conquers him so as to be invincible. There is a six-holed sling; for there are six seasons; it is by means of the seasons that he [establishes] Agni.
He takes hold [of the fire] above the navel; he carries it above the navel, for above the navel is the self. Indeed, the divine deities carry the divine self within themselves.

If he were to carry it below the navel, he would burn away his generative organ, and furthermore, it would become fatal to him. It strides forth; therefore domestic animals move away. And because it turns back again, therefore they return again.
For he indeed departs together with his vigor and his cattle; [the sacrificer says], "Return again with vigor," whereby he wins back both vigor and cattle.

They become "returning" for the sake of prosperity. He turns back with four verses; cattle are four-footed; verily he wins cattle. He turns around in this manner, for in this manner the sacrifice turns around; and furthermore—
This indeed follows the turning of that sun: "I have brought you; you have come within," for he is now indeed within.

With "O Varuna, loosen the highest bond from us," he loosens the bond of Varuna for his own safety. With "The great one has stood up erect at the forefront of the dawns," he causes him to prosper through light itself. "The swan dwelling in purity, the Vasu..."
He settles it with the words, "Seated in the intermediate space. Thus he establishes it in the seven *hotrā* offices;

moreover, by this [rite], he prospers in the seven groups of seven belonging to Agni, and he becomes an eater of food up to the seventh generation. Agni is indeed seed, and seed is poured into the intermediate space.
If he were to place it below, the embryos of cattle would be unsupported and would perish prematurely. Now...

In that he places [the brick] above, he has made it a dweller in the intermediate space for the support of embryos. He who is built up is indeed born from among the fires; therefore, [he says], "Sit down upon the throne; sit in the lap of this mother. This earth is indeed the womb of Agni;
verily, he causes him to settle in his own womb. He worships with three verses, for Agni is threefold.

*agre*: FN emended. Ed: *agne*. Cf. 2.7.8:85.14: "Now this is the Vātsapra. By means of this, Vatsaprī Bālandana attained the beloved abode of Agni; verily, by this one attains the beloved abode of Agni himself. It becomes dear to him and brings him back; for Vatsaprī Bālandana was indeed dear."
Thinking, "The thieves have spoken falsely," he saw this hymn; he defeated their denial and thereby attained honor.
By means of this [hymn], he indeed defeats the denial and attains honor. He worships with twelve verses; the year has twelve months:
having reached the year, he wins it. They are in the *triṣṭubh* meter for the attainment of power.

On one day he steps forward, on another day he stands near; thus he has secured the acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) of the creatures. Therefore, some creatures are migratory (*yāyāvara*) and others are settled (*kṣemya*). Now, because he stands near after having stepped forward, therefore a migratory person advances toward a place of security. Therefore, a place of security became the food of the migratory person. On whatever day he is about to sacrifice, that—

He should combine both [the days] during the day, and he should both step forward and stand still; for the sacrificer thus appropriates from his rival both security and the means of subsistence. With the words, "And all the gods shall lift thee up," [he offers], for all these gods are indeed here; with the words, "We who are men, O Agni, may they bear [thee] with their thoughts," he brings him into harmony with that very intention for which Agni is established.

"O Agni, go forth radiant," [he says]; having thus endowed him with light, he causes him to be propagated. "Agni has roared like the thundering sky"—this [verse] he should recite if the axle should creak; for when it creaks, it is liable to scatter the offspring and cattle of the sacrificer. By reciting this, he makes that very noise of his cease, and furthermore, having pacified it, he invokes a blessing. [He kindles the fire] with fuel.

He should kindle it for a Brāhmaṇa with the Gāyatrī verse, "duvasyata," for the Brāhmaṇa is connected with the Gāyatrī; for a Rājanya, with a Triṣṭubh verse, for the Rājanya is connected with the Triṣṭubh; for a Vaiśya, with two Gāyatrī verses, for those two Gāyatrīs together constitute a Jagatī. Moreover, he thereby makes the food of the people (viś) belong to the priesthood (brahman). If the ashes should become full again, he should cast them into the water, for the waters are...

Or [he should do so] because it is the womb of Agni; verily he places it in its own womb. He should make a layer of loose soil for one who desires cattle; loose soil is indeed cattle, and he becomes possessed of cattle. Or he should join the bricks together; thereby all his bricks become dedicated to Agni. Verily, he perishes along with strength and cattle; with the words, "Return again with strength," he wins back both strength and cattle.

With the two verses beginning "Be mindful of this my word, O youngest one," he worships; therefore, after sleeping, living beings awaken again. He worships with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet—for the sake of stability.
Let them bear; *yady*. (Emendation: Ed.
"Go away, depart, and creep away," he says. For this world has Yama as its deity; Yama has attained sovereignty over that world.
If one were to pile the fire-altar without having asked Yama for the sacrificial ground, his fire would have Yama as its deity and would not lead to heaven.

"When Yama made this dwelling-place on earth out of joy, saying, 'O Fathers, you have prepared this world,' it was by means of this [verse] that he begged for the place of divine sacrifice from Yama. When the place of divine sacrifice has been remembered, one piles the fire-altar; thus the fire-altar becomes dedicated to Yama.
They dig up [the ground] to the height of a fathom; whatever in it is unfit for sacrifice or impure, that they dig up."

They dig up [the earth] to this extent; for such is the vigor in man, and it is built up in accordance with that vigor. Moreover, such is the greatness in man, and it is built for the attainment of that greatness.

He sprinkles water; whatever cruel thing they did while digging it up, he makes that not cruel and pacifies it. Furthermore, water is indeed the womb of fire; thus it is built in its own womb. "Thou art the ashes of Agni, the soil of Agni."
He scatters eighty grains of sand. Sand is indeed the ash of Agni Vaiśvānara;
thus he is built upon his own ash. Sand is a womb, and saline soil is seed. When he scatters sand and then scatters saline soil, he places seed in the womb;
therefore, seed is placed in the womb, and from the womb seed is born. Prajāpati created offspring.

He created them from the womb of the saline soil (*ūṣa*); for saline soil is procreation, and it is in procreation that this Agni is built up. These two were together; as they were separating, they said, "Let there be a dear abode for us both together. The waters are the sacrificial and pure portion of this [earth], while those saline soils are the sacrificial and pure portion of yonder [sky]. When the waters and the saline soils come together, it is so that...

Verily, he thereby secures for these two that which is worthy of sacrifice and fit for the altar; moreover, he establishes him in the dear abode of these two. The saline soil (ūṣa) is indeed a means of recognition; both kinds of animals recognize it—both those that are domestic and those that are wild—and so both kinds of animals recognize him. He places four [bricks] facing eastward; for there are four meters.

By means of the meters, the gods went to the heavenly world; they stepped toward the quarters, but those [quarters] collapsed. They made them firm with these [bricks]. When these are laid down, it is for the support of the quarters. Bricks are indeed cattle, and cattle attend upon the Gārhapatya fire. He lays down two bricks joined together in front and two joined together behind; thus, on both sides, he [provides support] for him.
He lays down the *samīc* bricks for the securing of cattle. He lays down eight; the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables, and Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature:
as great as Agni is, so much of him he builds up. They should be made twenty-one in number for the sake of stability, for the twenty-one-fold is indeed a foundation.
Moreover, the *gārhapatya* hearth consists of twenty-one parts; it should be built with three layers, for these worlds are three; [he thus establishes] these very worlds.
He attains the worlds; [the altar] should be built with five layers, for the sacrifice is fivefold; having grasped the sacrifice in its entirety, he pours [the earth] together with four [verses].

There are indeed four meters; it is by means of the meters that he pours them together. Moreover, the meters are the Brahman; it is by means of the Brahman that he pours them together. That which is built among the fires is the Kṣatra, and that which is in the fire-pan (ukhya) is the Kṣatra, while [this] is the Brahman.

In that he pours together [the oblation] with a *yajus* formula, he thereby unites the *kṣatra* (the ruling power) with the *brahman* (the spiritual power); therefore, the *kṣatra* both unites with and separates from the *brahman*. Indeed, these two tigers come together, and being unappeased, they are capable of harming the sacrificer.
When he says, "Be you two of one mind for us, of one dwelling, of one thought, and stainless," he truly pacifies them; thus they are appeased.

Thus it is piled for the non-injury of the sacrificer. Indeed, the vigor of the earth was raised up by the seasons; it is released again by the seasons. When he says, "May Prajāpati Viśvakarman release [it]," it is Prajāpati Viśvakarman himself who releases it.
Now, these three oblations for Nirṛti are cooked in husks; for the husks are indeed the food of Nirṛti. They are black, for that is the form of Nirṛti.
They carry them toward that direction, for that is the direction of Nirṛti.
He places them face-downward in a depression he has dug himself; for this is seized by Nirṛti on earth, and thus he casts Nirṛti away from one who is seized by Nirṛti.
He delivers him from destruction; by the first [verse] he releases his out-breath (*prāṇa*), by the second his in-breath (*apāna*), and by the third his diffused breath (*vyāna*).

Now, man consists of three syllables; as great as man is, him he releases from the evil of Nirṛti. For Nirṛti is the supervisor of action; having appeased her with her own share, he then piles the fire-altar, impelled by Savitṛ.
With the words, "The net which the goddess Nirṛti bound upon you," he places it upon the bricks; thus he releases the noose of Nirṛti for his own safety.
That wonderful light which has been born beyond this great expanse,
may that Vaiśvānara Agni carry us across our enemies.

Saying "Svāhā!", he goes around sprinkling water so that Nirṛti may not follow after him; saying "Homage to Bhūti!", he turns back. Having become prosperity itself, he turns back for his own safety. They return without looking back so that Nirṛti may not follow after them. They cleanse themselves outside the cow-pen; thus they expiate Nirṛti outside the cow-pen. Indeed, by means of this power and vigor...

He who piles the Nairṛta bricks comes to ruin. With the verse, "The gatherer of dwellings, the bringer together of riches," he worships the Gārhapatya fire with an Aindrī verse; verily, by means of Indra’s power, he makes himself prosper. He worships with a Triṣṭubh verse; the Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor and strength;
verily, he establishes himself in vigor and strength. The Gārhapatya is piled first for the sake of stability. Indeed, [it is] in the Gārhapatya...

The gods, having established themselves, went forward to conquer the heavenly world. He measures with a bamboo as long as a man with upraised arms; for as much vigor as there is in a man, by that very vigor he measures. Moreover, such is the greatness in a man, for the sake of attaining greatness. Of trees, that which bears fruit most abundantly is the most vigorous among them.

The bamboo is indeed the most fruit-bearing of trees; it is the most vigorous among them. Fruit is food, and food is the *arka*; the *arka* is Agni. By means of the *arka*, he measures out this food and the *arka*-Agni. He measures seven men;
verily, from seven men he finds a world, and he becomes an eater of food as far as the seventh generation. It is one cubit in measure.
He lays down the bricks on the two wings; for the wing is indeed the great bird. He ploughs with six [oxen]; for there are six seasons;
verily, he ploughs by means of the seasons. He ploughs turning towards the east; for this is the turning of the gods, and it is also the turning of yonder sun that they follow.
He brings about three furrows each time; for Agni is threefold. There are twelve furrows.

Twelve months are a year; indeed, this [ploughing] conforms to the measure of the year. This earth was afraid, thinking, "Agni will burn me up. When he ploughs, he makes it double for her, so that he does not burn her excessively; moreover, by means of this doubling of the earth, they lift up the vigor of Agni. They cast [the furrow] toward this direction, for this is the direction of the gods; and furthermore—
They release her toward the heavenly world itself.
[The commentary on] the *parṣad*:

"He sows in the ploughed [ground], for in the ploughed [ground] plants most quickly take root. He sows of every kind of food; [he sows] with the *ṛc*-verses of the plants. The *ṛc* is indeed Brahman; verily by means of Brahman he secures for himself food. He sows with fourteen [verses]; twelve..."

The months are the year; and as for these fourteen [days], they are indeed the day and night. By means of this year and by means of the day and night, he secures for himself food. Food is the fruit, and food is the *arka*; Agni is the *arka*. With the *arka* (the sun/fire), he thus sows the *arka* (the fire) which is food—namely, that food for which he pours out the seed; whatever of that food he should eat, those are the things secured.
If these [materials] are not available, he should prepare them for him; furthermore, he should meditate upon them with his mind, and by that very means he secures them.

If he cannot find everything, he should sow barley mixed with honey. In that the barley is domestic, he secures domestic food; in that the honey is wild, he secures wild food; by that very means he secures both. Now, these are the ritual materials (*saṃbhārāḥ*); they indeed come from the quarters.

He gathers this vigor from the earth; with vigor the fire-altar is built. If he should desire of a certain people, "May they be hungry," he should take [the earth] from half of that place, saying, "I take food and vigor from here. That people will indeed become hungry.
He touches it, saying, "O yielder of desires, milk forth every desire! Thereby all his bricks become yielders of desires. [He then prepares] the high altar...

Having strewn the *uttaravedi*, his fire-altar is thus built; moreover, it is for the sake of not separating the joints of the sacrifice. Indeed, this *uttaravedi* which is strewn is Agni himself; when he builds the fire-altar after having strewn the *uttaravedi*, it is as if Agni is being built upon Agni.
With the words, "O Agni, thy fame is [like] fat," he scatters sand; these are indeed the unlimited *vaiśvānara* bricks.
This is piled as an unlimited [number] for Agni; this is indeed the hymn of Agni Vaiśvānara. Vaiśvānara is indeed the beloved body of Agni;
thus Agni is piled in his own beloved body. The *arka* is deposited with its body;
this metre is hairy and beneficial to cattle. It consists of eighty syllables, being deficient and redundant for the sake of procreation. By means of this, indeed, the gods...
They went to the heavenly world; that is its state of having eighty syllables. This metre is indeed the ocean, the womb; Soma is the ocean, the placer of seed.
In that he arranges [the altar] with two verses addressed to Soma, he places the seed in the womb; therefore the seed placed in the womb swells.
The two [verses] are swelling; therefore the seed in the womb swells. By means of the metres, Agni [established] the high altar.

That which is hurled into the fire while the *anvāhārya* is being offered, he should then meditate upon that mentally; thus by means of the *chandas* (metres) he hurls it onto the *uttaravedi*. He recites it mentally, for this [offering] is as if undefined (*anirukta*) and undifferentiated; [thereby] he goes forth separated from evil and the enemy. They lead the horse in front to drive away the *rakṣases*, and they make it step upon [the altar].
Whichever rival is equal to him, him they press down with the thunderbolt; they cause him to step forward facing eastward, and whichever rival surpasses him, him he drives away with the thunderbolt;

they turn him back facing westward, and whichever rival follows him, him he repels with the thunderbolt. This, indeed, is the removal of the rival; for Agni, having become black, [enters the fire-pan].
He entered the horse; he went to that place where the hoof-print of the wild animal is. When they cause the horse to step upon it, it is for the attainment of whatever of Agni was deposited there.

He places the lotus leaf with the formula, "Thou art the womb of penance. For the lotus leaf is indeed the womb of Agni; the *vadhaka* brick is the navel. Thus, being provided with its womb and its navel, the altar is built. This earth, indeed, was afraid, thinking, "Agni will burn me through. By placing the lotus leaf, it is for her protection from being burnt through. He places it below the navel for the stability of the plants; and also those...
"These are the fires; verily, he wins them. Prajāpati created offspring; those which he created before the Brahman, with them he did not succeed;

but those which he created with the Brahman at their head, with them he succeeded. By reciting, "The Brahman that was first born in the east," he places the gold plate for the sake of prosperity; he indeed prospers, and also for the sake of pairing. Not on the earth..."

"The fire is to be piled neither in the intermediate space nor in heaven," they say; "for gold is indeed immortality, and thus the fire is piled upon immortality. For these fires are piled as if for a cemetery; at each layer he throws down a piece of gold. By this means, this [fire] is not piled for a cemetery, and by this it is heavenly. Now, this golden man—he supports the world of the sacrificer; for this sacrificer is indeed he.

"He for whom this fire-altar is properly laid up in yonder world, moreover, has light itself piled up in its center. With the words, "The drop has fallen upon the earth, following after heaven," he touches it; thus he establishes it in the Hotṛ-offices. Now, these are the names of the serpents; the names of the serpents are indeed death. If he were to pile them up [directly], he would be liable to die prematurely; therefore, he assigns them [by name].

Some [of these] are for the tiger, one for the snake; thus he secures them all. He sprinkles with Vāmadeva’s demon-slaying formula. By means of this, Vāmadeva indeed set ablaze the head of Kusitāyī to strike away the Rākṣasas. He sprinkles with five formulas; the sacrifice is fivefold: he thus seizes the sacrifice in its entirety, and from as much as the sacrifice extends, from that much he [secures it].
It drives away the Rakṣases. Then he places these two spoons: one made of *kārṣmarya* wood to the south, for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.
For from the south the Rakṣases sought to strike the sacrifice of the gods; they drove them away by means of the *kārṣmarya* tree itself.
In that he places the *kārṣmarya* spoon to the south, it is for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases. It is filled with clarified butter; for this [spoon] is indeed...

Ghee is the dear body of Agni; verily, he endows him with his own dear body. He settles it with a *gāyatrī* verse; the *gāyatrī* is indeed brilliance, and Vedic luster is brilliance; verily, he wins both brilliance and Vedic luster. He settles a ladle full of curds to the north with an *udumbara* branch; the *udumbara* is strength and curds are food; verily, he bestows strength and food upon him. [He does so] with a *triṣṭubh* verse.

He settles [the oblation]; the Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor and strength; verily, he wins vigor and strength for himself. He settles it when full; [thus] they attend upon the world of the sacrificer as something inexhaustible.
He settles with two verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhanvatī*); [thinking], "May I be pre-eminent. They say, "The fire-altar is to be piled upon the Virāj.
The two offering-spoons (*sruc*) are indeed the Virāj; in that he places [the bricks] with the spoons, the fire-altar is thus piled upon the Virāj. Now, this...

This first naturally perforated brick is indeed this [earth]; the second naturally perforated brick is the intermediate space; the third is yonder [sky]. He thus lays down these very worlds. Having made the horse sniff it, he sets it down; thus it becomes a piling for Prajāpati, and also for the emission of the vital breaths.
"Thou art the earth," he should push it forward (eastward) if a rival should be excessively powerful against him; "Thou art the ground," if [he should push it] backward (westward).

With the words, "Thou art Aditi; thou art the earth," he places a transverse brick. If this [earth] is indeed Aditi, it is by means of her that the sacrificer drives away his rival so that he is utterly removed; he repels him with this one, he pushes him away with this one. This, then, is the driving away of the rival. With the verse, "Growing up from joint to joint," he lays down a *dūrvā* brick for the firm establishment of plants.

"From joint to joint, indeed, does this [Dūrvā] take root. The bricks are cattle; cattle do not delight in a place that is bare. In that he lays down the Dūrvā-brick, a resting-place is thereby created for the cattle. Now, this Vāmabhṛt brick has two Yajus formulas: by one he supports the world of the sacrificer, and by the other he excludes the world of his rival. By means of this, indeed, the gods [attained their goal].

The Asuras seized the desirable cattle; that is why the Vāmabhṛt has its name "Vāmabhṛt" (bearer of the desirable). The desirable of the gods is the meters, and the cattle are the meters; by means of this [offering], the sacrificer seizes the desirable cattle from his rival.

Now, these two are the Retahsic (seed-shedders): this earth is Virāj, and yonder sky is Svarāj; it is yonder sky that sheds the seed, and this earth brings it forth. Agni becomes an eater of food beyond measure.

If these two [bricks] are laid down for one who has sons, he should lay down one on the first layer and the other on the last layer, for the sake of securing the poured seed. If he is sonless, both should be laid down on the first layer;
for having become united, they pour forth the seed.
He establishes himself: FN emended. Ed: pratitiṣṭhatīti.

Now, these are the Viśvajyotis bricks; verily, he thus places the luminous Agni in these worlds. Moreover, it is for the separation of the vital breaths. Now, this one is marked with three lines; these worlds indeed are marked with three lines; he thus bestows these very worlds. Both the gods and the Asuras placed this brick; the gods placed it with the mark above, and the Asuras placed it with the mark below.

Then the gods became superior and the Asuras were defeated. One who has rivals should place it with its mark facing upward; he prospers in his own person, while his rival is defeated. This indeed is the *asapatneṣṭakā*; he becomes one who has no rival who places this brick. Moreover, this is the mark of the gods; he places the very mark of the gods which was on the fire-pan (*ukhā*).
The clay that remains over should be used to make this [brick]; by doing so, all his bricks become dedicated to Agni.

Now, these [funeral mounds] are built like burial grounds; a living tortoise should be placed there, for by that he is not a burial ground. It is the sacrificial essence of cattle; seeing this sacrificial essence, cattle attend upon him in yonder world.

He places it facing westward, for cattle stand facing westward toward the sacrificial offering. He places it with a verse addressed to Heaven and Earth, for cattle attend upon Heaven and Earth. Verily, he establishes him in harmony with the cattle. "Agni is to be piled upon the navel of Viṣṇu," they say; the mortar should be made one span in measure, for Viṣṇu is indeed of such extent, or rather, [it is] of Viṣṇu's [extent].
"This fire is piled upon the navel; 'The fire is to be piled upon strength,' so they say. The Udumbara is indeed strength;
in that there is an Udumbara mortar, the fire is thus piled upon strength. He settles it with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, for the mortar belongs to Viṣṇu;
he settles it by its own deity. Now this pan: on it the vigor and power of the earth are gathered; it is indeed vigor and power."

It is placed in the middle of the fire; thus, light itself is piled up in the center. If he were to look at it empty, the sacrificer would become hungry; but since he looks at it full, he does not become hungry. It should be filled with sand;
for sand is the ash of Agni Vaiśvānara—thus he gratifies it with its own ash. It should be filled with curds.

Verily, by means of curds he secures strength; this is what must be filled for one whose heart has been pierced. Ghee is indeed the dear body of Agni; verily, he prospers him with his own dear body. This is what must be filled with honey for his offspring; a honey-sweet child is born to him.
The heads of the sacrificial animals are indeed deficient in power, unfit for sacrifice, and impure; [therefore] gold chips are placed in the openings.

He thus endows them with power by means of the very organ that emits; he makes them pure and fit for sacrifice. Half of a thousand belongs to man, while the other half belongs to the other animals; therefore, he places this one in the middle and the others on both sides, so that the animal may possess full vigor and have its proper abode. For whomsoever he should desire, "May he be rich in cattle," [he should do so].

He should place the animal heads facing together; verily he places the animals facing together for him, and he becomes possessed of cattle. Now, for one whom he desires, "May he be without cattle," he should place the animal heads facing away from each other; verily he places the animals facing away from each other for him, and he becomes without cattle. These indeed are the thousandfold bricks, the animal bricks; they were [invented] by Somadakṣa.

Kauśreya understood them and laid them down for Śyāparṇa; he obtained a thousand cattle. He for whom these are laid down obtains a thousand cattle. This Agni is indeed named Yaviṣṭha; therefore, one should pile him. One should not pass between [the layers]; if one were to pass between, he would cut off his vital breaths. He should worship with the utsarga offerings; thus he transfers the affliction onto the wild animals alone.
He does not release it.
He should pile this;
he piles the human head, for this is the most vigorous of animals; he places vigor in it; he piles one [brick].

He bestows vigor upon it in a single way; he makes an offering over the human head with a verse addressed to Sūrya for the attainment of the heavenly world. Although this [verse] belongs to Sūrya, it is dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. Mitra is indeed the day and Varuṇa is the night; thus he finds firm support in both day and night. He offers with two half-verses; the half-verse is this [earth] and the half-verse is that [sky]; thus he finds firm support in these two. Now, as for what...

He offers twice with a single verse; therefore, though being one, man has two feet. Or rather, whatever he performed here, he thereby fashioned the womb, for when he sets down these Apasyā bricks, he places seed in that very womb. This earth, indeed, was afraid, thinking, "Agni will burn me up"; she saw these bricks. And they say, "Prajāpati saw them. He sets them down.

"That these [bricks] are laid down is so that there may be no excessive burning of this [earth]," he said; "for she who lays these down is indeed food. He becomes an eater of food for whom these are laid down. From that emitted semen, this animal comes into being.
In that these are the *chandasyā* bricks—the meters (*chandāṃsi*) are indeed animals—if he were to lay them down on the south, offspring would perish.

Varuṇa would seize him if he were to place them on the north side; therefore, he places them on the west side, for it is from the west that one drives away evil. Now, these are the breath-supporting bricks (prāṇabhṛt);
when that animal has been produced, he thereby bestows upon it breath, sight, hearing, and speech. He lays them down crosswise;
verily, he thus makes the animal step across, and therefore animals move along with their limbs crossing over. Or rather, they are placed by tens and tens.
By means of bricks the seers prospered; he prospers with those same prosperities for whom these are laid down.
Now, this semen is poured forth when the fire-altar is built; when these [bricks] are laid down, it is for the support (*saṃyati*) of the semen that has been poured forth.
"Fill the space! Fill the gap!"—this indeed is the "gap-filling" brick (*achidreṣṭakā*); by means of this, the layers are built without gaps. Indra and Agni...

"May Bṛhaspati [place] thee"—Indra and Agni are indeed might and vigor; by means of this might and vigor, the fire-altar is built. "Those [waters] of his with *sūdadohas*," he says; thus, joint by joint, he bestows sap. "They mix the Soma with the speckled [cow]," he says; the speckled cow is indeed food; verily, he wins food. "In the lineage of the gods," he says; this is for the sake of procreation. "In the three bright realms," he says.
"By day"—the three pressings are indeed the "lights"; he has thus made him one who is built up by the pressings.

This [verse] is indeed an Anuṣṭubh; speech is the Anuṣṭubh, and speech is breath. Since this [verse] moves along after all the bricks, therefore breath moves along after all the limbs. This [verse] belongs to Agni by its color; by its own metre, Agni is thus piled, and not the Adhvaryu.
He who knows thus does not suffer distress.

This piled fire-altar is indeed one whose sacrifice is destroyed; who indeed knows what is done for it and what is not? The Aśvins are the physicians of the gods; they are the restorers of that which has not been restored. Since these bricks of the Aśvins are laid down, it is for the restoration of that which was unrestored.
He lays down five; the sacrifice is fivefold: he thus seizes the sacrifice in its entirety, as great as the sacrifice is.
He fashioned that; then these seasonal (ṛtavyā) bricks are laid down following the Ashvinī bricks. Indeed, he thus placed the seasons for the seed that had been shed;

therefore, seed is deposited during all the seasons, and therefore seed is produced in accordance with all the seasons. Then these seasonal bricks are laid down following the Vāyavyā bricks; therefore, Vāyu moves about in accordance with all the seasons. Then these Vāyavyā bricks are followed by the Apasyā bricks.

They are not laid down; therefore, although animals have various vows, they become of one vow with respect to water alone. He lays down four bricks in front, for the head is fourfold: breath, eye, ear, and speech.

He settles them with verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), thinking, "May I be possessed of a head. He lays down five on each side for the sake of the animal's possession of strength, and also for the sake of providing it with a foundation.

Therefore, the animal is better when facing westward, for it has broader haunches; therefore, while moving eastward, [he says], "O Indra and Agni, make this brick firm so that it does not waver. This layer is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and these creatures are the intermediate space.
Indra and Agni are indeed the bearers of vigor among the gods; vigor is strength, and Indra and Agni are vigor. Thus, this vigor and strength is placed in the midst of creatures.

The gods indeed went to the heavenly world from this quarter; they stepped upon the quarters, and those [quarters] were distressed. They made them firm with these [bricks]. When these are laid down, it is for the support of the quarters. He lays down five; the sacrifice is fivefold: he thus seizes the sacrifice in its entirety. He places these ten in front; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is indeed the eye, the light.
This light, the eye of the meters, he places in front of the animal; therefore this eye is here in front.

Moreover, the Virāj is food; verily, he thus places food in the mouth. "The Mā metre, the Prama metre, the Pratima metre"—this world is indeed the Mā, the intermediate space is the Prama, and yonder sky is the Pratima; verily, he thus establishes these very worlds, and also the divine metres.
Verily, he lays down these as the metres of the gods; he lays them down twelve by twelve, which makes thirty-six.

The Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables, and the Bṛhatī among the metres has indeed attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). He for whom these are laid down attains self-sovereignty. The Bṛhatī is indeed cattle, and the middle layer is cattle; therefore, in this layer—

These are laid down. The higher ones have the Ādityas as their abode; they are the vital breaths (prāṇa). The lower ones have the Aṅgirases as their abode; they are the vital breaths. With the words, "Thou art the head, the ruler," he supports by means of these [bricks] those vital breaths which are above. With the words, "The controller, the ruler," he supports by means of these those vital breaths which are below. Thus, indeed, these [bricks] serve for the separation of these vital breaths. He settles them so that they share equally; they share equally.
"These are the vital breaths for the support of the vital breaths. If he should hate someone, he should set it down crosswise; he confuses that person's vital breaths, and he becomes liable to die.
He sets it down with verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), thinking, "May I be preeminent."
He places the *trivṛt*-verse brick in the east; for the *trivṛt* is indeed the beginning of the sacrifice, and thus he bestows the beginning of the sacrifice from the front.
He places the *saptadaśa*-verse brick on the south; for the *saptadaśa* is food, and thus he places food on the south.
Therefore, food is eaten with the right hand; therefore, the right half of the body is more powerful. Therefore...
The birds turn around following the southern half. [He places] a [stotra] consisting of fifteen verses on the north; the fifteenfold is indeed vigor, and thus he bestows vigor from the north.
[He places] one consisting of twenty-one verses on the west for the sake of stability. He sets down one consisting of three verses in the east;
the threefold is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice, and thus he places the mouth of the sacrifice at the beginning. [Then he places] one consisting of fifteen verses.
He places [the cup] on the south with seventeen verses, and on the north with seventeen verses, for the sake of providing vigor to both wings and for the sake of providing a proper abode;

therefore food is eaten with both hands. Furthermore, the fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, the sacrificer excludes his rival from both sides. He places [the cup] behind with twenty-one verses for the sake of stability; it is a firm foundation.
This is indeed the twenty-first [brick] of the sun; it conforms to the form of the sun. He becomes food and an eater of food for whom these are laid down.

"Thou art the portion of Agni, the overlordship of Dīkṣā; the Brahman is protected, the Trivṛt-stoma," he says. For these bricks are indeed named "the Protected" (spṛtaḥ). By means of these, Prajāpati protected whatever he desired; whatever—whatever... it was, that he protected.

In this way, whatever the sacrificer desires with these [bricks], that he secures. "With one they praised; offspring were produced"—these bricks are indeed named 'Creations' (sṛṣṭi). By means of these, Prajāpati created whatever he desired;
and whatever the sacrificer desires with these, that he creates. "O Agni, drive away our born enemies"—thus [he places them] in front.

He sets it down; by this [verse], he drives away those rivals who have already been born and repels those not yet born with the words, "O Jātavedas, drive them back. Thus, by this [verse], he repels those rivals who have already been born. This, indeed, is the dispelling of the enemy.
He sets it down on the south with the words, "The forty-fourfold Stoma is splendor, the wealth"; the sixteenfold Stoma is vigor, the wealth.

Thus, on the north side, there are forty-four syllables; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the *ṣoḍaśī* is a thunderbolt. The thunderbolt is grasped with the left hand and struck with the right; indeed, the sacrificer hurls this thunderbolt, grasped with the left and struck with the right, at his enemy. He places [the brick] containing loose earth in the middle, for this [universe] has loose earth in its center.

The dung of the animal is the middle of the self; thus he piles the fire-altar together with its very self. Now, these are the Virāj bricks. Speech indeed is the Virāj, and these bricks are cattle; verily, he places the highest speech within cattle. Therefore, one who possesses cattle speaks the highest speech.
Thus ends the second chapter, named Dṛṣāna, in the Upper Section.
[Page III,32] Now, these are the *stomabhāgās*. Bṛhaspati indeed brought this foundation of the sacrifice from among the Asuras;
when these are laid down, it is for the establishment of the sacrifice. The sacrifice, indeed, fell away from the gods; the gods [recovered] it by means of the *stomabhāgās*.
When these are laid down, they serve as a prop for the sacrifice. Indeed, Prajāpati gathered together this splendor of Agni from the earth;
thus, it is the very splendor of Agni that is now being gathered. Now, these are the "Nākasads" (those seated on the firmament).

For one who has piled the fire-altar, the firmament indeed becomes his; there is nothing at all that goes there, nor is there any comfort for one who has gone thither; therefore they are called Nākasads.

He places the five-crested *nākasad* bricks upon them for the attainment of the heavenly world. Indeed, this sacrificer is fully united with his wives and with Agni in that world when these [bricks] are laid down for him; moreover, light itself is built up in the middle.
These, indeed, are the wives of the sacrificer in that world; therefore, a woman should not approach one who has piled the fire-altar (*agnicit*), for she will become envious of her afterwards.

He places the last one facing east, for the wife sits behind him facing east. Now, these are the *kḷptis*: Prajāpati created offspring; once they were created, they disregarded him. Prajāpati saw these bricks and laid them down; then indeed he was established (*akalpata*). In that these are laid down, it is for the establishment of offspring. And these are the rain-bringers; rain is...
Food indeed departed from the gods; thereupon all this [world] withered away. Those gods ran to Prajāpati for help.
Prajāpati saw these bricks and laid them down; through them he secured rain and food for them.
Because these are laid down, it is for the securing of rain and food. The last layer is indeed a sowing-ground, for the bricks are one after another.
He lays down others and yet others; verily, he causes cattle to be born for him. The *svayamātṛṇṇā* is breath, and the *vāyavyā* is life;
he lays them down facing each other. He has thus made life and breath yoked together.
Moreover, it is by means of life and breath, joined together, that one enjoys. The *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed breath; he lays it down as the uppermost, for life is the highest.
If he were to place another brick above it, he would obstruct its vital breath, and he would be liable to die; therefore, he places that one last, for life is at its highest when it is at the end.
Now, this is the layer of the meters (*chandaściti*). The meters are indeed the desirable wealth of the gods, and cattle are the meters;

by means of this [layer], the sacrificer secures for himself that desirable wealth, namely cattle. Yajñasena Caitra once laid down this [layer], and he prospered. He who lays it down prospers. He settles it in front with *gāyatrī* verses; the *gāyatrī* is indeed brilliance, and brilliance is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Brilliancy...
Thus he acquires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). He lays down three [bricks], for Agni is threefold.

He settles them with verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), thinking, "May I be preeminent. With *triṣṭubh* verses on the south—since the *triṣṭubh* is force and vigor—he acquires force and vigor.
With *jagatī* verses on the west—since cattle are of the *jagatī* nature—he acquires cattle. With *anuṣṭubh* verses on the north—the *anuṣṭubh* is...

The left side is the station of cattle and the station of the sacrificer; the Āhavanīya fire is the station of the enemy. If he were to place them behind, he would place the desirable cattle in the station of the enemy. But since he places them in front, he thus places the desirable cattle in the station of the sacrificer. He places eight; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. As great as Agni is, so much [he establishes].

One who amasses [merit] should place eight *gāyatrī* verses before the *bahiṣpavamāna*; if his rival should be excessively powerful, he should place eleven *triṣṭubh* verses before the *mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna*, and twelve *jagatī* verses before the *ārbhava-pavamāna*. He should place these very same verses after the *pavamāna* chants if his rival should be excessively powerful.

The purifying wind (pavamāna) is indeed the vital breath; the purifying wind is the brilliance of Agni. By means of this brilliance, the sacrificer drives away his rival, repels him with brilliance, and pushes him aside with brilliance; for this is the repelling of the rival.
When building the first layer, he should build it knee-deep, as a layer built with the Gāyatrī metre; when building the second, he should build it navel-deep.

One building [the altar] should build it piled with Triṣṭubh verses, reaching as high as the chin; one building for the third time should build it piled with Jagatī verses. If, having built a larger [altar], one builds a smaller one, he would resort to a smaller sacrificial rite, [resulting in] fewer offspring, fewer cattle, and less food; he would become worse off. But if, having built a smaller one, he builds a larger one, he builds the larger one.
Thus he enters upon the sacrificial rite; he obtains more offspring, more cattle, and more food, and he becomes more prosperous.
This indeed is the layer of Agni called "the upward-leading" (*uttaravatī*); day by day he becomes better and better who knows this.

It should be built with five layers; the sacrifice is fivefold, cattle are fivefold; therefore it has five layers. There are five layers and five fillings (purīṣas), and thus it becomes the Virāj. Since it becomes the Virāj, the stotra of Agni should be performed [in that manner].
If it were to have five layers, it would depart from the Virāj; if it were to have ten layers, it would depart from the sacrifice and from cattle.

And in that it has five layers (*citikā*), he does not go away from the sacrifice and from cattle; and in that there are five layers and five fillings (*purīṣa*), he does not go away from the *virāj*. Thus, by means of both these forms, he wins cattle for him: that which of theirs is fivefold (*pāṅkta*) and that which is related to the *virāj*. Hair is two-syllabled, skin is two-syllabled, and flesh is two-syllabled.

The bone has two syllables, the marrow has two syllables; that makes ten. The *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the *virāj*; thus he wins cattle. It should be built with five layers: these worlds are three layers and the sacrificer is two; he has thereby established the sacrificer in these worlds. "What is the first layer? What is the filler? they ask; [the answer is: "This [earth]."

"The first layer is indeed this [earth], and the filling soil is the plants. "What is the second layer? What is the filling soil? they ask. "The second layer is indeed the intermediate space, and the filling soil is the birds. "What is the third layer? What is the filling soil? they ask. "The third layer is indeed yonder [sky], and the filling soil is the stars. "What is the fourth layer? What is the filling soil? they ask. "The fourth layer is indeed the sacrifice..."

"The fourth layer is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the loose soil (purīṣa); what is the fifth layer, and what is its loose soil? they ask. "The sacrificer himself is indeed the fifth layer, and his offspring is the loose soil. As much as there is, so much does he secure; that much he wins.
Now, these are the seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā). Agni Vaiśvānara is the year; Vaiśvānara is indeed the dear body of Agni."

Or rather, its very days and nights are laid down as bricks; he lays them down two by two for the sake of stability. Having inserted an *avakā* plant, he settles it for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. He lays down four in the middle layer, for the intermediate region is, as it were, unstable; [he does this] for the sake of stability. He lays down twelve; the year consists of twelve months, and the year is...
