Or rather, Vaiśvānara is indeed Agni; for Vaiśvānara is the dear body of Agni. Thus Agni is piled with his own dear body, and the *arka* brick is deposited with its body. "Thou art the internal bond of Agni"—Agni is indeed firmly joined for him for whom these bricks are laid down.
Indeed, Agni is firmly joined for him for whom these are laid down. "May Heaven and Earth be in harmony."

Thus it is indeed ordained for one who has piled the fire-altar: he who knows this attains preeminence among his peers. Verily, when he piles the fire, he kindles it; he causes it to blaze forth with the seasonal bricks.
Darkness indeed stands between [this world and] the heavenly world. These golden chips are indeed luminous bricks;
when he sprinkles them with water, he dispels that darkness and bestows light upon the sacrificer. There are a thousand of them, for Prajāpati is thousandfold;
verily, he attains Prajāpati. As far as a thousand extends from here, so far extends that heavenly world.
"May these bricks of mine be milch-cows for the world's totality in Agni. For these bricks are indeed named "milch-cows";
by means of them Prajāpati milked whatever he desired; and whatever the sacrificer desires by means of them, that he milks.
With the words, "You stand in the seasons, increasers of the season," he has made them stand in the seasons and increased them with the season; they drip with clarified butter.

With the words, "Dropping honey," he has indeed made them drop ghee; with the words, "Dropping honey, full of vigor, full of milk," he has indeed made them full of vigor and full of milk; with the words, "Sustaining the self, nest-like," for these are indeed nest-like. With the words, "The Virājs by name, the wish-fulfilling cows," for when those wish-fulfilling cows milked out every desire for the gods over there, then these [cows] also milked that; that is nourishment.

Thus he wins these [worlds] here; "in yonder world, in that world," for it is for yonder world that the fire-altar is built. Indeed, the gods excluded Rudra from the sacrifice; he turned toward them with his bowstring drawn, and therefore they were afraid of him.
Those gods ran to Prajāpati for help; Prajāpati saw this Śatarudriya, and with it he appeased him.

Therefore, he who knows thus—Prajāpati indeed knows him, and this god Rudra does not strike him down. Wherever he would wish to bring peace upon the creatures, he should go northward and move about while saying this very thing; for in his own quarter, with his own share, he thus appeases Rudra. First he offers at the height of the knee; by that, he appeases him in this very earth. [Then] at the height of the navel.

The second [offering] he makes from the intermediate space; by that, [the height reaches] as far as the chin. The third he makes from the sky; by that, he offers three times. For these worlds are three; verily, from these worlds he pacifies Rudra. Three times he offers again from there, returning [the offering];
those Rudras whom he sacrifices to from here, those he propitiates from there. Three times he offers from here, three times from there—that makes six; for the seasons are six.
Or rather, he thereby propitiates Rudra by means of the seasons from the seasons; he offers the oblations in equal portions, for the shares of the Rudras are divided equally.
He offers for twelve days, for with twelve days he indeed appeased him; verily, by means of twelve days, he appeases him.
He offers with an *arka* leaf; for with twelve days he indeed appeased him, and by means of twelve days, he appeases him.

He offers with a leaf of the *arka* tree; for by means of the *arka*, he thus performs a sacrificial expiation for the *arka*. If he were to offer with a vessel, he would bring Rudra down upon his offspring; therefore, he offers with a wild [branch]. Agni is indeed an animal; he is born at the very moment he is piled up. He seeks his own portion, just as a newborn calf seeks the udder; he seeks both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer.

He who offers the Śatarudriya looks upon him; verily, he pacifies him with his own portion. On that [cow] whose hind part is on the northern half, on the hip, one should offer; for having thus turned back Rudra in his own direction with his own portion, he pacifies him. The Aṅgirases, while going to heaven, poured the Gharma-vessel onto a goat's skin; it, burning, scorched a leaf.
As he touched it, it became the *arka* (flame-tree). Therefore, when one offers with an *arka* leaf, one thereby performs a sacrificial expiation (*avayajati*) with the *arka* against the *arka*.
If one should hate someone, one should cast [the leaf] into the path where his cattle move; whichever [cattle] first steps upon it meets with ruin.
This: [FN emended. Ed:
*etam*] he offers; [FN emended. Ed: *juhoti*] he pacifies: [FN va] Pattern (P).
The gerundive is this:
"O stone, [the strength] resting upon the mountain, the *ṛk*— sprinkling water, he goes around with the words, 'of Prajāpati indeed is this essence.'"

He sprinkles around with the very essence of Prajāpati, saying, "May hunger be upon your stone," and thus he consigns hunger to the stone itself; saying, "May that vigor be in me," he bestows vigor upon himself; saying, "May your heat strike him whom we hate," he consigns the heat of Agni to him whom he hates. He goes around sprinkling three times; for these worlds are three, and it is from these worlds that he [drives away the evil].

He pacifies the heat of Agni by sprinkling water around him three times; he goes around three times without sprinkling. That makes six; for there are six seasons, and it is from the seasons that he thus pacifies the heat of Agni. If he should practice sorcery, he should go around again without sprinkling while reciting this very sacrificial formula; whatever heat belongs to Agni, with that he strikes him down, if he should practice sorcery.
This one, the son of such-and-such a person from such-and-such a lineage, I cast away toward that direction.
Thus he should pour the pitcher onto the lower hip; for whatever he pours out, he meets with misfortune following that very thing.
Now, when he utters the name, he cuts off its very abode. He sings the Gāyatra on the Āgneyapāvamānī verse;
Pavamāna is indeed breath, and the Gāyatrī is the head. In that he sings the Gāyatra on the Āgneyapāvamānī verse, [he places it] upon the head.

Verily, he thereby bestows the vital breaths. This [earth] is the Rathantara; the intermediate space is the Vāmadevya; yonder [sky] is the Bṛhat. Thus the threefold Arka is deposited. The Vāmadevya is the self; the Yajñāyajñiya is the foundation; the Bṛhat and Rathantara are the two wings.
In that they sing the Bṛhat and Rathantara on both sides, he places the two wings upon the self. The sacrifice belongs to the gods.

Desiring to destroy those Rākṣasas, they struck them down with the Bṛhat and Rathantara; because the Bṛhat and Rathantara are sung on both sides, it is for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas. He sings the Heart of Prajāpati over the two shoulder-blades (apipakṣa); therefore this heart of one's own self is situated between the shoulder-blades.
He sings it without a Ṛc verse; therefore the heart is boneless. With Sāmans that are not Ṛks, they chant around the Arka.
The seven-bodied Arka is deposited.

This: *etaṃ* [is the correct reading]; the edition reads *etam*. Varuṇa is indeed this *menī* (the curse/disease) now; it stands blazing against him at that time. It would then depart by means of his breath. He recites over it with a frog; thus it departs by means of its very breath. It does not harm domestic animals, nor wild ones, [if one uses] *avakā* grass.

The *avakā* plant is indeed the womb of the waters; by means of this womb of the waters, he pacifies the heat of Agni. The *avakā* is indeed the form of the waters; by means of this form of the waters, he pacifies the heat of Agni. He approaches it with *vetasa* reeds; the *vetasa* is indeed the flower of the waters; by means of this flower of the waters, he pacifies the heat of Agni. He draws it across with seven [reeds].
There are indeed seven meters; by means of the meters he thus pacifies the heat of Agni. Moreover, the meters are the Brahman;

by means of the Brahman he thus pacifies the heat of Agni. Indeed, when Agni was created, he sought his own portion. He ran to Prajāpati, who gave him food. That became "ka" for him—for "ka" is food—and it was through food that it became so.

Verily, he thus approaches Agni for the sake of comfort; comfort indeed comes to him who has piled the fire-altar. He goes toward the one turned away, for the animal, once appeased, is turned away; for the animal, once turned away on the chariot, deposits seed. "May your missiles burn others than us; O Purifier, be auspicious unto us"—for *pāvaka* is food; verily, by means of food he interposes a barrier against the heat of Agni.
He sprinkles [the fire] with fragments of gold. Gold is indeed immortality, and Agni is brilliance; thus he sprinkles this brilliance with immortality.

He sprinkles with five [fragments]; the sacrifice is fivefold; he thus seizes the sacrifice in its entirety. There are two kinds of gods who come to the house of the sacrificer: by sprinkling [the fire] with curds mixed with honey, he [satisfies] them.

He gratifies everything; he sprinkles all of them, and thus he gratifies them all. He sprinkles with three verses, for Agni is threefold. He sprinkles with *triṣṭubh* verses for the attainment of power. He sprinkles with verses containing the word "food" for the attainment of food.
He sprinkles with a handful of *darbha* grass, for he is connected to Prajāpati. Indeed, he is deprived of his vital breaths when he approaches the fire.

When he says, "Giver of out-breath, giver of in-breath," he places the vital breaths within himself. Indeed, he who studies the Agnicayana is deprived of offspring and cattle; offspring are splendor (*varcas*) and cattle are prosperity (*varivas*). When he says, "Bestower of splendor, bestower of prosperity," having placed both offspring and cattle within himself, he descends [to earth].
He pacifies.
Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; he fell forward, and as he was falling, Vṛtra encompassed Indra with sixteen coils.
Having indeed scorched the coils of Vṛtra with Agni alone, he was released from evil and darkness by means of the two Vaiśvakarman [verses].

When he offers with the verse, "Agni with his sharp flame," it is as if he scorching the coils of evil with Agni is thereby released from evil and darkness by means of the two Vaiśvakarman [verses]. He offers separately with the two hymns for the sake of distinct powers; he offers with [the ladle] drawn sixteen times.
For with sixteen coils he (Vṛtra) encompassed him; by this [hymn], indeed, he was released from Vṛtra’s coils.
Thus, by this [hymn], one is released from the coils of evil. Now, this is the Apratiratha [hymn]; by it, indeed, the gods conquered the Asuras in opposition.
That is why the Apratiratha is called "unconquerable. By this [hymn], the sacrificer likewise conquers his rival in opposition.

One should cause him to sacrifice with this very [offering] if he desires victory; he conquers the battle. One should cause him who has rivals, or one who is dear to him, to sacrifice with this very [offering]; he prospers in himself, while his rival is defeated. With this very [offering], Bharadvāja indeed equipped Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa; he became the ruler of a kingdom. Whomever one should desire to be a ruler of a kingdom—this...
Thinking, "May he possess a kingdom," one should equip him with this [hymn]; verily, he becomes a possessor of a kingdom. By means of this, the gods indeed conquered the Virāj;

he recites ten verses, for the Virāj consists of ten syllables; by means of this, he conquers the Virāj itself. From the south, the Rakṣases sought to strike at the sacrifice of the gods; they indeed drove them away by means of the Apratiratha hymn. Therefore, when the Brahman priest recites the Apratiratha from the south...
He goes saying this for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasas.
"Victory! [jayati].
He places the fuel-sticks with the words, "Lead him upward," thereby providing a share for him as he is being offered. He places three;
for Agni is threefold. With the words, "Upward thee, all the gods," he places them, for all these gods are indeed present here. "We are humans, O Agni, let them bring [offerings]."

With the words "By thoughts," he causes him to prosper with that very thought for which the fire was established. With the words "May the five divine directions, the goddesses, protect the sacrifice," he endows these very five directions with splendor for him. With the words "Winged by hymns, worthy of praise, grasped," for he is indeed winged by hymns; and with the words "coming while grasping the sacrifice," for they indeed come having grasped him.

"Harikeśa, with sun-like rays, in front"—for that sun indeed is Harikeśa, with sun-like rays, in front; "Savitṛ, the light, rising eternally," he says for the sake of impulsion. "In his impulsion, Pūṣan goes, the knowing one"—Pūṣan is indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle. "Then may the prayers and our blessings be pleased"—this is for the sake of blessings.
This milking is indeed the milking of blessings. With the verse "All have made Indra grow," they go with a verse containing the word "grow";
thus they attain growth. They go with an *anuṣṭubh* verse; the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech belongs to the Viśvedevas, while Agni belongs to the Viśvedevas;

therefore they go with an *anuṣṭubh*. They go from the *āgnīdhra* shed with six verses; there are six seasons, so it is by means of the seasons that they go. He stands in the midst of heaven as a measurer.

Thus he sets down the stone: "For this Aditya is the measurer of the heavenly world; may the sacrifice, the bringer of bliss, bring hither and let Agni the god worship the gods, and bring them hither"—this is indeed the prayer. "May the sacrifice, the bringer of the gods, bring hither and let Agni the god worship the gods, and bring them hither"—this is indeed the fulfillment of the prayer. "By the impulse of strength, with the upward-lifting, he has lifted me up. This is the securing of the blessing.
Thus, this sun is indeed the *udgrābha* (the up-grasper) and this [moon] is the *nigrābha* (the down-grasper). Rising, he grasps the sacrificer upward;
setting, he holds his rival downward. "The *udgrābha* and the *nigrābha*"—the *udgrābha* is indeed the Brahman, the *nigrābha* is the Brahman.
By means of the Brahman he thus grasps the sacrificer upward, and by means of the Brahman he holds his rival downward, and likewise his enemies.

"May Indra and Agni scatter my enemies in all directions. For Indra and Agni are indeed might and vigor; by means of this might and vigor, the sacrificer drives his rival away in every direction. They proceed from the Āhavanīya fire with four [verses], for there are four meters;
they proceed by means of the meters themselves. Moreover, the meters are the Brahman; thus they proceed by means of the Brahman itself.

utthapatrā. 2.10.5: 136.17:

"O you whose vessel is the hymn, stride forth with Agni to the firmament," he says for the attainment of the heavenly world. "Having gone to the back of heaven, to the light," he says, for they go by way of the *pṛṣṭha* (ridge/back). "Bestow strength upon us, bipeds and quadrupeds," he says, [bestowing it] both upon bipeds and quadrupeds.
"And he bestows vigor upon the cattle, saying, 'Striving together with the Bhr̥gus,' for the Bhr̥gus indeed prospered first through sacrifice; [he does this] for prosperity.

'From the earth I have ascended to the atmosphere; from the atmosphere I have ascended to the sky'—this is the ascent of these worlds. He strides with five [verses]; the sacrifice is fivefold; verily, by means of the sacrifice he thus ascends the sacrifice."
He offers with the milk of a black cow that has a white calf, so as not to exclude Kṛṣṇā. The calf is indeed the day, the mother is the night;

he thus causes the night to yield itself to the day. Verily, day and night yield themselves to him who knows this. All cattle, though being of various forms, are of one form in their milk alone. In that they are of one form in their milk, he thereby secures them.

"O Agni, Night and Dawn! You are thousand-eyed, you are the fair-winged Garuḍa; sit upon the back of the earth!"—with these words, he indeed places this luminous Agni in these worlds, and also for the separation of the vital breaths. He sets it down with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet, [and this is] for support.
"Being invoked, fair-faced, in the east," he says, for the attainment of the heavenly world.

"Of Savitṛ, the most excellent, that wondrous one"—with this [verse], Kaṇva Śrāvasa indeed discovered the milking of Agni; for this is the milking of Agni. By means of this, the builder of the fire-altar (agnicit) milks Agni. Indeed, Agni milks all milkings and all desires for him who knows thus. "We would worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni," he says; this is for the sake of prosperity. "Kindled, O Agni... he says.
"Shine forth before us, O people"—this is indeed the fire-rod with knobs (*karṇakavatī sūrmi*). It is an unceasing light; verily, he has bestowed this unceasing light upon him.

Vasiṣṭha Sātyahavya once asked those sitting at a sacrificial session, "Do you know the fire-rod with knobs? They replied, "We know it. He said, "Do you know that which is in the woods? "We know it," they said. The "knobs" of this [fire-rod] are indeed cattle; thus, one becomes possessed of cattle.

The gods indeed launched this thunderbolt, the hundred-slayer, the repeller, against the Asuras; it crushed them by the hundreds. In the same way, the sacrificer launches this thunderbolt, the hundred-slayer, the repeller, against his rival;
he crushes him by the hundreds. "O Agni, strike him down"—with this *paṅkti* verse he offers; the *paṅkti* is indeed the sacrificer; [he thus strikes] the sacrificer.

Verily, he has thus established this [sacrifice] upon the Virāj; moreover, by means of the Paṅkti oblation, he undertakes the sacrifice. "Seven, O Agni, are thy fuel-sticks, seven thy tongues"—for so many indeed are the bodies of Agni, sixfold and seven by seven. Whoever, while piling the fire-altar, causes these [bodies] of his to wither, he himself withers away. He satisfies them for him with the words, "I offer the layer with the mind."
This indeed is Agni’s invincible Vaiśvakarman oblation; it does not harm the one who has piled the fire-altar, and his rival does not overcome him.

He who knows this attains preeminence among his equals. Agni thought, "I shall not bestow this splendor upon myself without a share. He secured it for himself with this share. This is indeed Agni’s Agnihotra; by means of this, the piler of the fire-altar secures Agni.
Agni indeed milks all milk-yields for him and grants all desires for one who knows thus. Truly, when he piles the fire, he kindles Agni; he causes that very Agni to blaze through the Agnihotra.

They said: *hotur* (FN Corrigenda;
Ed: *hotur*). *atṛṃhan*: (FN Correcturen und Conjecturen zu dem ganzen Werk). *tṛṃhati*: (FN Correcturen und Conjecturen zu dem ganzen Werk).

Now, this [offering] is for Agni Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; verily, he gratifies the year. Moreover, he has made a portion for him as one who has been brought hither. Through the firm foundation of the oblations, the sacrificer finds a firm foundation; through the lack of a firm foundation of the oblations, he does not find a firm foundation. In that he offers this [oblation], it is for the firm foundation of the oblations.
As they settle down, the sacrifice settles after them; as the sacrifice settles, the sacrificer settles. Furthermore, Vaiśvānara is indeed desire;

whatever desire he may have, that desire is fulfilled for him. If he were to turn toward the east, the divine subjects would become bewildered; if toward the south, it would belong to Yama as its deity; if toward the west, it would belong to Sūrya; if toward the north, it would belong to Rudra. It should be offered straight on for the sake of stability.
He offers the *sarvahuta* for the sake of stability. Vaiśvānara is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*), and the Maruts are the people (*viś*).
In that he offers to the Maruts after having offered this [Vaiśvānara], he thereby subjects the people to the ruling power; moreover, he makes the people obedient to the ruling power.
Prajāpati created animals with Agni at their head; the Maruts are the animals. In that he offers to the Maruts after having offered this [Vaiśvānara], [he ensures the continuity of the sacrifice].

Prajāpati produces cattle for him with Agni as their mouth. There are cakes on seven potsherds; there are seven groups of Maruts, therefore they are on seven potsherds. He offers group by group; thus he gratifies the Maruts group by group. That group which is to be recited in the forest, he should offer that in the middle; for this [group] of the Maruts is the nobility (*kṣatra*), while the others are the common people (*viś*); thus he places the nobility in the midst of the common people.

He makes the *kṣatra* (the ruling power) pre-eminent in the middle. If he should desire, "May I destroy the *kṣatra* by means of the *viś* (the common people)," he should confuse that group which is to be recited in the forest with the other groups; for by this he destroys the *kṣatra* by means of the *viś*. If he should desire, "May I destroy the *viś* by means of the *kṣatra*," he should confuse the group which is to be recited in the forest with the other groups; for by this he [destroys the *viś*] by means of the *kṣatra*.
He destroys the people; for him, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* should be in the *triṣṭubh* metre. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed force and vigor;
having taken this force and vigor from the people, he bestows it upon the ruling power (*kṣatra*). If he should desire, "May I destroy his ruling power with my own ruling power;
may he fall from his own abode," then with that group of verses which is recited in the forest, he should strike the chariot-stand at the fire-altar.

This chariot-stand for the Maruts is indeed the *kṣatra* (nobility) of the Maruts; it bears the *kṣatra* of the Kṣatriya. By means of this *kṣatra*, he strikes down his [enemy's] *kṣatra*. He falls from his own abode with the words, "The divine clans, the Maruts, follow Indra as their path.
This, indeed, is the path of the gods. Thus, he makes both the divine clan and the human clan follow him as their path.
Verily, when he piles [the fire-altar], he kindles Agni; he indeed makes him blaze with the [bricks] belonging to the Maruts.
Thus ends the third chapter, named Stomabhāga, in the Upper Section.

He offers the *vasordhārā* for the sake of the ordering of what is disordered, for the pacification of what is unpeaceful, for the conquest of what is unconquered, and for the acquisition of what is unacquired.
He offers it continuously for the continuity of the vital breaths, for the continuity of these worlds, and for the continuity of food; [he offers it] without interruption.
He offers for the non-interruption of food; if he were to interrupt it, he would interrupt the vital breaths. Whomever he hates, of him he interrupts the food-eating.
He cuts off his food with the words, "Hunger and food. These indeed are the forms of food; verily by means of its forms he secures food.
"Agni and the waters"—this indeed is the womb of food; verily from its own womb he secures food. Of the Vasu...

Thinking, "May it flow for me," he offers the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*). This is indeed a stream of clarified butter; they attend upon the sacrificer in yonder world. He offers twelve by twelve; the year consists of twelve months; verily, he wins the year.
He offers the *ardhendrāṇi* oblations; with the *ardhendras*, the gods indeed seized the power and vigor of the Asuras; [it is] power.

In this way, by means of these [oblations], the sacrificer wrests away the strength of his rival. Once, the gods and the Asuras were in conflict. The gods said to Indra, "Conquer them with you as our leader. He replied, "Let there be a share for me. They said, "Choose one. He said, "May I be entitled to half of the deities' portion. Thereupon they conquered; therefore, he (Indra) is the one who possesses a half-share.
Since the portions for the deities are offered with Indra as their chief, they become supreme through Indra after victory; for Indra is indeed power and vigor.
Thus, the sacrificer finds firm support in that power and vigor of the sacrifice.
With the words "Aṃśu and Raśmi," he secures the very mouth of the sacrifice, for Aṃśu and Raśmi are the mouth of the sacrifice. [He offers] Adhipati and Adābhya.

And thus his rival does not harm him who has piled the fire-altar; he attains preeminence among his peers, he who knows this. These are the cups (grahas); these indeed are the forms of the sacrifice; by means of the forms, he wins the sacrifice.
"The offering-spoons (srucaḥ) and the chalices (camasāḥ"—thus he collects the sacrificial implements (yajñāyudhāni). Having collected the sacrificial implements, [he wins] the sacrifice.

He employs the vessels; he offers with the vessels, or food is eaten by means of the vessels; thus he secures food in accordance with its proper form. "The sacrificial grass and the altar"—this is indeed a prayer for blessings; "the purificatory bath and the utterance of Svaga"—this is for the sake of firm establishment.

"Agni and Gharma"—this indeed is the luster of Agni that brings spiritual splendor; by this, he obtains both luster and spiritual splendor. He becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual splendor. "The Season and the Vow"—the season and the vow are indeed day and night; by this, day and night become propitiated and pleased for him. "One and three"—this is the meter of the gods.
Or [if he recites] "one and three," he wins the *devachandas* (divine meters); and "four and eight"—since four and eight are indeed the *manuṣyachandas* (human meters), he wins the *manuṣyachandas*.
By means of the *devachandas*, he prospers in the world of the gods; by means of the *manuṣyachandas*, he prospers in the world of men. "One and three, four and eight"—this is indeed an ascent.
This is the transition to these worlds, to the heavenly world. By means of the *stoma* increased by two, the Ādityas went to the heavenly world;
by means of the one increased by four, the Aṅgirases [did so]. When he offers these two *stomas*, it is for the attainment of the heavenly world.
These two *stomas* are indeed paired, even and odd, a couple for procreation; by means of the one increased by two, he places seed. Seed.

With the four and one, he produces welfare—the one and the three—up to thirty-three; those thirty-three deities become gratified and drunk by this for him. With the four and eight, [he produces] the forty-eight;
the Jagatī has forty-eight syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī; verily, he wins cattle, as well as the three-year-old ram and the three-year-old ewe.
And these indeed are the birds; [thereby] he wins animals, for animals are indeed animals. "May life be perfected through sacrifice;

may breath be perfected through sacrifice"—this is the perfection of the sacrifice; thus he has here brought the sacrifice to perfection. "To Vāja, svāhā! To Impulse, svāhā!"—these are thirteen oblations; thirteen months are a year; verily, he [establishes] the year for him.

He lays this down; he finds firm support in that very world of heaven. "The *stoma* and the *yajus*": the *stoma* and the *yajus* are indeed food; having thus placed food within himself and become an eater of food, he finally enters the domain of the gods.
Agni is indeed the Vasu, and this is his stream; for him, Agni milks all milkings and milks all desires.
He who knows thus: Agni indeed kindles this food for himself when he piles it; he truly causes him to blaze with a stream of wealth.
He performed the rite: he offers the *vājaprasavya* oblation. By this, Agni won *vāja* (strength/food) and the eating of food; by this, the sacrificers win *vāja* and the eating of food.
He offers it with each kind of food using the *vājaprasavyā* verses. *Vāja* is indeed food; [he does this] for the attainment of the eating of food.
He offers both the domestic and the wild; he does so for the attainment of both kinds of food. He offers with a ladle made of Udumbara wood;

the Udumbara is strength, [he does this] for the attainment of strength. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the speech of Sarasvatī, by the restraint of the restrainer, I consecrate Bṛhaspati unto sovereign rule. Thus [he says].

If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should consecrate him with the Bṛhaspatisava, for this is indeed [the sacrifice] of Bṛhaspati; he should consecrate him with the words, "I consecrate Indra for sovereignty.

If a Rājanya should sacrifice, he should consecrate him with the Indrasava, for this is indeed [the sacrifice] of Indra. On a black antelope skin, he should consecrate one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
for this is the form of the *ṛc* and *sāman* of the Brāhmaṇa. The *ṛc* and *sāman* are spiritual luster; verily, he attains spiritual luster.

One who desires cattle should [be consecrated] on a goat-skin; for the goat-skin is indeed cattle—he thus wins cattle. He who is piled with these fires is consecrated by them; he thus endows him with his own consecration. When the plants had ripened, the gods entered a contest; Agni won it. This is indeed the consecration of Agni; it is the consecration of food. Of all consecrations, this one is the Bṛhaspatisava.

This Brāhmaṇa of Bṛhaspati’s lineage is consecrated by his own consecration according to his deity. Regarding this they say: "One must certainly offer; for one who has been consecrated does not descend to anyone. Indeed, he who has piled the fire-altar is consecrated by his deity. The seasons indeed support the kingdom of one who is consecrated; there are six seasons, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛts are the seasons. In that he offers with six [verses], [he supports the kingdom].
Verily, he establishes his kingdom in the seasons; they support the kingdom for him. He offers with [an oblation] drawn twelve times;

the year has twelve months; having attained the year, he wins it. These offerings are indeed pairs: "To him svāhā! Vaṭ! To them svāhā! Vaṭ!"—in that very pair he places seed upon the head of the chariot.

He offers the seventh oblation for the conquest of the quarters; indeed, the quarters are conquered by means of the chariot. Now, these are the Vāta-homas (wind-oblations) for one who has piled the fire-altar. Indeed, yonder day and night are piled with fire, and this wind blows here; the wind is indeed breath. Verily, he secures breath for himself. He offers with joined palms, for there is no formal cutting-off (avadāna) of this [wind]; moreover, it is for the sake of grasping it. The wind is breath, and the hand is the means of grasping.
He has provided the most excellent [oblation] for the vital breaths; therefore, he offers with joined palms. He offers three times, for these worlds are three;
thus these very worlds shake the wind for him. "Thou art the ocean, windy, yielding moisture"—these indeed are the forms of Vāyu;
verily, by means of his forms, he wins Vāyu. "Thou art the Marutian, the host of the Maruts"—for Vāyu is indeed the Marutian. He thus unites this [wind] with Agni.
In that he kindles and piles [the fire], he truly makes it blaze with the Vātahomas. The Gāyatrī is indeed the out-breathing (prāṇa); the Havirdhāna shed is Gāyatra.

The Jagatī is the in-breathing (apāna); the Sadas is Jāgata. The Triṣṭubh is the diffused breath (vyāna); the Āgnīdhra is Traiṣṭubha. "The speckled life-spirit (asu), the speckled stone, is placed in the midst of heaven"—verily, by this, he places that [stone] in the middle of his out-breathings and in-breathings.

He places nine stones for the support of the vital breaths in the Āgnīdhra fire-hall; there are indeed nine vital breaths, and thus he places the vital breaths of this sacrificer in the world of the sacrificer. He places twenty-one in the Hotṛ’s station for the sake of stability, for the twenty-one-fold is a foundation. Eleven in the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s station; the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor; verily, he finds support in vigor. Eight each...

In the others, there are eight-syllable *gāyatrī* verses; the *gāyatrī* is Brahman, and thus he establishes himself in Brahman. There are six [verses] at the *mārjālīya* altar; for there are six seasons, and the seasons indeed carried him around from the south. The seasons are the Fathers; moreover, there are six meters, and it is with the meters that he yokes this [fire] at the beginning of the sacrifice. With the words, "In harmony with the year, with the Āyavas," these indeed are the deities of Agni.
These very [deities] have their portions at the beginning; he thus gratifies them. Moreover, these are indeed the dear bodies of the gods; he thus gains possession of them.

With the words, "In harmony with the year, with the Āyavas,"—the year is indeed the *abda*, and the seasons are the *āyavāna*s; by this, his seasons are sacrificed to and become gratified. With the words, "In harmony with the Dawn, with the ruddy ones," he gratifies the Dawn itself. "In harmony with the Aśvins... [and so on].
"With their wondrous powers"—the Aśvins are indeed day and night; thus by this [verse], day and night become worshipped and gratified for him.

"In harmony with Sūra through Etaśa"—he thereby gratifies Sūrya (the Sun). "In harmony with Vaiśvānara, with the *iḍā* and with ghee—Svāhā! Vaiśvānara is indeed the year, the *iḍā* is cattle, and ghee is cattle; thus by this [offering], the year and cattle become worshipped and gratified for him.
They exist; he offers oblations upon a clump of *darbha* grass. This is indeed his immortal body, and it is in the immortal that the fire-altar is built.

Having placed gold down, he offers; thus he offers upon what possesses fire, upon what possesses a foundation. The officiating priest (*adhvaryu*) would become blind if he were to offer where there is no foundation. Indeed, the chariot of the gods is yoked for the sake of the heavenly world, while the chariot of men is yoked for the sake of desire. [He offers] the fire...
With the words, "I yoke [thee] with power and ghee," he indeed yokes Agni; by means of him thus yoked, he goes to the heavenly world.

If he were to yoke with all [three verses], his sacrifice would be yoked but the oblations would lack a firm foundation. He does not yoke with two either, for the sake of the firm foundation of the oblations.
As those [oblations] find a firm foundation, the sacrifice finds a firm foundation after them, and the sacrificer finds a firm foundation after the sacrifice.

He yokes with three verses, for Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, him he yokes. When he is yoked, every oblation is placed within him. He yokes with five verses, for the sacrifice is fivefold; as great as the sacrifice is, it seizes that. Indeed, these two burn this [Agni]:
both the one who is being piled and Vaiśvānara. When [he recites] the two verses containing the word "water" before the Yajñāyajñiya chant—
He touches [it] for the sake of peace; this indeed is the measure of the sacrifice, namely the Agniṣṭoma, yet even more than that is performed for it thereafter.

He who, when the time for yoking has arrived, does not yoke the fire, nor yokes it among those who are yoking, [commits an error]. With the verse, "O Agni, yoke those that are thine," he indeed yokes the fire when the time for yoking has arrived; he yokes it among those who are yoking. He who, when the time for unyoking has arrived, does not unyoke the fire, nor unyokes it among those who are unyoking, [commits an error]. With the verse, "I loosen thy reins, I loosen thy traces," he indeed unyokes the fire when the time for unyoking has arrived.
When [the fire] has arrived, he releases it; while it is being released, he releases it. Just as the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) is, so is the re-piling (*punaściti*).
He who prospers through the establishment of the fires establishes them again; and he who, having piled the fire-altar, should think, "May I prosper," let him pile this re-piling.
Even one who piles for the first time should pile it; thus he prospers, and indeed he prospers. Furthermore—

Whatever oblation the fire-piler offers that is not made with bricks, it flows away; as it flows away, the sacrifice flows after it, and the sacrificer flows after the sacrifice. In that he piles this *punar-citi* (re-piling), it is for the support of the oblations;
as they find support, the sacrifice finds support after them, and the sacrificer finds support after the sacrifice. He piles eight [bricks]; the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables.

The Gāyatrī is Agni’s metre; as great as Agni is, so much of him he builds. Having laid down eight *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and having covered them with loose soil—the Gāyatrī has eight syllables and the Gāyatrī is the Brahman—he builds him by means of the Gāyatrī metre, by means of the Brahman. Having laid down eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and having covered them with loose soil—the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables and the Triṣṭubh is vigor—he builds him by means of the Triṣṭubh metre.

With vigor he piles [the altar]; having laid down twelve *lokapṛṇā* bricks, he covers them with loose soil. The *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the *jagatī*; verily, by means of the *jagatī* metre and by means of cattle, he piles it. This indeed is the high-altar (*uttaravedi*) of Agni; this Agni is piled as the high-altar.
If one’s fire should have been previously piled, he should settle down and sacrifice after it, just as...
Just as one adds more wood to a fire that is already burning, so indeed does he bestow upon him an ever-increasing brilliance.
Regarding this, they say: "Who will awaken one who is sleeping better than a superior? For by means of the oblation, he diminishes him who sacrifices.
Indeed, he who piles the fire-altar makes a home for himself; or rather, whatever he finds elsewhere, he brings it to his home when he performs the sacrifice.
Or he may sacrifice with an animal or with Soma; he should sacrifice after settling down beside that fire of his which was piled previously.
Just as one, having obtained wealth from elsewhere, brings it to his home, so is that. Regarding this they say: "Verily, the sacrificial ladle (sruva) is used again in this sacrifice.
Wherever he may sacrifice, having placed these twenty-one [bricks], he should sacrifice for the sake of stability; [it serves as] a firm foundation.
"Indeed, it is the twenty-first. //MS_3,4.5 //

He should pile [the fire] with the verses beginning, "May the seasons increase thee in unison; may the seasons increase thee. Thus he kindles it both with the half-years and with the seasons. With the verse, "Shine forth with the heavenly light," he piles it as possessed of light. With the words, "Illumine all the four quarters," therefore—

"Agni illumines all the quarters; from that state beyond, O Bṛhaspati, release him from the curse of Yama"—this one should perform for one who is ill. Yama is indeed death, and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; by means of the Brahman as far as it extends, he heals him.
"May the Aśvins ward off death from him"—the Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; they [ward it off] from him.

With the verse, "We drive death away from around the darkness," he indeed strikes away the darkness that is evil and ascends to the heavenly world. Indeed, he was the Hotṛ-priest for Agni Citya, the all-encompassing, whose name is "the Bringer. They said to him, "Go for those [verses] containing the word *ap* (water). It was these *sāmidhenī* verses containing the word *ap* that the Gandharvas and Apsarases revealed to him.
They serve for the sake of peace. He recites twenty-four verses; the Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the mouth of the sacrifice;
thus he seizes the very mouth of the sacrifice. Moreover, there are twenty-four half-months in a year, and the year is established prosperity (*śrī*);
indeed, this [year] does not waver from prosperity, nor does his prosperity waver. He recites Gāyatrī verses; brilliance (*tejas*) indeed is...

The *gāyatrī* is spiritual luster; verily, he wins spiritual luster and splendor. He recites the *triṣṭubh*s; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor and strength; verily, he wins vigor and strength. In that there are both *gāyatrī*s and *triṣṭubh*s, by that very means he wins both. Those verses addressed to Agni which are unexpressed (*anirukta*) should be performed; for this [sacrifice] is, as it were, unexpressed.

It goes forth unturned, yet turned away from evil and the rival; one should perform these rites for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, for who would ascend the field of the gods twice? "Having carried the fire for three nights, the fire-altar should be built," they say;
the Virāj consists of three feet, and thus he attains the Virāj. "Having carried the fire for six nights, the fire-altar should be built," they say; for the year consists of six seasons.

The Virāj is dependent upon the year; verily he attains the Virāj. "Having carried [the fire] for ten nights, the fire should be piled," they say; the Virāj has ten syllables; verily he attains the Virāj. "Having carried [the fire] for twelve nights, the fire should be piled," they say;
twelve months are a year; the Virāj is dependent upon the year; verily he attains the Virāj. Twenty-four...

"One should pile the fire after carrying it for nights," they say; for twenty-four half-months make a year, and the Virāj is dependent upon the year: verily he attains the Virāj. "One should pile the fire after carrying it for a month," they say; verily he attains the year month by month. Eight Vasus indeed carried it for a month; they won this world and the Gāyatrī metre. Eleven...

The Rudras won for themselves the intermediate region as their world and the *triṣṭubh* as their metre; the twelve Ādityas won for themselves yonder world and the *jagatī* as their metre. They prospered; he who, knowing thus, maintains the fire for a year, prospers.
Therefore they say, "Agni is indeed maintained for a year. Now these are the *āprī* verses; having created the creatures, Prajāpati—
Being emptied, he reflected; he saw these Āprī verses, and with them he gratified himself. Prajāpati is indeed Agni;
in that these are the Āprīs, the sacrificers gratify Agni by means of them. This metre is hairy and cattle-bestowing;
it is deficient and redundant for the sake of procreation. They consist of Virāj verses, for the Virāj is all the metres; [all] the metres...
Thus his meters are established; he should make them "all-seeing" (viśvacit). These [meters] are indeed the vital breaths;
they are both greater and smaller, for these vital breaths are both greater and smaller. Thus he places the vital breaths within himself.
Or: *vā* (emended; Ed.: *ā*).

If the fire in the *ukhā* pot goes out, it is just as if a son who has been born were to die. If it should go out, he should kindle that same *ukhā* again; this indeed is the womb of Agni; verily, he procreates it from its own womb. It is indeed capable...
This is the progenitor who piles the fire-altar.

O Agni, those moist wombs of yours, those nest-like ones, those drops of yours, O Agni, and those navels— with all these twofold ones, being in harmony and knowing [the way], sit down here for this body.

Thus, because this [verse] contains the word "moist" (*ārdra*) and the word "nest" (*kulāya*), it serves for peace. Indeed, offspring are a nest and cattle are a nest; by means of the word "nesting" (*kulāyinīḥ*), it serves for procreation. He who piles the fire-altar, having piled the fire-altar, approaches his wife—he has indeed become an oblation.
It would be just as if an oblation had been spilled; just as they seek an expiation for a spilled oblation, so too for him.

If one should approach [the fire], they should desire an expiation; he should sacrifice with a curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. Thus he attains the state of Mitra and Varuṇa for the sake of his own non-spilling. Agni is indeed an animal; whoever approaches the animal from the front harms it.
Therefore, one does not step upon it from the front toward the back; rather, one approaches it from behind toward the front for one's own sake.
"Indeed, he who piles the fire according to its proper course and according to its form ensures that offspring and the seasons are established.

Those bricks which turn to the right, he places on the south; those which turn to the left, he places on the north. He places the triple-lined bricks behind, facing eastward. Thus he piles the fire according to its proper course and according to its form, so that offspring and the seasons are established."
And they deliberate thus: "There is truth; the fire-altar is to be piled," so they say.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.

Thus, as far as the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks extend from the front, this indeed is the truth of speech; he thus piles the fire-altar with truth itself. The *svayamātṛṇṇā* is breath, and gold is immortality. In that he places a gold brick and then places the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, he places breaths in him that are immortal. "Thou art brilliance, grant me brilliance," with these [formulas] he places the gold bricks.

Or rather, these worlds are supported by them; moreover, it is with these very [bricks] that one piles the fire-altar. These worlds shine forth. Having slain the Asuras, the gods were afraid of death; they saw the meters and entered into them. Whatever [part of themselves] was exposed to them, they covered that with [the meters].
That is the reason for the "metrical nature" (*chandastva*) of the meters. Having laid down each layer (*citi*), he touches the layer with a verse addressed to Agni, beginning with the word *dhāma*.
He enters into his very own deity for the sake of his own non-injury.

One who desires heaven should pile the *śyena-citi* (falcon-altar). Having become a falcon, the Gāyatrī flew to that world; [this is] for the attainment of the heavenly world. One who has rivals should pile the *rathacakra-citi* (chariot-wheel-altar). The gods, having made the chariot wheel into a thunderbolt (*vajra*), hurled it against the Asuras; they shattered their hundredfold host. Having made this very altar into a thunderbolt, [he should do likewise].
The sacrificer causes [the fire] to roll forward against his rival; he indeed crushes him a hundredfold. One who has rivals should pile the *prauga* altar;
for on both sides the Asuras surrounded the gods—some from the front, others from behind—and it was by means of this that they drove them away.
This, then, is the driving away of the rival. One who desires food should pile the *droṇa* altar; for by means of a wooden trough (*droṇa*), food is eaten.

One obtains food in accordance with the *anurūpa* (corresponding) [brick]. There is a rice-pot offering (*caru*) at the back for the sake of correspondence. He who desires, "May I go directly to the world of the fathers," should pile the funeral mound (*śmaśānaciti*);
he goes directly to the world of the fathers. Another should pile it if he desires a village;
just as he piles this one, so he piles a village for him. One desiring cattle should pile it by gathering [the earth] together (*samūhya*).
Just as he sweeps this [fire] together, so does he sweep the cattle together for him from all directions.
