*FN Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.*
Prajāpati indeed built this fire-altar first by means of the seasons and the year:

he built the front part with spring, the right wing with summer, the left wing with the rainy season, the tail with autumn, and the middle with winter; he built the front part with the Brahman, the right wing with the Kṣatra, the left wing with the Viś, the tail with cattle, and the middle with hope.

There is only as much as there actually is; he pervades that, he secures it. Indeed, the fire-altar is built for the sake of the heavenly world, and the set of eleven [sacrificial stakes] is a thunderbolt. If he were to set up the eleven stakes, the thunderbolt would strike him from the front and he would be excluded from the heavenly world. If he were not to set them up, he would be without cattle. Therefore, let eleven animals be tied to a single stake; by that means he becomes rich in cattle, and by that means he attains the heavenly world.

If one were to measure [the altar] according to the wingspan, he would enter upon a lesser sacrificial rite, obtain fewer offspring, fewer cattle, and less food, and would become more wretched. But when he measures it according to the altar-site, he piles it as something greater;
indeed, he enters upon a greater sacrificial rite, obtains more offspring, more cattle, and more food, and becomes more prosperous.

This indeed is the layer of the fire-altar called the "Successive" (uttaravatī). He who knows this becomes superior day by day. Indeed, for one who has piled the fire-altar, his glory and power depart in two ways: they go either to the fire-altar itself or to his own self.
Bestow radiance upon our Brahmins; maintain radiance among the kings; grant radiance to the Vaiśyas and the Śūdras; through radiance, bestow radiance upon me.
Thus, when he offers this oblation, he impels his own self toward Agni with glory; for he who studies the Agni [section] is liable to become afflicted with skin disease.
That I implore of you, worshipping with sacred prayer; that the sacrificer seeks from you with oblations. O Varuṇa, be mindful here without anger; do not steal away our long-lived span of years.

Thus, as for why he offers [these oblations]: this is indeed a pacification of Agni, a protection for oneself; Agni is vitality. Therefore, one who has built the fire-altar (*agnicit*) must not eat birds, nor should one who knows the fire-altar eat them; if he were to eat them, they would devour him and lead him to ruin. Prajāpati indeed built this fire-altar first, desiring preeminence; he attained preeminence and greatness—preeminence.

He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, attains greatness. Prajāpati, having created offspring, entered into them. He said, "Whoever shall pile me together, he shall prosper. The gods piled him together; they prospered.
That is why the fire-altar is called *citya* (the piling). Therefore, he who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, piles Prajāpati himself and prospers.
Therefore they say: "Agni is indeed piled by Prajāpati."
The light did not shine forth for the gods who had piled the fire-altar. They offered an oblation into the fire, saying, "Shine forth first for you;
thus it will shine forth for us. Through that [oblation], the light shone forth for Agni; the light shone forth for Agni, but it did not shine forth for the oblation.
Through the sacrifice, the light shone forth for that oblation; the light shone forth for the oblation, but it did not shine forth for the sacrifice. [They offered] for that sacrifice.

Through the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) they shone forth; for the sacrifice they shone forth, but it did not shine forth for the sacrificial fee. Through the *brāhmaṇa* they shone forth for that sacrificial fee;
for the *brāhmaṇa* they shone forth, but it did not shine forth for the *brāhmaṇa*. Through the sacred word (*brahman*) they shone forth for that *brāhmaṇa*;

for the *brāhmaṇa* they shone forth, but it did not shine forth for the sacred word. Through ascetic fervor (*tapas*) they shone forth for that sacred word. These indeed are the stages culminating in ascetic fervor.

The dawns dawn for prosperity and greater well-being for him who, knowing thus, lays down the dawns. Verily, he for whom the dawns dawn in their proper sequence knows the dawns according to their proper sequence, and for him they dawn in their proper sequence. The first dawn is indeed that of Uṣas;
they say it is "Vyavāt" (the Pervader) because of what arises at dawn, what shines forth, when the fire is kindled, when the sun rises, and when the hands [are raised].
Whatever he eats and whatever he drinks, these indeed are the dawns in their proper order; for him who, knowing this, lays down the dawns, the dawn breaks in its proper order.
Whoever piles the fire-altar without a womb and without a foundation becomes himself without a womb and without a foundation; for water is the womb of the fire.

In that he places the jar-bricks, he piles the fire-altar as one possessing a womb and a foundation; he becomes possessed of a womb and possessed of a foundation. "The fire-altar should be piled with its rival below," they say; for water is the rival of the fire. In that there are jar-bricks...
He places them down; he thus piles the fire with its rival subdued; his evil becomes inferior to him, and his rival becomes inferior.

Fire is indeed heat, and water is the pacification; in that he places the jar-bricks, it is for pacification. In that there are both jars (kumbha) and jar-shaped bricks (kumbhyā), that is a pair; in that there is a pair, it is for procreation. He places twelve; the year has twelve months.

Having obtained the year itself, he secures it. The rice-oblation (caru) of wild rice consists of thirteen portions; since there is a thirteenth month, it is by means of this that he obtains and secures it. It is prepared in milk: by the milk which is domestic, he secures food-eating;
by the wild rice, he secures that which belongs to the forest; thus, by that very means, he secures both.
Thus ends the fourth lesson concerning the Vasordhārā in the Upper Section.
Verily, he who piles up only the head [of the fire-altar] cuts himself off from Prajāpati, but not from his other limbs; he becomes one who has piled bones, one who has piled a cemetery.
In that he piles this "man-pile" (puruṣaciti), he does not cut himself off from Prajāpati; he does not become one who has piled bones, nor one who has piled a cemetery.
There are thirty-six of these; he lays them down. The *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables; cattle are connected with the *bṛhatī*, and man is connected with the *bṛhatī*.
An image of man is thus laid down, for it is he who is being established here. Indeed, that sacrificer for whom these are laid down does not die prematurely in yonder world.

Now, these are the five *pañcāpañcīnā* bricks. The fire-altar when built is, as it were, loose; in that he lays down the five *pañcāpañcīnā* bricks, it is for the support of the fire and to prevent its looseness. He lays down five; the sacrifice is fivefold: having grasped the sacrifice in its entirety, [he says], "Thou art the maker of abundance, thou art the maker of wide space"—thus he bestows abundance upon the fire itself; he becomes more abundant in progeny and cattle. [He lays down] the *apsuṣad*.

"Thou art a falcon; thou art a vulture"—Agni is indeed a bird; verily he makes him a bird to be looked upon, and having become a bird, he goes to the heavenly world for whom these [bricks] are laid down.
With the words, "Ye are piled; ye are piled around," he encloses the pebbles.

For if he were to pour down the sand without enclosing it with pebbles, the emitted seed would be spilled away; therefore, when he pours down the sand after enclosing it with pebbles, it is for the sake of containing the emitted seed.

The sacrifice is indeed severed when they release the animal before it has been completed. Āśokeya used to restore it by completing it with clarified butter for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice.
He who piles the fire-altar ascends to the heavenly world; when he offers the *anvāroha* oblations, having caused him to go to the heavenly world, he then moves according to his desire.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Upper Section.

One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu. Agni is indeed all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus one seizes both the deities and the sacrifice. Agni is the end of the sacrifice from below, and Viṣṇu is from above; thus one seizes the ends of the sacrifice from both sides. Regarding this they say: "The sacrifice must not be without Indra. In that it is on eight potsherds, it belongs to Agni; in that it is on three potsherds—[it belongs to Viṣṇu].

In that it becomes a cake on eleven potsherds for Viṣṇu, by that it is for Indra; for Agni is the purifier of the sacrifice and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice—it is indeed a sacrifice purified by the purifier that he undertakes. This form of the sacrifice is indeed the sacrificial oblation (*medha*); since the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is that very form, therefore a cake must be prepared. They prepare a cooked rice offering (*caru*), for ghee is the milk of the cow and [the milk] of the ox.

The rice grains are a pair; verily he places a pair at the beginning of his sacrifice. Ghee is indeed brilliance; verily one is born from brilliance. This man is indeed sacrificed for the sake of wisdom, for this image is like a man, since its form is as it were that of a person;

therefore, the sacrificial pap (caru) must be prepared. He undergoes initiation upon the altar-ground (*vedi*); "he finds" (*vindate*), indeed, is what is meant by "upon the altar-ground" (*vedimati*). Verily, he finds.

Verily, he who undergoes initiation upon the sacrificial altar (vedi) has indeed undergone initiation upon the very path of sacrifice. By means of the altar, the gods found this [earth] from among the Asuras; so too, he who undergoes initiation upon the altar finds this very [earth]. Moreover, he has seized the very path of sacrifice. They construct the hall with its beams pointing eastward;
for when they fashioned these quarters, it was this [earth] they fashioned for the gods, this for the ancestors, and this for men.
From the Asuras he approaches these humans; for him who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*), this deity approaches. He turns toward the very quarter of the gods;

he turns toward the eastern quarter indeed. Moreover, he enters the domain of the gods. They enclose it [with a screen], for the human dwelling is indeed separated from the divine dwelling. Thus, they separate him from the human dwelling, and also from the Rakṣases.

"He who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*) indeed departs from this world so as not to return; for he goes to the people and ascends to the world of the gods. By enclosing [the fire-hall] and making it free of openings, he does not go away from this world; by that, he is supported in this world. One desiring heaven should perform the commencement in the east. Yonder sun is indeed the heavenly world; [he thus places him] within the sight of yonder sun."

He should cause [the sacrificer] to go toward the south and perform the commencement if he should desire of someone, "May he prosper in the world of the fathers. This indeed is the direction of the fathers;

verily, he prospers in the world of the fathers. He should perform the commencement from behind for one who desires offspring; for from behind the seed is deposited, and the consecrated one is seed—he thus places seed in him. He should perform the commencement from the north if he should desire of someone, "May he prosper in the world of men."

"May he prosper"—this indeed is the direction of men; in the world of men alone does he prosper. He should make his departure from the north-east if he should desire of someone, "May he prosper in both worlds. For this is indeed [the way] for both worlds; thus he prospers in both worlds. He should make his departure from all sides if he should desire of someone, "May he prosper in all directions. Thus he prospers.
Thus, [he prospers] in all directions; he thus succeeds.
He undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*). He shaves his hair and beard, cleans his teeth, cuts his nails, and bathes; for this skin is indeed dead and impure.

This impurity is in his own self; he thereby removes that very [impurity]. Being pure, he approaches the sacrificial essence. Having caused the consecration (*dīkṣā*) to enter the waters, the gods went to the heavenly world. When he bathes in the waters, he takes hold of that very consecration.
Then, when he descends into the waters for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he causes that consecration to enter the waters once again. "O plant, protect him! he says.
"Protect him, O Svadhiti; do not harm him!"—the Svadhiti is indeed the thunderbolt, and it is capable of harming the sacrificer if it is not appeased.
When he places a blade of grass in between, it is for the sake of the sacrificer's safety. "O God-hearer, shave these [heads]!"—for he shaves them while they are indeed being heard by the gods.
"May I attain well-being in the end"—that is to say, "May I reach the successful conclusion of this sacrifice."

"May the waters, my mothers, purify me"— for the waters are indeed the sacrifice— "may those who purify with ghee purify me with ghee"— thus he purifies himself by means of the deities— "may the goddesses carry away all defilement"— whatever defilement, impurity, or stain there is in his self, that they carry away from him— "I emerge from them bright and purified"— he becomes bright.

Thus, from these [waters], he rises as one worthy of sacrifice, fit for the altar, and purified; for the consecrated one is indeed the oblation (*havis*). When one sprinkles the oblation with the *yajus*-formula, then it becomes the oblation; when he bathes him with the *yajus*-formula, he has made him into the oblation. He eats [the food]; for eating is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*);
having placed the vital breaths within himself, he undergoes consecration. Man is indeed hollow; he is truly whole only when he has eaten.

When he has eaten, he becomes pure and attains the sacrificial essence (*medha*). Just as one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) here [on earth], so indeed is he in that world; for it remains [in his body] even when he has overeaten. Therefore, one should not eat excessively. That [excessive eating] is not to be desired; one should eat only having eaten moderately. For just as one who is consecrated should eat less and less, so should he eat. Indeed, that which is less while being consecrated—

He bathes; with that, the initiated one anoints himself, or he rubs oil on his body and puts on a garment. These indeed are the bodies of man; verily, with his full body, he approaches the sacrificial state. He anoints himself with fresh butter (*navanīta*). Fresh butter is the portion of the gods, ghee (*ghṛta*) is that of men, melted ghee is that of the Gandharvas, and self-melted ghee is that of the Pitṛs. This [fresh butter] belongs to all the deities; therefore, he anoints himself with fresh butter.
He mixes [the butter] with two bunches of *darbha* grass; that indeed was the ointment he made, and thus he now pours it on for the sake of wisdom (*medha*).
He says, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," for this is indeed the milk of the great ones; "the essence of the waters and the plants," for this is indeed the essence of the waters and the plants;
"thou art the bestower of splendor (*varcas*), bestow splendor upon me"—thus he invokes a blessing.
He causes to disappear;
FN emended. Ed: antar dadhāti.
[The text] reads *svid*.

[He] anoints himself for procreation; he anoints with a blade of *iṣīkā* grass, for humans anoint themselves with *śala* grass. He anoints with the tufted [grass], for humans anoint themselves with the tuftless. He anoints the right [eye] first, for humans anoint the left first. Three times [he anoints] one [eye], three times the other.
He anoints with something else, for men anoint themselves with an unlimited amount; he does not use it again, for men anoint themselves so as to return [to worldly life] again.

Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; his eye-pupil flew away and went to the Trikakubh mountain. That is the Traikakuba collyrium which he anoints. The eye is truth; one does not place trust in speech as in the eye. Having grasped truth itself, he enters upon the consecration (dīkṣā).

"I approach within with you; I place hatred and enemies within by means of a great mountain"—by means of the mountain, he thus places hatred and enemies within. "Thou art the protector of sight; protect my sight"—thus he invokes a blessing. He purifies both upward and downward, for this breath moves both upward and downward. If he hates anyone, he should purify him crosswise, [thereby] [purifying] his vital breaths.
"It deludes him; he becomes subject to death. "May Citpati purify you"—Citpati is indeed the sacrifice;

"may Vācaspati purify you"—Vācaspati thus purifies him for the sake of the sacrifice. "May the god Savitṛ purify you"—impelled by Savitṛ, he purifies himself for wisdom through these deities. "With a flawless strainer"—this, indeed, is the flawless one.

"The purifier which belongs to the sun—verily with that flawless purifier he purifies him. "O Lord of the Purifier, with thy purifier... The Lord of the Purifier is indeed the sacrifice; it is for the sake of the sacrifice that he thus purifies his own self.
He anoints: "May I be able to perform the sacrifice."
Thus, when Indra struck Vṛtra upon the waters, that which among them was worthy of sacrifice and fit for the altar rose upward;

it became these plants. Of these, the Darbha grass is indeed their splendor. These [Darbhas] are the waters when they are dry; he thus secures for himself whatever splendor they possessed. There are three kinds of waters: those of heaven, those of the earth, and those of the ocean. All of these are spread out within the Darbha.

Therefore, the *darbha* grass is a purifier; with two [blades] he purifies him, for there are two purifiers, and the sacrificer has two feet: as great as his self is, that much he purifies. He purifies three times, for the gods are true in three ways; moreover, these vital breaths are three—the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the in-breath (*apāna*), and the diffused breath (*vyāna*)—as great as his self is, that much he purifies. He purifies with seven [verses], for there are seven meters; by means of the meters...

Thus he purifies him; moreover, the meters are indeed the Brahman, so it is by means of the Brahman that he purifies him. He purifies him with twenty-one [stalks]: there are ten fingers, ten toes, and the self is the twenty-first; as great as his body is, that he purifies. There are three things belonging to Nirṛti: dice, women, and sleep. When he undergoes initiation, he thereby separates himself from dice and from women. As for the woman...

On the first night the initiated one keeps watch; by that he is freed from sleep. That first night which the initiated one dwells upon, by that he wins the sacrifice; that which [he dwells upon] when the Soma has been purchased, by that he wins offspring; that which [he dwells upon] on the eve of the pressing, by that he wins cattle.

"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, Svāhā!"—for by means of intention (*ākūti*), one intends, "I shall sacrifice"; and indeed, they employ him for the sake of the sacrifice as *Prayuj*. "To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, Svāhā!"—for by means of wisdom (*medhā*) and the mind (*manas*), one attains the sacrifice.
"To Dīkṣā, to Tapas, to Agni, Svāhā!"—for by means of consecration (*dīkṣā*) and austerity (*tapas*), one attains the sacrifice. [To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan...]

"To Agni, svāhā!"—Sarasvatī is indeed speech; by means of speech one utters, "He shall sacrifice" and "He shall prosper. Pūṣan, indeed, brought this sacrifice to him and caused it to prosper. "O divine waters, vast, all-beneficent"—for the sacrifice is indeed the waters.
"O Heaven and Earth, wide atmosphere"—for the sacrifice rests upon heaven and earth and the atmosphere. From there [it proceeds].

"Thus having seized the sacrifice, may Bṛhaspati increase us with the oblation, Svāhā! Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; by means of the Brahman he thus seizes the consecration after first attaining all desires. For wherever his sacrifice is supported, wherever it rests, from each of those places he thus seizes the entire sacrifice together with the Brahman. Indeed, a single oblation does not [suffice for] one who is consecrated.

In that he offers these oblations, he does so for the sake of obtaining a second [partner]. Whatever Prajāpati envisioned with his mind, he obtained that very thing through the *ādhītayajus* formulas; that is why they are called *ādhītayajus*. Therefore, whoever, knowing this, offers the *ādhītayajus*, obtains whatever he has envisioned with his mind as he offers them. These indeed are the materials of the sacrifice; this, verily, is...

Thus he sacrifices with a sacrifice whose materials have been fully gathered, for those [oblations] are offered by him. Indeed, Āruṇa Aupaveśi used to say: "What kind of man would sacrifice with a sacrifice if he did not know the materials of the sacrifice? He offers with five [verses]; the sacrifice is fivefold; having thus grasped the sacrifice in its entirety, he offers with six [verses]; there are six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons.

When the sacrifice was created, it stretched out the *Sāman* and the *Yajus*, but the *Ṛc* alone held it up. Either one *Ṛc* held it up, or twelve *Yajus* and nine *Sāmans*. Therefore, they chant the *Bahiṣpavamāna* with nine [verses], for nine *Sāmans* held it up.
For this reason, those who know the lineage of Vatsa offer the *Audgrabhaṇa* oblation with twelve [verses], for twelve [units] held it up.

The Yajus formulas held it fast at that time; indeed, he is now being created when he undergoes consecration (dīkṣā). When he offers the Audgrabhaṇa oblation with a Ṛc, he thereby holds fast the sacrifice that has been created by means of the Ṛc. Therefore, those who know the Āruṇi-offering offer the Audgrabhaṇa with a Ṛc, for one single Ṛc held him fast.
[The text] *prāpipat*: FN Corrigenda. Ed: *prāpibat*.
Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; the *anuṣṭubh* is this meter belonging to Prajāpati. When one offers with the *anuṣṭubh*, one wins him by means of his own meter.
One offers with a single [verse], for Prajāpati is one. One offers with an undefined [verse], for Prajāpati is undefined.
He offers with a full [ladle], for Prajāpati is full. If he were to offer with one that is deficient, he would leave a portion for his rival;
but since he offers with a full one, he leaves no portion for his rival. That which is full is indeed the form of *ūrj* (vital energy);
in that he offers with a full one, he places *ūrj* into the sacrifice. "Of every god who leads..."—this is a verse to Savitṛ; "the mortal..."—[is the next].

"May he choose friendship"—this verse has the Pitṛs as its deity; "Everyone seeks wealth"—this belongs to the Viśvedevas; "May he choose glory"—this belongs to Bṛhaspati; "For prosperity"—this belongs to Pūṣan; the *svāhā*-utterance belongs to Sarasvatī. Indeed, this *ṛc* belongs to all the deities; therefore, although it is a single verse, it has encompassed the *audgrabhaṇa*. They say that at the sacrifice, [the victim] is to be offered for all the deities, for it belongs to all the deities.

This *ṛc* is indeed [the essence], for when he offers the *audgrabhaṇa* with this *ṛc*, he offers the sacrifice to all the deities. Of this very *anuṣṭubh*, there are three feet of eight syllables each and one foot of seven syllables. Of that foot which has seven syllables, four syllables go into one foot, and three into another; where the four go, [that constitutes a complete foot].

That which has three [feet] is the Jagatī; that which has eight syllables is the Triṣṭubh, by which it is the Gāyatrī; that which is the Anuṣṭubh, by that it is the Anuṣṭubh. Thus, his oblation is offered with all the meters. The sacrifice is indeed established upon the meters;
verily, he has thus established this sacrifice in the meters. This Paṅkti is indeed characterized by the exclamation *svāhā*; the sacrifice is fivefold, beginning with the fivefold.
The Paṅkti has its rising and the Paṅkti has its beginning; thus he made his sacrifice one that rises with the Paṅkti. Moreover, the meters are indeed speech;
having reached speech in the middle, he thereby secures it. Therefore, this speech speaks from the middle, for this speech is in the middle.
Prajāpati indeed approached his own daughter, Uṣas; his seed fell away, and the gods gathered it together.

Therefore, once consecrated, one does not give gifts nor cook; then people approach him, and they took hold of that [essence], which is why the Audgrabhaṇa cup is called "the taking-hold. With it they stretched out the sacrifice. When the sacrifice first came into being, it divided into three parts: with one-third it took refuge in the Ṛg-verses, with one-third in the Sāmans, and with one-third in the Yajus-formulas; and with that which was his beloved body, [it took refuge] therein.
The Yajus is recited loudly, while the Ṛc is performed loudly and the Sāman in a low voice; the Yajus is performed in a whisper, for here the beloved body of the sacrifice is the Yajus.
If one were to perform it loudly with the Yajus, one would strip away the beloved body of the sacrifice; [the sacrificer] would lack spiritual luster and would become naked.

This man, being one who has established the sacred fires, neither offers the Agnihotra nor performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices; thus he causes those deities who are entitled to the oblations to become envious of him and he emaciates his own self. By that very act, his [sacrifice] becomes offered. When the gods had slain the Asuras, they drove them out from these worlds; their vital breaths (asavas) entered into human beings, and that is this impurity (ripra).

Furthermore, there is something black within a man, as it were, inside his eye; one should not eat that, for by doing so, one strikes away what belongs to the Asuras. When there is indeed nothing black within a man, and when the blackness in his eyes has vanished, then he is fit for sacrifice (*medhya*).

If he should perform [the rite], he should do so at night; for the night belongs to the Asuras, and thus what belongs to the Asuras is performed as something belonging to the Asuras. "It is speech indeed that they consecrate," they say.
Āruṇi Aupaveśi said: "He who, having anointed himself and rubbed his body with oil, speaks the speech of one consecrated—he indeed is the consecrated.

Indeed, the food ordained by the gods for humans is [to be taken] in the evening and in the morning. Having passed over the evening meal and having passed over the morning meal, he partakes of the vow-food. This is for the sake of distinguishing himself from the human state. Regarding this, they say of cows, "They do not eat," and of humans, "They eat. [The sacrificer says: "Offer [the oblation]! for humans [eat].
Or rather, they say this [is for] the gods.
Not the Agnihotra. (FN emended. Mittwede. Ed:
nāgnihotraṃ)
At dawn,
O one bound by vows, enter upon the vow.

Such indeed is his vow; by means of this vow the sacrifice is continued, and by means of the vow alone he continues the sacrifice. Now, the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman* were once far removed from the sacrifice. Having set aside their two greatnesses (*mahiman*), they returned to the sacrifice.
Those two greatnesses became day and night. Of these two, that which is black is the form of the black antelope skin, and that which is white is [the form of] the white [antelope skin].

That which is the black form of the day belongs to the night; he indeed takes hold of these two greatnesses for the sake of crossing over, thinking, "May you two carry me across. Day and night became a couple, and their brilliance departed; it entered the black [form]. He indeed takes hold of that very thing. Heaven and earth became a couple, and their vigor departed.

He entered that black [skin]; and this very thing he now takes hold of. Just as one here who intends to cross to the other shore boards a boat, even so has he boarded the *Ṛc* and *Sāman*. These two carry him across to the conclusion of the sacrifice. For where the hair of the black antelope skin is, there is the sacrifice; where the sacrifice is, there are the deities. If he were to spread it with the hair facing outward, the consecrated one would be separated from the sacrifice.

It might be argued that because the inner-fleece [skin] is hidden, the sacrifice is hidden from the deities; however, by fastening two [skins] in opposite directions, the consecrated one becomes unhidden from the sacrifice, and the sacrifice becomes unhindered from the deities. If there were only one [skin], one would consume its end;

by that very means, one obtains both. Indeed, the consecrated one is the oblation (*havis*); if he were to sit elsewhere than on the black antelope skin, it would be as if [he were sitting] upon the oblation itself.
It would indeed be as if [the oblation] were spilled; just as one seeks an expiation for a spilled oblation, so too they should seek an expiation for this.
For he ascends upon both the meters and the deities, and they are capable of repelling him.
When he says, "Homage be to thee! Do not harm me!"—this is a gesture of homage to prevent being repelled. The deities are indeed the sacrifice.

"The sacrifice is the protection of the sacrificer when he says, 'Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu; grant me protection. For by this [formula] he has made the deities the protection of the sacrifice, and he covers the sacrifice for the sacrificer. For the consecrated one is, as it were, covered; moreover, that which is covered is indeed the form of the consecrated one. Therefore he covers himself. He puts on a garment; for the garment belongs to all the deities, with all [the deities]..."
Verily, by means of these deities, they enclose themselves.
Let it be:
*āstām* (emended by Mittwede; Ed: *āstām*). Having set aside (*apanidhāya*).
FN emended. Mittwede. Ed: *apinidhāya*.
Of the sacrifice when it was created, the caul clung to it; that became the linen garment (*vāsaḥ kṣaumam*). Therefore, they consecrate [the sacrificer] with linen.

For the sake of providing a common womb for the sacrifice, they initiate the wife in the eastern shed. Indeed, Indra’s power is the eastern shed, and offspring are the power of a woman; by initiating the wife in the eastern shed, he bestows power upon her. The initiation-hut of the initiated is the womb, the black antelope skin is the placenta, the garment of the initiated is the amnion, the girdle is the navel, and the initiated one is the embryo.

The consecrated one indeed lies within his own womb; therefore, the consecrated one must not step out of the consecrated shed except at the proper seasons, for this is his womb, and from it he is born. The consecrated one is an embryo;

if he were to reveal himself during the proper season, embryos would be born with teeth. If he were to smile at an improper time, his vital splendor (*tejas*) would be liable to fly away. Therefore, he must not [smile] at an improper time.
One must be patient so that one's vital energy (*tejas*) does not fail; for a person is indeed unborn, and he is born only through sacrifice.

He is born at that very moment when, after the *soma* has been purchased, he covers himself from here first—just as a person is born first [covered] by the placenta—and at that very moment he is born whole when he enters the waters for the final bath (*avabhṛtha*). Therefore, at that time, he is complete.

By means of the threefold *stoma*, Prajāpati was entirely liberated; he created offspring by means of the threefold. When the girdle is threefold, it is for the sake of procreation. The thunderbolt is indeed threefold; the belly is Vṛtra, evil, hunger, and the enemy of man.
When one fastens the girdle around oneself, one hurls the thunderbolt at one's rival and enemy. Whomever one hates, him [one strikes].

Then he should meditate with his mind; verily he hurls the thunderbolt at him and strikes him down. The Aṅgirases, while ascending to heaven, cast away their girdles, and from that place the Śara grass was born; therefore it is made of Śara grass. Plants are indeed strength;
verily he bestows strength upon his own middle and upon that of the subjects. With a cord the wife is girded, but the initiated one is girded with a girdle.

It is for the sake of pairing; indeed, what is above the navel of a man is pure, while what is below is impure. When the girdle is fastened around him, it is for the separation of the pure from the impure. He who undergoes consecration offers himself as a sacrifice to the deities. Indeed, he binds himself as it were when he fastens the girdle; therefore, this becomes his food.

For he is bound like one distressed for food; therefore, the food of one who is bound is indeed "annādya" (food for the bound). Or rather, just as in this world there is the swallowing of poison, so it is in yonder world for him who eats the food of one consecrated (*dīkṣita*); for by means of the sacrifice alone is his release from that. The consecrated one is indeed the oblation (*havis*); if one were to offer [ordinary food] belonging to him, he would be offering that very thing [as an oblation], and he would be liable to die prematurely. For he [the consecrated one] is [bound] to all [deities].

He who undergoes initiation (dīkṣate) is nourished by the deities; if he were to offer an oblation, he would milk away his sacrifice. His sacrifice would be miscarried. Therefore, when the proper time arrives, he should milk for the deities that entire sacrifice which has fully matured. Indeed, they divide the evil of him who undergoes initiation into three parts: one-third belongs to him who eats his food, and one-third to him who speaks unseemly words to him.
He proclaims the third [portion]; those ants that bite him, they [consume] the third. Therefore, this is his food and sustenance;

for that reason, one must not proclaim anything indecent concerning him. For that reason, the garment of the consecrated (dīkṣita) must be worn, for it is there that those ants which bite him [reside].
Regarding the intention:
*dakṣiṇā* was indeed among the gods and the *yajña* was among the *asuras*. The *yajña* desired that *dakṣiṇā*; he turned toward her and united with her.
Indra perceived this, thinking: "Whoever shall be born from this womb of mine, he will become this [world]."

Indra entered it; from that Indra came into being, from that Indra was born. As he was being born, he perceived: "Whoever else shall be born from this womb of mine, he shall be like me. Wrapping himself up with her, he was born; because he wrapped himself up (*nyaveṣṭayat*), therefore [the fetus] is called *niveṣṭita*. Because she became dark (*śyāvā*) while being wrapped up, therefore one should offer to Indra as *kṛṣṇa* (the dark one).

And indeed, he seeks to obtain both the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the womb of Indra. Having seized this very womb of the sacrificial fee for himself, he thus seizes the sacrifice together with its source. With the words, "May the plowing be rich in grain," he strikes the earth with his horns;
thereby he causes his plowing to prosper through the grain. He scratches himself with a *yajus*-formula, for by means of a *yajus*-formula do men scratch themselves.

He scratches with a *yajus* for the sake of distinction; therefore, offspring are not prone to disease, nor are they prone to disease. If he were to scratch without a *yajus*, [the result would be different]. [With the formula] "Make the plants full of good fruit," he scratches his head; verily, he causes the plants to bear fruit. Therefore, plants bear fruit upon their heads. Speech, once created, became divided into four parts.
Then that which remained over entered the trees; this same [speech] is what is in the lute, in the drum, and in the flute.

When he hands over the staff to the lute-player, he hands over that very speech to him; moreover, he hands over the thunderbolt to him for his protection. He hands it over as high as the navel, for this much is the extent of this speech that speaks, and for this much indeed is the power of speech.

It is performed such that he should give his own voice to the senior [priest]; the Maitrāvaruṇa distributes it, and he gives it to the Maitrāvaruṇa at the next day's Soma-pressing; on the following day, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest distributes it among the officiating priests.
O Hotṛ, sacrifice! O Potṛ, sacrifice! O Neṣṭṛ, sacrifice!
Thus, together with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, she goes to the Āhavanīya fire; the Adhvaryu divides her in front of it.
O Hotṛ, sacrifice! O Potṛ, sacrifice! O Neṣṭṛ, sacrifice!
Thus the Adhvaryu divides the speech in front, and the Maitrāvaruṇa behind.
Svāhā! [I offer] the sacrifice with the mind.

Thus they approach the sacrifice with their mind; from that very place he seizes the sacrifice, saying, "Svāhā! From heaven! Svāhā! From earth! For the sacrifice rests upon heaven and earth along with the intermediate space; from that very place he seizes the sacrifice, saying, "Svāhā! From the wide intermediate space! For the sacrifice is indeed the intermediate space—whether it be the wind or the cattle—from that very place he seizes the sacrifice.

"Svāhā! I take it from the wind; svāhā!"—this wind that blows is indeed this sacrifice; he has seized it and restrains his speech. He thus restrains the sacrifice. If he were to release his speech, he would release the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "Having been consecrated again, one must restrain one's speech. If he were to consecrate himself again, he would exceed the number of oblations. Therefore, having recited a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, one must restrain one's speech.

Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; having recited the verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu, one should restrain one's speech, for Agni is all the deities and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus one has grasped both the deities and the sacrifice. Having recited the verse addressed to Sarasvatī, one should restrain one's speech, for Sarasvatī is Speech; by Speech the sacrifice is extended, and by Speech alone one extends the sacrifice. Having recited the verse addressed to Bṛhaspati, one should restrain one's speech.
Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; the sacrifice is joined together by the Brahman; verily, by means of the Brahman he joins together the sacrifice.
Thus: this *saṃdhi* arises from *manasaḥ* and *iti*. Cf. 1.2.2:11.13 [Page III,72]:
"This one here is initiated, the son of such-and-such."

Thus he calls out or says: "The consecrated one is indeed dear to the gods; he announces him to the gods. He says it three times, for the gods are characterized by triple truth; moreover, these worlds are three, and thus he announces him to these very worlds. Therefore, they hear the consecrated one from afar, for he announces him to these worlds. Having seen a star, he releases his speech; for there are two...

The seasons, day, and night—having reached another season—he releases his speech; he releases his speech with the words, "Perform the vow," for his sacrifice is continuous by means of the vow; verily, by the vow alone he makes the sacrifice continuous. With the *yajus* formula, "Meditating on the divine thought," he washes his hands; for by means of the *yajus* humans wash themselves, for the sake of distinction.

"For the sake of the Brahmin's possession of the gods, and so that the waters may not steal away my consecration. Food indeed loathed men; he desired to establish it among men. The waters said, "We shall purify this for you; then return [to us]. Thereupon food returned to men; thus this food is established among men. Therefore, a Brahmin should eat [only] what is brought to him.

Having brought the food, he should wash his hands for the sake of securing food; furthermore, by this act, he purifies himself for the sake of food. With the mantra, "The gods born of Manu, whose yoke is the mind," he performs the vow. These indeed are the gods born of Manu whose yoke is the mind—namely, these vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
This deity is present in him at this time; he gratifies her and offers the vow-food into her. If he were to do otherwise than this, it would not be so.

He would deprive him of his vital breaths; he would be weakened and liable to die. He should say, "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," whether he is about to sleep, has already slept and is waking up, or speaks the words of one consecrated (*dīkṣita*). Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods; therefore, from him alone he undertakes the vow. He should not sleep on his back; for if he were to sleep on his back, these worlds would pass away, and he would not rise again from Agni.

If he should turn his back, he would turn away from the sacrifice; therefore, let the sun neither set nor rise while the consecrated person is outside the consecrated hut (*dīkṣitavimita*). That is indeed the consecrated vow. The sacrifice did not come together for the gods;
they brought it together by means of service (*bhṛti*). When one seeks service, it is for the sake of the completion of the sacrifice. "O Soma, grant this much!"—thus [he says].

He should say, "Let there be this much for him, and no more," for what he says, "Bring more," is for the attainment of the unlimited. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ, the giver of wealth, [bestow] wealth," he accepts these with those deities impelled by Savitṛ, for his own protection. With the words, "Vāyu is the guardian, Tvaṣṭṛ is the overlord, Pūṣan is the receiver," he makes Vāyu their guardian.

Tvaṣṭṛ is the overlord; Pūṣan is the receiver. The waters indeed are the sacrifice. If one who is consecrated were to plunge into the waters, he would tear asunder the sacrifice. When he says, "O divine waters, O child of the waters," he does not step upon that which of these is sacrificial and pure. If one who is consecrated were to plunge into the waters, they would become swollen with water; therefore, he should not plunge into them. If he should plunge into them...
Crushing a clod of earth, he crosses; he crosses along that very bridge. Indeed, the deities do not cross after the consecrated one as he crosses;
he crosses together with the two kindling woods, and thus he crosses together with the deities. Indeed, the sacrifice does not cross after the consecrated one as he crosses;
he crosses with a part of the chariot, and thus he crosses together with the sacrifice.

All speech goes unto this sun; when he rises, all [speech] is emitted. When he says, "Those words which are in the bull of cattle," he thus takes hold again of the speech that was being emitted. With "To Vāyu thee," he points out the lost one;
with "To Varuṇa thee," the one submerged in water; with "To Rudra thee," the one struck by Mahādeva; with "To Nirṛti thee," the one who has collapsed; [with "To Indra thee," the one stolen by Indra].

With "To thee! [he offers] that which has been struck by a splinter or has become shattered; with "To the Maruts, thee! [he offers] that which has been struck by hail. These gods indeed have their portions spilled; he thus gratifies them. One set of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā) is given to the gods, and another to men;
these [gifts of the Maruts] are indeed given visibly to the gods. Through these, one obtains more than through the other [ordinary] gifts.

The gods and the Asuras contended with one another. At that time, the sacrifice consisted of only this much: the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and the Four-Monthly sacrifices. The gods perceived the sacrifice; they consecrated themselves for it. They adopted the Agnihotra which they possessed as their vow. Therefore, one must remain under a vow, for the Agnihotra is offered twice—once at the full moon when there is an offering to Agni and Soma.
The sacrificial oblation existed; on the previous day they immolated that animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, and on the new moon day that one dedicated to Indra and Agni;

on the following day they immolated that animal dedicated to Agni. They performed the morning pressing as the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the midday pressing as the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, and the third pressing as the Sākamedha sacrifices, the Pitṛyajña, and the Tryambaka offerings; therefore, [these are performed] at the third pressing.
The "all-formed" (*viśvarūpa*) is praised, for this form is indeed all-encompassing. The Asuras did not follow after that sacrifice of theirs; by means of it, they drove them away.

Consequently, the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows thus prevails by his own self, and his rival is defeated. They departed, thinking, "This has become a non-sacrifice (*adhvara*). That is the reason for the name of the *adhvara*. Therefore...
One should be of a single vow, for the Agnihotra is offered but once.
One might fall into doubt:
thus ends the sixth chapter, named the Āgnāvaiṣṇava, in the third book.
[Page III,75] This was indeed unformed; they did not discern these quarters. Then the gods sought one another;
they did not find it. Those gods said to Aditi, "With you as our mouth, let us discern these quarters. She said, "A share [for me]."

"Let it be mine," they said; "Choose [a boon]," they replied. She said, "Let the introductory offering (prāyaṇīya) have me as its deity, and let the concluding offering (udayanīya) have me as its deity;
may you follow after me when you enter, and may you follow after me when you emerge. Thus, this *āditya* oblation is for Aditi;
indeed, they go forth following Aditi and they emerge following Aditi. From that, these quarters became known. He sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti; by that, he [wins] this very [earth].
They discerned the quarters: by that [verse] they discerned this [quarter] where Agni is; by that, this [quarter] where Soma is; by that, this [quarter] where Savitṛ is;

and by that, this [quarter] where Aditi is—for Aditi is indeed this [earth], and this quarter of hers is directed upwards; thus they discerned the upward direction. From that, it was made fit; for the sake of making fit what was not yet fit, there is the Prāyaṇīya [offering]. Therefore, he who, knowing thus, performs the Prāyaṇīya, finds success.

The seasons were prepared for them; from that they beheld these quarters. In that they sacrificed to Pathyā Svasti, they thereby beheld this very quarter. In that they sacrificed to Agni and Soma—the eyes, indeed, are Agni and Soma—they beheld by means of those two. In that they sacrificed to Savitṛ, being impelled by Savitṛ, they beheld these quarters. In that they sacrificed to Aditi—Aditi is indeed this [earth], and it is upon her that one stands firm.

The gods performed the sacrifice. When he sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti, Vāc (Speech) indeed is Pathyā; verily, he wins Speech. In that he sacrifices to Agni, he does so for the sake of the deities; in that he sacrifices to Soma, he does so for the sake of the sacrifice; in that he sacrifices to Savitṛ, it is for instigation; in that he sacrifices to Aditi—the Ādityas are these creatures—he has won them and made them edible. Whatever they omit in the sacrifice, that is a flaw; by that [flaw], the sacrifice is affected.
By that [leakage], the sacrificer flows away; therefore, he makes an oblation together for Agni. Agni is indeed the *samiṣṭi* (the completed sacrifice), Agni is the foundation.
For the sake of the *samiṣṭi* and for the sake of the foundation, he sacrifices first to Agni and last to Agni. This deity is indeed one and the same, for the sake of the fivefold nature (*pāṅkta*).
The sacrifice is fivefold; having grasped the sacrifice in its entirety, he sacrifices for well-being. [He offers] to Pathyā for the well-being of the sacrifice.

He sacrifices; Pathyā is indeed speech, and they follow after speech itself. At the concluding sacrifice (udayanīya), he sacrifices that same Pathyā as the last; Pathyā is indeed speech, and they utter speech after it. There are verses for Pathyā addressed to the Maruts; the Maruts are indeed the clans of the gods, and he has thus fashioned the clans of the gods.
When the clans of the gods have been fashioned and pacified, the human clans follow them in being fashioned. Therefore, one becomes a thief or a robber as the oblation.
They understood; [the correction reads *imān prajānan*. The edition reads *imān aprajānan*]. She said; [the correction reads *sābravīt*. The edition reads *so 'bravīt*].
Thus [he] has enclosed.
(FN emended. Ed:

With the [verse] beginning with *juṣāṇa*, other portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) are offered; but here he recites the *ṛc* on both sides for the sake of firmness and to prevent looseness. Seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses should be performed: five seasons and twelve months—this is the year; it is from the year itself that he extends the mouth of the sacrifice. Regarding this, they say: "Fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses should be performed, not seventeen, for the course of the year itself."

"One should perform seventeen [offerings] for the prosperity of the year"—this is not to be heeded; rather, they should be performed as seventeen. The Prāyaṇīya [offering] should be like the Prayājas (without Anuyājas), and the Udayanīya should be like the Anuyājas (without Prayājas). For this sacrifice is bound on both sides by Prayājas and Anuyājas, since this sacrifice is the same. He sets down both the scrapings and the stirring-stick.
By that, the sacrifice is made continuous; the self is indeed the *prayāja*s. The *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are the field of the gods; the sacrifice is the field of the gods.

If he were to omit the *anuyāja*s while stepping across the field of the gods, he would exclude his offspring. If he should omit the *anuyāja*s, it should be like the *prayāja*s at the opening rite (*prāyaṇīya*); it should be like the *anuyāja*s at the concluding rite (*udayanīya*).

It should be like the *anuyāja*s at the opening rite, and like the *prayāja*s at the concluding rite. The opening rite should be performed with milk, and the concluding rite should be performed with milk—of the waters.
This Śukriya is indeed the essence of the waters; he thus secures the essence of the waters. The Śukriya is cattle; he thus secures cattle.

Moreover, he places cattle for him both at the beginning and at the end. The opening oblation (prāyaṇīya) should be dedicated to Aditi, and the concluding oblation (udayanīya) should be dedicated to Aditi.
For Aditi is this earth; verily, by means of the mouth of the sacrifice, he establishes himself upon her, and finally upon her.
In that part of the sacrifice where prosperity is first brought about, whatever is performed subsequently indeed prospers for him.

For the sake of the prosperity of the sacrifice, the *prāyaṇīya* [opening] offering should be completed. Those verses which are the *anuvākyās* at the *prāyaṇīya* should be the *yājyās* at the *udayanīya* [concluding] offering;
those which are the *anuvākyās* at the *udayanīya* should be the *yājyās* at the *prāyaṇīya*. This is for the sake of recognizing the path, and also—
For the sake of continuity; if they were to do otherwise than this, they would perform a futile act.

This Kadrū is indeed speech; Suparṇī is the meters. Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī—she is Kadrū, and she conquered Suparṇī as her own self. She said, "Bring Soma; with that, ransom yourself. She sent forth the meters: "Bring Soma from yonder; with that, ransom me. Then Jagatī flew up together with the cattle.
She came through the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and through austerity; therefore they say, "The Paśus are the Jagatī. Therefore, when one obtains cattle, then one undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*).

Then the Triṣṭubh flew up; she came through the sacrificial fee and through austerity. Therefore, in the world of the Triṣṭubh, the sacrificial fee is given; and therefore it is said that at midday one should perform austerity. Then the Gāyatrī flew up; she...
He brought the Soma; while it was being brought, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole it. It remained with him for three nights after having been offered.

Therefore, once purchased, [the Soma] stays for three nights. They said, "Let us ask it back. The gods replied, "The Gandharvas are indeed fond of women; let us ransom it by gathering speech together, just as one might ransom a woman who is most difficult to part with."

They ransomed it from him; therefore they say, "Speech is indeed the cow for purchasing Soma," for one thus ransoms speech with a cow. They said, "Let us follow after it," and so they followed after it. That is the birth of falsehood. Therefore, he who, knowing this, speaks speech that is both true and false, falsehood does not harm him. They said, "Let us call it apart," and so they called it apart.

The gods sang the *gāthā*, the Gandharvas spoke the *brahman*; it returned to the gods. Therefore, at a wedding, the *gāthā* is sung; therefore, women love singing. Thus, he who, knowing this, takes her hand while singing the *gāthā*, they both grow old together, reaching the full span of life, and he is not led away from here with affliction. Regarding this, they say: "It indeed went back to them, and not at all [to us]."

||| MS_3,7.3 ||| "Is this the cow for purchasing Soma? ||| MS_3,7.3 ||| "Is this the cow
He conquered; [the variant] *ajayat* is corrected by the editor to *ayajat*.

That which is two-colored is the *vārtraghnī*; if one were to purchase [the Soma] with such a cow, his kingdom would become subject to ruin. Now, for whomsoever such a cow becomes the *anustaraṇī* (the cow sacrificed over the body), another among them dies immediately thereafter. That which is red, with black eyes, black tail-hair, and black hooves—

That [cow] has the Pitṛs as its deity; if one were to purchase [Soma] with her, the sacrificer would be likely to die. Now, for whom such a cow becomes an *anustaraṇī* (the cow to be slaughtered at the funeral), another of his kinsmen dies within the year. She who is reddish-brown, with brown hair, white in appearance, and with clear eyes—that is the form of the *somakrayaṇī* (the Soma-purchasing cow).
It is purchased by means of its own proper form. She should be one-eyed, not stunted, lame, and seven-hoofed; likewise.

It is purchased entirely with a one-year-old cow; for speech is indeed the Soma-purchasing cow, therefore offspring speak speech only after a year. It is to be purchased with water; for Soma is the plants, and water is the essence of plants—thus that essence is secured. "At the purchase, I win a third pressing of the Soma," so said Āruṇa Aupaveśi; [it is] cattle.
The third pressing belongs to the cattle; in that he pours [the grains] upon the hide, by that very act he secures the third pressing.
He pours them upon a red hide; therefore the reddish form belongs to cattle. He pours them upon the hide of an ox; for the ox is indeed all ages among cattle.
Having thus obtained all the ages of cattle, he secures them; moreover, he secures much of the sacrifice itself.

They sift the *soma* for the sake of warding off evil and inferiority; moreover, they thus purify it for the gods. Neither the *adhvaryu*, nor the sacrificer, nor the sacrificer’s men, nor onlookers should sift the *soma*.
If there were onlookers while it is being sifted, offspring would be led to hunger, and misfortune would seize the sacrificer.
The Adhvaryu priest would become hungry.
They investigate.
Purify the Soma that has entered, having cast out [the impurities].
He should say: "That which has been obtained is indeed swallowed by Soma; those who sort out the Soma extract what has been swallowed from him.

Therefore, the sellers of Soma, though they buy much and gain much, are hungry, for they extract what has been swallowed by Soma. With the words, "Thou art ours," he performs the *abhitsāra* (the final seizing); with the words, "Thine are the cups, O Śukra," he [takes] the Śukra.

Thus he draws it; with the verse, "Towards that god Savitṛ," he draws it, for he is impelled by Savitṛ. He draws it with the *aticchandas* metre; the *aticchandas* indeed comprises all the metres; thus he draws it with all the metres. This [metre] is the summit of the metres; he causes him to reach the summit among his equals. He draws it with five [verses]; the sacrifice is fivefold—just as great as the sacrifice is...

In this very way, having seized the sacrifice, he measures it out while releasing each [strand] one by one. He measures with that which is not exhausted; indeed, he measures with that which is not exhausted. For such is the vigor obtained from each of these [strands]. Therefore, these [strands] extend at will and contract at will. He measures ten times; the Virāj consists of ten syllables; verily he attains the Virāj. Moreover, cattle are of the nature of the Virāj; verily he wins cattle.

He takes twice, for there are two pressings. As much Soma as is taken belongs to the sacrificer; that which he pours over belongs to the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*). With "For offspring," he pours it over, for they move forth from clan to clan. Soma is indeed plants; it is an unlimited life-force. If he were to take a limited amount, his life-force would be limited; but since he pours it over, [it becomes unlimited].

For the attainment of the immeasurable. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrificer; the shoots are his offspring. When he ties up the Soma, he thereby ties up the breath of the offspring. When he says, "May the offspring breathe after you," he establishes breath within them.
He ties it up with linen; linen is indeed an herb, and herbs are the womb of Soma; thus he places him in his own womb.
The sacrifice bestows [this] when it first went among the gods; the Rakṣases sought to strike it down. It retreated among the deities.

Garment is indeed possessed by all the deities; in that he ties on a linen garment, he drives away the Rakṣases from the sacrifice by means of all the deities; moreover, he prospers the sacrifice through all the deities.
They extract [the one] who has fallen [into misfortune]. (Emended from *niṣkhidanti* as noted in the corrections and conjectures to the entire work;
Ed.)
They take it out; there is clarified butter taken in four portions. Cattle indeed have four feet; verily, he wins cattle by placing gold within.

He offers ghee pertaining to Agni, gold born from fire; thus he is offered with his own body and his own splendor. Ghee is indeed the dear body of Agni, and gold is his splendor. When he offers after placing gold [in the ladle], he thereby endows the dear body of Agni with splendor; moreover, he causes him to assume his very forms. Ghee is indeed cattle, and gold is seed.

In that he offers after placing gold [within], he thereby places seed in cattle; therefore, from boneless seed, cattle are born with bones. He offers with something bound; therefore the embryos of cattle are not born already developed.
If he were to offer with something unbound, the embryos of cattle would be born already developed. [He offers with the mantra] "Thou art swift"; for in this manner one indeed moves swiftly.
"Thus has she been, thus has she been"—this is her state of being impelled; "held by the mind"—for one holds speech with the mind;

"pleasing to Viṣṇu"—he makes her pleasing to Viṣṇu for the sake of the sacrifice; "at the impulse of thee, whose impulse is true"—for that which is impelled by speech is performed; "may I attain the restraint of the body, Svāhā!"—thus he invokes a blessing; "Thou art bright, thou art shining."
He draws it out with "Thou art a sword," for the sake of attaining union with the heavenly world. Speech indeed is the Soma-purchasing cow; he thus commands her.
Therefore, having created offspring, they are born again. When a calf is born, it seeks the teat; a child seeks the teat.
With "Thou art thought" (*cit*), [he says this because] when one reflects, "Is it thus? Is it thus?"—that is its quality of being thought (*cittvam*). "Thou art mind" (*manas*).

For what one conceives with the mind and what one approaches with the mind, that one speaks with speech. "Thou art thought" (*dhīḥ*): insofar as one reflects, thinking "let it be thus, let it be thus," that is her state of being thought. "Thou art the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*): insofar as something is given by means of speech, that is her state of being the sacrificial fee. "Thou art worthy of sacrifice" (*yajñiyā*): for speech is indeed worthy of sacrifice. "Thou art a kṣatriya": for he whom speech favors is a kṣatriya.
"Diti art thou, double-headed"— since the Prāyaṇīya is the Āditya cup and the Udayanīya is the Āditya cup,
that constitutes her being double-headed. "May she be well-forward for us and well-backward"— for she is indeed well-forward at the Prāyaṇīya and well-backward at the Udayanīya.
[The text] *asāt* has been emended. [The editor's reading:
"If he were to purchase her with [a cow] held by the ear, she would belong to Vṛtra-slayer; if she were held by the horns, she would belong to humans;
if bound at the foot, she would belong to the ancestors; if unbound, she would be aimless. As for what he says, 'May Mitra bind you at the foot'—"

Thus, with the noose of Mitra himself, he binds her. "May Pūṣan protect the paths"—Pūṣan is indeed this earth; it is she who prepares the path for her. "For Indra as overseer"—Indra is the strongest of the gods; him he has made her overseer. "May your mother permit you, may your father permit you"—with the permission of Mother, Father, Brother, and Friend, he purchases her. That [is the purchase].
"O Goddess, go to the God," for she is indeed a goddess; "Soma the God [goes] to Indra for Soma," for she indeed goes to Indra for Soma;

"May Rudra turn you back," he thus places Rudra behind her; "Return safely, O friend of Soma," he has thus directly obtained her. Indeed, when he says, "May Rudra turn you back," he entrusts the cattle to Rudra.

When he says, "Hail! O friend of Soma, come back again," he bestows well-being upon her as she returns. Speech indeed is the cow for purchasing Soma; she enters into the forms of the gods. When he says, "Thou art a Vasu, thou art a Rudra," it is as if he says to her, "Thou art this, thou art that.
Whatever she becomes, or whatever she speaks, by this he attains and secures her.
He steps out six steps; for speech is divided over six days. Indeed, on the sixth day speech does not speak beyond [its limit];

on the sixth day, all speech whatsoever is attained. He attains as much speech as there is. With the right half [of himself], he steps out following the right half; therefore food is eaten with the right hand, and therefore the right half of the self is superior.
Therefore, the right side is more vigorous; birds turn around following the right side. He offers at the seventh step;
there are seven meters, and speech is the meters. Having obtained as much as speech is, he secures it by this oblation.
There are seven meters, seven officiating priests (*hotrās*), and seven domestic animals; verily, he secures those animals. "May Bṛhaspati cause you to rest in happiness."

"Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; verily with the Brahman he bestows it. "Rudra, together with the Vasus, has drawn it forth," he says; thus he makes Rudra its drawer-forth by means of the Vasus. "On the head of the earth I sprinkle thee," he says; for the place of sacrifice is indeed the head of the earth. "The station of Iḍā," he says; for Iḍā is indeed a cow, and this is her station, rich in ghee.
With "svāhā," by means of the utterance of "svāhā," he indeed restrains her.

Thus: [the word] *iti* should be *ācakā iti* (*ācake* and *iti*). Having placed gold down, he offers; he offers indeed upon that which possesses fire and possesses a foundation. The Adhvaryu would become blind if he were to offer where there is no foundation. Ghee is indeed cattle, and the footprint is cattle. The wooden sword (*sphya*) is a thunderbolt. As for the footprint with the wooden sword—
He traces around with a vajra; verily, he encloses the cattle for the sacrificer. He traces around with a horn;
verily, he encloses the cattle for him together with their source. He pours the footprint into a pot; this [earth] indeed is under her authority, for she is the source of cattle;
verily, he places them in their own source. Verily, the cattle grieve when they are cut off from their source if [the footprint] is poured into water.

He pours it out; he indeed pacifies it for the sacrificer. He hands over the footprint, and thereby the Adhvaryu becomes devoid of cattle, for he has delivered the cattle to the sacrificer. When he says, "With your wealth," he thereby causes the Adhvaryu to participate in the cattle; thus the Adhvaryu becomes possessed of cattle. He places the footprint in his own house; verily, he establishes the sacrificer's cattle in his house. The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the world of heaven.

If he were to scatter [the grain] on the Āhavanīya fire, he would place his cattle in another world; he scatters it on the Gārhapatya, for cattle stand near the Gārhapatya; thus he establishes him in harmony with cattle. The footprint is indeed cattle, and Agni is Rudra; if he were to scatter it on a spot where there is fire, he would hand over his cattle to Rudra. Therefore, one should scatter it on a spot where it is calm, for the sake of the cattle.

They cause the wife to touch the Soma-purchase cow so that there shall be no burning; they do this for the sake of pairing. With the words, "Thou art accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ," [he addresses her], for Tvaṣṭṛ fashions forms. With the words, "May we be united," [he says], for offspring are indeed born from union. With the words, "I have mounted the eye of the Sun," [he says]; for this is the path that is unobstructed and free from danger, by which yonder Āditya moves; it belongs to yonder Āditya.
"He chooses the path"; "he finds wealth," for he who buys Soma indeed finds wealth.

"O Soma-seller, let me buy Soma from you for a great price, for much worth, for much beauty; I will buy it from you for a *kalā*, I will buy it from you for a *kuṣṭā*, I will buy it from you for a hoof, I will buy it from you for a foot.
This he says as the greatness of the cow; thus he magnifies her. Moreover, he measures out the sacrifice syllable by syllable:
"Suvāṅ," "Nabhrāḍ," "Aṅgāre," "Bambhārā"—these indeed are the guardians of the Soma of the gods; it is from them [that he buys it].
The *chandases* brought Soma; he assigns her to them alone. Moreover, whatever part of the sacrifice is attached here, that he purchases.
He purchases with ten; the *virāj* has ten syllables; thus it is made *vairāja*. He purchases with eleven;
there are ten breaths in an animal, and the self is the eleventh; thus it is made complete. He purchases with a cow for the sake of the milk-mixture (*āśira*).

Thus he buys it; moreover, he thereby secures speech. He buys it with gold; thus he buys its brilliance, and moreover, he secures luster. He buys it with a garment; thus he buys what belongs to all the gods. He buys it with a goat; thus he buys its heat. For when the meters brought Soma here, they could not discern him because of darkness; then the Gāyatrī...
Taking a she-goat, he flew up; she indeed made it pleasing to them. Thereupon the meters brought Soma. Therefore they say, "Soma is our goat";
thus he buys [Soma] with a bull, for he buys it with a draught-animal. He buys it with a bull; verily he buys it together with Indra.
If he were to buy it with a bull, he would sell himself to Prajāpati. [He should buy it] with a young bull that has testicles, so that Indra may be present in the purchase.
He buys [the Soma] by day; he does not sell it with Prajāpati. He buys it with a pair of cows; thus he buys its very pairing.
seller of soma:
FN Corrigenda. Ed:
seller of soma.
vikrīṇīta: FN emended. Ed: vikrīṇīte krīṇāti: FN cf. Oertel, *Zur Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha-Saṃhitā*, p. 25f.
Soma was indeed there in yonder world. The gods sent forth Gāyatrī, saying, "Bring back that Soma from there.
She beheld the sacrifice spread out; she thought, "If I go into the midst of the sacrifice, I shall go into my own self.
To her, Soma spoke this "seizing of the living one": "Thou art self-born; thou art self-existent. This is indeed the "seizing of the living one" of Soma, or rather, it belongs to Soma.
He who knows this takes the *jīvagrāha* cup as one who is truly an *adhvaryu* and does not come to ruin.

Indeed, at this moment he is Varuṇa, having Varuṇa as his deity; for when he is bound, Varuṇa, having become Varuṇa, might enter him. When he says, "O Mitra, come to me, bestowing good friendship," he makes him Mitra and thus pacifies him. [With the words: "Enter the right thigh of Indra."

The sacrifice belongs to Indra, and Indra is the womb of the Soma; thus he places him in his own womb. Indeed, when he first arrived, Indra closed his thighs upon him; in imitation of that, he now places him upon his thighs. He uncovers [the altar], just as one uncovers for a superior who is approaching; that is the same. "Go through the wide mid-air," he says, for at this moment he has departed from here and has the mid-air as his deity.
"He has reached Aditi there; Aditi was always present"—for the sacrifice is indeed Aditi, and Aditi is the womb of Soma; verily, he places him in his own womb.
Since he says this while he is actually Varuṇa, he makes him Mitra; thus he deprives him of his own deity.
The Bull propped up the sky and measured out the expanse of the mid-air;
as sovereign lord, he took his seat upon all beings—all these are the sacred ordinances of Varuṇa.

Thus he makes him Varuṇa; he causes him to prosper through his own deity. "In the forests he has stretched out the atmosphere," [with these words] he wraps him around with a garment. The garment indeed belongs to all the deities; he thus encloses the purchased sacrifice with all the deities. "Thou art the shoulder (dhūḥ), O shaker (dhvara), shake the one who shakes!"—so he says for the destruction of the Rākṣasas and for the overcoming of the Rākṣasas.

"Thou art Varuṇa’s; may Varuṇa support thee!"—for at this time he belongs to Varuṇa and has Varuṇa as his deity. They approach him mentally; they approach his very greatness. They carry him on a wagon; therefore, plants bear fruit that is wagon-borne.
Plants would bear fruit that is carried on the head; if they were to carry the purchased Soma on the head, therefore [it is carried] with a song (*girā*).

"The plants bear fruit that must be carried on the head, for they carry the purchased Soma on the head. "Move forward, O Lord of the World!"—for he is indeed the lord of beings. "Toward all abodes"—for he moves toward all abodes. "May the waylayers not find you, nor the highwaymen; may the wicked wolves not find you!"—thus [he says].

Or rather, when he was being brought here, Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva of the Soma-fragrance, stole him away; it was indeed from such demons that Varuṇa made this blessing for him out of fear. This purchased [Soma] is carried to the house of the sacrificer; if unappeased, he is liable to harm the sacrificer. When he says, "Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa," he pacifies him.

Thus he is carried in peace for the sake of the sacrificer’s non-injury. Indeed, he is carried for all the deities; if he were to halt with a single fire-brand, his sacrifice would belong to the Pitṛs as its deity. A great fire must be maintained; Agni is indeed all the deities.
With all these deities, he thus establishes the sacrifice as it proceeds. These two, Agni and Soma, come together.

These two [Agni and Soma] were about to seize either the sacrificer or the sacrificer’s cattle; therefore, they seize that very animal which is held as their allotted portion. Indeed, when this animal was being held, the deities did not turn toward it, for they hoped for that other one in this sacrifice. Agni and Soma, however, turned toward this one; therefore, this [animal] belongs to Agni and Soma.
He who undergoes initiation offers himself as a sacrifice to Agni and Soma for their sake. By means of this very [offering], he ransoms his own self from the animals;

therefore, one should be stout and fat for the sake of ransoming oneself. For this reason, one must not eat of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, for by this [animal] a man ransoms his own self. Therefore, when the offering to Agni and Soma has been completed, one may eat in the house of the sacrificer.

Then he is ransomed and freed from debt; for this is the slaying of Vṛtra. Soma indeed is Vṛtra. On the previous day Indra slew Vṛtra; on the previous day, having run toward him, he now presses [the Soma] on the following day. Furthermore, he who undergoes consecration is bound by the two nooses of Varuṇa; day and night are the two nooses of Varuṇa. If he were to conclude [the sacrifice] during the day, he would remain unliberated from the two nooses of Varuṇa.
He should conclude [the rite] at night; thus he is released from the nooses of Varuṇa for his own non-injury.
One ox is yoked and the other is unyoked; then he offers the guest-offering for the continuity of the sacrifice.
He pours out [the grains] from the hand of the wife; for the wife is the mistress of the household goods (*pārīṇahya*). It is thus performed as something granted and approved by the wife herself.
Whatever the wife does at the sacrifice constitutes a pair; it is for the sake of pairing that he pours out [the grains] from the hand of the wife.

This indeed is the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice, that he performs [the ritual acts] at the sacrifice; for the sake of taking hold, he pours out [the grains] from the hands of the wife. "Thou art the body of Agni, for Viṣṇu thee!"—with this *gāyatrī* metre he takes [the portion]. "Thou art the body of Soma, for Viṣṇu thee!"—with this *triṣṭubh* metre [he takes it]. "Thou art the hospitality for the guest, for Viṣṇu thee!"—with this *jagatī* metre [he takes it] for Agni.

With "Thee for Viṣṇu, the bestower of the increase of wealth," he takes up the Anuṣṭubh; with that [verse], "Thee for Śyena, the bearer of Soma, for Viṣṇu," he takes up the Gāyatrī—for Śyena, the bearer of Soma, is indeed the Gāyatrī. He thus takes her up again so that she may not be exhausted, for the sacrifice is fivefold (pāṅkta); as great as the sacrifice is, so much of it does he take up. Verily, he has grasped the meters; by means of those meters being grasped, [he accomplishes this].

He takes up the sacrifice for as many as follow after the guest; even for them there is a share. Indeed, the meters follow him from yonder, and for them this share is prepared. The sacrifice, when purchased, belongs to Varuṇa, but when extended, it belongs to Viṣṇu.
Now the sacrifice is indeed extended; therefore, there is an offering on nine potsherds for Viṣṇu. For they extend this threefold sacrifice at its opening.

They proceed with the *trivṛt* [stoma]; those three cakes on three potsherds are indeed dedicated to Viṣṇu by deity. For the gods, having made Viṣṇu a dwarf, led him along, thinking, "As far as he strides three times, so much shall be ours. He first strode across this [earth], then this [atmosphere], then that [sky];
therefore, the cake on three potsherds is dedicated to Viṣṇu. This is indeed the hospitality for Soma. As for that...

This is indeed the guest-offering for Agni; for they churn fire within the fire. Moreover, it is for the sake of the purchased sacrifice that they generate a deity; moreover, they generate brilliance for him; moreover, during the Upasad rites, they truly generate a hero for him, and a hero is born to him. As for those Sādhyas among the gods who disregarded the sacrifice, their—

Whatever is done in excess in the sacrifice is redundant; indeed, that which is done in excess in the sacrifice is when they offer fire into the fire, and when [they place] the *upara* stone above the *caṣāla*. He touches it right there. They deliberate: "Should it be concluded, or should it not be concluded? If he were to conclude it, he would conclude the sacrifice at its very beginning—the *ātithya* [rite] of the *upasads*.

The fore-offerings (prayāja) are the *tānūnaptra* and the prayer for blessings; therefore, the guest-offering (*ātithya*) must conclude with the *iḍā*. The fore-offerings belong to the Upasads; therefore, those Upasads are without fore-offerings. Or rather, the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) belong to the guest-offering; therefore, those [Upasads] have three [after-offerings], for there are indeed three after-offerings.
The guest-offering is the head, the Upasads are the neck; then this other sacrifice is joined together as the body of Prajāpati. These [are his parts].
The horse-riders are its eyelashes; the stalks of sugarcane are his eyebrows. Prajāpati is the mouth of the sacrifice; from the very mouth of the sacrifice he extends the mouth of the sacrifice.

The horse is indeed the sacrificial victim, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice; the horse belongs to Prajāpati. Therefore, the prastara-bunch consists of horse-hair, and the enclosing sticks are made of *kārṣmarya* wood, for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases.
He is the master of his personal belongings.
(FN: Corrections and conjectures to the entire work.
[Page III,90])

The gods, each contending for preeminence over the others, went forth in four divisions: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, and Varuṇa with the Ādityas. Bṛhaspati caused them to sacrifice with this very [rite], and among them, Indra became preeminent. Therefore, he who sacrifices with this becomes preeminent. They were indeed afraid of mutual hostility; of those [gods], their beloved [wives]—
They touched their bodies; they conversed together; they stroked one another.
May he who would harm us,
or our offspring, or one another— from him alone let destruction fall away.

When they thus touched it together, the gods became superior and the Asuras were defeated. Therefore, those who, knowing this, touch it together, prosper in themselves, and their rivals are defeated. If he should desire of someone, "May he prosper," he should let that person touch it first; he prospers. If he should desire, "May they all be equal," he should let them all touch it together; then they all [become equal].
Those who are indeed alike, even when they touch one another, do not now bear malice toward each other;
therefore, one should not bear malice toward the *satānūnaptrin*. If one were to bear malice, he would be bearing malice toward his own dear body.
They, indeed, deposited their dear bodies in yonder sun; therefore, that [sun] burns most fiercely, and therefore they have Sūrya as their deity.

For indeed, all the Soma draughts are drawn; moreover, it is here that the dear bodies of the gods are obtained. With "I take thee for the protector," he draws for Agni, and thereby for the Vasus; with "for the defender," for Soma, and thereby for the Rudras; with "for Tanūnapāt," for Indra, and thereby for the Maruts; with "for Śakman, the powerful one," for Varuṇa, and thereby for the Ādityas—from these [deities] he draws them.
