Verily, it is first taken for the gods; thus he takes it for them. He takes four times, for they went forth in four directions.
With "I take thee for the one who flies away," he thereby takes his own self; with "for the one who flies around," he thereby takes his offspring;
with "for Tanūnapāt," he thereby takes the sacrifice; with "for Śakman, the powerful," he thereby takes cattle. Verily, [he takes] those gods who are the Sādhyas...

The Veda indeed succeeds for him wherever he may desire, "May it succeed here for me. These worlds are the Sādhyas, the gods; by means of the consecration (*dīkṣā*), he protects his own self, and by means of the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*), he protects his offspring. He tightens his girdle more closely and undertakes a lighter vow, for the offspring stands between himself and [the external world]. He must observe two vows, for there are two seasons: day and night.

And during the night, he should observe the vow alone; he should pass the night with his wife. With the words, "O Agni, that body of yours which is Rudriya," he observes the vow. For at this time, that deity is present within him; he gratifies her, and in her he offers the vow-food.
If he were to observe the vow otherwise than this, Rudra would be intent on harming him. Indeed, he who [observes it correctly] attains union with the deities.
He undergoes initiation; if he were to sprinkle himself with cold water, they would quench him, and it would be as if fire were thus assailed by water.
But when he sprinkles himself with heated water, it is for the sake of pacification; moreover, the *madantī* waters are indeed brilliance, and so he wins brilliance for himself.
Whoever should desire: *yad eto*. (Note: The sandhi is not functioning here;
the manuscripts read *yad eto*, while the edition reads *yad etas*.)
Thus ends the seventh lesson in the upper section.
In these worlds, the Asuras had fortresses: one of iron in this world, one of silver in the intermediate space, and one of gold in heaven.
The gods, repeatedly repelling them, defeated them; for those [fortresses] were without a foundation. They then conceived these counter-fortresses.

The *havirdhāna* was in heaven, the *āgnīdhra* in the intermediate space, and the *sadas* on earth. They said, "Let us sit down; for by means of the *upasad*, one conquers a great city. So they sat down; that is the reason for the name of the *upasads*. They drove them out from these worlds. Having been driven out from these worlds, they took refuge in the day. This is why they performed the *upasad* in the morning.

By means of that [day], they drove them away during the day; being driven away from the day, they took refuge in the night. When they performed the *upasad* in the evening, by means of that they drove them away during the night. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. Therefore, he who, knowing this, performs the *upasad*, drives his rival away from these worlds by means of both day and night; he prospers in himself.
His rival is defeated; for at that time there was no arrow. Those gods fashioned this arrow:
Agni as the barb, Soma as the shaft, and Viṣṇu as the tip. They said, "Who shall discharge this arrow?
The gods replied, "This very Rudra. He said, "Let there be a share for me. "Choose," they said.
He said, "It is not so; one should not deliberate over an arrow that has been shot. Therefore, an arrow that has been shot should not be deliberated upon.
"Truly, I am!"—thus indeed one should say. Rudra, indeed, released that [missile], for he is the most cruel of the gods;
with it he shattered these fortresses. He shattered them with Agni, with his brilliance; therefore Agni is sacrificed to first.

If one were to sacrifice to another deity first, the [fortresses] would be devoid of strength. Eight times he takes [the portion] in the *juhu* ladle, four times in the *upabhṛt*; [this is] the eastern half.

The arrow of the bow, most perfectly concentrated, passes beyond once; for once indeed did the arrow fly away when it had passed beyond. He causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*) after having passed beyond, for the conquest of the sacrifice.

If he were to cause the announcement without having passed beyond, his sacrifice would be unconquered. He offers the *upasad* oblations with the *sruva* ladle; this is the ascent after the forts have been conquered. Day by day he offers one [oblation]; day by day he offers one, for they [the days] were one by one.
Having conquered one [day], he offers one [oblation] on each day; there are three *upasads* which he offers for the conquest of these worlds.

By means of Agni as their mouth, the gods entered these worlds; by means of the *upasads*, they drove away the Asuras. Verily, by means of Agni as his mouth, the sacrificer enters these worlds; having driven away his rival by means of the *upasads*, those [oblations] which are in the evening...

Those which are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) in the morning should be the offering verses (*yājyā*) in the evening; those which are the invitatory verses in the evening should be the offering verses in the morning; in this way, both sets become endowed with power.

He offers iron, having placed it on the first [altar], silver on the middle one, and gold on the last. Bṛhaspati indeed created this as a fortress for the gods; wherever they might wish to fight a battle, there he should offer these. This is indeed the rampart of the sacrifice;
therefore, whatever is prior to the offering to Agni-Soma, that they perform in a whisper. Now, this [offering] belongs to Agni-Soma.

They release their speech; having reached the sacrifice, they release their speech. Indeed, the gods, having made the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles their thunderbolt, struck Soma; therefore, the two ladles do not partake of the oblation to Soma.
They have indeed slain this Soma, since they have brought his two ladles and the clarified butter close to him. When he says, "O divine Soma, may thy stalk by stalk swell," [he thereby heals it].

Whatever cruel thing they did while striking him, that they made non-cruel; they cause it to swell, and all the officiating priests cause it to swell, for all of them heal what is exhausted. Those who rise up to swell the Soma depart from this world, for they go away turning their backs; they are liable to perish. When he says, "Desired are riches, desired are boons; I send forth blessings," by that [he preserves them] from this world.
He does not go to the worlds; therefore he is supported in this world. Or rather, this embryo belongs to these two; he who strikes at the Soma cuts himself away from these two.

When he says, "Homage to Heaven! Homage to Earth!", he thus pays homage to these two. The fore-offerings of the Upasads are indeed hospitality; the Tanūnaptra is the prayer for blessing. Therefore, he does not choose a Hotṛ nor an Ārṣeya.
He said:
"Sit down, O Hotṛ!"—thus indeed says the one of four vows (*caturvrata*). There are three feathers on the shaft (*hīṣu*), four on the nock (*parṇa*);
the one of three vows (*trivrata*) has three joints (*triṣandhi*), a shaft, a barb (*śalya*), and a socket (*kulmala*). The one of two vows (*dvivrata*) has two joints, a shaft, and a barb.

There is one *kulmala* for one who observes a single vow, and three for those who observe more; for this initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed progressively superior. One who observes a single vow enters a lesser vow but conquers a greater world. There are three days for one who observes a single vow, three for one who observes two vows, three for one who observes three vows, and three for one who observes four vows. This [initiation] indeed ascends for one desiring heaven; day by day he becomes better and better.

He who knows thus: if there were twelve *upasads* for the *agniṣṭoma*, they would burn it down unappeased; if there were three for the *ahīna*, it would be as if one were to cause a heavier burden to crush the *uṣṇih*s. Therefore, exactly three *upasads* should be performed for the *agniṣṭoma*, and twelve for the *ahīna*, for the sake of its possessing full vigor.
He pierces [it]. The sacrifice was indeed far removed from the gods; they did not know whether it was here or there, though they knew that "the sacrifice exists.
They desired union with it; they sought the impulse for it; they did not find it, but birds [found it] above and above.
Indra passed right over him without delay. He observed him and realized, "He has indeed perceived me. He said, "Who is this?
"I am the slayer in the difficult place," he replied. "And who are you? "I am the one who brings [the prey] out from the difficult place," he answered.
He said, "You have called yourself the slayer in the difficult place; here is a boar at the entrance, beyond twenty-one fortresses made of stone."

"In that [place] is the wealth and treasure of the Asuras; slay him! Indra, approaching with a *druṃbhūlī* (a club or weapon), split him in the front and cut open his heart. This very verse was recited concerning him.
Deeply pierced even by the unsteady bow, he struck the thrice-seven ridges joined together of the mountains;
neither god nor mortal could surpass those deeds which the mighty Bull performed.

Thus he said: "From the stronghold you have spoken of him as one who shall bring him back; bring him back! Viṣṇu indeed brought him back. Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; it was the sacrifice that brought the sacrifice away from the Asuras. By means of the sacrifice, the gods thereby recovered the sacrifice from the Asuras.
This very thing has been declared in the following verse.
All these things Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one, impelled by you, brought hither:
a hundred buffaloes, rice cooked with milk, and a boar that had stolen Indra’s food.
Thus, it was there that the gods found the sacrifice. Because they found the sacrifice there, that is the reason for the sacrificial ground of the gods being called *devayajana*.

When they seek a *devayajana*, they seek the sacrifice; when they find it, they find the sacrifice. Whatever the sacrificer approves as a site, that is the *devayajana*; for it is the sacrifice itself that the sacrificer approves. In the beginning, this earth belonged to the Asuras.

As far as he could see while sitting there, so far did he behold the gods. Those gods said to the female wolf, "As far as she goes three times around this [earth] on all sides, that shall be ours. She indeed went three times around this [earth] on all sides;
thus the gods found this [earth]. That is the reason for the name of the *vedi* (the sacrificial altar). The gods brought Viṣṇu, having made him a dwarf; as far as this...
"He strides three times; that is ours. He indeed first strode across this [earth], then this [space], then that [heaven].

The gods found him here; therefore, it is called the *vedi* (altar) because of his being found (*vidita*). This entire earth is the *vedi*; "this [girdle] is my *mekhalā*," thus the sacrificer encloses it. For as much as the sacrificer makes of the *vedi*, by so much does he [gain] from it.
One conquers through the earth; therefore, it should be made large, ever larger. Now, the gods and the Asuras contended.

Whatever belonged to the Asuras, that the gods discovered on the *vedi*; that is why the *vedi* is so called. With whatever dear wealth they possessed, they fled, thinking, "By this we shall free ourselves. That the gods discovered on the *uttaravedi*.

"We have indeed found that which is higher and better," they said; that is why the high altar (uttaravedi) is called the "high altar. He who, knowing this, prepares both the altar and the high altar, goes forward, seizing the wealth of his rival and adversary, taking it in succession.
"Let us know," [FN Corrigenda.
Ed: *vidāmahīti*.]

It is thirty-six steps long toward the east, twenty-four at the front, and thirty at the back; thus it is commensurate with the Virāj, for the Virāj is indeed the metres, and he thereby yokes the metres at the beginning of this sacrifice. This very [verse] has been addressed concerning it: The altar is thirty-six steps long toward the east, Twenty-four at the front, and thirty at the back; By means of the Virāj it is measured out, For the Virāj is the metres. The metres, verily, he thus yokes at the opening of the sacrifice. This indeed is the verse that was spoken regarding it.
Indrāṇī won the well-won prize from her husband; with her tooth she split open the secret of the husband.
Her loins extend thirty *yojanas*, and her lap bears the mighty Indra.

Thus, that which indeed slopes toward the east is the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), for they found him lying facing the east. Therefore, he who desires, "May I prosper in both worlds," should sacrifice on a site that slopes toward the east and inclines toward the north; for this [site] belongs to both worlds, and thus he prospers in both worlds. Now, as for that sacrificial ground from which the northern side...
One who desires, "May the higher sacrifice incline toward me," should sacrifice on another place for the divine sacrifice;

for that is indeed the place for the divine sacrifice called "the higher" (*uttarāvat*), and thus the higher sacrifice inclines toward him. Now, one who desires cattle should sacrifice on a place for the divine sacrifice where the plants are abundant in the middle; for plants are indeed cattle, and he becomes possessed of cattle. [And] where it is level...
One who has lost his fortune (*gataśrī*) should sacrifice on a consecrated site; for this [site] is indeed consecrated, and he who has lost his fortune is one who is already established.

Thus, it establishes him. For he is indeed wicked when falling away from that [fortune]. Now, he who desires, "May the subsequent sacrifice incline toward me," should sacrifice at a place where the waters are to the east; for that is called *purohavir* (the oblation in front).

A higher sacrifice inclines toward him who has chosen a place for the sacrifice (*devayajana*). Now, if one who has rivals should sacrifice on a place for the sacrifice where the path lies to the east, or where there is a salt-flat or a pit, this indeed is a secured place for the sacrifice, possessed of the gods; for if he were to leave over a portion of the place for the sacrifice from [the previous] place for the sacrifice, he would be leaving over a world for his rival. Now, regarding that place for the sacrifice which [is defined] by the *āhavanīya* fire...

Other waters flow eastward from the *gārhapatya* fire, and others flow westward; one should perform that sacrifice for whom they might deliberate regarding a bed or a vessel, for he is indeed closely joined with evil when they deliberate upon this. This [fire] is indeed separated from evil;
they thus separate him from evil by means of evil itself. Indeed, when the sacrifice is completed, what was successful of it goes toward the east.

The westward direction is unsuccessful; cattle are indeed the success of the sacrifice, and water is indeed cattle. If he were to descend for the *avabhṛtha* bath facing westward, he would be deprived of the success of the sacrifice. But in that he descends for the *avabhṛtha* bath facing eastward, he attains the success of the sacrifice.
That [altar] which has three elevations—one who has rivals should sacrifice upon it, provided his *āhavanīya* fire...

If the *havirdhāna* shed is higher in the middle, and if both the *havirdhāna* and the *sadas* are higher in the middle, and if both the *sadas* and the *gārhapatya* fire are higher in the middle—from this very fact Viṣṇu conquered these worlds;
following Viṣṇu’s victory, he conquers these worlds and drives his rival away from these worlds. Now, as for that place of sacrifice...
That [altar] which is elevated on the south—let one who has rivals sacrifice upon it. For the gods, having driven away the Asuras from this quarter, went to the heavenly world;

then they placed yonder sun around them as a boundary to prevent their return. In like manner, the sacrificer, having driven away his rival from this quarter, goes to the heavenly world; then he places yonder sun around him as a boundary.

He puts on [the garment] so that there may be no returning again. He who desires, "May I go into the light of both gods and men," should sacrifice on dry ground; for this place of sacrifice is indeed called "Light," and he goes into the light of both gods and men. One should cause him who is being falsely accused to sacrifice. They should perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants out of sight, in secret in the forest; for he is indeed out of sight.

Regarding that which they accuse him of behind his back, he makes his speech more wicked in secret; however, for one whose Hotṛ-priest, while reciting the *prātaranuvāka*, should look upon Agni, the waters, and the sun—desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should perform that sacrifice.
For Agni is spiritual luster, the waters are spiritual luster, and the sun is spiritual luster for him; thus, he truly unites him with spiritual luster.
One becomes endowed with the splendor of Brahman (*brahmavarcas*). Now, one should sacrifice on that sacrificial ground where various thick plants grow in the middle;
for it was from there that the Aṅgirases released cattle, so one desiring cattle should sacrifice there. Now, one should sacrifice on that sacrificial ground where the middle is elevated;
for it was from there that the Aṅgirases went to the heavenly world, so one desiring heaven should sacrifice there. One practicing sorcery should sacrifice on barren soil.
Just as he determines this [earth], so does he determine that [altar] for whom he performs the *abhicāra* (sorcery). He should sacrifice that which might be like a task;

he who might be like one who has a task—verily, the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*) is the self. He makes it so; those young, lineage-descended (*ārṣeya*) priests who are carriers (*vahnayaḥ*), that is the place of sacrifice. Therefore they say: "Only the young are fit for the priesthood. Verily, Agni is the place of sacrifice; that—
He who, knowing thus, performs sacrifice after establishing the fire anywhere at all, performs sacrifice on a true sacrificial ground.
[The reading] *praibhyaḥ* is an emendation; the edition reads *praibhyau*.

Whatever in her was worthy of sacrifice, pure, and possessed of the gods, that, having stepped forth, stood between the gods and the Asuras as they were contending, having assumed, as it were, the form of a lioness. They knew: "To whichever side she shall turn, those will become this [world]."
Both [the gods and the asuras] desired her, but she did not turn toward either side. The gods sought her, saying, "Turn toward us!

She said, "Let there be a share for me. They said, "Choose it. She said, "They should sprinkle me first upon the fire; whatever desire he has when he sprinkles me, that very desire he shall attain. The gods then sprinkled her first upon the fire.

Then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. Therefore, he who, knowing thus, pours this [ghee] as the first libation for Agni, prospers in himself and his rival is defeated. Indeed, that which stood apart after stepping out, between the gods and the Asuras when they were arrayed for battle, having become like a lioness—that was the high altar (uttaravedi). "Thou art the path of heat," [he says], for they found it heated.
"Thou art my way to wealth," for they indeed found that wealth of thine; "protect me, the protectorless," for she protected them who were protectorless;
"protect the distressed," for she protected them who were distressed. By this very means the gods seized [the wealth] of the Asuras;
by this very means the sacrificer seizes [the wealth] of his rival. "O Agni Angiras, he who is upon this earth..."
He says, "I sit upon," for those which are the fires in these three worlds—those he thereby secures. "O Agni, find the one named Nabhas," he says;

for that fire was indeed named Nabhas. This trench is knee-deep; for this much of this earth is living and fit for sacrifice, and that he thereby secures. "Thou art a lioness, thou art a buffalo-cow," he says; for it has the form of a lioness and the form of a buffalo-cow.

Having become as it were [a woman], he stands [over her] with the words, "Be purified for the gods! Be adorned for the gods! Thus they purify her for the gods; they adorn her for the gods. He removes [the earth] with the words, "Whatever cruel thing you have committed while digging this out, make that not cruel. He thus removes that which was cruel.
With the words, "May the roar of Indra protect you from the east with the Vasus," he acts; for these quarters indeed belong to those deities.
He sprinkled it according to the respective deities. For by this means the gods, having driven away the Asuras with their mind, went to the heavenly world;

they placed these deities at the end to prevent the Asuras from following after them. In the same way, the sacrificer, having driven away his rival with his mind, goes to the heavenly world; he places these deities at the end to prevent his rival from following after him.

They desired, "May we overcome our rival and adversary. [With the mantra] "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals; svāhā! they attained that very desire by it, having overcome their rival and adversary. They desired, "May cattle be ours.
[With the mantra] "Thou art a lioness, winning increase of wealth; svāhā! they attained that very desire by it, having overcome their rival and adversary.
Having roasted and split the victims, they desired, "May we have offspring. [They offered: "Thou art a lioness, winning good offspring, svāhā!

By this they attained that very desire. [They offered: "Thou art a lioness, winning the Ādityas, winning kinsmen, svāhā! For she was together with those offspring belonging to the Ādityas. They desired, "May the gods know our sacrifice. [He offers: "Thou art a lioness; bring hither the gods!"
With "Svāhā to the god-like sacrificer," they attain that very desire by means of it. With "To the beings, thee! he makes the dedication;
for the beings are indeed the gods. When Agni, out of fear of the office of the *hotṛ*, fled from there, he dwelt among all beings.
That [portion] which he dwelt upon in cattle, he dwelt within the hair-tuft of an animal whose tail-hair was unclipped; that which he dwelt upon in trees, [he dwelt] in the *pūtudru* tree.
That which is in the plants, that is in the fragrant *tejana* wood; when he collects the materials, he collects whatever of Agni was deposited there.
Or rather, those bones which Agni shook off over there became the *pūtudru* tree; what was flesh became *guggulu*;
what was putrid and adhering became the fragrant *tejana*. Since these materials exist, [he gathers them]. What...

Thus, what is placed here is deposited for Agni; for the sake of attaining it [he says], "Thou art all-living, steady the earth!"—for these enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are laid down for the support of these worlds. "Thou art firmly seated, steady the atmosphere!"—for the sacrifice is the atmosphere. "Thou art of unshakable seat, steady the sky!"—verily, he has thus caused him to go to the sky. "Thou art the ashes of Agni, thou art the soil of Agni"—[thus he says] for Agni.

This is indeed the ash of the fire, or rather the vessel of the gods; the high altar (uttaravedi) is the vessel of the gods for the gods. Having consecrated it as the vessel of the gods, he says, "O radiant one, let the great [Soma] drink the Soma-mead," for he has thus declared this vessel of the gods to the gods.
He obtains the vessel of those who are more excellent. However, one should not question a Brahmin regarding his vessel, even if he should appear to be merely a man of the vessel.
Out of fear he departed.
(FN emended; Ed:
*hotrādiṣāpākrāmat*)
This earth is indeed as large as the sacrificial altar; thus, having excluded the rival from that which is unlimited, he secures it for the sacrificer.
When he sprinkles water upon what is rough or impure, it becomes an oblation; he thereby makes it pure.
When he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) over what is rough or impure, he thereby makes it pure. This earth is indeed as large as [the altar].
The altar is offspring, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is offspring; when he spreads the sacrificial grass, he thereby establishes offspring upon this [altar].

The *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer, and the sacrificial grass is offspring; when he places the *prastara* above the sacrificial grass, he thereby places the sacrificer above these offspring. Now, as for the fact that he places two blades of grass in between, by that means the sacrificer is separated from the sacrificer.

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is turned away from [the altar] in abundance; his cattle become free from hunger. He spreads the sacrificial grass facing eastward, for the sacrifice is directed toward the east. If he were to spread it facing westward, his kingdom would be struck down and become destructive.

The altar-ground (*vedi*) is indeed the arrow of the gods; wherever one aims with a drawn arrow against the gods, there one strikes. In that he prepares the altar-ground, [he ensures the success of the sacrifice].

They bend this toward the gods; with it thus bent, they strike down whatever the sacrificer desires. Indeed, three former fires went forth, carrying the oblation to the gods; the *vaṣaṭ*-call cut them off. Then this one here now fled in fear, thinking, "He will harm me in such a way. The gods sought to restrain him, saying, "Come back to us!"

He said, "Let there be a share for me. They said, "Choose one. He said, "Three brothers of mine indeed went before me, carrying the oblation to the gods; the *vaṣaṭ*-call cut them off. Let there be a share for them. They said, "Choose one.
He said, "Whatever remains unoffered that spills outside the enclosing sticks—let that be their portion."

"This is non-existent," they said; for their portion was indeed boneless, and so they ran away. He said, "I shall now build up bones; then I will return. They followed him and settled all around him for the protection of the sacrifice.
Indeed, this [brick] is laid down for the sacrifice, this for the sacrificer, this for the enemy, and these two for the furtherance [of the sacrifice].
He makes this [sacrificer] more prosperous; indeed, by means of the sacrifice he makes the sacrificer more prosperous and by means of the sacrifice he makes his rival less prosperous.

He offers the oblation at the junction, for no oblation passes over Agni; thus he gratifies them right from the beginning. Moreover, he causes the oblations to cross by way of a good ford. Verily, this is the lord of the earth (bhūpati), this is the lord of the world (bhuvanapati), this is...
Now, he who is this Lord of Beings (Bhūtānām Pati) is Bhūti; if that which has been offered should spill outside the enclosing sticks, one should consecrate it with the following mantra:
He performs [the offering]:
*bhūpataye svāhā*, *bhuvanapataye svāhā*, *bhūtānāṃ pataye svāhā*.

Thus he indeed gratifies them with their own share; moreover, by means of this spilled oblation, he secures a second blessing. Regarding this, Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say: "What would he achieve by performing a sacrifice who does not know how to secure a second blessing by means of a spilled oblation? By this [rite], he secures that very second blessing.

They loosen those knots which were previously there for the sake of the human’s turning away; he washes them with water to cleanse whatever impurity or uncleanliness has settled upon them. He offers the oblation with the verse, "They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts," for this is indeed the means of harnessing.
He offers with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, so that the two [cart-sheds] proceed only when impelled by Savitṛ; for the two Havirdhāna cart-sheds are indeed the sacrificial oblation.
When he anoints [the axle], the two [wheels] set forth as having become the oblation; moreover, the wife anoints them when they have already turned toward each other.
Whatever the wife does at the sacrifice constitutes a pair; it is for the sake of pairing that the wife anoints. This indeed is the wife’s participation in the sacrifice:
that which she performs at the sacrifice is for the sake of participation. She anoints while facing eastward, for the sacrifice is directed toward the east.

He anoints one part three times and the other part three times, for humans anoint to an unlimited extent. He anoints on the right side, for these two turn toward the world of men from the north. This [sacrificial post] is indeed seized by Nirṛti and bitten on both sides;
when he anoints it, he pacifies it. It is dry and ill-spoken; it utters a cry at the house of the sacrificer, and it is liable to bring misfortune.

"The sacrificer is indeed harmed by the calm [Soma]; therefore, they go while bestowing grace upon him. If he should cry out, he should say, 'O God, speak auspiciously to the dwellings'; thus he pacifies him, and having pacified him, he invokes a blessing. The oblation is indeed in the two *havirdhāna* sheds; having strewn the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), they set down the oblation. Therefore, having strewn the *prastara* [grass-bundle], they cause it to proceed; for the oblation is indeed in the *havirdhāna* sheds."
While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, they set down the sacrificial oblations; therefore, while the two *havirdhāna* carts are being turned, the Hotṛ recites:

"These indeed are these; these indeed are turning here. Because of this, a later generation of people desires to take over the land from a previous generation. When they turn [the carts], then the Hotṛ, reciting, should mentally step upon that generation with his foot.

"He drives away the fear of the enemy; he drives away the common folk. For this [place] is indeed the common folk; thus he drives away the common folk. His subjects are not inclined to descend upon his field. The Rakṣases indeed pursue the sacrifice when it is being led away. In that he offers on the path, it is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. He offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; the sacrifice belongs to Viṣṇu. By means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, he smites away the Rakṣases from the sacrifice.

In that he offers with a *gāyatrī*, he thereby ascends this [earth]; in that [he offers] with a *triṣṭubh*, [he ascends] the intermediate space; and in that they go to the *āhavanīya* fire, [they ascend] the heavenly world. He strides three steps forward; for these worlds are three, and thus he bestows these very worlds upon the sacrificer. "Thou art Vaiṣṇava; may Viṣṇu support thee!"—for the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) belongs to Viṣṇu.
With the words, "O Viṣṇu, from heaven or from earth," they drive in the stakes of the southern *havirdhāna* cart; thus he secures the blessing at the very mouth of the sacrifice.
The knot that the Adhvaryu ties first, that he unties first. If he were to untie another first, he would die of urinary obstruction. "Now, indeed, the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu... [he recites].
Saying, "I have spoken," he drives in the pegs of the northern *havirdhāna* cart with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, for the *havirdhāna* belongs to Viṣṇu;

thus he establishes it by its own deity. With the words, "He who propped up the higher dwelling-place," he fixes the *havirdhāna* in that very higher dwelling-place, for yonder [sky] is indeed the higher dwelling-place.
May the worshipful gods, free from malice, sit upon your lap here today for the drinking of the Soma.
Thus, he places those very gods who are worthy of sacrifice upon the two *havirdhāna* carts; on the following day, he sacrifices to them.
Indeed, the staff [of the Adhvaryu] struck this [roof-covering] down with the *vaṣaṭ*-call; when he lays the covering down, it is for concealment and to prevent leakage.
"Thou art the back of Viṣṇu"—this [is the roof]; "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu"—this [is the front]; "Thou art the two nostrils of Viṣṇu"—these [are the two sides].

Thus, from the very beginning, he prepares the head of the sacrifice with its own deity by means of the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s seam. Therefore, this head is manifested in six parts. With the words, "Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic deed," he steps forward and speaks;
for from there Viṣṇu conquered these worlds. Following Viṣṇu’s victory, he conquers these worlds and prevails over them.
He repels the rival from the worlds.

With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes it up, for he is indeed impelled by Savitṛ. With the words, "With the arms of the Aśvins," for the two Aśvins are indeed the Adhvaryus among the gods; with the words, "With the hands of Pūṣan," [he takes it] by means of the deities themselves. With the words, "Thou art a spade, thou art a woman," for this spade is, as it were, cruel; thus he pacifies it. With the words, "Here do I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas."

He says, "For the destruction of the Rākṣasas, for the exclusion of the Rākṣasas—here do I cut off the necks of him who, whether equal or unequal, acts as an enemy toward Soma. For it is he who, whether equal or unequal, acts as an enemy; with this [formula] he wards off everything.
The sounding-holes are indeed the vital breaths, and the oblation-holder (havirdhāna) is the head; these vital breaths are in the head, therefore they are within the oblation-holder.

Or rather, these vital breaths in the head are four; therefore there are four [holes] on the inside. Or rather, these vital breaths in the head are four; therefore there are four [holes], for the vital breaths are held apart from one another.
They are pierced further back, for the vital breaths are held apart from one another further back. They are pierced above, for these vital breaths are held apart from one another above.
These vital breaths are in the front part of the mouth; indeed, the southern Havirdhāna cart is the front part of the Havirdhāna.
Therefore, at the southern *havirdhāna* shed, he says, "Thou art great, of great lineage," for the gods are indeed great;
"Speak the great speech to Indra," for the sacrifice belongs to Indra. He says, "The demon-slayer, the spell-destroyer," for the sake of warding off the demons and for the exclusion of the demons.
"Belonging to Viṣṇu," for the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu. The Asuras, indeed, [placed] these spells within the vital breaths of the gods.

They dug them out; they found them at the depth of an arm's length. Therefore, they should be dug to the depth of an arm's length. Whatever is a magical spell (*kṛtyā*), whatever is a hoof-print, and whatever is an act of sorcery—it is all this that he removes. The sounding-holes (*uparava*) are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). When he pours water [into them], it is because these vital breaths are watery. The sounding-holes are indeed the vital breaths. When he spreads [grass] over them, it is because these vital breaths are hairy. And then...

In that he pours [the liquid] and spreads [the grass], this [altar] is made as the brain; the two pressing-boards are the jaws, and the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*) is the head. For these jaws are indeed upon the head; therefore, they are within the oblation-holder. Since these jaws are within the head, they are thus within it.

If one were to join them together, one would be joining these very two [jaws] together. Therefore, they should be joined so as to leave a space of two finger-breadths between them. It should be made with a space of two finger-breadths.

Indeed, this [altar] is between; the *nāka* is the head, the *havirdhāna* shed is the back, the *āgnīdhra* is the belly, and the *sadas* is the chest, for the sacrifice is joined together facing eastward.

The two pressing-boards are the jaws, the lower pressing-skin is the tongue, and the pressing-stones are the teeth. From his mouth, as it were, Prajāpati drinks the Soma. Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; he entered this [earth], and the deities sought him out. That...
The beings did not find him who had been our overlord; they cried out, "We do not find him!"—that is why the *uparavas* (the sounding-holes) have their name.
Because they cried out (*upāravanta*), they are called *uparavas*. They sought him fourfold below, and they found him singlefold above.
Therefore, he is fourfold below and singlefold above. When one touches the *uparavas*, it is for the attainment of sensory power (*indriya*).

He sprinkles [the sacrificial post] with the formula, "For the earth thee! For the intermediate space thee! For the sky thee! for it is thus that this [post] is measured for the support of these worlds.
He sprinkles three times, for the gods are characterized by the number three; moreover, there are these three worlds, and it is from these very worlds that he has sprinkled it.
Barley is indeed food, and the udumbara is vigor; when he sprinkles with barley-water, he thereby provides nourishment for this food.
Roughness is impure, while water is an oblation; when he pours water over it, he makes it pure. Roughness is impure;
when he spreads grass over it, he makes it pure. That which is dug in belongs to the Pitṛs and is impure, whereas that which belongs to another deity is pure.

Indeed, these are the most excellent parts of this [earth] where he spreads the grass; thus he fixes it in the most excellent part of this very [earth]. It has become as if unburied. Barley is indeed food, and the *udumbara* is vigor; when he scatters barley, he bestows both food and vigor upon this [post].
For food does not nourish vigor, nor does vigor nourish food without food. "Nitāna, the Marutian... [he says].

"May he strike down"—the mind is indeed the *nitāna* (the fastening), and the Maruts are the vital breaths. "By the firm law, O Mitra and Varuṇa"—Mitra indeed supports it, and Varuṇa arranges it for the sake of separation and for the well-being of these creatures. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed the upholders of the cosmic order (*dharma*) among the gods; they have upheld this divine law.

When he says, "I pile thee around, O Audumbarī, winner of the Brahman, winner of the Kṣatra," this is indeed a prayer for blessing; when he says, "Strengthen the Brahman, strengthen the Kṣatra," this is the acceptance of that very blessing; when he says, "With ghee I fill heaven and earth," he thus moistens heaven and earth with ghee.
The Sadas is indeed the belly, and the Udumbara is strength; in that there is an Audumbarī post, he thus places strength in the middle of his own self.
This is indeed the belly of Prajāpati, for the *sadas* belongs to Prajāpati; the Udgātṛ priest is related to Prajāpati, therefore the sacrificer takes hold of the Udgātṛ.

The Audumbarī post should be made the tallest, for he thus causes him to reach the pre-eminence among his equals. With the words, "Thou art the shade of all people," he lays down the roof-covering, for they move forward from clan after clan. The *sadas* is indeed the belly; [he does this] so that it may not be by one thing and then another.

He piles it together; therefore the belly is filled with various kinds of food. The *sadas* is indeed the belly. If he were to pile it lengthwise, what has been eaten would pass through him. But since he piles it crosswise, therefore what has been eaten pervades all the limbs. He piles this together facing toward himself; offspring turn back toward him from all sides. Thus it is joined together.
He becomes like that; the *sāṃkāśina* rite should be performed in common, for these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are common. If he should hate someone, he should measure [the altar] diagonally for him;
he confuses his vital breaths, and he becomes liable to die. If he should desire, "May Parjanya rain," he should measure the *sadas* low;
thus he brings down the rain. If he should desire, "May Parjanya not rain," [he should measure it] high.
One should not have a hall; thus one has taken hold of rain itself. There should be a hall with nine roofs in the Agniṣṭoma, commensurate with the threefold (stoma) for the sake of splendor;

there should be a hall with fifteen roofs in the Ukthya, commensurate with the fifteenfold thunderbolt; there should be a hall with seventeen roofs in the Atirātra—for Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and the night belongs to Prajāpati; it is in the Ānuṣṭubh meter. This is the distinction among the sacrificial rites. [The hall] should have its beams facing east.

He erects the *havirdhāna* shed, for the sky is upright; the *āgnīdhra* shed has its beams directed eastward, for the intermediate region is upright; the *sadas* has its beams laid crosswise, for this [earth] is laid crosswise. He erects the *havirdhāna* with a *yajus* formula, for the sky is defined; he erects the *sadas* with a *yajus* formula, for this [earth] is defined; he erects the *āgnīdhra* without a *yajus* formula, for the intermediate region is, as it were, undefined. Half of the *āgnīdhra* is within the altar.
He obtains half outside the sacrificial altar; for half is in the intermediate space, half in this world, and half in yonder world.
He applies himself to the Dharma;
he exerts himself.
He places [the stone] down.
He says:
"Suvāṅ, Nabhrāj, Aṅghāri, Bambhāra. These indeed are the guardians of the Soma among the gods; from them, indeed, the meters [proceeded].

While they were bringing the Soma, he was excluded from the drinking of the Soma; he then assumed these second names: "Soma-drinker," "Nā," "Upanamād," and "Maṅgalechā. Therefore, these [deities] have two names. They followed after him, but they did not reach him;
therefore, the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered having passed them by, for they did not reach him. This world belongs to them as far as it is piled up.
Therefore, he who steps forward without knowing this meets with distress; but he who steps forward knowing this does not meet with distress in the assembly.
Indeed, that which is sprinkled [with ghee] is their portion; thus they become propitiated and pleased for him.
The Pavamāna is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; when the fires are carried forth while the Pavamāna is being chanted, they are carried forth from the very mouth of the sacrifice.

There was once an Asura named Jambha; he swallowed the sacrifice, but he did not reach the Āgnīdhra fire-shed. From the Āgnīdhra, he split it apart again. This, indeed, is life; therefore, they carry [the fires] away from the Āgnīdhra. To the south, the Asuras conquered the sacrifice of the gods; they stood facing north at the Āgnīdhra, and from the Āgnīdhra, the gods conquered them back. This, indeed, is...
It is unconquered; therefore, they carry it away from the Āgnīdhra fire-altar. For it was here that the Asuras defeated the sacrifice of the gods.

Having conquered the sacrifice by means of the Bahiṣpavamāna from the Āgnīdhra, and having established the fires, they spread the sacrificial grass (barhis). When they creep forward while about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna, they do so as if desiring to be defeated. When he says [the signal] at the chanting of the Bahiṣpavamāna, [it serves to prevent this].
O Agnīdh,
distribute the fires; strew the sacrificial grass.
Thus, having conquered the sacrifice by means of the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant from the *āgnīdhra* fire-pan and having established the fires, he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
For at this very moment the sacrifice is present where the chant has not yet been sung; returning to that very place where the sacrifice is, he offers the oblation.
Indeed, the two earlier pressings are full of light (*śukravat*), while the third pressing is without light; therefore, they sprinkle with ghee containing light during the third pressing.
Therefore, the third pressing belongs to Śukra; the Agniṣṭoma is indeed the year. These Dhiṣṇya hearths are its very bodies;
having excited them and made them luminous, they then chant the Agniṣṭoma.
The Agniṣṭoma is the year, for there are twelve months in a year. When the oblations are offered eastward, the Dhiṣṇya hearths face westward.

They are sprinkled for the separation of the year. On both sides the Asuras were surrounding the gods; some were in front, others were behind. When the oblations are offered facing eastward, they thereby drove away those who were in front.
When the hearths (dhiṣṇyas) are sprinkled facing westward, they thereby drove away those who were behind. This is the [means] against the enemy.
This is indeed a diversion for the Adhvaryu, for the sacrifice is held apart by him. These hearths (dhiṣṇyas) are, as it were, the very body of the sacrifice;

if the Adhvaryu were to pass behind the hearths, he would draw away from his vital breath and would be liable to die. If he must pass them, he should recite verses addressed to Indra, for the Sadas belongs to Indra; thus he serves it with its own deity.

For one's own non-injury, the Adhvaryu’s place is indeed to the east of the hearths (dhiṣṇyas). If the Adhvaryu were to pass beyond the hearths facing westward, another people would be intent on seizing his domain; some [seeds] would be sown and others not. Of these, there is a productive pairing:
those that are defined (nirukta) and those that are undefined (anirukta). Those that are defined belong to this world, while those that are undefined belong to yonder world.

"For such a dwelling, just as this girdle is wound around for the separation of the pure and the impure, so indeed these are piled up for the separation of the sacrifice. That which is east of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths belongs to the gods; that which is westward belongs to men. Therefore, one should not pass beyond the *dhiṣṇyas* while drinking the Soma, for he goes toward the people."

He ascends to the world of the gods from the *cātvāla* pit; for this is the womb of the fires, and thus they are carried forth from their own womb to ensure that nothing is spilled. Now, the space between the *cātvāla* and the *āgnīdhra* hearth is both the descent and the ascent of those fires;
this indeed is the ford of the sacrifice. Therefore, one moves along by this path; if one who is ignorant moves by it, he meets with ruin.
Now, he who, knowing thus, moves about, does not meet with any misfortune in the sacrificial assembly.
stṛṇāhi: FN emended. Ed: stṛṇāti. TS.6.3.1.2: stṛṇāhi, ŚB.4.2.5.11: stṛṇīhi.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Asuras," in the Upper Section.
[Page III,112] This sacrifice indeed proceeds as it passes on: from the Prāyaṇīya it goes to the Ātithya; from the Ātithya to the Upasads; and from the Upasads it is led forward.
If they were to lead it forward without having taken the clarified butter, they would strike away the sacrificer; but when they have taken the clarified butter...

The sacrificer indeed takes hold of this sacrifice as it is being led forward; they proceed eastward with the Soma, and the wife goes out first toward the eastern fire. Verily, they go forth conquering by means of King Soma. For when the king of men enters a man's house, he possesses authority over him only so long as he remains there; but once he departs from that place, then [the authority] belongs to those [of the house].

That, moreover, occurs for that reason; therefore they say they are "under a vow" (*apivratāḥ*), for even then their vow remains. King Soma indeed reached this house; at that time, he possessed sovereignty over it. When he departs from there, he then releases it to them; that is why these [oblations] are called *vaisarjana* (releasing). "O Soma, you who diminish the body..."—this is what [he says].

Thus he expiates with this [offering] both the sin committed by himself and that committed by another. He offers twice with two verses at the Gārhapatya fire; the sacrificer has two feet, [and it serves] for support.

With a verse addressed to Agni at the Āgnīdhra fire, having reached the intermediate space, he makes it another form. With a verse addressed to Viṣṇu at the Havirdhāna shed, having reached this very world, he makes it Viṣṇu; for the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu, so he makes it the sacrifice itself. The Asuras, indeed, [attacked] this [sacrifice] of the gods.
The gods, having made him a fish, took him to that world; when one offers with the *aptu* verse, they take him to that world after having made him a fish.
Indeed, he is taken away from all beings when one offers the *saumya* oblation: by means of it, he is taken away from men;
by means of the *aptu* verse, from the ancestors; by means of the *āgneyī* verse, from the gods; and by means of the *vaiṣṇavī* verse.

For the sake of the sacrifice; by this, Varuṇa seizes all these creatures. When he offers the oblation to Soma, he thereby releases men from Varuṇa; when with the verse addressed to the Waters, he releases the Fathers; when with the verse addressed to Agni, he releases the Gods; when with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he releases the Sacrifice.
Indeed, by this he releases all these creatures from Varuṇa. For by means of Agni as their mouth, the Gods generated these worlds.

By means of the *gārhapatya* fire he wins this world, by the *āgnīdhra* fire the intermediate space, and by the *āhavanīya* fire yonder world; therefore, the fires are established in three ways for the conquest of these worlds. Indeed, Indra and Agni are the latter two fires—Agni is the latter and Indra is the former—and Prajāpati is the *āhavanīya*. Therefore, it is placed on a spot that has been rubbed smooth, for the father is superior to the son and superior to the rival.

He who knows thus prospers. One who has lost his fortune should lead [the fire] forward along the front for the sake of regaining fortune. The Brāhmaṇa has Soma as his deity; [thus he leads it] by its own deity. Offspring are indeed the *aṃśu* plants, and Rudra is the Āhavanīya fire.

If one were to lead it forward along the front, one would deliver over his cattle to Rudra. Therefore, it should be led forward from behind toward the east, for the protection of the cattle, across the broad mid-air.

"Vīhi!"—for at this time he belongs to the deity of the intermediate space; fallen from here, yet not having reached there, he has come to the seat of Aditi. The sacrifice indeed belongs to Aditi, and Aditi is the womb of Soma; thus he places him in his own womb. "O God Savitṛ, this Soma is thine"—for previously he was among men; he has now delivered him over to the gods. "This, O divine Soma..."

"Having turned toward the gods," he says, for this god indeed turns toward the gods. "May I now turn toward men with increase of wealth and offspring"—thus he invokes a blessing. "Homage to the gods! Svadhā to the fathers!"—this is the act of homage to the gods and the utterance of *svadhā* to the fathers. "I have been released from the noose of Varuna"—thus he is truly released from the noose of Varuna.
"For the sake of non-injury to myself, I shall manifest the *svar*," he says; for the sacrifice is indeed the *svar*, and thus he gazes upon the sacrifice itself.

"The light of Vaiśvānara," he says; for yonder sun is the light of Vaiśvānara. He who undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*) exchanges his body with Agni. Rudra is Agni; if he were not to exchange his body again with Agni as was before, Rudra [would seize him].
One might become conceited [thinking], "What has been said?"—[namely] "O Agni, Lord of Vows, that body of yours which was in me, let it be in you;
O Agni, Lord of Vows, that body of mine which was in you, let it be in me. For by this, one exchanges one's body with Agni according to the proper order, for the sake of self-protection from injury.

One who is about to drive this sacrificial post [to the site] with the *gārhapatya* fire must offer an oblation; for they do not offer into the fire of one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*). Having recited the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he should drive it.

"For the sacrificial post is indeed Vaiṣṇava; they say that one must certainly offer [the oblation] upon it, for one offers upon a joint as a place of refuge. This is not to be heeded. Having churned fire at the very end of the post, one should then offer the oblation. Thus he performs both [acts]. He says, "I offer," yet he does not offer in the fire of one who is consecrated. "I have passed beyond some, I have not approached others"—for he passes beyond some and does not approach others, but he turns back toward you.
"Higher than the high, lower than the low, I have found [thee]"—for he indeed finds him who is higher than the high and lower than the low.

"We delight in thee for the sacrifice to the gods"—for he indeed delights in this. "Pleasant to Viṣṇu"—he has thus made him pleasant to the sacrifice and to Viṣṇu. "To Viṣṇu, thee!"—with these words he anoints it all around; he cuts it when it has become the oblation, and moreover, it is sprinkled with clarified butter.

Thus, that which one knows in this way or that way is the *medha*; that which is turned away is the *medha*. That which is straight with upward splinters is indeed the *medha* when it has arrived; that which is straight and bent downward at the top is the womb (*yoni*). He who is born from this [womb] is "possessed of a womb" (*yonimān*), for this earth is the womb of trees. It is to be cut at a joint (*paruṣi*); if he were to cut it where there is no joint, it would be as if he were cutting at a joint.

If it were cut off in this way, the part of the body that is not fit for the axle would remain; if he were to leave the stump with the axle-socket remaining, it would become a thunderbolt and strike down the sacrificer’s cattle. It should be made five cubits long, commensurate with the *paṅkti* meter; it should be made six cubits long, commensurate with the seasons (*ṛtu*); it should be made seven cubits long, commensurate with the *śakvarī* verse consisting of seven feet; [it should be] eight cubits long.
It should be made nine cubits long, commensurate with the Gāyatrī; it should be made ten cubits long, commensurate with the Trivṛt;
it should be made eleven cubits long, commensurate with the Virāj; it should be made twelve cubits long, commensurate with the Triṣṭubh;
it should be made thirteen cubits long, commensurate with the Jagatī; and it should be made fifteen cubits long, commensurate with Prajāpati of the thirteenfold form.
It should be made fifteen cubits long, commensurate with the thunderbolt; it should be made seventeen cubits long, commensurate with Prajāpati;
it should be made twenty-one cubits long, commensurate with the twenty-one-fold [stoma]; it should be made twenty-three cubits long, commensurate with the twenty-three-fold [stoma];
it should be made twenty-five cubits long, commensurate with the twenty-five-fold [stoma]; it should be made twenty-seven cubits long, commensurate with the twenty-seven-fold [stoma].
It should be made thirty-one cubits long when measured by the *triṇava* [stoma]; it should be made thirty-three cubits long when measured by the *ekatriṃśa* [stoma];

it should be made as large as a man with his arms raised when measured by the *trayastriṃśa* [stoma]. Or else, it should be as large as a man standing on a chariot; for such is the smallest measure of a man with his arms raised, and from that point it may be larger and larger.

In this very way it should be made; it should be made with many branches and many leaves, for from abundance he has grasped the abundance of this [tree]. He grasps its abundance, and cattle attend upon his abundance.
hurṇo: FN *Corrections and conjectures for the entire work*.
kāryā: FN *kāryas sa*: FN emended. Ed: *su*

"O herb, protect him! he says; thus he indeed protects him. "O axe, do not harm him! he says; the axe is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra), so he interposes this between himself and the thunderbolt for the sake of non-injury. Whatever splinter falls away from the front of this [wood] when it is struck, his brilliance follows after it and departs; in that he brings it back again, it is for the sake of possessing brilliance. He causes it to be thrown forward.

He causes him to turn toward wisdom. The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt; therefore, these worlds are afraid of it being carried forth, for it is capable of harming these worlds if it is carried forth while unappeased.

When he says, "Do not harm the sky with your top, do not harm the intermediate space with your middle; arise from the earth, go to radiance," he truly pacifies it. Thus, it is carried forth only when pacified, for the sake of these worlds.

He who is consecrated is indeed a friend to all for the sake of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). He has harmed this [tree]; therefore, the trees are liable to destroy him when he reaches the sacrificial hearths (*viṣṇya*). In that he offers an oblation on the cutting-block (*āvraścana*), he causes it to be born again; therefore, more [wood] is produced from the cutting-block. It should be made equal in size to an animal. There are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in an animal, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh. It has eight supports (*aṣṭāśraya*); [this] is the sacred formulation (*brahman*).

In the tenth [measurement], it is eleven [units] including the self; likewise, it should be made eight-cornered, commensurate with the sacrificial animal. It is the form of the Gāyatrī, for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. Indeed, when the Gāyatrī was falling, the leaf that fell off her became the *parṇa* tree; therefore, it is made of *parṇa* wood. Moreover, the *khadira* is indeed the very essence of the *parṇa*; therefore, it is made of *khadira* wood. Here, indeed, this sun was present.
They brought him from here to that world; because they brought him from here to that world, the *bilva* fruit was born from that light.

Therefore, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should make [the sacrificial vessel] of *bilva* wood, for the sake of attaining spiritual luster. Moreover, by means of that very light, he overcomes the darkness. Indra, indeed, gave the *yatīs* to the *sālāvṛka*s; of them, this student (*brahmacārī*) is the *camasādhvaryu*.

That which was this deer, its Soma-drinking became the porcupine; therefore the deer eats the porcupine, for this is its Soma-drinking. Where it overturned the cup, from that the Rohītaka tree was born; therefore it is called Rohītaka, and therefore the porcupine is found on the Rohītaka. [He offers with: "For the earth thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the sky thee!"
He sprinkles them; for this [post] is measured out for the support of these worlds. He sprinkles three times, for the gods are threefold in truth;
moreover, he has thus sprinkled it with the three-footed Gāyatrī. The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt, and barley is food;
in that he sprinkles with [water] containing barley, he thereby wins food by means of the thunderbolt. The sacrificial post is indeed brilliance, and barley is truly the brilliance among plants.
Therefore, the cool herbs breathe after this; when he pours out the barley, he places brilliance within brilliance.
That which is rough is impure, while water is an oblation; when he sprinkles it with water, he makes it pure. That which is rough is impure;
when he spreads [grass] beneath it, he makes it pure. This [barley] is indeed naked when it is unshelled; when he pours it out, he makes it non-naked.

Thus he has made him; he places him in his very own place. He has become uninjured. "With ghee, may I fill heaven and earth"—with this, he fills heaven and earth. The sacrificer is indeed the Agniṣṭha; he anoints him with ghee, which is brilliance, continuously to the end; thus he anoints the sacrificer himself with brilliance. "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey"—this, indeed, belongs to the gods.
Honey indeed is clarified butter; impelled by Savitṛ, he thus anoints it with honey. "Thou art the pinnacle of Indra," he says, for the pinnacle belongs to Indra.
"Make the plants bear good fruit," he says; he thus causes the plants to take on fruit, and therefore plants bear fruit at their tops.
"Supporting the sky with thy top, fill the mid-region with thy middle, and make firm the earth with thy base," he says.

"For this [post] is measured for the support of these worlds; we desire to go to those abodes of yours"—with these words he sets it down with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, for the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu; by means of its own deity he intends, "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu," for the sake of its being properly established.
With the words, "I pile thee around, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility," this is indeed a prayer for blessing; [he says], "Strengthen the priesthood, strengthen the nobility."
"Make firm"—this is the acceptance of the blessing; he sprinkles water around for the sake of stability.
In Rohītaka,
with [waters] containing barley.
FN Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.
*agniṣṭhās*: FN *agniṣṭhā*. Oertel, *Zur Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha-Saṃhitā*, p. 26.

The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt. If he were to set it up within the altar, it would burn [the sacrificer]; if outside the altar, it would not be secured. He sets half within the altar and half outside the altar; thus it becomes secured and does not burn. One must not make the top part visible.
If he were to make the top part visible, the sacrificer would be liable to perish, as if standing in a pit. It should not be made too thick.
"Let not hunger lead away our offspring; let there be no lack of food for both. By means of the sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world.

They thought, "By this [sacrifice], others will surely ascend after us to the world. They secured it with a sacrificial post (yūpa); that is the reason for the name of the sacrificial post. Since the sacrificial post is erected in front, it serves as a guide toward the heavenly world. That is Viṣṇu’s supreme...
He wipes it all around with the words, "The step," for the attainment of the heavenly world. He girds it at the height of the navel;

plants are indeed strength, and thus he bestows strength upon the center of his own self and of offspring. If he should desire, "May hunger seize the offspring," he should set up stakes without ropes; then hunger seizes the offspring. If he should desire, "May Parjanya rain," [he should set them up with ropes].

Thinking, "May I prosper the sacrificer with vigor," he should, after encircling it, lift it upward; thus he presses down upon this earth with rain and prospers the sacrificer with vigor. If he should desire, "May Parjanya not rain, and may I deprive the sacrificer of vigor," then, after encircling it, he should lower it downward; thus he presses down upon this earth with rain and deprives the sacrificer of vigor. It belongs to all the deities.
That part of the sacrificial post which is buried belongs to the ancestors; that which is above belongs to human beings; where the rope is fastened belongs to the plants;

that which is above the rope belongs to the Viśvedevas; and the top-ring (*caṣāla*) belongs to Indra. As for those Sādhyas who disregarded the sacrifice, this part of the post which is above the top-ring—one finger-breadth in height—belongs to them; it should be made one finger-breadth high.
For that was the tip; if he were to make it larger than that, it would become a thunderbolt and strike down the sacrificer’s cattle.
Indra indeed raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra; it recoiled. This *caṣāla* is for the purpose of binding it [to the post].
It should be made the size of a span (*pṛthu*), for that was the size of its tip. Because he grasped it from the narrow end (*aṇimat*), therefore [it is used] from the narrow end.
Because Indra drew [the sacrificial post] up, it belongs to Indra. If he should desire, "May others ascend after him to his world," he should make the *svaru* from another tree;
others will ascend after him to his world. If he should desire, "May I extend my progeny," he should make the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*);
thus he extends his progeny. The sacrificer is indeed the *agniṣṭha*; Agni is brilliance.

If one were to measure [the sacrificial post] in this way or that way, he would deprive the sacrificer of his splendor by means of the fire; therefore, it should be measured equal to the fire for the sake of the sacrificer's possession of splendor. Formerly, indeed, when the sacrifice was completed, they used to throw the sacrificial post into the fire after breaking the *sruks*.
The gods reflected, "This will cause a destruction of the sacrifice," and they said, "With the enclosing-sticks (*paridhis*)."

"Thus may our offering-spoons be consecrated with the *svagā* call; may the sacrificial post be consecrated with the *svaru*, and the *prastara* grass-bundle always. This, indeed, is their consecration with the *svagā* call.

Formerly, Mahādeva did not slay a human being; it was only thereafter that Rudra followed after him. The gods perceived this ritual entrapment (*aveṣṭi*) of Rudra: he anoints [the post] three times from above and three times from below—that makes six; for there are six seasons, [and it is] from the seasons [that he is bound].
Verily, by this he propitiates Rudra. The seasons are indeed the sharers of the oblations; they are the sharers of the *stomas*. They become worshipped and gratified for him by this [offering].
When he offers from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he thereby propitiates the lords of the forest (*vanaspati*). When [he offers] from the rope (*raśanā*), he thereby [propitiates] the plants.
When [he offers] from himself, he thereby [propitiates] men. When he says, "Let your smoke go to heaven," he thereby [propitiates] the atmosphere from the *havirdhāna* cart.

"Light!"—with this he offers from the Āgnīdhra fire; "The earth, the ash, svāhā!"—with this from the Sadas. Thus he propitiates Rudra on all sides. Indeed, they cause him to move away from the trees; having performed the secondary sacrifice, men depart, and thus he is hidden from his own deity. The sacrificial post (yūpa) indeed takes upon itself whatever part of the sacrifice is ill-performed; if one were to touch the sacrificial post, [he would incur] that of the sacrifice.

One might incur a defective sacrifice; therefore, the sacrificial post must not be touched. For it is being measured out as pain, and if it were left alone, it would be liable, while still unappeased, to afflict these worlds with pain.
This is for you, Vāyu.
He should say this if there are many [students].
These are yours, O Vāyu.

Thus he should say: "The trees have Vāyu as their guardian; verily, he releases for them their own deity for the non-injury of these worlds. Just as a wagon-pole is bound with ropes, so are these worlds bound by the sacrificial posts (yūpa); [therefore] they lead him to ruin if [the priest] says [otherwise]."
Homage to the sacrificial posts!
Thus, homage indeed to them; they make way for him, they find a world for him. These gods did not grant favor;

they are the sacrificial posts (svaravaḥ) established in this world, the obstructors whom he does not see—those are the ones established. And those whom he sees are the great ones; when he says "with strength" (ūrjā), it is to them.
Homage to the great Svarus belonging to the Maruts; may I not encounter those who are struck down.
Thus he excludes those very ones; for these indeed are the givers of food in yonder world, and they bestow food upon him.
Standing in the pits; *mīyate* is emended [from the edition's *mīyeta*].
*agniṣṭhāḥ*: *agniṣṭhā*. Oertel, *Zur Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha-Saṃhitā*, p. 26.
*vyūtam*: Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.
May I never be one who lags behind in attaining food.
*vyūtās*: Corrections and conjectures for the entire work. *ta*: Corrections and conjectures for the entire work. *apaścāddaghvānnaṃ bhūyāsam*.
Thus, one becomes a person who does not leave food behind.
[Page III,121] The gods were indeed those who were to be accomplished; at that time, there was no other oblation. Those gods, having churned the fire, offered into the fire.
Having created cattle by means of that very oblation, they then seized a beast for sacrifice. In that he churns the fire and offers into the fire, [he acts as the gods did].

Having created the animals by means of this very oblation, they then seize an animal; moreover, those very animals are seized when they produce a deity. Furthermore, they produce splendor for him [the sacrificer]. With the words, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni," he prepares as it were a dwelling-place; with the words, "Ye two are the testicles," he places seed, for the seed of one whose these two [testicles] exist is not withheld.

"Thou art Urvaśī"—for speech indeed is Urvaśī; "thou art Purūravas"—for breath indeed is Purūravas. Thus he unites that pair. "Thou art life"—with these words he anoints it; verily in that very pair he places seed. "Thou art the Gāyatrī, thou art the Triṣṭubh, thou art the Jagatī"—verily by means of the meters he causes him to be born.
He recites the Sāvitrī first for the sake of impulsion, being impelled by Savitṛ.

For offspring are born from these two; furthermore, regarding the verse addressed to Heaven and Earth, cattle are indeed born after the likeness of Heaven and Earth, for cattle are born in accordance with Heaven and Earth. He recites Gāyatrī verses, for Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature and the Gāyatrī is the metre. He recites them in an unlimited number, for unlimited are the bodies of Agni. With Agni as his vanguard, Indra slew Vṛtra; when Vṛtra was thus overwhelmed, [the waters flowed forth].

Where [the sacrifice] of one who was afraid failed, from that smoke was emitted; therefore, the *dhūmavatī* verse should not be recited, for it belongs to the Rakṣases and leads to failure. The enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are placed around [the altar] so that the Rakṣases may not follow after and seize the sacrifice.
One should strike [the sticks] in front of the enclosing-sticks, so that the Rakṣases do not follow after and seize the sacrifice.

Indeed, something cruel is done in the sacrifice when they offer Agni into Agni; when he says, "Be you two of one mind, of one dwelling, of one thought, and stainless," he truly pacifies them. Being thus pacified, [the fire] is cast forward for the non-injury of the sacrificer.
He makes an offering with the *sruva* ladle; he thereby bestows a share upon these two as they come together. [This applies also to] whatever is crooked or earless.
Or he may be one-eyed, or withered, or twisted; that which is worn-out belongs to him, for that is the impurity of cattle.

A beast for Agni is to be offered at the Agniṣṭoma, for the Agniṣṭoma belongs to Agni. A beast for Indra and Agni is to be offered at the Ukthya, for the Ukthya-stotras belong to Indra and Agni. A ram for Indra is to be offered at the Ṣoḍaśin, for the ram belongs to Indra and the Ṣoḍaśin belongs to Indra. A female sheep is for Sarasvatī.
A ewe is to be offered at the Atirātra. Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and speech is the Anuṣṭubh; the night belongs to the Anuṣṭubh among the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*).
This is their distinction. Just as a fish, when not caught, shakes off the people, even so these [sacrifices], when being performed, shake off the people.
But he who knows them thus—those [sacrifices] shake him off. How do the pressings (*savana*) come to possess cattle?

He should ask: "In that they proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, thereby the morning pressing becomes possessed of the animal; in that they proceed with the sacrificial cakes at the midday pressing, thereby the midday pressing becomes possessed of the animal; in that they proceed with the limbs at the third pressing, thereby the third pressing becomes possessed of the animal. To what extent do they perform the rite of the animal? To what extent [do they perform it] when they proceed with the omentum? "To that extent. "And to what extent [do they perform it] when..."

"In what way do they proceed with the sacrificial cakes? In what way do they proceed with the forms of the animal? In what way do they proceed with the omentum? In what way with the body? In what way with the portions? "If one asks: 'For what purpose is the animal bound facing west, led eastward, placed to the south, and offered as a libation facing east?'—[the answer is: When it is bound facing west, [it is for] this earth..."
By that he conquers the quarter: when it is placed to the south, by that he conquers this [earth]; when it is offered toward the east, by that he conquers this [earth];
when it is carried forth toward the north, by that he conquers the world of men; when it is placed to the south, by that he conquers the world of the fathers;
when it is offered toward the east, by that he conquers the world of the gods; and when the smoke rises upward from the oblation, by that he conquers the heavenly world.

When they carry this [victim] westward after it has been invited with the *iḍā*, by that he conquers this world; indeed, he conquers all these quarters through the animal sacrifice, all the worlds, and all these quarters as well as all the worlds become conquered for him.
Having churned [the fire] into the fire:
FN emended. Ed: mathitvāgau.
Dhūmnī; Dhūmavatī; Samayā.

Now, having created offspring, Prajāpati felt himself depleted. He perceived these Āprī verses; with them he gratified himself. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; in that there are these Āprīs, the sacrificers gratify the sacrifice itself by means of them. By means of the omentum of the animal, the gods went to the heavenly world at the morning pressing; in that [there is] the omentum at the morning pressing—

By means of the omentum, the sacrificer indeed goes to the heavenly world at the morning pressing. As they were departing for heaven, they shook off their bones—their bodies—when they perform [the rites] with the limbs at the third pressing; this is for the redemption of the bony remains.
They wash the animal for the purification of whatever impurity or uncleanliness has settled upon it. Having brought the animal forward, [he approaches] the fire.
They churn for the sake of obtaining cattle. There are indeed two kinds of *vajras*: one is terrible, the other is auspicious;
that which is dry is terrible, and that which is moist is auspicious. By means of the *vajra*, vigor is indeed produced; he thus takes hold of this *vajra* for the sake of vigor.
"For the impulse (*iṣe*) thee!"—thus he impels him. "Thou art manifest" (*upāvīr asi*)—for he is indeed manifest. "The divine hosts have approached the gods"—these [are the words].

"Truly divine are the clans," [he says], for cattle are indeed the clans. "The carriers, the eager ones"—these are indeed the carriers and the eager ones, namely the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and those on the hearth-mounds (*dhiṣṇya*).
"O Bṛhaspati, bestow riches!"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred formulation (*brahman*); thus he holds them by means of the sacred formulation.
"May thy offerings be savory"—thus he offers him as something already made savory. "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, delight in the wealth!"—Tvaṣṭṛ is [the deity].
For the *revatīs* transform forms; [he says] "the *revatīs* are impure," for cattle indeed are the *revatīs*; thus he restrains them.

With "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes it up, for he is indeed impelled by Savitṛ. With "By the arms of the Aśvins," for the Aśvins are indeed the *adhvaryu*s among the gods; with "By the hands of Pūṣan," he takes it by means of the deities themselves. There are two nooses: one is terrible.

The one who is other than Śiva is the one fit for sacrifice; he who is fit for sacrifice is Ghoras; he who is unfit for sacrifice is Śiva. With the words, "O divine oblation, with the noose of *ṛta*," he seizes him with that very noose which is fit for sacrifice. With the words, "I bind you," for humans indeed fasten [the victim] upon it. With the words, "For such-and-such a deity, you who are beloved," he makes him beloved for whichever deity the animal is seized; "Be bold! [he says].
"Men"—for men indeed maintain [the sacrifice]. This [animal] is dry and impure when one binds it; he makes both of them fit for sacrifice.

He binds it facing westward, for animals approach the sacrificial food facing westward. When he binds the animal, the deities have already approached its vital breaths; by binding it, he brings the deities themselves to face him.

"From the waters, from the plants"—for he sprinkles him who is dear to the waters and the plants; "I sprinkle what is dear to [the deity] for whom the animal is sacrificed"—he thus makes him dear to that very deity. "May your mother permit you, may your father permit you"—he sacrifices him with the permission of his mother, his father, his brother, and his friend. "Bring the gods hither for the god-loving sacrificer"—[this is] for the sake of the deities.

He points him out with the words, "Thou art the drinker of the waters," for he is indeed the drinker of the waters; with "The well-prepared oblation—may the divine waters make it savory," he offers him once he has been made savory. Now, when he pours [the water] over and sprinkles it around, he endows him entirely with the essence of wisdom (*medha*). With the words, "May thy breath unite with the wind," he [unites] his breath with the wind.
"He unites him with the sacrificial portions," he says; verily, he makes him worthy of sacrifice. "The lord of the sacrifice is united with his blessings," he says;
verily, he causes the sacrificer to prosper through the blessing of the sacrifice. The *āghāra* libation is indeed the head, and the oblation is the body.

When, having poured the *āghāra*, he unites it with the animal victim, he thereby restores the head to the body of the sacrifice. The wooden sword (*svaru*) is a thunderbolt, and the *āghāra* is a thunderbolt.
When he anoints it with the knife, he strikes it down with the very thunderbolt; with that which has been anointed, he cuts off a portion of the cooked offering.
For this [part] has indeed become an oblation; thus, by means of an oblation, he cuts off from the oblation.

By means of Agni as their mouth, the gods conquered these worlds; when he performs the *paryagni* rite, the sacrificer likewise conquers these worlds by means of Agni as his mouth. The *rakṣases* seek to destroy him; when he performs the *paryagni* rite, it is for the repelling of the *rakṣases*. He performs the *paryagni* rite three times, for these worlds are three; it is from these worlds that he [drives them away].

From the sacrifice he drives away the *rakṣases*. He goes around even the *cātvāla* pit; for this is indeed the womb of the fires. This oblation spills when it drips or when it is smeared. Agni is all the deities; here indeed is the deity for whom the victim is seized. In that he performs the carrying of fire around (*paryagni-karoti*), he causes that very deity to reach it. How much of the animal is this, and how much is that?

Since the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) are indeed everything when they are satisfied, therefore, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he gives the *upapreṣya* call. Previously, he had called for the *śrauṣaṭ* for the deities; now, however, he calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* for the victim. Therefore, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he gives the *upapreṣya* call.
Both kinds of animals follow this one as it is being bound—those that are domestic and those that are wild—which follow the one being bound.

"Being bound, they looked on with their minds"—this is what he recites when he offers the oblation.
