Indeed, this is their release: that he should not offer [the subsequent oblations], for they would remain unreleased. "Go through the wide atmosphere!"—for at this time he has the atmosphere as his deity. Verily, the Rakṣases seek to slay him when he has departed from here but has not yet reached yonder world. They carry Agni before them to drive away the Rakṣases. For the destruction of the Rakṣases.

Having driven away [the evil], they thus bring the deities forward for this oblation being led forth; he places the fire in front to prevent spilling. Indeed, when the victim is being led to its slaughter, the sacrificial essence approaches the Āhavanīya fire.
Whoever then touches the victim, him the blessing of the sacrifice reaches. When he says, "O wealthy one, prosper the lord of the sacrifice,"...

"Enter!"—wherever the blessing of the sacrifice reaches the sacrificer while he is present, there he takes hold of the two omentum-spits. By saying, "Both of you, together with the divine Vāta, [enter] the wide mid-region," he places the cattle—the mid-region—and the vital breath—the Vāta—into him. By saying, "Sacrifice the oblation for yourself," he gratifies the deities.
"May he be united with his body"—with these words, he restores him to life. "Greater by the greater"—by this, the sacrificer becomes more prosperous.
When they speak of the sacrifice as the victim, and when they direct their thoughts toward it, where then does the sacrifice reside?
When he says, "I place the sacrifice in the lord of the sacrifice," it is by thus establishing the sacrifice in the lord of the sacrifice that he then [proceeds] to the victim.
That which drips or is smeared from this oblation when it is being immolated is lost. When one throws down a blade of grass, it is for the sake of preventing spilling.
They cause the animal to be quieted facing westward, for animals approach the sacrificial offering facing westward; they turn it with its feet toward the north for the sake of distinction.
Having caused [the Hotṛ] to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*,
he gives the command to the *upapreṣya*.

FN: Corrections and conjectures for the entire work. "He chooses the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); the meters (*chandas*) indeed are the officiating priests; he chooses the meters when he chooses the *hotṛ*. When he chooses the *hotṛ*, he chooses the *jagatī*; when he chooses the *adhvaryu*, he chooses the *paṅkti*; when he chooses the *agnīdh*, he chooses the *aticchandas*; when he chooses the *maitrāvaruṇa*..."
The Gāyatrī is that which he says for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the Triṣṭubh is that which he says for the Potṛ; the Uṣṇih is that which he says for the Neṣṭṛ; the Kakubh is that which he says.
Agni is the leader of the divine hosts.

Thus, he chooses the sacrificer; being chosen, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call. He does not choose the *achāvāka*, for this *achāvākya* office is the last of the *hotṛ*-functions leading to heaven. When he recites the two-deity verses, it is for the sake of the sacrificer’s support, since the sacrificer is two-footed. Now, as to why he chooses the *agnīdh* from the middle: therefore this fire is in the midst of the plants; and as to why he performs the final sacrifice.
He offers together; therefore, when churned from above, it is born. Indeed, his meters have become harnessed and joined;

for if they were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call while unjoined, the blessing of the sacrifice would go to the rival. But since they utter the *vaṣaṭ* call while joined, the blessing of the sacrifice settles in a single place upon the sacrificer. Therefore, one person utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for the animal, and one [for the other].

For indeed, ten deities choose the victim; there are ten vital breaths in it. When there are ten *prayāja* offerings, he thereby sacrifices to those very deities that are in it. And as for this eleventh [offering], he thereby sacrifices to whichever deity the victim is being offered.
Then, as for the eleven *anuyāja* offerings, he thereby gratifies with these those very deities whom he has sacrificed to. It is slain.

Or rather, he who has died and become one there is indeed this [sacrificial animal]. There are ten deities of the animal, for there are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in it; the vital breaths are indeed the deities of the animal.

In that there are ten *prayāja* offerings, he offers the very vital breaths of this [animal] as a sacrifice. The self (*ātman*) is the eleventh among the vital breaths, and the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal is the self.
In that this eleventh [offering] remains over, he thus places the self around the self. And as for the eleven *anuyāja* offerings—
He bestows the vital breaths upon this one.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third book.
The wife, indeed, when she steps forward, would step toward the world of that sun; he surely harms him who steps toward his world.

When he says, "Homage to thee, O outstretched one," he thereby pays homage to that [sun]. By saying, "Go straight forward," he means, "Go sinless. "Along the stream of ghee, together with the increase of wealth"—[he says this for the sacrificer].
He utters a blessing: "O divine waters, you are pure; purify the gods. For they indeed adorn the waters;

being purified by these [waters], they move about purified. Therefore, even though she moves about with much filth and impurity, the waters do not harm her. He has indeed been slain and is dead there in the other world; for from the waters offspring are born, and the wife gives birth.

In that he sprinkles him with water, he causes him to be born again; he touches all the vital breaths and all the limbs, for such is the extent of the animal. Indeed, when the animal is being slain, pain reaches its vital breaths. When he says, "Do not harm its speech! Do not harm its breath!"—it is by means of water that he thus releases the pain from its vital breaths. Whatever [pain] is yours...

"Whatever cruel thing has been undertaken, may you purify that with this [verse], 'Be beautiful for the gods'!"—whatever cruelty they have committed while preparing it, he makes that non-cruel; he pacifies it. For those drops which fall down, they reach this earth unpacified, and from that, pain reaches this earth. When he says, "Peace to the waters," he indeed pacifies them; thus, being pacified, they reach this earth.

"O herb, protect him from injury! he says; thus he indeed protects him. "O axe, do not harm him! he says; the axe is indeed a thunderbolt, so he interposes this between himself and the thunderbolt for the sake of non-injury. For the animal is offered to all the deities; when he says, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," by this portion he [drives away] the Rakṣases.

"I drive away this Rakṣas; I strike down this Rakṣas; I lead this Rakṓas to the lowest darkness," he says for the destruction of the Rakṣases and for their exclusion. The omentum is indeed cattle; if he were to pierce it [before cutting], he would injure the cattle;
if he were not to pierce it, they would be uncontrolled. He should pierce it at the place where it is firm, for the sake of the cattle. "For sap, for strength, thee! [he says].

"Thou art for food, for thou art food; thou art for strength, for thou art strength; be pure for the gods, be beautiful for the gods"—thus he purifies it for the gods and makes it beautiful for the gods. "May Heaven and Earth cover thee with ghee"—thus he covers Heaven and Earth with ghee.
"Thee, acceptable to such-and-such"—thus he makes it acceptable to whichever deity the animal is being offered.

He makes obeisance with the words, "Obeisance to the appearance of the Sun"; thus he makes obeisance to that very one. In this way he turns around, for in this way the sacrifice turns around. Moreover, he turns around following the turning of that sun. With the words, "Go through the wide atmosphere," he does so because at this time he has the atmosphere as his deity; for the Rakṣases seek to strike him down when he has moved away from here.
"Two omentum-spits made of *kārṣmarya* wood have been obtained there for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases.

For whomsoever they carry the fire from there to the east, for him the deities follow this oblation as it turns back from here. He receives it close to the end to avoid a failure in the sacrifice. If he were to carry it beyond, he would carry this very Agni beyond; for Agni indeed faces in every direction."

"The *rakṣas* is burnt away; the enemy is burnt away," he says for the destruction of the *rakṣases* and for the exclusion of the *rakṣases*. "Of Vāyu, of the drops," with these words he throws down a blade of grass for the support of the drops, for Vāyu indeed releases them from yonder. It is for the well-being of creatures; this is the first of the oblation, the first of the plants. By means of the first, he brings the first into fulfillment; moreover, it is for the sake of the foremost.

This is indeed the first portion of the oblation among the plants; he piles the fuel as the oblation itself. These drops of the oblation spill over—namely that which drips away, that which is smeared, and that which he says: "Accept this most expansive word, most delightful to the gods, as you offer the oblations into your mouth."
"You [plural]," he says;

thus, by that very means, those offerings of his become offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call, unspilled, and dedicated to various deities, for the animals in the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice are indeed dedicated to different deities.
Now, at this point, the verses addressed to Agni are recited first. Agni, indeed, is all the deities;

thus he causes that very deity for whom the animal is sacrificed to reach it. When the meat is cooked so that it is as if red, then it belongs to Rudra; if he were to offer it then, he would hand over his cattle to Rudra. When it is cooked so that it is as if pale (śyenī), then it belongs to Agni; it should be offered then, and thus it is for him.
Rudra becomes one who does not look with favor upon the cattle; for at this time the animal is indeed raw meat when it has been cooked.

If he were to sprinkle the *pṛṣadājya* after having sprinkled the omentum, he would deliver the cattle over to Rudra. But since he sprinkles the omentum after having sprinkled the *pṛṣadājya*, he thus approaches the animal in the proper order; and so, in this way, Rudra does not seize his cattle.

He becomes free from arrogance; for some gods have the *svāhā*-utterance before them, while others have the *svāhā*-utterance after them; both these types are obtained here in this sacrificial animal which is worthy of sacrifice.
Svāhā to the gods!
Thus he should offer before the omentum.
Svāhā to all the gods!
Thus, above, both of these are secured for him. Indeed, when the victim is being slaughtered, its vital breaths are struck by pain;
having gathered the vital breaths, he should release the omentum. The omentum is the self of the victim; thus he places the vital breaths back into its very self.
"One should cut from the front of the right foreleg," so said the Dākṣāyaṇas; thus [he secures] all of it for him.
"The portion of the victim has been cut off," he says; then, with the words, "Svāhā! Go to the god Māruta Urdhvanabhas," he throws the two omentum-spits after [the offering].
For these two are indeed the share of Māruta Urdhvanabhas; he causes him to go to that very one by means of this.
Or rather, he throws these two apart in opposite directions for the sake of keeping them separate.
Śug: [emended; Ed: śag].

The gods, indeed, immolated a man for the sake of the sacrificial essence (medha). His sacrificial essence departed; it entered a horse. They immolated the horse; its sacrificial essence departed; it entered a cow. They immolated the cow; its sacrificial essence departed.

He entered the sheep; they sacrificed the sheep, but its sacrificial essence departed. It entered the goat; they sacrificed the goat, but its sacrificial essence departed. It entered barley; they sacrificed the barley, but its sacrificial essence departed. It entered rice; they sacrificed the rice, and it reached the rice—therefore [the cake] consists of rice.

There is a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); for it is from the middle of the animal that the essence (medhas) is placed. At that time, when they extract the omentum (vapā), the animal is indeed hollow; since the sacrificial cake is made of rice, it is for the sake of covering [the cavity] and to prevent hollowness. It is offered on twelve potsherds; twelve months are a year, and cattle are produced in accordance with the year—for the sake of procreation. [Alternatively,] it may be on eleven potsherds.

The *kārya* consists of eleven syllables; the *triṣṭubh* belongs to Indra. Since cattle belong to Indra, he thereby bestows cattle upon cattle. The gods offered one another as a victim and went to the heavenly world. They thought, "By this [victim], others will surely ascend after us to the world. They let its sacrificial essence (*medha*) flow away, and it became the *plakṣa* tree. That is why...
The Plakṣa-ness of the Plakṣa tree indeed came from the lungs and the heart; the Plākṣāras [the ancestors] drew it out from there, and therefore this [part] is hollow.
When he cuts a portion from a branch of the Plakṣa tree, he cuts it from the very essence. Having taken some speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), he goes away.
The oblation has been cooked; [it is] the Śamitṛ.

Thus he says three times for the sake of declaring it cooked, for the gods are true to the triad; furthermore, just as one announces "the rice-porridge is cooked" to the Brahmins, so too does one announce "the oblation is cooked" to the gods. Having gone around to the north, he pours the clarified butter over it for the attainment of cattle. The speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) is indeed out-breathing and in-breathing, while the heart is the self; when he anoints the heart with speckled butter, [he unites] the self with the breaths.

Verily, he thereby places the out-breath and the in-breath in the middle of the animal. That which is the *barhis* belongs to Soma; and that which is the *uttarabarhis* belongs to the animal. He does this so that his oblation may go to the deities as something faithful, unspilled, and undisturbed, thinking, "May my oblation reach the deities. Indeed, when the animal is being immolated, it reaches the minds of all the gods.

The mind, indeed, is the Manotā. In that he recites the Manotā, he brings their minds together. He has indeed been slain and is dead, having gone to yonder world; but in that he recites the Manotā, he brings him back to life once again.
He cuts from the heart; thereby he cuts from the mind itself. Moreover, as much as the animal is, so much of it becomes cut off.
He cuts from the tongue; thereby he cuts from speech itself. Moreover, for by means of this [tongue], one tastes the essence of plants at their very tip.

He cuts from the hawk’s breast; he cuts from that very place, for it is there that the essence is established. Having cut from the foreleg, he cuts from the two sides for the sake of securing the sacrifice. He cuts from the liver; he cuts from that very center. He cuts from the two kidneys; he cuts from that very form. Having cut from the hip, he cuts from the rectum; he thus cuts from the highest part.

For the life-force is at the top; if he were to cut from another [part] that is higher than that, he would obstruct its breath and it would be liable to die. Therefore, he cuts from that which is the highest, for the life-force is at the top. Having cut from the heart, he cuts from the tongue; for thus he approaches the animal from front to back, and in this way, a portion of this entire animal has been cut. Eleven times [he cuts].
He cuts off [the portions]. There are ten vital breaths in an animal, and the self is the eleventh; thus, of this entire animal, the portion has been cut off.

Indeed, there are these eleven cut-off portions; he cuts them off twice each, which makes twenty-two. Three parts consist of three limbs each, which makes twenty-five. By means of the twenty-five-fold *stoma*, Manu created offspring; therefore, this is the *manus-toma*.

This indeed is the portion taken from every animal for the sake of procreation; yet, truly, there is no portion taken from the out-breath, the in-breath, and the diffused breath. When he cuts portions from the three limbs, by that very act a portion is taken from the out-breath, the in-breath, and the diffused breath of those [limbs].
Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, spat upon the animals; therefore, animals are called "spat upon" (abhivānta) and are of various forms (viśvarūpa).
The animal indeed becomes putrid; therefore, the marrow of the ribs is not to be eaten. It did not reach [the fire] from below;
this [part] is indeed living, therefore he cuts from it. He cuts transversely from the limbs;
he thus causes the animal to shrink away, and for that reason animals move about with their limbs turned crosswise. The entire animal belongs to Agni, yet it may also belong to another deity.

That which is taken from the fore-part of the right shoulder he cuts off for Agni; from the middle of the rectum and from the hind-part of the hip—thus, of this entire animal, it becomes cut off for Agni. He divides the rectum threefold, for at this time the animal has three parts. Having made the three-fold portioning, he cuts off the sacrificial portions; as great as the animal is, into that he places life. Threefold.

Fat provides fat, for cattle are of the nature of fat; indeed, all the limbs of a fattening animal become fatty. In the animal itself, he thus bestows the form of fat. "Many are the mortals who are but carrion at the sacrifice," so said Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana.
"From here men drive away the animal, but they do not go to yonder world. Therefore, having placed gold [within], he offers the oblation.
Verily, he causes him to go to the heavenly world with golden light.
He does not cause [them] to hear;
there are many boundaries.

FN: Corrections and conjectures for the entire work. He offers the *vasā-homa* (fat-oblation); he thus offers the essence. He offers it with the *svadhiti* (knife), for with this one cuts portions from the other limbs; thus he has indeed performed a formal cutting (*avadāna*). Moreover, by means of the *vajra* (thunderbolt/knife), he secures the oblation. It is accompanied by this broth.

He pacifies it; for *ūrj* is indeed sap, and *yūṣ* is *ūrj*. Thus, by means of *ūrj* and sap, he causes the animal to prosper. Moreover, he unites the animal with its full extent. He covers it with the side-flesh to secure the *ūrj*. Verily, this animal has been slain and is dead, having become that which is beyond; when he touches the animal, he brings it back to life again. Having first caused the oblation to go to the deities, he then—

"The body should be made to ascend [the fire]," they say. When, having offered the oblations, he touches the animal, he first causes the sacrificial food to go to the deities and then makes the body ascend. He offers at the half-verse;

for this earth is one half-verse and yonder sky is the other half-verse. Between these two is the intermediate space, and the intermediate space is these creatures. Thus, he places the essence within the creatures themselves. [He offers] to the Vanaspati.
He sacrifices; Soma indeed is the lord of the forest, and these creatures belong to Soma; verily, he bestows sap upon the creatures.

The speckled butter is indeed out-breathing and in-breathing, and the oblation is the body; in that he offers the speckled butter, he places out-breathing and in-breathing into the very self of the animal.
He offers to the quarters; verily, he unites these very quarters with sap. He offers the last one toward the east; verily, [he unites] the eastern quarter.
They turn back again; they carry [the omentum] to the Hotṛ on the *adhyūdhnī* (the upper part of the udder). The Hotṛ belongs to the Viśvedevas, and these creatures belong to the Viśvedevas;
for indeed, creatures live upon the udder. He thereby makes all these [creatures] rich in milk. He performs the supplementary offerings with the rectum;

the rectum is indeed the vital breaths, and from the vital breaths creatures are born—for the sake of procreation. He performs the supplementary offerings with the thick parts, [offering] from the thick parts.
For offspring are born from what is solid; if he were to offer from what is minute, he would destroy procreation. Therefore, he offers from what is solid.
He offers without piercing [the offering], for the non-piercing of the vital breaths. If he were to pierce, he would pierce the vital breaths;
he should pierce [the offering] of one whom he hates, for he thus pierces his vital breaths. One should not offer [in this manner]; if he were to offer, he would [destroy] the vital breaths.

If one were to perform the *upayaj* offerings, he would be likely to die; regarding this they say: "The *upayaj* offerings are indeed procreation; even he who performs the *upayaj* offerings is procreated.

Śucivṛkṣa Gaupālāyana used to say, "Ābhāradvāja!"—"What then? There were no offspring when the sacrifice was performed without the various *upayaj* offerings; offspring were not produced, nor did plants bear fruit. When...
Verily, through the *upayaj* offerings, the sacrifice became complete; then creatures were born, and then the plants bore fruit.

There are eleven *prayāja*s, eleven *anuyāja*s, and eleven *upayaja*s—that makes thirty-three. Thirty-three are the deities; it is they who are thus worshipped and gratified by him through these offerings. This, indeed, is the portion of the victim that has been sacrificed and yet not sacrificed.
Whatever portion of it was left on the ground, he causes that to go to him. Every animal is indeed connected with heaven;

if one were to offer elsewhere than at the Āhavanīya fire, it would not be conducive to heaven. They bring the fire from the animal-cooking hearth; by that means, every animal becomes conducive to heaven.
From the very same place where he first cuts the portions, he subsequently cuts the others; therefore, animals of various forms are born from a single womb.

The sacrifice indeed overreached the gods; the gods covered it with the *upayajas* so that it would not overreach. In that there are these *upayajas*, they cover the sacrifice with them so that it does not overreach. Now, just as a man is perforated when facing backward, so the sacrifice is perforated when facing backward;
the gods closed it up with the *upayajas* so that it would not be perforated. In that there are these *upayajas*...
Verily, he completes the sacrifice with these [verses] for the sake of its being free from flaw.
Whatever animals are for the later *ekādaśinī* sacrifice, one should bind them to the northern half of the sacrificial post;
for animals belong to Rudra, and Agni is the separator. They place the Soma in the southern *havirdhāna* cart; thus Rudra does not become hostile toward his animals.
"In the vessels indeed, I distinguish between the Adhvaryu and the non-Adhvaryu," so said Āruṇa Aupaveśi.

If one should ask, "How many vessels are there? [the answer is] twelve vessels; the *upāṃśusavana* is the thirteenth. Regarding that, they deliberate: "Is it a vessel? Is it not a vessel? For they deliberate upon the thirteenth month: "Is it a month? Is it not a month? There are five *puroḍāśa* cakes at the morning pressing, four at the midday pressing, and four at the third pressing. From this [thirteenth], indeed, he fashioned her.

Prajāpati fashioned this [brick] from his very self; therefore it is covered over with these [bricks]. The gods and the Asuras were in competition; the Asuras possessed a firm foundation, while the gods were without a foundation. These worlds were the foundation of the Asuras.
The gods, being repeatedly struck down, were defeated, for they were indeed without a foundation. The *savana*s (pressings) are truly their foundation.
They sought those [abodes], but they did not hold them fast. They indeed discovered the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) to be the proper abode for the pressings;

they offered them, and those [pressings] held fast. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. Therefore, sacrificial cakes should be offered at each pressing.

For the support of the pressings, therefore a *puroḍāśa* cake is to be eaten at each pressing for the support of the Soma-drinking. The gods, having made ghee into a thunderbolt, slew Soma; indeed, they sprinkle him [with ghee] when one eats it. If he were to eat it, he would strike at the Soma-drinking; if he were not to eat it, he would be deprived of the Soma-drinking. Therefore, he should eat that which is not sprinkled with ghee, for the sake of the Soma-drinking.
Therefore, that must not be overlooked; indeed, having consumed it, Indra slew Vṛtra, yet he did not digest anything of him;
the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) alone digested it. Therefore, the sacrificial cake is to be consumed for the support of the Soma-drinking. There are five sacrificial cakes at the morning pressing:

the sacrificial cake, the parched grain (parivāpa), the fried grains (dhānāḥ), the groats (karambha), and the curd-mixture (payasyā). This is the "cake-row" (puroḍāśapaṅkti), consisting of two sets of nārāśaṃsa cups.
At the morning pressing there are two *nārāśaṃsa* cups; at the midday pressing there is one *nārāśaṃsa* cup; at the third pressing, that is the *narāśaṃsa-pañkti*.
The three pressings, the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the *anūbandhyā* cow are the fifth of the pressings; that is the *savanapañkti*.
This indeed is that *pañkti* which those who discourse on Brahman call "the *pañkti* by which they neither praise nor recite. Now...
"They carry the sacrifice and they establish the sacrifice," so it is said.

The gods and the Asuras were contending. Their vital powers and strengths departed from them; the *Ṛc* and *Sāman* departed from them, as did the cattle, speech, the sense-faculty, and the out-breath and in-breath. By means of these, Indra desired: "May I attain union (*sāyujya*)."
May Indra, the possessor of bay horses, eat the parched grains.
Thus, the *ṛc* and the *sāman* are indeed Indra’s two bay horses; through the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, he attained union (*sāyujya*).
Accompanied by Pūṣan, [he partakes of] the groats.
Thus, Puṣan is indeed cattle; through cattle he attained union. The Parivāpa offering belongs to Sarasvatīvat and Bhāratīvat.
Thus, Sarasvatī is indeed speech; through speech alone she attained union.
Karambha: FN Ed.:
karambhaḥ. Oertel, Zur Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha-Saṃhitā.
Mittwede: *karambha*.
A cake for Indra.
Thus, either the sense-faculty is Indra, or he attained union with Indra by means of the sense-faculty itself.
The curd-mixture is for Mitra and Varuṇa.

Thus, Mitra and Varuna are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing; through out-breathing and in-breathing he attained union (*sāyujya*). Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows thus attains union with these very senses, these powers, and these greatnesses;
he prospers in himself, while his rival is defeated. Dīrghajihvī indeed licked the morning pressing of the gods.
That [intestine] fermented; it became *payasyā* (curd-mixture). Therefore, the *payasyā* for Mitra and Varuṇa at the morning pressing should be as if of a fermented nature.

Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing; thus, out-breathing and in-breathing are established at the beginning of the sacrifice. One must not turn back the rectum. If one were to turn back the rectum, a disorder of the bowels (*udāvarta*) would destroy the offspring, so that the Rākṣasas may not follow after them in conquest.
The sacrificial post is erected in front; if they were to lead the animal past the front of the post, the Rakṣases would follow and overcome the sacrifice.
Therefore, it should be led between the fire and the post to prevent the Rakṣases from following and overcoming it.
"Go to the ocean, svāhā!"—he thus offers it into the waters, for these are the ocean. "Go to the intermediate space, svāhā!"—he thus bestows seed.

"Go to the god Savitṛ, svāhā! he says for the sake of impulsion. "Go to day and night, svāhā!"—for it is after day and night that offspring are born. "Go to Mitra and Varuṇa, svāhā!"—Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breath and in-breath; [he thus bestows] out-breath and in-breath.
"Thus he places them in heaven and earth; go, svāhā!"—by these two he thus encompasses them once they have been released.

"Go to the meters, svāhā!"—the meters are indeed speech; he thus places speech in them. "Go to Soma, svāhā!"—Soma is indeed food; he thus places food in them. "Go to the sacrifice, svāhā!"—he thus makes them worthy of sacrifice. "Go to the celestial firmament."
With "Svāhā! they pour rain down upon them. With "Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, to your own [place]!"—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year;

thus he establishes them in the year and makes their life-span equal to the year. He says, "Bestow mind upon the heart," for the protection of the vital breaths. With "For the plants, thee! he places sap in the plants. He who...

Whether he is learned or unlearned, the Upayaja offers with a pair; verily, by this he creates a union of the vital breaths when he says, "O mind, bestow warmth upon the heart. Verily, he thus arranges the vital breaths according to their seasons. When the animal that has been seized suffers, its pain gathers toward the center; it reaches the hearts. If he were to touch a man, the pain would strike the men.

If he were to touch a cow, pain would strike the cattle; if he were to touch wood, pain would strike the trees; if he were to touch grass, pain would strike the plants; if he were to touch water, pain would strike the waters.
That which is moist but devoid of water is pacified; one should fast there, for by that he offers up the pain to the deity.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, named "The Pātnīvanta Offerings," in the Third Book.
Kindled at the face of the dawns, O Indra, increasing through the preceding light, you, the first-doer with thunderbolt in hand, struck Vṛtra with the thirty-three gods; you threw open the doors.
The one praised by men, the hero who measures out [the sacrifice], Tanūnapāt, the upholder of the station of the sacrifice—
he, rich in fatness, anointing himself with milk and honey, radiant with gold, the wise one, performs the sacrifice.
Praised by the gods, accompanied by the bay steeds, the one who is sought with prayer, being invoked with the oblation and exulting;
the breaker of forts, the sustainer of the cow-pens, the wielder of the thunderbolt in his arm—may he come to our sacrifice, graciously accepting it.

May Indra, the lord of bay horses, taking pleasure in the sacrificial grass, sit down facing the east upon the earth’s appointed place; may he, wide-expanding and spreading out, sit upon the pleasant seat anointed by the Ādityas and the Vasus, in harmonious accord with them.
The wooden doors, running like women with noble husbands, hasten toward Indra, the bull;
let the divine doors open wide on all sides, providing heroic sons as they expand with greatness for the sake of the Hero.
Dawn and Night, the lofty ones, rich in milk, yielding well for the mighty Indra;
they, the two deities adorned with beautiful ornaments, weaving with their thread, worship the God among the gods.
Measuring out with divine mind in many places, the two first invokers with beautiful voices, placing Indra at the head of the sacrifice,
strengthening the eastern light with the oblation of honeyed sweetness.
The three goddesses, growing through the oblation and delighting in Indra, the bull, like wives [with their husband]—
Sarasvatī with her milk, the goddess Iḍā, and Bhāratī who overcomes all— [maintain] the unbroken thread.

May Tvaṣṭṛ bestow vigor upon Indra; may the far-reaching one, for the sake of glory, perform many deeds. As a bull sacrificing to the bull, he of abundant seed shall anoint the gods at the head of the sacrifice.
The Lord of the Forest, released though not by snares, anointing himself by his own power like the divine immolator,
filling Indra’s belly with oblations— may he sweeten the offering with honey and ghee.
For those who offer but little, Indra is the hero; acting as a bull, he is the bull, the subduer of the swift.
With a mind that sprinkles clarity, may he moisten the oblation; may Indra enjoy the oblation consecrated with Svāhā.

Let the Hotṛ worship Agni with the kindling-stick in the place of Iḍ; let him worship the Aśvins, Indra, and Sarasvatī. As a smoky goat [is offered], so may there be healing medicine from wheat, jujube fruits, and honeyed shoots;

as vigor and sensory power, so may milk, Soma, foaming liquor, ghee, and honey enjoy the clarified butter—O Hotṛ, sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ worship Tanūnapāt and Sarasvatī; as a ram and a ewe [provide] healing medicine, so may the path be sweet.

Bringing heroic strength for Indra, with jujube fruits, parched grains, and young sprouts, [they provide] medicine; with milk, Soma, foaming liquor, ghee, and honey—let it enjoy the clarified butter! O Hotṛ, sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ worship Narāśaṃsa, who is not naked, the lord of the Surā, the medicine; the ram is the physician, Sarasvatī is the chariot, and the omentum belongs to the Aśvins and to Indra.
May vigor [be pleased] with jujube fruits, the remedy with *upavākā* sprouts, milk with young shoots, Soma with foaming liquor, ghee with honey;
let it partake of the clarified butter, O Hotṛ, sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ, impelled by *iḍ*, being invoked, sacrificing, increase Sarasvatī and Indra with strength;
with the bull and the cow, [increase] the power of the senses; for Indra and the Aśvins, a remedy with barley, jujubes, honey, and parched grain like *māsara*.
Milk, Soma, foaming liquor, ghee, and honey—let them enjoy the clarified butter; O Hotṛ, sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ worship the grass-cushion, soft as wool;

let the two physicians, the Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, be present; let the mare with her foal be the physician, and Sarasvatī the cow be the physician; for Indra she milks forth the milk of power, Soma, foaming liquor, ghee, and honey—let them enjoy the clarified butter; O Hotṛ, sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ worship...
The doors of the quarters are wide-expanding like those of the Kavaṣas; for the Aśvins, the doors of the quarters yield as Indra yielded the two worlds.
Sarasvatī, the milch-cow, yields the bright light, the power of Indra, the milk, the Soma, the foaming liquor, the ghee, and the honey. Let them enjoy the clarified butter;
O Hotar, sacrifice! Let the Hotar sacrifice to the well-adorned Dawn and Night, and to the Aśvins, who, being in agreement, anoint themselves with beautiful forms.
May Sarasvatī with her brilliance, Indra with his healing power, and the falcon with the dust of heaven, [grant] milk, Soma, foaming liquor, ghee, and honey.

O Hotṛ, sacrifice of the clarified butter! Let the Hotṛ sacrifice; let the two divine Hotṛs, the Aśvins, the physicians, [and] Indra, ever-watchful by day and night, [grant] healing powers. Let Sarasvatī, the physician, with lead, milk out vital strength, milk, Soma, and foaming liquor.

Let the *parisrut*, the ghee, and the honey enjoy the clarified butter; O Hotṛ, sacrifice with the oblation! Let the Hotṛ sacrifice to the three goddesses for our medicine—the three who possess triple nature, the active ones, whose form is gold: Indra, the two Aśvins, and Iḍā. Let Sarasvatī, as Bhāratī, with her speech, yield for the great Indra his power and milk: Soma, the *parisrut*, the ghee, and the honey. Let them enjoy the clarified butter; O Hotṛ, [sacrifice]!

Sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ worship Tvaṣṭṛ, the fashioner of forms, the well-adorned, the bull of manly deeds. Let him worship Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra, the Aśvins our physicians, Sarasvatī, vigor, speed, and virility. Like a fierce wolf is the physician; glory is the remedy for the *surā* liquor. Like beauty is the *māsara* mixture, milk, Soma, the foaming liquor, ghee, and honey. Let him enjoy the clarified butter.

Hotṛ, sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ sacrifice to Vanaspati, the immolator, the one of a hundred powers, the terrible like wrath, the king, the tiger—with homage, let the Aśvins [sacrifice]; let Sarasvatī, the physician, milk out for Indra her fury, the power, the milk, the Soma, the foaming liquor, the ghee, the honey;
let him enjoy the clarified butter. Hotṛ, sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ sacrifice to Agni with Svāhā to the drops of clarified butter; Svāhā to the portions of fat!

Svāhā to the goat individually; svāhā to the ram for the Aśvins; svāhā to the bull for Sarasvatī; svāhā to Indra, the lion, for power through force; svāhā to Agni with medicines; svāhā to Soma with powers; svāhā to Indra the Good Protector, to Savitṛ, to Varuṇa, the Lord of Physicians; svāhā to Vanaspati, the beloved, as a path with medicines; svāhā!
May the gods who drink the clarified butter, Agni enjoying the medicine, Soma with the milk, the foaming liquor, the ghee, and the honey, partake of the clarified butter;
O Hotṛ, sacrifice!
O Aśvins, Agni is kindled by medicines; the Gharma is heated, the Virāj is pressed out.
Sarasvatī, the cow, milks forth here the pure Soma, the power of Indra.
When the soma is pressed, may both Aśvins, the physicians who protect the body, and Sarasvatī,
carry the honeyed essence through the paths to Indra, bestowing vital power upon him.
For Indra, Sarasvatī and the Aśvins, the physicians, have placed the Soma-drop with the Narāśaṃsa; they have set down the honey-medicine at the pressed juice.
Being invoked, Sarasvatī has bestowed upon Indra vital powers and heroism; with the *iḍā* offerings, the Aśvins have provided food, strength, and wealth.
The Aśvins [took] the bright Soma, the pressed juice from Namuci;
Sarasvatī brought it upon the sacrificial grass for Indra to drink.
Like wide-opening doors for the Aśvins, like the quarters of space,
Sarasvatī milks both worlds like Indra— she milks all desires.
Uṣas and Night, the Aśvins, and Indra with his powers at evening— these well-adorned deities, being in harmony, anoint themselves together with Sarasvatī.
Protect us by day, O Aśvins; protect us by night, O Sarasvatī!
O divine Hotṛ-priests, the physicians, protect Indra together at the pressed juice.

The three goddesses—Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, and Iḍā—and the two Aśvins have pressed the sharp, circling Soma with the *parisrut* ferment for Indra as a means of exhilaration; they have prepared it in three ways.
The Aśvins have bestowed healing medicine and honey; Sarasvatī and Tvaṣṭṛ, along with Indra, have bestowed glory, splendor, and every beautiful form upon us when the soma is pressed.
In due season, Indra, the Lord of the Forest, exerts himself with the *parisrut* liquor;
Sarasvatī, the milch-cow, yields for the Aśvins the honeyed *kīlāla*.
O Aśvins, with milk, with *māsara*, and with the foaming liquor, Sarasvatī has prepared the pressed honey for Indra; Svāhā!
The Aśvins, through their inspired thought, and Sarasvatī brought forth for Indra from Namuci the oblation, the vital power, the bright wealth of the Asura, and the exhilarating draught.
The oblation with which the Aśvins and Sarasvatī strengthened Indra—
he, together with the Asura Namuci, shattered the intoxicating strength [of the demon].
The cattle, both Aśvins, and Sarasvatī, bestowing power upon that Indra, have acclaimed him; they have offered the sacrificial oblation for his Indra-strength.
May he who bestowed power upon Indra— Savitṛ, Varuṇa, and Bhaga— he the good protector, attend to the sacrificer, the lord of oblations.
Savitṛ and Varuṇa bestow wealth upon the worshipful sacrificer;
the Good Protector has taken from Namuci the power and the strength of Indra.
Varuṇa bestows sovereignty and sensory power; Savitṛ, with Bhaga, bestows glory; and Sutrāman, with fame, bestows strength—bestowing these, they have attained the sacrifice.
O Aśvins, you two, together with the Asura Namuci,
drinking the surā-liquor, and Sarasvatī, aided Indra in his deeds.

Let the Hotṛ worship the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra. These Soma juices, mixed with *surā*, have been pressed with goats, rams, and bulls; they are great exhilarants like young grass, sprouts, and parched grain. Accompanied by *māsara* and *parisrut*, these bright, milky, immortal draughts, dripping with honey, have been set forth for you. May the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra enjoy them; may they drink the Soma-sweetness.
May they partake of the boiling [milk]; O Hotṛ, sacrifice! Like parents [protecting] a son, both Aśvins have protected you, O Indra, with their wisdom and wondrous deeds.
When you drank the intoxicating [Soma] with your powers, Sarasvatī, O Maghavan, refreshed you.
The Aśvins increased Indra’s sensory power with cattle, Sarasvatī increased his heroic vigor and strength with horses, and they strengthened the sacrificer with the oblation.
May those two Nāsatyas, well-adorned, whose paths are golden,
O heroes, and Sarasvatī, rich in oblations, protect Indra in his deeds.
Those two physicians of skillful deeds and that well-milking Sarasvatī—
he the Vṛtra-slayer, Śatakratu— bestowed Indra-power upon Indra.
The oblation has been poured into your mouth, O Agni, like clarified butter into the ladle, like Soma into the cups.
Bestow upon us wealth that wins booty, accompanied by brave sons—praiseworthy, glorious, and vast.
In whom horses, bulls, oxen, cows, and rams have been released and offered as oblations—
to that Agni, the drinker of sweet draughts, whose back is laden with Soma, the Ordainer— I generate a beautiful hymn from my heart.
The divine sacrificial grass, Sarasvatī, and the two Aśvins have bestowed godly splendor upon Indra. Like brilliance, they have placed sight in his eyes through the sacrificial grass;

may he enjoy the power of the senses for the winning of wealth and the granting of riches. Sacrifice! O divine Doors, the two Aśvins as physicians and Sarasvatī have bestowed vital breaths upon Indra.

They have placed vigor in your nostrils; they have established the sense-faculty for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure—sacrifice! Let them partake. Sacrifice to the divine Dawn and the Aśvins, to Indra with the Good Protector, and to Sarasvatī. They have placed strength and speech in his mouth through the two Dawns; they have established the sense-faculty for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure—sacrifice! Let them partake. Sacrifice to the two divine Delighters, to Sarasvatī, and to the Aśvins. They have strengthened Indra; they have placed the sense of hearing in his ears.

The two who delight in glory have bestowed vital power; for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure, let them partake. Sacrifice to the two goddesses, the two offerings of strength (*ūrjāhūtī*), the well-milking ones; may Sarasvatī and the Aśvins, the physicians, protect Indra. Like bright light, the two offerings place vital power within his breasts; for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure, let them partake. Sacrifice to the gods, the physicians of the gods, the two Hotṛ-priests, Indra, and the Aśvins.
With *vaṣaṭ*-cries, Sarasvatī and the two Hotṛ-priests have placed brilliance in the heart and mental power, as well as sensory vigor, for the winning of wealth and the granting of riches;

sacrifice to them! O three goddesses—Aśvinī, Iḍā, and Sarasvatī—like strength, they have placed sensory vigor in the very center of the navel for Indra, for the winning of wealth and the granting of riches; let them partake; sacrifice! O god Indra, Narāśaṃsa, the triple-protecting one.

The chariot of Sarasvatī and the Aśvins is driven forth; like seed, it is an immortal form, a source of generation. Tvaṣṭṛ, bestowing powers upon Indra, let him enjoy the gift of wealth for the winning of wealth. Let the divine Vanaspati, with the gods, golden-leaved and well-berried, ripen for the Aśvins and Sarasvatī, and for Indra, as honey, as vigor, as speed, as the bull’s brilliance—Vanaspatis! Yaja! (Sacrifice!)

Bestowing the senses, may he enjoy the wealth-bestowing gift of the treasure-store; sacrifice to the god Barhis, who is spread with water-plants at the sacrifice, soft as wool for the Aśvins, and pleasant for Sarasvatī—O Indra, this is your seat. Through their lordship, they have established the King Manyu upon the sacrificial grass; may he enjoy the wealth-bestowing gift of the treasure-store; sacrifice. May the divine Agni Sviṣṭakṛt [enjoy] the gods...
May the two Hotṛ-priests sacrifice to Indra according to his due; may they sacrifice to the Aśvins with speech, to Sarasvatī with speech, and to Agni and Soma. May Agni Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice well.
Sacrificed well are Indra the Good Protector, Savitṛ, Varuṇa the Physician, and the god Vanaspati. Sacrificed well are the gods who drink the clarified butter.
Sacrificed well is Agni by Agni, the Hotṛ for the office of the Hotṛ, as Sviṣṭakṛt. May he bestow upon us power, vigor, honor, and the ancestral offering.
May he partake of the gift of wealth and the bestowal of riches; sacrifice!
The camel-milked [juice]:
the bright Soma,
the king, the pressed nectar, the essence of plants and of the waters.
By means of cosmic order (ṛta), truth, and power, this is the drinking of the bright essence of the soma-plant;
it is Indra’s own power, the milk, the nectar, the honey.
From the waters, Kruñ Āṅgirasa drank forth the milk by means of his inspired thought:
the truth through the cosmic order, the potent power, the pure draught from the soma-plant;
this is Indra’s own power, the milk, the nectar, the honey.
From the waters, the swan dwelling in purity drank the Soma with the meters; by means of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), he drank the truth, the power of Indra, the bright draught of the plant-juice—
this milk, the immortal honey, which is the very power of Indra.
From the food, the Kṣatra drank the essence that flowed forth by means of the Brahman;
through the cosmic order (ṛta), it drank the truth, the power of the senses, the purified draught of the soma-plant.
This is Indra’s vital power, this milk, the nectar, the honey.
The semen and urine are discharged as the organ enters the womb;
the embryo, enveloped by the placenta, casts off the amnion at birth.
By means of the cosmic order (ṛta), the truth, the power, the drinking of the bright essence of the soma-plant—
this is Indra’s power, this milk, the nectar, the honey.
Having observed form, Prajāpati distinguished truth from falsehood;
Prajāpati placed lack of faith in falsehood and faith in truth.
By means of the cosmic order (ṛta), this is the truth, the power of Indra, the drinking of the bright essence of the soma-plant;
it is Indra’s own power, the milk, the nectar, the honey.
By means of the Veda, Prajāpati drank the forms [of the Soma], both the pressed and the unpressed;
by means of Cosmic Order (ṛta), he drank the Truth, the sensory power, the distilled essence of the plant-juice.
This is the sensory power of Indra—this milk, the nectar, the honey.
Having seen the flowing essence, Prajāpati drank the pure milk with his pure [organ]— the Soma, the truth through the cosmic order, the drinking of the bright juice,
the sensory power of Indra; this is the milk, the nectar, the honey of Indra’s vital force.
Pour out the pressed juice on every side—the Soma which is the supreme oblation, the manly one that has flowed within the waters; he has pressed the Soma with the stones.
Thou art Soma; be cooked for the Aśvins, be cooked for Sarasvatī, be cooked for Indra the Good Protector.
May the daughter of the Sun purify for you the flowing Soma with her eternal, continuous fleece.
The wind is purified by the filter, as is Soma when it has flowed forth;
he is the fitting friend of Indra.
Purified by the filter of the wind, Soma has flowed through;
he is the fitting friend of Indra.

The Brahman, the Kṣatra, splendor, and sensory power flow forth from the pressed Soma, the well-pressed liquor for exhilaration. O God, satisfy the deities with your bright radiance; bestow nourishment upon the sacrificer with your essence.
For are you not indeed different from one another?
May that [goddess] who protects against the tiger and the viper,
and both the wolf and the winged falcon, and the lion— may she protect this [person] from distress.
With obeisances, the mighty ones impel the sacrifice, rich in Soma, seated upon the sacred grass, and abounding in heroes;
offering Soma among the gods in heaven, these sacrificers, chanting beautiful hymns, exhilarate Indra with their joy.
That essence of yours which is gathered in the plants, the vigor of Soma, and the power of the pressed Surā—
by that exhilaration, quicken the sacrificer, Sarasvatī, the Aśvins, Indra, and Agni.
That which Sarasvatī pressed out from the Asura Namuci for the sake of Indra’s power—
that bright, honeyed drop, this King Soma, I partake of here.
Whatever remains here of the pressed juice of the Soma, that which you, O Indu, drank with your powers—
I, with a gracious mind, consume that King Soma here.
At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I take you up.

The three groups of gods, the eleven, and the thirty-three, the bounteous ones, with Bṛhaspati as their domestic priest— at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may the gods protect you along with the gods.

May the first [verses] consecrate you with the second; may the second with the third; may the third with truth; may truth with the sacred word (*brahman*); may the sacred word with the *yajus* formulas; may the *yajus* formulas with the *sāman* chants; may the *sāman* chants with the *ṛc* verses;

may the *ṛc* verses with the introductory invocations (*puronuvākyā*); may the introductory invocations with the offering verses (*yājyā*); may the offering verses with the *vaṣaṭ* calls; and may the *vaṣaṭ* calls consecrate you with the oblations.
May the oblations sprinkle you; may they fulfill your desires. With the splendor of the Aśvins, I sprinkle you for the sake of sacred luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
with the vigor of Sarasvatī, I sprinkle you for the sake of glory and the eating of food; with the power of Indra, I sprinkle you for the sake of vital force and strength. Bhūḥ! Svāhā!
My head is glory, my face is fame; my hair and beard are splendor.
My breath is the king, my sight is the immortal sovereign, and my hearing is the far-shining one.
My tongue is prosperity, my speech is greatness, my mind is fury, and my wrath is self-ruling splendor; my joys and raptures are my fingers, my limbs are my strength, and my friend is my power.
My arms are strength and power; my hands are action and vigor;
my chest is the self and the ruling power.
My ribs are the kingdom; my belly, shoulders, neck, and hips;
my thighs, forearms, and knees—these limbs of mine on every side are the subjects.
My navel is consciousness; my mind is the anus, the seat of honor; my testicles are joy and delight; my generative organ is fortune and prosperity.
My body hair is my effort; my skin is my bowing, my coming hither; my flesh is my approach; my wealth is my bone; my marrow is my bowing.
Through my shanks and feet, I am wise; I am established as the king over the people. O Brahman, I establish myself in the Kṣatra; I establish myself in horses and in cattle.
I establish myself in offspring, I establish myself on the back, I establish myself in the vital breaths, in the self, in heaven and earth, and in the sacrifice.
With the head as the warp, the wise weave the ritual with their minds; the seers weave it with woolen thread.
The Aśvins, Savitṛ, Sarasvatī, and Varuṇa heal the sacrifice, which is the form of Indra.
The three deities, acting in harmony with their powers, bestowed that immortal form upon him;
his body hairs became like young grass, his hair like sprouts in many ways, and his skin and flesh became like parched grain.
Then the Aśvins, the physicians whose path is red, and Sarasvatī weave a beautiful form within;
placing bone and marrow, they fashion the *māsara* with the *kārotara* strainer upon the hide of cows.
Sarasvatī weaves with her mind a beautiful treasure for the two Nāsatyas—a lovely form, like the red juice of the flowing soma; the wise one [weaves] it as a shuttle upon the loom.
From milk comes the seed, the immortal source of liquor; from urine they produce semen.
Driving away ignorance and ill-will, may all that waste be far removed by the wind.
Indra the Good Protector generated truth with his heart; Savitṛ generated it with the sacrificial cake;
Varuṇa, acting as physician, heals the liver and the lungs; he does not diminish the gall-bladder and the spleen by means of the Vāyu-vessels.
The intestines are the cooking-pots overflowing with honey; the bowels are the vessels like a cow that yields milk well.
The spleen, by its powers, is like the wing of a hawk; the navel is the throne-seat, and the belly is like a mother.
The cauldron is the rectum, the progenitor by its powers, in which, at the beginning, the embryo dwells within the womb;
the bladder is manifest as a fountain with a hundred streams; like a jar, it yields the *svadhā* offering for the ancestors.
The mouth is the head of the assembly; with truth, the tongue is the filter. The Aśvins are its two lips, Sarasvatī is its palate.
The water-skin is its anus; the physician is its tail-hair. The bladder is its penis, vigorous with its heat and speed.
From the two Aśvins, [he received] immortal vision; from the two cups, splendor through the goat-oblation and clarified butter;
the eyelashes were fashioned with the smoke of cow-dung and jujube fruits; like a weaver, he puts on the white and the black.
Like a ram upon its nose for heroic power, the immortal path of breath is formed by the two cups;
Sarasvatī, with her invocations, has generated the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the nasal passages, the sacrificial grass, and the jujube fruits.
The bull is the form of Indra for the sake of strength; from his two ears, the immortal [soma] is taken by means of the two cups.
With barley, the sacrificial grass is formed upon his brows, and the filaments are produced; the jujube fruit was born as honey in his mouth for the bees.
On his body there is no hair like that of a wolf; on his face there is no beard like the fur of a tiger;
on his head there are no hairs for the sake of glory, but a crest for the sake of splendor; the hair of a lion is his radiance and his vital powers.
With his limbs the physician restored himself; with his limbs Sarasvatī restored him.
Assuming the form of Indra, a hundredfold lifespan, and the bright, immortal light like radiance, she healed him.
Sarasvatī, the consort, bears within her womb a well-fashioned embryo for the Aśvins;
like Varuṇa with the essence of the waters, the King generates Indra for glory within the waters through the Sāman.

The brilliance of cattle, the potent oblation, the honeyed mead from the bee, with milk and the flowing liquor—these have been milked by the two physicians, the Aśvins; the pressed and unpressed Soma, the immortal drop, has been milked by Sarasvatī.
May the Soma-loving fathers purify me; may the grandfathers purify me.
Through the purifier that grants a hundred-year life, may I attain a full span of life.
May my grandfathers purify me; may my great-grandfathers purify me.
Through the purifier that grants a hundred-year lifespan, may I attain a full span of life.
O Agni, you purify our lifespans.
May Pavamāna, the light-maker, the all-seeing one, who is the purifier, cleanse me with the filter.
May the divine folk purify me; may the sages purify me with their inspired thought;
may all beings purify me; O Jātavedas, do thou purify me.
May Pavamāna purify me for wisdom, for skill, and for life,
so that I may long behold the sun.
O God Savitṛ, purify me on all sides with both the filter and the impulse.
O God Agni, shining with brilliance, purify me with the purifier, with the bright one, according to our mental powers.
O Agni, with that purifier of yours which is spread within your flame, we purify our sacred prayer (brahman).
The purifying goddess belonging to all the gods has come, she whose many forms have smooth backs;
rejoicing with her in our common feasts, may we be masters of riches.
May Vaiśvānara purify me with his rays; may Vāta, the impetuous bringer of bliss, purify me with his breath;
may Heaven and Earth, the observers of Truth and worthy of sacrifice, purify me with their milk and waters.
O divine Savitṛ, with three great and most exalted hymns of praise, O Agni, we purify ourselves through our skillful insights.
Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—
for them let there be a world, *svadhā*, obeisance, and may the sacrifice be prepared among the gods.
Those living beings who are equal and like-minded among the living, my own kin—
may their prosperity be ordained for me in this world for a hundred years.
There are two paths.
May this oblation be productive for me, providing ten heroic sons, a complete retinue, and well-being;
may it grant me self, progeny, land, cattle, the world, and fearlessness.
May Agni make my progeny abundant; bestow upon us food, milk, and seed.
O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, O gods,
may Agni release me from that sin and from all distress.
Whether we have committed sins while sleeping or while awake,
may Vāyu release me from that sin and from all distress.
Whether by day or by night we have committed sins,
may Sūrya release me from that sin and from all distress.
From station to station.
That which is in the village.
You are the purifier, the purifier of the sacrifice and of the sacrificer. May that purify me from all sin against the gods, from every sin against the gods.
Like one released from a trap, like one perspiring cleansed from dirt after bathing,
like clarified butter purified by a strainer— may all release me from mental affliction.
The earth has been encompassed, as have the dawn and the sun.
May I become the light of Vaiśvānara; may I attain the all-pervading desire. Bhūḥ! Svāhā!
The fire is kindled by fuel, well-kindled and most excellent;
Gāyatrī as the meter, Indra-power, and the three-year-old bull have bestowed vital strength.
Tanūnapāt of pure vows, Tanūpā, and Sarasvatī have bestowed the Uṣṇih meter, sensory power, and the Dityavāt bull as vital strength.
Sarasvatī:
Agni is to be praised with *iḍā*-invocations; the immortal god Soma, the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the sense-power (*indriya*), and the five-colored cow have bestowed vital strength.
Agni with fine sacrificial grass, accompanied by Pūṣan, the immortal one for whom the grass is strewn;
the Bṛhatī meter, sensory power, and the three-year-old bull have bestowed vital strength.
The divine quarters, the great goddesses; the god Brahmā, Bṛhaspati;
the Paṅkti meter, the sense-power, and the four-year-old ox—these have bestowed vital strength.
The two young Dawns, well-adorned, and all the immortal gods,
have bestowed the Triṣṭubh metre, sensory power, the Pṛṣṭhavāṭ cow, and vital strength.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the physicians, together with Indra as their companion,
have bestowed the Jagatī metre, sensory power, the ox, and the cow as vital strength.
The three goddesses— Ṛtā, Mahī, and Bhāratī— and the Marut clans have bestowed the Virāj metre, sensory power, and the cow as nourishment, like life-sustaining food.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the swift and wonderful, Indra, and Agni, the increasers of prosperity, have bestowed power through the two-footed metre; they have granted vigor like a bull or a cow.
May Vanaspati pacify us; may Savitṛ, impelling, bestow fortune.
May the Kakubh metre, Indra’s power, and the bull-cow bestow vigor here.
Svāhā! May Varuṇa, the one of good dominion, make the sacrifice a healing medicine.
The Atichandas meter, the Bṛhat, the barren cow, and the cow that miscarries have bestowed vital power and life-force.
With the spring season, the Vasu gods, through the threefold hymn and the splendor of the *rathantara*, have placed the oblation and vital strength in Indra.
By means of the summer season, the gods, the Rudras, have praised the fifteenfold [stoma];
with the Bṛhat [sāman], with glory, they have bestowed strength, the oblation, and vital vigor upon Indra.

With the rains, with the season, and with the seventeenfold hymn, O Ādityas, you have been praised; through the Vairūpa chant and with the power of the people, you have placed the oblation and vital strength in Indra.
By means of the autumn season, the twenty-one-fold hymn, and the Vairāja melody, the divine Ṛbhus have, through glory, bestowed glory, the oblation, and vital strength upon Indra.
By means of the winter season, the gods—the Maruts in their thrice-ninefold host—have offered praise;
through strength and power, they have placed the *śakvarī* verses, vigor, and the oblation within Indra.
By the winter season, the thirty-three gods have praised the nectar;
through truth, the Revatī verses have placed dominion, the oblation, and vital strength in Indra.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, named the Sautrāmaṇī, in the third book.
The ancient seers grasped this rein of Order at the early age during the sacrificial assemblies;
she has appeared for us at this pressing, proclaiming the course of Order at its boundary.
[Page III,160] You are speech, you are the world, you are the controller, you are the sustainer. As such, go to Agni Vaiśvānara, the far-extending.
Being consecrated by *svāhā*, may you go well to the gods and to Prajāpati. O Brahman, I shall bind the horse for the gods and for Prajāpati.

By that may I prosper; bind it for the gods, for Prajāpati; by that do thou prosper. I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Prajāpati; I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Vāyu; I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Indra and Agni; I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the Viśve Devas; I sprinkle thee, acceptable to all the gods.
I sprinkle:
*juṣṭam*.
He who seeks to kill the courser—him Varuṇa strikes down.
The mortal is beyond; the dog is beyond.

Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to the Delight of the Waters! Svāhā to Vāyu! Svāhā to Savitṛ! Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ! Svāhā to Bṛhaspati! Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Mitra! Svāhā to Varuṇa! Svāhā to the Hiṃ-sound! Svāhā to the one who has uttered the Hiṃ-sound! Svāhā to the one who bellows! Svāhā to the one who bellows down! Svāhā to the one who snorts! Svāhā to the one who snorts forth! Svāhā to the scent! Svāhā to the one who smells! Svāhā to the one who has settled down! Svāhā to the one who has sat down! Svāhā to the one who is bound! Svāhā!

Hail to him as he leaps! Hail to him as he sits! Hail to him as he lies down! Hail to him as he sleeps! Hail to him as he wakes! Hail to him as he moans! Hail to him as he awakens! Hail to him as he stretches! Hail to him as he yawns! Hail to speed! Hail to strength! Hail to coming! Hail to departing! Hail to him as he goes! Hail to him as he runs! Hail to him as he flees! Hail to him as he has fled! Hail to him as he snorts!

Svāhā to the one who has made the sound *śūkṛt*, svāhā to the one who has approached, svāhā to the one who is gathering together, svāhā to the one who is seated, svāhā to the one who has risen, svāhā to the one who is standing firm, svāhā to the one who is turning around, svāhā to the one who has turned around, svāhā to the one who is shaking,
svāhā to the one who has shaken, svāhā to the one who hears, svāhā to the one who is listening, svāhā to the one who looks, svāhā to the one who has looked, svāhā to the one who is looking about.
Svāhā to the winking; svāhā to that which eats; svāhā to that which drinks; svāhā to that which urinates; svāhā to the one who acts; svāhā to the act performed.

Abundant through thy mother, powerful through thy father; thou art a horse, thou art a steed, thou art a racer, thou art a joy-giver, thou art a man, thou art a courser, thou art a swift steed, thou art a stallion, thou art one whose mind is directed toward men;

thy name is "The Wanderer. Follow the flight of the Ādityas! O gods who guard the quarters, protect this horse sprinkled for sacrifice here for the gods! Here is steadfastness, here self-steadfastness, here is delight; let them find delight here.

To the body, svāhā! To whom, svāhā! To which one, svāhā! To Savitṛ, svāhā! To Savitṛ the impeller, svāhā! To Savitṛ the inspirer, svāhā! To Aditi, svāhā! To Aditi the great, svāhā! To Aditi the very gracious, svāhā! To Sarasvatī, svāhā! To Sarasvatī the vast, svāhā! To Sarasvatī the purifying, svāhā! To Pūṣan, svāhā! To Pūṣan the path-finder, svāhā!
Svāhā to Pūṣan, the protector of men; svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ; svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ, the bestower of seed; svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ, whose form is the joints;
svāhā to Viṣṇu; svāhā to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; svāhā to Viṣṇu, the protector of what is hidden. Svāhā!

O Brahman, may a radiant Brahmin, endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge, be born; in this kingdom, may a Kshatriya be born who is a hero, skilled in archery, and a great chariot-warrior; may there be a milch-cow that yields milk, a draft-ox that carries the load, a swift steed, a youth worthy of the assembly, a wife of noble mind, and a victorious warrior standing upon the chariot—may such a hero be born to this sacrificer. May Parjanya rain for us according to our every desire, and may our crops be fruitful.
May the plants ripen; may our security and prosperity be established.

Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to the Earth! Svāhā to the Atmosphere! Svāhā to Heaven! Svāhā to the Quarters! Svāhā to the Directions! Svāhā to the Wide Quarter! Svāhā to the Eastern Quarter! Svāhā to the Constellations! Svāhā to those belonging to the Constellations! Svāhā to Day and Night! Svāhā to the Half-months! Svāhā to the Months! Svāhā to the Seasons!

Svāhā to the seasons! Svāhā to the year! Svāhā to Heaven and Earth! Svāhā to the Moon! Svāhā to the Sun! Svāhā to the rays! Svāhā to the Vasus! Svāhā to the Rudras! Svāhā to the Ādityas! Svāhā to the Maruts!
Svāhā to the All-gods! Svāhā to the roots! Svāhā to the branches! Svāhā to the trees! Svāhā!
Hail to the flowers! Hail to the fruits! Hail to the medicinal herbs!

Hail to the eastern quarter, hail to the intermediate quarter; hail to the southern quarter, hail to the intermediate quarter; hail to the western quarter, hail to the intermediate quarter; hail to the northern quarter, hail to the intermediate quarter; hail to the upward quarter, hail to the intermediate quarter.
Hail to life! Hail to out-breath! Hail to in-breath! Hail to diffused breath! Hail to equalizing breath! Hail to upward breath! Hail to the eye! Hail to the ear! Hail to the mind! Hail to speech!

Hail to the earth! Hail to the intermediate space! Hail to the sky! Hail to the sun! Hail to the moon! Hail to the stars! Hail to the waters! Hail to the plants! Hail to the trees! Hail to the floating creatures! Hail to the reptiles!
Hail to all things moving and stationary! Hail!

Hail to Asu, hail to Vasu, hail to Vibhu, hail to Vivasvat, hail to Gaṇaśrī, hail to Gaṇapati, hail to Abhiṣāh, hail to Abhibhū, hail to Adhipati, hail to Śūṣa, hail to Saṃsarpa, hail to Candra, hail to Jyotis, hail to Malimluca!
Hail to Dharaṇa, hail to Draviṇa, hail to Prasava, hail to Upayāma, hail to Sindhu,
hail to Samudra, hail to Kāṭa, hail to Arṇava, hail to Sarasvatī, hail to Viśvavyacas, hail to Subhūta, hail to Antarikṣa!
Svāhā!
Hail to Madhu, hail to Mādhava! Hail to Śukra, hail to Śuci! Hail to Nabhas, hail to Nabhasya! Hail to Iṣa, hail to Ūrja! Hail to Sahas, hail to Sahasya! Hail to Tapas, hail to Tapasya!
You are the gliding one; hail to Aṃhaspatya!

Hail to one of equal age! Hail to one of superior age! Hail to one of ascending age! Hail to one of great age! Hail to the more powerful! Hail to the conquering one! Hail to the victorious! Hail to the one possessing power!
Hail to the one who overcomes by command! Hail to the one who overcomes! Hail to the one who overcomes the adversary! Hail to the slayer of the adversary! Hail!
Hail to one! Hail to two! Hail to ninety-nine! Hail to a hundred! Hail to one hundred and one! Hail to the dawning! Hail to heaven! Hail!
In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. He supported this earth and yonder heaven. To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. This is your womb; the sun is your greatness.
He who is the king of all that breathes and blinks, the lord of the entire world;
he who rules over its bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati. This is your womb; the moon is your greatness.
They harness the ruddy, bright one as he moves; those who stand around him behold him. The luminous realms shine in the sky.
Or when the wind has gone to the waters, to Indra’s beloved body—
O singer of praise, by this path bring our horse back to us again.
May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre; may the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre; may the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Lājī, O Śācī, O Yavyā, O Gavyā—eat this food, O gods; eat this food, O Prajāpati.
Who indeed wanders alone? Who indeed is born again?
What is the remedy for cold? What is the great place of sowing?
The sun moves alone; the moon is born again;
fire is the remedy for cold; the earth is the great vessel for sowing.
What indeed was the primordial thought? What indeed was the great vital power?
What indeed was the slippery one? What indeed was the devourer of flesh?
The sky was the first thought; the horse was the great vital power;
the sheep was the slippery one; the night was the reddish-brown one.
Hail to the out-breath, hail to the in-breath, hail to the diffused breath!
O Ambā, Ambikā, and Ambālikā, no one leads me away;
the little horse sleeps with Subhadrā, who dwells in Kāmapīlava.
We invoke you, the lord of hosts; we invoke you, the lord of beloved things; we invoke you, the lord of treasures, O Vasu. May I be born as one who brings forth offspring;
may you be born as one who brings forth offspring.
May we two together extend the four quarters; may they cover us in the heavenly world. May the stallion horse, the bestower of seed, bestow seed upon you both.
May Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Anuṣṭubh, along with Paṅkti, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇihā, Kakubh, the wives of the gods, and the Viśvedevas, pacify you with their needles.
Whether they have two feet, four feet, three feet, or six feet;
whether they are irregular in meter or possess regular meters—may these [verses] pacify you with their needles.
Let the silvery ones and the tawny ones, yoked together, harness themselves with their functions;
let them form the weaving-threads upon the skin of the vigorous horse, bringing peace.
May the Mahānāmīs, the Revatīs, the divine quarters, the prolific ones,
the clouds, the lightnings, and the words— through their needles— pacify you.
May women, your wives, comb your hair as is fitting;
O Steed, may we, as wives with good husbands, enjoy offspring.
Is it not so?
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the third book.
Raise this one upward, like one carrying a load upon a mountain;
then let its middle swell, like one purifying himself in a cold wind.
The two anklets, like little birds, tinkle as she moves;
when her foot is struck, they ring out clearly.
"Both your mother and your father climb to the top of the tree.
"I am getting it," says your father.
When the deer eats barley, it does not consider the animal to be well-nourished; when a Śūdra woman has an affair with an Ārya, she does not desire wealth for the sake of prosperity.
I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan.
The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—these are for Prajāpati; the black-necked [goat] is for Agni; the ewe with a white mark on the forehead is for Sarasvatī;
the dark [goat] below the jawbones is for Pūṣan; the two reddish-brown [goats] at the navel are for the Aśvins;

the two hairy-thighed [goats] at the thighs are for Tvaṣṭṛ; the white and the black [goats] at the sides are for Sūrya and Yama; the white [goat] at the tail is for Vāyu; and [the others] are for Indra.
The ewe for Svapasya, and the dwarf for Viṣṇu.

The tawny, the ruddy-tawny, and the parrot-tawny—these belong to Varuṇa. The red, the smoke-colored red, and the jujube-colored red—these belong to Soma. The white-armed, the one with a white arm on one side, and the one with white arms all around—these belong to Bṛhaspati. The white-nosed...
The *nyataḥśitirandhra*, the *samantaśitirandhra*—these belong to Savitṛ; the *pṛṣatī*, the *kṣudrapṛṣatī*, and the *sthūlapṛṣatī*—these belong to Mitra and Varuṇa.

The pure-tailed, the all-pure-tailed, and the jewel-tailed are for the Aśvins; the white, the white-eyed, and the ruddy are for Rudra Paśupati; the spotted-eared, the smeared, and the smoke-colored are for the Rudras; the speckled, the cross-speckled, and the upward-speckled are for the Maruts; the pale, the red-wooled, and the white-eyed are for Sarasvatī;
the spleen-eared, the snout-eared, and the overgrown-eared are for Tvaṣṭṛ; and the black-necked, the white-flanked, and the marked-thighed [are for Agni].
They are dedicated to Indra and Agni: Kṛṣṇañji, Alpāñji, and Mahāñji; they are dedicated to Uṣas.
A cow of artistic skill for the Viśvedevas; three-year-old cows of the Rohiṇī breed for Vāc; unmarked cows for Aditi; cows of uniform color for Dhātṛ; and heifers for the wives of the gods.

Those with black necks belong to Agni; those with white eyebrows belong to the Vasus; the ruddy ones belong to the Rudras; the white, speckled ones belong to the Ādityas; and those with the color of the sky belong to Parjanya.

The humped ones with white forelegs and white backs are for Indra and Bṛhaspati; the humped bulls and dwarfs are for Indra and Viṣṇu; the swift ones with the appearance of boars and variegated spots are for Agni and the Maruts; the dark ones are for Pūṣan; these two-colored ones are for Indra and Agni; the dwarfs that are oxen are for Agni and Viṣṇu; the ones striped on one side are for Mitra; and the barren cows are for Mitra and Varuṇa.

Those with black necks are for Agni; the tawny ones are for Soma; the white ones are for Vāyu; those of unknown color are for Aditi; those of uniform color are for Dhātṛ; and the heifers are for the wives of the gods.
The black are terrestrial, the smoky are atmospheric, the great are divine, the variegated are lightning-born, and the speckled are stellar.

Those with black necks are for Agni; the brown ones are for Soma; the speckled ones are for Savitṛ; the heifers are for Sarasvatī; the dark-grey ones are for Pūṣan; the dappled ones are for the Maruts; the ruddy ones are for the Viśve Devas; the barren cows are for Heaven and Earth. Those with black necks are for Agni; the brown ones are for Soma; the speckled ones are for Savitṛ; the heifers are for Sarasvatī; the dark-grey ones are for Pūṣan; these [others] are for Indra and Agni; the dappled ones are for the Maruts; the black hornless ones are for Varuṇa; and the hornless ones are for Ka.
He sacrifices first-born [calves] to Agni Anīkavat; Savātyas to the Maruts Sāṃtapanas;
Vaṣkihās to the Maruts Gṛhamedhas; Saṃsṛṣṭas to the Maruts Krīḍins; and Anusṛṣṭas to the Maruts Svatavantas.

Those with black necks are for Agni; the tawny ones are for Soma; the speckled ones are for Savitṛ; the heifers are for Sarasvatī; the dark ones are for Pūṣan; these hornless ones are for Indra-Agni; those of many colors are for Indra; those for Viśvakarman have black necks; those for Agni are tawny; those for Soma are speckled; the heifers are for Savitṛ; those for Sarasvatī are dark; those for Pūṣan are white; those for Vāyu are white; the hornless ones are for Indra; those for Sūrya are white.

Three-year-old oxen are for the *gāyatrī*; five-year-old oxen are for the *triṣṭubh*; two-year-old oxen are for the *jagatī*; three-year-old heifers are for the *anuṣṭubh*; and four-year-old oxen are for the *uṣṇih*.
The draft-oxen are for the Virāj; the bulls are for the Bṛhatī; the bullocks are for the Kakubh; the milch-cows are for the Jagatī; the oxen are for the Paṅkti.
Smoke-colored for spring, white for summer, and black for the rainy season.
Red for autumn, speckled for winter, and tawny for the cool season.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the third book.
For Spring he immolates *kapiñjala* partridges; for Summer, *kalaviṅka* sparrows; for the Rainy Season, *tittiri* partridges; for Autumn, quails (*vartikā*); and for Winter, *kakara* partridges.
To the Ocean he sacrifices porpoises; to Parjanya, frogs; to the Waters, fish; to Mitra, *pulīkāya* birds; to Varuṇa, crocodiles.
He sacrifices swans to Soma, cranes to Vāyu, curlews to Indra and Agni, water-fowl to Mitra, and ruddy geese to Varuṇa.
He sacrifices *kuṭaru* birds to Agni; *ulūka* owls to the Vanaspatis; *cāṣa* blue jays to Agni and Soma; peacocks to the Aśvins; and pigeons to Mitra and Varuṇa.
He sacrifices *laba* birds to Soma, *kaulīka* birds to Tvaṣṭṛ, *goṣādī* birds to the wives of the gods, and *pulīka* birds to Agni Gṛhapati.

He offers the *pārāvata* birds to the day, the *sīcāpuṣ* birds to the night, the *jatū* birds to the junctions of the day, the great *suparṇa* birds to the year, and the *dātyauha* birds to the months.
He offers mice to the earth, porcupines to the intermediate space, lizards to the sky, mongooses to the quarters, and brown mongooses to the intermediate directions.
To Prajāpati he sacrifices men with an elephant; to Speech, gnats; to Sight, mosquitoes; to Hearing, bees.
He sacrifices the Ṛṣya deer to the Vasus, the Ruru deer to the Rudras, the Nyaṅku deer to the Ādityas, the spotted deer to the Viśvedevas, and the Kulaṅga deer to the Sādhyas.
He sacrifices the *parasvat* animals to Īśāna, the *gaura* to Mitra, the *mahiṣa* to Varuṇa, the *gavaya* to Bṛhaspati, and the camels to Tvaṣṭṛ.

To Prajāpati and Vāyu, the *gomṛga*; to Varuṇa, the wild ram; to Yama, the black antelope; to Manurāja, the monkey; to Śārdūla, the female deer (*rohit*); to Vṛṣabha, the *gavayī*; to Kṣipraśyena, the quail (*vartikā*); to Nīlaṅgu, the worm; to the Ocean, the porpoise (*śiśumāra*); to Himavat, the elephant.

The mayu belongs to Prajāpati; the ulūka, the halikṣṇa, and the vṛṣadaṃśa belong to Dhātṛ; the kaṅka belongs to the Quarters; the dhūṅkṣā belongs to Agni; the kalaviṅka, the puṣkarasāda, and the red snake belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; the krauñca belongs to Vāc.

The *kulāṅga* for Soma; the wild goat, the *nakula*, and the *śaka*—these are for Pūṣan; the jackal for Māyā; the *gauramṛga* for Indra; the *nyaṅku* for Pidva; the *kakuṭha* for Anumati; the *cakravāka* for Pratiśrutkā; the crane (*balākā*) for Sūrya; the *śārga*, the *sṛjaya*, and the *śayāṇḍaka*—these are for Mitra; the porcupine for Bhūmi; the *śāri* that speaks like a man for Sarasvatī; the tiger, the wolf, and the *pṛdāku*—these are for Manyu; the parrot that speaks like a man for Sarasvant.

The *suparṇa* is for Pārjanya; the *āti* bird is for Vāyu; the woodpecker is for Vāyu; the *kṛkavāku* (cock) is for Savitṛ; the swan is for Vāta; the *plava* and *madgura* fish are for the Lord of Rivers; the tortoise is for Heaven and Earth.
