The *puruṣamṛga*, the *godhā*, the *kālakā*, and the *dārvāghāṭa*—these belong to the trees. For Bṛhaspati Vācaspati [are offered] the *paiṅgarāja*, the *alaja*, the *āntarikṣa*, the *nākra*, the *makara*, and the *pulīkāya*; for Hrī [is offered] the *śalyaka*.

The female antelope belongs to the Day; the frog, the mouse, and the partridge belong to the Serpents; the jackal belongs to the Aśvins; the black bear, the owl, and the chameleon belong to the Night; the female mongoose belongs to the Itarajanas; and the female snake belongs to Viṣṇu.

The anyavāpa is for the half-months; the ṛśya, the peacock, and the eagle are for the Gandharvas; the otter is for the Waters; Kaśyapa is for the months; the rohit, the kuṇḍṛṇācī, and the golattikā are for the Apsarases; the asita is for Death; the varṣāhū is for the seasons; the rat is for Kaśa; the mānthālava is for the Pitṛs; the kapiñjala is for the Vasus; the python is for Strength; the pigeon, the owl, and the hare are for Nirṛti; the black one is for Night.

The variegated one belongs to the Ādityas; the camel, the glowing one, to the Vārdhrīṇasas; the *sṛmara* antelope, for the sake of thought (*matis*), to Araṇa; the *ruru* deer, to Rudra; the *kuvaya*, the *kuṭaru*, and the *dātyauha*—these belong to the desire for swift steeds; the cuckoo (*pika*) [belongs to the same].

The rhinoceros is for the Vaiśvadevas; the hyena, the dog, the black-eared donkey—these are for the Rakṣases; the boar is for Indra; the lion is for the Maruts; the chameleon, the pippakā bird, and the śakuni bird—these are for Śaravyā;
the spotted deer is for the Viśve Devas.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the third book.
With his teeth he [takes] the young grass, with the roots of his teeth the *avakā* plants, with his gums the clay, with his tusks the stepping-stones,
with his roar the palate, with his jaws the prize, with his tongue the foremost tongue of Sarasvatī, with his mouth the springing forth of water, with his testicles the two virile ones,
with his beard the Ādityas, with his eyebrows the path, with his eyelids heaven and earth, and with his pupils the lightning.
From the ears come the two ears; from the ears the ears are to be excluded. The eyelashes are to be included; the sugarcanes are to be included. The eyelashes are to be included;
the sugarcanes are to be excluded.

With the side-posts [he offers] to Vāta; with the breath-inhalation and breath-exhalation to the nose; with the lower lip to the Upayāma; with the upper lip to the Sadas; with the cry "Svāhā! to the white [light], with the cry "Svāhā! to the black [darkness]; with the Nirbādha [cup] to the thunder; with the Niveṣya [cup] to the head; with the Mastiska [cup] to the lightning-bolt; with the two pupils to the lightning-flash.
By the light [he attains] the inner space, by the radiance the outer; now, by the lower throat the waters, by the parched throat the mind;
by the neck-tendons Aditi, by the head Nirṛti; by the motionless head the vital breaths, by the throes of anger the wind, and by the crown of the head the thunderbolt.
With his hair [he overcomes] mosquitoes; with Indra, through his skillful vehicle; with Bṛhaspati, through the sitting of the bird; with tortoises, through his hooves;
with the *sthūra* [thighs], the act of mounting; with the *kuṣṭha* [feet], strength; with the shanks, speed; with the arms, the path; with the *jāmbila*, the forest;
with the *atīrūk*, fire; with the *rorā*, Rudra; with Pūṣan, through his forearms; with the Aśvins, through his shoulders.
The first belongs to Agni; the second to Vāyu; the third to Soma; the fourth to the Waters; the fifth to Aditi; the sixth to Agni and Soma;
the seventh to the Maruts; the eighth to Bṛhaspati; the ninth to Pūṣan; the tenth to Tvaṣṭṛ; the eleventh to Indra; the twelfth to Varuṇa; and the thirteenth to Yama.

The first rib belongs to Indra and Agni; the second to Sarasvatī; the third to Indra; the fourth to Bṛhaspati; the fifth to Nirṛti; the sixth to Indrāṇī; the seventh to the Serpents; the eighth to Viṣṇu; the ninth to Aryaman; the tenth to Dhātṛ;
the eleventh to Indra; the twelfth to Varuṇa; the thirteenth to Yamī; and the right side belongs to Heaven and Earth and to the Viśvedevas.
The answer.

The shoulders belong to the Maruts; the first vertebrae to the Viśvedevas; the second to the Rudras; the third to the Ādityas; the tail to Vāyu; the two buttocks to Agni and Soma; the two *kruñc* birds to the two hips; Mitra and Varuṇa to the two thighs; Indra and Varuṇa to the two *alga* joints;
the stepping-place to the two *kuṣṭha* joints; and the *kapiñjala* birds to the *atsarā* tendons.
The breast-bone belongs to Indra; the belly to Aditi; the collar-bones to the quarters; the buttocks to Aditi; the heart and the pericardium to the clouds;
the atmosphere to the ligament; the sky to the abdominal cavity; the anthills to the liver; the mounds to the globes; the *cakravāka* birds to the kidneys;
heaven to the two kidneys; the flowing rivers to the veins; the mountains to the large intestines; the stones to the spleen; and the lakes to the two sides of the belly.
The ocean indeed with his belly, and Vaiśvānara with his ashes.
He placed the *vidhṛti* in the navel; ghee with the juice, water with the broth, dew with a drop, mist with heat, cold with fat,
hailstones with the *dūṣīkā*, spray with tears, the *rakṣases* with the flesh, the variegated stars with the limbs, and the constellations with the forms.
To Jumbaka, the earth with its skin, svāhā!
Pūṣan with the rectum; the Andhāhīs with the thick intestine; the serpents with the entrails; the Vihrutas with the intestines; the waters with the mouth;
the two stallions with the testicles; Śeṣas with the semen; the Cāṣa birds with the bile; the Pradaras with the anus; the Kūṣmas with the balls of flesh.
He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni—associated with the *gāyatrī* meter, the *trivṛt* stoma, the *rathantara* sāman, and the spring season;

a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra—associated with the *triṣṭubh* meter, the *pañcadaśa* stoma, the *bṛhat* sāman, and the summer season; a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas—associated with the *jagatī* meter, the *saptadaśa* stoma, the *vairūpa* sāman, and the rainy season; and [a cake] to Mitra and Varuṇa.
To Bṛhaspati, who is associated with the Anuṣṭubh meter, the twenty-one-fold Stoma, the Vairāja Sāman, the autumn season, and the curd-mixture (payasyā), [he offers] an oblation;

to Savitṛ, who is associated with the Paṅkti meter, the twenty-seven-fold Stoma, the Śākvara Sāman, the winter season, and the Atichandas meter, the thirty-three-fold Stoma, the Raivata Sāman, and the dewy season, [he offers] a cake on twelve potsherds;
to Anumati, [he offers] a caru-oblation; and to Vaiśvānara-Aditi, [he offers] a cake on twelve potsherds.
An offering of cooked rice (caru) for the wife of Viṣṇu, and a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla) for Ka.
[Page III,181] He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the Deliverer from Distress; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, the Deliverer from Distress;
curdled milk to Mitra and Varuṇa, the Deliverers from Cattle-stealing; milk to Vāyu and Savitṛ, the Deliverers from Cattle-stealing; and [milk] to the Aśvins.
To the Maruts, the sin-removers, parched grains; to the Viśvedevas, the sin-removers, a cake on seven potsherds;
to Anumati, a pap; to Vaiśvānara, a cake on twelve potsherds; to Heaven and Earth, the sin-removers, a cake on two potsherds.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the third book.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts not hold us in contempt when we proclaim the heroic deeds of the prize-winning steed, born of the gods, in this assembly.
When they lead before him the seized gift of the ram covered with wealth and cleansed by washing—
the bleating, multiform goat, moving forward well— may it go to the beloved path of Indra and Pūṣan.
This goat, possessing all forms, is led as the portion of Pūṣan, belonging to all the gods, before the vigorous horse.
When Tvaṣṭṛ impels this beloved sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) along with the steed for the sake of glorious renown.
When men lead the horse, fit for oblation and the path to the gods, three times around in due season—at that moment, Pūṣan’s first portion goes forth: the goat, announcing the sacrifice to the gods.
He has come near; my prayer has been offered well. With his smooth-backed form, he has approached the regions of the gods.
The wise seers rejoice after him; for the prosperity of the gods, we have made him our close kinsman.
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āvayāj, the Agnimindha, the Grāvagrābha, and the wise Śaṃstṛ—
with this well-prepared, well-offered sacrifice, fill the channels of the belly.
May the approval of those who hew the sacrificial post, those who carry the post, those who carve the top-ring for the horse's post, and those who prepare the cooking-vessel for the steed,
further us.
Whatever halter binds the prize-winning steed, whatever head-stall or cord belongs to him,
or whatever grass has been placed in his mouth as fodder— may all those things of yours be among the gods.
Whatever undigested contents from the belly escape, whatever odor of raw flesh there is—
let the immolators make that well-prepared, and let them cook the sacrifice until it is thoroughly cooked.
Whatever of the horse's raw flesh the fly has eaten, or whatever impurity remains on the sacrificial post or the axe,
whatever is on the hands of the slaughterer or on his nails— may all that of yours be with the gods.
Whatever from your body, as it is being cooked by fire after you have been impaled on the spit, drips down—let that not cling to the earth, nor to the grass; let it be offered to the longing gods.
May the approval of those who look upon the cooked horse, of those who say, "It is fragrant,
take it out," and of those who wait for a portion of the steed's meat, further us.
That which is the inspection of the cauldron for cooking meat,
the vessels for pouring the broth,
the warming covers for the pots, the hooks, the carving-boards— they all attend to and adorn the horse.
The garment they spread beneath the horse, the upper covering, the golden ornaments, the halter for the steed, and the foot-rope— these dear things they offer among the gods.
The stepping forth, the sitting down, the rolling over, and the tethering-rope of the steed;
that which he drank and that which he ate as fodder—may all these of yours be among the gods.
Let not the smoke-scented fire consume you, nor the glowing cauldron, smelling of fatness, overflow.
The gods accept that horse which has been offered, enjoyed, approved, and consecrated with the *vaṣaṭ* call.
He should cause it to resound: "Enkindled and anointing the interior of the hymns, O Agni, swelling with honeyed ghee."
O Jātavedas, bearing the sacrificial food, carry the oblation to the beloved assembly-place of the gods.
May Tanūnapāt, the steed, knowing the paths that lead to the gods, go unto the gods.
O Steed, may the quarters of space attend you; bestow sacrificial food upon the sacrificer through the gods.
You are worthy of praise and you are worthy of worship, O swift steed; you are fleet and you are fit for sacrifice, O courser.
May Agni Jātavedas, in harmony with the gods and the Vasus, carry you—the beloved bearer—forward.
The sacrificial grass is strewn, well-spread; may Aditi, in harmony with the gods, accepting it as it extends wide and broad upon the earth, making it pleasant, establish us in prosperity.

May these blessed goddesses, who possess all desirable things, leaning upon their wings and uplifted by their heights—lofty yet sounding like rushing waters, being adorned—be easy of access for us as they open. May the divine Doors be propitious to our departure.

Moving between you, O Mitra and Varuṇa, being in agreement regarding the mouth of the sacrifices— O Uṣas, you two who possess beautiful gold and beautiful forms, I seat you here in the womb of Cosmic Order (Ṛta).

First, O two gods of golden hue, sharing one chariot, beholding all beings, have you come hither; measuring out your impulses, as Hotṛ-priests, pointing out the light by means of the quarters of space.
May Bhāratī, together with the Ādityas, desire our sacrifice; may Sarasvatī, along with the Rudras, protect us.
Invoked as Iḷā, in harmony with the Vasus, may she, making our path pleasant, establish us in prosperity.
Tvaṣṭṛ begot the hero who loves the gods; from Tvaṣṭṛ was born the swift, fleet horse.
Tvaṣṭṛ has generated all these worlds; O Hotṛ, worship here the maker of much.
Let the horse, anointed by itself with clarified butter, go according to the seasons to the god;
let the Lord of the Forest, knowing the world of the gods, carry the offerings made savory by Agni.
Increasing through the ascetic fervor of Prajāpati, as soon as you were born, O Agni, you took possession of the sacrifice.
As the leader, go with the oblation consecrated by Svāhā; let the Sādhyas, the gods, eat the offering.
They harness the ruddy, flaming one as he moves; those who stand around him behold him. The luminous realms shine in the sky.
They yoke his two beloved bay horses to the chariot on either side—
red, bold, and carrying the hero.
Making a signal for the signalless, making a form for the formless, O men—
you were born together with the dawns.
Like a cloud, his appearance becomes formidable when the armored warrior goes into the lap of battle; conquer with an uninjured body, and may the greatness of that armor protect you.
With the bow may we win cattle, with the bow may we win the battle; with the bow may we conquer fierce conflicts.
May the bow cause the enemy's desire to depart; with the bow may we conquer all hostile armies.
As if about to speak, she approaches the ear, embracing her dear friend;
like a woman, this bowstring twangs upon the stretched bow, carrying us across in the assembly.
Moving together like two women toward a husband, may they bear [the arrow] in their lap like a mother her son;
acting in concert, may these two bow-ends pierce the enemies and strike down the foes.
He has many fathers; his son is many. Having entered the fray, he makes a whizzing sound. The quiver, bound upon the back, wins all encounters and all battles when it is set in motion.
Standing in the chariot, the skillful charioteer leads the horses forward wherever he desires;
marvel at the greatness of the reins—the tethers follow behind according to the mind.
Making loud noises, the stallions with strong hooves, striving for the prize along with the chariots,
trampling the enemies with their forefeet, destroy the foes without turning back.
O Lord of the Forest, may you be firm-limbed, our friend, a furtherer, and a possessor of noble heroes;
you are bound with thongs of cowhide, so be steadfast, and may your rider win all that is to be won.
From heaven and from earth, from the mid-air, from the lords of the forest, victorious might has come forth;
it is encompassed by the waters, enveloped in cattle—worship with an oblation the chariot, the thunderbolt of Indra.
The thunderbolt of Indra, the vanguard of the Maruts, the offspring of Mitra, and the navel of Varuṇa— O divine chariot, enjoying this our offering of oblations, accept these gifts.
The Fathers who sit at the sweet draught, bestowers of vitality, dwelling in hardship, powerful, profound,
possessing diverse armies, strong with arrows, never-failing, truly heroic, vast, and conquerors of hosts.
May the Brahmins and the Fathers worthy of Soma be present; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious to us.
May Pūṣan protect us from misfortune, O increasers of Truth; guard us, and let no one who speaks evil have power over us.
O straight-flying one, protect us; may our bodies be like stone.
May Soma speak in our favor, and may Aditi grant us shelter.
She wears the feathers of an eagle; her tooth is that of a deer; bound with cow-hides, she flies forth when discharged.
Where men run together and apart, there may the arrows grant us protection.
Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm, warding off the strike of the bowstring;
the hand-guard, knowing all the ways of action, as a man, shall protect the man from every side.
Let it strike their shoulders; let it strike their hindquarters. O horse-whip, you who are wise, urge the horses forward in the battles.
Cause the earth and the sky to resound; let the world scattered in many places take heed of you. O drum, in harmony with Indra and the gods, drive the enemies far away to the distance.
Shout forth strength and vigor; bestow power upon us. Thunder aloud, driving away misfortunes. Blow away all calamities from here, O drum; you are Indra’s fist—be firm!
O Indra, drive those away and bring these back; the drum resounds as a signal.
Let our men, winged with horses, come together; O Indra, let our chariot-warriors be victorious!
The kindling-stick of the quarters, lying prostrate, winning the light, may Mādhava protect us with his honeyed seed;
may the god Agni, invincible and undeceivable, guard this dominion and protect us.
May the Rathantara protect us with the Sāmans; may the Gāyatrī, the omniform among meters, protect us;
may the Trivṛt Stoma with its arrangement and the day, and the ocean and the wind, fulfill this power for us.

Fierce, the overcomer of the quarters, bestower of vitality, pure, resplendent on the bright day, dwelling in might—may he, through the lordships of Indra, nourish us from here; may he maintain this great dominion for us on every side.

May Indra protect this middle realm with the *bṛhat* sāman, which sustains dominion, which is grown strong and virile, which is the *triṣṭubh* meter, radiant with vigor, and possessed of fierce heroes— by means of the fifteenfold hymn (*pañcadaśastoma*) together with the wind and the ocean.
The eastern direction is glorious among directions, full of fame; all the gods are radiant with the rainy season among the days.
May I be capable regarding that which rests upon the Vairūpa Sāman; through the Jagatī meter, I cause him to enter into the people.
May this dominion be invincible, an unassailable force, powerful and victorious.
O All-Gods, through the seventeenfold [stoma], grant splendor to this fierce dominion that possesses the wind of the waters.
The upholder of the quarters has established this sovereign power; may the strength of the regions be friendly toward us.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, being mindful of us through the autumns and the days, grant great protection to our kingdom.
Upon the Vairāja Sāman my thought rests; through the Anuṣṭubh, heroic power and force have been gathered.
This sovereignty, accompanied by Mitra and yielding gentle rain—O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect it with your lordships.
The sovereign of the quarters, the powerful one with a thousand powers, may the winter season protect us with its fixed order.
May the wind, seeking aid, like the great Śakvarī verse, and the ghee-anointed quarter of the quarters, protect us.
May she who is rich in sound, easy to milk, full of milk, and dripping with ghee protect this sacrifice;
O Bṛhaspati, you are the guardian both in front and behind—yoke the voice for the journey to the world of Yama.

May the upward direction of the quarters, the nourisher of plants, together with the year and the day, and Savitṛ— may the wealthy Sāman, the Atichandas metre, and the metre that has no enemy be gracious and pleasant to us.
O Stoma, lord of the thirty-three, O Bhuvanasya Patnī, O Vivasvat, O Vāta, sing for us! May the gift be rich in clarified butter under the sovereignty of Savitṛ; may our portion be full of milk.
May Anumati favor our sacrifice among the gods today;
and may Agni, the bearer of oblations, be a source of joy to the donor.
Truly, may you grant us understanding; bestow welfare upon us. Impel us toward wisdom and skill; may he prolong our lives.
May Vaiśvānara come to us with his aid from afar,
Agni, through our hymn as his vehicle.
He was questioned in heaven.

May Dhruvā, the wife of Viṣṇu among the quarters, Īśānā of the non-terrible face, she who is the mental inspirer of strength, Bṛhaspati, Mātariśvan, and Vāyu— the winds that roar together— sing our praises.
The support of heaven, the sustainer of earth, mistress of this world, the consort of Viṣṇu— may she, the spacious,
the nourishing, the auspicious one, be gracious to us in the lap of Aditi.
By what means [will you come] to us?

Who today yokes to the pole of the Eternal Law (Ṛta) the vigorous, impetuous, and fiercely angry bulls—those who have arrows in their mouths, who pierce the heart, yet bring delight? Only he who fulfills their service shall live.
I meditate upon Agni, the first of the immortals, whom many kindle as the one belonging to the five peoples;
having entered into every clan, we implore him: may he deliver us from distress.
I praise Agni, whose alone is this breathing, whatever stirs, and whatever has been born or is being born; seeking protection, I call upon him repeatedly: may he deliver us from distress.
I meditate upon Indra, the first, the wise, the slayer of Vṛtra; his hymns of praise have come unto me.
May he who goes to the call of the donor who performs good deeds deliver us from distress.

He who leads the battle, who is masterful in combat, and who gathers together the three kinds of prosperity—I praise Indra; seeking protection, I call upon him repeatedly: may he deliver us from distress.
I think of you both, O Mitra and Varuṇa; take note of that, O you whose power is truth, as to whom you, being ill-disposed, drive away.
You two kings who travel on one chariot, O fierce ones, release us from sin.

That chariot of yours which, with straight reins and true laws, approaches the one who walks in falsehood, corrupting him—I praise Mitra and Varuṇa; seeking protection, I cry out to you: release us from sin!
We meditate upon the ordinances of Vāyu and Savitṛ, who maintain that which possesses a self and who protect it;
you two who have become the encompassers of the universe—release us from sin.
The most excellent ordinances of the two gods have been established for us;
I praise Vāyu and Savitṛ, and in my need I call upon them repeatedly: may you two release us from sin.
I have invoked for aid the two best of chariot-warriors among chariot-warriors, those most swift in their journey to glory with well-governed horses—
O Gods, you whose power among the gods is unsurpassed, deliver us from sin.

Those who came with the three-wheeled bridal vehicle of Sūryā, seeking a place of assembly—I praise the divine Aśvins; beseeching them, I call upon them repeatedly: may they release us from our transgression.
I call upon the Maruts; may they speak for us, and may all of them protect this entire speech.
I invoke the swift ones, easy to guide, for our aid; may they release us from sin.
Sharp is the weapon, firm and victorious; the divine host is triumphant in battles.
I praise the gods, the Maruts; seeking protection, I call upon them repeatedly: may they release us from sin.
I call upon the gods; may they speak for us, and may all of them protect this entire speech.
I invoke the swift ones, easy to control, for our aid; may they deliver us from sin.
That which here afflicts me, whether by human or divine means—I praise all the gods; being beset, I call upon them repeatedly: may they release us from sin.
May Anumati follow us today; may you, O Anumati, as Vaiśvānara, follow us with your protection.
O Agni, flaring up with your brilliance at birth, you filled the two worlds,
heaven and earth; O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, by your greatness, you released the god from the curse.
O wide Heaven and Earth, grant us room; as the two mistresses of the field, speak for us!
I praise Heaven and Earth; seeking protection, I call upon you repeatedly. Deliver us from distress.

Those two who have spread themselves out with immeasurable powers, who have become the two foundations of all treasures—I praise Heaven and Earth; seeking protection, I call upon them repeatedly: may you two deliver us from distress.
Whatever offense we have committed against you among men, O youngest one, through lack of thought or by our intentions—make us sinless before Aditi; loosen these sins from us on every side, O Agni.
Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of worship, released even the Gaurī cow that was stuck by the foot, so indeed release us from this distress; O Agni, crossing over [it], prolong our lifespan further.

[Page IV,1] The fierce god indeed burnt the trees; they pacified him with the *śamī* tree. That is why the *śamī* has its name *śamī*. When one drives away the calves with a branch of the *śamī*, it is for the sake of peace (*śānti*). It should be made leafy; this is the form of cattle, and thus he becomes possessed of cattle. When...

The *aparṇā* is the form of the staff; the staff is a thunderbolt (*vajra*). With the thunderbolt he should drive forward the cattle. In the third heaven Soma was; Gāyatrī, having become a hawk, carried him off. His feather was cut off, and from that the *parṇa* tree was born.
That is the reason for the name of the *parṇa*. Therefore all other trees have leaves (*parṇin*), but this one is called *parṇa*.

It is said: when he drives away the calves with a *parṇa* branch, he thereby secures that very Soma. The gods indeed deliberated upon the *brahman*; the *parṇa* heard it; therefore this tree is named Suśravas (the Good-hearer). He who knows thus does not become deaf. The *parṇa* is indeed the *brahman*. When he impels [the cows] with a *parṇa* branch, he impels them by means of the *brahman*. [He says: "For food (*iṣe*) thee!"—[it is] for food.

"He has placed vigor in the sacrifice and in the lord of the sacrifice" [with the words] "O Vāyus, you are! For Vāyu is the overseer of the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*), and cattle have the intermediate region as their deity;

thus he entrusts them to Vāyu for the sake of the intermediate region. Indeed, he releases them by saying "O Vāyus, you are!", for Vāyu belongs to the wild. "May the god Savitṛ impel you forward"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he [impels] them.
"He dedicates them with a rite for the most excellent one"—the sacrifice is indeed the most excellent; thus he dedicates them for the sake of the sacrifice.

"Swell up, O inviolable ones, for the gods!"—formerly these cows swelled for the sake of both calves and men, but now he makes them swell for the sake of the gods alone. "May no thief master you, may no malevolent person!"—thus he invokes a blessing.
"May you be many and firm under this lord of cattle"—thus he causes them to propagate.
O Brahman,
drink the pure waters at the excellent watering-place.
Thus, he indeed purifies them.
May the weapon of Rudra spare you.
Thus, they protect them from Rudra himself.
May Pūṣan be your protector from afar, Aditi your leader on the journey; may Indra be your overseer; return home unharmed!

Thus, these worlds are three; from these very worlds he causes them to return. [With the words] "Protect the cattle of the sacrificer," it is for the protection and non-injury of the sacrificer's cattle.
He embraces a westerly branch; therefore, domestic animals come from the forest to the village in the evening. Those who know thus become western-facing cattle for him.

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up with the deities. Prajāpati indeed knows the plants joint by joint; the horse belongs to Prajāpati;

when he mows the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with an animal’s hoof, it is for the non-injury of the plants. "Thou art cattle-haunting," [he says]; he bestows wealth upon the sacrificer. "Burnt away... [is said].
"Protection"—this is for the driving away of the *rakṣases*. "The prayer has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass"—the prayer is indeed knowledge;
thus he approaches it with knowledge. "Made by Manu, fashioned by *svadhā*"—for it was indeed made by Manu and fashioned by *svadhā*.
"The sages bring it from the front"—the Brahmins are the sages, the seers are the sages, the wise ones are the sages.
They are carried by that [speech].
(FN emended. Ed:
tayā vahante. cf. MS.1.1.2:1.7)
[Page IV,3] This sacrificial grass, pleasing to the gods, is here for them to sit upon.

Thus he makes it acceptable to the gods. With the words, "Thou art chosen by the gods," he cuts the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Whatever exists here, all that is chosen by the gods. Just as one performs a task after announcing it to a superior, even so he cuts the *barhis* after announcing it to the gods. As far as he points out, so much he cuts; and that which he does not cut entirely—that is a deficiency of the sacrifice.

Whatever is redundant in the sacrifice, by that he increases his rival; he points out one tuft [of grass] and cuts it all down so that there is no redundancy in the sacrifice. "The crest of Viṣṇu"—for Viṣṇu’s crest was indeed severed; it entered the earth. If he were not to release the first [tuft], he would meet with misfortune. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ..."
"With the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I cut the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he cuts it with the deities.
May I not be below, nor above; may I prosper in the middle.
Thus for the non-injury of the plants.
He will be the one who cuts you down, O worthy sir.

Thus, for as long as the Adhvaryu, being ignorant in this way, cuts the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), for so long is his own self diminished; but his own self is not diminished for one who knows thus. [With the words] "O grass, grow with a hundred shoots," he bestows abundance upon the plants.
[With the words] "May we grow with a thousand shoots," he invokes a blessing. [With the words] "Thou art the girdle of Aditi"—Aditi is indeed this earth; [he says this] regarding her.

Thus he makes this girdle, saying, "The binding of Indrāṇī. For Indrāṇī was the first among the deities to bind herself, desiring prosperity; she prospered. He who knows thus prospers through prosperity. He binds the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); the sacrificial grass is indeed offspring. This is for the continuity of offspring and so that offspring may not be lost; therefore, offspring are continuous by means of sinews. "May Pūṣan [tie] your knot..."

"Let him tie it," he says; for Pūṣan is indeed nourishment (puṣṭi), and thus he bestows nourishment upon the sacrificer. "May it not stand against thee," he says, for the sake of the sacrificer's non-injury.
sahasravalśāḥ:
FN emended. Ed: sahasravaliśā. cf. MS.1.1.2:2.1.
The waters have cleansed you, the Aśvins have cleansed you, and the seven seers have cleansed you;
I grasp the sacrificial grass, the banner of the dawns, with the rays of the sun.

Thus: "The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; let them heal this. With "I lift you up with the arms of Indra," he lifts it up with the very arms of Indra. With "I carry you on the head of Bṛhaspati"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman—he carries it with the Brahman.
With "The wide atmosphere," he [carries it] for the sake of the *samiṣṭi*. With "I set you down on the back of the Ādityas," [he sets it down] on this earth.
Or Aditi; he has thus seated it upon this very [earth].
You are the sacrificial grass that goes to the gods.

Thus he consecrates the nearby [fire]: "Much indeed of this [oblation] spills here and there when it is being brought here on the day before; he has delivered it unspilled to the deities for the sake of the sacrificer’s non-injury.

On the day before, they prepare the fuel and the sacrificial grass; having thus taken hold of the sacrifice, he observes the fast. Prajāpati created offspring; his two fire-pan lids (ukhās) became loose; he set them right with these two fire-pan lids. That these two fire-pan lids exist is for the sake of Prajāpati."

At this point he places [the strainer] back with the words, "Be purified for the divine rite"; thus he purifies these very things for the gods. With the words, "You are the filter of the Vasus," he makes this the portion of the Vasus for them. He covers it with a filter; he mixes the milk of both plants and animals. He restrains his speech for the support of the sacrifice, holding it firm.
"He sits as if supporting [the world]," for they indeed milk her; with the two formulas, "Thou art heaven" and "Thou art earth," he thus prepares her.
With the words, "Mātariśvan’s Gharma," [he does so]; Mātariśvan’s Gharma is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa), for the support of the intermediate space.
With the words, "What hast thou milked? She is all-life, she is all-being, she is all-action"—verily, yonder sky is all-life, and the intermediate space is all-being.

"O Viśvakarman, cause these worlds to be bestowed upon us in their proper order. He who knows this milks these worlds, already bestowed, in their proper order. He consecrates three [drops] with a *yajus* formula; for these worlds are three, and he thus places essence into these worlds.
Therefore, creatures subsist upon these worlds. "The drop is offered, the speck is offered."
Thus he consecrates it for the sake of freedom from disease.
This: [the text] has been emended by FN to *etal*; the edition reads *etaṃ*. [He says:
"Yield much sacrificial food for Indra and for the gods."

Thus he draws out [the milk] three times, for the gods are true to the triad. One should not milk into a wooden vessel; indeed, a wooden vessel contains fire, and one would thus sacrifice with a sacrificial offering that has already been used up. Regarding this, the Dātreyas say: "The sacrificial offering has the cake (puroḍāśa) as its mouth; there is no further course for the sacrificial offering beyond this, so it must simply be milked. A Śūdra should not milk, for he is produced from what is unreal; he would become unreal.
Whatever indeed passes through the strainer is the oblation; the Agnihotra alone a Śūdra should not milk, for they do not purify that.
Unite, O you who dwell in Truth, with your wave, most rich in sweetness;
mingling your milk with milk, O delightful ones, for the winning of wealth.

Thus he pours it back for the sake of cooking, for the gods desire cooked [food]. With the words, "I mix you, Indra’s portion, with Soma," he makes it indeed Soma. His drinking of Soma is continuous indeed, who, knowing thus, drinks the *sānnāyya* offering.
Thou art taken; for Viṣṇu, thee!

Thus, Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he makes this very thing ready for the sacrifice. With the words, "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation," he says to Viṣṇu exactly as one would say, "This is your portion; protect it. He says, "This is your oblation; protect it. One should not cover it with an earthen vessel, for the oblation would then belong to the Pitṛs as its deity; one should cover it with a wooden vessel, for a wooden vessel contains fire.

Agni alone protects the oblation; the water-filled vessel is the task [to be performed]. Water indeed is the slayer of Rākṣasas; the Rākṣasas do not cross over the waters, for the purpose of striking down the Rākṣasas.

Verily, he who sacrifices without having grasped faith—neither gods nor men place their trust in his sacrifice. He brings forward the waters; for the waters are indeed faith. Having grasped faith itself, he sacrifices. The sacrifice is the waters; having established the sacrifice, he proceeds. Water is the beloved abode of the gods; having brought forward the beloved abode of the gods, he proceeds. Water is truth; having grasped truth itself...
He offers water that slays the Rākṣasas for the purpose of striking down the Rākṣasas; water is a thunderbolt, and he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival for the purpose of felling him.

Water is faith; the gods and men place their faith in one who knows this and for whom one who knows this thus leads forward the waters with the words, "O divine waters, you who go before. He thereby leads forward the sacrifice itself. With the words, "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ... [he proceeds].

"At the impulse of the Aśvins, with their arms, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take it"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it by means of the deities. "The wide atmosphere"—this is for the sake of the *samiṣṭi* (the completed sacrifice). "The Rakṣas is burnt up"—this is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases.
"Thou art the yoke-pole; drive away the driver"—this fire is indeed named *dhurya*; if one were to pass over it without touching it, he would afflict the sacrificer with pain.
There are indeed two types of rivals for a man: him whom he hates and him who hates him; it is these two alone that he afflicts with pain.

"You are the best carrier of the gods, the most liberal, the most satisfying, the most beloved, the best invoker of the gods"—thus he makes this [sacrificial vessel] the best carrier for the gods, the most liberal, the most satisfying, the most beloved, and the best invoker of the gods. "You are the unswerving sacrificial receptacle;
stand firm, do not waver"—thus he makes it firm. "You are the stride of Viṣṇu; wide is the wind"—thus [he says]. What...
Whatever wind blows not toward it, he thereby makes that very thing Varuṇa’s own domain; by saying, "With the eye of Mitra I gaze upon you," he indeed makes them Mitra's own.
Take up vigor!
Thus he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer.
For your abundance.

Thus he causes them to prosper. "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, may they offer [the oblations] for your protection against the enemy; I pour out what is pleasing to Agni for you. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he pours them out with the deities. "May they offer [the oblations] for the five"—for there are indeed five seasons; it is thus the seasons he gratifies, and they [gratify] him.

"May they, being pleased, be intent upon your protection; let not the non-friends [approach]," he says for the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*. "To Agni, for you, those that are acceptable," he says;

thus he makes them acceptable to Agni, and also to whichever deity he offers them, to that deity he makes them acceptable. "This is for the gods, and this is for us," he says for the sake of separation. "May the dwellings be firm," he says; these worlds [are strengthened] once the oblation has been taken.
The gods trembled; they made them firm with this *yajus*. In that one knows this *yajus*, it is for the support of these worlds.

"I have released myself from Varuṇa’s noose"—thus he is indeed released from Varuṇa’s noose, for his own safety. "I have beheld the sun"—for he enters as it were into darkness and confinement; [by saying this] he beholds the very light, the Vaiśvānara light.
Thus, this sun is indeed the Vaiśvānara light.
I traverse the wide mid-air.
If he were to say, "Bring the rice," the Adhvaryu would become exhausted.
I traverse the wide mid-air.
Thus the Adhvaryu becomes unwearied; with the words, "I place you in the lap of Aditi," he places them upon this very earth, for this earth is indeed Aditi.
O Agni, protect the oblation.
Thus he places it in front; Agni himself protects the oblation.
You two are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu.

"Thus, Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he purifies them for the sake of the sacrifice itself. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ purify you," he purifies them as impelled by Savitṛ. With the words, "Pleasant to Agni for you," he makes them pleasant to Agni; furthermore, he makes them pleasant to whichever deity he sprinkles them for. With the words, "Whatever of yours was taken while impure, that do ye purify," he purifies them.
With the words, "Aditi’s skin art thou," he makes this very earth its skin, for Aditi is indeed this [earth]. With the words, "The Rakṣases are shaken off," he strikes away the Rakṣases.
He spreads out the black antelope skin with its neck toward the west; therefore, animals approach the sacrificial food facing westward.
With the words, "Thou art the separate stone, belonging to the tree," he makes it a pressing-stone; "Thou art the tongue of Agni."

"The release of speech"—for this is indeed the tongue of Agni, the release of speech; for when cattle eat the plants, they then release their speech. "For life"—he thereby bestows life upon the sacrificer. "Thou art the great pressing-stone, made of wood"—he thus makes it a pressing-stone. "Prepare the oblation for the gods"—he thus prepares it for the gods.
The Rakṣas is struck down.
Thus, for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasas.
O preparer of the oblation, come!

Thus, he invokes him who prepares the oblation for the gods; he invokes him thrice, for the gods are true to the three [truths]. For the speech of Manu Śraddhādeva, the sacrificer, which slays the Asuras, had entered the sacrificial implements. As many Asuras as heard her while she was speaking, on that day they simply ceased to exist. Knowing this, a Brahmin should perform sacrifice after settling in the midst of his rivals.
As many as of his rivals hear the sacrificial implements, from them he takes away brilliance, sensory power, and strength.

"Thou art a *kuṭaru* bird, honey-tongued; through thee may we conquer host after host"—with this, the sacrificer indeed conquers the rival host after host. "Utter prosperity, utter vigor, utter abundance of wealth"—this is the benediction.
Thus he prays.

"You are increased by the rains; may that which is increased by the rains accept you"—this is for the sake of stability. By means of the husks, the gods drove away the *rakṣases* from the cattle, and by means of the chaff, from the plants. When he says, "The *rakṣas* is blown away;
the enemy is blown away," by this much alone he drives away the *rakṣases* from the sacrifice.
May the god Savitṛ separate you.
Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed separates them.
O wise ones, discern with careful deliberation.

Thus he utters a blessing; he makes them well-winnowed, thereby making them pure and fit for sacrifice. He winnows them thrice, for the gods are threefold in truth. "Aditi’s skin art thou"—Aditi is indeed this earth; he thus makes it her skin.
"The Rakṣases are shaken off"—this is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. He spreads out the black antelope skin with its neck toward the west; therefore they [the cattle] go backward.
The animals approach the sacrifice. With the words, "Thou art the pillar of Aditi," he places a *śamyā* (wooden pin). These two [worlds] were indeed together;
they moved apart by the measure of a *śamyā*, by the measure of a *śamyā*. In that he places the *śamyā*, it is for the separation of these two. With the words, "Thou art grain;
satisfy the gods," it is by the power of this sacrificial formula (*yajus*) that as much as one deity desires, so much does another desire.
So long does his oblation spread—that is, it spreads—through progeny and cattle for him who knows thus.

With the words, "For out-breathing thee, for in-breathing thee, for diffused-breathing thee," he places out-breathing, in-breathing, and diffused-breathing within the sacrificer. With the words, "Touch [the butter] along its long extension for the sake of life," he bestows life upon him. With the words, "With the eye of Mitra, gaze," he [bestows] Mitra.
"Thus the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, shall take hold of you"— with these words, he takes hold of them while they are indeed impelled by Savitṛ.

"The Rakṣases are burnt away," he says, for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases. In that he turns the ember downward, he thereby bestows light upon this world; in that [he turns it] upward, he thereby bestows light upon the intermediate space. For him, that Āditya becomes light in yonder world;
moreover, for him, it becomes as if day in yonder world. All these worlds become luminous for him.
He who knows thus becomes so. He lays down three bricks facing together; for these worlds are three, and it is for the support of these worlds.
With the words, "O Agni, strike away the raw-eating Agni," he strikes away that raw-eating flesh-eater and lays down the sacrificial bricks on the place of sacrifice fit for the gods.
With the words, "Thou art firm; steady the earth," he indeed steadies the earth. With the words, "Thou art the supporter; steady the atmosphere," [he steadies the atmosphere].
He makes firm the intermediate space itself with [the words], "Thou art the support; make firm the sky"—thus he makes firm the sky itself. With [the words], "Thou art the law;
make firm all things"—thus he makes firm the quarters themselves. When Prajāpati came into being, he came into being as precisely this much:
first one skull of the head comes into being, then a second, then a third, then a fourth.

Then the fifth, then the sixth, then the seventh, then the eighth. In that he lays down eight, the sacrificer thereby prepares his own self; having been prepared, he follows after it in yonder world. In that he lays down eight, he thereby obtains the Gāyatrī metre; in that eleven, the Triṣṭubh; in that twelve, the Jagatī; and furthermore—
He lays down all of them measured according to the meters.
You are piled; you are piled around.

Thus he makes them possessed of sacrificial formulas: "By the fervor of the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Bhṛgus, and the Aṅgirases—be heated by the heat of the Gharma. By this, he heats them with the heat of these deities.
Those potsherds which the wise ones collect for the heat—
may Indra and Vāyu release them as well under the ordinance of Pūṣan.
Thus, they are yoked by the Yajus itself and unyoked by the Yajus.

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I mix you together"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he mixes it with the deities. He mixes it with a strainer; he prepares the oblation. "May the god Savitṛ purify you"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he purifies them. He pours water upon them; water is indeed immortality; verily he makes the oblation immortal.

"May the waters unite with the plants; may the plants unite with the sap. One set of these [verses] invigorates the others: the waters invigorate the plants, and the plants [invigorate] the waters. "The auspicious ones have united with the auspicious; the waters [have united] with the waters"—the waters are indeed the *revatī* (wealthy) ones, the plants are the *madhumatī* (honey-sweet) ones, and the cattle are the *jagatī* (moving) ones. He [unites] those waters, plants, and cattle for him.
Having mixed them together into one, he makes them full of sweetness.
You are the head of Makha.

Thus he says: "The sacrifice is indeed Makha; this head of his is being prepared. With the words, "May the subjects sit down for the sake of procreation," he creates a pair. With the words, "Thou art the Gharma, the life of all; O Gharma, rest upon the Gharma; spread wide, spread wide! May the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee," he causes him to expand.
Spread yourself out across the earth and the sky.

Thus he spreads these [fires]. This Gharma is indeed kindled every half-month; if it were not appeased, it would be liable to burn up the cattle of the sacrificer with its heat. In that he carries fire around it, he makes it a sacrificial animal for the sake of appeasement, so that there may be no burning.
He carries fire around it three times; for these worlds are three; verily, from these very worlds he pacifies it. [He prepares] the sacrificial cake.
Or when it was placed upon the fire, desiring to destroy the *rakṣases*, that fire named Nāka, the slayer of *rakṣases* in heaven, drove the *rakṣases* away from him.

When he says, "May the god Savitṛ bake thee upon the highest vault of the earth," it is for the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*. The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *veda* grass-bundle is its hair; just as there are skull-bones on the head, so is this [the case].

Just as the skull-cups are for the brain, so the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) must be well-cooked for the sake of its purity. If one were not to cover the cake, the brain would be exposed; because he covers it, therefore the brain is hidden. He causes the skin to adhere [to it]; therefore the brain is enclosed. He sprinkles it with ashes; therefore the bone is covered by flesh. He covers it with glowing embers; therefore the flesh is joined with the marrow.

Therefore, if one were to cut off the head with hair and, without taking hold of the skin, cover it with ashes, the Adhvaryu would become grey-haired; [but] he covers it with flames, and thus the Adhvaryu does not become grey-haired. Indeed, those gods could not find that upon which they might perform the cruel act of the sacrifice. Agni said, "I shall produce him for you."

In that [spot] where [the gods thought], "The cruel part of the sacrifice has been licked by the wolf," he struck it with a coal; from that, Ekata was born; from that, Dvita was born as the second; from that, Trita was born as the third. Because he brought them forth from the waters, that is the reason for the *āpeya* (water-born) nature of the *āpeyas*;
because he brought them forth from himself, that is the reason for the *ātmeiya* (self-born) nature of the *ātmeiyas*. He offers within the altar; thus he secures that very [essence].

He pours [the butter] over from above for the sake of cooking, for the gods are lovers of cooked food. Those gods went away while still being cleansed; they were cleansed when the sun had risen. He who falls asleep while the sun is rising is one "at whom the sun has risen" (*sūryābhyudita*). He who falls asleep while the sun is setting is one "at whom the sun has set" (*sūryābhinimrukta*). One who has black teeth is a "black-toothed man" (*śyāvadant*); one with deformed nails is a "deformed-nailed man" (*kunakhin*). One who eats before his elder is an "eater-before-the-elder" (*agredadhuṣ*); one who marries before his elder brother is a "younger brother who marries before the elder" (*parivitta*). He who is superseded by a younger brother is a "superseded one" (*parivitti*).
In the act of displacing [the fire], while displacing it, the sin of killing a hero, the slaying of a hero, does not exceed the sin of killing an embryo.
One should cover the sacrificial cake with ashes.
He should cover it with ashes.

With the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee," he takes it up; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up with the deities. With the words, "Thousand-edged, hundred-pointed," he whets this thunderbolt against his rival.

"About to strike, O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods, may I not harm thee"—[he says this] for the sake of not harming the roots of the plants. "Go to the fold, the cow-pen"—the fold and the cow-pen are indeed the *chandases*; verily, he makes the *chandases* his fold and cow-pen for him. "May Parjanya rain for thee"—verily, from Parjanya he wins rain. "Bind, O God... [he says].
"O Savitṛ, with a hundred nooses in the furthest distance," he says; for there are indeed two kinds of enemies to a man:

him whom he hates and him who hates him—it is these two he binds in the furthest distance. "Him who hates us and him whom we hate, bind him here; let him not escape from this"—thus he invokes a blessing. "May thy drop not leap up to heaven."
Thus, whatever is its essence is that drop; upon it living beings subsist; he offers it into this [earth] so that it may not spill.
Let not your splinter fly up to heaven.

Thus, there was an Asura named Araru; he lay having pressed down upon the earth. Indra perceived him and struck him away from the earth, saying, "Araru, the non-sacrificer to the gods! He sought to fly up to heaven;
[Indra said], "O Araru, do not fly to heaven!"
Thus he drives away from heaven [the enemy]; for he who, knowing this, carries the *stambayajus*, thereby excludes the rival from these worlds.
He carries it three times; for these worlds are three; thus he excludes the rival from these very worlds.
He carries it silently a fourth time; that world which is undefined and unlimited—from that he excludes the rival.

This earth belonged to the Asuras. The gods said, "Give us a share of this earth. They replied, "Then you yourselves must speak [among yourselves]. Thereupon, the Vasus won the eastern quarter, the Rudras the southern, the Ādityas the western, and the Maruts the northern. Then indeed the gods seized this [earth] from the Asuras; thus the gods drove the Asuras away from these [quarters].

They apportioned [the world] from the worlds; then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. In that he thus encloses the altar with these deities, the sacrificer thereby appropriates this [earth] from his rival and excludes the rival from it. He prospers himself, and his rival is defeated. Indeed, the pure and the impure separated themselves from the earth; [the pure went] toward the east.
The pure (medhya) part moved toward the north, while the impure (amedhya) moved toward the south. One should make the sacrificial altar (vedi) sloping toward the east and the north;

thus one makes these [parts] pure and fit for sacrifice. Furthermore, whatever cruelty they committed while digging it up, that they have now made non-cruel and pacified. Moreover, this is for the sake of distinguishing between the pure and the impure; the two arms [of the altar] extend toward the east.

He leads [the earth] to the Āhavanīya fire; by that he encloses it. The two buttocks face westward; he encloses the Gārhapatya fire. Indeed, the Rakṣases suck up the root. If he were to cut with his fingernail, he would become one with deformed nails. He cuts with the wooden sword (sphya); the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt;
with the thunderbolt itself he slays the Rakṣases.

He who, not knowing the connection of the offering-spoons (*srucaḥ*), answers when called "O Adhvaryu," cuts himself off from the deities; he becomes destitute of cattle. But he who, knowing the connection of the offering-spoons, answers when called "O Adhvaryu," does not cut himself off from the deities;
he becomes possessed of cattle. The *juhū* is the sky, the *upabhṛt* is the intermediate space, the *dhruvā* is the earth, and the quarters are the vessels for the clarified butter.
This Āditya is the dipping-spoon; that which is he...
Oṃ, cause [them] to hear!
Thus he says; with this, he joins the *juhū* ladle.
So be it; let there be hearing!
Thus [is the formula] for the *upabhṛt* ladle.
"Perform the sacrifice!"—thus [he says] regarding the *dhruvā* ladle.
We worship those whom we should sacrifice to.
Thus, with the *vaṣaṭ* call, he pours butter from the *ājyadhānī* into the *sruva*, and from the *juhu* into the *dhruvā*; from the *dhruvā* into the *juhu*.

For that [person] gives this [world] to him, and this [world] gives that [world] to him; thus food is handed over continuously and without interruption for him in both this world and that world. And the fame of one who knows thus reaches the people of his former generation.

Ghee and honey: Prajāpati was [the source]. From where there was honey, from that he created offspring; therefore, there is no offspring born from honey. Therefore, they do not perform the ritual with honey, for that is exhausted. They perform it with clarified butter (*ājya*), for this ghee belongs to Prajāpati and is unexhausted. Unexhausted is Prajāpati among the gods; he places it over the *gārhapatya* fire.
The wife looks [at the butter]; this is indeed the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice; he causes her to take hold of the sacrifice.

Moreover, whatever the wife does at the sacrifice, that constitutes a union for the sake of procreation. That which the wife looks upon is impure and unfit for sacrifice; therefore, he places it over the Āhavanīya fire; he thus purifies it and makes it pure and fit for sacrifice.

He places the path of the wooden sword; it is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ purify thee," he purifies this very thing as impelled by Savitṛ. "Thou art the oblation for Vaiśvānara"—these are twelve utterances (*vyāhṛti*). Twelve months are a year;
by means of the year, the sacrificer appropriates the splendor, sensory power, and vigor of his rival. On both sides [of the offering] is that which belongs to Vaiśvānara.
It becomes both ways; for his rival is born deprived of splendor and deprived of virility, and he indeed becomes more feeble.

The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict; Indra perceived this opening and by means of it overcame the Asuras. He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice, overcomes his rival through the sacrifice.

They sprinkle the other sacrificial offerings with clarified butter (*ājya*). Regarding this, the exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) ask: "With what is the *ājya* sprinkled? Indeed, the *ājya* is sprinkled with truth; when he says, "I sprinkle thee with truth," sight is indeed truth. By closing his eyes while reciting this formula, the sacrificer does not bestow sight [upon himself]. The *ājya* is indeed the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is Viṣṇu.
Vishnu strode across this [universe]; in three places he planted his step; that which was gathered together in his footstep-dust.

Thus, when he places [the oblation] on the fire for cooking rice, then on the Gārhapatya, and then on the Āhavanīya, it is indeed in this way that Viṣṇu strides his three steps. With the words, "The Rakṣases are burnt up," he strikes away the Rakṣases. He cleanses the offering-spoons; he thus purifies them, making them pure and fit for sacrifice.

"Unsharpened, destroyers of rivals. For these [ladles] are indeed unsharpened destroyers of rivals. He cleanses the *sruva* first; he thereby sharpens the male among them at the beginning, then the *juhū*, then the *upabhṛt*, and then the *dhruvā*. This *sruva* is the Āditya, the *juhū* is the sky, and the *upabhṛt* is the intermediate space.

He thus sweeps these worlds firmly, in their proper order; he delivers himself from these worlds for the sake of non-injury. He first sweeps the *juhū* spoon; the *juhū* is indeed the self—he thus approaches his own self. Then he sweeps the *upabhṛt*;
the *upabhṛt* is offspring—he thus approaches offspring, for offspring are, as it were, beyond the self. Then he sweeps the *dhruvā*; the *dhruvā* is cattle—he thus approaches cattle.
For if he were to wipe them while they are lying on their backs, it would be as if one were approaching another’s offspring; the seed would be unstable.
If he were to wipe them while they are facing downward, the seed would be unstable. He wipes them crosswise;

for seed is poured out crosswise, and thus the seed becomes stable. If he were to wipe along the front of the mouth and the handle, [it would be] for the sake of the Rakṣases and the malevolent beings.

He places the base of the *samidh* downward; with the front part he wipes the mouth [of the spoon], and with the rear part he wipes the handle. Thus he places the base of the *samidh* against the Rākṣasas and the *Abhūs*.

Internally he wipes the *juhū* eastward, externally westward; externally the *upabhṛt* eastward, internally westward. Having gathered them together from all sides, he wipes the *dhruvā*; thus he restores his vital breaths in their proper order.
The *juhū* ladle has the sacrificer as its deity, while the *upabhṛt* has the rival as its deity. Taking four portions, he takes more clarified butter in the *juhū*;
taking eight portions, he takes less in the *upabhṛt*. Thus he has made his rival a subordinate attendant.
Having gathered himself, he should set down many [prokṣaṇī-ladles]; for as many *prokṣaṇī*-ladles as he sets down, so many waters are there for him in yonder world; therefore—

Having approached many [places], the sacrificial essence (medhya) departed from Agni; becoming black, it entered the trees. When he says, "Thou art black, dwelling in the lair; become ghee for Agni," he thereby secures that very sacrificial essence. "Thou art the altar;

I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the sacrificial grass (barhis)"—the sacrificial grass is indeed offspring, and the altar is the earth; thus he makes the offspring go to their own place upon this earth.
Because he sprinkles below after having sprinkled above, therefore, when it rains from above, plants grow from below.

With the words, "Support the earth with strength," he placed strength in this [earth]; therefore, living beings subsist upon this [earth]. With the words, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft," he places the *prastara* grass-bundle at the front.

He takes this [soma] from the principal [part]; by that he makes it "head-like" (*śīrṣaṇya*). He should take as much as he can grasp with his hand; the sacrificer then becomes free from hunger. He should not wipe upwards, for if he were to wipe upwards, he would wipe away whatever wealth and what is to be known belongs to him. He should not wipe downwards, for if he were to wipe downwards, he would drive away whatever was coming to him. He should not shake it, lest he lose his offspring and cattle.
Whatever might shake off, he should grasp; just as one adds to what has been eaten, even so he spreads the cord (śulba) to the south.
Therefore, [he says] "O wide-expanding, wool-soft one," for he indeed spreads it from the south.
"A good seat for the gods"—thereby he makes it a good seat for the gods. Holding the prastara-bunch, he lays down the enclosing-sticks (paridhi).
The sacrificer himself thus clothes his own self for the sake of non-injury. He does not place [the enclosing sticks] in front;

for as that sun rises, it drives away the Rakṣases; indeed, as it rises, that sun drives away the Rakṣases from him. He places two upright fuel-sticks; by means of them he drives away the Rakṣases from above him. He places two for the sake of pairing. They are separated.
With "sthā," he indeed makes them two separating-spacers.
I set you down in the lap of Aditi.

Thus this Aditi; in her he has seated him. "Thou art the seat of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas"—for these deities indeed first won this [earth]; for them he makes this seat. "Thou art the sky by birth;
Juhū by name, the dear one of the gods; by thy dear name, sit in the firm seat"—this indeed is their dear name.

"Rich in ghee, he indeed secures that very thing. "O Viṣṇu, protect these; protect the sacrifice; protect the lord of the sacrifice; protect me, the leader of the sacrifice"—thus he says to Viṣṇu, as if saying, "This is your portion; guard it. "These are the clarified butter; guard them"—thus he says. The altar (vedi) departed from the gods; the gods found it by means of the wooden sword (veda); that is why the wooden sword is called *veda*. It was a woman.

The altar is male and the Veda is female; when he sweeps the altar with the Veda, it is for the sake of pairing. He goes from the Āhavanīya fire, spreading [the grass] continuously, for the continuity of the sacrifice. He sacrifices to him continuously during the latter half-month. This Upaveṣa is indeed the distributor of the trees; his dwellings become prosperous for one who knows thus. He strikes it down from the front toward the west.

Therefore, those who have settled in their dwellings turn westward and take up the fire-wood from the largest [piece]; thus the dwellings do not overstep him. Indeed, everything is prepared for the sacrifice; the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) is a snake, and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) is an anthill. In that he throws the *upaveṣa* onto the rubbish-heap, therefore the anthill is the dwelling-place of snakes.
As it has been said: "yathāhaiṣa. (The editor's reading was *yathāhaiṣa*; the emendation is *yathāhaiṣa*.)
You are the world.
Thus he prays for prosperity.
Spread forth!

Thus he makes this very thing manifest: "Standing here, Indra performed heroic deeds, having taken hold with the deities"; for from there indeed, standing here, Indra performed heroic deeds, having taken hold with the deities.

O Juhū, come; Agni calls you; we two shall sacrifice to the gods for the sake of the worship of the gods. O Upabhṛt, come; the god Savitṛ calls you; we two shall sacrifice to the gods for the sake of the worship of the gods.

Thus, these [steps] are not for one who lacks knowledge, for he would step upon the nooses of Varuṇa as if they were something to be tasted; rather, with these deities he takes them up so that there may be no stepping upon the nooses of Varuṇa. With the words, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he strides across, so that there may be no stumbling of the sacrifice.

With the words, "The sacrifice of the Lord of Sacrifice is upright, reaching heaven, unshaken," he pours the *āghāra* oblation straight upward, so that the sacrifice may not be overturned. It belongs to Indra and Vāyu.
"Having a horse" means he has performed a sacrifice for Indra; thus, by that, he obtains power.
O Vasumata, may I attend upon your shadow.
Thus, Agni is indeed possessed of wealth; he stands in the shadow of Agni itself. He should pour the *āghāra* oblation straight upward.
The *āghāra* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the sacrificer attains a full lifespan. If he should hate someone, having poured the *āghāra* for him, he should cut it short;
he cuts off that person's vital breath, and that person dies quickly. The *āghāra* is the head of the sacrifice, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) is its body. What...
Having poured the Āghāra libation, if he were to anoint with the Upabhṛt ladle, he would cut off the head of the sacrifice; therefore, he anoints with the Ājyadhānī.
The oblation is anointed with fire; the clarified butter is anointed with the oblation.

Thus he replaces the head of the sacrifice upon himself; moreover, he restores the mind to the sacrifice. "The offspring, possessing breasts, live upon the breast"—thus say the exponents of sacred knowledge: "What [is there] for those who are breastless? "Licking with their tongues, let them go forth as birds" (VS 29.13)—it is indeed upon this that they subsist. "Becoming a dappled cow, go to the Maruts"—for the Maruts indeed rule over rain.
They pour down rain for him; thus he prays, "May you favor us with rain," and so he wins rain from the Maruts themselves.

"O Agni, you are the protector of the eye; protect my eye"—thus he protects his eye. "O Agni, you are the protector of the ear; protect my ear"—thus he protects his ear. "O Agni, you are the protector of the body; protect my body"—thus he protects his body. "O Agni, that which is mine... [he says].
"What is deficient, that do thou fill for me"—thus he invokes a blessing.
O divine Agni, that enclosing-stick which you placed around yourself when you were being carried away by the Paṇis—
that very one I bring back to you according to your pleasure, so that it may not cause you to be forgotten by them.

Thus they are yoked by means of the *yajus* formula and unyoked by means of the *yajus* formula. [With the words] "You are portions of the remnants, great ones," he throws the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire and makes an offering over them. These are indeed the fires; he gratifies them and pacifies them with their allotted portion. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "He alone should be the *adhvaryu* who, from wherever he initiates the sacrifice, establishes it. O Gods!

"Knowing the way, having found the way, go the way, O Lord of the Mind! Place this well-prepared sacrifice in heaven among the gods, Svāhā!"—it is from this [formula] that the Adhvaryu impels the sacrifice; thus he establishes it.
Prajāpati alone existed. He desired, "May I be many; may I procreate. He meditated upon himself with his mind and became pregnant.

As he was being born from the womb, he became exhausted; being exhausted, he turned black and dark-brown. Therefore, one who is exhausted becomes as if black and dark-brown. His vital breath (*asu*) alone remained alive; by means of that vital breath, he created the Asuras. That...

The "asura-nature" of the Asuras is that [quality]. He who knows that asura-nature of the Asuras becomes possessed of vital breath (*asu*); the *asura* does not abandon him. Having created the Asuras, he thought of himself as a father; with that [thought], he created the Pitṛs. That is the "pitṛ-nature" of the Pitṛs.
He who knows that pitṛ-nature of the Pitṛs becomes like a father among his equals; his ancestors come to his call.
For him who created the ancestors, it became day; with that, he created the gods. That is the godhead of the gods.

He who knows that godhead of the gods, for him it becomes day among the gods; the gods come to his invocation of the gods. Having created the gods, he was, as it were, dissatisfied; with that, he created human beings. That is the humanity of human beings. He who—

The wise one indeed knows that which is the human nature of men; his mind does not desert him, nor does he abandon his mind. Even when he speaks excessively or acts beyond bounds, men stand by him for the sake of the human being. Then, that which remained as the womb became the cow.
This is indeed its name, "the Womb" (*yoni*); this is its manifest name, though they also say it is its secret name. He [uttered] a thousand...

He who knows this obtains cattle. On her, indeed, they beheld milk; the gods milked her with a golden vessel; he who knows this milks immortality. Then the ancestors milked her with a silver vessel; he who knows this milks *svadhā*. Then humans milked her with a wooden vessel; he who knows this milks food, food indeed. He who knows this milks food, food indeed.
The Vedas and the Asuras milked the Surā in a leaking vessel of iron; they milked out the Surā. The rival of him who knows this leaks away.
Therefore, one should neither wash one's hands with what is leaking nor drink from it. These indeed are its milkings;
he who knows this enjoys all its milkings and all desires. There are indeed four worlds: the gods, the ancestors, humans, and...
In all these [worlds], water indeed becomes like a cloud for those who know thus; the Asuras desired it, thinking, "May it be in me!
May it be in me! and so the gods [placed] it in the object of desire (kāmye).
Thus he calls out, and she indeed desires them; for both gods and men desire him who knows this, and they become well-disposed toward him in his office as officiating priest.

"Manuṣe" means "in what is to be heard. Thus, they are human beings. Indeed, she (Speech) does not fail those who listen; for both gods and humans listen to him who knows this. The fame of one who has come from a previous generation reaches him. Both gods and humans indeed listen to him who knows this. And she (Speech) attends upon those who do not listen. Thus, both gods and humans attend upon him who knows this; the fame of one who has come from a previous generation reaches him. He who knows this—his fame comes from his former lineage.
"O Ilānda!"—thus [he says]. From them the Pitṛs stood away; cattle stand upon him who knows thus.
Now, just as the Asuras called out, from them [the cattle] were terrified. Whomever he hates, he should call out to him in that manner within the cow-pen;
the cattle are terrified of him. With these very [verses] he should offer oblations.
One desiring cattle should [anoint] the head of a cow with *saṃśṛṅgī* plants that have the same names as the cows.
They tremble: svāhā to Kāmyā, svāhā to Śravyā, svāhā to Helāndā.
Thus, this is indeed named the *goṣṭha* (the cow-pen); it is his own cow-pen, and in it the sacrificer appropriates the cattle of his rival.
By these [verses] they indeed appropriated them; by those very ones he appropriates them. It has horns, for the sake of encompassing cattle.
Verily, he who knows the distribution of the eye becomes possessed of sight; the eye does not desert him when [he recites] during the day.

When we see by means of the eye of the gods, we see with that; for yonder sun is indeed the eye of the gods. He who knows this, seeing among the gods, performs his rites among the gods and recognizes the path leading to the gods. When we see by means of the eye of the fathers in the moonlight, we see with that; for the moon is indeed the eye of the fathers. Verily, he does not [perish] in yonder world.

The eye leaves him who knows thus; he knows the path leading to the fathers. That which we see in the darkness, we see with the eye of men; this indeed is our own eye. Verily, the eye does not leave him in this world who knows thus; he reaches a full lifespan. That which we see at the edge of the fire, that is with the eye of the Asuras.
"Behold, he indeed shines aloft; he will roar. While he is shining, one should carry away wealth from the house of the rival;

thus one carries away his very prosperity. One should remain awake until the rising of the sun. If one should fall into affliction through sleep, that is why one must stay awake; for by staying awake, one follows after wealth and prosperity."
He will not come to harm; [the editor notes:
*ni ca riṣyati* is the correction and conjecture for the entire work.]
From the *Svapna*:

"He who knows the cow Iḍā—for him indeed all the quarters become cows, and all people desire to give to him—he discovered her as the arrow-shaft, the thunderbolt, and the burner of enemies; for him all the quarters became cows, and all..."
All people were desirous of giving; therefore, he was dealt with by all the peoples.

As he went along, all the quarters became milch-cows for him, and all the peoples were desirous of giving. He who knows thus—for him all the quarters become milch-cows, and all the peoples are desirous of giving. Of that [Vāk], this [earth] indeed is one quarter, and the intermediate space is [the second].

One quarter is heaven, one quarter is the earth, and one quarter, they say, is agriculture. Therefore, it stands firm for you at one time, but not for you at another; when there is good grain, then it stands firm, and when there is no grain, then it does not stand firm.
Indeed, he who knows this has grain, and his grain is never lost. Of her—

Yonder sky is indeed its back, the intermediate space its body, this earth its belly, the quarters its sides, the two oceans its flanks, the sun its head, fire its mouth, and the wind its breath. The Gāyatrī is its tether; he who knows this attains a full lifespan. The high altar is its udder, the lower altar its teat, and the Pavamāna is the calf. Verily, he who knows this causes this [cow] to low, and she milks these worlds when they have been bestowed.

The *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* are two teats, and the *Vāmadevya* and *Yajñāyajñiya* are two others. By means of the *Rathantara*, he milked plants for the gods; by the *Bṛhat*, cattle; by the *Vāmadevya*, water; and by the *Yajñāyajñiya*, the sacrifice. He who knows this milks plants for himself by means of the *Rathantara*; cattle by the *Bṛhat*; water by the *Vāmadevya*; and the sacrifice by the *Yajñāyajñiya*. This [world] is indeed the *Iḍā*.
He obtains a thousand cattle; he who knows thus obtains a thousand cattle.

Where there is ground sloping toward the east with its roots intact, at the rising of the sun, having washed his hands, he should pour out a water-pot upon a clump of Darbha grass, saying: "Make me turn [toward my desires] according to each desire."

Thus, by means of desire itself, he brings about the fulfillment of the desire for him; whatever desire he may have, that desire comes to him immediately. For he who knows desire directly—whatever desire he may have—that desire indeed comes to him at once. Now, our desire lies in cattle, the desire of cattle lies in plants, and the desire of plants lies in the waters. He has thus distributed the plants according to desire; they fulfill the desire for him, whatever desire he may have.

This very skin of hers moves about released as water; it is hairy because she is hairy. Therefore, she goes puffing and blowing, for fire is her mouth and the wind is her breath. Wherever she should come into contact with cattle, there one should speak.
"You are praised, O auspicious ones! [eṣā] FN Ed: erṣā. Praśastāḥ stha kalyāṇyaḥ.
This [earth] indeed makes this [heaven] its counterpart; cattle become miserable for him from whom they depart, provided he knows thus.

The gods and the Asuras were in conflict. Aditi was among the gods, and Kustā was among the Asuras. Those gods reflected, "If we shall conquer, we will strike off the head of Kustā. "If we shall conquer," the Asuras reflected, "we will [strike off the heads] of the Ādityas."

Thinking, "I shall strike the veins," the gods struck her after they had conquered. Indeed, wherever there is conquest and wherever there is victory, it is in that person's house that this [cow] is struck. This [cow] is indeed hunger; thus, one strikes hunger. Therefore, he who, knowing this, strikes a cow on the Ekāṣṭakā day, strikes hunger for the sake of the year. In the beginning, Prajāpati was alone; he desired, "May I become many."

"Let me procreate," he thought; he brooded upon himself, and he created the mind (*manas*). That mind was single; it brooded upon itself, and it created speech (*vāc*). That speech was single; it brooded upon itself, and it created the Virāj. That Virāj was single;
it brooded upon itself, and it created the cow (*go*). That cow was single; it brooded upon itself, and it created the ewe (*eḍā*). That ewe was single.
She desired a self and created these enjoyments by which men here enjoy this world; these indeed are her enjoyments.

He who knows this enjoys with all enjoyments and with all desires through every one of her enjoyments. The Cow is indeed speech, the Cow is the Virāj, the Cow is Iḍā, the Cow is truly the Cow; the Cow is all this. Verily, all these [powers] resort to him who knows thus.
Verily, when he sought his own self, it became *iḍā*; that is the reason for the name of *iḍā*. He who knows that reason for the name of *iḍā* truly seeks his own self for prosperity.
She who is Rohiṇī is Aruṇā; she is Gaurī; she is Babhru.
Indra raised up that wealth, the name and form of cattle.

He who knows this finds wealth; wealth does not elude him. She who has a white back—she is the gladdening one, she is the dark-spotted one, she is the dappled one, she is the white-armed one, she is the pure-tailed one.
Bṛhaspati raised that up as the form of cattle, named Iḍā.

Many indeed are the *iḍā* offerings that accrue to him who knows thus: that which is spotted, that which is tawny, that which is dappled, that which is speckled, that which is brindled, and that which is white.
The Maruts then raised up that light, the name and form of cattle.
He becomes luminous who knows thus; whichever is well-formed, let him sacrifice that one—whether it be white, or ruddy, or black.
Prajāpati extracted that from the cattle: life-force as their name and form.

He who knows thus becomes long-lived: there are four first [verses], four last, and twice six in the middle; those are twenty, and the Virāj consists of ten syllables. Cattle are of the nature of the Virāj; verily he wins cattle. Utter the *hiṃ* for the Vasvī; chant the *prastāva* for her; [do this] for my acquisition of her.
Thus one should speak before the Bahiṣpavamāna chant.
Sing the *hiṃ* for Iḍā; chant the *prastāva* for her, so that she may be secured for me.
Thus one should say before the offerings of clarified butter.
Sing the *hiṃkāra* for Jyotis; chant the *prastāva* for it, for my attainment of it.
Thus one should recite before the midday *pavamāna* chant.
Sing the *hiṃ* for life; chant the *prastāva* for that; [do so] for my attainment of it.
Thus one should recite before the Ārbhava Pavamāna.
