The sacrifice is indeed the abode of cattle; thus, in his own abode, the sacrificer appropriates the cattle of his rival, and the cattle do not depart from him.

Come as the more excellent one; come as the better one; come as the more abundant one; come as thought; come as boldness; come as play; come as joy. You are intelligence, you are mind, you are wisdom; you are the good, the delight, and the benevolent one.
O noble one, let all beings breathe after you; you, breathe after all beings. You are the abundance of life; you are the sacrifice; you are the rain of uniform form—come!
Crawl along after these two; approach these two auspicious draft-oxen; as it were, smooth down their heads.
May she be our swift victor, our dear one, our kind bringer of gifts, our dear friend, our bountiful giver; come as the beloved, come hither, come as Aditi!
Invoked, may I share in your invocation. Come with abundance of wealth! O goddesses, goddesses, turn toward me!
O pleasant one, sprinkle me with pleasant ghee.
The bold Brahman took that which was to be seized;
from the ocean he drew it forth for you with the sacrificial ladle.
At the beginning of the day, the bull of the sage stands with his ten horns pointing toward every direction.

"Come, O superior one!"—the Brahman is indeed the superior; he thus calls out to the Brahman. "Come, O better one!"—the Kṣatra is indeed the better; he thus calls out to the Kṣatra. "Come, O more abundant one!"—the Viś is indeed the more abundant;
he thus calls out to the Viś. "Come, O conscious one!"—the mind is indeed consciousness; he thus calls out to the mind. "Come, O courageous one!"—this is Speech.
"O bold one, come hither!"—with these words he indeed challenges speech. "O *iḍā*, come hither!"—the *iḍā* is cattle; he thus challenges cattle.

"O *sūnṛtā*, come hither!"—*sūnṛtā* is food; he thus challenges food. These, indeed, are the seven divine cows (*devagavyas*). Vitahotra Vaida knew them; with them he challenged away the cattle of the Kurus from Kunti. Those [cattle] were the Kurus'.
They sought them among the Brahmins; they found them as the horse-sacrifice fees belonging to Kumāravatī. He said, "Do not be negligent!

With these I shall challenge those [horses], and with the others the other ones. For indeed, one who has been purchased does not know what their beloved abodes are. When the battle was joined, he saw a shelter and thought, "With these very ones I shall challenge those, and with the others the other ones."
Whichever side these [cups] are indeed called across to, toward that side the cattle move; where the cattle are, there are the gods;
where the gods are, there is Indra. Whichever side these [cups] move toward, those win; he wins the battle.
Once created, she indeed held herself in contempt above both gods and men. The gods covered her over with the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
they reached her when they [reached] the *iḍā*. Having reached her, they think they are carrying her away when they invoke the *iḍā*.
When he should invoke silently, then he should recite these seven [verses]; when aloud, then the latter seven, verse by verse.

He approaches each of their colors; indeed, he approaches him unopposed, who knows thus. Wherever he might approach plants with their roots or cattle, there he should recite these very seven [verses]. He approaches each of their colors; indeed, he approaches him unopposed, who knows thus. One should cause seven [persons] to sacrifice with the *sthāvīrya* [offering].

If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra should be very prosperous, one should cause a bull among his cattle—a young steer—to be driven away while chanting: "O you for whom there are seven elders as the last and most excellent, come, O more wealthy one! Come, O better one! This indeed is the challenge he issues to him. One should then drive away a bull-calf from the herd of that man who is a Vaiśya or a Śūdra and is very prosperous.
samūlā: FN emended. Ed: sa mūlā sthāvīryeṇa:
FN Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.
Caramā: FN Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.
Apagamayeta: FN emended. Ed:
He should drive them away. Cf. MānŚS 9.5.5.21:
"You are the Ilānds."
Thus, for cattle are indeed the *ilāndas*, and the lunar mansion of Pūṣan is nourishing.
Thus, this indeed moves among the common people; it is the constellation of Pūṣan, which is nourishing. One should cause that very one to suckle [the child] and ward off that [other one].
Grant me long life; grant me luster; grant me wealth; grant me nourishment.
Thus he takes away his wealth and prosperity; having released him from there, one should then call out to him from here, saying, "Come to what is more prosperous!

Come to what is better! It is thus that he calls him beyond her [the cow]. Nothing whatsoever remains for him. One should perform the sacrifice for one who desires a village with the two Sarasvatī verses.
Sarasvat is indeed the Year; by means of the Year itself, he causes the village to move toward him. "Come to what is more prosperous! he says.
"Come, O more excellent one!"—with these words he thus challenges her. One desiring cattle should perform this sacrifice to Sarasvatī with two *ṛc* verses. Sarasvat is indeed the Year;

by means of the Year itself, he causes cattle to come forth for him. "Come, O more wealthy one! Come, O more excellent one!"—with these words he thus challenges her. When all [the cows] have been milked, one desiring cattle should cook four *śarāva* measures of rice for the Brahmins.

In that there is a four-platter [offering], he thereby wins cattle from the very quarters; in that it is given to the Brahmins, he thereby wins the Brahman; it should not be given in a fragmented manner, for he is like one desiring cattle. Either a garment or gold should be given; for him who has sacrificed, his cattle become more numerous.

Prajāpati indeed did not speak; he gathered merit within himself alone and did not discharge his merit from himself. This is that sacrificial formula (yajus) which one should recite, and one should not speak otherwise.
Merit is praiseworthy.

Thus he should say; he bestows merit upon himself alone and does not disparage his own merit. Whatever he gives to one who is unworthy, his cattle follow after that gift and depart from him. If he should think, "I have given to one who is unworthy," he should recite this very *yajus*: "The bold Brahman has not deceived me. By this, he fills that very thing and causes it to swell, like the ocean.
Verily, for one who knows this, even while being expanded, it does not diminish.
May you be full of heroes, you who have made us rich in heroes.
Thus one should consecrate the newborn male child with this mantra.
May those [powers] of yours be more abundant, which have made us more abundant.
Thus [is the rite] for one born as a woman.
May those who have made us eaters of food become eaters of food themselves.
Thus he should consecrate the offerings of the bali-oblation.
May those who have done us much harm become even more numerous than we are.
Thus he should touch the feet of the members of the assembly; for these indeed are cattle, and cattle approach him and do not depart from him who knows thus.

The auspicious has brought forth the auspicious; the manifold has brought forth the manifold. O Blessed One, you have been born for me as one belonging to the lineage of Iḍā; O Maitrāvaruṇa, O Blessed One, you have been born together with vigor for me; find harmony for me.
Thus he should consecrate the newborn male with this mantra: "Strength indeed is born together with him; he goes to the fellowship of cattle."
Aiḍī:

O blessed one, you have been born for me from the Puṇyā and the Puṇyā, from the Citrā and the Citrā; O blessed one, you have been born for me as Aiḍī, as Maitrāvaruṇī. May you be born together with me in the abundance of wealth; find for me the knowledge of kinship.

Thus, when a woman is born, he goes forth together with her as the increase of wealth (*rāyaspoṣa*). Those who are born before the Ekāṣṭakā belong to the first crop; those who are born after [the Ekāṣṭakā] belong to the second crop. He should consecrate both types together; thus he secures both types together.
Aiḍī: [FN emended. Ed:

daiḍī] He who knows power (*śakti*) is able to teach that which he has learned. This earth, indeed, is power; he who possesses the greatest share of it is able to teach that which he has learned. And he who knows thus indeed comes to possess the greatest share of it.
Cattle indeed are power (*śakti*). He who possesses the greatest share of cattle is able to accomplish whatever he teaches;
for one who possesses cattle becomes most abundant in that way, provided he knows this. Its observance (*vrata*) is: "One should not say, 'It has been killed.'"
He should say, "Perform [the rite]"; he should not say, "She is pregnant," but rather he should say, "She is about to give birth. "Thou art the world; a thousandfold, Sṛma gave thee to Indra."

Thus, there was indeed an Asura named Sṛma; this earth belonged to him and was filled with cattle. Indra appropriated them; therefore they say, "Cattle belong to Indra. [With this formula: "Of as many as these I make, may I make more in a future year."

Thus he should make the mark for the cows; he makes the subsequent year more abundant. When cattle were first created, they each resorted to a single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); by that they multiplied, yet they did not attain abundance.
Therefore, whatever rite one performs for cattle, one should perform it under the *Revatī* constellation, for cattle resort to him and he becomes possessed of cattle.

Thus one should know: for him whose [vessel] is split on the right side, he should use that which is used on the right side; that is the mark of Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine mark, worthy of sacrifice; the one desiring sacrifice should employ it, for the sacrifice inclines toward him. For him whose [vessel] is split on both sides, he should use that which is used on both sides; that is the Gāyatra mark, beneficial for cattle; the one desiring cattle should employ it, and he becomes possessed of cattle. For him whose [vessel] is split on both sides...
That which is split on both sides is the mark of the *triṣṭubh*; it is the form of the purified one. One who desires a firm foundation should employ it;
he attains a firm foundation. The *sthūṇākarṇī* belongs to Vasiṣṭha. Vasiṣṭha indeed beheld wealth and placed it within himself.
In that he employs the *sthūṇākarṇī*, he places wealth among his cattle. The *karkarikarṇī* belongs to Jamadagni.

Jamadagni indeed perceived prosperity; he placed it within himself. When one makes [the ears] like those of a *karkarikarṇī* (a small bird), he places prosperity in the cattle. Those with ears shaped like the dewlaps of Asuras become numerous quickly, but they perish quickly;
they are impure ears. Those with perforated ears become numerous quickly, but the sacrifice overcomes them excessively as if by Nirṛti.
If one were to make the ears perforated, Nirṛti would seize that animal; therefore, one should not cut them off.
They should be made with natural ears, nor should they be "sickle-eared," for that is turned away and does not return.

They are "Viṣṭi-eared" after Agastya, "Kambu-erected" after Kaśyapa, and "unbroken" after Indra; moreover, they say [they belong] to Prajāpati—both of these are marks of the eldest, so he who desires preeminence [should choose them].
One should perform [this rite] among his equals; he attains preeminence. Prajāpati created cattle; indeed, he did not create blood. That [blood] was uncreated;
therefore, its nature is that of non-blood (*asṛk*). He did not create blood because it is cruel for cattle.

Truly, he who sharpens [the horn] makes it cruel for cattle. Because it has been sharpened (*akṣita*), it is called "sharpened" (*akṣitā*); and because it is not sharpened (*anakṣita*), they are heard of as "unsharpened" (*anakṣitā*).

Therefore they say that those [points] which are not sharpened do not go to yonder world; for this reason, they must be sharpened. One should not sharpen them with a reed-shaft (*tejana*), for the reed-shaft is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*); if one were to sharpen them with a reed-shaft, he would strike the cattle with a thunderbolt.
Nor should he use dark iron, for that is cruel and unappeased. Having soaked a stalk of sugarcane in water, he should sharpen them with that; for that is auspicious.
They call that peaceful, and also "with red iron"; for that is auspicious, that is peaceful.
*kaṃbunyuddhatās*:
FN Corrections and Conjectures to the Entire Work.
May the offspring of every form rejoice here in this cow-pen, the all-sustaining mothers.
Entering the fire as their nest, let them be united with milk and clarified butter.

Thus he should consecrate the cows as they return in the evening: "Agni indeed is their source; Agni is their nest. He causes them to settle in their own source, in their own nest. His cattle do not meet with misfortune at night—he who knows thus.
May Aryaman unite you; may Pūṣan unite you; may Bṛhaspati unite you;
and may Indra, the winner of wealth, unite you.
Meeting together, unerring, rich in cattle in this stall, come hither,
O well-disposed ones.
"Pūṣan"—thus he should mingle the cows that were his previously and those he finds from elsewhere. Ghee is indeed cattle; Agni is Rudra.
If he were to offer [the ghee] into the fire, he would deliver over his cattle to Rudra. Therefore, he should indeed mingle them; thus both kinds become more numerous.
"May Aryaman unite you"—Aryaman is indeed the sacrifice; thus he unites them with the sacrifice.

"May Pūṣan [unite you]"—Pūṣan is indeed nourishment; thus he unites them with nourishment. "May Bṛhaspati [unite you]"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred formulation (*brahman*); thus he unites them with the sacred formulation. "Indra, the winner of wealth, [unites you]"—Indra is indeed power (*indriya*); thus he unites them with power.
The Revatī is the cord; the Earth is the mother; the waters and the plants are the Revatīs.
May they impel us toward gain and inspired thought for your pleasure.
Thus one should extend the thread and smooth it along.
I anoint you with wealth and with nourishment.

Thus, with wealth and nourishment itself, he strokes her. Her vow is this: she must not be empty; they must not walk over one another; it must not rain upon her; and it must not shine (the sun) upon her. Basta Rāmakāyana discovered this—the stretching out by means of a thread—and he obtained a thousand cattle. He who knows thus obtains a thousand cattle.
He is the father of calves, the lord of the inviolable cows, and he is also the father of the great jars;
may he release you for the increase of wealth—him who bestows seed and bestows glory.
Saying this, as he releases [the bull] from the ear of the Ṛṣabha, he should say: "Verily, he releases him who bestows seed and bestows glory for the increase of wealth.

If there should be a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who is very prosperous, one should bring twenty-one dung-clods from his cow-pen and offer twenty-one oblations; for there are twenty-one worlds of men—it is from the worlds of men that he secures cattle for him.

One who desires cattle should offer these very oblations with the *gonāman* verses while seated on the afterbirth of a cow; for this is the mouth of cattle, and thus he brings cattle to him from the very mouth.
Whose wealth Indra has raised up—the name, the form of cattle, and the abode of the Dawn—beholding them all.
This is their source, this is their stall; here is wealth and prosperity.
Svāhā!
Thus one should offer the oblation.
Of those for whom Bṛhaspati utters praise, beholding the gathering of cattle, whose form is named *iḍā*, their abode.
Of these, this is the source, this is the stall; here is wealth and prosperity.
Svāhā!
Thus one should offer the oblation.
Those Maruts who raised up the light called the form of cattle, beholding the midday station.
This is their source, this is their stall; here is wealth and prosperity.
Svāhā!
Thus one should offer the oblation.
Of those whom Prajāpati raised up, beholding their life-span, their form, their cattle, and their abode in the afternoon.
Of these, this is the source, this is the stall; here is wealth and prosperity.
Svāhā!
Thus he should offer these; for these are indeed the forms of the day, and in these forms of the day the gods appropriated the forms of the cattle.

Therefore, in these very forms of the day, the sacrificer appropriates the cattle of his rival. He offers with ghee; ghee is indeed cattle, so by means of cattle he appropriates cattle. One should not pay heed to this [delay]; rather, it should be done in the morning while the cows are still inside the cow-pen.
One should offer oblations; by these very [verses], one secures all these [cows] together. One should offer with these when the cows have been driven in:
"From their very source he has seized the cattle; they make them stray, each in turn. One should offer with these in battle, and then one should consecrate the horses with mantras.
Supported by friends, supported by the ruling power, supported by vital energy, supported by strength—may we conquer, may we prevail, may we come to be, may we prosper.
Thus he wins the battle.
I choose for you the *rohiṇīs* with the *gāyatrī* metre; I choose for you the *aruṇās* with the *triṣṭubh* metre;
I choose for you the *gaurīs* with the *jagatī* metre; I choose for you the *babhrus* with the *anuṣṭubh* metre;
I choose for you the embryos with the *paṅkti* metre; I choose for you the forms with the *śakvarī* metre; I choose for you all [beings] with the *anāpta* metre—so be it.
The Śakvarī consists of seven steps; cattle are connected with the Śakvarī; verily he wins cattle. The first is a Gāyatrī, the last is a Gāyatrī;
the Gāyatrī is indeed splendor and spiritual luster. With both splendor and spiritual luster, he encloses cattle on both sides for him.

Prajāpati indeed created three greatnesses: Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya. These four—father and sons—performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). They wiped away their sweat, and that became this; "That indeed was his name," they said, "he has become everything.
These are his two names, both cruel and unpeaceful; therefore, these two should not be taken, for they are cruel and unpeaceful.

Prajāpati indeed desired his own daughter, Uṣas; she became a red deer, and he, having become a buck, approached her. He concealed his transgression from her, but she turned toward him with a longing gaze. He was afraid of that, and he said, "I make you the lord of cattle; do not stay with me. That, indeed, is his name: Paśupati (Lord of Cattle). Him—

As he approached, he pierced him; he wept, and that is why his name is Rudra. These indeed are his two names, both auspicious and peaceful; therefore, these two may be taken at will, for they are auspicious and peaceful. Then, the first semen that fell away, Agni consumed with fire; that is the reason for the inviolability (*aghnyātva*) of these cows. Then, what flowed over, Bṛhaspati caught.

"We were able to milk them," thus they became the *usriyās*; "we have found the way," thus they became the *śakvarīs*. These indeed are their names; he who knows this enjoys all their names and all their desires.
When cattle were created, they fled toward these constellations: the full moon, the eighth day (*aṣṭakā*), the new moon, and the Citrā.
Therefore, among those [trees], one should not exclude the *aśvattha*; for if one were to exclude it, his cattle would follow after and depart from him.

All the gods indeed were pregnant together; they all gave birth together. That [embryo] lay there as a single whole, rolled up. The gods moved about here and there in various ways. Mitra and Varuṇa perceived this: "Surely, someone might alter this. They made the cow two-footed, but she did not stand firm. From one side of her, they took away the two ears.

Therefore, she supported herself by means of these [verses] which were unbound; having become four-footed, she established herself. He who knows this establishes himself with offspring and cattle. Indeed, they beheld milk in her; the gods milked her with a green vessel; he who knows this milks both the sacrifice and immortality. Then the ancestors...
They milked with a silver vessel: vigor and the ancestral offering (*svadhā*). He who knows thus milks vigor and the ancestral offering.
Then humans milked with a wooden vessel: food and offspring. He who knows thus milks food and offspring.
Then the seers milked with a cup (*camasa*): the meters and cattle. He who knows thus milks the meters and cattle. And then...

The Gandharvas and Apsarases milked it with a lotus leaf; he who knows this milks holy fragrance for himself. Then the serpents milked it with a *alāpuna* plant; he who knows this milks poison for his rival. Then the Asuras milked it with a leaking iron vessel;
he who knows this milks both prosperity and misfortune for his rival.

Indra indeed worshipped her with this very [formula]; he milked out all this, whatever exists here. Having milked her, he pushed her away. Pushed away, she stood there dejected and brooding. Prajāpati perceived her, thinking, "She is indeed brooding. He said, "Why are you brooding? She replied, "Those who have milked me have pushed me away. He said, "Do not [be so]."
"I shall indeed treat you with such care that you will become dear to both gods and men.
As he spoke, ghee flowed from her feet; taking some of that ghee, he wiped his face.
I make you beloved by both gods and men.

Thus, for this reason, he is dear to both gods and men; with this very [ointment] one should wipe the face of a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), for both gods and men know him by this. With this [one should wipe the face] of a young girl who desires a husband. This indeed is the radiance of cattle;
one should not do this for just anyone, but for whomsoever one does it, he shall become radiant.

He who has a white mark on his forehead, whose feet are white, whose horns are white, whose face is white, whose tail is white, and who is brindled—he attains eight herds, eight herds indeed, he for whom such a bull exists; or he for whom there is one with a white tuft firmly established—that is "firmly established," and he stands firm through offspring and cattle, he for whom such a bull exists; or he who is all-white with white forelegs.
He becomes surrounded on all sides by offspring and cattle whose bull is such as that which has a white back;

he becomes possessed of cattle whose bull is such as that [which is] the *tanti*. Furthermore, he whose bull, though being of a single color, bears a mark, his enemies do not scatter his cows; he becomes such whose bull is such as that.
That which has wool on its belly is nourishing; like goats, offspring are born from one who has such a bull. That which is dark-brown is nourishing;
they quickly become numerous, though they are prone to miscarriage. That which is reddish is nourishing; they quickly become numerous, though they have rough skin.
That which is white with black spots is nourishing; they quickly become numerous, though they have diseased skin.
But one should not apply ointment to him, nor should he be spotted; for that is not a pairing. Moreover, the spotted bull has the form of a tiger, and cattle are afraid of it;

thus, the cattle of one who possesses such a bull become fewer. Regarding this, they say: "The seed itself must be cast away," for the red form is indeed their seed. He becomes rich in cattle who possesses such a bull.

He becomes a bull; he who is smoke-colored or copper-smoke-colored is Prajāpati, and he whose bull is such as that is propagated with offspring and cattle. He whose hump is hairy is "stambin" (thorny/firm); like a thorn, he becomes possessed of offspring and cattle, he whose bull is such as that. He whose hump is upright—those [cattle] are upright, they swell upwards, they are upright.

The cattle of him prosper for whom there is such a bull, whose right side is depressed—that is the evil one, that is the flowing one; and whose left side is elevated—that is the auspicious one, that is the bringing-up one. Those which have a hump on their backs, being upright, they prosper upwards; the cattle of him prosper upwards for whom there is such a bull, whose left side [is elevated].

That which flows away to the south is sinful; it carries away merit. That which flows toward the left is meritorious; it brings back merit. That which has a horn-like swelling is a cow-pen; one should not cut it off. These two should belong to the cattle that have been let loose among the herd.
Indeed, these two are the unspilled oblation of animals; for him whose cattle are let loose among the herd, his oblation becomes unspilled.

The bull and the heifer should be among his cattle; for these two indeed carry the vigor of livestock. His cattle become free from hunger, he for whom there is both a bull and a heifer among his cattle.
[Page IV,39] Some men are hostile toward another man, while others are not; those who are hostile are Nirṛti, and those who are not hostile are Anumati.
To both of these they offer together, they cook both together, and they proceed first with the offering to Nirṛti.
Having gone toward the south, he offers on a hollow dug by himself; for this is seized by Nirṛti, and thus he expiates Nirṛti right where she has seized him on earth.

Having placed a single firebrand, he makes two offerings from the stalks of a withered plant, saying: "May Nirṛti, being pleased, accept [this], Svāhā! A black garment with a torn hem is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), for that is the form of Nirṛti. Indeed, it constitutes half of a person.
Half of it is seized by Nirṛti, half is not seized by Nirṛti; that which is seized by Nirṛti, he thereby expiates from himself with that.
Having returned, they proceed with a cake on eight potsherds for Anumati; having thus expiated from Nirṛti, Anumati is indeed this [earth], and speech is Anumati;
verily, he causes him to ascend the sacrifice that has been approved. It consists of a cake on eight potsherds, for this [earth] is a Gāyatrī, and the Gāyatrī is speech.

A cow is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), for this is the form of Anumati. Then, having gone northward to where the pegs (śamyā) extend beyond [the altar], he should dig up a mound of anthill earth and offer it with the formula: "I here appease the field-disease (kṣetriya) of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so. He then covers it back up again with the formula: "I here cover up the field-disease of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so. This is the [remedy for] the field-disease.
He takes this [offering] for those who follow him; this earth is the mistress of the field, and thus he expiates the *kṣetriya* (the disease of the womb) in her.

Then he causes it to ascend the *sava*. On the following day, there is an oblation of ghee for the Adityas, the Bhuvadvats. For the Adityas indeed went from here to the highest heavenly world; having announced it to them, he goes to the heavenly world. The Adityas, indeed, are in this world...

The Ādityas prospered in this world; he prospers in both worlds. The choice is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); by means of the choice itself, he ascends to the heavenly world. On the following day, there is an offering to Agni and Viṣṇu on eleven potsherds. Agni is indeed all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus he has obtained both the deities and the sacrifice. Agni is the end of the sacrifice from below, and Viṣṇu is from above.

He has grasped both ends of the sacrifice; having grasped both ends of the sacrifice, he pours it out just as one would pour something into the hollow of one's lap—thus indeed does he pour out the sacrifice.

As he proceeds to pour it out according to his desire, the sacrificial fee is a dwarf ox; because it is a draught-animal, it belongs to Agni, and because it is a dwarf, it belongs to Viṣṇu; thus he endows it with its very form. On the following day, the offering belongs to Agni and Soma.

"Eleven potsherds"—for by means of the power of Agni and Soma, Indra slew Vṛtra; and indeed, he who is consecrated by the Rājasūya slays Vṛtra. Therefore, this gold, which is the sacrificial fee, is truly "Vṛtra-slaying. Gold is indeed truth;
by truth itself he slays. On the following day, there is an offering on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni—for by means of the power of Agni and Soma, Indra [slew Vṛtra].

He slew Vṛtra, but he was deprived of his vigor and manly strength. He beheld this offering to Indra and Agni; with it, he placed vigor and manly strength within himself. Indeed, he who is consecrated by the Rājasūya is deprived of vigor and manly strength. Indra and Agni are vigor and manly strength; verily, through vigor and manly strength, they endow him with them. An ox that has been a draught-animal is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); in that it is a draught-animal, it belongs to Agni, and in that it is a bull, it belongs to Indra.

Thus, by means of Indra’s very form, he causes him to prosper. On the following day, there is an offering to Agni on eight potsherds and curds for Mahendra; this is for the sake of prosperity. It belongs to Agni. Indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra, but he held himself in contempt above the other gods; he became Mahendra. Having slain Vṛtra, he took out this special portion (uddhāra) for himself. Therefore, this is his share as a special portion; thus, he is like a king.
Having won the battle, he won the prize; for he who is consecrated by the Rājasūya is deprived of milk and of vigor.
In that there is milk, he thereby endows him with milk. He who is consecrated by the Rājasūya is deprived of sensory power and of vigor.
In that there is [the offering] to Indra, he thereby endows him with sensory power and vigor. He who... is deprived of the deities.
He consecrates him with the Rājasūya sacrifice. Cloth is indeed sacred to all the deities; since linen cloth is the sacrificial fee, he thereby causes him to prosper through the deities themselves.
Indeed, when the plants had ripened, the gods entered the race. Indra perceived: "Agni will surely be the first to win these."
He said, "Whichever of us two shall first win, that we shall share together. Agni won them first; Indra won them after him.
Therefore, the offering belongs to Indra and Agni. Moreover, they say it should be made for Agni and Indra, for Agni won them first.
It is on account of this victory that the Āgrayaṇa cake consists of twelve potsherds; the year has twelve months, and it is from the year that this [offering] arises.

There were seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses to be recited: five seasons and twelve months—this is the year; for it is from the year that this [offering] arises. At that time, there was indeed one handful of barley, one of rice, one of beans, and one of sesame.
Then the Viśve Devas said, "We shall spread this out for you; let there be a share for us. And so it was.

The All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ) spread it out; therefore, it belongs to the Viśve Devāḥ by virtue of its abundance. Moreover, one spreads it out by means of this [offering]. It should be prepared in milk, for milk belongs to the Viśve Devāḥ. Now, Earth said: "This [offering] indeed rests upon me; yonder [Sky] cooks it with rain. You shall not win it away from me; let there be a share for me. Therefore, this share is indeed made for these two.
It is for victory and also for stability. Now, plants belong to Soma, and Soma is the overlord of plants;
his portion is that which ripens without being ploughed. This is indeed his special share (*uddhāra*); this is his very portion.
Therefore, having won a battle, a king carries off the prize. Some plants are domestic, others are wild; by this [offering], he obtains both of them.
Those [grains] which have been ploughed by the plough are for those he performs the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice with this [rite]; those which are wild, for those he performs it with the latter [portion].

Indeed, he who has established the sacred fires is brought near to the gods; if he were to eat of the new grain without having performed the *āgrayaṇa*, he would be eating a portion of the gods that has not been assigned to him, and he would meet with ruin. Verily, he who performs the *rājasūya* is consecrated above all others; [this *āgrayaṇa* is] for the attainment of food.
The first-born calf is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), for it is like seed not yet born; it serves for the sake of procreation.

[Page IV,42] Now, as for these Cāturmāsya offerings: the Cāturmāsyas are indeed performed throughout the year; it is from the year itself that he obtains and secures them. This is a sacrifice that has fallen into disuse; it is from the year that this neglected sacrifice is recovered.
Having obtained it from the year itself, he secures it for himself. These Śunāsīrya offerings are indeed cattle that exceed the Cāturmāsya sacrifices;
he thus obtains them. He should sacrifice in rain-water, for that is the nearest [source] of cattle.
Now, these five oblations are for the sake of continuity. One who desires a village should sacrifice; Vāyu indeed has these creatures tied to his nose, leading them hither and thither.

And he is led away; for Vāyu, indeed, leads the people bound by the nose to him. One who desires food should sacrifice to Śunāsīra Indra. Śunāsīra Indra is the year, and the year is the bestower of food. He approaches him with his own portion, and he grants him food.
One who desires rain should sacrifice in rainwater, for that is the nearest source of food. One who desires rain [should sacrifice].
Or he should sacrifice to Vāyu; for Vāyu sets these [winds] in motion, he causes [the waters] to swell, and from that it rains. Or Indra Śunāsīra is the year;
following the year, it rains.

The gods and the Asuras were contending. Vṛtra said to Indra, "You are the best of the gods, and I am the best of the Asuras; let us two make an alliance so that neither of us may slay the other. They made a compact for the sake of non-hostility.
The gods suspected Vṛtra, thinking, "He will surely take over this world. Indra desired, "I will kill him. He...

He said, "Let there be a compact for me, that they shall not harm me when they are united. Agni said to him, "I myself will protect you from this [earth]," Varuṇa said, "I [will protect you] from the intermediate space," and Rudra said, "I [will protect you] from heaven. Then indeed the gods slew Vṛtra;
for he who is consecrated by the Rājasūya slays Vṛtra, and so this is truly the slaying of Vṛtra, as it was for the gods.
The gods and the Asuras contended; Agni, having divided himself threefold, confronted them:
Agni, becoming manifest in this world, Varuṇa in the intermediate space, and Rudra in heaven. Indra thought, "This one indeed will become all this.
He said, "I [will win] from all the quarters. Then they conquered; it was by means of that very victory that they won.

One should cause him to sacrifice in battle; he conquers the battle by this very [rite]. One should cause him who has rivals, or one who is dear to him, to sacrifice with this; he prospers in himself, while his rival is defeated. Indeed, because Indra then attained the fourth part (*turīya*), it is called the *Indraturīya*. A cow and a draught-ox are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); because she is a draught-animal, she belongs to Agni; because she is a milch-cow (*dhenu*), she is so called.

Because it is tamed, it belongs to Varuṇa; because it is a cow, it belongs to Rudra; because of its milk, it belongs to Indra. Verily, he endows it with these very forms. Indra could not seize Namuci. Having made his rays a nest, he ascended after him—that Sun up there.
He (Indra) called out to him, "O friend, here I am! He (Namuci) said, "I will not kill you. He (Indra) said, "I will make a covenant with you, so that—"

"I will not slay you by day, nor by night; neither with the dry, nor with the wet"—thinking thus, at the very rising of the sun, he cut off Namuci's head with a continuous stream of mist and the foam of the waters. Yet it followed after him, saying, "Thou art a betrayer of a friend. The head of Namuci was indeed evil; evil indeed followed after him. By that [act], he struck away that evil; he struck away that evil.
Thus he strikes them away. They bring Apāmārga plants from the gathering-place of the waters; for the waters are slayers of the Rakṣases, and the Rakṣases do not cross over the waters;

it is for the striking away of the Rakṣases. A boon is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); by means of a boon he wins a boon, for the self is the boon, and his self indeed followed after that. "The gods who sit in the front, led by Agni, slayers of the Rakṣases—may they protect us; may they [protect] those..."

"May they protect us; to them, Svāhā!"—these quarters indeed have those deities as their presiding powers; thus, according to the respective deities, he drives away the Rakṣases from these quarters. He offers while moving around [the fire] in succession; thus he drives away the Rakṣases from all the quarters.
"Here I sweep together the Rakṣases; O Agni, burn up the Rakṣas! Burnt up is the Rakṣas!"—he says this for the destruction of the Rakṣases.

Having driven away the Rakṣases from within, he then offers the oblations after piling them up together; thus he makes those very quarters from which he has struck away the Rakṣases share in the offering, for the sake of non-injury. A chariot drawn by five oxen is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); there are five directions and five deities, for the sake of prosperity.
Of the asuras:
[of the asuras, of the asuras].
He slew: [he slew].

One should cause him who has performed the Soma sacrifice to perform [the Devikā-homas]. For a year, the meters of one who performs the Soma sacrifice become exhausted; the minor deities (Devikās) are indeed the meters. Thus, he makes the meters for him fresh again and restores their power.

One should cause him who is being consecrated by the Rājasūya to perform [the Devikā-homas]; a four-year-old cow is the sacrificial fee. For he is consecrated in the hope [of attaining all things], and the four-year-old cow is hope.
He has indeed created hope for him; one desiring cattle should cause him to sacrifice. The Devikās are the meters, and cattle are the meters:

Gāyatrī is Anumati, Triṣṭubh is Rākā, Jagatī is Sinīvālī, Anuṣṭubh is Kuhū, and Dhātṛ is the *vaṣaṭ* call. That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati, that which is the later is Rākā; that which is the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī, that which is the later is Kuhū; [and] the Moon itself.
When Dhātṛ [places] two below and two above, that is a pair; when one fills another, that is a pair;
when they see one and not the other, that is a pair; when the moon is born from the new moon (amāvāsyā), that is a pair.
Therefore, from this very pairing he produces cattle for him. One who desires offspring should sacrifice to Dhātṛ; he should make Dhātṛ the last [deity].

The Devikās are indeed women, and Dhātṛ is the man; offspring deposit seed in those who are turned away (*parācī*). He deposits seed in these very [Devikās] as they are turned away. Regarding this, they say: "He does not indeed place it far away when it is inserted between. One should interpose Dhātṛ in the middle;
thus he makes them all truly "delighting in the bull" (*vṛṣamodinī*). Regarding this, they say: "It is born indeed, yet it is as if it moves backward."
For they lead him around from behind the women; when he is born, then one should offer to Dhātṛ in front.
Dhātṛ is indeed the beginning; verily, he leads him around by means of the beginning.
[Page IV,45] One should cause one who is ill to sacrifice to Dhātṛ; he should place Dhātṛ in the middle. Dhātṛ is indeed the year;
for the year, indeed, has become bewildered for him, and then he falls ill. Verily, they have thus established the year for him in the middle, and then him.
From this pair he procreates. Indeed, these meters are lords; apart from the animal, they would sweep away [the sacrificer] unappeased.
Even when an animal is offered, it is for the sake of appeasement and to prevent being swept away. Rice and barley are indeed animals;
in that there is a rice-cake (*puroḍāśa*), by that very means the animal is offered for the sake of appeasement and to prevent being swept away. Or rather, they are the abodes of heroes.

Other animals are in the state of the non-heroic; those sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) which are in front are in the state of the heroic, while those sacrificial cakes which are behind are in the state of the non-heroic.
Those sacrificial cakes which are in front attend upon [the sacrificer] as he eats, for they were created by Prajāpati as a firm foundation.
Those sacrificial cakes which are behind pass him by; the *caru* offerings should be prepared in the same vessels in which the Soma juices were contained.

Soma is indeed the bestower of seed for procreation. One should cause him who has performed the *sarvavedasa* sacrifice to sacrifice with cattle; for he who gives away everything is deprived of cattle. Indeed, it is at this point that he last sees his cattle—namely, when he distributes them. From the very place where he distributes them, he recovers them again. Whosoever should sacrifice with Soma, one should cause him to sacrifice for a year.
The meters of him who sacrifices with Soma become exhausted; the Devikās are indeed the meters. Verily, he thereby makes the meters for himself fresh again and full of vigor.
Now, as for this first *triṣaṃyukta* chant: by means of it, he established these worlds above from here;

and as for the latter *triṣaṃyukta*: by means of it, he established these worlds below from there. Thus, the first *triṣaṃyukta* serves to sustain these worlds, while the latter is the progenitor of heroes.

That which is the first *triṣaṃyukta* produces offspring; by it he produces heroes for him. That which is the latter produces cattle; by it he produces cattle. That which is the first *triṣaṣyukta* deposits seed; by it he impels [the birth]. That which is the latter, by that one who desires sacrifice should sacrifice. Agni indeed is all the deities, Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; [thus] the deities [are satisfied].

And indeed, Indra seized the sacrifice; for Indra is the sacrifice and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice—thus this is the commencement of the sacrifice itself. Now, as to why it belongs to Viṣṇu: Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus he establishes himself in the sacrifice. With that which follows, the *triṣaṃyukta* (threefold-conjoined) offering, one who desires cattle should sacrifice. Soma is the depositor of seed and Pūṣan is the progenitor of cattle; it is Soma who bestows seed upon him.

Pūṣan procreates cattle; cattle are indeed procreated by means of vital power (*indriya*), and Pūṣan procreates them by means of that very vital power for him. Furthermore, as for the offering to Pūṣan: Pūṣan is indeed cattle; thus he establishes himself firmly in cattle.
Now, this [offering] belongs to Vaiśvānara and Varuṇa. Agni Vaiśvānara is the year; the seasons are indeed his own.
Of these, he is the consecrated king; Varuṇa is indeed the consecrated king of the gods. These two are the two pressers (*sūtau*) of the gods; these two are the lords of the pressing (*savapati*);
these two are the masters of the pressing (*savasya*). They press for him. As many as are his own people (*svāḥ*), they are indeed followers (*anukāḥ*);
those who are followers of Varuṇa among the gods—just as many as are his own people, so many followers does he make for him, free from dispute. This is the *caru* offering.

The self becomes only as large as this [offering] which is his self; having released him from Varuṇa, Agni Vaiśvānara—who is indeed the year—establishes him in the year and makes his life-span equal to the year. Therefore, the teeth of one consecrated by the Rājasūya fall out through old age, for he establishes him in the year and makes his life-span equal to the year.

Whoever has been long ill, him one should cause to sacrifice with this [offering]. For he is indeed seized by Varuṇa through evil, and thus he is long ill; since it is dedicated to Varuṇa, he thereby releases him from Varuṇa. It is a pap of *iyām* beans; for the self is only as large as this, and having released that self of his from Varuṇa—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year, and the year...
Thus he establishes him; he makes his life-span one year.
Now, these are the jewels; these are indeed the limbs of the kṣatra. For whichever [kṣatra] possesses these as its powerful limbs, that kingdom becomes powerful;

he thus makes those very limbs powerful for it. These are indeed the limbs of the kṣatra; for whichever [kṣatra] possesses these as its brilliant limbs, that kingdom becomes brilliant; he thus makes those very limbs brilliant for it by means of the *brahman*.

"A pap of cooked rice for Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; a kingdom with Bṛhaspati as its domestic priest surely prospers. He has thus driven the Brahman forward at the head of the kingdom; furthermore, he makes the kingdom subject to the Brahman. "An eleven-potherd cake for Indra in the house of the King"—Indra is indeed power; verily, he becomes established in power.

"The *āditya* oblation is for the chief queen’s house"—for Aditi is this earth; verily, he causes him to go to her as his measure, and he makes him one to be subsisted upon by these very creatures. A cow is the sacrificial fee, for that is the form of Aditi. "The *nairṛta* oblation is for the house of the woman who has been rejected and whose nails have been pared away"—for she is indeed seized by Nirṛti, and they now reject her [as] Nirṛti.
Thus she is cleansed; this is the permission for her, and by means of this he causes him to attain his proper measure. He makes him subsistence for these very creatures.

A white, tailless, quivering ewe is the sacrificial fee, for that is the form of Nirṛti. There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni in the house of the commander of the army; for Agni is indeed all the deities. By means of the deities, he sharpens the front of his army for victory. Gold [is given].
Gold is indeed the sacrificial fee; by truth alone one conquers. The cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins is in the house of the charioteer;

by that he makes amends to him for the splinter of the chariot. "Two swift horses are the sacrificial fee," they say, for the two drivers seated on the left are indeed like swift horses with respect to the chariot.
The cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ is in the house of the attendant, for it is for the sake of impulsion; moreover, he is like Savitṛ toward all creatures.

A cake on ten potsherds made of barley for Varuṇa is offered in the house of the *sūta*; a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts in the house of the *vaiśya* village-chief. For the *viś* (the common people) have the *sūta* as their mouth; thus he approaches the *kṣatra* with the *sūta* as its mouth. Verily, he thus places the *viś* with its mouth toward him for the sake of eating food. A pap for Pūṣan is offered in the house of the *bhāgadugha*; for Pūṣan is prosperity—verily, [he offers] prosperity.

Thus he assigns a share to him: a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu in the house of the carpenter and the chariot-maker; for the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu, and thus it finds firm support in the sacrifice itself.
There is a pap of Gavidhuka grain for Rudra in the house of the dice-player and the butcher;
thus, right to the end, he propitiates Rudra with that for himself, for these two indeed regard cattle as if they were Rudra. Eleven [offerings].

These oblations indeed consist of eleven syllables; the Triṣṭubh is vigor, and thus he finds firm support in vigor itself. If they were to offer them together, they would be without a cubit's reach [of distinction]. There is an eleven-potherd cake for Indra in the king’s house; for Indra is power. Thus, the blessing of the sacrifice comes to rest one-pointedly upon the sacrificer.
For the sacrificer is indeed [a form] of Indra.
He conceives [the following]:
"One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc for whatever sin he commits subsequent to his birth."
Then, for him who speaks ill of him or seeks to harm him, he offers this cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman;
thus Sutrāman protects him from that [enemy]. Now this [offering] is dedicated to Mitra and Bṛhaspati: Mitra is truth and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman;
having obtained both truth and the Brahman, he undergoes consecration. Mitra is indeed the Kṣatra and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; [thus he obtains] the Kṣatra.
And having obtained the *brahman* [priesthood], he undergoes initiation; for him whose kingdom might be as if loose, one should cause him to sacrifice with this offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati.

Mitra is indeed the *kṣatra* (nobility), and Bṛhaspati is the *brahman* (spiritual power). He thereby establishes the *kṣatra* in the *brahman* for the sake of firmness and to prevent looseness. Now, these are the "divine riches" (*devasva*). These are indeed the draft-horses of the gods; they are the lords of the pressing, and they have mastery over the pressing.
They press him [the Soma]; therefore they say of him: "On the previous day he is pressed, and on both sides he is poured.
Now this cake for the Maruts is on twenty-one potsherds; thrice seven are the Maruts, and the Maruts are the people (*viś*). Thus he is pressed in the midst of the people;
therefore he is dear to the people, for he is pressed in the midst of the people. Indeed, the power (*indriya*) of Varuṇa when being consecrated—

Vital power departed; it became threefold: Bhṛgu became one third, the Śrāyantīya became one third, and Sarasvatī entered as the third. When the Bhārgava is the Hotṛ and the Śrāyantīya is the Brahman-sāman, and the waters are those of the Sarasvatī, he thereby obtains that very vital power, vigor, and splendor. Indeed, they consecrate with speech him whom they consecrate; [for] speech is vital power.
Sarasvatī is the Sarasvatī waters; when [the Soma] is pressed with the Sarasvatī waters, it is pressed by as much speech as there is.
These are indeed the wonders of the waters; these they collect from the waters, and with the wonders of the waters they consecrate him. They bestow wonder upon him;

therefore, he who has been consecrated is heard of as "the wonderful king," for they consecrate him with the wonders of the waters and bestow wonder upon him. Just as the honey-makers here collect honey, so do they collect it.
In this very way, they collect the essence of the waters and the plants; they consecrate him with the essence of the waters and the plants and bestow that essence upon him.

Therefore, they say of him, "O King, you are holy," for they consecrate him with the essence of the waters and the plants and bestow that essence upon him. This is indeed a Varuṇa-consecration (varuṇasava), for the waters belong to Varuṇa; in that he consecrates him with water, [he performs this rite].

He has indeed made him Varuṇa. Sarasvatī is the Viṣuvat; the waters belong to Sarasvatī. Since he is pressed with the waters of Sarasvatī, he becomes the Viṣuvat. Sixteen cups are drawn and sixteen oblations are offered; that makes thirty-two. The Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-two syllables.
With as much as is speech, with that he is pressed.
One wave fights against the current, while another flows with the current for the sake of pairing. He takes [the milk] from that which fights against the current;

for it is with strength and vigor that this one fights against the current. With strength and vigor he thus bestows power and vigor upon the kingdom. Then, as for his taking [the milk] from that which flows with the current—the buffalo-milk—with that he procreates offspring.

Now, as for the river-lord: this is indeed the pairing of the waters; by means of this pairing of the waters, he establishes a pairing within the kingdom. Furthermore, because it is situated in the midst of the *aprahāvarī* waters, he thereby secures [the kingdom]. Because it is on the further bank of the *parivāhinī* waters, he thereby procreates offspring. And as for those waters which are *añśerā*: these waters are indeed *añśerā* by vigor and by strength. By vigor and by strength...

By this [offering], he bestows vigor and strength upon the kingdom through its virility; and as for the waters of the wells, by them he secures both kinds of waters—those that belong to the ocean and those that do not. These flowing waters, if unappeased, are capable of wiping him out; therefore, when he takes the water of standing pools, it is for the sake of appeasement and to prevent being wiped out. Those waters which fall as heat, those which rain down, and those which are visible on the surface—these are the waters.

They are conducive to spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); with them he bestows spiritual luster upon the kingdom. Now, in that there are *hradunī* plants, by that he secures heroism for the people (*viś*). Now, in that there are flowers, by that [he secures] the wild [plants]. Now, in that there are *ulbyā* plants—the cattle are indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the *ulbyā* plants are a thunderbolt—with the thunderbolt he thus places the thunderbolt in the kingdom. Now, in that there is milk—with milk he thus...

He places milk in the kingdom; now, as for the ghee—these waters are indeed invincible, and with them he makes the kingdom invincible. And as for the honey—it is the essence of the waters and of the plants; thus, by means of the essence of the waters and of the plants, he bestows essence upon the kingdom. These sixteen cups belong to Prajāpati; when brought together, they are seventeen, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
Verily, he attains Prajāpati.

"O divine waters, full of sweetness, mingle together, winning great dominion for the kṣatriya"—for these are indeed the winners of dominion, unassailable; "sit down, full of vigor, bestowing great splendor upon the kṣatriya"—for these are indeed the sustainers of dominion;
"thou art uncrushed"—for the kingdom is indeed uncrushed; "born of fervor"—for the kingdom is born of fervor.

"The gift of Soma"—for this is indeed the gift of Soma; "the bright ones I purify for you with the bright, the radiant ones I purify for you with the radiant"—gold is indeed life; he has thus made them long-lived. Gold is indeed luster; he has thus made them lustrous.
"May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer"—that which is the sun is indeed the flawless strainer.

With rays he purifies them by means of an unbroken strainer; "Svāhā to the Rājasūyas," for these [waters] are indeed the Rājasūyas. "The joyous ones, radiant with splendor and strength, united," with this he causes them to flow apart. With a verse addressed to Varuṇa, for the waters belong to Varuṇa; thus he satisfies them through their own deity. "O Rudra, that name of yours which is beyond the mountains"—with this he makes amends to Rudra on his behalf. "In it you are offered; you are sacrificed to Yama."

"Svāhā!"—Mṛtyu is indeed Yama; by this, he expiates Mṛtyu from him. "O Soma, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni—may these gods who uphold the Law maintain the Law for you. These gods who uphold the Law are indeed these vital breaths (*prāṇas*). If they were to consecrate him without having announced [the rite] to them, they would seek to exclude him; but when they have announced it to them...

Having proclaimed it, they consecrate him; thus they become ones who do not exclude him. At the tip and the end of the *parṇa* leaf, the Brahman spoke together; that indeed was "well-heard" (*suśravas*) because he heard it. He consecrates him with a vessel made of *parṇa*; he consecrates him with the Brahman;
verily, he consecrates him with the splendor of the Brahman (*brahmavarcasa*). Moreover, the Brahman-priest is indeed the Brahman; with the Brahman itself, the Brahman-priest consecrates him.
By means of the *aśvattha* wood, the Vaiśya departed with the vigor of the people (*viś*); it entered the *aśvattha*. Through that vigor, it became full (*bharbharā*).
Thus, by this [wood], he secures for himself the vigor of the people. With one made of *udumbara* wood, the rival [is addressed]; the *udumbara* is indeed strength (*ūrj*);
thus the sacrificer appropriates from his rival that strength, that food-eating power. He who is a friend of the enemy [should use] one made of *nyagrodha* wood, for it is a friend.
The *nyagrodha* tree is indeed the most firmly established of the *kṣatra*; with Mitra he thus establishes the *kṣatra* for the sake of firmness and to prevent it from becoming loose.
"O seed! ... *svāhā*!
"Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra, thou art the amnion of the Kṣatra, thou art the navel of the Kṣatra"—thus [he says]. Indeed, when Indra was born...
This was indeed his birthplace: the *tārpya* garment was the womb, the white membrane was the navel, and the turban was born from the birth-cord.

The four-footed slaughter-stool was the udder; the wild rice (*nīvāra*) was the first milk. Therefore, the sacrificial cake is made of wild rice. He anoints fifty [hairs] on one eye and fifty-one on the other. Man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold strength; thus he bestows both life and strength.

He obtains water; he touches water; water is indeed immortality; verily with immortality he causes him to be consecrated. "Agni, lord of the house, has accepted [him]"—verily he announces him to the Gārhapatya fire. "Indra, of far-reaching fame, has accepted [him]"—Indra is indeed power; verily he announces him for the sake of power. "Mitra and Varuṇa, whose vows are firm, have accepted [him]"—Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night; verily by means of day and night [he accepts him].

Thus he announces him; with the words, "Announced are Heaven and Earth, the increasers of *ṛta*," he announces him to Heaven and Earth. With the words, "Announced is Pūṣan, the knower of all,"—Pūṣan being cattle—he announces him to the cattle. With the words, "Announced is the goddess Aditi,"—for these creatures belong to the Ādityas—he announces him to them. "This one here, the son of such-and-such... he announces him.
"He is the son of such-and-such a woman, of such-and-such a clan"—thus he makes him known to the clan; therefore, he is dear to the clan, for he makes him known to the clan.
"He is the king of this people"—thus he makes him known to the people. "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas"—thus the Brahman priest takes it up;
he thereby makes him known to all other beings. The Brahman priest takes it up.

Therefore they say, "The *brahman* has been extracted," for he indeed extracts the *brahman*. With the words, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; with thee may this man slay Vṛtra," he hands over the bow. The bow is indeed the thunderbolt, and the Rājanya is the thunderbolt; verily by means of the thunderbolt he empowers the thunderbolt.
With the words, "Thou art the repellers of enemies," [he hands over] the arrow-case. The arrow-case is the end, and the Rājanya is the end; verily by the end he reaches the end.
He makes [the sacrificer] prosper; he bestows three [protections]. There are indeed three kinds of arrows: those of heaven, those of earth, and those of the ocean; may they keep him away from us.
"Protect him facing forward; protect him facing backward; protect him facing crosswise; protect him facing downward; protect him from above;
protect him from the quarters"—thus they protect him from the quarters. He consecrates this [victim] with the words, "Thou art Mitra," for this is the form of Mitra.

With the verse, "Varuṇa art thou," he should consecrate him with this form of Varuṇa; with the verse, "The golden-colored one at the dawning of the Dawn," he should consecrate him while he stands on high ground with his arms raised. A Bṛhat Sāman is performed; verily, he causes him to extend toward the heavenly world.
Form:
[the word] *rūpam* has been emended; the edition reads *rapam*.
With arms raised upward.
FN emended. Ed: ūrdhvabāhus. Dharmadhikari, p. 485:
"He establishes him in these directions; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus conquers these directions; therefore, all [of this belongs] to him."
He turns toward whichever direction he intends to conquer; for the directions are indeed the world of heaven, and these directions have those deities as their presiding powers.
Thus, according to the respective deities, he goes from these directions to the world of heaven. "Thou art the brilliance of Soma;
may my brilliance be like thine, full of brilliance!"—with these words, he wraps himself in a tiger skin. For there is one brilliance in Soma and one in the tiger.
One [is for the snake] and one for those very [creatures]; thus he secures them both. "Cast down the head of Namuci," with these words he throws a lead weight at the eunuch;

for the head of Namuci is indeed evil, and it is evil that he thus casts away from himself. "As he ascends to the heavenly world, may the biters be averted," with these words he throws a piece of red iron at the hair-cutter; by this means, he expiates the biters for him.

Therefore, there is no sorcery against this [altar]. For as many deaths as there are, he expiates them for him with the words, "Protect me from death! He places a silver plate underneath; for the tiger is the form of death, and gold is immortality—by means of immortality, he thus interposes a barrier against death. With the words, "Protect me from the sky," he places a golden plate above; for that which belongs to the sky...
Thus he should drive him away with the lightning-bolt; for this [earth] is silver-colored and yonder [sky] is golden. Having encompassed him with these two, they flow over him:
gold is indeed life, so they flow over him as things pertaining to life; gold is indeed splendor, so they flow over him as things pertaining to splendor.
When Varuṇa was being consecrated, the waters struck away his power and vigor; in that he places a gold disk in between, it is for the sake of power.
It consists of a hundred syllables to ensure that his vigor is not destroyed; for man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold vigor; thus he attains both life and vigor.
Now, these are the *pārtha* offerings; the *pārtha* offerings are indeed the year. He thus enters the year from the middle;
therefore, this [sacrifice] is difficult to complete. For he enters the year from the middle. These two are the mountains of the Rājasūya:
that of Bṛhaspati is for others the last, and that of Indra is for others the first. Bṛhaspati is indeed vigor.

Indra is vigor; he bestows vigor upon him. These are indeed the names of the Ādityas; the Ādityas are these creatures; it is for them that he is consecrated. With the words, "With the splendor of Soma, with the brilliance of Agni, with the power of Indra, with the will of all the gods, I consecrate thee," he consecrates him with these very powers and these very deities. Of Indra...
"You are the womb; beget!"—from this very [source] Indra was born; verily, he causes him to be born from his own womb.
"Protect beyond the days," he says, for the attainment of the heavenly world. "They have turned together, downward and upward"—thus he wipes upwards.
Verily, the power and vigor of one being consecrated departs; that he recovers by wiping upwards; thereby he causes him to prosper.

With an Aindrī Triṣṭubh verse, the Brahman priest follows after him; for the Rājanya is connected with Indra, and the Triṣṭubh is his metre—he thus follows him with his own metre. Moreover, Prajāpati is the Brahman of the sacrifice; from Prajāpati, Indra was born; he is thus born from Prajāpati himself. "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the winner of booty; through thee may this man win booty"—with these words he brings down the chariot by means of its own [formula].

With the words, "By the deity Mitra and Varuṇa, the two directors, I yoke you by their direction," he yokes [the chariot] by its own deity. With the words, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, overcoming the rival," he mounts the chariot. For from there indeed Viṣṇu conquered these worlds;
following after the victory of Viṣṇu, he conquers these worlds. He drives his rival away from these worlds. Of the Maruts...

With "At the impulse, conquer! he becomes the host of Maruts and conquers; he overcomes the nobleman and has stepped upon the very end. Therefore, no one remains unconquerable by him. He hurls that arrow at him; it has been hurled at him so that it is not in vain. Having said, "The mind has reached its goal; [it is] united with the sense-power," he turns back. Having gone to the very end, he turns back for his own non-injury; for this is a thunderbolt.

"O most excellent winner of booty, may our son win booty through that! With these words, he hands a bow and arrow to the wife; this indeed is the wife's participation in the sacrifice, and thus they both dwell together in the heavenly world.

"Such is your life; give me life"—thus he bestows life upon him. "You are a yoke; you are splendor; give me splendor"—thus he bestows splendor upon him. "You are vigor; place vigor in me"—this [earth] is indeed silver-colored, and yonder [sky] is golden;
having thus taken hold of these two, and since the udumbara is vigor, he places vigor in the very center of himself and of offspring. "You are Mitra"—thus [he addresses] this one.

He brings it down with the formula, "Thou art Mitra's," for this is the form of Mitra; "Varuṇa thou hast been," for this is the form of Varuṇa. With the formula, "Thou art the seat; may I be united with all the gods," he pours the *āmikṣā* over his hands. The *āmikṣā* is indeed the seat; thus he pours it down upon the very seat. There he gives gold as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Truly, this [offering], when descending onto the earth, harms the cattle.

"Obeisance to the mother Earth"—with these words he descends upon the sandals; he thus descends upon wild animals alone. Yet the boar is indeed fit to tread upon it; therefore, the boar itself treads upon it. "That name and sovereignty have been established for thee; Varuṇa has clothed his own body"—this is the Varuṇasava; he thus announces him to Varuṇa himself. Trita...
With "He has reached old age," he indeed bestows old age upon him; with "Thou art pleasant, a good seat," for she is indeed pleasant and a good seat;
with "Sit on the pleasant one, sit on the good seat," he causes him to sit on a truly good seat.
Varuṇa, firm in his vows and wise in action, sat down within the dwellings for the sake of universal sovereignty.

Thus, this is indeed the Varuṇasava; he has made him Varuṇa himself. He offers the oblation for unyoking the chariot with the formula: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Indra’s vigor, svāhā! To the Maruts’ strength, svāhā! By means of the Yajus they are yoked, and by means of the Yajus they are unyoked.
With the verse, "The swan dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere," he praises the chariot together with its driver while it stands on the chariot-stand.

They set up the chariot for the sake of completeness and for instigation. "Thou art the Brahman!"—this he says because [the sacrificer] thinks, "What have I become? What have I become? "Thou art Savitṛ of true impulsion"—this he says to him, "Whatever thou art, that thou art.
"This is the thunderbolt; with it, prosper me," he says as he hands over the wooden sword (sphya). The wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus [wins] the kingdom.

He subdues him; he hands him over from one to another. By means of that, he goes about subduing the kingdom from one to another. Therefore, these [people] bring tribute to him, subdued from one to another. With that wooden sword (sphya), they prepare the gambling-ground. There they gamble with a four-year-old cow. Indeed, he has consecrated himself to hope; the four-year-old cow is hope. Thus, he has created hope for him. From that...
He said, "Four hundred dice must be cast."
It was revealed to the king.

Thus there are indeed four classes of men: the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra; it is among these very classes that he causes him to excel. Then, handing over five dice, he says, "He has overcome the quarters. He thus bestows these five quarters upon him for the sake of food.
He gives a field; by means of that field, he becomes firmly established. He chooses a boon; that desire of his is fulfilled.
Whatever desire he may have, he calls upon one whose name is auspicious, thinking, "May that which I have previously uttered not be in vain.
He interchanges the two names, saying, "He is the son of so-and-so; so-and-so is his son," for the attainment of the heavenly world.
This sacrificial rite is equal to the year; indeed, the Daśapeya is interrupted when they go down for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Therefore, they come back while offering oblations, saying: "Svāhā to Apāṃ Napāt! Svāhā to Urjaḥ Napāt! Svāhā to Agni Gṛhapati!"

For the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice: the sacrifice indeed disappeared from the gods; the gods sought it while moving together. In that there is an offering to Savitṛ, they sought it while impelled by Savitṛ. In that there is an offering to Sarasvatī—Sarasvatī is speech—they sought it in speech itself. In that there is an offering to Pūṣan—Pūṣan is cattle—they sought it in cattle themselves. In that there is an offering to Bṛhaspati, [they sought] the *brahman*.
That which belongs to Bṛhaspati, they sought in the Brahman; that which belongs to Indra, Indra sought in his own power (*indriya*);
that which belongs to Varuṇa, Varuṇa sought in himself; that which belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ—Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the year—they sought in the year;
that which belongs to Agni, Agni is indeed all the deities—they sought in the deities; that which belongs to Soma—the plants are indeed of Soma.

They sought him among the plants; since the sacrifice belongs to Viṣṇu, they sought him in the sacrifice itself. They found him in Viṣṇu on the tenth day; therefore this [day] is the tenth, for they found him on the tenth. There are ten cups and ten cup-officiants (camasādhvaryus);
they announce the cups by tens down to the tenth man for the sake of success, for this sacrifice is successful in ten ways. This [cup]—
Verily, they sought after that sacrifice of his and they prospered; therefore, he who sacrifices with this prospers. It consists of seventeen parts and is complete;

Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold, and thus he attains Prajāpati. This is a sacrifice that has fallen into ruin; for it is from the year that a ruined sacrifice is lost. Having obtained it from the very year, he secures it. Indra, indeed...
He slew Vṛtra; these are his various forms which they have approached: these [stars] are the stars, and yonder [sun] is the stars.

Indeed, in the space of the stars the white lotus (puṇḍarīka) is born; this is the form of the kṣatra. He puts on the very form of the kṣatra. There are twelve white lotuses; the year consists of twelve months. Having attained the year, he secures it.
The *rūpa* (golden ornament) belongs to the Hotṛ;

the Hotṛ indeed pertains to Agni, and it does not dawn upon him [directly], yet he causes it to shine for him. The wreath (*sraj*) belongs to the Udgātṛ; the Udgātṛ indeed pertains to the Sun, and thus, having reached yonder Āditya, he leads him upward. The *prāvepas*...
For the Adhvaryu is like the two Yamas; indeed, he is the Adhvaryu.

The horse belongs to the Prastotṛ; for the horse is connected with Prajāpati, and the Prastotṛ is connected with Prajāpati. Moreover, this horse indeed neighs forward, and the Prastotṛ likewise chants forward. The milch-cow belongs to the Pratihartṛ; for she carries [milk] toward [the calf], and the Pratihartṛ likewise chants toward [the response]. The barren cow belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa, so that she may not lead him away from his will. The bull belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, for the sake of possessing virile power. The garment belongs to the Potṛ, for the sake of purity. The ox belongs to the Neṣṭṛ.

The chariot of the Neṣṭṛ belongs to the Agnīdh; it is yoked by means of a hitching-block and is covered with barley. That of the Acchāvāka is like a hitching-block, for this office of the Acchāvāka is a heavenly *hotṛ*-function;
furthermore, it is for the sake of freedom from Varuṇa’s noose. At that time, no sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are given to the members of the assembly (*sadasya*);
they alone are thereby gratified and pleased by her. To the Brahman, twelve pregnant heifers are given.
Speech is indeed the cow, and the mantra is the calf; he places the mantra in speech itself. He becomes worthy of being addressed. They become like cows that are yet to be milked.
There are twelve kinds of milk; he bestows these upon him. Therefore they say of him: "The king is full of milk, he is holy," for as much milk as there is, that is placed within him.

The *Śrāyantīya* is the *Brahmasāman*; they chant the *Yajñāyajñiya* in *Anuṣṭubh* verses; the *Vāravantīya* is the *Agniṣṭomasāman*. Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; he was deprived of his vigor and his heroic power. He beheld this *Sāman* and thereby restored himself. He who is consecrated by the *Rājasūya* is deprived of vigor and heroic power; thus, by means of this very [Sāman], he restores himself to the Brahman.
In the beginning, when [the Veda] was divided, it became the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the *yajus*. Of that, the essence is the *yajñāyajñiya*;
when one sings the *yajñāyajñiya*, he places the essence in the *brahman*. He who is consecrated by the *rājasūya* is indeed deprived of speech;
the *anuṣṭubh* is speech. When the *yajñāyajñiya* occurs in *anuṣṭubh* verses, he places the essence in his speech, or rather, in his sensory power.

He who is consecrated by the Rājasūya falls away from vigor; the Vāravantīya is power and vigor. In that the Vāravantīya becomes the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, it is for the attainment of power and vigor. With the Śrāyantīya they indeed made him hear, and with the Vāravantīya they caused him to restrain himself.
These two are for the complete grasping of power and vigor. Or rather, when he establishes him there in the quarters at that time—

He ascends to that heavenly world so that he may not descend again to this world, or else he might go beyond the people or become intoxicated. Since these are the offerings to the quarters (*diśām aveṣṭayaḥ*), he descends again to this world; one who desires food should sacrifice with these, for these quarters have those deities as their presiding powers, and thus he secures from these quarters the enjoyment of food according to their respective deities.

If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed an offering for Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should pour over each oblation as it is offered; if a Vaiśya, [an offering] for the Viśvedevas; if a Rājanya, [an offering] for Indra. Thus he establishes food-eating in him all at once. This sacrificial rite is indeed the same throughout the year; yet the sacrifice is indeed cut asunder when it comes to a conclusion.

When he employs these *prayuj* verses—some at evening and others in the morning—he thereby employs the two seasons, namely day and night. Six are one set and six are another; there are indeed six seasons, so he employs the seasons themselves. Those two sets together make twelve;
twelve months are a year, so he employs the year itself. A pair of oxen is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for they are already yoked.
"A spotted, four-year-old mare belonging to the Maruts, pregnant"—the Maruts are indeed the clans;
he thus makes him (Agni) the child of the clans, and therefore he is dear to the clans, for the child is dear. "Born from Aditi, a white cow, pregnant"—Aditi is indeed this earth;
he thus makes him the child of her, and therefore he is difficult to overcome, for he is her child. And these...

The messengers of truth, the offspring of Savitṛ, the gods, when approaching for victory over the Asuras, deposited their truth with the Aśvins and Pūṣan; Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and by means of speech one sends forth the truth.
I instructed him in this; he became a king.
Thus they place faith in him as he is consecrated; he offers the Agnihotra for a year for the sake of continuity.

First he performs the Agniṣṭoma, which is the Jyotiṣṭoma; for the Agniṣṭoma is the mouth of the sacrifice, and by seizing the very mouth of the sacrifice, he ascends to the Soma-pressing. Now this [next] is the Triṣṭoma; its morning pressing is the Trivṛt-stoma and its midday pressing is the Pañcadaśa-stoma.
The Trivṛt is indeed brilliance, and the Pañcadaśa is the ruling power (kṣatra); thus he bestows brilliance upon his ruling power. Indeed, even here there is no [lack thereof].

It is extended as seventeenfold; Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati. Since the sacrifice is extended, it is thereby seventeenfold and uninterrupted. The midday pressing is fifteenfold and the third pressing is twenty-onefold; the twenty-onefold is the people (*viś*), and the fifteenfold is the nobility (*kṣatra*). Thus he has established this nobility within the people for him. All [is thus accomplished].

The Pavamāna lauds of the Abhiṣecanīya consist of thirty-four verses; there are thirty-three deities, and it is they who are thus gratified and pleased by this. Now, as for this thirty-fourth [verse], Prajāpati is indeed the thirty-fourth; thus he attains Prajāpati himself.
This is indeed a transition between the Stomas, occurring out of sequence when the Stomas are unequal; but because the Pavamānas are equal, there is no such transition.

By that, as before, he prospers through himself by means of the Agniṣṭoma; he becomes meritorious through himself. The Ukthas are offspring, the Ukthas are cattle; in that there is the Ukthya, it is for the sake of continuity. He who departs from the Sava does not attain the Sava; he who departs from the Sāmans becomes worse off after having performed the consecration. By [departing] from those Sāmans which belong to the kings of the gods, it is by that very [means] that he [does not depart].

He does not depart from the Sāmans; for the Pṛṣṭhas are indeed these Sāmans. In that they perform the Pṛṣṭhas, he thereby does not depart from the Sāmans. By means of those Sāmans which belong to the kings of the gods, he prospers in this world; by those which belong to the kings of men, he prospers in yonder world.
Thus, by means of these, he prospers in both worlds—both in this one and in yonder one—as they flow forth in the *udvatī* verses.
The form of the *anuṣṭubh* is indeed a height, and the Rājanya is connected with the *anuṣṭubh*; therefore, they press [the Soma] on heights. The *anuṣṭubh* is first, and the *anuṣṭubh* is last;

the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and by means of speech they thus set forth and by means of speech they impel. The *anuṣṭubh* dedicated to Sūrya is the last, for the attainment of the heavenly world. The *bahiṣpavamāna* of the Keśavapanīya sacrifice consists of the twenty-one-fold stoma.

"The twenty-first is the highest of the consecration (abhiṣecanīya)"; for the twenty-first is the *viḍ* (the people), and the seventeenfold is the *kṣatra* (the ruling power). Thus he is consecrated from the midst of the *viḍ*; therefore, he is dear to the *viḍ*, for he is consecrated from the midst of the *viḍ*.
