When he establishes him there in the quarters, he ascends to the heavenly world; were he not to descend again to this world, [he would remain there].
Or he may go among the people, or he may become intoxicated; for when this [sacrifice] has a *pratīcīna-stoma*, it descends again to this world.
He prospers;
he prospers by means of the Agniṣṭoma itself through this very [rite].
Vṛtra was indeed the waters; they lay encircled by him. Those that were released from him became living, worthy of sacrifice. Vṛtra was indeed the mountain;

those that run forth after having broken through it are living, worthy of sacrifice. When he takes [the water] of flowing rivers, he takes from those very ones that are living and worthy of sacrifice.
He draws it against the current to avoid a useless offering. He takes it in the sight of the sun, so that it may be accompanied by Indra.

He draws [the water] with the words, "These waters are rich in oblation"; thus he draws them as indeed rich in oblation. He draws them while the sun is visible; thereby he takes hold of the subsequent sacrificial rite. He draws with an *anuṣṭubh* verse; the *anuṣṭubh* indeed comprises all the meters;
thus he draws them with all the meters. This [meter] is the summit of the meters; he causes him to attain the summit among his peers.

He takes [the water] with four [verses] and deposits it with three; that makes seven. The Śakvarī metre has seven feet, and cattle are connected with the Śakvarī; thus he wins cattle. Night indeed enters the waters when it becomes day; therefore the waters are black by day. Day enters the waters at night; therefore the waters are white by night. In that he takes [them] by day, he takes both day and night. By day, indeed, belong men...
The gods perform the sacrifice by night; therefore, one seeks glory through the nights. Having completed the sacrifice, men indeed descend [from it].
The waters are truly all the gods; when they carry water around, they bestow the sacrifice upon the waters.
Whatever else is performed for him at his sacrifice, that which they omit from the sacrifice becomes a flaw, and he follows after that flaw.

The Rakṣases descend upon the sacrifice; the waters are indeed slayers of the Rakṣases, for the Rakṣases do not cross over the waters. When they carry the waters around, it is to prevent the Rakṣases from following after. Those waters which he takes by day are the womb of those offspring that are sighted; after them these [waters] are born. Those which he takes by night are the womb of those offspring that are not sighted; after them these are born. Thus, both kinds [of offspring] are produced.

He procreates offspring; he places the Ātrī and Ādya [cups] in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed. This, indeed, is the unconquered [portion]; moreover, it is here that the deities observe the fast for that night. The gods did not perceive the morrow of the sacrifice; they perceived this very thing as the morrow of the sacrifice, namely the Vasatīvarī waters. In that they take the Vasatīvarī waters and observe the fast, [they secure] the morrow.
Verily, they fast after having offered this sacrifice; moreover, the Viśve Devas are indeed the waters, so they fast after having offered all these deities.

If the sun should set while the [Soma] has not yet been drawn for one who has established the sacred fires and is a Soma-sacrificer, then the portions should be taken from his water-jar, for from that [jar] they have already been drawn. They should hold the fire above and then draw [the Soma]; thus he draws them with light. [He should take] gold.

When it is in his hand, he then takes it; gold is indeed truth, so by means of truth he takes them. A boon is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), so by means of a boon he takes them. Whatever wealth there may be that one does not intend to give away, that should be given.
He takes [the butter] first in the *pracaraṇī* ladle, for this indeed moves forward first. Water is the essence of Soma that has entered within;

Agni is all the deities, and water belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*). The pressing-stones are the mouth of the sacrifice. Impelled by Savitṛ, he thus seeks the essence of Soma in the waters with all the deities. "May Agni hear my call with the fuel!"—in whatever fire [this is done].

He offers; regarding that, he says, "May the waters hear. He thereby addresses those very waters which he approaches. "And the goddess Dhiṣaṇā"—Dhiṣaṇā the goddess is indeed speech; he thereby addresses speech. "Hear now the sacrifice, O pressing-stones, you who know!"—for the pressing-stones are the mouth of the sacrifice.
"May the god Savitṛ hear my call," he says, for the sake of impulsion.
O Hotṛ, impel the oblation!
Thus he says this when he gives the *praisha* for the sacrifice.

With the words "Forward with the sacred prayer," he approaches the sacrifice by means of the sacred prayer itself; he approaches with the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa, for he moves forward first, and moreover, Mitra and Varuṇa are the lords of the waters. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice, and the waters are the mouth of the sacrifice; thus, by means of the mouth of the sacrifice, he approaches the mouth of the sacrifice, wherever he may hear the Hotṛ reciting the morning litany.

The Adhvaryu should take up that water which he does not hear; for if he were to hear it, he would become deaf, since his speech is thereby cut off. Now, when he offers it, he takes it up as having already become an oblation, and indeed as being already sprinkled with ghee. Having thrown a blade of grass into it, he offers; thus he offers in that which possesses fire and possesses a proper receptacle. The Adhvaryu would become blind if he were to offer where there is no receptacle. Ghee, indeed, is the gods’...

Having made [the vessel] into a *vajra*, they indeed pour [the Soma] over it while slaying the Moon; therefore, he causes the oblation to float away. Furthermore, thinking "lest the oblation be poured out," he causes the oblation to float away with the words, "Thou art the furrower. He brings it near with the words, "For the imperishability of the ocean, lift ye up! This is for the imperishability of the waters; for the essence of the Soma has entered into the waters, and the essence of the waters has entered into the Soma.

Now, indeed, Night and Dawn are the mistresses of the water, of the Soma, and of its essence. It was by means of this oblation, as their allotted portion, that he begged for the water, the Soma, and its essence from them.
"Both Day and Night should be drawn as *vasatīvarī* waters," they say; on the previous day he draws one set, and before the rising of the sun the other.
Thus, both Day and Night have been drawn by him as *vasatīvarī* waters on the previous day.
One [priest] takes [the waters] before sunrise, while another takes them after; thus he has made both of these taken at once.

Those which are taken in the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa and those which are the *nigrābhyā* waters—these two kinds he anoints together above the *cātvāla* pit; he thereby effects their unification and bestows friendship upon them. They are drawn out from the *cātvāla*; this indeed is...
The womb of the waters is from its own womb; they are taken out for the sake of non-spilling.
"Bring forth the waters, O Adhvaryu! Om! (The editor has emended *pra* to *praḥ*).
"Thus [is] the sacrifice of the ignorant"—this is what he thereby says.
And so we have bowed down; look upon this one as well.

"This one has been subdued by me"—this is what he says when he offers [the oblation] if it is an Agniṣṭoma; for they do not pass beyond the Agniṣṭoma by means of either the Stotra or the Śastra. He thus continues the sacrificial rite of the Agniṣṭoma itself. If it is an Ukthya, he touches the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*);
for the enclosing-sticks are outside of the fire, and the Ukthas are outside of the enclosing-sticks. Thus, he continues the sacrificial rite through the Ukthas themselves.

If it is an Atirātra, he should enter the Havirdhāna shed while reciting this very Yajus formula. For the Havirdhāna is beyond the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), and the night is beyond the Pr̥ṣṭha-stotras; thus he continues the sacrificial rite through the night itself.
[The text asks: "The mind is a thief, speech is a liar; by what, then, are the Soma-draughts taken, and by what are they offered? One should reply: "By the *r̥ta*, indeed, by the truth."
Gold is indeed grasped by means of the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and by means of truth; it is offered by means of the cosmic order.
The sacrifice is indeed brought forth for the gods, for men, and for the heavenly world. When he says, "For the heart thee," by that it is for the gods;

when he says, "For the mind thee," by that it is for men; and when he says, "For heaven thee, for Sūrya thee," by that he causes the sacrifice to ascend after him to the heavenly world. Indeed, the sacrifice is split apart for whomever it is brought; therefore, it follows after him.

He causes [the sacrificer] to ascend to the heavenly world when he says, "Bestow the priestly offices among the gods in heaven. For by the priestly offices the sacrifice is extended; indeed, by means of the priestly offices he extends the sacrifice.
Recite the invitatory verse for the gods who come at dawn.

Thus, the meters are indeed the gods who travel at dawn; he recites this from the meters before the utterance of speech. He recites the *prātaranuvāka* (morning litany) before the first sound of speech; verily, he takes hold of speech for the sacrificer. At this time, the sacrificer does not wash his hands;
when he recites the first verse containing the word "water," that is the sacrificer’s morning bath (*prātar-avanega*). It is where those waters [are found].

They indeed carry away the sacrifice from the waters when one recites that first verse containing the word "water" (apsumatī). By reciting that first verse containing the word "water," he takes the sacrifice back from the waters. The morning litany (prātaranuvāka) belongs to all the gods, for the waters are indeed the All-gods (viśve devāḥ).
In that he recites that first verse containing the word "water," he attains all these deities and pervades them all, just as [one would pervade] water.
Having thus seated the *sāmidhenī* verses for the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), they indeed recite the *sāmidhenīs* after the oblation;
for at this time, the Soma is indeed the oblation. Therefore, having brought down the Soma, he recites [the *sāmidhenīs*] and brings together both the *gāyatrī* and the *jagatī*.
Thus, he brings two meters together into one meter: the *bṛhatī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and the *kakubh*.

He unifies those two meters into one meter—the Bṛhatī and the Anuṣṭubh—and thus he unifies those six meters into one meter. One should make the meters have the Bṛhatī and the Anuṣṭubh as their introductory parts for one who has violated the sacrifice;
the Anuṣṭubh is indeed speech, and by means of speech he heals him. [He should do so] equally with the Triṣṭubh and the Jagatī.

And he should recite [the *jagatī*] for one who desires cattle; the *jagatī* is indeed cattle, so he becomes possessed of cattle. He recites all the meters; the meters are Prajāpati, and thus he attains Prajāpati himself. This morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) is the hymn (*uktha*) of Prajāpati;
he should recite it when the dawn has broken but before the sun has risen, for this is the world of Prajāpati. The morning litany is indeed a means of purification.
By this, he purifies the sacrificer himself. He should recite a hundred [verses] for one who desires long life; man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and a vigor of a hundredfold;
thus he attains both life and vigor. He should recite seven hundred and twenty [verses] for one who desires cattle;
there are indeed as many days and nights in a year; by means of the year itself, he secures cattle for him. He should recite a thousand [verses] for one who desires heaven.
As far as a thousand [bricks] extend, so far this world is the counterpart of the heavenly world. He recites an unlimited number for the attainment of the unlimited;
he concludes with a *paṅkti* verse, thereby securing the subsequent sacrificial rite.
These are indeed the foot-washing waters of the sacrifice: the Agnīdh for men and the Neṣṭṛ for women. When he sits upon the lap of the Neṣṭṛ, it is a productive union that comes into being;
when he then pours the water forward, he places seed into that very union. The wife pours it forward, for from the wife offspring are born; she pours it forward with her thigh.
For offspring are born after the thigh; he causes them to proceed along the right thigh, for offspring are born after the right thigh.

He causes them to proceed from within, for offspring are born from within. If he were to cause them to proceed toward the south, he would consign them to the world of the fathers; but since he causes them to proceed upward toward the north, he causes them to be born into the world of men.

The Udgātṛ is indeed related to Prajāpati; when being sprinkled with water, the Udgātṛ takes the seed from his wife when he says, "In the sight of you two, may I deposit all my seed. Thus he does not take it away. At the twelfth Stotra he pours forth water;
twelve months are a year, and there are twelve Stotras in the Agniṣṭoma. Water is peace; when he pours forth water at that time, he brings about peace.

With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes it up, for he takes it up impelled by Savitṛ. With the words, "By the arms of the Aśvins," for the Aśvins are indeed the two Adhvaryu priests among the gods; with the words, "By the hands of Pūṣan," he takes it by means of the deities themselves. With the words, "Thou art a pressing-stone (grāvan)," for this [stone] has been given to the gods; with the words, "The performer of the sacrifice for the gods," for he performs the sacrifice for the gods; [and] "For Indra."

"Thee, most well-pressed, honeyed, and full of milk"—for the sacrifice belongs to Indra; indeed, at this time, the other deities follow after Indra. "Thee for Indra, accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras"—for at this time both the Vasus and the Rudras follow after him. "Thee for Indra, accompanied by the Ādityas"—for at this time the Ādityas follow after him. "Thee for Agni, the bestower of increase of wealth."

Agni, indeed, is all the deities, for these deities now follow him. "For Viṣṇu, thee!"—for the sacrifice is Viṣṇu; the Upāṃśusavana stone is the vyāna breath, and the Aṃśu vessels are the progeny; thus he places the vyāna breath within the progeny. "Ye are strengthening, slayers of Vṛtra"—this, indeed, is the Soma-drink of the waters; Viśvāmitra discovered this Soma-drink of the waters for him.
The rivers bend down to avoid being milked; water indeed is this Soma-drink.
He who knows the Soma-drink of the waters truly unites himself with that Soma-drink, and he does not come to ruin among them; he exerts his virility among them.
"O Soma, that light of yours in heaven"—Soma is indeed *vāja*; the moon is its third part, and this which purifies is the third part.

That with which they sacrifice—that third [element]—he has sustained through the embryos; by this he bestows the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). This one who purifies (the wind) sustains food by means of this. That with which they sacrifice is indeed the truth of that *vāja* (strength/food); the *vājina* (possessor of strength) is food, the *vājina* is the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*), and the *vājina* is the thunderbolt.
Having gathered these bodies of his together, they cause him, having become possessed of a whole body, to swell—the thunderbolt.

The two pressing-stones are indeed the jaws; the two pressing-boards are the palate. Now, something cruel is done in the sacrifice when he says, "O two *dhiṣaṇās*, you who are praised, be praised! [By saying this] he truly pacifies it.
They cause the Soma to swell with the *vasatīvarī* waters; for Soma is not made to swell by Soma, but Soma is made to swell by water.

With the *nigrābhya* waters they swell the *upāṃśu* cup, for from it the other Soma cups are drawn. The *upāṃśu* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the other cups are the limbs. If they were to swell [the Soma] from another source, they would sever the sacrifice from the vital breath. Eight times he presses in the morning; the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables.

The Gāyatrī indeed stretches out the Gāyatrī at the morning pressing. Of old, the gods and the Asuras were in conflict. Those gods saw that the sacrifice was to be completed in the Upāṃśu cup; they completed it in the Upāṃśu cup. Therefore, the sacrifice is to be completed in the Upāṃśu cup itself. He presses eight times at the morning pressing; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables; verily he obtains the Gāyatrī.

In that there are eleven [syllables], it is by means of the *triṣṭubh*; in that there are twelve, it is by means of the *jagatī*. He separates [the breaths] three times; for there are three pressings (*savana*), and thus he obtains the pressings themselves. Indeed, they completed the sacrifice in the *upāṃśu* cup; with that sacrifice being completed, unharmed, and having become [realized], they proceed. He separates [the breaths] three times, for these vital breaths are three: the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the in-breath (*apāna*), and the diffused breath (*vyāna*); moreover, these worlds are three.

He attains these very worlds: the *upāṃśu* cup is yonder world, the *antaryāma* is the intermediate space, and the *upayāma* is this earth; for when they are drawn with the *upayāma*, they are indeed drawn by means of this [earth]. Thus, these [soma juices] are not spilt, for they are drawn by means of this; since they are drawn with a vessel (*sthālī*), they are drawn by means of this, for this [earth] is the foundation for that. Thus, these [juices] are not spilt, for they are indeed drawn by means of this.

They are taken with a wooden vessel, or rather, they are taken by means of this [earth], for she is the womb of the trees; thus these [Soma cups] are not spilt, since they are taken by means of her. He sets them down with the words, "This is thy womb"; for this earth is indeed the womb of Soma, and from her Soma is born; he thus places him in his own womb. This earth is indeed the vessel of the gods; he who knows thus [attains it].

One obtains a vessel that is more excellent; however, one should not scrutinize the Brāhmaṇa as a vessel. He who would be worthy of a vessel is taken without being held with a *upayāma* formula, for creatures subsist upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is not held with a *upayāma*. It is taken unpurified by the strainer, for creatures subsist upon the vital breath which is unpurified by the strainer. It is offered unseated, for creatures subsist upon the vital breath which is unseated. [It is] purified by the strainer.
Or rather, these other *soma* juices are [impure], whereas this *upāṃśu* cup is purified by speech; therefore he says, "Flow clear for Vācaspati," for it is indeed purified by speech.

He purifies it with the stalks (*aṃśu*); the stalks are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), so he purifies it by means of the vital breaths. He purifies it with two [stalks] at a time, for these vital breaths come in pairs. With the words, "O god, you are the purifier of the gods," he purifies the *soma* with *soma*.

"Thou art made one's own," he says; verily, he makes the breath his own. "May Tvaṣṭṛ fashion thee with the mind," he says; by means of the mind alone, he attains the breath. "Svāhā! Thee, O well-being, for Sūrya! he says; for all Soma offerings are indeed offered to the deity Sūrya. Moreover, these are the dear bodies of the gods; verily, he wins them.
"Thee for the gods who drink through the rays," he says; the rays are indeed the gods who drink through the rays.

The enclosing-sticks are the rays; that Āditya is the Āhavanīya fire; he thus gratifies them. He offers while standing upright, for standing upright one is more powerful. If he should hate someone, he should offer while standing crookedly; he strikes down the vital breaths of that person, and he becomes afflicted with consumption.
If he should practice sorcery, he should remain standing until he collapses; Agni, hastening toward the oblation, [destroys] him instantly.
If he should desire, "May Parjanya rain," he should wipe [the fire] around it and then wipe upwards;

for from yonder, from the plants, this [fire] rains; thus he brings the plants closer to the rain. If he should desire, "May Parjanya rain," he should wipe around it and then wipe downwards; by means of Vaiśvānara alone he strikes down the rain. It must not be covered; for if he were to cover it, [the rain would be obstructed].

He should block the breath of one whom he hates; that person will be liable to die. He should block the breath of him whom he hates if he intends to practice sorcery; thus he indeed blocks his very breath.
Here I shut off the breath of such-and-such a person, the son of such-and-such a lineage.
Thus he should cover it; verily, he covers his very breath.
Thus:
"Here I place [this] in the breath of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so."

Thus, when performing a malevolent rite, he should set it down; he sets it down upon the vital breath itself, and the sacrificer becomes liable to die. When not performing a malevolent rite, he should set it down with the formula: "For the vital breath!"

They spread out the filter for the sake of supporting the out-breath and the in-breath; it is taken with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support," for by the in-breath the out-breath is indeed supported, for the sake of supporting the out-breath. The Antaryāma cup is indeed the intermediate space, and these creatures are the intermediate space; in that he sets down this vessel containing the *sūda* (clarified butter), he places essence within the creatures. The gods and the Asuras were contending; those gods...
They saw the Upāṃśu cup and took it; before the Stotra and before the Śastra, they rose up to offer it.
The Asuras perceived them, thinking, "They are indeed offering it! Taking up their thunderbolt, they rushed at them. The gods saw the Antaryāma cup and took it;
with it, they shielded themselves from the Asuras in these worlds. Then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. That—

He who, knowing thus, draws the Antaryāma cup, by means of the Antaryāma itself excludes his rival from these worlds; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing, while the Upāṃśusavana stone is the diffused breath (vyāna). When this pressing-stone is placed between these two vessels, it serves to separate the out-breathing and the in-breathing. He who sacrifices with these [cups] by means of which these two [breaths] exist...

This very pressing-stone is indeed the *upāṃśusavana*; the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* [libations] are the out-breath and the in-breath, while the *upāṃśusavana* is the diffused breath (*vyāna*). Because these two vessels do not leave this pressing-stone until the third pressing, therefore, when a man is asleep, all his other senses depart, but the out-breath and in-breath do not leave him; and so it is that he awakens again.

Therefore, having slept, they wake up again. The out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*) are the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* cups; the through-breath (*vyāna*) is the *upāṃśusavana* stone. Because these two vessels do not leave this pressing-stone until the third pressing, therefore birds, though flying in the air with their wings spread, do not fall. And because it strikes [the stone] again, therefore they draw themselves back together again—the out-breath and the in-breath.

The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [cups] are the out-breath; the Upāṃśusavana stone is the diffused breath (vyāna). Because these two vessels are used again, therefore these two breaths below strike [the body]. They indeed injure the Soma when they press it; the Adhvaryu is the first to press, and he becomes one who is deprived of his strength.
Having pressed that part which is the root, this part of it is most connected with the gods; thus, indeed, he does not become deprived of his strength.
Indeed, he who, knowing the field of the gods (*devakṣetra*), hands it over to another, meets with calamity. The vessels are indeed the field of the gods.

Wherever the Adhvaryu first offers the Soma, there the deities sit waiting for him, thinking, "He will surely come here; he will not go elsewhere. If he were to offer elsewhere than that, he would hand over what is his own to others and would become destitute.

This indeed belongs to the Adhvaryu: when he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, if he were to depart without having offered after calling for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he would depart from that which is his own; he would become one who possesses nothing. This indeed belongs to the Adhvaryu: namely, the [animal] dedicated to Vāyu. If he were to call for the *āśrāvaṇa* without having seized the victim for Vāyu, it would be cut off from that which is his own; he would become one who possesses nothing. Therefore, he who knows thus...
Whether he calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* after having offered the oblation or without having offered it, he falls away; much of his own property is lost, and he is severed from his own.
By offering an animal to Vāyu and calling for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he becomes possessed of his own property.

The exponents of Brahman say: "What is done at the sacrifice because of which some animals take food with their hands while others take it with their mouths? Because the *upāṃśu* cup is taken with the hand, therefore the monkey, man, and elephant take food with their hands; for the *vāyavya* cup is indeed the mouth, and since the other cups are not taken in the *vāyavya* manner, therefore the other animals take food with their mouths—the exponents of Brahman say.

They ask: "What is performed at the sacrifice because of which animals established themselves immediately after birth, while humans do so only after a year? The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [libations] are indeed like other animals, but man is measured by the sacrifice itself. The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma are the out-breath and the in-breath; because these two cups are offered while still unpressed, therefore animals established themselves immediately after birth.

The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the year; the year consists of twelve months. Since these other cups are set down, therefore a person, once born, becomes firmly established in the year. "O Soma, that which is thy invincible name, O watchful one"—this is indeed the drinking of Soma for Soma;
he truly provides the drinking of Soma with the drinking of Soma for him who knows the drinking of Soma for Soma.

One is not deprived of the drinking of Soma; for Soma indeed desired these quarters—east, west, south, and north—and by means of these quarters he sweeps him clean, he prospers through them, he attains his desire, and he truly goes according to his wish.
Women become desirous of him; whichever woman he should desire, let him meditate upon her with his mind at that time, and she will surely desire him.
When he says, "Remember me, O Amba! Remember! he means, "May the enemy know [me]"; or rather, he means, "Know [me] together with him.
There were indeed four teats of Pṛśni; with three she milked for the gods, while one remained tied up with a cord.
Indra alone perceived it, and with that he milked for Indra himself. That is his "Kauśika-ness" (the state of being connected by a cord), which he expresses when he says this.
Like the Brahmins of Kauśika.
Thus he approaches the four *nigrābha* [libations]. There are indeed four kinds of milk; verily, he obtains as much milk as there is. He gathers it three times;

therefore, on this [earth] there are three portions: in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. He approaches the four *nigrābha* and gathers it three times; that makes seven. The *śakvarī* [verse] consists of seven feet, and cattle are connected with the *śakvarī*; verily, he wins cattle. Nine times...
He approaches the *nigrābha* water; he gathers it thrice. That makes twelve. Twelve months are a year, and there are twelve stotras in the Agniṣṭoma;
this is the measure of the sacrifice. Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness. The gods drove away that darkness from him.
That first darkness they drove away became a black cow; that second became a red one.

That which was the third was Balakṣī; she was released in her own form. Because Balakṣa becomes the filter (*pavitra*), the bright [Soma] is drawn from it. This is indeed the filter of the sacrificer; by means of this, he purifies the sacrificer himself.
It should be unsewn; for he has thereby made it for himself. If it were sewn elsewhere, that would be a non-filter for the sacrificer.
The Aindravāyava cup is indeed speech; for at first, that speech was one-fold, as long as it had not yet been differentiated. Indra said, "Let them draw Soma for me here as well;
I shall cause this speech of yours to be differentiated. He indeed caused speech to be differentiated by means of speech itself.
In that the cup for Indra and Vāyu is drawn, it is for the separation of speech; he draws first for Vāyu and last for Vāyu, while for Indra he draws in the middle.

For this speech is held apart in the middle by means of power (*indriya*); he who knows thus speaks speech endowed with power. The gods indeed sought to slay Soma, but they were unable to slay him, for Vāyu was within him.
The gods desired to seize that vital breath (*prāṇa*), saying, "Come back to us! He said, "Let there be a share for me. They said, "Choose it.

He said, "Let the vessels belong to my deity alone. Therefore, one-fourth of the vessel belongs to Vāyu; thus they are called *vāyavya* vessels. Then the gods slew Soma; being slain, he began to stink. Therefore the gods were repulsed by him.
That Vāyu said, "I shall make this Soma palatable for you; let there be a portion for me. They said, "Choose [your boon].
He said, "Let the cups be drawn with me at their head. Vāyu blew through it from the middle; he made it palatable.
Therefore the cups are drawn with Vāyu at their head, and therefore they pour out what has been fermented in a windy place. The gods, indeed, [performed] the morning pressing.

They were unable to lift it up at the third pressing; at that time Vāyu was present, and the gods directed him toward the morning pressing. By means of him, they lifted up the morning pressing. This is why the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*) is drawn at the morning pressing. Vāyu is indeed breath; it is by means of breath that they thus lift up the sacrifice from the beginning. The gods, indeed, desired to slay Vṛtra; he [Vṛtra] said to Mitra:

"I am Mitra; I will not kill," they said. "Kill him! he replied. "Let there be a share for me," he said. "Choose it," they said. He said, "Let me mix the Soma with milk alone. Therefore, the cattle departed from him, thinking, "He is Mitra, yet he is a deceiver. For milk belongs to the cattle. In that he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk, [he wins] through the cattle.

Verily, he establishes him in proper order when he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk; it is for the sake of its being for two deities: that which is cold belongs to Mitra, and that which is heated belongs to Varuṇa. Mitra is indeed the Brahman and Varuṇa is the Kṣatra; thus he places milk in both the Brahman and the Kṣatra. Therefore, the Brahman and the Kṣatra are most rich in milk. There are five [cups].

The deities of the Brāhmaṇa are Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, and Sarasvatī; therefore, other men resort to the Brāhmaṇa, for his deities are the most numerous. Among those, three belong specifically to the Śrotriya: Agni, Bṛhaspati, and Sarasvatī; therefore, non-Śrotriyas resort to the Śrotriya, for his [deities] are the most numerous among them.

The deities approach the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; when he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa with milk, he bestows milk upon those very deities. Formerly, they used to draw the Soma-libations separately for Mitra and Varuṇa; consequently, those creatures were seized by one another in mutual conflict. Then they drew the Soma together for Mitra and Varuṇa, and from that it became well-ordered. Therefore...
He mixes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk; indeed, by means of Mitra he thus makes Varuṇa fit, and by means of Varuṇa he makes Mitra fit.

When Mitra had slain Vṛtra, Varuṇa seized him; he (Mitra) then sought protection among the gods. They said, "Seek protection from Varuṇa. He sought protection from Varuṇa. He (Varuṇa) said, "Let there be a share for me. They said, "Choose one. He said, "Together with [the other]."

Regarding the formula, "Mixing Soma with milk," when he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk, it is for the sake of the sacrificer's freedom from Varuṇa’s noose. If an enemy should be excessively powerful over him, he should grasp the thumb with the finger; if [the enemy] follows after him, he should grasp the finger with the thumb.
Therefore,
O Bṛhaspati, whatever rival or kinsman should assail us, or whoever should overwhelm us, O Mitra and Varuṇa.
I cast this lower one down, so that I may think myself supreme.
Thus the highest one indeed perceives.

The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session at Kurukṣetra—Agni, Makha, Vāyu, and Indra. They said, "Whichever among us first succeeds, that shall be for all of us. Of them, Makha indeed succeeded; he desired that [success] for himself and did not share it with them. They sought to seize it from him by force. He produced three [steps] from this very place, and from this, the bow; that belongs to the three and to the bow.
And having fixed that [bowstring], he stepped aside; it did not dare to strike him. He, the archer, stood firm, warding off the pain.

Indra said to the ants, "Eat this bowstring! They replied, "If we are touched by this, we shall not be able to live; let there be a share for us. He said, "Then you shall subsist on its sap. Therefore, these [ants] [survive] even from dry [wood].

They licked the moisture while it was still wet; for they subsisted upon its sap. They indeed bit through its bowstring, and the pain from that bow caused its head to burst forth, whereupon it became the *samrāj* (sovereign). Then the others divided the rest into three parts: Agni took the fore-part, Indra the middle, and Vāyu the hind-part. Therefore, the morning pressing belongs to Agni, the midday pressing to Indra, and [the third] to the Viśvedevas.

The third pressing is Vāyu, for the All-gods are indeed the out-breath and in-breath; the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups are the out-breath and in-breath, while the Upāṃśusavana stone is the diffused breath (vyāna).
The cup for Indra and Vāyu is speech; that for Mitra and Varuṇa is skill and will; that for the Aśvins is hearing; the Śukra and Manthin cups are the two eyes; the Āgrayaṇa vessel is the self;
the Ukthya cups are the limbs; the Dhruva cup is life-span; the Ṛtu vessels are the breasts; the Droṇakalaśa is the head; the two Kalaśas are the belly; and the two [smaller] jars are the jaws.

The two pressing-boards are the tongue; the pressing-stones are the teeth; the axle-pins are the enclosing-sticks; the nose is the high altar; the crest-lock is the sacrificial post; the head is the oblation-holder;

the back is the Āgnīdhra shed; the belly is the Sadas; what is within the belly are the hearths (dhiṣṇyas); the two hands are the Āgnīdhra and Mārjālīya sheds; the two heels are the Gārhapatya fire; the feet are the altar. This, indeed, is Prajāpati.
He is worthy of the sacrificial vessel; indeed, he knows him who knows thus.

These nine cups are drawn in the morning; indeed, these are drawn as the nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The tenth, the cup for the Aśvins, is drawn;
this is the out-breath (*vyāna*) that is drawn, for the navel is the tenth that is drawn. The third [of each set] is offered, for this breath is the third among the breaths;
it is for the continuity of the breaths. All these cups possess a *stotra*, a *śastra*, and a *nidāna*; they are provided with a foundation.
He who knows thus becomes [successful]. The Hotṛ indeed sacrificed the Upāṃśu cup this morning; by that these [cups] possess the *uktha*.
And as for the *tūṣṇīṃśaṃsa* which the Hotṛ recites, by that alone these possess the *uktha*. These nine cups are drawn in the morning; they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* with nine verses;
by those [verses] these [cups] possess the *sāman*. The Āśvina cup possesses the *sāman* through the *hiṃkāra*; the Aindravāyava cup [possesses it] through the Aindravāyava [verse].

The Maitrāvaruṇa cup is drawn with a verse addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa; the Śukra and Manthin cups with one addressed to Indra; the Āgrayaṇa with one addressed to the Viśve Devas. The Ukthya is drawn for the sake of the Uktha, and the Dhruva for the sake of the Uktha—for the sake of continuity. The Aindrāgna is for the sake of continuity. The Adhvaryu offers the Marutvatīya cups and the Hotṛ utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.
By means of this, they bestow the vital breaths; with the same mantra with which the Adhvaryu hands over [the offering], the Hotṛ [responds].
He accepts [the offering] for the protection of the vital breaths. Prajāpati himself was the Hotṛ; he became exhausted.

The gods ran toward him with the offerings to the dual deities (dvidevatya). The dual-deity offerings are indeed the vital breaths. When the Adhvaryu, having offered the dual-deity oblations, quickly hastens toward the Hotṛ, he thereby fortifies the Hotṛ with the vital breaths at each and every *vaṣaṭ*-call. At each and every *vaṣaṭ*-call...

The Hotṛ reaches the end of the vital breaths; for the dual-deity offerings are indeed the vital breaths. When the Adhvaryu, having offered the dual-deity oblations, hastens toward the Hotṛ, he thereby pierces the Hotṛ with the vital breaths. For the dual-deity offerings are the vital breaths, and the *iḍā* is cattle. If he were to invoke the *iḍā* without having partaken of the dual-deity offerings, he would exclude the vital breaths from the cattle. Now, when...
Having consumed the portions belonging to the two deities, he invokes the *iḍā*. Having thus placed the vital breaths within himself, he then invokes the cattle.

Soma is indeed power (*indriya*), and cattle are power; in that he consumes the Soma, he places power within himself. He consumes the portion for the Aśvins by moving around on all sides; therefore, he hears from all directions.
In the morning: whatever vessel is empty and not released, the *rakṣases* follow it and descend upon the sacrifice; this applies to the cup for Indra and Vāyu.

He places the sacrificial cake for Mitra and Varuṇa, the curd-mixture for the Aśvins, and the parched grains; this is so that there may be no deficiency. Indeed, the sacrifice is torn asunder when the pressings conclude. If these vessels remain set out until the third pressing, it is for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice. He releases the vessels while the Vāyavyā verse is being recited; for Vāyu is breath, and by means of breath [the sacrifice is sustained].
The sacrifice is continuous through the vital breath; by means of the vital breath alone, one continues the sacrifice.
With one and with ten, O Vāyu, you travel for your own sake; with two, twenty, three, and thirty yoked horses you carry us for our welfare; unyoke them here.

Thus he says: "The Adhvaryu's vessel, which has been understood through its release and set aside for the Pratiprasthātṛ, if he should desire: 'May I place that which is outside within the village, and that which is within the village outside,'" [he should do so].
I hereby drive out this man, the son of such-and-such a father and such-and-such a mother, from such-and-such a clan.
Thus, having set aside the Adhvaryu’s vessel.
Here I establish this man, the son of such-and-such a person and of such-and-such a woman, in such-and-such a clan.

Thus he should set down the *pratiprasthāna* cup; that which is outside he places within the village, and that which is within he places outside. Indeed, the *adhvaryu*’s vessel belongs to the sacrificer, while the *pratiprasthāna* vessel belongs to the enemy. If he should desire, "May I make him equal in strength with his enemy," they should both draw [the soma] in parallel, set them down in parallel, and offer them in parallel.
He thus makes him equal in vigor with his rival. The Adhvaryu’s vessel is indeed a superior vessel, while the Pratiprasthātṛ’s vessel is inferior.
If he should desire, "May he become more wretched," he should draw [the cup] first, set it down first, and offer it first;
by this means Vipūjana Saurāki made [his enemy] more wretched. Thus, by this very act, he makes him more wretched.
When the sacrifice had been created, its head was cut off. The gods sought an atonement for it.

Now, at that time, the Aśvins were the two physicians of the gods, yet they were not drinkers of Soma. The gods approached them, just as one approaches a physician, saying, "Restore this head of the sacrifice. They replied, "Let there be a share for us. [The gods said,] "Choose [your reward]."
They said that; the two [Aśvins] replied, "Let them draw a draught for us, so that we may partake of the Soma-drink. The Aśvins then accepted that;

therefore they chant the hymns for the Aśvins, for it was the Aśvins who accepted it. Having purified them by means of the *bahiṣpavamāna* itself, once they were purified and fit for sacrifice, they drew the draught for them; therefore, [the draught is drawn] during the *bahiṣpavamāna*.
The two Aśvins are praised; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa should run forward toward the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, for that is a means of purification.
Therefore, he should exclude one whom he hates from it; that indeed is a remedy. They distributed it threefold:

a third part in the fire, a third part in the Brāhmaṇa, and a third part in the waters. Thus, knowing this, having announced it to a Brāhmaṇa at the end of the fire, [he should place it] in the waters.

It acts as a medicine and becomes effective; for as far as that which is made is a medicine, so it is here. These cups become a loss of the dwelling when, having drawn the draughts, they go out for the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant. Having returned, he touches them with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. The sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu; by means of Viṣṇu, that is, by the sacrifice itself, he causes them to ascend to the heavenly world.
These two, the Śukra and the Manthin cups, are indeed the two eyes of Prajāpati: the Śukra is this Āditya (the sun), and the Manthin is the Moon.
Of that Prajāpati, the left eye swelled; from it, those drops fell down, and by them it rains here.
Twenty-one drops indeed fell; Vāyu releases them from yonder for the well-being of creatures. Now, as for its pupil—
That [Soma] which fell away became barley. In that he mixes the *manthin* cup with barley-meal, he thereby restores his eye-sight.

Soma and barley-meal are indeed a pair; in that he mixes the *manthin* cup with barley-meal, it is for the sake of pairing. This *manthin* cup is indeed afflicted; if one should hate anyone among the officiating priests, let him take [the portion] for him; he will meet with affliction, [namely] the *ṣaṇḍa* and *marka* demons.
There were two priests of the Asuras; the gods were unable to slay them, for they were possessed of the power of Brahman.

The gods desired to remove them, saying, "Come back to us! They replied, "Let there be a share for us. [The gods said,] "Choose one. They chose these two, the Śukra and the Manthin cups. The gods reflected, "If we shall offer these two Soma-libations belonging to the Asuras, then..."
"The Asuras will prevail over us; they will prevail because we shall not offer," they thought. Therefore, having driven them away, they offered to Indra.

For this reason, these two are taken for other deities, yet they are offered to Indra; thus, by driving them away together with that [offering], one drives him away along with the expulsion of Śaṇḍa and Marka—whomsoever we hate.
Protect his life; protect his progeny; protect the heroic power of that man.

Thus he should set it down for one who is dear to him, thinking, "His *śukra* indeed is the kingdom; let the *manthin* be churned out for him. For they say that when a kingdom is besieged, it is the *manthin*. If he should desire, "May he who is outside be brought into the village, and he who is in the village be sent outside," [he should act accordingly].
Here I drive out that man, the son of such-and-such a father and such-and-such a mother, from this clan.
Thus, having set aside the vessel for the semen.
Here I establish so-and-so, the son of such-and-such a man and of such-and-such a woman, in this clan.

Thus he should set down the *manthin* cup; for he who is outside he places within the village, and he who is within the village he places outside. This *manthin* cup is indeed afflicted, as is the *śukra* cup, yet they are used again; therefore these two possess equal power, and therefore one looks upon them with equal regard. That sun is the *śukra*, and the moon is the *manthin*; when [the *manthin*] has been covered...

Because they go forward from here while covering [the fire], they do not see them as they go forward; but because they offer while standing facing backward without covering [the fire], they see them as they go backward. Because they go forward from here while covering [the fire], the breath goes away; but because they offer while standing facing backward without covering [the fire], therefore the breath comes back again.

Because they offer while covering [the altar] facing eastward from here, therefore embryos are deposited facing away from here; but because they offer standing facing westward without covering [it], therefore offspring are born facing toward here. The Śukra and Manthin cups are indeed the two eyes, and the high altar (uttaravedi) is the nose;
when they step upon [the altar] with their two thumbs, they thus place the two eyes, and then they step upon it from above.
Therefore, with the words, "Thou art Tutha, the nourisher of men; may the gods who drink the *śukra* lead thee forward," he offers [the cup] for those offspring that are yet to be born (*atrīḥ*);

they are its womb, and they are born after it. With the words, "Thou art Tutha, the nourisher of men; may the gods who drink the *manthin* lead thee forward," he offers [the cup] for those offspring that have already been born (*ādyāḥ*); they are its womb, and they are born after it—both kinds of offspring.

In this way he procreates offspring, both the Atris and the Ādya clans; they take hold of the *śukra* (the bright cup). The *śukra* is indeed brilliance (*tejas*) and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); verily, they take hold of brilliance and spiritual luster. With the words, "Yoked with Indra and with wrath," they proceed with the *śukra*.
For with wrath as his ally, Indra struck down the Asuras; with wrath as his ally, the sacrificer likewise strikes down his rival.
With the words, "Meeting together, O Heaven and Earth," they join the two elbow-boards (*aratnī*). Indeed, he joins these very things when they should join the two vessels;
for were they to join the vessels, this [space] would not exist between them. But because they join the two elbow-boards, therefore this space exists between the eyes for the sake of separation.
With the words, "Place a male embryo within the two *gavinyau*," thereby cattle come to the wives of the sacrificer.

"The wife gives birth to a hero; you are the receptacle of the *śukra*, you are the receptacle of the *manthin*," with these words they throw two wood-shavings [into the fire]. This is indeed their fuel-stick (*samit*), and furthermore, it is for the firm establishment of the oblations. "Cast out is the eunuch, cast out is the impotent one, along with him whom we hate"—with these words they throw away the two wood-shavings. As far as the dug-out space extends, so great is this world; indeed, it is as great as the world itself.
Therefore, the sacrificer excludes his rival. They mix some of the Soma juices with milk, but not others; that constitutes a pairing of the Somas.

It rains following those which they mix, while it withers following those which they do not mix. Some vessels are made of wood, others are made of clay; that constitutes a pairing of the vessels. Verily, he who knows this pairing of the Soma and the vessels [attains success].
Pairs of animals attend upon him.

The Āgrayaṇa cup is indeed Prajāpati. With the words, "O gods who are eleven in heaven," he draws it; for there are as many gods as are mentioned here. From them the Āgrayaṇa is drawn. Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, the gods went to the heavenly world, while the Asuras were cast down. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras perished. Therefore, he who, knowing thus, draws the Āgrayaṇa, prospers himself and his enemy perishes.
He who is a rival or one who is inferior in rank should draw the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa; for the Āgrayaṇa is the foremost, provided he intends to practice sorcery.
O gods,
if Saramā found the breach of the mountain, [then] you have made your great, ancient protection a common refuge.
Leading the foremost of the syllables with her beautiful feet, she who knows has gone toward the sound with joy.

"Rugṇam"—thus one should make the *puroruc*; for it indeed breaks [the enemy], and furthermore, Saramā is speech; he thus seizes their speech. This [cup] is indeed the flow (*sarā*) of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior to the *āgrayaṇa* cup, that they perform in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), and then this...

They release their speech at the Āgrayaṇa; having thus reached the sacrifice, they release their speech. Speech indeed departed from the gods; those gods performed the sacrifice in silence. That Speech thought, "They are indeed excluding me from the sacrifice," and she ran toward the Āgrayaṇa.
Therefore, they release their speech at the Āgrayaṇa. They release their speech after uttering *hiṃ*; [for] breath...

The *hiṃkāra* is indeed speech and breath; it is the harnessing of speech itself. He utters the *hiṃkāra* three times, for this speech speaks in a threefold manner: softly, loudly, and then very loudly. As much as there is of speech, that much of it is thereby harnessed for him. There are three priests belonging to Prajāpati: the Udgātṛ, the Prastotṛ, and the Pratihartṛ. These, at this time, are unturned and unharnessed for him; by the very fact that he utters the *hiṃkāra*, they are harnessed for him.

Having become disciplined and composed, Speech and Mind disputed with one another, saying, "I am superior! I am superior! They went to Prajāpati to ask him for a decision. Speech said, "Nothing at all should be done by me that has not been uttered.
Then Mind said, "Nothing at all should be done by me that has not been conceived. He (Prajāpati) spoke in favor of Mind.
That speech said, "I shall indeed not be a carrier of the oblation for you. Therefore, she is not a carrier of the oblation for Prajāpati;
hence, whatever is performed in a whisper, they say, "This has been done; let it be performed," for it is performed for Prajāpati.
At the morning pressing he draws [the Soma] with two streams, at the midday pressing with three, and at the third pressing with four.

At the third pressing, there are nine of those [cups]; the *āgrayaṇa* is the self, and thus he places the vital breaths within himself. The sacrifice is indeed split asunder when the pressings conclude. With the words, "O gods who are eleven in heaven, who are eleven upon earth, who dwell in the waters, eleven by your greatness," he [reconnects it] with the deities; for the sacrifice is connected by the deities—it is by means of the deities that he [reunites] the sacrifice.

Prajāpati is indeed the Āgrayaṇa; in that he pours [the Soma] over at all the pressings, Prajāpati thereby smells his offspring. Prajāpati is indeed the Āgrayaṇa; in that he draws [it] at all the pressings, he continues the sacrifice by means of himself.
Prajāpati is indeed the Āgrayaṇa; in that this [cup] remains as a surplus, therefore man is the foremost among animals.
The *āgrayaṇa* cup has gone farthest; the year is indeed the *gāyatrī*. He thus runs after it as far as the third pressing.
For in the world of the *gāyatrī*, all the *soma*s are drawn. All the pressings, therefore, run after it.
Now, as for the fact that it is drawn with a vessel (*sthālī*)—should one offer from a known vessel, or from one made of wood? Therefore, it is offered from an unknown [vessel].
Now, because the slayer of an embryo discards the cooking pot but not the wooden vessel, therefore a male is an heir, while a female is not an heir.
And because they discard the cooking pot but not the wooden vessel, therefore they discard a girl when she is born, but not a boy; thus, women alone remain in excess.
*Sa-rā*: [Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.
*adāyāt*: [FN] *adāyādā?* Indra, indeed, raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra; seeing the thunderbolt raised, he was afraid and said, "There is..."

"Or rather, this vigor which is within him—that I shall give to you; do not kill me. He indeed gave it to him; he gave him the sacrifice, for the Ukthya is indeed cattle. When the Ukthya is drawn, it is for the attainment of both the sacrifice and the cattle. The sacrifice is indeed as great as the Ukthya; the other cups are merely internal cement. This [Ukthya] is indeed a raft.
As one who has performed the Ukthya sacrifice, just as here one might bathe after having girded himself with a float, so indeed does he bathe after having offered the Ukthya;
it carries him across to the conclusion of the sacrifice. The limbs of the sacrifice are the Ukthya; it is drawn for the sake of continuity.
"For thee, for Viṣṇu," [he says]; the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu; by Viṣṇu the sacrifice is made continuous, through Viṣṇu alone.

By means of this sacrifice he extends the sacrifice; for by this indeed are the hymns (ukthas) made continuous. Therefore, a man is held together by his sinews. He pours it out from the Sadas; having thus extended and reached the sacrifice, he pours it out. The Śukra is indeed sight, and the Ukthya is sight; thus sight is maintained in front. Moreover, it is just as here in front.

Looking back, he follows after it; thus it is. Now, as to why that which was one is made threefold: therefore the one remains preeminent in the front half. Because these two cups are followed by the most numerous Soma-libations, it is for the sake of warding off misfortune. Because many Soma-libations follow this cup, therefore many follow behind the one who goes on as the preeminent leader.

The vessels follow after the Adhvaryu; the *ukthāmadā* verses carry him forward from the front. He attends upon the *sadas* with a verse addressed to Indra, the *āgnīdhra* shed with one addressed to Agni, and the *havirdhāna* shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu; thus he attends upon them according to their respective deities, and so they do not carry him away.
Between the Āhavanīya fire and the *havirdhāna* shed is the world of the Adhvaryu; between the *havirdhāna* shed and the *sadas* is [the world] of the sacrificer.

And for the sacrificer, the *sadas*, and the members of the assembly (*sadasyās*): if he should desire, "May glory fall upon the *adhvaryu*," he should cause [the cart] to descend between the *āhavanīya* fire and the *havirdhāna* shed; for glory is indeed Soma, and this is the world of the *adhvaryu*; thus he causes the *adhvaryu* himself to attain glory.
If he should desire, "May glory fall upon the sacrificer," he should cause it to descend between the *havirdhāna* shed and the *sadas*; for Soma...

This indeed is the glory of the sacrificer; he leads the sacrificer himself to glory. If he should desire, "May the members of the assembly (sadasyas) attain glory," he should pour it out within the assembly-hall (*sadas*). Glory is indeed Soma; this is the world of the members of the assembly; he leads the members of the assembly themselves to glory.
He pours it out while touching the *sadas*, for the *sadas* belongs to Indra, and the hymns (*ukthas*) belong to Indra; it is for the continuity of the hymns.
For the non-interruption of the hymns.
Hymns and intoxications.
You are taken with a support; I take you for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Thus he takes [the cup] for the Maitrāvaruṇa at the morning pressing.
For Indra, you!
Thus [he spoke] to the praising Brahmins.
For Indra and Agni, you!
Thus for the Achāvāka.
You are taken with a support; for Indra you, for Indra you!
Thus he takes [the draughts] from all [the cups] at the midday pressing.
You are taken with a support; I take you for Indra and Varuṇa.
Thus he takes [the draught] for the Maitrāvaruṇa at the third pressing.
For Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee!
Thus [he spoke] to the praising Brahmins.
With the formula, "For Indra and Viṣṇu, thee," [he takes it] for the Achāvāka; thus his cups are taken according to the hymn-form and according to the deity.
Life is indeed the *dhruva*; he draws it as the last, for life is the highest. He draws it with a vessel for the support of life;

he draws it full, so that he attains a full span of life. The *gāyatrī* is breath, and the *dhruva* is life; because this [dhruva] remains until the third pressing, therefore breath lasts as long as life. Life is indeed the *dhruva*; when he performs the *agniṣṭoma*, having attained life itself—
Life indeed slips away; if one were to offer only the *dhruva* [ladle], he would deprive living beings of their life.

He pours [the remainder] down while the *paridhānīyā* verse is being recited, for that is the conclusion. He pours it down into the *hotṛ*'s cup, for the *hotṛ* belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*) and these living beings belong to the All-gods;
thus he bestows life upon all these beings. "Of the people," they say—this [refers to] all of them.

The life-span of creatures is drawn from all creatures; Vaiśvānara is drawn on both sides, for this breath is indeed Vaiśvānara on both sides. That which is this downward breath—because he is set down alone in the northern *havirdhāna* cart, therefore he is a sharer of half the vital breaths, while the others are sharers of half. One should set him down upon gold for one who desires long life; [gold is] immortality.

Gold is indeed life, and the *dhruva* cup is immortality; thus he bestows life upon him. The other cups are set down on ground that has been strewn with sand, but the *dhruva* is set down on unstrewn ground; therefore, other animals stand firm by means of bone, while man stands firm by means of flesh.

The sounding-holes (*uparavas*) are indeed the vital breaths; since these cups are set down on strewn ground, they are set down in their own womb, for these [holes] are in the front part of the mouth.
The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed this eastern half of the *havirdhāna* shed, which is the southern *havirdhāna*;
therefore, these other cups (*graha*) are the vital breaths. The *dhruva* cup is life (*āyus*). There are nine vital breaths, and life is the tenth;
therefore, this [cup] is drawn as the tenth, for life is the tenth. The prince guards the *dhruva* as the guardian of all these creatures.
It protects one's lifespan; therefore, a prince should be most diligent in this regard, even if he should practice sorcery.
[He] lies down: "I here set in motion the life-span of such-and-one, the son of such-and-one."
Thus he should certainly set it in motion; verily, he sets his own life-span in motion.

If he were to set it in motion, he would set the life-span of all creatures in motion; the offspring would perish, the sacrifice would not proceed, and the Adhvaryu would become hungry; therefore, it should be performed with a limb that is deficient.
I displace you, who are firm and possess a firm foundation, from that station.

Thus, by this very act, he causes him to fall from his station; he becomes liable to die. Indeed, when one who is firm falls, all beings fall after him; the sacrificer falls from his station. Therefore, having touched it, he says: "In heaven, make firm those things that belong to heaven; in the atmosphere, those that belong to the atmosphere; on earth, those that belong to earth. In this way, he makes the subjects firm according to their respective stations, each in its own abode.
The sacrificer is deprived of life-span and vigor when the *dhruva* ladle spills; therefore, it should be touched with the formula, "Life-span and vigor, you are the *dhruva*."
You are the upholder of life; bestow long life upon me.

Thus he bestows life itself upon him; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a choice (*vara*); by means of a choice, he wins a choice, for the self is indeed the choice. Dhruva Upadadāsa, the son of Sena Bhaimaseni, once heard that [the bricks were] being laid down; hearing it, he caused them to swell for these worlds through the *ṛta* of the Sthairabrahmaṇas.
Svāhā! From heaven, may you swell with nourishment.
Thus, he became the third.
Svāhā! From the intermediate space, swell!
Thus, he became divided into two parts.
Svāhā! From the earth, may you swell.
Thus he purified it by means of that very truth; it is to be made full for these worlds, being fixed, and he pours it out at the twelfth laud.

Twelve months are a year; the year is the sacrifice; the sacrifice is Prajāpati; the person is of the nature of Prajāpati. In the person, as large as he is, he bestows life. If he were to cause [the breath] to descend while the *stotra* is being chanted, embryos would be born prematurely; if while the *śastra* is being recited, young men would die; if while the *śastra* has been recited, he would place the vital breaths outside. When the *śastra* has been recited once, [he should place it] in the middle.
He places this life-span of living beings in the middle.
You are self-existent, the most excellent ray, beloved by the gods, worthy of being gathered together.
O auspicious one, may the gods enter into you completely.
You are the upholder of life; bestow long life upon me.
Thus he bestows life itself upon him.
You are the bestower of splendor, O steadfast one; bestow splendor upon me.
Thus, he bestows radiance upon him.

You are the impeller; you are the radiant one; you are manly vigor; you are the sacred law; you are skill; you are dexterity. May I partake of that impelling power of yours, of your radiance, of your manly vigor, of your sacred law, and of your dexterity—of my own kin, of the wanderer, of the Śūdra, and of the Ārya. Just as you, O Sūrya, are visible to all, so may I become visible to all.
Thus he becomes visible to all; for that sun is the self-existent, most excellent ray. Just as it became self-existent, so does he who knows this become self-existent.

Now, these seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*) are drawn for the sake of the support of the year; the year consists of twelve months, therefore there are twelve seasonal cups. "Madhu and Mādhava, the two spring seasons," they are offered while not yet present, for these seasons are not yet present;
one does not enter into another. If one were to enter into another, season would run over into season.
Now, because one follows after the other, therefore these seasons follow one another in succession and revolve;

the season-cup has openings on both sides, for these seasons indeed have openings on both sides. Truly, we do not know which is the mouth of the seasons; they take up the first together and the last together; they are yoked together and they are unyoked together. Indeed, they perform fourteen [rites], or rather, this exceeds that.
There is an additional month, the thirteenth; by means of this [rite], having attained that very month, he secures it. From the seasons, indeed, creatures are born.
When [he performs it] six times with the word "season" (*ṛtu*), he procreates four-footed cattle for him from the seasons;
and when four times with the word "season," he procreates two-footed cattle for him from the seasons; and when twice—[the same applies].

By means of the *ṛtu* [cup], these two seasons are indeed [grasped]; and as for why there are two *ṛtu-pātra* vessels, it is because these seasons are in pairs. He does not perform an after-offering (*anuyāja*), for the *vaṣaṭ*-call belongs to Vaiśvānara; were he to perform an after-offering, he would cast Vaiśvānara into the seasons. This world was indeed blind, undifferentiated; there was no day, nor was there night. Then the gods differentiated them by means of the *ṛtu-grahas*; thus, when the *ṛtu-grahas* are drawn, [it serves] for the differentiation of day and night.

For the sake of distinction, the heavenly world is indeed the year; these seasonal cups (ṛtugraha) are its steps. In that the seasonal cups are drawn, it is for the purpose of ascending to the heavenly world.
One should not resort to one another. (Variant reading: *nānyo'nyam abhiprapadyeta*)
They approached one another.
Indeed, the Ādityas were the last to go from here to the heavenly world; they, having been gathered together from here, [placed] another [form] in front.
The year is indeed the heavenly world; these two Adhvaryus move about to fashion the year.
When he draws the [cup] for Indra and Agni with the *ṛtupātra*, he thereby takes hold of the year for the sake of the heavenly world;
furthermore, he places light above for the attainment of the heavenly world. That bright [cup] is indeed the sun, the person.

The Vaiśvadeva cup: because he draws the Vaiśvadeva with the Śukra vessel, therefore man alone faces that [sun], while all other animals and the gods alike face downward. The gods and the Asuras were in conflict; those gods, at the morning pressing, saw that the sacrifice was to be completed at the Vaiśvadeva rite, and they completed it at the morning pressing—this is why the Vaiśvadeva belongs to the morning pressing.

This [cup] is drawn at the morning pressing; indeed, one thereby establishes the sacrifice at the Vaiśvadeva [offering]. With it, being thus established and unimpaired, they proceed. All the gods indeed approached the morning pressing; they did not remain for the two subsequent pressings.
Since the Vaiśvadeva is offered at the morning pressing, the deities are [present] at the morning pressing through this Vaiśvadeva [offering].
When they have been satisfied, those [cups] go forth being poured out at the later pressing. The Marutvatīya cups are indeed the thunderbolt;
the first is the preliminary strike, the second is the discharge, and the third is the felling. The bow is indeed the thunderbolt;
the first is the drawing back, the second is the aiming, and the third is the release. These Marutvatīya cups are indeed the two wheels of the sacrifice, and the [Aindrāgna cup] is the axle.
The two flanks were the midday [pressing]. With the Maruts, indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra through his heroic power; he was not able to perform heroic power without the Maruts.
Because the cup for the Maruts (marutvatīya) is drawn and the hymn for the Maruts (marutvatīya) is recited, the midday pressing thereby becomes possessed of heroic power.
"How do you know that the pressings possess the seasons? one should ask; [the answer is: "By means of the seasonal cups (ṛtugraha), the morning pressing [is made to possess the seasons]."

The midday pressing belongs to the Marutvatīya [stotras] with the *ṛtu* formulas; the third pressing belongs to the Sāvitra [cup]. When the two Marutvatīya cups have been set down, the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are given. Indeed, these gifts are given in their own womb. These Marutvatīya cups are the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) of the sacrifice; therefore, the sacrificial gifts are not given beyond the Marutvatīya cups. If he were to give them beyond, it would be as if [giving] outside the enclosing-sticks.

It would indeed be spilled if he should desire, "May the *viś* be more powerful and the *kṣatra* weaker. He should make that *puroruc* which has the *marutvatīya* verse as its first half-verse; for he has thus made the *viś* more powerful and the *kṣatra* weaker.
If he should desire, "May the *kṣatra* be more powerful and the *viś* weaker," [he should use] that which has the *aindra* verse as its first half-verse.

One should make that the *puroruc* (introductory verse). Indeed, he has thus made the Kṣatriya more powerful and the Vaiśya weaker. A kinship is indeed created in the sacrifice when the Marutvatīya cup is drawn and the Marutvatīya hymn is recited. The Maruts are cattle; thereby, that kinship among cattle is avoided. Having touched the *ṛtupātra*, he receives [the cup]; for the Maruts are the seasons, and the year is the seasons.
The seasons are life, and the year is life; in life, indeed, the Adhvaryu establishes this. He who draws the Marutvatīya cups slays Vṛtra;

in the Mahendra cup, all desires are contained, and thus he obtains all desires and pervades them all. Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; he held the other gods in contempt, and he became Mahendra. He took for himself this special portion.
Having slain Vṛtra, this [libation] is indeed his specific share and his very portion; therefore, having won a battle, a king distributes the prize of victory.
He draws the cup for Mahendra with the Śukra vessel. "The pressing-stones speak, the mortars speak," they say;
"they churn the milk-mixture (āśir). Indeed, when Indra had first arrived, they made a sound; thus they bestow brilliance upon the sacrificer himself.
*vā*: corrected; Ed: *vā*.
*vettheti*: corrections and conjectures to the entire work.
[Page IV,92]
This very [truth] has been declared in the following verse:
Of the eight sons of Aditi who were born from her own body, she approached the gods with seven; she cast away Mārtāṇḍa.
Thus, this very Upāṃśusavana pressing-stone is indeed that; its Soma-drinking is when they cause the Āditya cup to be mixed.
O Vivasvat, O Āditya, this is your draught of Soma.

Thus he causes him to prosper by means of the Soma-drinking itself. The Upāṃśusavana stone is indeed the vyāna breath, and the Āditya cup is offspring; verily, he thus places the vyāna breath within offspring. The Āditya cup is cattle; in that he mixes it with curds in the middle, he thereby places milk in the midst of cattle. Now, as for the *taptātaṅkyam* (the heated vessel): therefore, though being raw, she yields cooked milk. If he should so desire—
"May Parjanya rain."
With that which is the divine rain, I mix you.

Thus, one should mix the *dadhi* with the *āditya-graha* from above; for the *āditya* is indeed cattle, and it rains from yonder for the sake of cattle; verily, he sprinkles the cattle with rain. If he should desire, "May the embryos coagulate," he should lift up the *āditya-graha* and look at it;
then the embryos indeed become coagulated. For the first two pressings are full of *śukra*, while the third pressing is without *śukra*. If...
He pours out the residues of the dual-deity cups and pours them over the Āgrayaṇa vessel; by means of that, the third pressing becomes possessed of the *śukra*.

When the gods had slain the Asuras, they were afraid of death. Seeking protection and seeking a place of refuge, they entered these most abundant deities, namely the dual-deity cups. Therefore, the Āditya cup is drawn from the dual-deity cups with two *bṛhatī* verses.

The *bṛhatī* verses are indeed cattle, and the *āditya* cup is progeny. As far as this world extends—that is, as far as [the space] dug out—when he draws [the cup] after stretching it out, the sacrificer thereby seizes from his rival this world and its food; furthermore, he secures these very subjects for the sake of food.
If his rival should sacrifice, he should stand outside the sacrificial ground (*vedis*), for thus he does not seize him. The *āditya* cup is indeed cattle.

Agni is Rudra; these hearths are the bodies of Agni. In that he takes [the portions] after having spread them out, he thereby interposes the cattle from Rudra. He goes out after covering [them], for the protection of the cattle. The Aditya is indeed the after-offering (anuyāja) of the offerings belonging to the two deities;
therefore, one does not perform an after-offering for them. The two-deity offerings are indeed the fore-offerings (prayāja) of the Aditya; therefore, one does not perform an after-offering for them.

The sun is indeed the cattle, Agni is Rudra, and the Brahmin is the overseer. If he were to offer while looking [at them], he would become an overseer of these [cattle] as they are being led away; therefore, one should offer while looking elsewhere, so that he does not become an overseer of them.
śukravatī: FN emended. Ed:
śukravatīr aśukraṃ: FN emended. Ed: aśakraṃ. cf. MS.3.8.10:110.11.
For those seeking a protector: Savitṛ is indeed the Gāyatra among the gods; Soma is taken in the world of the Gāyatrī, which is the Āgrayaṇa; therefore, [it is taken] from the Āgrayaṇa.

The Sāvitra draught is drawn; it remains here until the third pressing for the impulsion of what is being performed and what has been performed. The Antaryāma cup is the intermediate space, and these creatures are the intermediate space. In that he draws the Sāvitra with the Antaryāma vessel, Savitṛ impels these creatures for procreation. It is offered while not yet placed upon the fire, for these creatures do not move when they are not yet settled; nor does he perform an after-offering.

If one were to perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), he would cut off the creation of offspring; moreover, these two *soma* draughts are drawn in the same vessel, therefore he does not perform the after-offerings. The gods, indeed, were unable to lift up the third pressing; at that time Savitṛ was still in the morning pressing.
The gods carried him around to the third pressing, and by means of him they lifted up the third pressing. That [cup] which belongs to Savitṛ—
It is drawn at the third pressing; for this third pressing is indeed impelled by Savitṛ. They lift it up;
into the dregs of the libation to Savitṛ, he draws the cup for the Viśve Devās. These creatures belong to the Viśve Devās;
indeed, creatures are born only when impelled by Savitṛ. Savitṛ is the mind; these creatures belong to the Viśve Devās, and thus [he places it] in all these creatures.

He fixes his mind; being desirous of blessings, he draws [the cup] for the sake of the sacrifice belonging to all the gods (*vaiśvadeva*). "Thou art good protection, thou art a firm foundation"—when Soma thus establishes itself upon Soma, [he says this]. "To the great bull, homage!"—by saying "great" he [offers] to the gods, and by saying "homage" he [offers] to the fathers. For the fathers have a share in the *uktha*, not a share in the *stoma*; therefore, this [cup] is drawn for the sake of the *uktha*.
Where it is taken for praise, that is recited in its own proper place.
pariśaye: FN emended. Ed: pariśayet;
ukthāyaiṣa: FN emended. Ed: ukāyaiṣa.

He offers with clarified butter. This Āhavanīya fire is indeed the first of the Dhiṣṇya hearths; it is this one that he sprinkles first. He sprinkles it with a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu. At this stage, the sacrifice has turned away; Agni is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice. Thus he has seized both the deities and the sacrifice. Indeed, they kill the Soma when they press it; therefore there is the cup for Soma (Saumya).
Verily, they thus honor Soma; they cause Soma to drink. For they have indeed slain Soma when they pressed him.

This offering to Soma is the "Soma-anustaraṇī" (the cow that follows Soma in death); for the Pitṛs' anustaraṇī is one belonging to the Pitṛs, therefore he sacrifices with a verse addressed to the Pitṛs.
Standing on the south side, he offers, for the south belongs to the Pitṛs. These after-offerings of the Upasads belong to Agni and Viṣṇu; [he offers] of ghee.

He performs the *saumya* offering; those very deities for whom he sacrificed during the *upasad*s, for them he now performs this [offering] there in the other world. Whatever of his was torn away or perished, that goes to yonder world; then, purified, he alone remains as the residue.
The *saumya* is indeed a means of purification; by this, he purifies the sacrificer himself. Soma has the *sāman* as its deity; it is indeed of Soma...
Verily, this Soma is supported by the Sāman.
Truly yours is this, whatever of yours is here.
Thus, he who has not departed from life perceives; he who has departed from life does not perceive. If one were not to perceive, then one might speak.
That mind of mine which has gone to Yama, or that which has not yet returned—
by means of King Soma, we cause that to be restored within us.
Touching the heart, touching the sacrifice, you are the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me.
Thus he invokes this very blessing.
Now, these are the *atigrāhya* cups. The gods indeed took hold of the Soma; then Indra also took hold of them. He reflected:
"I shall not be able to prevail over these without the *brahman*. He ran to the *brahman*; with the *brahman* he struck them down.
The *gāyatrī* is indeed the *brahman*; therefore they are drawn with *gāyatrī* verses. These [cups] belong to that supreme food which had not yet been secured.
They are taken for the sake of attainment. Those *stobhas* of the *Vairāja* which are redundant—by means of them these [verses] become possessed of the *Sāman*.

All these indeed belong to Indra; that Indra who is there is this Āditya. Agni and that Āditya are the same. The splendor of the *Virāj* belongs to Agni; that of the *Śakvarīs* belongs to Indra; that of the *Revatīs* belongs to Sūrya. Where the *Pṛṣṭha* hymns are to be joined together...

Therefore, one should offer these for the sake of the brilliance of the *sāmans*. Indeed, this sacrifice is supported from behind by both the *stotra* and the *śastra* when the *atigrāhya* cups are offered;
they are the two wheels of the sacrifice, while the *pṛṣṭhas* are the axle-tree and the *atigrāhyas* are the support.
Therefore, they are drawn at the morning pressing for the sake of support. That which belongs to Agni, by that he wins brilliance.
Whatever power belongs to Indra, by that; whatever luster belongs to Sūrya, by that—this threefold [offering] bestows upon him this successful spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Agni is indeed brilliance, Indra is power, and that sun is spiritual luster; thus, on both sides, he encloses power for him with both brilliance and spiritual luster.
With the splendor of Agni and of the Brahman, I offer you; O giver of splendor, may splendor not forsake me, may I not forsake splendor.
Svāhā! With the vigor of Indra and of the Kṣatra, I offer you; O giver of vigor, may vigor not forsake me, may I not forsake vigor.
Svāhā! With the luster of Sūrya and of the plants, I offer you; O giver of luster, may luster not forsake me, may I not [forsake luster]. Svāhā!

O Agni, maker of life, you have bestowed radiance; svāhā! You are long-lived and full of splendor among the gods; make me long-lived and full of splendor among men. O Indra, maker of vigor, you are vigorous and powerful among the gods; make me vigorous and powerful among men. O Sūrya, maker of luster, you are lustrous and radiant among the gods; make me radiant...
Make me radiant among men.
These oblations and the consumption [of the remains] come into being; indeed, by the power of these, Bamba and Viśvavayas came to know these worlds, both hitherward and thitherward.
