Truly, for one who knows thus, these worlds shine forth for him both hitherward and thitherward. Indeed, from here the worlds are well-known as being thus, but from yonder they are difficult to discern as being hitherward.
But indeed, those for whom these [oblations] are offered know these worlds from that [world] down to this one.
He draws the cup for the Patnīvat with the Upāṃśu vessel. The Upāṃśu is indeed breath; by means of breath they proceed, and by means of breath they rise up.
Furthermore, it serves as a recognition of the vital breaths. Moreover, that which is the first vessel employed is the last to be released.

For the protection of the vital breaths, the Hotṛ indeed offered the Upāṃśu cup this morning. If the Hotṛ were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call for this [cup], then what was in front would be left behind, and he would be liable to perish. Therefore, the Agnīdh utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for it; for the Agnīdh is in front, and the Upāṃśu is the vital breath.
From the vital breath, offspring are born. As for the Pātnīvata [offering] with the Upāṃśu vessel...

He draws [the cup] for procreation; it is offered while still near, for offspring are born while still near. He does not perform the *anuyāja* offerings, for if he were to perform the *anuyāja*, he would obstruct procreation. Moreover, these two Soma draughts are drawn in the same vessel; therefore, he does not perform the *anuyāja*. Ghee and Soma are indeed a pair; when he mixes the *pātnīvata* draught with ghee, it is for the sake of pairing. [This is the portion] of him pressed by Bṛhaspati.

"Those"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; from the womb of the Brahman Prajāpati created offspring. From this very womb of the Brahman the sacrificer is born. "O Indra, [make us] possessed of power," for the embryo is indeed power.
"O Agni, accompanied by the wives," for Agni and the wives are a pair. "Drink the Soma with Tvaṣṭṛ in harmony," for Tvaṣṭṛ fashions forms.

The gods, having made ghee their thunderbolt, struck at Soma. Indeed, they sprinkle him with ghee when there is the offering for the wives (*pātnīvata*). By means of this, the wife deprives him of his power; therefore, a woman is devoid of power, while a man possesses power. Therefore, men go to the assembly hall, but not women. If they were to mix the other Soma offerings but not the one for the wives, women would [possess power].
The men did not go to the assembly; indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra. When he split open his head, that became the *droṇakalaśa*.
The Soma that flowed from it was the *hāriyojana*; therefore, one offers this with the *droṇakalaśa*, for this is its womb.
Having slain Vṛtra, Indra poured out the Soma from his lungs and heart. That...
He became the Hāriyojana. Indra thought: "If I offer this Soma which belongs to the Asuras, then the Asuras will follow after it;

but if I do not offer it, they will still follow after it. At the conclusion of the rite, when the enclosing sticks had been cast into the fire, he offered it. In that he offers at the conclusion when the enclosing sticks have been cast in, he has indeed performed both; he does indeed offer it.

When [the sacrifice] has been completed, he offers [this oblation]. The Unnetṛ is indeed the one among the officiating priests who is redundant; therefore, they do not choose him, nor does he utter the *vaṣaṭ* call.
This Soma has flowed over; it flows over specifically toward the Unnetṛ. The Adhvaryu indeed offers the preceding Soma-pressings;
if the Adhvaryu were to offer this [final one], he would conflate the oblations and cause a conflict. Therefore, the Unnetṛ offers this.

Prajāpati, indeed, thought of offering this Soma. Agni said to him, "You shall not offer this non-divine Soma in me while it is uncooked and unfit for eating; let there be a second [offering]. When he mixes it with parched grains (*dhānā*), it is for the sake of cooking and also for the sake of providing a second [offering]. Moreover, these parched grains: when those wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadughā*) milked out every desire for the gods, then these [grains] were also [milked].

They milked that; verily by these [oblations] he secures nourishment. Prajāpati indeed is the Āgrayaṇa; in that this [cup] is left over, therefore this one is left over, unlimited, and it flows over these creatures. The two bay steeds of Indra are the Ṛc and the Sāman; the enclosing-sticks are their support. Truly, one provides fodder for a horse when it is not yet tied up; so it is when [the sacrifice] is completed after the [Soma] has been offered.

When he offers on the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), it is because they have been placed around and the rite is completed; when he offers after the enclosing-sticks have been cast into the fire, he thereby provides fodder for these two [fires] by means of their very foundations.
Parched grains (*dhānā*) are indeed cattle. If he were to chew them, he would injure the cattle; if he were not to chew them, they would be uncontrolled.
He scatters them with the words, "For sight thee! For prosperity thee!"—thus he has accomplished both, for the restraint of cattle.
While he is eating, the sacrificial animals attend upon him.
"They will come into being" (ābhaviṣyanti):
this alone is superfluous.
FN Corrections and conjectures for the entire work. *duduhre*: FN Corrections and conjectures for the entire work.
By means of the sacrifice (*yajña*), the gods went to the heavenly world (*svarga-loka*). They thought: "By this [sacrifice], others will surely ascend after us to the world."
They saw the meters; they interlaced them so that the world of heaven would not be pierced.
In that he interlaces the meters, the sacrificer confuses the world of his rival; it is for the non-piercing of the world of heaven.
Among the gods there were some meters, and among the Asuras there were others; those among the gods were fewer, while those among the Asuras were greater.

Those gods, by means of the smaller meters, appropriated the larger meters of the Asuras. When he recites the larger meters with the smaller meters, the sacrificer thereby appropriates the world of his rival; he has deprived him of his world and rendered him meterless. He recites all the meters together in the *anuṣṭubh*, for speech is all the meters.

Or [it is] the *anuṣṭubh*; man is of the nature of the *anuṣṭubh*, therefore man speaks all speech. The meters are indeed cattle, and speech is the *anuṣṭubh*; man is of the nature of the *anuṣṭubh*. Because he recites all the meters and recites the *anuṣṭubh* last, therefore man eats cattle from above, after speech. He recites all the meters; Prajāpati [is the one who does so].
Verily, he attains Prajāpati through the metres; six syllables remain over from the stotra. There are six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons.

From there, four syllables return to the śastra; by that, he wins quadrupeds. Then two indeed remain over; they exceed the Virāj by two, [representing] truth and untruth; verily, he attains the Virāj.
All [these].

Prajāpati indeed fashioned the sacrifices for the gods; he thought, "I have entered within myself. He then gathered together their senses and powers once more, and he became the *ṣoḍaśin* (the sixteenfold cup). Now at that time, Indra was among the gods.
It was most overcome and most weakened; he gave this *ṣoḍaśin* to him, and by it Indra became powerful.

Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. Therefore, he who, knowing thus, draws this *ṣoḍaśin*, prospers in himself and his rival is defeated. Prajāpati indeed fashioned bodies for the gods; of those, that which was associated with the bay horses (*harivatī*)—

He consecrated her within himself with love. Because the *puroruṅ* of the cup is accompanied by the word "bay" (*harivatī*), he obtains that very body of his which is dear to him as the one associated with the bay horses. They say, "There is no sacrifice named the *ṣoḍaśin*"; yet why is it called the *ṣoḍaśin*?
Because it is perfected through both the chant (*stotra*) and the recitation (*śastra*), therefore it is the *ṣoḍaśin*. By means of the sacrifice, the gods [attained] the heavenly world.
He went toward them, but he was not able to overcome them. They then fastened this *ṣoḍaśin* (sixteen-verse cup) onto him; by means of it, they pervaded that world.
Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśin* is drawn for the sake of pervading that world and for the attainment of that world.
One should draw it at the *agniṣṭoma* for a Kṣatriya; the unappeased thunderbolt kindles him for prosperity. One should draw it at the *atirātra* for a Brāhmaṇa.

The *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a thunderbolt; being unappeased, it would harm the sacrificer. By taking [the cup] at the night [rite], one appeases the thunderbolt. When taken at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the morning pressing is indeed brilliance; thus he fashions the thunderbolt from brilliance itself. When taken at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina savana*), the midday pressing is indeed vigor;
thus he fashions the thunderbolt from vigor itself. When taken at the third pressing, [it is] cattle.

The third pressing belongs to the cattle; he thus fashions the thunderbolt for the sake of the cattle. If he were to draw it at the morning pressing, the thunderbolt would be left over for the later pressings. If he were to draw it at the midday pressing, he would strike the thunderbolt in the middle. It is drawn at the third pressing;
thus he draws it at all the pressings, and it does not bring ruin upon the earlier pressings. A fifteen-fold stoma should be employed.

The *pañcadaśa* (fifteen-fold stoma) is indeed a thunderbolt; verily, he bestows a thunderbolt upon him, and by it he attains victory and prosperity. A *ṣoḍaśin* (sixteen-fold stoma) should be performed; the sacrificer is fifteen-fold and the thunderbolt is sixteen-fold; verily, he bestows a thunderbolt upon him, and it kindles him for prosperity and excellence.
A *saptadaśa* (seventeen-fold stoma) should be performed; Prajāpati is seventeen-fold, and the *ṣoḍaśin* belongs to Prajāpati; verily, he places him in his own womb.

The Ekaviṃśa [stoma] should be employed; for the Anuṣṭubh has twenty-one positions, and the Ṣoḍaśin is of the nature of the Anuṣṭubh—this is its most appropriate abode. Therefore, the Ekaviṃśa should be employed on the middle day of the Trirātra, for it is the middle day of the Trirātra that is the most fragile; [it is done] for the firmness of the day and to prevent fragility. On the fourth day of the Catūrātra, the Caturtha [stoma] should be employed.

Or rather, the day of the four-night rite is loose; it is for the firmness of the day, to prevent its looseness. On every fourth day of the Ahīna sacrifice, the Gṛhya cup is drawn; or rather, every fourth day of the Ahīna is loose; it is for the firmness of the day, to prevent its looseness. It is not appropriate for a two-night rite, for these two meters—the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh—are without meter and without a foundation.

The sacrificer becomes one who lacks a proper foundation when he takes [the draught] on the first day; on the second day of the two-night rite, it is taken as something to be grasped, and thus the night itself is left as his foundation.
It would exceed [it].
(FN emended. Ed: abhyatiricyate)
Now, this is the Adābhya. The gods and the Asuras were contending; the gods saw this [cup], they took it, and the Asuras could not deceive them.
That is why the Adābhya has its name "the undeceivable. An enemy cannot deceive him who takes this cup.
Indeed, they slay Soma when they press him. This is the body of Soma that delivers one from distress—namely, those which...

They pull these shoots out; in this very way the sacrificer is released from this world. Indeed, the sacrifice is cut asunder when the pressings conclude. In that he puts these shoots back again, it is for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice, and for rain—for Parjanya rains according to the names of the Maruts where this cup is drawn.
"May Agni protect us from the morning pressing"—with this, the gods deprived the Asuras of the pressings;

with this, the sacrificer deprives his rival of the pressings. "For Agni I pluck thee, with the Gāyatrī metre"—with this, the gods deprived the Asuras of both the metres and the deities; with this, the sacrificer [deprives his rival] of both the metres and the deities.

He appropriates the rival; he shakes [the vessel] four times, for by this the gods appropriated the quarters of the Asuras; by this the sacrificer appropriates the quarters of his rival. This is indeed a "living-draught" of Soma, for it is drawn from what has been offered but not yet pressed.

The sacrifice is continuous through both the Yajus formula and the oblation; when he offers the oblation while reciting the Yajus, it is by means of both the Yajus and the oblation that the sacrifice is maintained.

And he continues the sacrifice. The gods indeed took up the Soma; Prajāpati perceived: "Whoever here shall first take up the Soma, he shall become this [world]. He took up this [cup], and he became that which he was. Whoever should desire prosperity, let him take up this [cup]; he becomes prosperous if he is able to take it up. Both become prosperous even if he is not able to take it up.
Both [methods] are not correct: it should be drawn with the breath moving outward, for he had reached the end of his prosperity while his vital breaths were moving outward;

it should be drawn with the breath moving inward, for he had grasped that [cup] while his breath was moving inward; it should be drawn with the breath neither moving outward nor inward, for he had grasped it while his breath was neither moving outward nor inward.
If he were to breathe out, he would sever the vital breaths; if he were to breathe out, he should cover [the cup] with gold.

Gold is indeed immortality; with immortality he thus joins the vital breaths together. He presses once and draws once; Prajāpati is indeed one; verily he attains Prajāpati. It should be drawn with a four-cornered vessel;
with a four-cornered vessel Prajāpati drew it; he prospered in all directions; he who knows thus prospers in all directions.
The wise man draws this [cup] with a four-cornered [ladle]. Water indeed is the sap that has entered Soma; Soma is the sap of water.
Just as two cows, having come together, strike one another, even so these two, having come together, have struck out each other's power and vigor.
Of these two, the sap is curds. When he offers with curds, he [offers] with their own sap.
He pacifies it.
The black-headed animal is for Agni; the ewe is for Sarasvatī; the brown one is for Soma; the dark-grey one is for Pūṣan; the white-backed one is for Bṛhaspati;

the tawny one is for the Viśvedevas; the ram is for Indra; the speckled one is for the Maruts; the compact one is for Indra and Agni; the one with a dark belly is for Savitṛ; and the castrated bull is for Varuṇa. Having created living beings, Prajāpati felt himself emptied; he then beheld this set of eleven animals.

With it he gratifies himself. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; therefore, when one who knows this binds this set of eleven [animals], he gratifies whatever in his own self is deficient. Having created offspring, Prajāpati felt himself emptied.
He beheld these powers and strengths; he bound them together into pairs within himself: the Agni-animal is the self, Sarasvatī is speech, and Indra is the power.

Soma bound speech, the sense organ, and the self together; Pūṣan, the lord of nourishment, and Bṛhaspati, the sacred formulation, bound nourishment and the sacred formulation together with the self; the Viśvedevas, strength, and Indra, heroism, bound strength and heroism together with the self;
the Maruts, vital power, and Indra-Agni, force, bound vital power and force together with the self.
He binds himself with a Sāvitra [offering] for procreation, and with a Vāruṇa [offering] for freedom from Varuṇa’s noose;

all [the animals] are bound for the sake of Agni, for Agni is indeed all the deities; thus they are bound for the sake of all the deities. The Sarasvatī [offering] is for the sake of pairing. Now, as for the Saumya: Soma is indeed the placer of seed; he places seed in him. And as for the Pauṣṇa: it is for the sake of procreation.

Pūṣan [is the deity] for procreation; Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; these creatures belong to the All-gods (vaiśvadevīḥ). Verily, he has thus driven the Brahman forward before these creatures; moreover, he makes these creatures subject to the Brahman. The Maruts are the people (viś); verily, he yokes the people to the nobility (kṣatra); moreover, he makes the people subject to the nobility. By means of vigor, he [yokes] the people.

He takes hold for the sake of the *kṣatra*. When [the animal] has been seized, it is dedicated to Agni; when it has been seized, it is dedicated to Indra. Now this one dedicated to Indra and Agni is seized. He has made the *brahman* and the *kṣatra* companions, since Agni and Indra are the recipients of the greatest share among the deities;
therefore, the Brahmin and the king are the recipients of the greatest share among men. [The animal] belongs to Savitṛ for procreation, and to Varuṇa for release from Varuṇa’s noose.

Varuṇa is indeed the ocean, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the ocean; in that the animal dedicated to Varuṇa is sacrificed on the southern side, it is for the sake of the sacrificer’s freedom from Varuṇa’s noose.
Regarding this, there is this verse recited:
You are a good god, O Varuṇa, you whose palate the seven rivers flow over,
like a hollow, well-fashioned metal pipe.

Those who are the lords of the strength of the gods are offered on the southern half; therefore, offspring go forth conquering by means of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). As for the offerings to Agni, Soma, and Bṛhaspati which are offered together—it is vital power (*ojas*) that is thus joined.
In that the offering to Agni and the offering to Bṛhaspati are on both sides of the one to Soma, it is brilliance (*tejas*) and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) that are thereby bestowed upon him.

He grasps the organ from both sides; there are eleven deities for these animals, and the ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī is the twelfth among the deities. Because she remains in excess, therefore women exceed men. Now, there are two ropes for one animal and two for another;
therefore, when a female child is born, they cast her away, but not a male. Thus, it is indeed the females who remain in excess.
When Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, it became threefold: that which was its tip and its brilliance became the wooden sword (sphya);

that which was its middle became the chariot; and that which was its base became the sacrificial post (yūpa). With the wooden sword he traces the outline, with the axle of the chariot he measures it out, and it becomes the sacrificial post. This very thunderbolt is thus collected. For this earth is only as large as the altar.

He measures across with eleven *vajras*; for by means of the *vajra* he thus conquers this [earth]. It should be measured elevated toward the south, for that is the form of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). Moreover, the sacrificer thereby raises the *vajra* against his rival. Three [steps] should be measured equal in the middle, for the sake of equality; for cattle stand upon it evenly. Thus, by means of cattle, he makes it level.
If he should desire of someone, "May he prosper in the world of the fathers," for him he should fix [the sacrificial post] level with the top-ring; verily, he prospers in the world of the fathers.

Then, if he should desire of someone, "May he prosper in the world of men," for him he should fix it level with the middle-ring; verily, he prospers in the world of men. Then, if he should desire of someone, "May he prosper in the world of the gods," for him he should fix it level with the *caṣāla* (top-piece).

One prospers in the world of the gods; indeed, among them, that which is equal in measure to the *caṣāla* is the most prosperous. Therefore, it should be erected equal in measure to the *caṣāla* for the sake of prosperity. One should erect [the post] for him whose lap is behind and whose front is hollowed out, if he should desire:
"May I create a place for my rival and exclude the sacrificer. He thus creates a place for his rival and excludes the sacrificer.
Now, one should erect that [post] for which there is a pressure from the front and a depression from behind, if he should desire:
"May I create a world for the sacrificer and press down his rival. Thus, he indeed creates a world for the sacrificer and presses down his rival.
All [posts] should be made with the fire-side facing forward; those which have the fire-side as their support, those should be made with the fire-side forward; by that, all [are so].
The one standing nearest the fire is the *agniṣṭha*. Now, because the ropes are drawn out from the one nearest the fire, for that reason all are *agniṣṭhas*.

Indeed, their animals are diverse and their deities are diverse; yet he who is this twelfth [victim] is the sacrificer himself—the animal belonging to him. If he were not to designate an animal for him, the sacrificer would be liable to die; therefore, he should name one whom he hates.
Thus they exceed [the norm]:
FN emended. Ed:
evātiracyante.
This is your sacrificial animal.
Thus he points out that very animal to him; if he should practice sorcery, [the victim] becomes one who dies prematurely.
With this Indra’s thunderbolt, I strike down so-and-so, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman.
Thus he should press down; verily with Indra’s thunderbolt he presses him down, and he becomes liable to die; moreover, this is for the attainment of the twelfth month itself.
Manu indeed had sacrificial vessels; as they were being struck together, as many Asuras as heard them perished on that day.
Now, at that time, there were two Brāhmaṇas among the Asuras, Tṛṣṭa and Avarūtrī. They said, "Examine this for us.
They replied, "Manu is indeed a sacrificer and a believer; give these vessels to us."

He gave those [cattle] to the two of them; they caused them to be cooked by Agni. A bull licked those flames, and the Menī followed after him. As he bellowed, as many Asuras as heard him on that day ceased to exist.
Those two said, "Manu is indeed a performer of sacrifice and one who possesses faith; let us cause him to sacrifice with this bull. And so, with that...

They two performed a sacrifice for him; [the victim] was Śroṇi, and Suparṇa devoured it before the portions were cut off. She, being desirous of a husband, entered his lap. Menī followed after her. As she was speaking, as many Asuras as heard her, so many ceased to exist on that day.
They two said, "Manu is indeed a sacrificer and full of faith; let us perform a sacrifice for you with this woman as your wife. So they sacrificed for her.

Having sprinkled [the victim] and carried fire around it, he brought forward the fuel and sacrificial grass. Indra perceived: "These two have indeed deprived Manu of his wife through Asura-magic. Indra approached him while calling himself a Brāhmaṇa. He said:
"O Manu, you are indeed a performer of sacrifice and one whose god is faith; let me officiate for you. Which Brāhmaṇa are you?"
Manāyyā:
What do you ask about the Brahmin’s father, and what about his mother?
If the knowable has been heard within this [Veda], he is the father, he is the grandfather.

"By whom? "By these two Brāhmaṇas. "I am the master of the two Brāhmaṇas. "Indeed, you are the master," replied the host, "for you are the lord of guests. He then approached to dig out a second altar. Carrying fuel and sacrificial grass, those two came to him and said, "What are you doing here? "I shall perform a sacrifice for this Manu. "By whom? "By you two. They [consented].
Indra thought, "I have found them," and he cast down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; they fled, and as they ran away, Indra pursued them from behind.
The two fled; they became the vṛśa and the evāṣa; such was the birth of the vṛśa and the evāṣa. That Manu said to Indra:
"Establish my sacrifice for me; let my sacrifice not be disrupted. He [Indra] replied: "With whatever desire you have sacrificed this [animal]."

"May that desire of yours be fulfilled; now let her go"—with these words he released her, and it was for the sake of prosperity. The cup for Tvaṣṭṛ accompanied by the wives (pātnīvata) should belong to Tvaṣṭṛ, for cattle belong to Tvaṣṭṛ. It should be performed below the navel, for what is below the navel of a woman is vigorous.
Or rather, the set of eleven [cups] supports the sacrifice when the cup for the wives is used to prop it up.

In that world, indeed, the sacrificer desires to thrive; for that world of yonder sun belongs to him. When he offers with two verses addressed to Sūrya, the sacrificer thereby comes to be in that world. He offers with two [verses]; the sacrificer has two feet—for the sake of stability.

Having placed gold [on the ladle], he offers; verily, he causes him to go to the heavenly world with golden light. He offers with [the gold] bound [to the ladle]; this is the grasping of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās). "Go to heaven, go to the sky," he says as he lifts it up; it is for the attainment of the heavenly world. "With form I approach your form," he says; gold is form, and cattle are form. "Tutha, the all-knowing, [is yours]."

"Let him distribute," he says; for Agni is indeed Tutha, the all-knowing. He knows who is worthy of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇīya*) and who is not. "This gift of thine, O Agni, goes forth, distilling Soma"—for this is what is given to the Āgnīdhra, and that causes the Soma to flow. "Lead it by the path of Mitra"—for the path of Mitra is the sacrifice; [he leads it] to the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni.

He offers the oblation to Agni, for the office of the Āgnīdhra belongs to Agni; with the second verse addressed to Varuṇa, he offers if a cart or a chariot is given, for that belongs to Varuṇa. With the words, "Go by the path of Truth," he means that the sacrifice is indeed the path of Truth. With the words, "O you of shining sacrificial fee," he refers to the fact that a shining gift is being given. With the words, "May I today prosper as a Brāhmaṇa, having a father and a grandfather," he refers to the fact that such a person is indeed a Brāhmaṇa who has a father and a grandfather.

"He who is the descendant of his mother’s lineage, who is of Ṛṣi descent, and who has heard [the Veda]—he gives the sacrifice to him with a well-placed sacrificial fee (*sudhātu-dakṣiṇa*)," thus he establishes his sacrifice in a state of being well-placed.

"Behold the heaven! Behold the mid-region!"—having reached this very world, he speaks thus. "Exert yourself together with those in the assembly (*sadasyaiḥ*). For these Brahmins who drink Soma are indeed prone to hostility toward him as they give; they are capable of destroying him with their gaze. He pacifies them by saying, "Given by us."

"Go to the gods, full of sweetness; enter the giver"—thus they indeed come to him there. "Many mortals are like corpses at the sacrifice," so used Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana to say. "Mortals here cause the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) to fall away;
they do not go there. When he says, "Without abandoning us, sit in the world of the virtuous by the path that leads to the gods," that is for us.
It is called "the conditioned" (saṃskṛta), for in this way they come to it both here and in the hereafter.
Many indeed are the deaths;
for they slay this Soma when they press it, and they slay this sacrifice when the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) are given.

They indeed invigorate the sacrifice; that is the reason for the "gift-ness" (*dakṣiṇātva*) of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), in that they thus invigorate it. The midday pressing is indeed the heavenly world; since the sacrificial fees are given at the midday pressing, it is for the sake of ascending to the heavenly world. Much should be given, for he thereby builds a bridge for the attainment of the heavenly world. Gold is held in his hand.

Now he leads [the earth]. Gold is indeed truth; verily, by means of truth he leads them. Along the front of the *gārhapatya* fire and along the rear of the *sadas*, they release them toward the north between the *cātvāla* pit and the *āgnīdhra* shed. By this very path, the Aṅgirases went to the heavenly world;
it is that same path he leads them along. He offers two oblations on the *gārhapatya*; by means of these, he has stepped upon this [earth].

With the [portion] for Agni he gives the Āgnīdhra fire-shed; by that he wins the intermediate space. Now, as for the fact that sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) are given: by that he first bestows the heavenly world upon the Āgnīdhra. For the Āgnīdhra is the mouth of the sacrifice; thus he does not exclude the mouth of the sacrifice. Moreover, Agni is indeed all the deities; thus his deities are both worshipped and gratified by that gift. He gives to the Brahman priest; for the Brahman is related to Prajāpati; [thus he wins] Prajāpati.
With that [gift] he gratifies the officiating priests when he gives to the *ṛtvij*s; with that he gratifies the *hotṛ*s when he gives to the members of the assembly (*sadasya*s);

with that he redeems the drinking of Soma (*somapītha*) when he gives to one who is of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) and learned; with that he gratifies the meters (*chandas*) when he gives to one who is of noble lineage and learned—for they do not deserve to have the drinking of Soma redeemed from him; with that he prospers in the world of the gods when he gives to one who is of noble lineage and learned.
That which one gives to one who is not a descendant of a ṛṣi but is learned in the world of men, by that the trees spread forth;

that which one gives to one who has not approached [for instruction], by that he overcomes his rival; that which one gives to one who asks for it, by that he consumes the *brahman* while his *kṣatra* is terrified;
that which one pushes away—that sacrificial gift is a tigress. If one were to accept it back again, she, having become a tigress, would devour him.

One should cause it to melt together with another [vessel] after having taken hold of it; thus he does not cause it to overflow. When he gives a goat, since the goat belongs to Agni, he thereby approaches the beloved abode of Agni. When he gives a sheep, he conquers through its wooliness. When he gives a cow, since the cow belongs to the Viśvedevas, he thereby approaches the beloved abode of the Viśvedevas. When he gives a garment, it belongs to all the deities.

The deities themselves are his garment; by that [gift], they become propitiated and pleased. When he gives prepared food, he redeems himself with flesh. When he gives a cart or a chariot, he redeems himself with his body. When he gives gold, he lengthens his life-span. When he gives a horse—the horse belongs to Prajāpati—he thereby approaches the beloved abode of Prajāpati.
Moreover, he wins the world of yonder sun at the very end; it should be given to the *pratihartṛ* at the end. For the *pratihartṛ* is indeed related to Rudra;
if one were to give it to the *pratihartṛ* in the middle, one would bring Rudra down into the midst. Therefore, it should be given to the *pratihartṛ* at the end.
Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness; Atri beheld him there; therefore, [it should be given] to one of Atri's lineage.
He gives gold; he drives away darkness, and moreover, he places light above for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Āvyan: Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, considered this failure of the sacrifice to be a deficiency when the *ṛc* and *sāman* were separated.
He saw these [oblations] for the restoration of the sacrifice; whatever failure of the sacrifice occurs here, these are offered for its restoration.

There are six *ṛc*-verses; there are six seasons; verily he finds firm support in the seasons. There are three *yajus*-formulas; there are three pressings (*savana*); verily he attains the pressings. He offers these nine *sam-iṣṭayajus* oblations. They chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* with nine [verses]; that is nine; there are nine breaths; verily he places the breaths within himself. Standing upright, he offers the oblation; standing upright—
Standing [while reciting], one is more powerful; standing silently, he should offer for whomsoever he hates, thinking, "I cut off his vital breaths.

He offers continuously for the continuity of the vital breaths. He offers without breaking for the non-interruption of the vital breaths; were he to break [the continuity], he would cut off the vital breaths.
He should break [the continuity] for whomsoever he hates; thus he cuts off his vital breaths. [He offers] with equal [breaths], taking them separately.
He offers [the oblation], for these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed common. These two are the poles (*āṇī*) of the sacrifice. Viśvāmitra saw these two as the poles of the sacrifice;

thus these two poles of the sacrifice are made. "Where the sacrifice is taken up, there it must be set down again," so said Bharadvāja; for where this sacrifice is taken up, there it is set down again.

The sacrifice indeed has five pressings: three pressings, the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), the *anūbandhyā* cow, and the fifth is the pressing itself. The sacrifice is fivefold; he seizes the sacrifice in its entirety. Whatever exceeds the sacrifice, Varuṇa seizes that; it is the excess.

That which is the *ṛjīṣa* is indeed the pressing-wood of the sacrifice; therefore, with that they go down for the *avabhṛtha*. They go down into the waters, for Varuṇa is the waters. They go down into still waters, for he is Varuṇa manifest. If they were to go down into flowing waters, they would drive away the cattle; but since they go down into still waters, it is for the sake of not driving away the cattle. The waters, indeed...

Varuṇa is the wind; Varuṇa is the north. If they were to descend for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) from the north, Varuṇa would seize the offspring from the front. But because they descend for the purificatory bath from the south, it is for the sake of the sacrificer’s release from Varuṇa’s noose. "For King Varuṇa has made wide space," they say as they depart from the pit (cātvāla). This indeed is the path that leads nowhere else, free from danger, by which that Āditya [is reached].

They say, "This is the path of yonder sun," reciting: "A hundred physicians are yours, O King, a thousand. They speak thus while gazing at the waters; for they adorn themselves with water, and purified by these [waters], they move about purified. The cakes are offered on single potsherds;
for man cannot be reached by potsherds, but he reaches him all at once. Moreover, this earth is one; verily, he finds support upon her.

Having thrown a blade of grass, he offers into the fire; thus he offers into that which possesses fire and has a proper receptacle. If he were to offer without a receptacle, the Adhvaryu would become blind. He performs the *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*; the *barhis* is indeed offspring; verily, he releases offspring from death. He performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings for the sake of the nature of sacrifice. He sacrifices to Varuṇa for release from Varuṇa’s noose. He sacrifices to Agni and Varuṇa; verily, from both sides he [releases him].
He releases [the victim] from Varuṇa; he does not perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), nor do they conclude the rite, for they consider that to be redundant.

With the verse, "In the ocean is thy heart, within the waters," he wipes it together with the offering-ladle (*sruk*); whatever cruel thing has been done there, that he thereby pacifies. With the words, "O *Avabhṛtha*, thou who art deep-drenching," this is his *Avabhṛtha* bath. Then, whatever dregs (*ṛjīṣa*) float up, that—

For they consider it as if drinking the Soma-juice; indeed, the *ṛjīṣa* is Varuṇa, so if he were to consume it, he would smear Varuṇa upon himself. Regarding this they say: "It must certainly be consumed, for the *ṛjīṣa* is cattle; thus he smears cattle upon himself.
With the words, "The snares of Varuṇa are loosened," he unties the snare of Varuṇa. With the words, "The snare of Varuṇa is cast down," [he casts down] the snare of Varuṇa.

Thus he casts it aside with the words, "Homage to the noose of Varuṇa!"—verily, he has paid homage to the noose of Varuṇa. When the Aṅgirases were rising up, the Rakṣases rose up after them; Bṛhaspati followed after them with this [chant] and thereby drove away the Rakṣases from them. In that he follows with this, it is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. In that it has *ūrdhvastobha* (upward-stobhas), it belongs to Bṛhaspati. Now, as for that which...

It consists of three *stobhas*; for these worlds are three, and it is from these worlds that he drives away the *rakṣases* from the sacrifice. Because it is in the *aticchandas* metre—the *aticchandas* being all the metres—it is by means of all the metres that he drives away the *rakṣases* from the sacrifice. Because it is addressed to Agni—and Agni is indeed all the deities—it is by means of all the deities that he drives away the *rakṣases* from the sacrifice.

They descend into the waters; for the waters are indeed slayers of the *rakṣases*, and the *rakṣases* do not cross over the waters. For the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*, they return without looking back, so that there may be no following after by Varuṇa. They cleanse themselves outside the cow-pen; thus they appease Varuṇa outside the cow-pen. "Thou art fuel; may we prosper," they say; having become free from Varuṇa, they approach to kindle the fire. "Thou art a kindling-stick."
"May we prosper together"—this is for the sake of kindling.

He who should desire, "May my entire sacrifice be complete and full of essence," should immolate these three barren cows for the sake of the completeness and the essence of the sacrifice. He should immolate the one dedicated to the Viśvedevas in the middle; verily, he thus places seed in the middle, for seed is placed in the middle.
They proceed with one that is undefined, for seed is, as it were, undefined. The deities of this [sacrifice] have indeed become exhausted.

The *vaśā* dedicated to Brahmāṇaspati and the one dedicated to the Viśvedevas belong to both the deities and Brahmā, for the sake of preventing the exhaustion of their vital energy (*ayātayāmatva*). Indeed, the meters of this sacrificer have become exhausted; he thus places the essence back into the meters themselves. He should finally offer the one dedicated to Bṛhaspati; for Bṛhaspati is the Brahman, and it is thus at the very end that he establishes himself in the Brahman.

The sacrificer finds firm support through the sacrifice. Indeed, when the sacrifice is completed, Mitra takes over its well-offered portion and Varuṇa its ill-offered portion. Since there is a victim for Mitra and Varuṇa as the *anūbandhyā*, he thereby releases the sacrificer from the well-offered portion of the sacrifice by means of Mitra, and from the ill-offered portion by means of Varuṇa. Having released him from both sides, he delivers him to the sacrificer.
Just as they break up the soil with a plough, so do the *ukthāmadāni* (the hymns of praise and joy) break open the sacrifice.
Just as one covers over a grave, so does this [verse] rectify whatever in the sacrifice is ill-sung, ill-recited, or perverted.
One who has sacrificed is devoid of the gods, while one who has not sacrificed is possessed of the gods; for the deities are praised even for one who has not sacrificed. And just as...

Just as a draft-ox, once released, runs away, so do the deities depart from one who has performed the sacrifice. Since the concluding offering (*udavasānīya*) belongs to Agni, and Agni is indeed all the deities, he thus recovers the deities themselves. It consists of an eight-potherd cake, for Agni is connected with the *gāyatrī* and the *gāyatrī* metre; it should be made on five potsherds, for the sacrifice is fivefold—thus he recovers the sacrifice in its entirety.
Or, when they place a deceased man upon that fire, truth abandons him; all other deities abandon him, but Agni does not abandon him among the deities.

Verily, with the *ṛc* he bestows, and with the *yajus* he causes [the offering] to go; the *ṛc* is for the *stotra*, and the *yajus* is for the *śastra*. Indeed, the *stotra* and the *śastra* are connected, and the *ṛc* and the *yajus* are connected. The *ṛc* is performed loudly, and the *sāman* loudly; the *yajus* is performed in a low voice.
Those gods thought, "This part of the sacrifice is loose," and they placed the *puroruc* in order to make it firm.
Indeed, all the deities hope that while the cup is being drawn, "He draws it for me! He draws it for me! The *puroruc* verse is used for the sake of distinguishing the deities.
You are named Jīvas; revive him! You are named Jīvikās; revive him! You are named Saṃjīvas; revive him!
Having thus placed twenty-one barley grains and bunches of *darbha* grass, he should address them and then consecrate them with the following mantra.

May the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma grahas protect your out-breath and in-breath; may the Upāṃśusavana protect your diffused breath (vyāna); may the Aindravāyava protect your speech; may the Maitrāvaruṇa protect your skill and will; may the Āśvina protect your hearing; may the Śukra and Manthin protect your two eyes;
may the Āgrayaṇa protect your self; may the Ukthya protect your limbs; may the Dhruva protect your life-span and your breasts.
May those two protect him at the cup of the seasons; may the *droṇakalaśa* protect your head; may the two jars protect your two sides, O Lord of Nourishment!
Give back his sight for his sight, his smile for his smile, his speech for his speech, his breath for his breath—*svāhā* to this!

Thus one should offer the oblation. Regarding this, Vāsiṣṭha Sātyahavya used to say: "I know that Brāhmaṇa passage concerning the vessels, namely how a man is offered a single draught; one should indeed do it only once, not before that. If one were to do it again, he would die. If he should practice sorcery, having recited this very Yajus, he should then consecrate [the victim] with it."
Furthermore, otherwise.
Furthermore, other vessels are employed and others are not; those which are employed again are for this world, while those which are not employed again are for that world beyond.
Now, this Ukthya vessel is employed again.

This [cup] is for the wild animals; by this, he supports the very wild animals. Because it is used again, they kill these [animals] after surrounding them from all sides. Now, this ṛtu-cup is used again; it is for the horse;
by this, he supports the very horse. Because it is used again, therefore, beneath this horse—
The hoof-cup is then used again as the Aditya-vessel; indeed, it is for the sake of the cow that this is done, and by it he supports the cow herself.

Since Soma is drawn in the greatest quantity with the greatest number of verses, therefore the cow, though being slaughtered and eaten, remains the most numerous of animals. Then this Śukra-vessel is used again; indeed, it is for the sake of man that this is done, and by it he supports man himself.

That bright Āditya indeed supports the rays; the seasons are the intermediate [vessels]. The *śukra* vessel is used again, for from that bright Āditya the rays proceed again. Then this *upāṃśu* vessel is used again;
it is the sheep, and by this he supports the sheep. Then this *antaryāma* vessel is used again; it is the goat.

By this, Prajāpati supported the unborn itself. The Āgrayaṇa is indeed Prajāpati; because it is used again, therefore Prajāpati knows his offspring. This wooden trough (droṇakalaśa) is the vessel of Prajāpati; because it is used again, therefore this [world] exists as a dwelling-place. There are seven vessels that deserve to be used again, for they—
There are seven meters that have a manifest connection; the meters are speech, and thus he obtains as much speech as there is.

There are seven meters, seven officiating priests (*hotṛs*), and seven domestic animals; he thereby secures these very things. Indeed, there are three vessels whose connections are manifest, while everything else has a hidden connection: the Aindravāyava cup is connected with the *gāyatrī*, the Śukra cup with the *triṣṭubh*, and the Āgrayaṇa cup with the *jagatī*.

The severed [branch] should be made to flow; thus his desire becomes successful, and moreover, Parjanya rains without clouds. One should not place it near the *camasa* cup; for if one were to place it near the *camasa*, the offspring would suffer miscarriage.

They should creep back by the same way they first crept forward; if they were to creep by another way, the embryos would become entangled. Indeed, the oblations are like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

They go to the heavenly world by means of the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificial fees; the sacrificial post is erected upright, and he responds while standing upright, for the attainment of the heavenly world.

He who is the eldest kinsman should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu, for the cup for Indra and Vāyu is the foremost. He who is afflicted by illness should draw the cups beginning with those for Mitra and Varuṇa, for Mitra and Varuṇa are out-breathing and in-breathing. He whose Soma-drinking comes later should draw the cups beginning with those for the Aśvins, for these two attained their Soma-drinking as if from behind. He who desires spiritual luster should draw the cups beginning with those for Śukra; for Śukra is indeed splendor.
If one desires to practice sorcery against another, he should draw the cups beginning with the *manthin*; for the *manthin* cup is indeed a vessel of distress.

He who is inferior in birth should draw the cups beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*, for the *āgrayaṇa* goes to the forefront. Indeed, he who draws the cups other than those beginning with the *aindravāyava* departs from the mouth of the sacrifice; they should hold that [cup] for whatever desire he may draw it, and then [he should draw] the *aindravāyava*.

Or rather, he should set it down as before; thus this is performed, and it does not depart from the mouth of the sacrifice. If the Āgrayaṇa should spill or be lost, one should draw it from the other cups; that is just as when a father, having been displaced, seeks refuge with his sons.
If the other cups should spill or be lost, one should draw them from the Āgrayaṇa; that is just as when sons [seek refuge with their father].
They run toward their father while standing on the ground; in the same way, they are drawn out from the *droṇakalaśa*. This indeed is their source;
they are drawn out from their own source so that there may be no spilling. "Soma will spill; I shall draw him from here," he thinks.
For this is his resting place. When he pours it down, then it becomes bright on both sides, and indeed bright all over with its cattle.
He indeed comes to ruin whose Soma spills; his sacrifice is torn asunder. The speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) is indeed cattle;
in that he offers the speckled butter, he restores him with cattle. With the words, "May the mind, the light, enjoy the clarified butter;
may it join together this severed sacrifice," he truly joins the sacrifice back together.
It is performed:
May prosperity increase; may [the sacrifice] with curd and ghee release the patron of the sacrifice from distress. Svāhā!

Thus he should offer; for this [earth] indeed takes hold of that part of the sacrifice which falters. This earth is prosperity; verily, he releases it from her. With the words, "The drop has fallen upon the earth, after the heaven," he touches it; thus he establishes it in the *hotrā* offices.
He sprinkles thirty-three drops of water; for the sacrifice is indeed water. Verily, they tear apart the sacrifice of him whose sacrificial animal [falters].

Their sacrifice is disturbed and cut asunder if one cannot find a portion for the offering; in that case, one should take a portion from the clarified butter (*ājya*). For all other deities have their power exhausted (*yātayāmnī*), but Prajāpati alone has his power unexhausted. Clarified butter belongs to Prajāpati, and the gods belong to Prajāpati; thus, his offering becomes one made to Prajāpati himself. If he should desire, "May those who have disturbed the animal sacrifice meet with ruin," [he should act accordingly].

Thus, with the verse, "O, surely those who possess barley [offer] even the barley," one should offer oblations in the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word *namas*. By doing so, one appropriates for oneself their very utterances of homage; they immediately meet with misfortune. Now, regarding this eight-footed [verse]: if one were to cut portions from the embryo, one would exceed the prescribed portions; if one were not to cut portions, one would not cut from the consecrated offering. One offers with the essence; thus he cuts from the consecrated [offering].
He cuts the portions from the oblation so as not to leave any remnants.

Just as a hall is, so is the year; its two sides are like the two wings of the hall, and the central ridge-pole is like the *divākīrtya* chant. Just as here the two wings of a hall meet at the central ridge-pole, even so these two wings of the year extend continuously toward the *divākīrtya*, which is like the central ridge-pole.

Thus, if this [rite] were loose, it would fall apart. Because on this day these cups are drawn, it is for the firmness of the day, to prevent its loosening. On this day, the cups have the Śukra as their first; the Śukra belongs to the Triṣṭubh, and this day belongs to the Triṣṭubh, for the sake of support and stability. A cup for Sūrya is drawn, and there is an animal sacrifice for Sūrya.
That [victim] is sacrificed to Āditya on this day; he thus directly prospers. Six cups are drawn, and the animal is sacrificed as the seventh.

There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head; that [Āditya] is the head. Thus, he places the vital breaths in the head. Indra, indeed, slew Vṛtra; he conquered this world, but he did not conquer yonder world. Viśvakarman [conquered it].

Since he conquered [all] having become [the All], the Vaiśvakarman cup is drawn for the conquest of that world. Indeed, those who draw the Vaiśvakarman cup depart from this world, for they go away turning their backs; they are liable to perish. On the following day, they should draw the Āditya cup. Aditi is indeed this [earth]; she is the foundation. Since the Āditya is this [earth], they find firm support upon her.
They should take them one after the other up to the *parārdha* by turns; with one they perform all ritual work, and with the other they proceed.
Aditi is indeed this [earth]; in her they find support with the other. They should take both together at the end;
having reached the end, having indeed reached the end, they find support in both worlds—with the Āditya cup in this world and with the Vaiśvakarman cup in yonder world.
They find firm standing.
(FN emended. Ed:
pratitiṣṭhanti.)

The inspired singers yoke their minds and yoke their thoughts for the sake of the great, inspired, and wise one. He who knows the sacred ordinances has established the priestly functions; indeed, the great praise of the divine Savitṛ is unique.
At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I take you up.
You are a spade; you are a woman.
Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati! We, seeking the gods, call upon you.
May the Maruts, the bounteous givers, come forward; O Indra, be swift in our company.
May Brahmanaspati come forward; may the goddess Sūnṛtā come forward;
may the gods lead our sacrifice toward the hero, the manly one who bestows fivefold wealth.
O divine Heaven and Earth, may you both approve of me; may I today succeed with the head of Makha.
For Makha, you!
For the head of Makha thee! May I today prosper with the head of Makha—the divine ants, the first-born of this world, who are observers of the Eternal Law (Ṛta).
For Makha, you!
For the head of Makha, I take you.
So much was there in the beginning; from this, O Goddess, may I prosper today—the head of Makha.
For Makha, you!
For the head of Makha, I take you.
You are the vigor of Indra; you are the seed of Prajāpati.
May I today succeed in reaching the head of Makha.
For Makha, you!
For the head of Makha, I take you.
May honey make you sweet.
You are the head of Makha.
You two are stationed at the place of the sacrifice.
You are the Gāyatra.
You are of the Trishtubh metre.
You are related to the Jagatī meter.
You are the girdle of Makha.
Take refuge in the essences of the sun.
You are the residue of the potent horse; with the residue of the potent horse, we fumigate you.
May Varuṇa, whose vow is firm, fumigate you with Mitra and Varuṇa through their steadfast law.

May the goddess Aditi, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, dig the pit for you in the dwelling-place of the earth, like Aṅgiras. May the goddesses, the wives of the gods, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, place the great vessels (mahāvīras) for you in the dwelling-place of the earth, like Aṅgiras.
For radiance thee, for glow thee, for light thee, for splendor thee! By his greatness Mitra has become the far-reaching one who surpasses heaven.
And [he has covered] the earth with glory.
The fame of the divine Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is winning;
his splendor possesses most wonderful renown.
May the god Savitṛ, with his fair hands, his fair fingers, and his strong arms, dig thee out with power.
For the upright one, for the virtuous one, for the good dwelling-place, thee!
With splendor and with the luster of sacred knowledge, I enclose this person, the son of such-and-such a father.
With this, I enclose so-and-so, the descendant of such-and-such, on all sides with the power of the people and the power of the ruling class.
With this, I enclose so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, on all sides with offspring and cattle.
May speech hear you; may radiance hear you; may the oblation hear you.
O city of the gods, you move; may I prosper through you.
Homage to movement!

Homage to speech! Homage to the Lord of Speech! To that speech which is uttered and that which is unuttered—homage, homage to that speech! Homage to the seers, the makers of mantras, the knowers of mantras, the lords of mantras!
May the seers, the makers of mantras, the knowers of mantras, not manifest the divine speech against me.

This [offering], which has been raised up for the gods, which possesses the *svadhā* for the ancestors, and which is approved by humans— may the gods protect it for my splendor, and may the ancestors rejoice in it.

I take refuge in the Gāyatrī metre; I take refuge in the Triṣṭubh metre; I take refuge in the Jagatī metre; I take refuge in the Anuṣṭubh metre; I take refuge in the Paṅkti metre; I take refuge in the metres.
May they protect us; may they guard us; may they reach him who hates us and whom we hate.

O Brahman, we shall proceed with the Pravargya; O Hotṛ, recite the hymn for the Gharma; O Agnīdh, place the two Rajana-rohiṇa cakes upon the fire; O Pratiprasthātṛ, distribute the portions; O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāmans.

May the praises, being well-disposed, carry that which is yoked by the Yajus, gathered by all the Sāmans, perfected by all prayers, and provided with sacrificial gifts—stretched out and leading to the further shore.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, impelled by Bṛhaspati.
Impelled by Bṛhaspati, accompanied by Indra, proceed!
For Yama, you!
For Makha, you!
For the impetuosity of the Sun, I take you.
May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey.
Protect us as one who is in close contact with the earth.
For the flame thee, for the radiance thee, for the light thee, for the heat thee.
You are the flame, you are the glow, you are the light, you are the heat; perform the heat of the sun’s heat.
Sit down; you are great. Shine forth, O most beloved of the gods!
O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, O praised one, emit your ruddy smoke, beautiful to behold.
That which the inspired poets, spreading it out, anoint— not as those rich in fatness heating with fire—
but like a son in his father’s lap, the most beloved Gharma has sat down like immortal Agni.
You are unassailable from the east, under the sovereignty of Agni; grant me long life. You are possessed of sons from the south, under the sovereignty of Indra; grant me progeny.
Easy to sit upon from behind, under the overlordship of Savitṛ, grant me sight.
From the north, under the overlordship of Mitra and Varuṇa, may you grant me hearing.
The support above, under the overlordship of Bṛhaspati, grant me speech.
Grant me spiritual power; grant me sovereign power; grant me nourishment.
O Manor, you who have many sons, you who are easy of access—protect me from all tusks.
You are consciousness.
Svāhā! To the Maruts, enclose [the fire].
In the month.
You are the means of valid cognition.
Every month.
Two months.
I have honored him.
Unmāsi.
You are the inner concealment of the intermediate space.
Drink from the mixture of heaven.
Worthy, you carry arrows and a bow; worthy, you wear the worshipful, multiform golden ornament. Worthy, you bestow all this wealth with your bow.
O Rudra, that power of yours is indeed formidable.
You are of the Gāyatrī metre.
You are of the Trishtubh metre.
You belong to the world.
Honey! Honey! Honey!
The hot milk-rice is pleasing.
Ten you shine toward the east, ten toward the south; ten you shine toward the west, ten toward the north; ten you shine upward, being well-disposed.
As one who is not to be harmed, protect our offspring and our cattle.
May Agni with the Vasus cause you to shine from the east; once he has shone, may he cause me to shine.
May the ancestors, with Yama as their king, together with the Pitṛs, cause you to shine from the south; may you, being thus illumined, cause me to shine.
May Savitṛ cause you to shine from behind with the Ādityas; being himself illumined, may he cause me to shine.
May Mitra and Varuṇa together with the Maruts cause you to shine from the north; being yourself illumined, cause me to shine.
May Bṛhaspati cause you to shine from above with all the gods; being yourself shining, make me shine.
O God, you are beloved by the gods; make me beloved among the gods. O God, bestow luster upon me;
you are luster, you are the source of luster. Just as you shine with luster, so may I shine with luster.
May there be for me a luster shining like yours. You are speed, you are the source of speed. Just as you speed with speed, so [may I].
May I shine with splendor; as I am shining, may my splendors be like thine. Thou art splendor, thou art radiance.
Just as thou shinest with splendor, so may I shine with splendor; as I am shining, may my splendors be like thine.
I beheld the Herdsman, who never rests, moving hither and thither along his paths;
he, clothing himself in converging and diverging rays, revolves repeatedly within the worlds.
The embryo of the gods, the progenitor of hymns, the inspired thought of sages, the lord of creatures, and the upholder of sovereign power.
That god, worthy of sacrifice, shines together with the god Savitṛ, together with Sūrya.
For the heart you; for the mind you; for the sky you; for the sun you.
Direct this sacrifice upward to heaven among the gods; perform the priestly duties.
The upholder of heaven shines across the mid-air; he is the upholder of the earth, the upholder of the vast intermediate space.
The immortal god among gods, born of austerity, has entered the waters as their protector.
O Lord of all worlds, O Lord of the entire universe, O Lord of every mind, O Lord of every word, O Lord of the entire sacred formulation (brahman)!
O divine Gharma, you who are heard by the gods, protect the gods born of austerity.
Bestow upon him strength that seeks the gods.
Honey for the two honey-makers, honey for the two honey-gatherers; rich in honey, for the feast of the gods.
Agni has come together with Agni; the adorable god has come together with the god Savitṛ; he has shone together with Sūrya—svāhā!

Agni has come together with fervor; the god has united with the god Savitṛ, O worshipful one. He has joined with Sūrya; may he grant us long life, O Gharma. You are the giver of splendor; you are our father—be mindful of us.
Homage be to you; do not harm me.
May we serve you with skillful hands.
At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I take you up.
You are the girdle of Aditi.
O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O [Name], come! O Sarasvatī, come! O [Name], come!
That breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is a source of bliss, by which you nourish all desirable things—[that breast, O Sarasvatī, grant us].
You are the turban of the Ādityas.
May Pūṣan sit down near you.
O Vāyu, blow upon this for the sake of the Aśvins.
Be propitious for the heat.
May Bṛhaspati sit down beside you.
You are the Dānavas.
You are the impellers.
Overflow for the two Aśvins.
Swell for Sarasvatī; swell for Indra; swell for Indra.
Come near to me with a portion of strength.
You are honey, the oblation; svāhā! I offer you to Vāta, to the ray of Sūrya; bound for the winning of rain, I offer you with svāhā!
O Indra and Aśvins, drink the warm offering of the honey of the bees;
O Vasus, worthy of sacrifice, *veṭ*! [Page IV,128] O Indra and Aśvins, drink the warm offering of the honey of the bees; O Vasus, worthy of sacrifice, *veṭ*!
You are the Gāyatra.
You are of the Trishtubh metre.
You belong to the world.
I enclose you with heaven and earth.
I offer with the intermediate space.
O sky-touching one, do not harm me.
O you who touch the intermediate space, do not harm me.
O Earth-touching one, do not harm me.
You are splendor; follow after splendor.

To the wind that is the water, svāhā! To the wind that is the ocean, svāhā! To the wind that is the river, svāhā! To the wind that is the sea, svāhā! To the wind accompanied by *śimidvat*, svāhā! To the wind accompanied by *kumudvat*, svāhā! To the wind that is the helper, svāhā! To the wind that is the one to be honored, svāhā! To the wind that is unassailable, svāhā! To the wind that is invincible, svāhā!

Hail to Vāta! To you, Agni accompanied by the Vasus, hail! To you, Soma accompanied by the Rudras, hail! To you, Indra accompanied by the Maruts, hail! To you, Yama accompanied by the Pitṛs and the Aṅgirases, hail!
To Savitṛ, who possesses abundance, who possesses pervasiveness, who possesses vigor, who possesses Bṛhaspati, and who belongs to all the gods—svāhā!
May they enjoy the day with its banner; may they enjoy the light of heaven, svāhā!
May Night with its banner be pleased; may the light of heaven be pleased. Svāhā!
Place this sacrifice in heaven; place this sacrifice in heaven. Blessing for the Gharma; it flows for the drinking of the Gharma.
Seated in the south, he has sacrificed here to all the quarters and to all the gods.
Oṃ, cause [them] to hear!
So be it; let there be hearing!
Sacrifice to Gharma.
O Aśvins, drink the hot offering; may Hārdrānu follow me; may Heaven and Earth favor me; here indeed are the gifts. Together with the sacrificial formulas, Svāhā! To Indra, Svāhā! To Indra, Vaṭ!
Drink of the Gharma, the honeyed oblation consecrated with Svāhā, O Aśvins; you have drunk the Gharma, O Aśvins, brought hither with divine aids, just as Veṭ drank his own Pedravam.
For example:
*iṣe pipīhi*.
Swell for strength!
Pour forth for this sacred prayer.
Pour forth for this sovereignty.
Swell for us with nourishment and strength.
Pierce Subhūti!
Make me swell with the splendor of sacred knowledge.
Pronounce this for me, so that I may attain preeminence over this people.
You are the heat; I come to the heat. Sustain the sacred formulations within us.
Sustain the kṣatra-power.
Support the people.
To Pūṣan in the head, svāhā!
Hail to the pressing-stones!
Hail to the echoes!
Svāhā to Heaven and Earth! Svāhā to the Fathers who drink the Gharma!
To Rudra, to Rudra-hotr, svāhā!
This is the offered oblation, the honeyed oblation, in the most Indra-like fire; Svāhā!

May we partake of thee, O divine Gharma, who art accompanied by the Ṛbhus, by Vibhūman, by Vāja, by Bṛhaspati, by the Viśvedevas, by the Pitṛs, and by the Aṅgirases. We desire thee; homage be unto thee; do not harm me.
Recite for us as it is being set down.
To the day, svāhā!
Hail to Night!
You are the light of the cattle, distributed among the gods; you are the light that shines.
The essence of the trees, of the waters, and of the plants—O spirited one, I pour you down, the spirited one; may my mind be uplifted toward heaven.
You are milk; may I become possessed of milk.

O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in heaven, which is in the sky, which is in the *bṛhat* [sāman], which is in the thunder, which is in the *jagatī* meter—this is that [heat] of yours; I appease it for you; to it, Svāhā!

O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in the intermediate space, which is in the intermediate space, which is in the wind, which is in the Vāmadevya [sāman], and which is in the Triṣṭubh metre—this [heat] of yours I appease; for that [heat] of yours, Svāhā!

O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in the earth, which is in the earth, which is in Agni, which is in the Rathantara, which is in the Gāyatra metre—this [heat] of yours I appease; for that of yours, Svāhā!
O Prastotṛ, sing the Sāman.
"May he follow us today"—with this [verse], [one offers] for the protection of the Brahman from the beyond; "protect the body of the Kṣatra."
We, the people, follow you according to the law for the sake of new prosperity.
O Prastotṛ, sing the Sāman!
"Follow us today"—with these words [he offers]; "For the protection of breath, guard my body; for the protection of sight, guard my form."
By the power of the ear, we follow you for the sake of ever-new prosperity.
O Prastotṛ, sing the Sāman!
"Anv adya naḥ"—this [verse] is for the day; "tvā paraspāya" [is for the night].
Protect the bodies of the intermediate space.
By the law of the earth, we circumambulate thee for new-found prosperity; thou art the four-cornered navel of Order, the seat, the Gharma, the life of all, the far-extended shelter.
Free from hatred, free from guile, we have followed the one who acts according to another's law; you are auspicious, O bestower of peace and nourishment.
The infant of the one who nourishes people.
And you shall speak for our welfare.
And you shall protect us.
O Gharma, this is your food, this is your soil.
By that, may you grow and swell; may we also grow and swell. May he who hates us and whom we hate be separated [from growth].
He is Ranti by name, the divine Gandharva. After him, the oblation-chamber follows; Agni is its overseer, Rudra its sovereign lord.
The Waters beheld Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva of Soma; they followed after him according to the *ṛta*, and that belongs to Indra.
Truly, Rudra, as you hasten along, unfasten the enclosures of the sun for us; being praised with our heroes, O measurer of the mid-world, grant us that which is true, whether we know it or not.
Impelled by our prayer, may he protect us with his wisdom.
He found the Sasi in the course of the rivers; he threw open the doors of our chariots.
The Gandharva spoke of the nectars of these [somas].
He delivered the skillful Indu from the serpents.
Sing the Vārṣāhara Sāman.
You are consciousness; you have the ocean as your source.
The moon is skillful, a falcon, true to the cosmic order, a golden-winged bird, swift in motion;
seated firmly in the great assembly, homage be to you; do not harm me.
Come after me, who have drunk the Soma.
Sing the *iṣṭāhotrīya* Sāman with the words, "Return with strength and with wealth," or some say, "Sing the *śyaita* Sāman."
Some [recite] "ud u tyam citram" [as the first verse].
Sing the Vāmadevya Sāman.
And do thou truly favor this our newest song of praise, which seeks to win gain.
O Agni, proclaim [this] among the gods.
Bhūḥ svāhā!
O Gharma, let not the trembling heat pierce us; let it not shorten our life, whether long or short. Let not the Rudra-like powers strike us down with their shafts. Do not abandon us to destruction.
Do not be angry with us because of our ritual actions; O good leader, do not abandon those who hate us.
Let not Nirṛti seize us, nor let her afflict us; O Heaven and Earth, do not be displeased with us.
And come here to us, O Mitra and Varuṇa, contemplating our prayer; and come as our two friends.
The discharge of the Ādityas is a fierce weapon; may Vāṣṭra, with the oblation, ward off the arrows.
The gray-haired one has swallowed the young moon as it fled in the assembly of many;
behold the poetic power of the god through his greatness! He who was equal and enduring has died this very day.
He has swallowed [the curse];
O jaritṛ, you have been consecrated by him in the past.
He is the healer, the healer Maghavan, the possessor of many riches; he shall restore what was shattered again.
"Arise, O you of fair sacrifice; stand up straight for us"—thus some [recite].
svadhvaraḥ:
FN Pada. Ed: ... svadhvara ūrdhva ...
Some [recite] instead: "With vigor, with wealth."
Some [recite] "ud u tyam citram" (Up has risen that bright one).
Bhūḥ svāhā!
Bhuvaḥ svāhā!
Heaven! Svāhā!
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Place that sensory power in me, place vigor in me, place wealth in me, place protection in me, place skill in me, place creative will in me; bestow upon me great heroic strength.

With three [verses] the Gharma shines forth, together with intention and mind, together with sovereign splendor and light, together with fervor and the sacred word (brahman). May we partake of its milking; may we partake of its consumption. Of that [Gharma], being invited, I consume it as one who has been invited.
From his vital energy, like that of the sun, the earth bears his burden, as the lands bear the weight of the world.
She bears [the sacrifice];
may the divine *manīṣā* (inspired thought) go forth brightly from us, like chariots fashioned by a craftsman, like the voices of singers.
Thou art truly well-fashioned.
May Bṛhaspati settle you upon the back of the earth; with that seer, with that ritual procedure, with that metre, with that sacred formula, with that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.
May Prajāpati settle you upon the back of the earth; with that seer, with that ritual procedure, with that metre, with that sacred formulation, with that deity—sit firm like Aṅgiras!
Ugra, Bhīma, Dhvānta, Dhanavant, Sahasāvant, and Sahīyas.
Distraction.
One should cast [the arrow] when the bowstring is slack and when it is taut.
You are the Saṃvatsara, you are the Parivatsara, you are the Idāvatsara, you are the Udāvatsara, you are the Vatsara.
Of that [year], spring is the head, summer the right wing, the rainy season the left wing, and autumn the tail.
Winter is its center, and the cool season is its foundation; its months, half-months, seasons, and years are those very things.
May day and night be favorable to you; come, go forth, enter, unite, and move upward!
With blood on his face and smeared with gore, Yama’s messenger runs about, crying out.
The vulture, the fair-winged one, frequents the corpse; sent as a messenger of Yama, he goes forth: "May he who hates us and whom we hate be separated!"
That eye, ordained by the gods, the bright one, rises in the east.
May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns; may we speak for a hundred autumns; may we hear for a hundred autumns.
Nidhāyo vā3 nidhāyo vā3 nidhāyo vā3 oṃ vā3 oṃ vā3 oṃ vā3 e ai oṃ svarṇajyotiḥ.
Great light! Great light! Great light! O great light, come! O great light, come! O great light, come!
im im im, O golden light!
The earth is the fuel; Agni kindles it; it kindles Agni; I kindle it; may it, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—svāhā!
The intermediate space is the fuel; Vāyu kindles it, and it kindles Vāyu. That I kindle; may it, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—*svāhā*.
Heaven is the fuel; Āditya kindles it, and it kindles Āditya. That I kindle; may it, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—*svāhā*.

The quarters are kindled together; Prajāpati kindles them, and they kindle Prajāpati. I kindle them; may they, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—svāhā!
O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; I declare it to you. Guard it for me; may I be able to do it; through it may I be capable; through it may I prosper.
O Vāyu, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow; I declare it to you. Guard it for me; may I be able to do it; through it may I be empowered; through it may I succeed.
O Sūrya, lord of vows, I shall perform a vow; I declare it to you. Guard it for me. May I be able to do it; may I be capable through it; may I succeed through it.
O Lord of Vows, I shall perform a vow; I declare it to you. Guard it for me; may I be able to do it, and may I succeed through it.

The earth is the fuel; may Agni kindle it, and may it kindle Agni; may I kindle it, and may it, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—svāhā! The atmosphere is the fuel; may Vāyu kindle it, and may it kindle Vāyu; may I kindle it, and may it, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—svāhā!
Heaven is the fuel; may Āditya kindle it; may Āditya kindle that [fuel]; may I kindle it. May she, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—svāhā!

The quarters were kindled; Prajāpati kindled them; they kindled Prajāpati; may I kindle them; may they, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge—svāhā!
O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I have declared it to you; I was able to perform it; through that I was able, and through that I shall succeed.
O Vāyu, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I have declared it to you. I was able to perform it; through that I was able, and through that I shall succeed.
O Sūrya, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I have declared it to you; I was able to perform it; by that I was able; by that I shall succeed.
O Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I have declared it to you; I was able to perform it; by that I was able; by that I shall succeed.
May the wind blow auspiciously upon us; may the sun shine auspiciously for us.
May the days be auspicious for us; may the night be ordained as auspicious.

The earth is peace through its herbs; the atmosphere is peace, which is peace through the wind; the sky is peace, which is peace through the rain; the waters are peace; the herbs are peace; the trees are peace;
all the gods are peace; the sacred word (*brahman*) is peace; the Brahmins are peace. Peace, total peace—through you, that peace, through total peace, may I [attain] for myself...
I bring peace to those who have two feet and those who have four; peace has come to pass. You are peace; may there be peace for us; may there be fearlessness for us.
O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength for great joy and for vision.
Whatever most auspicious flavor you possess, grant us a share of it here,
like longing mothers.
Therefore, let us come quickly to you, for whose dwelling you quicken us;
O Waters, give birth to us as well.
Mistresses of precious things, rulers of the people,
may those waters that flow without healing power provide us with healing.
With what aid has he appeared as our wondrous friend, the ever-increasing one? With what most powerful host?
Which true one among the exhilarations, most bountiful, shall intoxicate you with the soma-juice, so that you may break open even the firmest wealth?
Be truly our protector, O friend of those who sing your praises; may you come with a hundred aids.
I invoke Indra the protector, Indra the helper, the hero Indra who is easily invoked at every call;
I now invoke Śakra, Indra who is invoked by many. May the bounteous Indra bestow well-being upon us.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Just as the suns cause the ray to swell, and just as the imperishable ones drink from the imperishable,
so may Indra, Varuṇa, and Bṛhaspati— the guardians of the world— cause us to swell.
Beholding the higher light beyond the darkness,
we have gone up to Sūrya, the god among gods, the supreme light.
May we look upon you with the eye of a friend.
Behold with the eye of Mitra.
You are the under-layer for the Brahman; I spread you as an under-layer for the Brahman.
May Agni, kindled, bright, and invoked with oblations, slay the Vṛtras, desiring wealth through our song of praise.
O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous; you are the king and the slayer of Vṛtra; you are the auspicious power of will.
Agni is the head of the earth and of the sacrifice.
Satisfy the longing gods, O youngest one; knowing the seasons, O Lord of Seasons, sacrifice here.
With those who are the divine officiating priests, O Agni, you are the most excellent sacrificer among the Hotṛ-priests.
O Agni, Hotṛ of the sacrifice, you who possess purifying luster, come today to the people; for you are the sacrificer.
Sacrifice according to the Truth with your greatness as you manifest yourself; O most youthful one, carry the oblations that belong to you today.
Broad-chested, immortal, clothed in clarity, well-invoked with *svāhā*,
Agni is the bearer of oblations for the sacrifice.
Those who possess the sacrifice, with uplifted ladles and with such devotion, have brought Agni here for their protection, though he is beset by adversaries.
O Agni, protect us from distress; O God, burn against those who seek to harm us with your most scorching, ageless flames.
O Soma, O King, protect us from every side against the one who intends us evil; the friend of one such as you shall never come to harm.
May Vaiśvānara come to us with his aid, he who is enthroned in heaven.
O Jātavedas, carry us across all difficulties and across misfortunes as if across a river by boat;
O Agni, being praised with homage like Atri, be the protector of our bodies.
O Agni, do you, as a new protector, carry us across all difficulties with blessings;
be a broad, vast, and wide fortress for us, and grant welfare and peace to our children and descendants.
O Agni and Viṣṇu, may these songs of praise increase you both in harmony;
come hither with splendors and with strengths.
O Agni and Viṣṇu, your great and dear domain is the secret names of ghee;
bestowing the seven treasures in every house, let your tongue rise up toward the ghee.
May Sarasvatī, the purifier, rich in prizes and possessing wealth through our inspired thought, desire our sacrifice.
May Sarasvatī, the worshipful goddess, come from the high heaven and from the mountain to our sacrifice;
may she, the butter-dripping one who delights in our invocation, graciously hear our effective speech with longing.
O Sarasvatī, those waves of yours which are honeyed and dripping with clarity—
of them we seek your favor.
We invoke for our protection Sarasvat, whose vow all cattle follow, whose vow the waters attend, and under whose vow the Lord of Prosperity is established.
Agni, beautifying his own body with an ancient hymn,
